en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Minor Training: The Root Training.
The Minor Training.
The Introduction to the Book (Ka):
From the beginning, the training to be undertaken by one who is fully ordained; the summary.
Having paid homage to the Triple Gem, I shall explain the *Khuddasikkhā*.
Herein is the table of contents:
(Kha)
The four *pārājika* offenses, the nine heavy offenses,
robes, dyeing, the bowl, basins, and the invitation ceremony.
(Ga)
(Kālikā), receiving [food], and among meats, what is unallowable;
the Nissaggiya-Pācittiya rules, and the grounds for the ascetic’s practice.
(Gha)
(Ṅa) Duties toward the preceptor and teacher; the place for excrement and urine;
asking for permission; not being naked; the rules for bathing; and those who are not to be saluted.
Leather, sandals, a mirror not being looked into,
a collyrium stick, unallowable beds, and one who shares the same seat.
(Ca)
One who is not in communion, formal acts, avoidance of wrong livelihood,
duties, assigning [robes], dependence, and the waistband—
these are the six.
Earth and requisites, medicine, and the defilement of receiving;
the invitation for the rains retreat and the section on non-breaking—these are the miscellaneous topics. (Ja)
Instruction, giving with zeal, and so forth; the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā;
restraint, purity, contentment, the fourfold watchfulness, and insight—thus [ends] the Exposition of the Pārājika Offenses.
1. Pārājikaniddesa.
And the four *pārājika* offenses:
one who has not laid aside the training in the three paths; when a rug is spread over a rug; in a non-public place;
the sign; even as much as a sesame seed’s worth of a rug.
One who enters what has not been spread out and is clung-to, or one who has already entered or departed;
one who effects the moments of entering, abiding, and exiting;
one who would take up, carry away, or misappropriate the postures.
One who would steal, cause [an object] to be moved from its place, or pass by a signal [to take it];
one who, with a thieving mind, takes what is not given— whether it be by theft, by force,
by means of grass or straw, or by a prearranged plan— would incur a *pārājika* offense.
One who intends death [for another] is one who provides weapons, poisons, or places in a dangerous location; or one who provides means of enjoyment with the intent [of causing harm];
or one who, having abandoned the human form, deprives [another] of life;
or one who, with the intention of killing, places a weapon-bearer near [the victim].
One might cause [another] to take the means of death, or speak of the virtues of death;
[the offense occurs] upon the completion of the effort, whether by one's own hand, relinquishment, command, or by something stationary;
[it may also occur] through psychic power, spells, time, place, weapons, or bodily postures.
The occasion is a specific activity; there are six determinants of instruction.
Having made each individual section—which does not lead to a mere self but to the true self—dependent upon the present existence, [one should understand] the distinctions of jhāna and so forth.
One who, being free from the use of synonyms and devoid of overweening pride, explains [the offense] while the path of intimation is known through body or speech, falls from his state.
These four are *pārājika*; they are not to be lived with, just as before.
They are incapable of the state of a bhikkhu, just as one whose head is severed is incapable of living.
The method [of offense] is by command in the third and second [cases];
in the remaining cases, there is only by command. These two [factors] are not obtained in those [remaining cases].
The mind desiring to engage in sexual intercourse, and the entry into the path of that act—
these, the wise say, are the two factors of sexual misconduct.
Likewise, perceiving the object as a human being, and the intention of theft;
Garuda-birds and thieves are the causes for taking what is not given. A human being,
the perception that it is a living being, the intention to kill, the effort,
and death by means of that— these five are the causes for killing.
The non-existence of evil within oneself, the desire for it,
and the confession thereof constitute one's human birth;
there is no other designation, and knowing this is precisely that.
There are five factors here for illuminating what is non-existent:
four unique [grounds for suspension],
the eleven types of monks who have renounced the training, and the nun Mudupiṭṭhikā.
Taking [the organ] with the mouth, taking another’s sexual organ,
sitting down right there, and the four that are in accordance [with the path].
Entering the path, entering upon the path, and having come here for sexual intercourse.
"Four" means twenty-four; "offenses involving defeat" (pārājika) when combined [with the others].
2. The Exposition of the Saṅghādisesa Offenses:
"Nine heavy [offenses]."
Desiring to emit semen, one who releases it through well-prepared [action],
except in a dream, that ascetic incurs a grave offense.
Perceiving a human woman as a woman, and possessing lust for bodily contact;
By intentionally making physical contact, a recluse incurs a grave offense.
Likewise, by addressing sexual intercourse to a wise woman who understands,
or by speaking lewd words with lustful intent, he incurs a grave offense by causing her to blush.
For one who lusts after sexual intercourse, praising the attendance of a woman who has already spoken her consent;
speaking with words associated with sexual intercourse; requesting sexual intercourse from a superior;
and having received a message from a woman or a man—these are [offenses].
Having investigated and then taking it away, the ascetic incurs a heavy offense.
Having requested building materials and having designated a site,
if he builds a hut exceeding the prescribed dimensions for his own use, he incurs a heavy offense.
If a monk, for his own residence, has a large dwelling built on a site that has been formally designated,
he incurs a grave offense (garukāpatti). Likewise, one who accuses another with groundless charges,
or causes another to be accused by means of a formal charge, [incurs an offense].
If one causes another to fall away from the final [offense] while that person is listening, one incurs a heavy offense.
If, having seen the action of another, one accuses them on that basis alone,
one incurs a heavy offense for causing another to fall away from the final offense by means of that other matter.
If he conceals it after becoming aware of it, he should live in probation for that length of time;
having completed the probation, he should practice the *mānatta* penance within the Saṅgha for six nights.
Once the *mānatta* has been practiced, the Saṅgha consisting of a group of twenty should rehabilitate him.
Being suspended for an offense,
being free from obstacles, perceiving it as such,
and desiring to conceal it— then there is the concealment.
"Covered in the ten parts at the rising of the sun.
3. The Description of the Robe (*cīvara*): "Robe" means—
Silk, linen, cotton, hemp, and wool— these six are allowable [robes],
being permissible by their very nature. Furthermore, dukūla,
paṭṭuṇṇa, paṭa, and those produced from soma and China are likewise permitted.
That which is produced by supernormal power, that given by deities, and whatever is suitable for each [of these],
such as the three robes, requisites, cloth, and the rainy-season robe—
one may determine their use but not exchange them; this applies to the face-cloth and the sitting mat as well.
The bedspread, the itch-covering cloth, and here the triple robe;
one should not dwell apart for more than one night, nor [be separated from] the sitting mat for more than four months.
“I resolve upon this outer robe (saṅghāṭi),” thus one should always resolve upon the outer robe.
"Within the range of an outstretched hand"—this same method applies to the remaining cases as well.

When making a formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna), one should first relinquish (paccuddharati) the earlier robes, such as the outer cloak (saṅghāṭi) and so forth, and then determine them. The same applies when determining the alms bowl.
"This outer robe (saṅghāṭi), or this one, I relinquish"— thus,
having spoken by name for all [robes], the wise one should relinquish them.
The outer robe is five handspans in length from the edge of the back seam.
Even with the Sugata’s robe as the upper limit, it is permissible.
For the *muṭṭhittika* (the "fist-length" robe) measured crosswise, and likewise for the *ekaṃsika* (the "shoulder-covering" robe);
and for the *antaravāsaka* (the inner robe), it is five fist-lengths in length.
It is two and a half cubits or two spans in length; it is suitable as two spans in width.
For the sitting mat, the length is two spans and the width is one and a half spans;
the border is one span according to the span of the Sugata.
For a kaṇḍuppaṭicchādika (itch-covering cloth), there are two spans across;
from the long end, it is four spans of the Sugata’s span.
For a vassikasāṭikā (rain-cloak) as well, there are six spans in length.
Horizontally, it should be two and a half spans of the Sugata’s span.
For one who makes it beyond this, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for cutting [the excess].
Bedspreads and face-cloths are of the desired measurement.
Regarding the robe-material for requisites, neither its number nor its measurement is specified;
having spoken thus, one should determine [the size] and designate the bag and so forth.
The outer robe (saṅghāṭi) may be double-layered, provided it consists of cloth that is either new or nearly new.
The upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) and likewise the inner garment (antaravāsaka) should each be of single thickness.
The outer cloak (saṅghāṭi), however, should be made of four layers of cloth that has been taken out of the weather;
the remaining robes should be double-layered, while for rag-robes (paṃsukūla) it may be according to one's preference.
Of the three [robes], two, or even one, he should cut away whatever is superfluous;
if none of them is sufficient, he may take an extra piece.
He must not wear the triple robe unless it has been cut and marked.
In a village, a dwelling, a well, a sitting-hall, a palace,
a stone chamber, a boat, a pavilion, a park, a caravan, a field, a threshing floor,
under a tree, in the open air, or in a monastery— having deposited his triple robe there, [he may go].
Except by formal authorization from the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, it is not permitted to wear [robes] beyond [the prescribed limits].
Regarding the robe for the sick, the robe for the rainy season, the limit [of size], the itch-covering cloth, and the inner garment:
beyond that, one may determine [the size]; the rest are without a fixed limit.
A bedspread, requisites, a face-cloth, a fringe,
and even a ten-day period for what has not been formally given— these are permitted; likewise a sitting mat,
and the five types of robes other than those that have not yet been dyed.
Just as with the "Kappa-tādiṇṇaka" (the cloth given for a specific purpose), one may use a sitting mat that has a fringe,
provided it has not been formally resolved upon or relinquished. Furthermore,
a rug that is a hand-span long and half a hand-span wide may be used after being formally resolved upon.
For a monk who possesses only the three robes, all of this has been explained:
all the requisites and the cloths, having spoken thus, he determines them. [The causes for loss are:
confiscation, relinquishment, seizure, and departure.
The relinquishment, the signs of death, and the training rules;
for all these are causes for separation from one's resolve,
as well as the tearing of holes in the three robes.
[It is a] thullaccaya for wearing garments made of *kusavāka* grass, *phalaka* wood, wool from a *kesavālaja* [yak], or the wings of an owl or a hide.
It is a *dukkaṭa* for [wearing] garments made of *kadali*, *eraka*, *kakkusa*, or *potthaka* cloth.
All those that are dark blue, madder-red, yellow, crimson, and black;
those dyed with mahāraṅga, mahānāma, and raṅgaratta dyes; those made of tirīṭaka fibers;
those with uncut long fringes, and likewise those with fringes made of fruits and flowers.
"Everything [is obtained] when wrapped in a tunic;
he obtains it when his robe is torn. 4.
The Description of Dyes: "And dyes"—
According to the distinctions of root, trunk, bark, leaf, fruit, and flower,
six kinds of dye were authorized by the Teacher:
turmeric for the root, and madder, saffron, and *tuṅga-hāraka* for the trunk.
Regarding leaves: *alli*, *nīla*, *lodda*, and *kaṇḍula* are permitted.
Regarding flowers: *kusumbha* and *kiṃsuka* are excluded; all others are obtainable.
Thus ends the instruction on leaves. 5. *Pattaniddesa*.
"And the bowl" means:
there are two types of bowls that are allowable by birth—iron bowls and clay bowls.
By way of measurement, they are of three kinds: large, medium, and small.
In Magadha, the superior person takes two *nāḷis* of rice cooked with sauce, curry, and appropriate condiments;
the middling person takes half of that, and the inferior person takes half of that again.
One who is superior may accept from one who is superior; one who has not yet reached the limit may accept from one who is inferior.
An extra bowl may be kept for a maximum of ten days as one's own;
it becomes subject to forfeiture once that period has elapsed.
By means of cutting, giving, and taking possession; by leaving the order, being brought up for death;
by the loss of gender, training, and the bowl—through these one abandons the formal determination of the bowl.
One should not store away the bowl, nor should one dry it over water.
One should not burn it on hot ground, nor place it there, nor let it stick to anything.
It is not permitted to place it on a floor-cover, a border-cloth, in one's lap, or on a sunshade;
nor is it proper to place it on the feet, on a bed, or on a stool.
One should not pour out used water containing food scraps or bones;
nor, with bowl in hand, should one push open the door.
[The latrine] should be well-prepared with a wooden staff support and a ground support.
One should place two bowls on the ground, having turned one upside down:
those made of wood, silver, gold, gems, beryl, bronze, glass, tin, lead, crystal, copper, and iron.
"Also those made from the heads of children, those born from jars, gourds, or basins, and all bowls that are not allowable—these are stated to have wrong-doing as their basis. 6.
The Description of the Platter.
And as for "bowls":
there are three kinds of allowable bowls—those made of copper, iron, and clay;
and those made of wood, gold, silver, gems, and beryl.
Those made of crystal, glass, or bronze are improper; those belonging to householders are improper;
those belonging to the Saṅgha are proper; those made of gourds or clay are proper only for the time being.
7. The Exposition of the Invitation (Pavāraṇā).
Regarding "invitation" (pavāraṇā):
by whatever posture one has been invited while eating,
if one should eat by means other than that, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for food that is not left over (atirittaka).
The seat, the food, the bringing forward, the proximity, and the abstention from body and speech—
these are the five factors of the invitation (pavāraṇā).
Rice, roasted flour, boiled rice gruel, fish, and meat are the types of food.
Rice, paddy, barley, millet, kudrūsa, wheat, and varaka—
of these seven grains there is boiled rice and food-gruel.
Also sāmāka grass, kudrūsaka, and coraka.
Varaka and śāli rice, as well as nīvāra, are included [among the permitted grains].
Flour made from bhaṭṭha grain, kummāsa made from barley,
meat that is allowable, and fish originating from water are also declared permissible.
While eating food, whether it be allowable or unallowable,
one may invite [another] to accept what has been brought, provided it is allowable, either by name or saying "this.
Fried grains, rice mixed with sesame, milk products, and pure solid foods— these are the types of food.
Rice, parched flour, roasted grain, bamboo shoots and the like,
food remaining after what has been mentioned, meat broth, rice gruel,
and even plain gruel, fruits, and so forth— these do not generate the *pavāraṇā*.
Having risen after being invited, one who has not yet eaten must not make food "leftover" (atiritta) by means of whatever was previously prepared.
If allowable (kappiya) food has been taken and placed within arm's reach, [it may be used].
When making something "leftover" (atiritta), one should say, "This is enough.
Even if one does not do so oneself, one may have it made by sending it into the hands of one who is fully ordained (upasampanna).
While all [the food] may be had made, he who did not make it himself is the one permitted to eat it.
8. The Exposition of the Timely:
"And the timely" means:
the four kinds received are timely, as well as that which is for as long as life lasts (yāvakālika).
That which is for a watch of the day, for seven days, and for as long as life lasts;
flour, roots, fruits, solid food, milk products, grain-based meals,
rice-gruel, soups, and so forth— these are "timely" (yāvakālika) foods.
Honey, grapes, lotus roots, coconut, mango, rose-apple, and water-lily;
coarse sugar heated by fire, and a beverage that may be taken until the watch of the night.
Grains that are suitable [for making flour], excluding juices derived from fruits.
Except for the *madhūka* flower, all other flower juices,
as well as all leaf juices— excluding the juice of the *pakkaḍāka*—
whether they are boiled with cold water or boiled with rainwater, may be kept for a watch of the night (*yāmakālika*).
Clarified butter, oil, honey, and molasses—these are the seven-day medicines.
Clarified butter is that for which meat is not prohibited.
Oil is derived from sesame, castor, and mustard seeds.
Honey is that made by small bees, bumblebees, honey-bees, and flies.
Sugarcane products such as juice and the like, whether cooked or uncooked, are called *phāṇita*.
Fat is that which is cooked with its own vessel or prepared by oneself at the proper time, provided it is not from a non-human source.
One should not cook for others any of the items belonging to the category of "what is to be used within the day" (yāvakālika),
namely: turmeric, ginger, lac, garlic, sweet flag,
usira root, bhadramusta, ativisa, and katurohini.
The five roots and so forth—those roots are for life-long use.
Biḷaṅga, black pepper, goṭṭhaphala, long pepper, and mustard;
the fruit of triphalā, eraṇḍaka, and the like—those fruits are for life-long use.
Having avoided the leaves used for curry— such as those of the cotton tree,
neem, *kuṭaja*, *paṭola*, and *sulasā*— those leaves are [permitted] for life.
With the exception of sugarcane juice, [all other liquids are permitted].
The sap of the sugarcane, its bark;
the juice and the skin—all of it;
likewise salt, iron, and stone.
Pure rice-scum, water-moss, and whatever is well-strained;
the various kinds beginning with vikaṭa—these should be known as "lifetime medicines.
Root, pith, bark, heartwood, leaf, flower, fruit, and creeper;
Whatever is not used as food, all that is "for as long as life lasts.
The enjoyment of all-season items is permitted at the proper time for everything;
when there is a requisite reason, it is permitted even at an improper time, including the three types of seasonal items.
If both have exceeded the time limit for what is kept for seven days, both incur a *pācittiya* offense;
they both incur [an offense] for that which was stored overnight and for the act of hoarding.
When seven days of what is to be used within seven days have been passed, [the offense arises].
Regarding ghee and so forth listed in the Pācittiya Canon, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
One should not smear [the medicine] with what was received after forfeiture, nor should one swallow it.
For one who is assigning [it to another], within seven days, it is as if it were designated for a novice (sāmaṇera).
There is no offense regarding clarified butter and the like, even when giving them to another.
When things such as those to be consumed at the proper time are mixed together with solid food, they manifest their true nature [as solid food]; therefore, it has been stated thus.
If one consumes pure *paṭiggahita* (received) food, or that which lasts for seven days, or that which lasts for life,
mixed with *sesakālika* (food to be consumed at the proper time), there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). Likewise,
if one consumes the other three types of food mixed with *yāvakālika* (food to be consumed during the day).
What has been received on that day should be consumed on that very same day.
One should understand it in this way regarding what is mixed with "time-for-a-watch" (yāmakālika) items:
likewise, when mixed with "seven-day" (sattāhakālika) items, it remains permissible for seven days.
9. The Exposition of Receiving "Receiving" means:
the presentation by one who desires to give, and that which is within the reach of the hand.
When giving is threefold and receiving twofold, there are five factors for the recipient.
In the case of what is immovable, grown in that very place, minute, or belonging to ants and the like;
or in the case of leaves and the burden of grass—there, the act of receiving does not take effect.
Through the signs of training and death, through the relinquishing of what is not looked after,
through cutting off, and through giving to one who is not fully ordained, there is the pacification of the offense regarding taking.
All that is not formally received, for one who consumes it, is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Pure water that is not too thick is likewise permitted.
[The following are forbidden: what remains on the tip of a finger, what is not separated [from the body], tooth-dirt, ear-wax, feces, salt, saliva, snot, phlegm, urine, and excrement.
Having personally taken dung, clay, urine, and likewise ashes,
one may use them when there is no barber available. [This applies] to those who have practiced wrongly,
those covered in dust, and those who have received gifts through begging.
"For what that has been killed inside [the house] and roasted by oneself, and for what that has been cooked inside [the house], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
10. The Description of Improper Meat:
"And among meats, those that are improper..."
The flesh of humans, elephants, and horses; of dogs and leopards;
of lions, tigers, and hyenas; of bears and snakes;
as well as meat specially prepared for oneself, and that which has not been examined.
For human flesh, there is a thullaccaya offense; for the rest, there is a dukkaṭa.
Bone, blood, skin, hair, and fat are not allowable;
these are [forbidden] when specifically intended with one's own mind, while the remaining [parts] are [forbidden] even when unintended.
11. The Exposition of the Forfeiture Offenses (Nissaggiya-niddesa) Regarding the "Forfeiture Offenses" (Nissaggiyāni):
Non-monetary goods [exchanged] for monetary goods, and monetary goods [exchanged] for other [goods];
One may exchange silver; here, silver is an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*).
A *kahāpaṇa*, *sajjhu*, *siṅgī*, or a coin used in commerce;
cloth, pearls, and other such items—these are permissible, as is an article for which there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

When one has entered into a state of concentration, thinking, “Having taken this, eat it,” or “Give this,” or “Bring this,” or “I shall give it,” there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture in the act of buying and selling.
[This applies to] one’s own gain from another, or what belongs to the Saṅgha, or what belongs to another.
One should forfeit it and dedicate it [to the Saṅgha]; otherwise, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) or an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

If one uses what has been forfeited without having forfeited it, or does not give it away, or if one perceives as one's own what has been forfeited, there is an offense of wrong-doing; otherwise, it is different.
12. Exposition of the Pācittiya Offenses:
Regarding "Pācittiya"—in the case of speaking falsehood, as well as in the instigation of slander;
In the case of a student living with one who is not yet fully ordained, in causing annoyance or revulsion, in striking with the palm of the hand, in showing disrespect, and in causing remorse;
in entering a village without asking permission, and in eating in succession.
In departing without having lifted [the bedding], or in leaving one’s bed or lodgings;
in traveling on a road with a woman, or sitting alone with each [of them];
in frightening, striking, or speaking otherwise [than the truth].
In the cases of causing vexation, grave offenses, public disclosure, and concealing [a fault];
laughing, spitting water, and ejecting from the monastery;
and lying down in close proximity—it is stated that these are *pācittiya* offenses.
13. The Exposition of the Ascetic’s Mode of Life:
Regarding the ascetic’s mode of life—when there is the destruction of living plants, it is a *pācittiya* offense; what has been made permissible is allowable.
With the nails or with the arrows of words, one may act in accordance with the ascetic’s code.
That which is produced from roots, trunks, joints, seeds, sprouts, and fruit-seeds:
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the initial undertaking regarding seeds that have been separated from their living habitat.
A seed from which the embryo has already emerged, as well as a seed that is not yet a seed, is permissible; seeds bound within a basket, or even those placed outside, are likewise allowed.
Regarding seeds that are connected together, whether in a vessel or on the ground:
And whatever is done by Kate in one allowable place shall be considered as done in all. If,
after the allowable thing has been set aside, roots or leaves grow up there,
one must make it allowable again, for at that time it is a "growth from the earth" (bhūtagāma).
Whether it has spread or not, the water-moss growing in ponds;
the moss on shrines and the like, having produced two or three leaves;
and even a seed of a plant, when its roots and leaves have emerged.
Algae on the surface of jars and such, flower-buds, and the *ahichattaka* mushroom;
these are the bases for an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), as is a blossoming flower that is not fit for trade.
Lac, extract, and mushrooms, having been shaken off from a living tree—
For one who takes [a coconut] from there, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya), as is the case for one who even cuts a single syllable.
It is not permitted to press coconuts and the like with a wooden monkey or similar device,
nor is it permissible to cut [the husk] or make a knot on grass and such.
"Do not cut, break, or gather living plants or seeds;
do not plow, pierce, or cook them. Having made a restriction, one should not speak thus:
'Make this allowable,' or 'Take this,' or 'Bring this.'"
"Give this; clean that"—it is appropriate to speak thus.
14. The Exposition of the Grounds (*Bhūminiddesa*): Regarding "grounds" (*bhūmiyo*)—
And [the rules concerning] formal authorization, the Gonisādī, and the householder;
those grounds which are deemed allowable, where both what is raw and what is cooked are permitted.
In a dwelling built for the purpose of residence, belonging to the Saṅgha, or dedicated to the Vekasaṇḍaka.
A suitable hut may be obtained, sufficient for one person to sleep in,
within a house belonging solely to the Saṅgha. While building it in this manner,
one should place the first brick, pillar, and so forth, after performing the formal proclamation (*ussāvanantika*).
“We shall build a kitchen,” “We shall build a kitchen.
When a monastery is for the most part unenclosed, or even entirely so,
it is conventionally designated by the Saṅgha as a “cow-pen area” (gonisādī).
Except for a bhikkhu, what is given by others belongs to those [donors] themselves.
A householder is considered dead when his house is for the sake of a hut that is not allowable.
[Likewise,] what is mixed with ghee and so forth from a hut that is not allowable;
One should avoid what was stored overnight, as well as the two preceding types of food.
Cooked by a monk himself is permitted for life;
likewise, non-material food may be kept for seven days, but when mixed with material food, it must be prepared by the monks themselves.
A boundary established by pillars and other such markers remains in effect even when those very markers are removed, as well as when others are removed.
When all have been removed, it becomes one whose basis has been abandoned.
"Goniṣādi is enclosed; the rest are variations on roofing.
15. The Exposition of Duties Toward Preceptors and Teachers:
Regarding "duties toward preceptors and teachers"—
Living in dependence upon his preceptor and teacher, being well-behaved,
he should always provide tooth-sticks, a seat, water, and rice gruel at the proper time.
He should perform the duties regarding the alms-bowl when entering the village and when returning from it.
Regarding the seat and the footstool, the wooden block, the sandals, and the robes;
regarding the places for food, drink, excrement, and urine;
and likewise regarding the cleaning of the monastery and its re-establishment—this is the proper conduct (*vatta*).
While cleaning, a bhikkhu should not shake his robes near a dwelling, near a water source, or near a bed or seat; nor should he do so when facing the wind or in a crowded place.
This applies when bathing is to be performed, or when dyeing or washing robes.
While sewing a robe, one should not leave it unattended while moving about.
Without asking permission from someone else, one should neither give away nor take back their bowl, robes, or any other personal requisites.
To place someone behind oneself, or to go behind them;
to carry away one's almsfood, or to have it brought out for oneself;
to perform a service or a preparatory task, or to have one's own hair cut—these are [grounds for offense].
It is not permissible to have something built or to do it oneself without having asked for permission.
Likewise, it is not permissible to go to a village, a cemetery, outside the monastery boundary, or in any direction,
nor even to attend to one's own business, without having asked for permission.
One should dispel any discontent, wrong view, or remorse that has arisen;
or one should exert oneself in matters dependent upon the Saṅgha.
One should attend to those who are ill, and assist them when they have recovered.
In all cases, by breaking the rule, it is an offense of wrong-doing due to lack of respect.
16. The Exposition on the Place for Feces and Urine:
Regarding "the place for feces and urine"—
One should not defecate according to seniority, but rather in the proper sequence.
Facilities for defecation and urination, as well as bathing places, are provided.
One should enter after making way for others and should not enter abruptly.
One should clear one's throat while standing right there on one's sandals.
One should not sneeze or pass stool while chewing a tooth-stick;
one should not do either of these things outside the chamber for feces and urine.
One should not throw wood into a well, nor spittle or urine into a cesspool;
one should not scrape at rough ground, nor wash one's head after it has been shorn.
One should not go out hastily, nor should one go out by forcing an opening.
One should not chew or eat making a *capu-capu* sound, and one should keep it clean.
17. The Explanation of Making a Request:
"Making a request" means—
Without being requested by the elder, he did not recite the Pātimokkha;
he did not speak on the Dhamma, nor ask questions, nor provide answers.
When he spoke after having asked permission, the elders returned once more.
There is no need for a further formal request [for permission to leave], nor when expressing thanks at the head of the meal-row.
While residing in a single dwelling with an elder,
one should not recite the scriptures or give instruction without having first requested permission.
One should not speak the Dhamma while lighting a lamp, nor extinguish it;
one may open or close a window or a door.
Even while walking on the meditation path (caṅkama), one should turn back when meeting an elder.
"By which the elder [monk] does not brush against him with the corner of his outer robe.
18. The Description of the Naked: "Naked"—
Naked, one should walk on the path, eat, drink, chew, and taste;
one should neither take nor give, nor should one pay homage or cause others to pay homage.
One should not perform services, nor should one have them performed for oneself.
"In the preparation [of robes], two cloths for covering are allowable everywhere.
19. The Exposition of the Allowance for Bathing:
"The allowance for bathing" means—
One should not bathe in front of or above the elders;
one who is ascending should yield the path to those who are descending.
While bathing, one should not strike against walls, pillars, or trees.
One should not rub the body against a Gandhabba-hand,
a Kuruvindaka-string, a water-pot, or against another person’s body. However,
it is permissible to use potsherds, bricks, fragments of stone, or a cloth-wick.
All kinds of broad-footed creatures, as well as a stone, a shell, a pebble, or a clod of earth, are allowable for rubbing the feet. 20.
The Description of Those Not to Be Venerated.
Those not to be saluted: those who have been suspended, those who have not received full ordination, women of a different communion,
one who is newly ordained, one for whom a grave offense has been committed, and a paṇḍaka— these are not to be saluted.
21. The Description of Leather:
"Leather" refers to the hides of deer and goats; these are permitted for use.
The deer Rohita and Eni, and the Kuruṅga species of antelope—
apart from these three permitted ones, any other skin is a basis for an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Regarding bags, sandals, and skins— all this is permitted by way of likeness (kappatimānusa).
22. The Description of Footwear "Footwear as well"—these are not permitted in the Middle Country;
they are new footwear for use in crowded places.
In every forest monastery, and for one who is always unwell;
there are sandals that are entirely blue, yellow, white, red, and black,
as well as those dyed with mahāraṅga, mahānāma, and raṅga dyes.
There are sandals made entirely of mañjeṭṭhika cloth, variegated, or adorned with blue, yellow, and other colors;
those decorated with partridge feathers, or with the horns of rams and goats;
those bound with leather straps, those bound in folds, and those filled with cotton.
The Pāliguṇṭhimaka [carpets] were sewn together with peacock feathers;
they were adorned with the skins of scorpions, lizards, lions, tigers, leopards, cats, black bears, and owls.
Shoes that are to be worn by walking over them: if anyone wears them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Having wiped away the entire blue or other colors, or even a single part, one may use the sandals after removing the leather linings and so forth.
23. The Exposition of Looking At (Anolokiya-niddesa) "Looking at" means:
looking at the private parts of a woman for lustful desire, or looking at the face of one who gives alms.
If one looks at another’s eye, perceiving it as a mirror, or at one’s own face in a mirror or in water, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). 24.
The Description of the Eye-Cosmetic Case.
"Anjana-box" means:
whether it has eight, sixteen, or twenty-four compartments, it is suitable as an anjana-box if it is smooth and round;
even if there are three lines at the base and the neck, it is sufficient provided there is only one line to bind it.
Any kind of embroidery work such as garlands, "crocodile-tooth" patterns,
or variations like the "cow's urine," "drawn," or "half-moon" designs— none of these are permitted here.
However, it is permissible to sew a bag using a single-colored thread.
A box with a lid, a key-casket, and even a tally-stick without markings;
likewise those made of conch-shell, navel-horn, bone, reed, ivory, wood, bamboo, lac, or iron.
Eye-salve boxes, applicator sticks, and smoke-tubes are permitted;
likewise, surgical knives and handles made of that [bone] and toothpicks are permitted.
25. The Description of Unallowable Beds.
"Unsuitable beds" means:
a high couch, a stuffed bed, a sofa, a woollen rug, a cow-hide rug, a floral-patterned rug,
a leaf-mat, a multi-colored rug, a rug made of sheep’s wool, and a rug with hair on one side only.
Cotton cloth, silk, and fine linen; rugs for elephants, horses, and chariots;
rugs made of *jinappaveṇi* and *kadalī* fibers, and rugs of the finest deer-skin.
A canopy with red borders, and a crimson pillow.
These are improper; there is an offense of wrong-doing for one who consumes them.
Regarding the three types of high seats and the remainder:
it is permitted to sit upon those belonging to householders, as well as on a Dhamma-seat, in the dining hall, or in a private house.
It is also permissible to lie down upon a brief ground-covering.
As for beds and chairs— whether four-legged, seven-limbed, or five-limbed, or those with high legs—
if they are upholstered with cotton wool, one may sit upon them only within the house.
It is filled with coḷa-grass, vāku-plant, kuṇṇa-grass, and leaves, as well as grass;
the five types of bark-fibers for robes and the mattress are everywhere allowable.
The three types of down, the stuffing of the mattress, and the fur of wild animals and birds [are likewise permitted].
The use of stuffed cushions is permitted, provided they are free from cotton;
likewise for pillows made of lentil-shaped stuffing. Human hair, wool, leaves, and *tamālaka* flowers—these are not pure seats and may not be used unless they have been inspected.
26. The Exposition on Sharing a Seat:
"And 'one who shares a seat'—a single seat for monks was permitted [to be shared] by those within three years of seniority."
For seventy-seven years, a five-year-old [novice] was permitted to sit.
Excluding the paṇḍaka, the woman, and the hermaphrodite,
the Sage authorized all others to sit on long benches.
The end of a long seat is that which is sufficient for three to sit upon;
on a couch or even on a chair, it is allowable for two to sit.
27. The Description of One Who Is Not in Communion.
"And one who is not in communion" means:
one who has been suspended, one who has not received full ordination, a nun, one whose roots [of training] have been severed,
one living in a different communion, one staying outside the boundary, and one who has departed by air.
The eleven who are incapable and those who are not in communion have been explained.
28. The Description of Formal Acts (Kamma): And as for "the formal act" (kamma) —
A formal act that is both incomplete and contrary to the Dhamma; one that is complete but contrary to the Dhamma;
one that is incomplete yet in accordance with the Dhamma; and one that is both complete and in accordance with the Dhamma:
only the fourth of these is authorized; for all other formal acts, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
The fourfold group, the fivefold group, the tenfold and twentyfold groups;
the group of more than twenty: these five Saṅghas have been explained.
Among them, the fourfold group consists of the rehabilitation (abbhāna), the full ordination (upasampadā), and the invitation (pavāraṇā).
A group of five is required for rehabilitation (*abbhāna*) and for full ordination (*upasampadā*) in the Middle Country;
a group of ten is required for rehabilitation, except for the "all-work" (*sabbakammika*) [officer];
the other is declared to be authorized for all formal acts (*kamma*).
In matters to be performed by a quorum of four, there must be four regular monks (*pakatatta*);
others who have reached the stage for the formal act (*kamma*) require consent (*chanda*). This same principle applies to the remaining cases.
That which is to be performed by a quorum of four and so forth, and which is subject to a formal act of exclusion from the community (*asaṃvāsa-kamma*), [is likewise governed by this rule].
Having made one of those subject to heavy offenses (*garukāpatti*) a filler for the quorum,
any formal act (*kamma*) such as probation (*parivāsa*) that is performed— whether it be a *kuppa* (invalid) or *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing)—
is an illegitimate act (*adhammakamma*). One should reject it, for there are two or three obstacles [to its validity].

These are the grounds for formal acts (kamma): one who holds a wrong view, one who persists in it, one deserving of a formal act, one excluded from the community, one whose mind is deranged, and one who is insane;
against these, a formal act of prohibition performed in the midst of the Saṅgha is not valid.
For a monk who is of the same communion as those residing within a natural or formally established boundary,
even if he protests in their presence, his protest is effective even if it is the very next [action] after the announcement. One may protest a legitimate formal act in order to cause it to fail.
"Concealing the integrity of one's bodily conduct, one should not give consent;
this is an offense of wrong-doing. 29. The Exposition on Avoiding Wrong Livelihood: Regarding "avoiding wrong livelihood"—
One should not give wood, bamboo, fruit, flowers, powder, bath-water, mouth-washing water,
clay, tooth-sticks, and so forth, for the sake of maintaining a family connection.
Nor should one provide servants, mung beans, lentils, or medical treatments for the household.
One should not live by the business of sending gifts, or by running errands on foot, nor by providing supplementary food,
nor by the practice of medicine, nor by any other means condemned by the Fully Awakened One.
One should avoid requisites that have arisen from corrupting families and so forth, by means of such things as hinting, seeking, exaggeration, and hypocrisy. 30.
The Exposition of Conduct.
They proceed thus:
A visitor should not enter the monastery wearing sandals,
nor with a sunshade, nor with his head covered, nor having placed his robe over his shoulder.
One should not wash one's feet with drinking water, even if they are senior;
one should greet the resident monks and inquire about the bedding and seats.
One who is departing, having put away the wooden and clay utensils, [should do so].
Having secured the monastery, one should take leave of the bedding and seats.
If there is no one to be asked for permission, one should carefully store them away; otherwise, it is not permissible to depart.
The resident monk should prepare a seat for the newly arrived senior;
he should set out water for washing the feet and so forth, as well as the bowl and robes.
Having gone out to meet him, he should receive them and inquire after his drinking water.
One should greet those who have arrived as guests, and prepare a place for their bedding and seats.
One should speak of whether they have already dwelt there or not, and whether the area is suitable or unsuitable for alms-gathering.
One should designate places for defecation and urination, establish agreements, and grant formal permissions for those in training.
At the time of entering and departing, the drinking water for use, and while seated, one should announce all of this to the junior [monks]. 31.
The Exposition of Formal Assignment (Vikappanā).
"And the act of assigning" means:
two types of assigning have been stated—face-to-face and behind one's back.
When assigning face-to-face, one does so in the presence of a single competent person.
One should say: “I assign this robe to you.
Up to this point, it is as if it has been stored away; it is neither allowable nor unallowable.
Therefore, because its state has not been relinquished, [acts such as] using it and so forth are not permitted.
223. “Use what belongs to me, or dispose of it, or do with it as you see fit”—if [the owner] has thus relinquished it, its use and so forth are permissible.
Another [form of relinquishment] is done in the presence of a single monk, in the vicinity of another monk.
Having taken the name of one among five who share the same Dhamma, he should say:
“I assign this robe to the bhikkhu Tissa, to the bhikkhunī Tissa, to the male novice Tissa, to the female novice Tissa, or to the trainee Tissa. Then that bhikkhu [should say]:
“To the bhikkhu Tissa, to the bhikkhunī Tissa, to the male novice Tissa, to the female novice Tissa...”
One should say: "Use the property belonging to that novice nun or that trainee, or dispose of it, or do with it as you see fit.
Regarding the assignment [of property] in the absence of the owner: one should direct it toward another.
“I give this robe-cloth for the purpose of assigning it to you.
He should then ask, “Who is your friend or acquaintance?
The other should reply, “The three monks,” or “The three nuns,” or “The three novices,” or “The three female novices.”
Or, [he says] “to the trainee nun Tissa. Then,
having made the designation by that same person, saying “I give [this] to the monk Tissa,
to the nun Tissa, to the novice Tissa, to the novice nun Tissa, or to the trainee nun Tissa,” by that very [act]...
"It should be relinquished [with the words]: 'Use it, or dispose of it, or do with it as you see fit.
Having understood the state of being distant or near, singular or plural, one should apply [the appropriate pronouns] here: "this is this" or "these are these."
Whether for ten days, one month, or five months while the *kathina* robe has been spread,
if there is an expectation that what is deficient will be fulfilled, one does not incur an offense of forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) for failing to produce it,
provided it has not been formally resolved upon or assigned as a gift.
32. The Exposition on Dependence (Nissaya-niddesa) Regarding dependence:
for one who is proficient and has five years of seniority, there is no requirement to take formal dependence.
As long as one is incompetent, one lives entirely dependent [on others].
Having arranged the robe over one shoulder, having raised the joined palms,
and sitting in a squatting posture, one should speak up to three times.
“Venerable sir, please be my teacher;
I will live under the guidance of the Venerable One.
When one has departed, or when one has gone over to another faction, or even when one has disrobed, the formal support (nissaya) ceases.
The matter is settled by death, by difference of preceptor, or by coming together.
One who is conscientious should not live dependent on [a teacher] who has come to a place where he was not before,
until four or five days have passed, so that he may know his status among the community of monks.
For one who is traveling, for one who is ill, for an attendant of the sick,
or for one who has requested [permission] to dwell in the forest— provided he observes that it is comfortable—
and with a donor who is like-minded and virtuous, he is permitted to stay for that long.
33. The Exposition of the Girdle (Kāyabandhana-niddesa) Regarding the "girdle":
if one who does not have a girdle should enter a village, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Wherever one remembers [to fasten it], there too mindfulness has gone.
There are two kinds of waistbands: the corded band and the pig-tail band;
the cloth strap and the rope are the one that conforms to those.
Fish-bone, date-palm leaf, smooth strips of cloth,
and even fringes of four kinds may be used, with double threads at the ends.
Having shown [the faults of] garlands and so forth, as well as the "crab-cover," one should show the quality of the threads.
A cut-out elephant-umbrella fringe is not allowable.
A border with a vase, a makara’s mouth, and so forth, is not allowable at the edge of the fringes;
nor are vases, lines, or other variegated patterns on both ends.
The deḍḍubhaka, the muraja, the maddavīṇā, and the kalābu—these two are not permitted for the fringes;
they may be used only for the middle fringe.
[These may be made] from bamboo, ivory, horn, bone, wood, lac, or fruit.
[Amulets] made of conch-shell, thread, reed, or even metal,
as well as knots made of those same materials, are fashioned in various ways and are allowable.
The first recitation section is finished.
34. The Description of Earth "Earth" is of two kinds:
that which is formed and that which is unformed; it consists of pure clay and dust.
The earth was born scorched, with much clay and dust;
there was a heap of dust and clay more than four months old from the rainless drought.
There were pure gravel, stones, pebbles, potsherds, and sand.
The ground is burnt, as is the earth with most of its pebbles and so forth;
the second is called the "heap," and there is the four-month rain-rest.
Of the three parts, two parts consist of clay for that ground.
This is for the most part regarding clay; this same principle applies to the others as well.
There is a *pācittiya* when digging has occurred for one who perceives it as such; there is a *dukkaṭa* for one who perceives it as such when it has not occurred;
for one who is in doubt or perceives it as not having occurred, there is likewise no offense in causing the ground to be dug.
For striking back at a blow, for digging by oneself,
there is one offense for each individual command, or for various commands,
there is one verbal offense. “Dig this spot, this bulb, and dig a well here;”
It is not permissible to say, "Know this to be a fire-pit," having restricted the meaning.
However, such a statement as, "Know this to be a pillar or a moat; fetch clay;
make it allowable (kappiya)," is permissible.
Dry mud and the like that are not connected to the earth may be stirred up,
as may thin mud fit for splashing; likewise,
the soil of anthills, termite nests, and mouse holes.
One should not become angry for more than four months regarding [damage to] walls,
nor regarding clods of earth and the like. When stones fall on the banks of ponds and such,
or when dust falls near water, or when it falls upon a new mat, one should not be provoked.
In an anthill, on a mound of clay, or likewise in an open space;
in a place where there is mostly bare ground—there one stands as a "standing-builder.
By moving and disturbing the ground in order to take up a pillar or the like;
To split the earth with a stream [of water], or to make the uneven level;
to scrub with brooms, or to plant thorns and the like;
thinking "I shall show it," one breaks the earth to walk upon it, leaving footprints.
It is not permissible for one suffering from skin diseases to rub their limbs or members against riverbanks and the like,
nor is it permissible to rub the ground with the hand in order to wash it.
[Nor is it permissible] to pull up pillars and such upright objects, or to roll stones and the like.
Dragging branches, cutting trees or creepers, and plowing; sprinkling urine and so forth—
these are permitted for one of pure mind, provided they are not done for the sake of sport,
nor is the stirring up of dust from the ground allowed.
When there is no fuel for the fire, one may cause the fire to fall onto a potsherd or a brick, or let it die out on the ground. 35.
The Description of Requisites.
"Requisites" means:
to sew inside and out with threads of five colors;
and to cut [patterns such as] mountain peaks, half-moons, and so forth, upon the parasol and the leaf[-shaped umbrella].
A jar, or a wild beast’s form—lines on a staff are not permitted;
they are permitted on the tip of a staff, resembling a mushroom.
To sew with a single color, or to weave a cage-like pattern;
A thong is suitable for fastening a parasol to its handle by means of a line; likewise,
at the edge or the tip of the cloth, a braid, a chain,
or even another needle-work device is not allowable on a robe.
Even the *kappabindu* (the decorative dot), the *pāḷikaṇṇika* (the scrollwork at the corners), and so forth;
the *gaṇṭhi*, *pāsaka*, and *paṭṭa* (the knots, loops, and bands)—these are indeed four-cornered as an offering-stand (*agghiya*).
A mallet, a crab, or any such modification is not appropriate here.
And there should be no boils at the corners, nor anything difficult to discern on the edge;
one should not put perfume, oil, lac, or dye into it.
It should not be dyed with conch-shell, gem, or anything else that might scratch it.
One should rub [the robe] after placing it in a wooden trough, but not with blows from the fist.
One may cut the threads at the corners of the ear-flaps when the robe is dyed;
however, drawing lines on the handle of the umbrella for the religious purpose of making a mark is not permitted.
It is permissible to draw lines for a jewel-casket, a swelling, and a key;
likewise, a line for a pepper-corn and a boundary-line on a staff are allowed.
[Also permitted are] garlands and so forth, a water-wheel, a bowl-design, and wall-paintings.
The two lines below and above are like a mushroom (ahicchattaka).
Excluding the handle of a small axe, needles, and tongs,
anything else that has the color and polish of a mountain peak or similar object is not permitted.
In the case of a bolster, a mattress, a bench, and other types of bedding and seats;
in a broom, in a place for discarding refuse, and in a dye-vessel;
in a water-vessel, on a footstool, and in a spittoon.
In the case of mat foundations and covers, palm-leaf fans, and handheld fans;
whatever floral designs and the like are polished and colored are not prohibited.
However, in the case of a dwelling, there is no prohibition regarding the various types of doors, panels, and so forth.
The use of golden vessels is permitted; what need is there to mention those that are polished and beautiful?
Among the various types of oil containers—such as those made of horn, bamboo, or gourd—if they are devoid of male or female forms and are polished and beautiful, their use is not prohibited.
36. The Exposition of Medicines (Bhesajjaniddesa) Regarding "medicine" (bhesajja):
it is not permitted to give medicine or to speak [of giving] medicine for the sake of a person.
The request for alms-food, [the use of] one's own requisites, and those belonging to fellow practitioners of the Dhamma, to one's parents, to the attendant bhikkhu, and to the furniture;
it is permissible to prepare medicine and to perform services for the attendant.
To one's grandfather, grandmother, brothers, sisters, and so forth—
these being one's own kinsmen— one may give things for temporary use.
For [the offense of] "requesting" refers to requesting items such as medicines and the like that would defile the family.
The alms-food does not fail to grow among relatives by blood or marriage of one’s mother and father; it is unclaimed and unrestrained for one’s mother and others,
as well as for the six types of robbers, thieves, and those with authority to give.
With their own water for drinking and bathing, one should provide protection for oneself;
when others request it, one should recite the protective charms (paritta) rooted in the Teaching.
Whether it be morality, the Dhamma, or a protective charm, let one come and give it, or let one speak it.
"It is permissible to give and to speak [of having received], once one has gone as sent by someone.
37. The Description of Receiving: "Receiving" (uggaha) means—
For one who accepts even the ten kinds of gems for the sake of a shrine, the Saṅgha, another person, or a group, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Among those [gems], if one renounces them for one's own sake, it is a forfeiture (nissaggiya); for the other two cases, it is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one has not mentioned the group, the Saṅgha, or the individual when asked,
one should not refuse by saying, "I give this for the new construction of the shrine";
rather, one should say to the kappiyakārakas, "They are speaking thus."
If someone offers a field, a building site, a pond, or slaves and cattle,
one may accept them after first declining them, provided it is done through a formal procedure involving a *kappiya-kāraka* (an officer for allowable goods).
When fields and such are offered to the monastery, it is permissible to say, "I give."
In the case of a new field, a pond, or a tank, there is the work of digging, the removal of earth, the embankment, and the making firm of the rim.
In the case of a new field, there is the taking of one-third from the bank. In the case of a new tank, there is the same.
In an uncultivated area, [saying] "give just this much" regarding a crop,
and the causing of a *kahāpaṇa* coin to be paid— all these are improper for everyone.
Without saying "plow," "sow," and so forth, [taking] from the ground [that has been prepared];
He establishes [the boundary] on the ground, saying, "This much is the portion to be given. Regarding the crop grown on that plot of land, he says, "Take this much,
take that much," thus speaking while establishing the measure with measuring rods and ropes for the purpose of taking it.
Standing by to guard [the goods], having them removed from the threshing floor,
or returning them to the granary and so forth— this is improper for him alone.
If he should return anything belonging to a householder, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Under the pretext of the treasurer, even if it belongs to one’s father—
since the property of one’s fathers must certainly be restored—
one may restore it after making it one’s own possession. It is permissible to restore it.
If one says, "Give it," and after having arranged it, [the owner] says, "I refuse";
or if, having caused it to be laid down, [the owner] departs, it may be taken. To guard it because it is an obstacle [to one's duties] is permissible.
While performing work in the monastery, [one may take] one's own [tools], such as carpenters' tools and so forth.
If those favored by the king, having set aside requisites or bedding and furniture,
say "Give this," whether out of their own desire or out of fear,
one should not comply; it is proper to show that the place is well-guarded.
When men had forcibly cast him down and departed,
they suspected that the monk had stolen [the goods], for such was the state of the property lost.
Within the monastery dwelling, there was a jewel or what was considered a jewel.
Having taken it, one should place it on another path of a similar kind, knowing that the owner has not arrived, thinking, "Let what is appropriate be done. 38.
The Exposition on Corrupting Families.
Regarding "corrupting families":
for one who gives flowers, bamboo, fruit, powder, tooth-sticks, or clay for the purpose of socializing,
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for corrupting a family.
A heavy object belonging to the Saṅgha, when given by one who is authoritative, constitutes a thullaccaya offense;
for one who gives it, there are offenses such as dukkaṭa, and so forth, regarding property belonging to the Saṅgha through theft.
In every way, [it is forbidden] to plant or cause to be planted [trees] for the purpose of winning over families.
It is not permitted to tend a tree that bears fruit and flowers.
However, from the perspective of signs and manifestations,

Even for one who has not received the formal instruction (sāsana), if they speak first again,

39. The Exposition of the Entrance into the Rains Retreat "Entrance into the rains retreat" means:
there are two entrances into the rains retreat—the earlier and the later.
In this context, attachment and verbal expression are as follows:
“I enter the rains retreat for these three months in this monastery;
here I enter the rains retreat. Herein, the arising of such a thought constitutes attachment.
One who does not wish to enter the residence, or who transgresses that very day, incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); so too does one who enters while knowing [the rules].
One may enter a second time, having entered with the rains-retreat cut short.
One should not set out on a wandering tour for three months without having stayed [there],
except for the sake of one's mother and father, or for the five who share the same Dhamma,
or for food for the sick and their attendants, or for medicine.
I shall go and question him, and attend upon him who is discontented;
I shall dispel his remorse and his heavy, primary views.
I shall either do it myself or cause it to be done—this dispelling and separation.
Whether for the purpose of emerging from seclusion, making an effort [to go],
or for such reasons as "I wish to go," one may obtain [permission] by means of the seven-day business, whether it be a sent [message] or unsent. Or,
when invited for the sake of hearing the Dhamma at a legal act of the Sangha, [one may go].
Whether sent by a teacher or to see one's teachers, one may go to wash goods,
to fetch alms-food, or to visit relatives; but one who has gone far away shall not receive what is obtainable on that very day, nor shall he reach it until he returns.
When sent by other relatives, or by one who has resided with a bhikkhunī;
when sent by laymen or laywomen after having been specifically pointed out—
there is no offense in interrupting the rains residence if there is an obstacle or for one's own sake.
Or, if there is no harmony in the Saṅgha, one who has completed his rains-residence should perform the Pavāraṇā ceremony.
It is not permitted to go to an open space, to the hollow of a tree, to its branches,
to a charnel house, to a canopy, or to a wooden trough.
Even for one who has no other lodging, it is not permitted to go [to another monastery] unless it is by way of a boat or on land;
however, it is permitted to go there to perform the *pavāraṇā*. This concludes the exposition on the "Inalienable" (*avebhaṅgiya*). 40. Exposition on the Inalienable.
"Those things not to be divided" are:
the pleasure groves and their sites, the monastery and its site;
beds, stools, cushions, bolsters, and other furniture for lying down and sitting.
The iron cauldron and the pan,
the iron vessel for drinking;
the axe, the adze, and the hatchet.
A spade and a pickaxe,
creepers, bamboo, grass, leaves, muñja-grass, pabbaja-grass,
and clay; these five types of wooden and earthen vessels are not to be divided.
For one who distributes [heavy goods], it is a thullaccaya offense; even if distributed, they are considered undistributed.
These are called heavy goods (*garubhaṇḍa*), and they must be disposed of.
Even a creeper as thick as a forearm, or a bamboo eight finger-breadths in length—
Even a mere handful of grass and such, or even a single leaf, or clay— whether natural,
five-colored, or consisting of lime, husks, and so forth—
even if it is only the size of a palm fruit, provided it has been given there or grown there.
Even ropes, cords, and the like belonging to the Saṅgha are not to be divided while they are still being guarded;
they may be divided once the work is finished, whether for the Saṅgha or for a Cetiya.
Alms-bowls and other items suitable for a Bhikkhu are likewise [not to be divided] while unfinished or unmade.
A vegetable dish among metal vessels, a water-pot worth one quarter of a *pāda*;
a wooden box for oil, an oil-spoon, and a pair of scissors;
a sunshade handle, tally-sticks, and likewise a sandal-stand.
The staff for one permitted to live [in the forest], the basket, the foot-hold;
the fire-drill, the needle, and so forth—likewise the requisites of a monk.
Woodwork that has been carved but not yet finished, and ivory, should be distributed.
Among the requisites of a bhikkhu, a water-pot for the feet is made of clay.
Leather that is suitable for distribution is allowable, while the skin of a sheep is not suitable for distribution.
Heavy goods are to be exchanged for heavy goods, and stationary property for stationary property.
One may exchange a fixed portion and eat it after doing so; one may take rice and the like by way of a formal act of exchange (*phātikamma*);
the remainder is not to be shared. 41. The Explanatory Section on Miscellaneous Matters.
Miscellaneous matters:
In a place where the doors are secured with bolts and there are wooden pegs for the latch,
one who sleeps during the day should fasten the door with a cross-bar.
When a wise man is present, even the act of arranging [the bedding] is permitted;

Jewels, women’s forms, grain, and women’s ornaments—
For one who touches weapons or armor, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For one who smoothes the hair with beeswax, oil, or water-oil, or with a fan-hand or a comb, or even with a cloth, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
They may lie down together under one coverlet or on one bedspread;
likewise, they may eat from the same couch or even from the same vessel.
[The height of the seat] should be less than four finger-breadths or more than eight finger-breadths.
One should not chew a tooth-stick, nor should one who is unwell eat garlic.

One should not, out of a desire for gain, speak ill of another—whether superior or inferior—in terms of birth and so forth, or speak falsely under the guise of a pretext, even if done in jest. This is called "ill-spoken."
One should not maintain long nails, long hair, or long hairs on the nose.
It is not permitted to remove the hair from the private parts even once every twenty days.
One should not cause obstruction according to seniority; that which is designated for the Saṅgha belongs to the Saṅgha.
One should not sleep on a bed or seat with unwashed feet;
nor likewise on one where the feet have been well-washed, if sandals are worn.
One should not lounge with the outer robe draped over the knees, nor should one lean against a wall or similar support.
When water has been prepared by preliminary work, one should not refrain from rinsing the mouth.
There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the undertaking of what is unallowable, in piercing a stone out of sport,
in a confession that is similar [to the offense], and in the failure to disclose [the offense].
In the case of deceiving after having given one's word, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one whose mind is pure;
however, for the other, it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) at the very moment of giving the word.
One should not climb a tree, even when there is a human-sized task to be done.
In times of distress, it is permissible to mount [the vehicle] according to one's need.
For one traveling on a journey without [a companion], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for not making an announcement to the assembly.

One incurs a thullaccaya offense for cutting off the genitals;
there is a dukkaṭa offense for injuring other parts of the body, except when it is due to illness or for the purpose of self-destruction.
One should neither make nor cause to be made images of the mind, such as paintings or statues.

If one makes a mistake regarding the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha while performing an act of service, it is a dukkaṭa offense;

Having uncovered it, one should not pour [water] upon it with mud,
water, or the like. For one who does not accept the instruction, nor for one who does not respond,

One should not recite the Lokāyata, nor should one grasp at the hair [of another];
one should not eat from a bowl, nor play at any game.
One should not wear what is worn by others, nor clothing worn by householders.
One may wear a robe that has been wrapped around, or one may have a forest grove whitewashed.
One may employ interest on a loan or request it, provided it is not from one who is unrelated or from what has been restricted.
One may use for one's own consumption what has been given, but one must not give it to another.
Having taken the best portion and eaten it, one may give some back after a few days.
Regarding a request made for a specific purpose, one should know that there is protection [from the offense] whether one knows [the donor's intention] or not;

however, if the person is punished, the penalty falls upon the one who caused the punishment to be inflicted. As for the one who personally causes the punishment to be inflicted: [the penalty applies].
The offenses, beginning with the *pārājika*, are to be known according to the value of the penalty.
When those who are stealing requisites are addressed as "thief,
thief," the penalty for one who seizes them for no purpose is equal to the value of the goods.
One incurs a dukkaṭa offense if one discards excrement, urine,
or refuse outside the walls or enclosures, whether or not one has looked around,
or if one does so upon greenery or upon planted crops such as rice or coconut trees.
It is not permitted to arrange, to employ, or to observe those already employed;
nor is it permitted to engage in dancing, singing, or instrumental music, even if it is connected with the Dhamma;
nor is it permitted to accept when it is said, "Let us make an offering."
Seeing him going for the sake of sport to the royal palace, the lotus pond, the park, or the pleasure house,
he committed an offense of wrong-doing by entering the monastery.
One should not ward off [rain] with a new [robe], nor should one wear a robe while it is still damp.
One should conceal it and ask for forgiveness; and when one has been dismissed by a teacher.
In the case of verbal abuse in the absence of the other, and regarding the seven offenses;
whether it be a monk or a lay follower, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) by another means as well.
It is not permissible to divert a robe offered out of faith;
it may be given to one's parents, but it is not permissible to give it to other relatives.
If one who has completed the rains residence takes a share from elsewhere, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is lost or worn out, he should return it; if urged, he should not pay a fine for it.
By abandoning his responsibility, he becomes liable for the value of the goods.
One should not enter a village wearing only an undergarment and upper robe, nor should one do so wearing sandals.
One may enter [the village], but one should not carry a yak-tail fan or a mosquito whisk.

one should not carry an umbrella from the monastery grounds, though it may be used for protection.
One may cause [another] to take up a double-sided basket, or a single-sided basket;
a burden on the head, on the shoulder, or on the hips, as well as one suspended from the hand, is permitted.
To accuse someone who has not been granted the opportunity regarding an offense is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
And for one who is pure, likewise when there is no basis or when permission has been granted:
one should not use a bed-leg more than eight finger-breadths [in excess];
nor should one have a bed with high legs exceeding seven standard finger-breadths.

One who was previously a barber should carry a razor-case;
whatever manual labor is required for begging, it should be performed accordingly.
It is permissible to take what has been obtained even without having asked, provided one does not exert effort to do so;

When householders give to their guardians, one may take as much as they give.
It is permissible [to take] according to the limit [set] regarding what belongs to the Saṅgha or a shrine.
One may incur an offense in two ways: by means of body and speech, or by the six [factors];
through shamelessness, ignorance, remorse, being of a fickle nature, and the loss of mindfulness.
Whether regarding what is improper or what is proper, with the perception of it as proper or improper,
one who is shameless and ignorant conceals their offense through body and speech;
[this is] the fourfold emergence from offenses within the mark, the Saṅgha, and the group.
Indirect speech, hinting, and intimation are not permitted regarding two of the requisites;

There is no giving to one's own kinsmen when it involves the destruction of living beings; [this applies] to the five who share the same Dhamma.
That belongs to the Saṅgha alone, yet it takes root among householders.
Should a bhikkhu or a sāmaṇera die while staying in a lodging, the bhikkhu-saṅgha is the heir;

"This was given to the first; take it and give it to so-and-so";

A weapon in an iron vessel, and a wooden item in a wooden vessel;

42. Exposition of the Confession:
Regarding "confession"—that which constitutes the state of being a monk is the confession of a *pārājika* offense.
The method of emergence is as previously described:

the confession of a grave offense. Sitting in the *ukkhuṭika* (crouching) posture and raising one's joined palms in reverence, one should confess a *thullaccaya* or other such offenses in the presence of a single person in this manner.
384. “Venerable sir, I have committed one grave offense; I confess it in your presence,” he should say.
When the other asks, “Do you see that offense, friend? he should reply, “Yes, venerable sir, I see it.
When the other asks again, “Will you restrain yourself in the future, friend? he should say, “Very well, venerable sir, I will restrain myself thoroughly.”
“Venerable sir, I have committed two *thullaccaya* offenses; venerable sir, I have committed many *thullaccaya* offenses;
I confess them before you,” he should say. Regarding the *nissaggiya* offenses, however, [he should say]:
“Venerable sir, this robe-cloth of mine, which has exceeded ten days and is subject to relinquishment (*nissaggiya*), I relinquish to the Venerable One.”

“I relinquish them. “Venerable sir, these robes of mine... [or] this robe of mine... [or] these robes of mine, venerable sir, which have exceeded ten days and are to be relinquished—I relinquish them to you, venerable sir.

386. (Ka) “Venerable Sir, this robe of mine, which was spent overnight apart from me except by the consent of the Saṅgha, is to be relinquished.”

44. The Exposition of the Uposatha:
Regarding "Uposatha"—
There are two Uposatha days: the fourteenth and the fifteenth.
There are three types [of observance] by way of the recitation of the Suttas, the formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna), and complete purity (pārisuddhi).
For the Saṅgha, there is the Uposatha consisting of the recitation of the Suttas, and the Uposatha consisting of formal determination.
For the individual and for the rest, there is the *pārisuddhi-uposatha*.
When the preliminary duties have been performed, the assembly having reached a state of readiness, the Saṅgha recites the *sutta*; this is explained in five ways.
The brief exposition is prohibited when there is an obstacle.
Because it is stated: "The Elder alone is the authority regarding two expositions here, or three in different regions," it is permissible even when [the Elder] is not present.
If they should arrive at the same time, let those who are few recite;
that which has been recited should be well-recited, and the remainder should be listened to.
Whether it is merely recited, or the whole, or a portion remains standing [unrecited];
If there are many [monks] present, they should perform the *pārisuddhi* (declaration of purity) in his presence.
Having performed all the preliminary duties (*pubbakicca*) in every respect, one should then announce [the Uposatha] again.
For fifteen resident monks, or for others, if there are fewer.
If the others follow along with those who are equal, and there are more of the former, let the former follow them; this same method applies to the rest of them as well.
For those residing on the first day of the fortnight, [the procedure] is different from that of the others regarding the Uposatha.
May those who desire it grant their consent for the unity of the Samathakas.
If they do not grant it, the Uposatha should be performed after going outside;
for there is no unity when there is no desire to give, even if many are present or one is outside.
This same principle applies to those who wish to go on the first day of the fortnight (pāṭipada).
If one should intentionally recite a discourse to someone who does not wish to hear it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
[Likewise for] sweeping, lighting a lamp, or preparing a water-seat.
One who has been sent by a Mahāthera should not act in such a way.

(421) Having swept the area, having lit lamps, and having prepared a water-seat, and having established the formal motion for the assembly, the Uposatha should be performed by three [monks] as follows:
"Let the Venerable Ones listen to me: today is the Uposatha of the fifteenth day. If it is the proper time for the Venerable Ones, [let them attend]."
“Let us perform the Uposatha by means of mutual purification.

Having arranged his robe over one shoulder, sitting down in the kneeling posture (ukkuṭika), and raising his joined palms toward the Elder, he should proclaim thus: “I am pure, friends; consider me to be pure. He should say this up to three times.
Those who have already completed their previous undertaking should address the newcomer in this way: “I am pure, venerable sir; consider me to be pure. He should say this up to three times.
424. Two things are to be done by the elder; having done them thus, the junior should address him: "I am pure, friend; consider me to be pure"—this must be said three times.
The elder should likewise address the junior three times:

426. Having completed his prior duties, he should make a formal determination alone, saying: "Today is my Uposatha, whether it be the fifteenth or the fourteenth—I determine this. If he does not make this determination, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

If they perform that particular Uposatha, there may be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

And while seated in the assembly, one who has committed a similar offense should likewise not recite the Pātimokkha when surrounded by those who have consented [to conceal it].
Without having confessed the offense committed, and without having cleared away doubt;
Or one may attempt to perform the Uposatha on the following day, yet the Uposatha is not valid.
Those who have not established their residence for the Uposatha should not depart on that very day without [one of] these:
an obstacle, the Saṅgha, a formal resolution (adhiṭṭhātuṃ), or the boundary itself.
45. The Exposition of the Invitation (Pavāraṇā) Regarding "invitation" (pavāraṇā):
there is mutual invitation among two, three, or four [monks].
For one person there is a formal resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*);

for the rest, it is the invitation of the Saṅgha (*saṅghappavāraṇā*). When the preliminary duties have been performed, the time has arrived, and the assembly has gathered—the invitation is to be conducted by the Saṅgha in this manner, omitting the motion (*ñatti*).
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: today is the Pavāraṇā of the fifteenth day. If it is timely for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the Pavāraṇā.
Having arranged his robe over one shoulder and sitting in the kneeling position, the Saṅgha, with palms joined in reverence, raised its voice through the Elder.
“Friends, I invite the Saṅgha regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
May the Venerable Ones speak to me out of compassion; seeing [my fault], I shall make amends. For a second time...
For a third time, friends, I invite the Saṅgha regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected. May the Venerable Ones speak to me out of compassion.”
"Having taken [the bowl], while observing, I shall return it.

he himself remained in that very squatting posture until the end.
438. Having completed the preliminary commencement, the junior [monk] should address the Saṅgha:
439. “Venerable sirs, I invite the Saṅgha regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
May the venerable ones speak to me out of compassion; seeing [the fault], I shall make amends. A second time... and a third time, venerable sirs...”
