"I invite the Saṅgha with regard to what has been seen, heard, or suspected. May the Venerable Ones speak to me out of compassion;
seeing [the fault], I shall make amends.
By means of giving, by discussion of the Dhamma, and regarding quarrels and the night...
Because it is spent when there is an opportunity for the *tevācika* (three-utterance) procedure;
and because, in the case of the ten kinds of obstacles, one must state a formal motion (*ñatti*) according to the circumstances. 441.
“Let the Sangha, venerable sirs, hear me: while people are giving gifts, and while two bhikkhus are discussing the Dhamma...”

Most of the night has been spent by those engaged in quarreling. If the Saṅgha performs the invitation ceremony with three utterances, the Saṅgha will not have finished its invitation before this night dawns.
This is an obstacle of kings, this is an obstacle of thieves, this is an obstacle of fire, this is an obstacle of water, this is an obstacle of humans, this is an obstacle of non-humans. This...
“There is this danger from wild beasts, this danger from reptiles, this danger to life, and this danger to the holy life.
If the Saṅgha performs the invitation ceremony with three proclamations, the Saṅgha will not have completed its invitation, and then there will be this danger to the holy life.
If it is appropriate for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the invitation ceremony with two proclamations, with one proclamation, or by way of equal seniority.”
One should perform the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) according to the appropriate procedure, as established by the formal motion (*ñatti*);
if [the monks] should arrive at the same time, the first one among them should initiate it.

(443) Thus, even a group of three or four should state the motion and then perform the invitation: "Venerable sirs, listen to me. Today is the fifteenth day of the invitation. If it seems appropriate to the venerable ones, let us invite one another."
Having arranged his robe over one shoulder and sitting in the kneeling posture, he raised his joined palms toward the elder and spoke thus:
“Friend, I invite the venerable ones regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected; let them speak.”
“Out of compassion for me, may the venerable ones speak to me regarding what they have seen, heard, or suspect; having seen it, I shall make amends. A second time... [and] a third time:
“Friends, I invite the venerable ones to speak to me regarding what they have seen, heard, or suspect;
out of compassion for me, may the venerable ones speak to me; having seen it, I shall make amends.”
Even a junior [monk] should say: "Venerable sirs, I invite the venerable ones regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
May the venerable ones speak to me out of compassion; seeing it, I shall make amends. A second time...
[and] a third time, venerable sirs, I invite the venerable ones regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected. May the venerable ones speak to me..."
“Venerable sirs, out of compassion for me, please look upon me; I shall make amends. 446.
Regarding two [monks], the senior monk must act; having acted thus, the junior monk should exert himself. 447.
“Friend, I invite the Venerable one regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected; let him speak.”
"Out of compassion for me, may the Venerable One speak to me, whether he has seen, heard, or suspects [an offense]; seeing it, I shall make amends. A second time... and a third time:
"Friend, I invite the Venerable One to speak to me regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected;
may the Venerable One speak to me out of compassion, and seeing it, I shall make amends."
The junior [monk] should also say: "Venerable sir, I invite the Venerable one regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
May the Venerable one speak to me out of compassion; if I see [the fault], I will make amends. A second time...
A third time also, venerable sir, I invite the Venerable one regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected. May the Venerable one speak to me..."
“Out of compassion for the Venerable One, seeing [the fault], I shall make amends.

Having completed the preliminary duties, one who is alone should make this formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*): “Today is my invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), whether on the fourteenth or the fifteenth day;
I make this determination. This applies when five, four, three, or two [monks] are dwelling together.
Having exchanged the invitation (pavāraṇā) with one another,
if they each perform that respective invitation,
there may be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
The remaining verses regarding the Uposatha should be recited here as well.
When the Saṅgha has already performed the invitation (pavāraṇā), the Uposatha of purification (pārisuddhi-uposatha) is held.
One who has completed his rains-residence, or one who has not rained, or one who has not entered [the Saṅgha], may do so.
Even when the Uposatha has been performed by the Saṅgha for the four-month period,
those who have completed their rains-residence may perform the Pavāraṇā, provided they are fewer in number.
46. The Exposition of Restraint (Saṃvara-niddesa):
"Restraint"—this refers to [restraint] regarding the spheres of visible forms, sounds, and so forth, by means of the divisions of the eye, ear, and so on.
One should ward off the arising of covetousness, dejection, and the like.
One should restrain one's own mind as one would a wild beast difficult to subdue with grain and such;
mindful and clearly comprehending, one should conduct oneself in all modes of behavior.
47. The Exposition of Purification Regarding "purification" (suddhi):
it is analyzed according to the divisions of teaching, restraint, wish, and reflection.
Purity is fourfold: that which is recognized as the restraint of the Pātimokkha;
because of its purification through confession, it is called purity of confession.
The restraint consisting of a mental resolve, [thinking], "I shall not do so again," is the purity of the mind.
When it is said "purity of restraint," the restraint of the sense faculties is purified.

For one who has abandoned improper search and procures [livelihood] in accordance with the Dhamma, because of that purity, it is called "purity of search"; thus is what depends on livelihood described.
Having reflected thoroughly, one uses the robe-cloth;
thus, through the purification arising from reflection as previously described,
it is said that "purification by reflection" is dependent upon the requisites.
48. The Exposition of Contentment (Santosaniddesa):
"Contentment" means: one who is content with even a small amount that is blameless and easily obtained.
Knowing moderation and being easy to support, one should live with reverence for the true Dhamma.
Not grieving over the past, nor yearning for the future,
but sustaining oneself with what is present— one is called "contented."
49. The Exposition of the Four Protections:
The four protections are:
recollection of the Buddha, loving-kindness, foulness, and mindfulness of death.

The recollection of the Buddha consists in the repeated mindfulness of the Blessed One’s qualities in nine aspects, such as his being worthy of offerings (*ārahanta*), his perfect attainment of sainthood (*sammāsambuddha*), and his right and personal realization from a Buddha.
"Over the Saṅgha dwelling within the boundary and the deities dwelling within the boundary;
over the people in the village that serves as their alms-resort, and over the humans there—
may all beings be happy, free from enmity, and so forth."
Having delimited [the body] again and again, there is the meditation of loving-kindness.

Having defined the parts, beginning with the head-hairs and so forth, in successive order according to their color, shape, location, direction, and boundaries; [then one should practice] the meditation of loving-kindness.
Neither too fast nor slow, warding off distraction,
having transcended the conceptual designation, as he releases [the mind] in successive order—
therein lies the meditation on color, location, shape, fragrance, and place.
“Repulsive” refers to the bodily parts;
taking the aspect of foulness in the objects such as a bloated corpse and so forth, the meditation that proceeds is called the “foul.
“Death will happen to me; my life will be cut off.”
Having reflected thoroughly: "Death is indeed death," [one sees] that prosperity is like the arrival of an executioner because of its potential for misfortune,
and likewise that the body is shared with many others.
Because of the frailty of life, because of the nature of the determination of time, and because of the delimitation of the duration, there is the development of mindfulness of death. 50.
The Description of Insight.
Vipassanā:
Having discerned name-and-form, and then its condition, [one sees it] as impermanent through its non-existence after having been,
and as oppressed by arising and passing away.
"By applying the three characteristics— suffering, lack of mastery, and non-self—
to conditioned phenomena, and contemplating them again and again,
one shall gradually attain the destruction of all fetters."
Concluding Statement:
Training in higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom constitutes the duty of a bhikkhu;
therefore, it has been set forth in this Minor Training Manual.
For him whose great fame wanders through the world,
no weariness arises at any time, just as there is none for the wind.
By that one who possesses the glory of the Dhamma, the banner of Tambapaṇṇi—
Composed by the Elder and praised by those who know the Dhamma and Vinaya,
this *Khuddaka-sikkhā* has reached its conclusion at this point,
being measured at approximately five hundred stanzas.
The *Khuddasikkhā* is finished.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Ancient Commentary on the *Khuddasikkhā*.
The Introduction to the Composition:
Having long known that people have been suffering for a vast duration of time,
yet still do not awaken to it, [the Buddha] was impelled by compassion.
Having made the aspiration for enlightenment, he attained supreme perfect awakening;
having paid homage at his feet, and having properly honored the Dhamma and the Saṅgha,
he placed his own head at the feet of the ancient teachers.
This concise analysis of the meaning of the *Khuddasikkhā*— composed by the Elder Dhammasiri,
who was firm in virtue, beginning with the words "First,
that which is to be trained in after full ordination," and so forth— is now presented.
For the benefit of beginner monks, I shall write here what is appropriate to be adopted and what is inappropriate to be rejected;
this is the commentary on the introduction to the book.
(Ka) Here it is asked: What is the *Khuddasikkhā*? How is it to be studied? Why is it to be studied? Who studies it?
Who has completed their study? It is said in reply: There are three trainings (*sikkhā*) by way of higher virtue (*adhisīla*), higher mind (*adhicitta*), and higher wisdom (*adhipaññā*).
Because they are stated here in an abbreviated form according to the text (*gantha*), the work that elucidates them is called the "*Khuddasikkhā*. Alternatively, "the minor... [text continues].

Like the terms *anelakaṃ* (free from insects) and *madhupaṭalaṃ* (a mass of honey), they are called the *khuddasikkhā* because they are both minor (*khuddā*) and trainings (*sikkhā*) due to their sweetness for those desiring training;

or alternatively, like the phrase *khuddaputtamhi samaṇa posa maṃ* ("O ascetic, support me, who have a small son"), they are called the *khuddasikkhā* because they are both manifold (*khuddā*) and trainings (*sikkhā*) because they are to be trained in.
Furthermore, the training in higher virtue (*adhisīlasikkhā*) herein consists of the basis of right conduct (*cāritta*) and the basis of restraint (*vāritta*).
One who practices both kinds of virtue as instructed should train by abandoning the defilements opposed to it through their specific abandonment (*tadaṅgappahāna*);

however, the training in higher consciousness should be practiced by applying oneself to the aforementioned objects and effecting the suppression-abandonment (*vikkhambhanappahāna*) of the groups of hindrances that are the opposites of meditative absorption (*jhāna*).
Furthermore, the training in higher wisdom must be practiced by one who, through its appropriate mode of eradication, eliminates the defilements along with their underlying tendencies.

As for the question "Why must it be practiced?", it is because [the world] is afflicted by many sufferings such as birth and so forth: By the various sufferings, such as birth and the rest, It is oppressed in manifold ways.
Having abandoned the world of aggregates, they seek to reach the secure and auspicious city.
Along with the virtuous worldling, the seven trainees (sekha) train; the Arhats have completed their training.
Those who are free from delusion belong to the Bull among Sages;
The sages praised as the foremost among disciples were those who had fully trained in the three trainings;
after them, who else has fully trained?

"From the beginning" (*ādito*) here means "at the very start," or "beginning from the beginning. "Training for one who is ordained" (*upasampannasikkhitabba*) refers to that which must be trained in by one who is ordained and by one who is ordained as a female.

"Together with the matrix" (*samātika*) means together with the *mātikā*. "I shall speak of the Minor Training" (*khuddasikkha*)—which was described in the manner previously mentioned—with care, or I shall speak of it in detail; the meaning is: "having paid homage to the Triple Gem."

Furthermore, by the word "from the beginning," the Elder arouses a sense of urgency in those sons of good family who have gone forth out of faith, but who fail to practice due to the fault of indolence, or who practice wrongly due to the fault of ignorance. How so?
Having obtained the convergence of the opportune moment, which is exceedingly difficult to find, one should not waste that moment through laziness or by being intent on useless talk.
What should be done? From the very beginning, one must continuously cultivate reverence for the three trainings. Here it may be asked:
what is this so-called "Three Jewels" (Ratnattaya), after paying homage to which the Elder will explain the *Khuddasikkhā*?
It is replied: the Buddha-jewel, the Dhamma-jewel, and the Saṅgha-jewel—these are the three jewels. For they are called "jewels" in the sense that they produce joy (*rati*).
“They are called ‘jewels’ (ratana). Furthermore:
‘That which is honored, of great value, incomparable, rare to behold, and used by extraordinary beings—for that reason it is called a jewel.’”
The meaning of the "Jewel" (Ratana) should be understood by means of this verse.
Regarding the commentary on the matrix (Mātikā):
now, because the word "matrix" (*mātikā*) was mentioned [in the previous section], in order to first show that matrix, [the text begins with] "The four *pārājikas*," and so forth.
It has been undertaken. However, because it is the foundation of all trainings, the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) was stated first; for it is said: "Being established in virtue.

Even therein, because they are the most blameworthy and because they function by way of cutting off the root, the offenses involving defeat (*pārājika*) were stated first as those to be known at the very outset.
Now, regarding the matrix headings (*mātikā-padāni*) as they have been set forth:

In order to show [the offenses] by enumerating them in sequence, the first phrase, "The four pārājikas," has been extracted; its meaning is as follows: *pārājikā* means defeated (*parājitā*), having incurred defeat (*parājaya*).
It refers to those who, having transgressed a training rule (*sikkhāpada*), have thereby committed an offense, or it is a designation for those who have been brought to defeat by that [offense].
Furthermore, it is said that "they are four."
1. Explanation of the Exposition of the Pārājika Offenses 1–2.
Now, in order to demonstrate those [offenses], the passage beginning with “in the three ways” is commenced.

Therein, based on humans, non-humans, and animals, there are three types of women, three types of hermaphrodites, three types of eunuchs, and three types of men; these constitute the bases for the pārājika offenses.
The bases for the signs are twelvefold; their paths are three, by way of the anus, the urinary passage, and the mouth.
Among these, there are nine for human females—three each for the anus, the urinary passage, and the mouth—and likewise three each for non-human females and female animals.
Similarly, there are [nine] for human hermaphrodites (*ubhatobyañjanaka*) and so forth. However, for human eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*) and others, they consist of the anus and the mouth.
By taking each pair as two, there are six; likewise for human males and so forth, there are thirty paths in total according to all these categories.

Having encompassed them all, it is stated here as "in the three paths" (*maggattaye*); the meaning is "in that triad of paths. "One who has not laid aside the training" (*anikkhittasikkho*) means one whose training has not been formally renounced according to its characteristics by a mind desiring to fall away from the state of a bhikkhu. "Santhatasanthatā" [means...]
"On anything," such as a cloth or the like, whether it be spread out or not.
"In an uncovered place" means in a location not touched by the natural wind of the three paths. "The sign" refers to the male organ.

"Whether covered or not" means one's own male organ being concealed or unconcealed by any of these things, such as a cloth. "Derived" (upādiṇṇa) refers to the sensitive matter of the body that has been appropriated [by consciousness].
The connection is: "one who enters [the body] in the three aforementioned ways of the path is fallen, having committed a *pārājika* offense.
However, for one who inserts a boil, a piece of scar tissue, a hair, or the like into a body whose sense-faculties have perished, there is an *dukkaṭa* offense.

But regarding the living bodies of human beings, even if only as much as a sesame seed is inserted into wounds made by a knife or other instruments in the eyes, nostrils, ear canals, or the vaginal opening, [it constitutes a *pārājika* offense] through lust for sexual intercourse.
For one who inserts it into the penis, there is a *thullaccaya*; for the rest of the body, such as the armpits and so forth, there is a *dukkaṭa*.

For animals—such as elephants, horses, oxen, camels, pigs, buffaloes, and so on—there is a *thullaccaya* for inserting it into their nostrils, and likewise into their vaginal openings (*vatthikosas*).
For all animals, there is a *dukkaṭa* for inserting it into their eyes, ears, or wounds; likewise...
[This applies] even to their remaining bodies.
Now, "entering" occurs not only through one's own effort, but also through the effort of another, such as an enemy of a bhikkhu;
furthermore, it is to show that in those cases too, if there is a mind of sexual intent, one becomes guilty of a *pārājika* offense.
“Or else,” and so forth, was said. Its meaning is as follows:

whichever bhikkhu consents at the moments of entering, having entered, staying, and withdrawing, and at that moment establishes a mind of sexual intercourse, he too becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense.
However, the bhikkhu who does not consent at all, but regards it as if he had entered the mouth of a venomous snake or a pit of glowing embers, is without fault.
It exists. Here, "situated" refers to its occurrence at the time of the emission of semen.
First. 3–4.
Now, in order to show the second [offense], he says: “should take,” and so forth. Regarding the phrases beginning with “should take,” [the object is] what has not been given...
The connection is with the phrase: “with a thieving mind, he would be one who has committed a *pārājika* offense. “Should take” means:

if a monk, having set his heart upon a monastery or similar property, should seize it, he would be one who has committed a *pārājika* offense; this is the meaning. The same applies to the remaining cases. “Should carry away” means:
while carrying away another’s goods for a wage or out of friendship, if a thieving mind arises again [regarding the act], [the text continues]: “the burden on the head...”
"Touches with a thieving mind"—the meaning is that he would take [it] by means of such [actions].
"Should misappropriate" means that when a person is told, "Give me the goods placed there," he should misappropriate them by saying, "I will not take it," and so forth.
"Should obstruct the posture" means that thinking, "I shall lead him away together with the goods," he blocks the path of that man in order to lead him away by that very same person.

Having intimidated him with another means, he leads him away; for that man leading him in this manner, there is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) when the first foot [has crossed], and a *pārājika* (defeat) upon lifting the second foot.
By the rule beginning with "if one touches property standing on dry land with a thieving mind," he would cause it to be moved from its place.
Or, while passing through a designated spot or a customs checkpoint, he would let the agreed-upon time elapse. Whatever...
“Something not given” (*adinnam*) refers to any property belonging to another, owned by a master, which has not been given by those owners either by body or by speech.
Now, to show that one who steals does not become subject to a defeat (*pārājika*) only in this manner, but also in other ways, the passage beginning with “Alternatively” (*atha vā*) was stated:
“one who steals by theft, one who steals by force, one who steals by deceit, and one who steals by concealment.”
"And one who takes by means of a pretext shall be one who has committed a *pārājika* offense"—this is the connection [of the text].

In this context, "taking by theft" (*theyyāvahāra*) means taking after having deceived [the owner] by means of breaking into walls and so forth, or by means of false weights, false measures, or false balances. "Taking by force" (*pasayhāvahāra*) is taking by means of physical violence.

"Taking by trickery" (*kusāvahāra*) means taking another's portion after having made a deceptive shift [of the goods]. "Taking by concealment" (*paṭicchannāvahāra*) means taking another's property after having concealed it with dust and so forth, while the owners...

The offense of taking what is concealed (*paṭicchannāvahāra*) occurs when one returns and seizes [an item] after others have departed without seeing them. However, the offense of taking by way of supposition (*parikappāvahāra*) is twofold, according to the object (*bhaṇḍa*) and the location (*okāsa*).
In this regard, having made a supposition regarding the object—thinking, "If it is a cloth, I will take it;
if it is thread, I will not take it"—one takes a bag in the darkness. If it is a cloth there, the offense of defeat (*pārājika*) occurs at the very moment of lifting it up.

If it is a thread, he guards it; yet, even though he knows it is "thread," if he takes what has been obtained and learns it while thinking, "I shall take what was acquired," he commits a *pārājika* offense through theft alone—this is the "conceit regarding the object" (*bhaṇḍaparikappa*).
The "conceit regarding the place" (*okāsaparikappa*) involves making a demarcation by way of a room, a door, the front of a dwelling, and so forth, [thinking]:
"If they see me within this interval, I will give it; if they do not see me..."
"I shall take it and go"—if he exceeds that imagined limit, it should be understood that he commits a *pārājika* offense with each step; this is the "imagined space" (*okāsa-parikappa*).

Now, in order to show the method of legal determination (*vinicchaya-naya*) regarding this taking of what is not given, the passage beginning with "the value of the goods, the place, and so forth" was stated.
"Herein" means in the case of taking what is not given. "A decision" means that a formal adjudication (vinicchaya) must be made; this is the sense.

In that regard, if a certain bhikkhu says, "I took such-and-such an article with the intention to steal," the presiding Vinaya master should not immediately charge him with that offense, but should instead investigate whether the owner of that article is present or absent. If it has an owner...

He is to be dealt with according to the offense based on the value of that property. If it was taken at a time when there was no owner present, he is not to be dealt with according to a *pārājika* offense; this is the determination based on the property.
"Time" refers to the time of the theft. For that very same property may sometimes be of great value and sometimes of little value; therefore—
At whatever time it was stolen, one must be dealt with according to the offense based on its value at that time; this is the determination according to time.
"Value" refers to the value of the article.
For the value of a new article decreases later on; therefore, [the value] is always...
The stolen goods (bhaṇḍa) must not be assessed according to their ordinary value; this is the determination based on value.
"Place" (deso) refers to the place of theft. For a stolen good may be of little value at the location where it was situated, yet of great value elsewhere;
therefore, one must be made to pay according to its value in the very place where the goods were stolen. This is the determination based on place.

Even by way of use, the value of goods such as a cloth or the like diminishes; therefore, its state of being diminished or not diminished must be examined by way of use. This is the determination by way of use.
Second.
Now, in order to show the third [method], the passage beginning with "a human being" is commenced. Therein, "a human being" means...

Beginning with the *kalala*-matter that arises together with the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*), the personal existence (*attabhāva*) that gradually reaches maturity until the time of death for a being whose natural lifespan is one hundred and twenty years—this is called the "human form" (*manussaviggaha*);
the meaning is: such a human form. Having willed and intended by means of the volition of a murderer (*vadhakacetanā*), [he says] "I shall kill."
The meaning is: having fully resolved upon it, there is transgression. "Or deprives of life" means:

whoever—whether by means of heating and crushing while [the victim] is still in the stage of *kalala*, or by the administration of medicine, or by any other appropriate means beyond that—should deprive of life a human being of the kind already described, by way of disrupting the continuity (*santati*) of existence, he is one who has fallen away; such is the connection [of the sentence].
Furthermore, it is said: “Or one who carries a weapon,” and so forth. Here, “carrier” (*hāraka*) means that which carries; what does it carry? Life.

Or, it is a “carrier” in the sense of that which is to be carried away, meaning it is to be placed down [as a threat]. Thus, “weapon-carrier” (*satthahāraka*) means that which is both a weapon and a carrier.
“Of him” refers to the person in human form. Just as a person in human form, at whatever moment he desires—
He obtains that weapon, such as a sword; likewise, having himself the intention for death and the purpose of dying, he might place it [near him].
"He too would pass away"—this is the meaning. By this, he shows the method of a stationary application (thāvarappayoga). 6–7.
Now, in order to show the procedure beginning with "or he might praise the beauty of death," [the text says]: "He might provide the means for death..."

It is said: "One might speak of the virtue in death. In this context, one would employ means for the sake of death according to such methods as: "Take up a weapon," or "Eat poison," or "Die by hanging yourself with a rope," and so forth.
Furthermore, the praise of death here is manifold: "One praises it by way of body, or by way of speech, or by way of both body and speech, or by messenger, or by letter."
Because it has been stated thus. In this context, "he praises with the body" means he makes it known by means of the body.

If he praises in such a manner as, "He who dies by throwing himself from a precipice and so forth will obtain wealth, or fame, or go to heaven," there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Having heard his words, if someone [thinks], "I shall die," and experiences suffering...
If she causes a feeling [of pleasure] to arise, it is a *thullaccaya*. If she dies, it is a *pārājika*. The same applies to the remaining cases.
Regarding praise by messenger, however, if she causes the messenger to announce the message, saying, "Announce it thus," or "Whoever dies thus will receive wealth," all is exactly as before.
To "praise by means of a letter" means to write a letter concerning a mountain, a peak, an ancient city, or the like.
“Whoever dies thus,” and so forth, follows the same method already stated. Here too, the connection is:
whoever would grasp at the means of death, or speak of the excellence in dying, he is one who has fallen from his state (*cuto bhava*).
Now, however, in order to show the sixfold application (*payoga*) of this human form, the section beginning with “the applications” is commenced.

The intention is that there are six modes of application for that human form, by way of: (1) by one’s own hand (*sāhatthika*), (2) by relinquishing (*nissaggiya*), (3) by command (*āṇatti*), (4) by magical power (*iddhimaya*), and (5) & (6) by means of science (*vijjāmaya*).
In this context, "by one’s own hand" refers to striking with the body or with something connected to the body when one is killing by oneself.
"By relinquishing" refers to [the act] of one who wishes to kill someone standing at a distance, using the body or other means to discharge arrows, spears, slings, stones, and so forth.
Relinquishment (*nissajjana*). "Commanding" (*āṇattika*) refers to the act of commanding another, saying, "Kill such-and-such a person.
"Permanent" (*thāvara*) refers to digging pits, preparing traps, laying down swords and other weapons, administering poison in ponds and the like, using physical charms (*rūpūpahāra*), and so forth.
"Application of psychic power" (*iddhipayoga*) refers to the employment of success born from the ripening of kamma (*kammavipākajā iddhi*) for the purpose of killing. For the sake of killing...
“Reciting spells for the sake of knowledge is ‘consisting of knowledge’ (vijjāmaya).
Now, in order to show the conventionality and non-conventionality regarding the command within these six applications, he says:
“Time, place, weapon, and posture,” and so forth. Therein, “time” refers both to times such as morning and evening, and to times such as youth and old age. Among these, whatever—
Having fixed a time, if one who is commanded with the words, "Kill him at such-and-such a time," kills him at that very time, there is a *pārājika* offense at the very moment of the command.
If he kills him either before or after the fixed time, the commander is released.
"The object" (*vatthu*) refers to the person to be killed. If, having been commanded, he kills that very person, for the commander there is [an offense] at the very moment of the command.

It is a *pārājika*. If he causes another to kill, the one who gave the order is released. In the same way, the analysis for the remaining cases should be understood according to the method already stated.
"Weapon" means a sword or the like. "Posture" means the walking or sitting of the one to be killed, and so forth.
"Specific action" means piercing, cutting, breaking, impaling on a stake, and so forth. "Opportunity" means...
"Whether it be a village, a forest, or a house," and so forth. In these cases, the offense belongs to the one who gave the order according to exactly how the executioner was commanded;
if it is done otherwise, there is a discrepancy (*visaṅketa*).

However, regarding the command, this distinction—that it is obtained from the textual tradition (*pāḷi*) where it is said, "having resolved (*adhiṭṭhāya*), he commands: 'Pierce thus, strike thus, kill thus'"—should be understood.
The third [section].
8–9. Now, in order to show the fourth, he says: “The classification according to jhāna, etc. Its meaning is as follows:
“Jhāna, liberation, concentration, attainment, knowledge and vision, development of the path, realization of the fruit, abandoning of defilements, and freedom from hindrances.”

If one were to speak of that superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*) which has been described as "delight in an empty dwelling" for the mind—though it does not exist within oneself because it is not present—by saying "it exists in me," or by attributing it to oneself saying "I am manifest here," one would be fallen.
Regarding the phrase "or a portion": here [it refers to] "one who has attained jhāna, one who has attained liberation, one who has attained concentration."
The meaning is that it is told by way of categories (*koṭṭhāsato*) according to such a method as, "I am an attainer of the meditative attainments" (*samāpatti*).
Or, the meaning is that it is told one by one according to such a method as, "I am an attainer of the first jhāna, I am an attainer of the second jhāna.
For one who says, "In a past existence I was a stream-enterer," there is no offense involving defeat (*pārājika*), because it was spoken with reference to a past existence.
Therefore, it is said to be “based on the present existence”; the meaning is that one has made it dependent upon the present existence.
“Devoid of indirect designation” means that it is free from indirect designation in such a manner as: “The monk who dwells in your monastery is an attainer of the first jhāna.
For by speaking in this way, one incurs a grave offense (thullaccaya). “Speaking” means...
The meaning is: he elucidates by way of such expressions as, “I attained the first jhāna; I am attaining it; I have attained it; I am a possessor of the first jhāna;
I am master of it; I have realized it. As for the term “adhigato,” this refers to conceit (māna) or overweening pride (adhimāna);
one who does not possess that is “anadhimānika” (free from overweening pride). If it is asked, “By what means does he elucidate thus?”—in order to show that:
“By body or by speech,” and so forth, was said; the meaning is: either by body, or by speech, or by both. Regarding “in the range of intimation” (*viññattipathe*):
standing where a human being—whether a householder or one gone forth—hears that person’s words with his ordinary ear and immediately understands, “This person is saying such-and-such”;
if one speaks while standing there, one would be fallen (*cuto*).
The meaning is that he has not been known by anyone among the gods, Brahmās, or others.
This is the fourth [section].
Now, in order to state the common determination for all four [offenses], he said, "These four are pārājika," and so forth. In this regard, this is...
In brief: all four of these pārājikas are "non-residents" (asaṃvāsa) because they lack the capacity for the communal life described as "one ritual act, one recitation, and equal training.
Just as previously—both during the time of being a layperson and during the time before full ordination—they were non-residents, so too after having committed a pārājika, they remain non-residents.
Furthermore, they are incapable of the state of a bhikkhu.
Furthermore, the meaning is that because of the lack of a basis for full ordination (*upasampadā*) through that same personal existence (*attabhāva*), they are incapable of being fully ordained.

If one asks, "How so?"—it is like one whose head has been cut off; just as one whose head is severed is incapable of living again through that same personal existence, such is the intention regarding these four.
11. Now, in order to show those instances (*pariyāya*) which arise through indirect instruction (*āṇatti*) among these four *pārājika* offenses, it is said:
“And the instance,” and so forth. In this context, an “instance” refers to either a physical effort or a verbal effort by one who intends death.
Therefore: “Whoever, at such a moment, having brought a weapon or having consumed poison, or having fallen into a ravine and the like...”

If someone, upon hearing [the words] "He will die, he will obtain wealth, or he will obtain fame," and so forth—in this manner rejoicing in death and saying by way of indirect speech, "Whoever hears this, let them die"—should anyone die accordingly as a result of hearing that, it is a *pārājika*.
However, if it was spoken with reference to a specific person, then it is a *pārājika* only upon the death of that very person. This is the instruction (*āṇatti*).

But the meaning has already been stated. In the third [offense], the connection is that it "is obtained" in the *manussaviggaha-pārājika*. In the second, however, the meaning is that in the case of taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*), only a direct command (*āṇatti*) is applicable, not an indirect method (*pariyāya*). Why is it not committed by an indirect method?
Because, whereas in the *manussaviggaha* it is stated, "or one should praise death," so too here in the case of taking what is not given...

“Or he might praise it”—this is because [the word] *saṃvaṇṇeyya* was not stated [in the rule]. “In the remaining cases” means that in the first and fourth methods (*pariyāya*), the two types of instruction (*āṇatti*) are not obtained.

12. Now, in order to show the division of factors (*aṅga-bheda*) as they occur in all four [methods], it is said: “The mind desiring to engage in sexual intercourse,” and so forth. Therein, “of the sexual act” (*methunadhammassa*) refers to the offense of defeat (*pārājika*) regarding the sexual act. “The Awakened Ones” (*budhā*) refers to the masters of the Vinaya (*vinayadhara*).
13. "Human" means belonging to humans. By this, it is indicated that there is no offense in the case of property belonging to ghosts (*petas*) or animals.

"Perceiving it as such" means perceiving it as belonging to another on account of its being human property. "The object is of great value" means that the article is worth five māsakas or more than five māsakas.
"And by 'taking away' (avahāra) means that there is taking away by any one of the twenty-five ways of taking away; this is the meaning. 'By reason of taking what is not given' (adinnādāna-hetu):
the intention is that these five factors constitute the offense of defeat (pārājika) for taking what is not given.
14. 'A living being, human': a living being of the human species. 'The perception of a living being in that living being': the volition to kill, the murderous volition."
“Application” (*payoga*) means one of the six types of application, such as “by one’s own hand,” etc., originating from that [intention].
Death by means of that application. “These five are the causes for killing” means these are the five factors (*aṅga*) for the offense of a *pārājika* involving a human being.
15. “The state of not possessing” means the state of not possessing within oneself the superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussadhamma*). “Proclaiming evil through wrong view” means...
By this, it is indicated that there is no offense for one who speaks solely out of desire for evil, but rather due to dullness and delusion.
"Of him" refers to the person to whom one reports, both in terms of their being human and in terms of using a pretext, such as saying, "The monk living in your monastery is an Arahant.
"At that very time" means knowing at that precise moment.
“Proclaiming what is unreal” means an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*) for announcing superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*).
Now, in order to present [the offenses] by combining them with those included by the word “and” (*ca*) in the phrase “the four defeats and,” it is said:
“The four non-common [offenses],” and so forth. Therein, [the two offenses are: one who touches [a woman] above the knee, and one who conceals a fault.

The *ukkhitānuvattikā* (one who follows one who has been suspended) and the *aṭṭhavatthukā* (one who commits eight offenses)— these four are called the rules for bhikkhunīs that are not shared with bhikkhus.
Among these, the offense called *ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalikā* refers to a woman who, being lustful due to passion for physical contact, with that very same lust,
touches a lustful human male with any part of her body below the collarbones, above the knees, and above the ankles.

"To consent to touching and so forth" is a designation for that [offense]. Furthermore, a bhikkhunī who knowingly conceals a fault classified as a *pārājika* offense committed by another bhikkhunī is called a "concealer of faults.
Moreover, a bhikkhunī who follows a bhikkhu who has been suspended by a unanimous Saṅgha by adopting the same view as his is [called one who] "follows along with the adoption of that view."
She is called one who follows after one who has been suspended (*ukkhitānuvattikā*).

However, she who—being moistened by lust for physical contact—consents to the grasping of the hand or the corner of the outer robe of such a man; or who stands within arm’s reach of a man for the purpose of practicing that which is not the true Dhamma, namely physical contact;
or who, standing there, converses with him; [she is also one who follows after one who has been suspended].

One should understand that this is called the "eightfold basis" when she goes to a rendezvous, consents to a man's arrival, enters a concealed place with anyone, or, standing within arm's reach, makes physical contact. Regarding the phrase "eleven incapable persons," these are:
a eunuch, one living in communion by theft, one who has gone over to another sect, and an animal.

The matricide, the patricide, the murderer of an arahant, the defiler of a bhikkhunī, the schismatic of the Saṅgha, the shedder of blood [of a Buddha], and the hermaphrodite—these eleven types of persons are called "incapable" (of ordination). Regarding "a bhikkhunī who has left the order":
when a bhikkhunī, desiring to leave the order, dresses herself in white cloth or even in saffron robes in the manner of a laywoman's dress, at that time...
"One who has fallen into a *pārājika* offense" means that she does not receive re-ordination again, and she is indeed one who has committed a *pārājika*.
"One with a soft back" means one endowed with a back that has been made supple through preparatory treatment. To this extent he is not yet *pārājika*;
rather, it is when, being oppressed by lack of lust (*anabhirati*), he [inserts] his own organ into either his own mouth-path or anus-path.
When he inserts it, he is then defeated (pārājika).
17–18. "Lambi" is said because of the length of the male organ.
He too, when oppressed by lack of lust, inserts his own male organ into his own mouth or anus; at that time, he is defeated. "Taking with the mouth" means:
In this context, the meaning is: he who, oppressed by lust, takes the sexual organ of another who is either asleep or heedless with his own mouth; "right there" means upon the other's sexual organ.
He who, oppressed by lust, seeing the sexual organ of another to be functional, sits upon it with his own anus. This...
The meaning is: he inserts it into his own anus; "he" refers to the one who does so. These four are "conformable to sexual intercourse"—this is the connection. If one asks how?
It is because of the similarity to inserting [a member] into a path, not because of a similarity to the mutual union of two who have attained a state of passion for one another.
"The four who have come here" refers to those who have committed a *pārājika* offense by means of sexual intercourse and so forth.
"Four each"—the meaning is that there are twenty-four *pārājikas* when taken together.

Here it may be asked: "Since the matricide, patricide, and murderer of an *arahant* have fallen into the third *pārājika*, and the violator of a nun (*bhikkhunīdūsaka*), the one who causes schism (*lambī*), and so forth—these four—have already fallen into the first *pārājika*, how can there be twenty-four? This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*).
In this context, there are four types beginning with the matricide who are intended here as those who have not yet received full ordination (*anupasampanna*).

Although the four beginning with Lambī are included under the first *pārājika*, they are mentioned separately because they can exist even for one who has not engaged in sexual intercourse by way of a particular method. This concludes the determination of the *pārājikas*.
The commentary on the exposition of the *pārājika* rules is finished.
2. Commentary on the Exposition of the *Saṅghādisesa* Rules: 19.

Now, in order to explain the *saṅghādisesa* rules, the passage beginning with “heavy, nine,” etc., is commenced. “Heavy” means those offenses involving a formal meeting of the Saṅgha (*saṅghādisesa*).
These are intended here; however, elsewhere, even those involving defeat (*pārājika*) are included.

If one asks why "nine" is stated instead of "thirteen," it is because the first offenses (*paṭhamāpattika*) are mentioned since they must be incurred at the very moment of transgression, whereas the four formal acts entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*)—which require a third admonition—are not mentioned because they are incurred over time due to their dependence on the Saṅgha. In that context, "the desire to discharge [semen]" means:
The meaning is "the desire to emit," as in the case of [terms] such as "shamelessness" (*alajjitā*). However, according to this method, eleven gratifications (*assāda*) have been stated:

the gratification of emission, the gratification of being emitted, the gratification of having emitted, the gratification of sexual intercourse, the gratification of touch, the gratification of scratching, the gratification of seeing, the gratification of sitting, the gratification of speech, worldly affection, and the "forest-clearing" [of passion].
Of these, taking only one—the gratification of emission—...
The remaining [offenses] are excluded.

This determination should be understood by way of the gratification (*assāda*) of those [acts]: the gratification in emission is the gratification in ejaculation. One undertakes an effort toward the sign of the intention for the gratification in ejaculation;
if there is emission, it is a *saṅghādisesa*. If there is no emission, it is a *thullaccaya*. Regarding the gratification in emission...
If he relishes [the emission] while it is occurring through his own natural state, but does not make an effort, there is no offense.

If, while relishing the emission, he makes an effort and causes it to be emitted, it is a *saṅghādisesa* offense. Relishing [the emission] once it has been emitted through one's own natural state is "relishing what is emitted.
Here too, because there is no effort, there is no offense. This applies in all such cases. For one who takes hold of a woman with the intent of sexual intercourse:
There is no offense even if emission occurs; this is the gratification of sexual intercourse. The gratification of touch is twofold: internal and external.

Regarding the internal, if one causes one's own organ to move—either with the thought, "I shall know whether it is hard or soft," or out of a lustful disposition—and emission occurs, there is no offense.
Regarding the gratification of external touch, [if one touches] a woman out of a passion for physical contact...

There is no offense in touching or embracing, or in emitting [semen]. There is no offense even in emitting while scratching, when one is scratching with the pleasure of scratching a mark that is being eaten away by scabies, itch, or the like.
There is no offense even in emitting while gazing, when one gazes intently at a woman in a place where she has no other space.
There is no offense in sitting, when one is sitting in private together with a woman.

There is no offense even if emission occurs. "Vocal delight" (*vācassāda*) means delight in speech. There is no offense even if emission occurs for one who addresses a woman with speech connected to sexual intercourse out of that vocal delight.

There is no offense even if emission occurs for one who performs acts such as embracing out of worldly affection (*gehasitapema*), that is, out of affection for mothers and so forth. And regarding "gathering forest flowers" (*vanabhaṅga*):
there is no offense even if emission occurs when gathering flowers and so forth—designated as "gathering forest flowers"—sent by a woman for the purpose of establishing intimacy (*santhava*).
If one touches a gift with the thought, “This was sent to me by such-and-such a person,” there is no offense even if emission occurs through that gratification (*assāda*).

However, it should be understood that among these [cases], an offense occurs only for one who makes an effort based on the gratification of emission, whereas there is no offense when acting through the remaining [motivations]. Regarding “of semen”:
blue, yellow, red, white, the color of buttermilk, the color of water, the color of oil, the color of milk...
"Of whatever color among the ten colors mentioned—such as the color of curd or the color of ghee—the meaning is 'of any white [color]' (sukkassa).

By means of a contrivance (upakkamma): by any one of the four methods stated thus: 'He emits upon an internal form, he emits upon an external form, he emits upon both an internal and external form, or he emits while shaking his hips in the air'—by such a method, in the stiffening of passion..."
"‘He releases [the emission]: he releases during an obstruction of feces, he releases during an obstruction of urine, he releases during an obstruction of wind,
he releases during an obstruction caused by being bitten by a high-lying insect’— when, among these five times thus mentioned,
at any one time the male organ has become functional, [one does so] for the sake of health, for the sake of pleasure, or for the sake of medicine."

The meaning is: by means of any one of these ten purposes—namely, for the sake of giving, for the sake of merit, for the sake of sacrifice, for the sake of heaven, for the sake of seed, for the sake of testing, or for the sake of sport—one applies some kind of effort to the hands or other parts [of the animal].
They release [the animal] even if it were only for a tiny fly to drink from it.
The meaning is: "even that much he would emit. "Except in a dream" means: setting aside that emission of semen which occurs in a dream.
"A recluse" (samaṇa) refers to anyone who is fully ordained. "A grave offense" (garuka) refers to a *saṅghādisesa*. "Should incur" (*phuseyya*) means: he would commit [an offense].
This is the first training rule concerning the emission of semen.
20. Now, in order to explain bodily contact (*kāyasaṃsagga*), the passage beginning with “perceiving it as a woman” (*itthisaññī*) is commenced.

Therein, “perceiving it as a woman” means that even if she is a human woman born on that very day, one must perceive her specifically as a woman. If, however, one is doubtful in that regard, or perceives her as a *paṇḍaka*, a male, or a non-human animal, there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*).
Likewise [there is a grave offense] for touching a woman’s body with one’s own body, or for touching what is connected to her body with what is connected to one’s own body.

In the case of female *yakkhas*, female spirits (*petīs*), and *paṇḍakas*, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for physical contact with their bodies and for touching them with one's own body.

However, in the case of human females and female animals, there is an offense of wrong-doing even for physical contact with their bodies and for touching them with one's own body; likewise for *yakkhīs* and others, there is an offense for contact with the body, with what is attached to the body, and so forth.

But in the case of a deceased female, it is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*). By the phrase "with lust for bodily contact," [the text] excludes maternal affection and the like, as well as the intention for liberation.
He rejects [the charge]. "Touching" means: having approached with a lust for bodily contact, he touches a human woman even by so much as a hair;
this is the connection of the meaning. By this, it is shown that there is no offense for one who, though embraced by a woman, does not exert himself with the body but merely experiences the touch.
The second training rule on physical contact.
21. Now, in order to explain "indecent speech," the passage beginning with "they hear in such a way" is commenced.

Therein, "in such a way" means perceiving her as a woman. The connection is "hearing a human woman. By the word "hearing," even in the case of a woman who is capable [of understanding], [the offense is established].

It is indicated that for one who makes an announcement by means of a messenger or a letter to a woman standing where she cannot be made understood through gestures, there is no offense of wicked speech (*duṭṭhullavācā*).

By the word "and a wise person" (*viññuñca*), it is shown that here one who is elderly, foolish, or mute, and who does not understand discourse connected with the unrighteous practice (*asaddhamma*), is not intended. This is by way of the urinary passage and the anal passage.
The connection is: "with reference to a path or sexual intercourse. "Lust for indecent speech" (*duṭṭhullavācārāgo*) means lust for indecent speech;
by that lust for indecent speech. The meaning is: relishing it, having made a disclosure and spoken ill words, one incurs a grave offense.
How does one praise or disparage with reference to two paths? In that regard, first, even regarding praise: "by the characteristic of a woman..."
If he says, "You are endowed with auspicious female characteristics," it does not yet constitute an offense.

If he says, "Your anus and urinary tract are beautiful, well-formed, and pleasing to look at; you are endowed with such auspicious female characteristics," it constitutes an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*).
However, in the case of censure, if he says, "You are a *sikharaṇī* (a woman who has borne many children), you are a *sambhinnā* (a woman whose organs are deformed)... [the rule applies].

The three [terms] beginning with "ubhatobyañjanāsī" (you are a hermaphrodite) alone head the list as pure cases, because the terms for the anus and the urinary tract are fixed and because they are extremely grave.

Other terms, however—such as "animittāsi" (you are without marks) and "nimittamattāsī" (you are merely marked)—head the list only when stated in connection with sexual intercourse, because the terms for the tracts are not fixed. In those connected with sexual intercourse...

However, it does not constitute an offense with respect to the head [of the penis] through such phrases as “give it to me” or “you ought to give it to me. Only when connected with sexual intercourse (*methunadhamma*)—such as by saying “give me sexual intercourse”—does it become a *saṅghādisesa*.
In the case of speaking in praise or the like while pointing to a woman’s anus or vagina, excluding the area from below the collarbone up to above the kneecaps, it is a *thullaccaya*;
likewise for a female *yakkha*, a female *petī*, or a hermaphrodite (*paṇḍaka*). Regarding the anus or vagina...

And in sexual intercourse as well. However, for these [offenders], such as female spirits (*yakkhī*) and others, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) if the act occurs in the aforementioned locations, such as below the collarbone;
likewise, for women and others, if it occurs above the collarbone, below the kneecaps, or on a part of the body attached to the person.
This is the third training rule concerning indecent speech.
22. Now, in order to show the service of one who desires oneself (*attakāmapāricariyā*), the passage beginning with “having spoken” (*vatvā*) is stated.

Therein, “having spoken” means having spoken to a woman—perceiving her as a woman—in the manner described for the offense of *duṭṭhulla*. Regarding the phrase “the praise of service for one’s own desire” (*attakāmupaṭṭhānavaṇṇa*):

here, “service for desire” (*kāmupaṭṭhāna*) refers to service characterized by the desire known as sexual intercourse; thus, it is “service for desire for one’s own sake. (*Attano atthāya kāmupaṭṭhānaṃ*)

“Attakāmupaṭṭhānaṃ” means service performed for one’s own desire; “attakāmaṃ” means that which is desired or wished for by oneself, the sense being that it is sought after by oneself through lust for sexual intercourse.
“Attakāmupaṭṭhānaṃ” is the compound of that which is for one’s own desire and that which is service.
“Attakāmupaṭṭhānavaṇṇo” is the praise of that service performed for one’s own desire. “This, sister, is the foremost of services... [and so on].
The connection is: “Having spoken thus: ‘One should attend upon one such as me—one who is virtuous, of beautiful character, and living the holy life—by means of this practice.
By the phrase “those with lust for sexual intercourse,” it is indicated that there is no offense for one who praises attendance by means of requisites such as those for the sick.
Regarding the phrase “with speech joined to sexual intercourse,” here it refers to the requesting of sexual intercourse with speech that is indeed joined to sexual intercourse.
The intention is that it is grave, not otherwise.
The fourth training rule concerning service according to one's own desire is concluded. 23.
Now, in order to demonstrate matchmaking (*sañcaritta*), the passage beginning with "having accepted" (*paṭiggahetvā*) is commenced. Therein, "having accepted" means:

The meaning is: having been told by a woman, a man, or both their mothers and so forth, "Venerable sir, please speak thus to such-and-such a woman or man," one makes a vocal utterance in any manner whatsoever—such as saying "Very well," "So be it," or "I shall say it"—or accepts [the message] by nodding the head and so forth. This refers to a "message" (*sandesa*).

In this context, however, there are ten kinds of women: one protected by her mother, one protected by her father, one protected by both parents, one protected by her brother, one protected by her sister, one protected by her relatives, one protected by her clan, one protected by her virtue, one who has guardians, and one who is subject to legal penalty.

There are ten kinds of wives: one bought with wealth, one who lives according to her own will, one who lives for her property, one who lives for her clothes, one who is like water in a bowl, and one whose head-covering has been removed.
A female slave who is a wife, a hired servant who is a wife, one captured under a banner, and a momentary wife.
Among these, if a woman protected by her mother sends a message to a monk, saying: "Go, venerable sir, and say to so-and-so:
'I am the wife of so-and-so, bought with wealth... [and so on] ...even a momentary wife,'" this is what is called a woman's message. If, by that woman protected by her mother...
If a mother, father, brother, sister, or others send a monk, saying, "Go, venerable sir, and say to so-and-so:
'Let her be the wife of so-and-so, purchased for a price... [and so on]... even a momentary wife,'" this too is indeed a message from a woman.
The same method should be applied to those protected by their father and so forth. A man sends a monk, saying, "Go, venerable sir..."

"Speak to so-and-so, who is protected by her mother... [and so on] ... speak to her as one who is under threat of punishment, saying: 'May she indeed become the wife of so-and-so, purchased with wealth...
[and so on] ... even for a single moment'—this is what is called a man's message. If the man's mother, father, brother, sister, or others send a monk, saying:
'Go, venerable sir, speak to so-and-so, who is protected by her mother... [and so on] ... speak to her as one who is under threat of punishment'..."
"Speak thus: 'Let her be the wife of such-and-such a man, bought for wealth... [and so on] ...even for a moment'—this too is indeed called a message from a man;
the meaning is that it is an order. Regarding the word 'having investigated':
having received the message in the manner described here, [he approaches] that woman or that man."
The meaning is: having informed those who must be informed, such as one’s mother, father, brother, sister, and so forth. They carry [the message] to wherever they have been dispatched;
having gone there, they inform that woman or man.
Whether that woman or man accepts it, saying “Very well,” or does not, or remains silent out of modesty—it is the same. Having returned, [they inform] that woman...
The connection is that one who steals [it] from a woman or a man incurs a grave offense (*garuka*).
Up to this point, the three factors mentioned—“accepts,” “examines,” and “brings back”—are fulfilled. By the fulfillment of these three factors, there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense;

for any two of these factors, there is a serious offense (*thullaccaya*); and for one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). This applies even in the case of *yakkhis*, *itthis*, or *paṇḍakas*.
[If it is] from one [person], it is a *thullaccaya*; if from two [persons], it is a *dukkaṭa*.
This concludes the fifth training rule concerning matchmaking (*sañcaritta*).

Now, in order to reveal the training rule concerning the building of a hut (*kuṭikāra*), the passage beginning with "requisites requested together" (*saṃyācitaparikkhāra*) is commenced. In this regard:

The summary of the meaning: "Saṃyācitaparikkhāra" (requisites obtained by requesting) refers to requisites taken up through a request personally initiated by oneself, such as saying, "Give me an axe," or "Give me a hatchet.

Having requested the Saṅgha three times according to the method stated in the word-commentary, one should go there with either the monks who have received them or with the Saṅgha itself, and having ascertained whether the site is contentious or non-contentious, and whether it has a surrounding space or not, [one may proceed].
A hut whose site has not been formally authorized (*adesitavatthuka*) is a hut defined by the characteristics stated thus:
"A hut is one that is plastered inside, or plastered outside, or plastered both inside and outside. It is one that exceeds the dimensions stated thus:

"In this regard, the measure is twelve *vidatthi*s in length according to the Sugata’s *vidatthi*, and seven spans across. It is one that [is claimed] as "this is my dwelling place," thus [appropriated] by oneself.

"Designation for oneself" (*attuddesa*) means that which has oneself as its designation; the connection is: "having made that designation for oneself, one incurs a *saṅghādisesa* offense that is heavy.

Herein, this is the analysis: [the ground] has not been designated for others, it exceeds the proper measure, it involves injury (*sārambha*) because it was built upon the dwelling place of ants, termites, and so forth, and it is such that one cannot travel by cart yoked to two oxen.

When one builds or causes to be built for oneself a hut that lacks an open space and is constructed with plastered walls and so forth, there is a *thullaccaya* at the first offering of alms-food with the thought, "It will now be finished.

With the second offering of alms-food, when the plaster has been applied, there are two *saṅghādisesas* and two *dukkaṭas*. This applies whether the hut has already had its site designated or whether it merely exceeds the prescribed dimensions.
...or there is one *saṅghādisesa* offense and two *dukkaṭa* offenses.
This concludes the sixth training rule, on building a hut (*kuṭikāra-sikkhāpada*).
Now, in order to show the training rule on building a dwelling (*vihārakāra-sikkhāpada*), the passage beginning with "large" (*mahallaka*) is commenced. Therein, "large" (*mahallaka*) means...
It is "large" because it possesses a great size due to being built by means of begging from those who have owners;

or, because it is permissible to build even by exceeding the prescribed measurements after having had the site designated, it is "large" by virtue of its large dimensions. The meaning is: "having built that large vihāra.
In this context, however, one *saṅghādisesa* offense arises through the state of the site not having been designated; the rest [is as previously explained].

It is exactly the same as the preceding case. However, there is no offense for one who builds in this manner, thinking: "In this place or that place, setting aside the dwelling quarters, there will be an Uposatha hall, or a sauna, or a fire-hall," and so forth.
This is the seventh training rule concerning the construction of a monastery.
26. Now, in order to explain the training rule concerning groundless charges, the passage beginning with “by what is groundless” (*amūlakena*) is commenced.
Therein, “groundless” (*amūlaka*) refers to that which has not been seen, heard, or suspected regarding the person being accused by the accuser;
this is called “groundless” because it lacks the grounds (*mūla*) consisting of seeing, hearing, and suspecting. The connection is: “by that groundless matter. Therein, “not seen” (*adiṭṭha*) means:
"Not seen" means not seen by one's own eye of faith (*pasādacakkhu*) or by the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*). "Not heard" means likewise not heard when it was being spoken by someone.
"Not suspected" means not suspected by the mind; that, moreover, is threefold according to what has been seen, heard, or sensed.
In this regard, having seen both a monk and a woman in such a place, [one thinks]: "Surely this was done by these two."
Or if one suspects, "They will do so," this is called suspicion based on what has been seen.

Having heard the conversation of a monk and a woman in the dark or in a concealed place, if one suspects—without knowing whether a second person is present—in the manner previously described, this is called suspicion based on what has been heard. [In cases where] with rogues and women in border regions...
Having experienced the fragrance of flowers, scents, wine, and so forth, and seeing the place where they have gone, one investigates, thinking, "By whom was this made?

If a certain monk there has performed an offering with scents and the like, or has drunk *ariṭṭha* as medicine, he smells that scent and suspects, "This must be it. This is suspicion regarding what has been excreted (*muta-parisaṅkita*).
"By name. The meaning is: "not suspected" because of the absence of the threefold suspicion mentioned above.
"Charging" means charging oneself with such words as, "You have committed an offense entailing defeat; you are no longer a samaṇa; you are no longer a son of the Sakyan," and so forth.
For one who charges [another] in this way, there is a *saṅghādisesa* for every single word. "Or causing to be charged" means...
The meaning is that by standing near him oneself and instructing another bhikkhu to charge him, one incurs a grave offense for every word spoken by that instructed person.

Then, if that other person also charges him with the intention of causing him to leave the Order, saying "I have also seen it," and so forth, there is an offense for both of their words. And "by the last [of the] grounds" refers to those grounds appropriate for a bhikkhu...
"By any one of the nineteen *pārājika* offenses" is the meaning. "To cause to fall away" means to cause [the person] to fall away from the holy life (*brahmacariya*).

The intention is that if one who holds a pure view toward a person—whether that person has been ordained legitimately or illegitimately—accuses them or causes them to be accused with the intent of causing them to fall away, for him there is an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*).
By the word "while hearing," [it is indicated that this applies even] when [the accusation is made] by messenger in the absence of the person.
Or he accuses him with a leaf [of a tree]. It is thus shown that for one who accuses in this manner, the charge does not hold.
However, for one who speaks in the absence of the person regarding the seven classes of offenses, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
This is the eighth training rule concerning groundless charges.
27. Now, in order to show the training rule concerning another (*aññabhāgiya-sikkhāpada*), he said: “the action of another,” and so forth.
Therein, “having seen the action of another” means having seen the action—consisting of the transgression of a *pārājika* offense—of another person belonging to a caste such as a Kṣatriya;

this is the grammatical connection. “By means of that mark (*lesa*)” refers to the ten marks: the mark of birth (*jātileso*), the mark of name (*nāmaleso*), the mark of clan (*gottaleso*), the mark of gender (*liṅgaleso*), and the mark of offense (*āpattilesa*).

The meaning is this: among the ten stains mentioned as "the stain of robes, the stain of alms-food, the stain of preceptors, the stain of teachers, and the stain of lodgings," whichever one is seen in that person, by charging another person with that same stain on account of the final ground (antimavatthu), one incurs a grave offense.
In this context, "another ground" means it is smeared or adhered to.

It is called a "stain" (*leśa*) because it clings slightly by way of mere conventional usage; birth itself is the stain, thus it is "birth-stain" (*jāti-leśa*). This same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
How does one who accuses by means of a stain accuse? Another person of khattiya birth was seen committing an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika-dhamma*) with this accuser;
later, seeing another bhikkhu of khattiya birth who is his own enemy...
Taking that stain of the khattiya caste, one thus accuses him: "I have seen a khattiya committing an offense entailing defeat;
you too, being a khattiya, have fallen into an offense entailing defeat," or "Being such a khattiya and no other, you have fallen into an offense entailing defeat.
In this same way, the stains of name and so forth are also to be understood.
The ninth training rule concerning those belonging to another category.

Having thus shown in detail what was briefly indicated by the phrase “the nine heavy [offenses],” the passage beginning with “if he conceals it, knowing he has committed it” is now stated in order to show the manner of procedure for one who has fallen into these offenses.
This is its summarized meaning: whichever monk—“this... [text continues]... [omitted] ...“this monk.”

Whether by way of the offense, as in “this is such-and-such an offense,” or by way of the matter, as in “this is not permitted for monks”—for as long as a monk knowingly conceals an offense he has committed, he must undergo probation against his will.
“He should practice” means he should dwell having undertaken the *mānatta* (penance). For how many days? Six nights. This is the *mānattavāsa*.
However, it is in the Saṅgha alone, not in a group (gaṇa) nor in an individual (puggala); therefore it is said, "in the Saṅgha.

"Parivuttho" means that he has completed the probation without causing a break in the nights, as it is said: "Upāli, there are three breaks of the night for a monk on probation: living together, living apart, and failure to announce.
In this context, "living together" refers to [living] with a regular (pakatatta) monk.
"Living under one roof" means residing within the same water-dropping area. "Separation" (vippavāsa) means residing without another regular (pakatatta) bhikkhu.
"Failure to inform" (anārocanā) means failing to inform incoming bhikkhus and others. Through any one of these three, there is indeed a breach of the night [of the saṅghādisesa offense].

In this regard, however, one should inform those who have entered the boundary of the precincts (upacāra-sīmā), not those standing outside; even for those standing outside, [one must inform them if they are within earshot].
If he hears or sees [the danger], he must certainly report it even after traveling a long distance;

for one who fails to report it, there is both a breach of the night-period and an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for violating the duty. If they enter and travel within the boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīma*) while he is still unaware, there is only a breach of the night-period, but no violation of the duty.

“Having practiced the *mānatta*”: this means that the *mānatta* has been completed by practicing it without having incurred the interruption of the nights (*ratticcheda*) as described thus: “Upāli, there are four interruptions of the night for a monk undertaking the *mānatta*:
living together, being away from the community, failing to announce [his status], and wandering in a group smaller than the required number.
Herein, “living together” and the other terms are of the same nature as those explained in the section on probation (*parivāsa*).
Regarding the phrase "walking in a deficient group" (*ūne gaṇe caraṇaṃ*), here a "group" (*gaṇa*) consists of four or more bhikkhus;
therefore, even if one dwells with only three bhikkhus, there is indeed a breach of the night (*ratticcheda*).
However, it is said in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) that "if they depart after he has informed them of his presence and they have seen him, there is no fault in walking in a deficient group."

"Let them rehabilitate him" means that a Saṅgha consisting of a group of twenty monks should rehabilitate—that is, accept—that monk and restore him by means of the act of rehabilitation (*abbhāna-kamma*). If a Saṅgha of monks consisting of a group of twenty minus even one should rehabilitate that monk, he is not rehabilitated;
those monks are blameworthy and incur an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); such is the meaning.
29. Now, in order to show the manner in which a concealed offense becomes "concealed," the passage beginning with "an offense" (*āpatti*) was stated.

Herein, this is the construction of the words: "offense-ness" (*āpattitā*), "not being suspended" (*anukkhittatā*), "absence of obstacles" (*anantarāyatā*), and "plurality" (*pahuttatā*)—these are "offense, non-suspension, absence of obstacles, and plurality.
Regarding these four, there is the perception of them as such, and the act of concealing while desiring to conceal; thus, by means of these ten factors at the breaking of dawn...

Regarding the phrase "it is concealed": here, however, one should take eight factors by way of perception (*saññā*), namely: the perception of it as an offense among the four [factors] beginning with the offense;
the perception of it as not having been suspended; the perception of it as being without obstacle; and the perception of its abundance.
Then, "desiring to conceal" is one [factor], and "concealing" is another—thus there are ten.
Now, regarding these [cases], the analysis starting from the beginning is as follows: "There is an offense, and one perceives it as such.

Herein, whatever offense has been committed is one of the thirteen; and if one, perceiving it specifically as a grave offense and knowing it to be so, conceals it, then it is concealed. If, however, one perceives it as no offense, or perceives it as another offense, or is in doubt...
It is either concealed or unconcealed. Furthermore, there are three kinds of acts of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*); one who has not been subjected to such an act is "not suspended.
If he conceals [the offense] while perceiving himself as a regular monk (*pakatatta*), it is concealed. If he conceals it while perceiving himself as not a regular monk, it is unconcealed.
However, when concealed by one who is not a regular monk—whether that person perceives him as a regular monk or perceives him as not a regular monk—it is indeed unconcealed.

"It happens" means: "one who is free from obstacles" refers to one for whom not even a single obstacle among the ten—namely, kings, thieves, fire, water, humans, non-humans, wild beasts, snakes, threats to life, or obstacles to the holy life—exists.
If such a person, perceiving himself as being free from obstacles, conceals [an offense], it is concealed.
If he is afraid of the dark and, despite there being no obstacles, conceals it while perceiving wild beasts and the like as obstacles, it is indeed unconcealed. "Able" refers to one who is capable.
If one goes near a bhikkhu who belongs to the same community and informs him, and that bhikkhu, being capable, conceals it, then it is concealed.

But if one who is incapable conceals it while thinking he is capable, or if one who is capable conceals it while thinking he is incapable, then it remains unconcealed. Regarding the phrase "at the rising of the dawn":
here, whether one has fallen into an offense before the meal or after the meal, [the concealment lasts] until the dawn.
It should be announced as long as [the dawn] has not yet risen. However, even if the desire to conceal it arises a hundred times within the interval before dawn, it remains unconcealed.
Furthermore, when announcing, it is not permitted to announce that one has committed a *saṅghādisesa* offense of the same class.
If one does announce it, the offense is indeed disclosed; however, by reason of the act of announcing, another offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) arises.

He commits an offense. By this, it is indicated that it is not permissible for him to report any other offense belonging to the same class as the basis [of the first]. However, when reporting, he should say:
"I disclose one offense in your presence," or "I declare it," or "I report it," or "Know that I have committed one offense," or "I disclose one grave offense."
Or it should be stated in such a manner as "I am doing [it]," and so forth; up to this point, it remains unconcealed.
If one says, "I confess a light offense," then it is indeed concealed. This concludes the determination of the *saṅghādisesa* offenses.
The commentary on the exposition of the *saṅghādisesa* is finished.
3. Explanation of the Description of Robes (Cīvaraniddesavaṇṇanā) 30.
Having thus shown the manner in which one must train in what is weighty, [the author] now mentions "robe" (cīvara) in order to show it among the requisites.
Therein, there are six types of robes by way of origin; if one asks what those are, this passage beginning with "linen" (khoma) is commenced to show them. Therein:
*Khoma* means cloth made from *khoma* fibers. *Sāṇa* means cloth made from *sāṇa* fibers.
*Bhaṅga* means cloth made by mixing five types of materials, such as *khoma* thread and so forth;
some say it refers specifically to cloth made of wool alone. *Kambala* means cloth woven from fibers, excluding human hair and animal hair.

“Cloth. “These six” means these six. “Together with the conforming [materials]” means including the conforming ones. By way of their origin, however, it is said that there are six allowable robes. 31.
Now, in order to show the conforming materials for those [robes], “Dukūla,” etc., is stated. Therein, *dukūla* is [a type of] hemp (*sāṇa*).
*Anuloma* means made from animal hair. *Paṭṭuṇṇa* refers to cloth produced by insects in the region of Paṭṭuṇṇa. *Somāraja* and *cīnaja* refer to cloth produced in the regions of Somāra and Cīna;
these are the cloths [mentioned]. The connection is that these three are also *anuloma* to silk (*koseyya*), because they are made from threads produced by insects.
*Iddhija* refers to robes produced through the power of merit (*puññiddhi*) of those who have "come as monks" (*ehibhikkhu*).
