That, moreover, is made from one of the materials such as linen (*khoma*) and so forth.
That which is produced by *kappa*-trees—such as the cloth given to the Elder Anuruddha by the celestial maiden Jālinī—is "given by the gods" (*devadinnam*).

Because it resembles cloth produced from linen and other materials, it is likewise suitable for all six types of robes; this should be understood to apply equally to that produced by supernormal power (*iddhi*). Regarding that:
“Of that” means of the linen cloth and so forth. “Suitable” means appropriate.

Having thus shown the six types of robes along with their origins, [the text] now states “the three robes,” etc., in order to show the procedure for them, beginning with the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
Here, prior to the formal determination, what is called the “three robes” is distinct.
Because it has been permitted that one who possesses enough cloth for a *saṅghāṭi* and so forth may resolve upon it even as a *paccattharaṇa* (bedspread) and the like.

Therefore, regarding the statement, "One should resolve upon the triple robe, but not dispose of it," the intention is that when the name is taken thus, "This is a *saṅghāṭi*," one should say only "I resolve upon it" (*adhiṭṭhāmi*), and one should not say "I dispose of it" (*vikappemi*). Thus...

The same applies to the others as well. "Face-cloth and sitting-cloth" means a face-cloth and a sitting-cloth; the connection is that one should determine it as a "kaṇḍucchādi" (an itch-covering cloth), and not as a "vikappa" (an extra cloth).
"In this" means among these nine robes. "The triple robe" refers to a triple robe determined according to the method of determining the triple robe.
Without [the formal] agreement, a monk who has not obtained the agreement for non-separation [from his robes] is in a place where he has not obtained the status of being in non-separation.
The meaning is: "One should not live even for a single day having abandoned the reach of one's hand. Because it is stated in the *Khuddakakkhandhaka*:

"Monks, one must not live apart from one's sitting mat (*nisīdana*) for four months; whoever should live apart [from it], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," the meaning is that one should not live for four months without one's sitting mat.
34. Now, in order to show the procedure for formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna-vidhi*), it is said:

“This outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*)... and so forth. Therein, “one should determine with the formula *iti adhiṭṭhaye*”: the meaning is that one determines the outer robe by saying, “I determine this outer robe.
Regarding “not beyond the range of the hand (*ahatthapāsametan*)”: having observed a place set aside even if it is situated at a distance, if there is only one [robe], one says “this (*etan*)”;...
The connection of meaning is that after saying "these many," one should resolve them. This same method applies to the others as well;

just as it was said, "I resolve this outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*)," so too, having spoken by means of its own name—saying, "I resolve this upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*)," "I resolve this itch-covering cloth (*kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi*)"—it is stated that one should resolve it according to the aforementioned method, whether in the presence [of the robes] or out of sight.
35. Now, if among these six robes— namely, the three robes previously determined, the sitting mat, the rain-cloak, and the itch-covering cloth—
one of these robes already exists, and one wishes to determine and carry another such robe,
then because it is stated that "two [extra robes] are not permitted," one must first relinquish the robe previously determined.
The phrase beginning with “one who resolves” is stated in order to show that [the bowl] must be resolved upon; that is self-evident.
Regarding the resolution for the bowl, the distinction lies merely in the name, such as “this bowl” or “that bowl”; the rest is exactly the same—this is the meaning. 36.
As for the expression “he spreads this or that outer robe (saṅghāṭi)”: if it is located inside the inner chamber or in a neighboring vihāra, [then...]
Having observed the place where it was laid down, one should utter the words: “I resolve upon this outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*).
If it is within arm’s reach, the meaning is that the words should be uttered according to the specific names of each [robe], saying:

“This outer robe. This same method applies to the act of relinquishing (*paccuddhāra*) as well. In this context, however, there are two ways of resolving upon a robe: one resolves by means of the body, or...

Because it is stated, "or he resolves by means of speech," one must resolve with the body by grasping the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) and so forth with the hand, making a mental application (*ābhoga*) in the manner of "I resolve this outer robe," and then performing a bodily movement;
it is not permissible for one who does not touch [the object] with any part of the body. For one resolving by means of speech, there must be a vocal utterance.
One must make a formal resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) after having [measured] it. The same applies to the bowl. *Vidū* means "wise.
Now, in order to show the measurement and limits for these, it is said: "The outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) by its lower edge," and so forth.
Therein, starting from five fist-lengths in length, this is the measure of the Sugata’s Sugata-cloak: [The text continues with the specific measurements.]
It is also permissible [to make a robe] of the size of the Sugata’s robe as described thus: "nine spans long by the Sugata’s span, and six spans wide.
However, it must be three fist-widths wide. By the word "and" (ca), the meaning is that even more than this is permissible.
To show that this same measurement applies to the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) as well, it is said: "The same for the one-shoulder robe (ekaṃsika) also. As for the inner robe (antaravāsaka), however—
Because of the commentary’s statement, “Indeed, it is possible to cover the navel even by wearing [the robe] over it,” the phrase “or two handspans” was said. 39.

Regarding the phrase “in length for the sitting mat (*nisīdana*): here, “sitting mat” is the name for a requisite similar to a rug (*santhatā*), which is made by spreading it out and cutting it at two places with the aforementioned measurement at one end, and then attaching three fringes (*dasā*).

40. "Itch-covering cloth" (*kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi*) means: for one who has an itch, a pustule, a discharge, scabies, or some other ailment below the navel and above the kneecaps, this robe is permitted for the purpose of covering it. The verses are easy to understand. 41. "Two and a half [robes]" (*aḍḍhateyyāva*):
here the meaning is that more than that is not permitted. 42. "In this regard" (*ettha*):
the meaning is with respect to the robes shown, starting from the outer double-robe (*saṅghāṭi*) up to the rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭikā*).
"Beyond that" means: for one who makes those robes larger than the stated measurement, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) involving cutting;
this is the elliptical remainder of the text. The meaning is that having cut off that excess, one must then confess the *pācittiya* offense. Regarding "bedspreads and face-cloths":
here [the text says], "Monks, I allow as large a bedspread as one desires."
Because it is stated, "to make a bedspread," there is no fixed limit for the measurement of the bedspread.
However, neither a maximum nor a minimum measurement has been stated for the face-cloth (*mukhapuñchanacoḷa*); therefore, that too is without a fixed measure.
Thus it is said, "of whatever size is desired," meaning its size is according to one's wish. [It may be used] until even a single [corner] is washed.
Therefore, two [robes] are both permissible, as another may be required for the purpose of use.
43. "It is not explained": where is it not explained? In the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
Why? Because: "At that time, the monks' triple robe (*ticīvara*) was complete, yet there was a need for water-strainers (*parissāvana*) and bags (*thavikā*)."
They reported this matter to the Blessed One. [The Blessed One said: "I allow you, monks, a requisite-cloth (*parikkhāracoḷaka*).
Because this was spoken for the purpose of including many items such as bowl-bags, water-strainers, and so forth, it is a separate means of storage.
However, since the Blessed One has stated: "Whatever is obtained, having formally determined each of those according to this procedure, then..."
Out of compassion, it was permitted [by the Buddha] saying, "Let them take whatever strainers or other items they require, having prepared them accordingly.

Therefore, it is indeed permissible to take even a bag that has reached the maximum size for a robe—provided it has not yet been formally assigned (vikappanupaga)—or even a cloth strainer, by combining many such items together and saying, "I resolve upon these as robes and requisites. It is likewise appropriate to perform the formal resolution (adhiṭṭhātuṃ).
Therefore it is said, "having spoken thus"; the meaning is, "having spoken [of] 'requisites-cloth'. "Vikappanupaga" means that which is suitable for assignment.
44. "Ahatakappānaṃ" means those that have been washed once. 45.
"Utuddhaṭānaṃ" means those taken out from the weather—that is, after a long period—and those pieces of rags for which the work of making cloth has already been done.

This has been stated. "The rest" refers to the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) and the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*). It is called *paṃsukūla* because it goes toward, or moves into, a state of being loathsome and disgusting like dust;
this is the name for pieces of rags. The meaning is: "in that *paṃsukūla*, according to one's preference. Why? Because [the Buddha said]:
"I allow you, monks, [robes made of] unwashed cloth or those that appear as if unwashed, [or] double-layered..."
Because it has been stated: "The outer robe (saṅghāṭi) should be made single-layered, the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) single-layered, and the inner robe (antaravāsaka) [single-layered];
for cloths taken from the weather, the outer robe should be fourfold, the upper robe twofold, and the inner robe twofold; for rag-robes (paṃsukūla), as much as required;
for shop-cloths (pāpaṇika), effort must be exerted. Therefore, [this applies] to rag-robes fallen in cemeteries and the like, and to cloth robes (cīvara) consisting of rags fallen in marketplaces.
And it is established that there is no limit to the number of pieces [required for] a robe;

even a hundred pieces are permissible. 46. Now, having said, "Monks, I allow a cut-up outer robe (saṅghāṭi), a cut-up upper robe (uttarāsaṅga), and a cut-up inner robe (antaravāsaka)," at that time, regarding a certain monk's triple-robe (ticīvara) ...
While it was being made, it did not suffice even when all [the cloth] was cut. They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow two pieces that are cut and one that is uncut. It did not suffice with two pieces that were cut and one that was uncut.
“Monks, I allow two pieces that are uncut and one that is cut. One piece that is cut does not suffice.
“I allow you, monks, to add an extra piece as well. But, monks, you must not wear anything entirely uncut;
whoever should so wear it, there is an offense of wrong-doing. To show the rule thus stated, the passage beginning with “In three” is commenced.
Its meaning is as follows: among the three robes, that which is the smallest of all measurements for cutting and sewing—
If it is sufficient, that [extra] must be cut away. But if it is not sufficient for all, one may take an additional piece.

In this context, "additional" (*anvādhi*) means that it should be gathered like the wind and placed over the robe in the manner of an outer cloak (*saṅghāṭi*). Some also call it the "incoming cloth" (*āgantuka-patta*).
This, however, is permitted when [the robe] is insufficient; if it is sufficient, it is not allowed.

It must indeed be cut off. "Not taken up" (*anādiṇṇa*) means not formally assigned as an extra robe. "One should not keep it" means that one should not keep it after having performed the formal act of determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) regarding the three robes; this is the intended meaning. 47–8.

Now, in order to show the method of the training rule concerning stored goods (*udosita-sikkhāpada*), the passage beginning with "in a village" (*gāme*) was stated. In this context, however, if there is a village...
In the case of a village belonging to a single king or a lord of a district, it belongs to one family and is enclosed by a wall or similar structure;
having deposited his robe in such a village, he is permitted to stay in whatever place within that village he desires.
If that village is not enclosed, he must stay in the same house where the robe was deposited.
Or, one must not leave the reach of one's hand from all sides of that house.
If that village— such as Vesālī, Kusinārā, and so forth— belongs to various kings or local lords and is surrounded by the aforementioned type of enclosure,
then in such a village, one may stay in whichever house the robe has been deposited.
One should dwell in the vicinity of that house—either in the assembly hall or at the city gate—on the street where that house is located;
one must not depart from the range of hand’s reach of those assembly halls or gates.
If it is unenclosed, one should dwell either in the house where the object was placed or within hand’s reach of it.
It should be understood that dwellings (*nivesana*) and so forth, ending with watchtowers (*hammiya*), are situated outside the boundary of the village.

Otherwise, since they would already be included by the mention of "village" itself, the definition would have to be stated solely on the basis of whether a village consists of a single family or various families, or a single precinct (*ekūpacāra*) or various precincts (*nānūpacāra*).
In the Canon, the meaning is analyzed specifically by way of dwellings and so forth, not by way of the village.
This method has already been stated in the *Udositavinicchaya*.
Regarding the term "dwelling" (*nivesana*): if there is the dwelling of a single family and it is enclosed by a wall, one may deposit the robe within the dwelling and stay within the dwelling.
If it is unenclosed, [one must stay] in whichever room the robe is located.
It has been deposited; one must reside in that [room], or not depart from the reach of the hand of that room.
If it belongs to various families and is enclosed, one must reside in the room where the robe was deposited, or at the common doorway of all, or at the doorway of those specific rooms.
Or one must not leave the reach of hand. If it is unenclosed, one must dwell in the same room where the robe has been placed, or one must not leave the reach of hand.
"Udosi" refers to a hall for goods such as vehicles and the like. "Pāsāda" refers to a long building. "Hammiya" refers to a pavilion with a flat roof.
Furthermore, a boat may be either hauled onto dry land or remain in the ocean.
If the boat belongs to a single family, one must place the robe inside the boat and reside within the boat.
If the boat belongs to various families with separate cabins and separate compartments, one must reside in whichever compartment the robe has been placed; [this applies] to the robe.
Or one must not leave the reach of hand.
An *aṭṭa* is a specific type of dwelling built with thick walls of brick, four or five stories high, for the purpose of repelling rival kings and the like.
A *māḷa* is a square palace encompassed by a single roof. Now, among these, such as the *udosita* and so forth—
The detailed explanation regarding the upper stories and the dwellings should be understood according to the method already stated.
"Dwelling" (*nivesana*), moreover, is a designation for a type of residence not constructed as a multi-storied building (*udosi*) and so forth.
A "park" (*ārāma*) refers to a flower park, a fruit park, and so on. If it is a park belonging to a single family and is enclosed by a wall, then within that park—
Having deposited the robe-cloth, one must dwell within the monastery. If it is unenclosed, one must not go beyond arm’s reach of the robe-cloth.
If it belongs to various families and is enclosed, one must either dwell at the gatehouse or not go beyond arm’s reach of the gatehouse.
If it is unenclosed, one must not go beyond arm’s reach of the robe-cloth.

A "caravan" means either a foot-caravan or a cart-caravan. If it is a caravan belonging to a single family, having deposited the robe in the caravan, one must not leave more than seven *abbhantara*s in front or behind;
one must not leave more than an *abbhantara* from sight. An *abbhantara* is twenty-eight cubits (*hattha*). If one is traveling...
If the caravan is interrupted— either because the carts have broken down or because the oxen have strayed— one must stay in whichever part of the caravan the robe is to be deposited.
If it belongs to various families, having deposited the robe with the caravan,
one must not remain outside the reach of hand's distance from the robe.
The determination regarding fields and threshing floors is exactly like that for a monastery (*ārāma*). "Under a tree" (*dume*) means at the foot of a tree.

If it is the foot of a tree belonging to a single family, one should deposit [the bowl] within the area touched by its shadow at midday—that is, in a place where the shade extends all around and in a spot free from gaps. If, however, it is a tree with sparse branches...
However, if he places it in a spot on the tree touched by the sun, and at the rising of the dawn that monk is not within arm’s reach of it,
or even if his shadow is upon it in another location, it is indeed subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*). If it belongs to a different family,
one must not let go of the robe’s arm’s reach.
However, if one has placed the robe in an open space— such as in forests like the Vindhya jungle, or on islands in the middle of the ocean that are not accessible by fishermen—
one may dwell anywhere within a radius of seven *abbhantara*s from that location.
If the dawn breaks after one has exceeded even a hair’s breadth beyond those seven *abbhantara*s, it constitutes an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).

In this context, although the *mātikā* (table of contents) has been set forth in the *pāḷi* without distinction as “a village with a single precinct (*ekūpacāra*) or with multiple precincts (*nānūpacāra*),” etc.,

the fact that village-settlements, watchtowers, fields, threshing floors, monasteries, and monastic dwellings have either a single precinct or multiple precincts is explained according to whether they are enclosed or unenclosed,
starting with: “A village with a single precinct is one belonging to a single family, whether it is enclosed or unenclosed,” and so forth.

[These] are divided. Without stating it thus for the watchtower, the palace, the hall, the boat, the dwelling, the foot of a tree, and the open air, [the text] proceeds by way of "belonging to a single family" and "belonging to various families," and finally concludes:

"The open air is called a single precinct (*ekūpacāra*); in a forest outside a village, an area extending seven *abbhantara*s all around is a single precinct, and beyond that, it is various precincts (*nānūpacāra*)."

Thus, the state of having a single precinct (*ekūpacāra*) and having various precincts (*nānūpacāra*) has been analyzed. Therefore, among villages and the like, that which is enclosed is a single precinct, while that which is unenclosed is various precincts;
and in the case of watchtowers (*aṭṭa*) and so forth, it should be understood that what belongs to a single family is a single precinct, whereas what belongs to various families is various precincts.
This should be understood according to the method explained in the section on the open air (*ajjhokāsa*).

"Except by agreement of the bhikkhus" means: setting aside that case where, for a sick bhikkhu who is unable to depart taking his robe with him, an agreement not to be separated from it (*avippavāsa-sammuti*) is granted by a formal act consisting of a motion and a second (*ñattidutiyakamma*), there is no offense.
However, for one who has received such agreement, as long as the illness has not subsided, or if another illness arises once the first has subsided, there is indeed no offense.
49. “Monks, I allow you to determine the use of a *kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi* (itch-cloth) for as long as there is an illness, and after that, to assign it [to another].
A *vassikasāṭika* (rainy-season robe) may be determined for the four months of the rains, and after that, it may be assigned.
Because this was said, the meaning is that the *kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi* has the illness as its limit, and the *vassikasāṭika* has the rainy season as its limit.
"Sesā" means that the three robes and so forth are "without limit" by way of time; this is the meaning.

Regarding the triad beginning with the "bed-covering" (paccattharaṇa): whether it has fringe or not, whether it is dyed or undyed, and whether its dimensions are permitted or not permitted—these are all allowable;
this is the meaning. As for the "sitting mat" (nisīdana): the intention is that both a sitting mat that is dyed and one whose dimensions are not permitted are allowable.
However, for bedspreads, requisites, and face-towels, even blue, yellow, red, or those with flower-patterned borders are permitted;
therefore, it is said, "even if they are with borders," and so forth. Such items, however, are not permitted to be worn as an undergarment or as an upper robe;
they are permitted only to be formally designated (adhiṭṭhāna) as bedspreads and the like.

51. Regarding the set of five remaining robes—the three robes (*ticīvara*), the itch-covering cloth (*kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi*), and the rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭikā*)—the meaning is that these are allowable only when dyed, and they must be those whose measurement has been formally determined (*ādinnakappa*).

As for the phrase "the sitting mat with fringes," since it was previously stated [in the rule] "even with fringes," they say this was spoken in order to prevent confusion regarding the fact that a sitting mat without fringes is also permitted.

52. "Not formally resolved upon" (*anadhiṭṭhita*) means not resolved upon by way of the three robes and so forth. "Not relinquished" (*anissaṭṭha*) means not given away to others; the meaning is that it may be used after having been assigned [to another].
Now, in order to show the measurement of what is fit for assignment according to the minimum limit, he said:
"A hand's length," and so forth. Therein, he said: "I allow you, monks, [a cloth] eight finger-breadths in length by the Sugata’s finger, and four finger-breadths in width."
Because it is stated, “one may assign the final robe,” the intention is that it should be assigned as one cubit in length and half a cubit in width. 53.
“Of the triple robe” means the triple robe of the Vinaya, not the triple robe of the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga). Of that [robe], however, among these nine...
Only the three robes are obtained, nothing else is obtained. "All this" means both the procedure for formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and the procedure for wearing them.

"All requisites-cloths" refers to all nine types of robes, beginning with the triple robe (*ticīvara*). "Having spoken thus" means having spoken [of it] as a "requisite-cloth. "He determines" means he performs the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāti*). But what?
"Is it permissible to determine the three robes as requisites-cloth? Yes, it is permissible.
'Requisites-cloth' refers to a separate category of storage; therefore, it is permissible to use the three robes after determining them as requisites-cloth.
However, in the *Udosita-sikkhāpada*, the exemption is stated for one who carries about the three robes after having determined them."
It is stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*): "Therefore, when one is determining the requisite robe-material as the three robes, it must be relinquished and then determined again. 54.
Now, in order to show the manner in which their determination is lost, [the text says]: "By theft, by giving away, by taking back, by departing," and so forth.
It has been stated. In that context, "seizure" (*acchedo*) means being robbed by thieves and others.
"Giving away" (*vissajjanaṃ*) means bestowing it upon others. But how is it that what is given is well-given, and what is taken is well-taken?
If one says, "I give this to you, I bestow it, I grant it, I offer it, I relinquish it, I renounce it, I surrender it," or "I give it to such-and-such a person... [and so forth].
If one says, "I relinquish it," whether in the presence of the recipient or behind their back, it is indeed given.
When told, "Take it for yourself," if one replies, "I take it for myself," it is well-given and well-received.
When told, "Make it yours; let it be yours; you shall make it yours," if one replies, "I make it mine; it is mine..."
If one says, "Let it be; I shall make it my own," it is wrongly given and wrongly received.
But if, when told, "Make it yours," one takes it saying, "Very well, Venerable Sir, I take it," it is rightly received. "I take" means taking with confidence (*vissāsaggāha*).
That, moreover, should be understood thus: "I allow you, monks, [to receive] by means of five factors..."
One who has these qualities may be trusted. He is a person one has seen, with whom one is intimate, with whom one has conversed, who is living, and whom one knows, thinking:
"If I take [something] from him, he will be pleased. In this context, "one who has been seen" means a mere acquaintance.
"Intimate" means a firm friend. "With whom one has conversed" means: "Whatever you wish for that belongs to me, you may take it; having asked permission..."

When told, "There is no reason for taking [it]," [the monk replies: "He is still living," meaning that even though he is lying on his back in a state of non-exertion, he has not yet reached the cessation of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
And "being glad when it is taken" means having a satisfied mind once it has been taken.
It is permissible for one who knows, "He will be glad when my property is taken," to take the belongings of such a person. And these [terms] are used in the sense of exhaustive inclusion.
Five factors have been stated; however, the taking on trust succeeds by means of three factors. How so?

One who is a personal acquaintance lives well and is pleased when the goods are taken; one who is a trusted friend lives well and is pleased when the goods are taken; one who has been addressed [as a friend] lives well and is pleased when the goods are taken—in this way.
But as for one who lives well yet is not pleased when the goods are taken, even if his property is taken on the basis of trust, it is not [validly] taken.
It must be given again. When giving, the deceased’s property should first be given to those—whether householders or renunciants—who have authority over that wealth.

However, if someone has already expressed their approval by means of a verbal utterance or even a mere thought, saying, "You have done well in taking what belonged to me," yet later becomes angry for some reason, he [is not entitled to it].
One is not permitted to ask for it back. Even one who does not wish to give, but accepts it mentally and says nothing, is likewise not permitted to ask for it back.
However, if someone says, "I have taken what belongs to you," or "I have used it," and the other does not accept this but says, "Give it back," then he is permitted to ask for it back.

By the term "one who has left the order" (*vibbhama*), the relinquishing of the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) by a bhikkhunī alone is included. When she leaves the order, she then ceases to be a female renunciant (*assamaṇī*).
However, even when a bhikkhu leaves the order, as long as he has not formally renounced the training (*sikkhā-paccakkhāna*), he remains a bhikkhu;
thus, he does not relinquish his formal determination. "The gender and the training" refers both to the transformation of gender (*liṅga-parivattana*) and to the renunciation of the training.
The meaning is as follows. "In all" refers to the nine types of robes. "Causes for the loss of the formal determination" means causes for the relinquishing of the formal determination;
the sense is that by any one of these, the formal determination is relinquished.
Furthermore, even a rent or hole torn in the three robes causes the relinquishing of the formal determination.

The meaning is as follows. In that regard, if a hole the size of the back of the nail of the little finger occurs within a distance of one span from the long edge and eight finger-breadths from the crosswise edge of the *saṅghāṭi* or *uttarāsaṅga*, it invalidates the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
For the *antaravāsaka*, [the same applies] within a distance of one span from the long edge and four finger-breadths from the crosswise edge.
If a hole occurs within the designated area, it breaks the determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*), but if it occurs beyond that area, it does not break it.
Therefore, once a hole has arisen, the triple robe (*ticīvara*) becomes an extra robe (*atirekacīvara*); after performing the needlework [to mend it], it must be determined again.
However, for the other robes, there is no such thing as "losing" [the status of being a robe] through a hole. Furthermore, regarding the triple robe, if one first applies a patch to a weak spot...
Having given it away, if one later cuts away a weak spot and removes it, the determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is not broken.
The same principle applies when turning over a mandala. However, if one who is making both ends meet in the middle first cuts and afterwards joins them, the determination is lost;
but if one joins them first and then cuts, it is not lost. Having had it washed by dyers, [if it becomes] white...
Even while making it, one does not abandon [the robe].
55. Now, in order to show what are improper robes (*akappiyacīvara*), the passage beginning with "grass, bark, and wooden planks" is commenced.
Therein, a "grass robe" (*kusacīra*) is a robe made by knotting together grass. A "bark robe" (*vākacīra*) is the bark garment (*vakkala*) of ascetics. A "wooden plank robe" (*phalakacīra*)...
A robe made by sewing together pieces of cloth. A hair-blanket (*kesakambala*) is a blanket made by weaving hair into thread.
A yak-tail blanket (*vālakambala*) is a blanket made by weaving yak-tail hairs. An owl-wing garment (*ulūkapakkha*) is a covering made from the wings of an owl bird.
A deerskin rug (*ajinakkhipa*) is the hide of a deer with its fur and hooves intact. Among these seven types of clothing:
The meaning is that for one who wears anything [of such a kind], there is a *thullaccaya* offense.
Just as there is a *thullaccaya* in these cases, so it is for one wearing an *akkanāḷa*. An *akkanāḷa* is a robe made by sewing stalks of grass and the like onto a reed frame.
For it has been said: "Monks, an *akkanāḷa* must not be worn; whoever should wear one, there is an offense of *thullaccaya*."
56. "In *kadaleraka*, *kakkadussa*, and *potthaka* cloth": here it should be understood that garments made from *kadali*, *eraka*, *akkama*, and *cīvaka* are what are thus described.
Among these, only *potthaka* is mentioned in the Canon (*pāḷi*); the others, being of the same category, are excluded in the Commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
For all four of these, there is only an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). [As it says: "Monks, one should not go naked, which is the practice of the heretics."
Because it is stated, “It must be undertaken; whoever should undertake it commits a *thullaccaya* offense,” even nakedness is not permitted.
“All blue” means entirely blue. The same applies to the remaining colors. Here, “blue” is the color of the flax flower (*umāpuṣpa*).
“Madder” is the color of madder itself. “Yellow” is the color of the *kaṇikāra* flower. “Red” is the color of the *jayasumana* flower.
*Kaṇhaka* is the color of black *addāriṭṭhaka*. 57.
*Mahāraṅga* is the color of the back of a hundred-footed centipede. *Mahānāma* is the color of mottled red;
it is also said to be the color of a lotus flower, meaning a pale red. *Tirīṭaka* refers to the bark of a tree. *Acchinnadīghadasaka* refers to a long strip of cloth that has not been cut.
The meaning is: entirely with fringes cut off, and with fringes cut off in the middle. That which has been made by sewing the fringes together is called a "fruit-fringe" (*phaladasa*).
That which is provided with fringes resembling the petals of flowers such as the *ketaka* is called a "flower-fringe" (*pupphadasa*).

Regarding these as well, it should be understood that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) by virtue of the word "also" (*api*) used in the phrase "and also in the case of a book. "In the same way" (*tathā*)...

Just as there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for wearing these items beginning with the *kadalidussa* and ending with those having flower-patterned borders, so too there is an offense of wrong-doing for anyone wearing anything such as bodices (*kañcuka*) or wraps (*veṭhana*).
However, regarding these, the following is the legal determination (*vinicchaya*): all dyes that are entirely blue and so forth must be vomited out [of the cloth], dyed again, and then worn.
If it is not possible to discard it, one should have rugs and such items made, or they should be given as a central patch for a three-fold robe (*tipaṭṭacīvara*).
If the borders and so forth are uncut, the borders should be cut off before wearing it. A tunic (*kañcuka*) should be unraveled, dyed, and then used.
The same rule applies to a turban (*veṭhana*). A *tirīṭaka* cloth should be made into a foot-wiping cloth. "All" means...
The meaning is that one who lacks a robe may obtain this aforementioned unallowable robe, such as one made of grass-cloth and so forth.
This has also been stated in the *Parivāra*:
"That which is not properly prepared, nor dyed with a dye..."
Clad in that, one may go wherever one wishes; there is no offense for him,
and this is the Dhamma taught by the Sugata.
“This question has been thought out by the wise.
This question was indeed spoken with reference to a bhikkhu whose robe had been stolen;
therefore, having put on or wrapped oneself in any kind of unallowable robe, one who is without a robe must seek another. In this context, however: “Here—”
However, monks, when people give robe-cloth to monks who have gone outside the boundary, saying, "We give this robe-cloth to [so-and-so]," I allow you, monks, to accept it;
it does not yet count as received until it has come into their hands.
Because this was said, [the robe] is not considered given until it has been brought and delivered, [only then can one say]: "Venerable sir, a robe-cloth has arisen for you."
If it has been sent but not reported, it does not count until that time; it is permissible as long as it has not been formally determined (*adhiṭṭhita*). The same principle applies to a bowl.
Once it has been brought back and given, or once it has been reported, there is no exemption; it must be determined within ten days. This concludes the analysis of robes.
The commentary on the description of robes is finished.
4. Explanation of the Description of Dyes (Rajananiddesavaṇṇanā) 58.
Now, in order to show the method for dyeing those robes, it is said: “And the dyes. Therein, [it continues]:
“I allow you, monks, six kinds of dye: root-dye, trunk-dye, bark-dye, leaf-dye...”
Because it was thus permitted by the Blessed One—saying, "flower-dyes and fruit-dyes"—it is said: "Six kinds were permitted by the Teacher.
59. Therein, *mūle* means "root-dye. The connection is: "all [dyes] are permissible except for turmeric (*haliddi*).
The same applies to the remaining [items]. A certain thorny tree named *tuṅgahāraka* has a trunk-dye the color of a green palm leaf.
[It] exists. However, it is permissible to dye [a robe] once using a sour-gourd leaf that has been used by a householder.
In the case of dyeing with fruit, there is nothing called "unallowable"; everything is permitted.
This concludes the determination regarding dye. The commentary on the description of dye is finished.
5. Commentary on the Description of the Alms Bowl (Pattaniddesavaṇṇanā) 60.
Now, in order to show the variety of vessels, the phrase "and the bowl" (patto ca) is cited. Here, however, the first verse is easy to understand.

61. In the second [verse], although one should have said "cooked with two Magadha-measures of nāḷi of rice," the case ending was not elided for the sake of metrical convenience in the composition of the verse.
"It is said, 'prepared with two *nāḷi* measures of rice from Magadha'; the meaning is that it has been cooked.
Here, a *nāḷi* from Magadha takes up one and a half *pala*. Regarding 'boiled rice' (*odana*), one should understand this as boiled rice of every excellent quality that has been properly drained.
And the amount of mung bean curry, which is neither too thick nor too thin and can be taken by the hand, should be a fourth part of the measure of the rice, [to be taken] as a mouthful."

The meaning is that the bowl which receives curry—such as fish, meat, and so forth—in an amount corresponding to the rice, up to what is sufficient for the final meal, is called "excessive" (*ukkaṭṭha*).
However, ghee, oil, cream, soup, sour gruel, and the like do not count toward the [limit of] portions;
for they belong to the same category as the boiled rice, and one cannot either subtract from or add to them. Thus, all this is [explained].

If, when thrown [into water], it remains level with the lower rim of the bowl, or if, while being cut by a thread or an iron blade, it touches the lower edge of the thread or the iron blade, this is called an "excellent" (ukkaṭṭha) bowl.
If it stands having surpassed that rim and is shaped like a stupa, this is called an "excellent-inferior" (ukkaṭṭhomaka) bowl. If it does not [touch] that rim...
It reaches [the mouth], and it remains entirely contained within; this is called the "superlative-superlative" bowl. 62.
Regarding the statement, "The 'middling' bowl holds a *nāḷika* of rice," it is said that "the middling is half of that.
Here too, according to the manner described, there is a triad of bowls: the middling, the middling-inferior, and the middling-superlative.
It should be understood as follows. Because of the statement, “A ‘small’ bowl (omaka-patta) takes a handful of boiled rice,” it is said to be “half of that.
It takes half a Magadhan *nāḷi* of boiled rice, along with a corresponding amount of curry and condiments;
that is called “small. Here too, the triad of bowls—small, very small, and large-small—should be understood. Now, among these nine...
Among bowls, the most excellent and the most inferior are not permissible as bowls. There is no need for them to be formally determined (*adhiṭṭhātabba*);
the meaning is that the remaining seven bowls must be both determined and assigned (*vikappetabba*).

"An extra bowl" (*atirekapatta*) means one that has not been determined and has not been assigned. "One's own" (*saka*) means belonging to oneself. "Permissible" (*kappa*) means allowable. This is the meaning here.
In brief: a metal bowl is permissible because there is no need to pay even a mere *kākaṇika* coin for it;

and a clay bowl is permissible because it has been fired five times, whereas a clay bowl is fired only twice. Such a bowl may be kept for up to ten days without being formally resolved upon (*anadhiṭṭhita*) or assigned to another (*avikappita*).
64. The types of damage regarding robes are exactly as previously described. Regarding the term "perforated":
here, a bowl is considered broken by a hole such that, from the rim downward at a distance of two finger-breadths, rice-grains can pass through it.
However, once that hole has been repaired with copper filings or other materials so that it is restored to its original state, it must be formally resolved (adhiṭṭhātabba) again within ten days.
"He abandons the resolve regarding the bowl" means he abandons the resolve concerning the bowl. 65.
Now, in order to show the method of carrying it, the passage beginning with "He should not put away the bowl while it still contains water" is commenced.
He should not put away the bowl while it contains water; the intention is that he should not dry the bowl in the sun while it still contains water. He should not hide it [away].
The intention is that even if one has made it waterless, one should not leave it out for too long. "On the ground" means on the earth.

"One does not place it" means one should not place it on anything whatsoever—such as a wooden board, a piece of leather, or the like—for the sake of convenience; rather, the meaning is that one should place it on ground mixed with dust and gravel.
"Nor should one hang it" means that if it is hung anywhere, such as on a peg or similar object, there is likewise an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

"66. At the edge of the itch (*miḍḍhanta*): at the limit of the itch. However, if it turns back and settles right there, it is permissible to define the internal boundary of such an extensive itch, but not its outer limit.
'At the border' (*paribhaṇḍanta*) means the end of a thin layer of itch applied to the outer surface. 'In the lap' (*aṅke vā*) means in the middle between the two thighs."
In this context, however, it is permissible to place food on the shoulder-strap after hanging it from the shoulder-blade, but not otherwise.
Regarding "in the sunshade": this refers to a parasol. Here, it is not permissible to place even a bowl of rice or a leaf hung from the shoulder-blade [inside the sunshade].
67. "Leftover water" means water used for rinsing the mouth; having spat that into the bowl, one should not carry it away with the bowl.

Meaning: "Cartilage" (*calaka*) and "bone" (*aṭṭhi*) together constitute "cartilage-bone" (*calakaṭṭhika*). For one who removes any of these with the bowl, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

One is not even permitted to wash the hand after using the bowl as a receptacle. It is not allowed to pour into the bowl water used for washing the hands or water used for washing clothes and then remove it.
Nor is it allowed to take a bowl that is not soiled by food with a hand that is soiled by food.
It is not permitted. However, it is permissible to take [food] after washing one's hand outside.

When eating fish, meat, fruits, or other such things, if one has been picking them out with the mouth bit by bit, one may not place in the bowl that which was picked from the mouth—whether it be the flesh itself or the bones and so forth—if one no longer desires to eat it and wishes to discard it.
This applies to pieces of ginger, coconut, and the like as well.
While eating, one may bite again and again and then resume [eating]. Because it was said, "Monks, the door must not be pushed with the bowl in hand;

whoever should push it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," one who stands holding the bowl with any part of the body is not permitted to push the door with any part of the body; therefore—
It is said, “or with bowl in hand. It is permissible [for the bowl] to rest upon the shoulder.
68. Regarding “supported by the ground”: here this refers to a ring-support made of ivory, rattan, cord, and so forth. Regarding “supported by a wooden staff”:
the meaning is a support made from a single piece of wood, as well as a support made from many sticks. A tripod (tidaṇḍa) is not permitted.
When these have been properly arranged, it is permissible to place one bowl on top of another, but three are not permitted.

Regarding the phrase "having overturned one upon the ground," one should spread out something such as a mat of straw or similar material on the ground, and then place one bowl either overturned or upright upon it; two should not be placed there.
The intention is that it is permissible. However, they say that when setting down two [bowls], it is permissible to set the bowl placed on top so that it touches the ground on one side.
69–70. Now, in order to show the unallowable bowls, the passage beginning with “wood, silver, gold” is commenced. Therein, “made of gems and beryl” means:
"Jewel" (*maṇi*) refers to [gems] such as sapphire (*indanīla*), emerald (*karakata*), and so forth.

If householders, while in the dining hall, serve curry or condiments using vessels made of gold, silver, or tin, it is not even permissible to touch them. "Made of metal bowls" (*ghaṭikaṭāhaja*) and "made of gourd bowls" (*tumbakaṭāhaja*);
here, "gourd bowl" (*tumbakaṭāhaja*) means a bottle-gourd (*alābu*). This concludes the analysis of the bowl.
The commentary on the description of bowls is finished.
6. Commentary on the Description of Dishes (Thālaka-niddesa). 71–2.
Now, in order to show the rules regarding what is allowable and what is unallowable concerning dishes, the phrase "and dishes" (thālakā ca) is cited.
In this context, "unallowable" (*akappa*) means that bowls made of wood and the like are unallowable.
Bowls made of crystal and the like, whether belonging to a householder or to the Saṅgha, are allowable. Those made of hollowed gourds or wooden troughs are for temporary use;
the intention is that after eating from them, they should be discarded and not kept. This is the determination regarding bowls.
The commentary on the explanation of the *thālaka* is finished.
7. Commentary on the Explanation of the *Pavāraṇā*. 73.
Now, in order to show the procedure for the *pavāraṇā*, the term "pavāraṇā" is extracted. Therein, "by means of posture" (*iriyāpathena*)...
The meaning is: "by means of one of the postures—standing, walking, sitting, or lying down. The meaning is:
if one were to consume what is not left over by means of a posture other than that [specific] posture, it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). Regarding the term *pācittinatirittaka*:
it is an offense of expiation for what is not left over.
74. Now, in order to show those factors by which the *pavāraṇā* (invitation ceremony) takes place, he said, beginning with "eating" (*āsana*).
Therein, "eating" expresses the state of not having finished one's meal; the meaning is that the person is in the act of eating.
And "food indeed" refers to that which one invites [others to eat] while eating—namely, among these: boiled rice, sour gruel, flour, fish, and meat.
The meaning is that it becomes something else. "Bringing forward" (*abhihāra*) means the donor brings that food to him with the body;

however, "bringing forward by speech" is not to be accepted here. "Proximity" (*samīpatā*) means the donor stands within a space measuring two and a half cubits after having taken the food sufficient for an invitation.
"Rejection by body or speech" refers to [the recipient] standing within arm's reach.
The meaning is that one should refuse almsfood brought forward either by body or by speech.
In this context, however, if the bhikkhu is sitting, it is from the edge of his buttocks; if he is standing, it is from the edge of his heels;
if he is lying down, it is from the edge of the side on which he lies—provided the donor is likewise situated.
Setting aside the outstretched hand, the delimitation should be made according to whichever limb is closest to it.

Regarding the phrase "the invitation [is valid] by five factors," the meaning is that the invitation occurs by means of these five factors mentioned in the Canon: "food is discerned, a meal is discerned, one offers while standing within arm's reach, and a refusal is discerned."
75. Now, in order to show the food among these five kinds, the words beginning with “rice” (*odana*) were spoken.

Next, in order to show that rice and the other items are produced from these [grains], he said the words beginning with “śāli. In this context, all varieties of *kaṅgu*—distinguished as white, red, and black—should be understood as *kaṅgu*.
*Kudrūsaka* is black and white. From these seven types of grain, both boiled rice (*odana*) and soft porridge (*bhojjayāgu*) are prepared.
And "odana" means rice; this is the meaning.
*Sāmākā* grass is included within *kudrūsaka*; this is the meaning.
*Varakacoraka* is included within *varaka*, and both *sāli* and *nīvāra* are said to be included within *setatta*. Of these aforementioned types...
If, having taken the rice from seven kinds of grain that are suitable for use, they cook it— whether intending to make rice-gruel (*yāgu*) or boiled rice (*bhatta*),

or whatever else— with the thought, "We shall cook this," and if, when they are eating it either hot or cold, a solid mass (*odhi*) is visible at each place where it has been taken up during the meal,
this is called "boiled rice" (*odana*), and it generates an invitation (*pavāraṇa*). This also applies to milk-rice (*pāyāsa*).
Or sour rice-gruel: as soon as it has been taken down from the stove while still steaming hot, it can be stirred and drunk;
even where it is held, no sediment appears, and thus it does not produce an invitation (*pavāraṇa*). However, when the heat has subsided, it becomes thick and sediment becomes visible;
it then produces an invitation again, for its former thinness is no longer maintained. But in the case of cooked food...
If they pour in water, sour gruel, milk, and so forth, and say, "Take this rice-gruel," even though it is thin,
it still generates an invitation (*pavāraṇā*) because of the absence of [actual] rice-gruel therein. However, if they add [ingredients] to boiled water and the like,
cook it, and then give it, it is included within the category of rice-gruel.
77. *Bhaṭṭhadhaññamayo*: Having taken all seven kinds of grain, one roasts them until they are hard-baked, then grinds their husked rice;
the resulting flour and bran is called *sattu*. However, the flour and bran of rice that has been roasted evenly or dried in the sun does not count as *sattu*.
*Yavasambhavo*: Furthermore, by others... [text continues]

The intention is that one who has made *kummāsa* (sour gruel) from green gram and the like does not perform the *pavāraṇā*. By the term "aquatic creatures," crabs, shrimp, conchs, and so forth are also included.

If, at the time of drinking rice-gruel, they eat fish or meat while keeping it in the same vessel, and if one who did not eat it rejects another portion sufficient for the *pavāraṇā*, he does not perform the *pavāraṇā*. Even if [the fish or meat] has been eaten, if...
If there is nothing remaining in the mouth, then even one who is refusing does not perform the *pavāraṇā*.
If there is something remaining in the bowl but none in the mouth, and if he does not wish to eat it, or wishes to go elsewhere to eat it,
then even while refusing at that moment, he does not perform the *pavāraṇā*.
78. "Food" (*bhojana*) refers to any kind of food among the five types of food. The connection is: "whether it be allowable (*kappiya*) or unallowable (*akappiya*), one eats.

They refuse [the gift] by physically bringing it back, or by moving a finger and so forth, or by a movement of the eyebrows, or by looking with an angry expression, or by physically rejecting it, or by saying "enough," or "I will not take it," or "do not pour it out."
The meaning is that he either rejects by way of such expressions as “Go away,” or he prohibits by means of speech.
He invites when rejecting only permissible food; he does not invite when rejecting unpermissible meat or food.
Why? Because he stands in the position of one who must reject it. If, while eating permissible food...
He rejects what is improper; he does not invite [the donor to choose]. Why? Because it must be rejected by him.
Now, in order to show the method of mixing, it is said: "By that name," and so forth. Herein, this is the summary of the meaning:
one should invite while prohibiting what is proper, whether brought under that name or as "this. What is meant? One who, however, [offers] rice-gruel mixed with fish and meat...
If, having brought a sauce, he says, "Take fish! Take meat! there is an invitation (*pavāraṇā*) for one who refuses it.
If he says, "Take rice-gruel! Take sauce," there is no invitation for one who refuses it. Why?
Because that [rice-gruel] also exists [as part of the meal]. If he says, "Take this," specifying a particular substance...

If one gives [something] and the other rejects it, there is an invitation (*pavāraṇā*). The same principle applies when food is mixed with other items. If one rejects what has been brought for someone else, there is no invitation at all. 79–80.
Now, in order to show those who do not effect an invitation, the words beginning with "parched grain" (*lāja*) are stated. Here, "parched grain" refers to rice mixed with that same parched grain.

The meaning is: parched grain and rice-balls made with parched grain. However, since there is an invitation (*pavāraṇā*) regarding fish, meat, and cakes, it is therefore called "pure solid food" (*suddhakhajjaka*).
"Roasted flour" (*bhaṭṭhapiṭṭha*) means that which was raw previously and must later be roasted.
The connection is: "the meal consisting of the remainder of what has been mentioned, such as bamboo shoots, etc. "Savoury gruel" (*rasayāgu*) means cooked gruel.
Plain gruel unmixed with meat and the like is pure. However, any kind of invitation consisting of various delicacies does not generate an *atiritta* (leftover).
81. "Having risen" means having risen from one's seat; the connection is that one must not make it a leftover.
If a monk does not rise from his seat after having invited [others], he is also permitted to make it a leftover. And "food by one who has not yet eaten": by whom...
The meaning is that even if not even as much as a blade of kusa grass from among the five kinds of cooked food has been eaten, one must still not make it *atiritta* (leftover).

However, if someone has already eaten—even if only at dawn—and has given his consent (*apavārita*), then even if he has risen from his seat and has not eaten anything again during the midday period, he is permitted to do so.
Regarding the phrase "whatever was previously done by whom": [it refers to the consent given].
Whatever was done by someone previously, that same person should not do it again afterwards; however, they say it is permissible for someone else to do it.
82. Whatever fruit or root has been made allowable by the five monastic modes of preparation (*samaṇakappa*), or any other allowable food, or allowable meat—this is called "allowable" (*kappiya*).
That which is the opposite of the aforementioned types is called "unallowable" (*akappiya*). Regarding that:
Making it "leftover" is not valid; furthermore, it is also not valid in the case of that which has been accepted but not taken up.
Therefore it is said: "Only when the allowable [food] has been taken up. "Uttered" means that the monk who has come to have it made allowable has moved it even slightly upward or aside.
It is not permitted to place it outside the reach of the hand; therefore...
It is said: “within arm’s reach. “While making it leftover” means that while making it leftover, one should speak thus, having made a verbal declaration:
“This is enough for all. This should be stated three times; this, it is said, is the established custom.
However, the holders of the Vinaya say that it should be stated only once. “This is enough for all. Alametam.
"Everything"—this too is an addition for you; the meaning is that you shall not obtain anything other than this.
83. Regarding "in the hand of one who is not fully ordained": when making something allowable (*kappiya*), it must not be done while [the food] is still in the hand of one who is not fully ordained.
However, having had another monk receive it, it may be placed in his hand as leftover (*atiritta*).
It is permissible to give it to one who is not fully ordained. The meaning is that one may have it prepared by coming oneself and sending it into the hand of another.
However, with the exception of the one who makes the *atiritta* (leftover) declaration, everyone else—whether they have invited themselves to eat or not—may eat it.
If one who has invited themselves eats it, it is as if it were not prepared.
There is no "leftover" (missa); likewise, one should eat after having made both the mouth and the hands clean.

For one who is ill, even the remains of what has been eaten—if it was brought [to him] with the thought, "He will eat this today or tomorrow"—is permissible to eat as long as it has not been formally declared as leftover (anatirittakata). This concludes the determination regarding the invitation (pavāraṇā).
The commentary on the exposition of the invitation is finished.
8. Explanation of the Exposition of the Timely (Kālikaniddesa) 84.

Now, in order to demonstrate those four "timely" (kālika) items spoken of by the Sage as "that which is for the time being (yāvakālika), that which is for the watch of the night (yāmakālika), that which is for seven days (sattāhakālika), and that which is for life-long (yāvajīvika)," the phrase "and the timely ones" was extracted. Therein, what are those timely ones?

To show this, he said, "that which is for the time being" (*yāvakālika*), and so forth. Among these, it is "for the time being" (*yāvakālika*) because it is to be consumed from sunrise until the midday meal has been completed.
It is "for the watch of the night" (*yāmakālika*) because, when there is thirst, it is to be drunk from sunrise until the end of the watch (*yāmāvasāna*) for the purpose of quenching that thirst;
thus, its time is the watch. When there is an illness to be cured by that [medicine], it may be used for up to seven days.
It is "seven-day medicine" because it is to be consumed for seven days. It is "lifetime medicine" because, when there is illness, it is to be kept and consumed for as long as life lasts. 85.
Among those, in order to show what is "timely," he said: "flour, roots, fruits, and hard food," and so forth.
Herein, "flour for hard food" refers to the flour of the seven grains, of grain-like foods, and of other vegetables, as well as jackfruit flour.
Laba-fruit flour, mango-flour, sal-tree flour, dhota-tala-palm flour, milk-creeper flour, and so forth— these are flours that,
according to the natural dietary habits of people in various regions, serve as edible food (khādanīya) and soft food (bhojanīya),
and are of the "within-the-time" (yāvakālika) category. By this same characteristic, the "within-the-time" definition applies to edible roots and the other [categories] as well.
This should be understood; it has been abbreviated for fear of excessive prolixity. "The essence of cow products" (*gorasa*) means the essence of milk, curd, and buttermilk.
"Grain-food" (*dhaññabhojana*) means the seven types of grain along with their derivatives and the five kinds of cooked food—this is the meaning.
Regarding the phrase "gruel, soup, and so forth," by the word "and so forth" (*pabhuti*), root-vegetables, bulbous roots, head-vegetables, and trunk-vegetables are included.
It should be understood that these are included: edible stalks, edible leaves, edible flowers, edible seeds, and edible sap.
Herein, this is merely an illustration of the types:
the lotus root known as *bhiṃsa*—that is, the bulb of the white and red lotus—as well as *piṇḍāluka*, *sāluka*, and so forth.

The bulbous roots such as the *vallikanda*, *āluvakanda*, and *tālakanda* constitute the edible bulbous roots (*kandakhādanīya*). The lotus rhizomes (*muḷāla*) and so forth constitute the edible rhizomes (*muḷālakhādanīya*).

The tops—referred to as *kaḷīra*—of trees such as the palmyra (*tāla*), *hintāla*, *kuntāla*, *ketaka*, coconut (*nāḷikera*), betel-nut (*pūga*), and date palm (*khajjūrī*), constitute the edible tops (*matthakakhādanīya*).

The stalks of sugarcane (*ucchukhandha*) and the flower-stalks of the blue lotus (*nīluppala*), red lotus (*rattuppala*), white water-lily (*kumuda*), and fragrant lily (*sogandhika*) [also constitute edible stalks].
Such things as these are edible stalks (*khandhakhādanīya*). Edible bark (*tacakhādanīya*) consists solely of the sugarcane bark;

it is permissible only for the duration of a day (*yāvakālika*), and it is flavorful. Edible leaves (*pattakhādanīya*) include radish leaves, *khāraka* leaves, *caccu* leaves, *tambuka* leaves, *taṇḍuleyyaka* leaves, and so forth.
Edible flowers (*pupphakhādanīya*) include radish flowers, *khāraka* flowers, *caccu* flowers, *tambuka* flowers, and so forth, as well as the *asoka* flower.
However, [some] are for as long as life lasts (*yāvajīvika*). The *labuja*, *panasa*, *ṭhiti*, and so forth, are hard foods consisting of seeds (*aṭṭhikhādanīya*).
Among the hard foods consisting of resins (*niyyāsakhādanīya*), there is nothing that is for the time being (*yāvakālika*).
The meaning is that these aforementioned types are for the time being (*yāvakālika*). 86. Now, "Monks, I allow eight drinks: mango drink, rose-apple drink, coconut drink, plantain drink..."

To show that the eight kinds of drinks mentioned as "honey drink, grape drink, lotus-root drink, and *phārusaka* drink" are called "allowable for a watch of the night" (*yāmakālika*), he said "honey," and so forth.

Therein, the meaning should be understood as follows: honey-derived, grape-derived, lotus-root-derived, coconut-derived, *moca*-derived, mango-derived, and rose-apple-derived. Here, "honey-derived" refers to [drinks made from] *madhuka* flowers.
That which is made from the juice of fruit is permissible only when mixed with water; pure juice is not permissible.
"Grape drink" means that which is obtained by crushing grapes in water and straining it. "Lotus-root drink" means that which is made from the filaments of red, blue, and other lotuses.
The remaining items are well known. However, in this context, if one [prepares] these things oneself as substances for the "time-limited" (yāvakālika) category...
Having accepted it, he crushes it in water, cooks it by the heat of the sun, strains it, and makes a beverage;
this is allowable before the meal. If he receives what has been prepared by one who is not fully ordained, it is permissible with food before the meal on that very day;
after the meal, it is permissible for consumption without food until the rising of the dawn. These...
Eight kinds of drinks are permissible whether they are cold or heated by the sun, but those heated by fire are not permissible;
therefore, it is said, "heated by fire. 87.
Because it was stated, "Monks, I allow all fruit juices, except for the juice of grain-fruits,"...
However, the juice of grain or fruit is not permitted; therefore it is said, "except for grains that are suitable.

Because it is stated, "I allow, monks, all flower-juice except the juice of the *madhuka* flower," the juice of the *madhuka* flower—whether cooked by the sun or cooked by fire—is not permitted after the meal; therefore it is said, "except for the *madhuka* flower."
88. “Monks, I allow all the juice of leaf-vegetables, except for the juice of raw *ḍāka*,” because this was said, the juice of even cooked leaf-vegetables is permitted only before the midday meal;
the juice of those crushed with cold water is *yāmakālika* (permissible until the watch of the night).
Therefore it is said: “except for cooked raw *ḍāka*. Regarding the juice of a leaf-vegetable that lasts for life (*yāvajīvika*) when [mixed] with water...
The juice of what is ripe lasts for as long as life. 89.
Now, in order to show those things that are to be used for seven days, he said, beginning with "ghee" (*sappi*).
Here, however: "Ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses;..."
The reading should be accepted as: "Clarified butter for seven days, and the meat of those [animals] whose flesh is not forbidden.
When this is accepted, fat (*vasā*) is already included by the mention of oil, because it is explained in detail in the Canon thus:
"'Oil' means sesame oil, mustard seed oil, *madhuka* oil, castor oil, and fat-oil. Thus...

However, if one were not to include *vasā* (fat) and instead adopt the reading “honey and molasses,” it would follow that *vasā*, being a substance belonging to the category of “what is to be used until the same day” (*yāvakālika*), would [absurdly] become something to be used for seven days.
For the Blessed One has stated that there are exactly five medicines to be used for seven days by sick monks, namely: ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses.
These have been permitted; yet, beyond that, one incurs an offense even by possessing a sixth medicinal substance for a seven-day period.

Furthermore, in the *Bhesajjakkhandhaka*, the Blessed One said: "I allow you, monks, the use of medicinal fats—namely, bear fat, fish fat, porpoise fat, pig fat, and donkey fat—if received at the proper time, cooked at the proper time, and mixed at the proper time, for use as oil."
"to be consumed"—thus, without permitting its use for a period of seven days, only the oil produced from it was authorized.
Therefore, if the reading "and honey and molasses" (*madhuphāṇitameva ca*) were not accepted, it would contradict both the Canon (*pāḷi*) and the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
However, the Elder spoke according to the method found in the *Khuddasikkhā* used by the residents of the Uttaravihāra. For them, however—
“Ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses as the fifth;
and clear [liquids], fish, fat, and so forth—these are ‘seven-day’ items. Thus it has come down in the texts.
However, they say that there is no separate place where our own [tradition] mentions the seven-day items; this should be investigated.
Now, in order to show the ghee among those [medicines], it is said: "For whom meat is permitted. Since it is stated in the Pāḷi:

"Ghee is called cow-ghee, or goat-ghee, or buffalo-ghee; the ghee belongs to those whose meat is allowable, and the butter belongs to those very same ones," butter has been included but was not explained in detail.
However, ghee received before the meal on that same day is permitted both when mixed with food and when unmixed with food.
From after the meal onwards, it may be consumed for seven days provided it is unmixed with food.

If the seven-day period has elapsed, then if it was kept in a single vessel, there is one offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*). If it was kept in many vessels, there are offenses of expiation involving forfeiture according to the number of items.
What is received after the meal is permissible for seven days, provided it is strictly non-fatty (nirāmisa). When one is heating ghee, there is no fault of cooking by oneself;
however, when heating fresh butter (navanīta), there is no fault of cooking by oneself, yet one must not consume fatty food together with that which has been cooked by oneself.
Furthermore, if a person who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna) [uses] fresh butter received before the meal...
"If one gives it after having made it into ghee, it is permissible [to eat] with meat before the meal. If one makes it oneself, it is permissible for seven days only as long as it is without meat.
Thus, in the *Samantapāsādikā*, the state of being "self-made" (*sāmaṃpākata*) is mentioned specifically regarding butter (*navanīta*), not regarding ghee (*sappi*).
However, that which is stated in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*—"It is permissible to cook either produced ghee or butter"—[is also relevant].

Furthermore, regarding the statement, "On that day, it is not even permitted to consume meat before the meal," what is meant by "it is permitted to cook" refers to well-washed butter that is unmixed with the category of *yāvakālika* (food for the time being).
If one eats meat together with the seven-day medicine (*sattāhakālika*) that he himself has cooked, that meat becomes mixed with his own seven-day medicine.

If one causes [an item] that is of a *yāvakālika* (temporary) nature to be accepted as being of a *sattāhakālika* (seven-day) nature, then even an uncooked *yāvakālika* item comes to possess the status of being "self-cooked.
Therefore, it is stated: "It is not permissible to consume what is 'with meat' (*sāmisa*).

Just as oil of *sattāhakālika* substances that have been self-cooked, and oil from self-roasted mustard seeds and other *yāvajīvika* (lifetime) substances, is considered "with meat," it is likewise [forbidden] even on the same day before the meal.
It is likewise to be understood that fresh butter and ghee are permissible. And the Teacher will say:
"Those things such as *yāvakālika* (timely food) and the rest, when mixed with honey, cause the true nature [of the mixture] to be grasped";
and, "Cooked by those very [monks], it is permissible for a monk as *yāvajīvika* (lifetime medicine)."
"And for seven days [the use of] non-material [medicines], and for material ones, [it is permissible] when prepared by oneself.
As for the statement in the *Samantapāsādikā* regarding butter being "prepared by oneself," that was said with reference to unwashed butter mixed with curd and other such substances.
Therefore, among the wise, both the *Samantapāsādikā* and the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī* agree on this matter; as for that butter—
The teachers say that this was spoken with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). This alone is appropriate.

If the cooking of ghee were done by oneself, it would certainly have been mentioned in the *Samantapāsādikā*; for there it is stated: "As for ghee, having been received before the meal, it is permissible to consume it on that same day before the meal, whether mixed with food or not," yet no rule regarding its cooking is mentioned.
If one exceeds seven days with human fat, ghee, or butter, or with the unallowable meat, fat, or butter of other animals such as elephants and horses, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
But is it permissible to consume that? Yes, it is permissible. Why?
Because there is no prohibition against it and because it is permitted in all the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā): "The meat of those [animals] whose meat is allowable..."
"But ghee, fresh butter"—this was stated in order to show the object of forfeiture (*nissaggiyavatthu*), not for the purpose of prohibiting others.
90. Now, in order to show oil, he said: "Oil is produced from sesame, castor, *vaseraṇḍa*, honey, and mustard," and so forth.
Here, the connection is: "oil is that which is produced or originated from sesame and the rest. In this context, having accepted sesame seeds before the meal...

Oil prepared before the meal is permissible even if it contains food particles; however, from the time after the meal onwards, because it has been received with a base [of food], it is not fit for consumption.
Oil prepared after the meal, having been received after the meal, is not fit for consumption;
it should be applied to the head and so forth. If, after receiving castor seeds, madhuka seeds, or mustard seeds, one roasts them and extracts oil, [it is permissible].
Therefore, on that day, even before the meal, it is not permitted [to use] anything containing meat, as it would be "self-cooked" (*sāmaṃpāka*).

If one prepares it without dividing [the ingredients], then on that day before the meal, even that which contains meat is permitted; however, from after the meal onwards, only that which is free of meat is permitted.
Since the items to be consumed are lifelong (*yāvajīvika*), there is no fault in accepting them along with their physical bases (*savatthuka*). Regarding the taking of oil...
For one who, having accepted castor seeds and the like, lets more than seven days pass, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Likewise, there are oils of the *kosambaka* and *kusumbha* plants that are not mentioned or shown in the Pāḷi.
Now, in order to show the varieties of honey, it is said: "made by small bees, bumblebees, honey-bees, and flies. Regarding this:
*Khudda* means small flies. *Bhamara* means large bumblebee flies. Among the *daṇḍaka* bees, there are those called honey-bee flies (*madhukara-makkhikā*).
The meaning is that honey is that which is made by these three kinds of flies.
Since it is stated in the Canon, "Honey is honey made by flies," it should be understood that honey made by other insects such as the *tumbaṭaka* does not have a seven-day period of validity.
Now, in order to show what *phāṇita* (molasses) is, he said: "The various preparations of sugarcane, such as its juice, whether cooked or uncooked, are *phāṇita*.

The meaning is that the various forms of sugarcane, beginning with its juice, whether cooked or uncooked, constitute *phāṇita*. Molasses made from *madhuka* flowers is permissible with meat before a meal;
from after a meal onwards, it is permissible for seven days only without meat. Upon the passing of those seven days—
It is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Both *ciñcaphāṇita* (mango-syrup) and *ambaphāṇita* (mango-juice concentrate) are strictly *yāvakālika* (to be consumed within the same day). 91.

Now, because among these [types of fat] the *vasā-tela* (fat-oil) has been specifically permitted, he says "boiled in its own source or prepared by oneself," etc., in order to set that aside and show it separately.
For there are seven kinds of what is called "specifically permitted": that which is specific to a disease, specific to a person, specific to a time, and so forth.

There are four types of specific allowances: specific to the occasion (*samayodissa*), specific to the place (*desodissa*), specific to the dwelling (*vasodissa*), and specific to the medicine (*bhesajjodissa*).
Among these, it is said: "Monks, I allow raw flesh and raw blood in the case of a disease caused by non-human beings.
This is called "specific to the illness" (*byādhodissa*). In this case, however, whether at the proper time or outside the proper time, both allowable and unallowable meat and blood are permitted.
“I allow, monks, the chewing of cud for one who chews cud”—this is what is called *puggalodissa* (specified for an individual), as it was thus authorized.

“I allow, monks, the giving of the four great foul things: excrement, urine, ashes, and clay”—this is what is called *kālodissa* (specified by time), as it was authorized at the time of snakebites even when not formally received.
Eating in a group and so forth is *samayodissa* (specified by occasion).
“By name”: “Gaṇaṅgaṇūpāhanāni” (sandals with many compartments) is [an example] by region. “By substance”: “I allow you, monks, medicinal fats”—thus it was allowed by the name of fat (*vasā*).

Excluding human fat, the oil of all fats—whether allowable or unallowable—is permitted for those in need of it to use as an oil-ointment. “By medicine”: [refers to what is specified] by the category of medicine.
“I allow, monks, those five medicines”—thus are the five, beginning with ghee, spoken of by the name of "medicine.
However, this [oil] is not like the cooked oil made from milk, curd, and so forth, which is not permitted after the meal;
rather, even oil that has been cooked with its base (the medicinal substance) is permitted. To show this, it is said: “or one that has been cooked with its base, or prepared by oneself.”
Having observed the *vāsa* (residue), it is said, "cooked with its own base" (*savatthupakkā*). The meaning is: "cooked by oneself.
Just as oil cooked with curd and other ingredients is not permitted—even before the meal—if it was accepted with its own base and cooked by oneself, this [medicine] is not like that.
However, the meaning is that this is permitted both before and after the meal, even if it was cooked by oneself with its own base.
In this context, however, fat-oil is called simply "fat" by way of figurative designation for its cause.
"At the proper time" means that it has been cooked either by others or by oneself during the period before the meal. But it is not permitted to cook it after the meal, because it is stated:
"received at the proper time, cooked at the proper time, mixed at the proper time. Therefore, [it is said] "at the proper time."
It has been stated. However, one who receives [food] at an improper time, cooks it at an improper time, strains it at an improper time, and then consumes it, incurs three *dukkaṭa* offenses.

Regarding the term "non-human" (*amānusa*), since the meat of creatures such as bears and hyenas is permitted, this excludes human flesh and applies to all other types of forbidden meat (*akappiyamaṃsa*).
It should be understood that fat is permitted. For among meats, ten types of meat—such as human flesh, elephant flesh, and so forth—are prohibited;
however, regarding fat, only human fat is [prohibited].
Fat oil prepared by one who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna) and returned to its original state, if received before midday, may be used even if it contains food remnants before midday.
It is permissible; from after the meal onwards, it is permissible for seven days provided it is entirely without meat.
However, whatever here resembles fine dust—whether flesh, sinew, bone, or blood—that is not subject to the rule (abbohārika).

If one prepares it oneself, having received it before the meal, cooked it, and strained it, it should be consumed for seven days provided it is entirely without meat. For consumption that is without meat...
This was said with reference to [the following]: “What has been received at the proper time, cooked at the proper time, and mixed at the proper time may be used for the consumption of oil.
“Others” refers to ghee and so forth. “The substance” refers to a substance that is *yāvakālika* (to be consumed within the same day).
The connection is: “one does not cook a substance that is itself a *yāvakālika* substance.”

92. Now, in order to show the permutation of lifelong medicines (*yāvajīvikavikati*), the passage beginning with "turmeric" (*haliddī*) is stated. Regarding this, the meaning of the words not yet explained is as follows:

in the phrase "and also the five roots, etc.," it should be understood that, along with the two sets of five roots (*dvipañcamūla*), other medicinal roots belonging to that same category are also included.
93–5. *Biḷaṅga* and so forth are medicinal fruits. In this context, they say that *goṭṭhaphala* is the same as *madanaphala*.
The connection is with the leaves of cotton and other such plants. However, all these aforementioned items—by way of medicinal roots, medicinal fruits, and medicinal leaves—are allowable (*kappiya*).
The flowers, fruits, leaves, and roots of these are all allowable and may be kept for life (*yāvajīvika*).
The connection is as follows: setting aside the juice of sugarcane, all other juice; and setting aside the sap of sugarcane and its skin, all other skin.

96. "Unmixed with honey" refers to pure boiled rice (*suddhasittha*). However, that which is mixed with honey is only permissible for seven days. "Whatever else there may be" means rice, meat, bones, and so forth. 97.
"Or whatever other things there are that do not serve the purpose of a solid food (*khādanīya*) among solid foods, nor [the purpose of] a soft food (*bhojanīya*) among soft foods..."
Because it is stated: "They distribute them for the purpose of food; having accepted them, one may keep them for as long as life lasts and consume them when there is a requisite [for their use];
if one consumes them when there is no requisite, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," it is therefore said:
"All that which does not serve as food is 'for-as-long-as-life'."
