98. *Sabbassa* means "of both the sick and the healthy. *Kālikattayaṃ* means that, excluding the *yāvakālika* (food to be taken during the day), the remainder is permissible (*kappati*) outside the proper time (*vikāle*) when there is a requisite reason (*paccaye*).

99. *Janayantubho* means "both produce [an offense]. What is meant? Both types of food designated as *yāvakālika* and *yāmakālika*, when consumed after their respective times have passed, produce a *pācittiya* offense. And what...

Furthermore, the meaning is that both of these—storing what was kept inside an improper hut and consuming it on the following day—give rise to a *dukkaṭa* offense for the former and a *pācittiya* offense for the latter due to hoarding (*sannidhi*). 100. Regarding "not mentioned" (*anāruḷhe*):
the meaning is "in [substances] such as human ghee, which are not included in the Canon" (*pāḷiyaṃ*).
101. "Obtained after relinquishing" means obtained again after a formal act of the Vinaya has been performed. Regarding "for seven days for one who designates":

within the interval of seven days, for one who designates it—whether in the presence or in the absence [of the recipient]—by taking the name of a novice according to the method beginning with "This is ghee, this is oil," and saying, "I designate this to you," or "I designate this to so-and-so."
The connection is with the phrase "there is no offense. In the Pāḷi, however, only this much is stated:
"There is no offense if, within seven days, one determines [the robe], relinquishes it, it is lost, it is destroyed, it is burnt, they take it away by force, or they take it on trust";
the phrase "I designate it" (*vikappemi*) is not there. Even though it is not there, nevertheless, if one perceives as determined what has not been determined...

This was shown by the Elder because it is stated in the section on offenses: “It is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya); if one perceives something as already assigned when it has not been assigned, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.

Even while demonstrating that, [he notes that] if one assigns it to one who is fully ordained (upasampanna), it remains the property of oneself alone and the act of acceptance is not relinquished; therefore, he did not demonstrate it by way of one who is fully ordained.

This is shown by way of one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*). For when [the requisites] have been assigned to such a person, even the act of receiving them is relinquished, and no offense occurs.
"Having determined" means that there is no offense for one determining [them] for the purpose of anointing and so forth.
However, if within seven days one becomes indifferent and relinquishes them to one who is not fully ordained, there is no offense because they have been relinquished.
Since the other [portion] has not been formally accepted, physical use of both is permitted. However, because they are not subject to forfeiture (*anissaggiya*), external use is also permitted.

It is stated that "there is no offense even for one who gives them to another," because they were authorized with the specific restriction: "Having accepted them, they may be used as stored goods for a maximum of seven days."

102. *Sabbhāvaṃ* means one’s own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). Because they cause [others] to grasp it, the meaning is that it is thus spoken and uttered. The word “thus” (*evaṃ*) is used with reference to what will now be explained. 103–5.
*Sattāhaṃ yāvajīvikam* means both the seven-day [medicine] and the life-long [medicine]. What is meant?
For one who consumes the two types—the seven-day and the life-long—having mixed them with other types of medicine so that their flavors are blended, [there is an offense].
"It is declared that there is an offense of expiation for storing. This means: "What was received on that very day, on that very day.
"The rest" refers to the two categories of seven-day-use and lifetime-use. "The other" refers to the lifetime-use.

Whether it was received previously or received on that very day, it should be understood that the lifetime-use is permissible for seven days when combined with the seven-day-use. "By means of the timely-use..."
“Monks, that which is for the watch of the night, for seven days, or for as long as life lasts—if received on that very day—it is allowable at the proper time, not at an improper time.

Monks, by means of what is for the watch of the night, [what is] for seven days, or for as long as life lasts—if received on that very day—it is allowable during the watch, but when the watch has passed, it is not allowable. Monks, by means of what is for seven days, [what is] for as long as life lasts—[if] received...”
"For seven days it is allowable; after seven days it is not allowable"—thus it is stated in the *Bhesajjakkhandhaka*.
Here, however, because there is no qualifying statement such as "received on that very day," it is established that even what was received previously is permissible.
This concludes the determination regarding the [medicines] limited by time.
The commentary on the explanation of *kālika* (timely) is finished.
9. Commentary on the Explanation of Receiving (*Paṭiggāhaniddesa*). 106.
Now, in order to elaborate upon the term "receiving" (*paṭiggāha*), the passage beginning with "the solicitation of one who wishes to give" (*dātukāmābhihāro*) and so forth is commenced. Therein:
"An offering from one who wishes to give" means an offering from one wishing to give.
By this it is illustrated that if, when someone is about to pour into another's bowl, droplets rise up and fall into yet another's bowl, the acceptance is not valid.
"Capable of being carried" means capable of being lifted by a person of medium strength; beyond that, the acceptance is invalid.
It does not grow. "Giving in three ways" means giving in three ways by way of [objects] connected to the body and objects connected to the body that are to be relinquished.
The meaning is that for that bhikkhu, there is a twofold acquisition through objects connected to the body and objects connected to the body. "Fivefold" means fivefold in this way.

There is one [factor] consisting of the solicitation of one who wishes to give, one consisting of being within arm's reach, and one consisting of being capable of enduring the rain; among gods, humans, and animals, it is threefold by way of one [of these].
Giving is one, and the two kinds of taking are one; thus there are five factors.
Now, in order to show that which, being connected with the body, does not permit receiving, he says "in what is immovable," and so forth.
It does not apply to a bedstead or the like, a plank, or a stone that has been fixed in place by being bound to a stake—anything that is immovable.
The meaning is this: it is not permissible on lotus leaves or *kiṃsuka* leaves and the like grown there;

nor does it take root on the delicate leaves of *ciñcā* and such plants; and furthermore, the acceptance of that which is an unbearable burden—one which a man of middle stature cannot support—is not valid. This is the meaning.
108. Now, in order to demonstrate the relinquishing of what has been received, the passage beginning with “by the renunciation of training, by death, and by the change of gender” is commenced.

Herein, this is the summary of the meaning: by the renunciation of the training, by death, by the change of gender, or by giving it away without regard—thinking either, “I will not use this now,” or “I will not receive and use it again”—[the object is relinquished].

And because it is not cut off by thieves and the like, and because it ceases and is relinquished through the giving [of the bowl] to one who is not fully ordained, and through its acceptance, it is abandoned.
However, in the case of a bhikkhunī, since there is no formal renunciation of the training, it should be understood that she abandons it through disrobing (*vibbhamana*).
Now, in order to show what should be used after having been accepted, it is said: “All that which has not been accepted,” and so forth.

The meaning of this is as follows: it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for one who uses anything at all, even so much as a speck of dust, that is included within the four times [of the day] without having formally accepted it.
Now, in order to show what may be used without formal acceptance, the passage beginning with “pure and not too thick” is stated.
Therein, “pure” means unmixed with the flavor of other things. Regarding snow-water, ocean-water, and so forth, there is no requirement for formal acceptance.
There is none. "Salt and tears" means *loṇassu*. Here, "salt" refers to that which has arisen within the body.
However, all of these are permissible only when they are continuous [flows], not otherwise. 111.
Now, in order to show those things that are not the tip of a finger (*anaṅgalaggāni*), he said: "Feces, clay, and urine," and so forth. "In such a manner" (*tathāvidhe*).

"At such a time" means at a time when one has been bitten by a snake. However, for others, that which has not been formally received (*appaṭiggahita*) and is not attached to a limb (*anaṅgalagga*) is not permitted.
Why? Because it was said: "Monks, I allow that which one receives while performing [an act]; that itself constitutes the reception; it need not be received again."

112. "Ill-performed" (*durūpaciṇṇa*) means that for one who shakes a crystal tree, a creeper, or the like, or for one who touches a vessel filled with food without having received it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) due to ill-performance; this is the meaning. "Dust-covered" (*rajo-kiṇṇa*):
for one wandering for alms, if dust fallen into the bowl is not removed and he takes more alms, there is an offense of wrong-doing according to the Vinaya.

The meaning is "it occurs. Now, regarding "having received after having taken up": that is, in the case of having received after having oneself taken up; the meaning is "having been grasped by oneself.

The intention is that it is an *dukkaṭa* offense in all cases: when [food] has been stored inside an improper shed, when it has been cooked by a monk himself anywhere at all, and when it has been cooked inside an improper shed either by oneself or by another. This concludes the determination of receiving.
The commentary on the exposition of receiving is finished.
10. Commentary on the Exposition of Improper Meat: 113.
Now, in order to show the manner in which one should deal with meats, the phrase "and improper meat among meats" has been raised.
When non-permissible meat (*akappiyamaṃsa*) is presented, permissible meat (*kappiyamaṃsa*) is indeed presented by way of elimination (*pārisesanaya*).
Regarding the phrase "and of a snake," here no snake whatsoever is permissible.
Having thus shown the ten kinds of non-permissible meat according to species, [the text now addresses] the permissible meats as well.
To demonstrate the improper procedure, it is said: "Meat prepared specifically for [the bhikkhu], and that which has not been inspected.
In this context, among the five types of fellow practitioners (sahadhammika), anything prepared specifically for anyone at all is called "prepared specifically" (uddissakata).
Having learned of this, it is not permitted for any of them to consume it; however, there is no offense for those who do not know. This also applies to fish.
The same method applies here. "Without having reflected upon" means not having examined; the meaning is "without having asked for permission. It is said:
"Monks, meat should not be consumed without having reflected upon it. Whoever should consume it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
However, they say that regarding fish, there is no requirement to ask for permission, because there is no such thing as "unfit" fish. Now...
In order to show the classification of these offenses, he said, "a grave offense" (*thullaccaya*), and so forth. All of that is self-evident. 115.

Now, in order to show that it is not only the flesh of these [beings] such as humans that is unallowable (*akappiya*), but also their bones and so forth are unallowable, he said, "bones too," and so forth.
Therein, "even hair" means that even the hair of these [beings] whose flesh is an unallowable object is [unallowable].

The meaning. Regarding the phrase "or that which has consciousness": among these, only that which is prepared specifically for [the recipient] is "with consciousness" (*sacittaka*); the rest are "without consciousness" (*acittaka*). This concludes the analysis of unallowable meat.
The commentary on the description of unallowable meat is finished. 11.
Commentary on the Description of the Forfeiture Offenses (*Nissaggiya-niddesa-vaṇṇanā*).
116–7. Now, in order to show [the offense] by way of those that are not of high value (*accodārika*), the passage beginning with “arūpiyan” is commenced.
The logical connection should also be sought in another way. Herein, this is the summarized meaning:
for one who would exchange non-monetary goods for monetary goods, or who would exchange monetary goods for other non-monetary goods, there is an offense of relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).
Now, in order to show both the material (*rūpiya*) and the immaterial (*arūpiya*), the passage beginning with "Herein, material" is commenced.
Here, *sajjhu* and *siṅgī*: *sajjhu* means silver; *siṅgī* means gold.

Whether it is made by producing a form from copper, iron, wood, leaves, or lacquer, or even without producing a form, or even that which consists of leather or seeds—whatever is used as currency in a particular region [is what is meant].
"It goes"—this is what is called "that which constitutes entering into worldly transaction. This is what is intended here by "money" (rūpiya).

"Clothing and so forth, pearls and so forth" refers to clothing, pearls, and the rest. "The other" refers to non-monetary items that are either allowable (kappiya) or items involving an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
What is meant? Clothing, thread, a plowshare, cloth, cotton, various kinds of secondary food, clarified butter, fresh butter...
Oil, honey, molasses, and other such medicinal substances—this is called "allowable property" (*kappiyavatthu*). Pearls, gems, beryl, conch shells, crystals, coral, rubies, and emeralds;
the seven grains; female and male slaves; fields, lands, flower gardens, fruit orchards, and so forth—this is called "offensive property" (*dukkaṭavatthu*).
It is stated that both of these together are termed "non-monetary wealth" (*arūpiya*).
118. Having thus far shown the exchange of money, he now says, "Having taken this," etc., in order to show buying and selling.
Therein, "having taken this" refers to having taken allowable goods such as rice, or having eaten boiled rice and so forth, [he says]:
"Give me this allowable goods such as cloth; perform this such as dyeing or cooking; bring these such as firewood for dyeing; or this..."
“I give this to you; however, you must bring and do such-and-such, and give me that”—when one has thus engaged in buying and selling, it is an offense of expiation (*nissaggiya*);
this is the connection. 119.
Now, in order to show the classification of offenses by way of transformation (*pariṇāma*), the passage beginning with “one’s own” is commenced. In this regard, this is...

The summary of the meaning: if one should divert to oneself or another a gain—whether belonging to the Saṅgha or another—that has been intended and assigned for the requisites such as robes, there are offenses such as *nissaggiya*. How so?
If one diverts to oneself what belongs to a mother and has been assigned to the Saṅgha, it is a *nissaggiya* offense. If one diverts it to another person...
This is a *pācittiya* offense of the pure class (*suddhika*). If one dedicates it to another *saṅgha* or to another *cetiya*, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

Furthermore, if one who has already dedicated it to a specific person or to a *cetiya* then redirects it to oneself, to another person, to a *saṅgha*, or to another *cetiya*, for that person as well, it is likewise a *dukkaṭa* only.

120. Furthermore, if one should use an article that ought to be relinquished without having relinquished it, and without the formal legal act (vinaya-kamma) having been performed, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Or, if one should not give back an item that has been relinquished by another for the purpose of a formal legal act, thinking it to be one’s own, there is likewise an offense of wrong-doing.
Regarding the phrase "otherwise than this" (aññathetaraṃ): here, "otherwise" means if one should not give it with the perception of theft; "the other" [refers to the offense].

The meaning is that, according to its value, there is an offense of defeat (pārājika), a grave offense (thullaccaya), and an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). The determination of the offenses involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-vinicchaya) is concluded.
The commentary on the exposition of the offenses involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-niddesa-vaṇṇanā) is finished.
12. Commentary on the Exposition of the Offenses of Expiation (pācittiya-niddesa-vaṇṇanā).
121. Now, in order to show the *pācittiya* offenses, the matrix phrase (*mātikā*) "Pācitti" is cited, followed by the statement:
"In false speech, in slanderous speech, in inciting strife," and so forth. Therein, the connection is that *pācittiya* is stated for false speech, for slanderous speech, and for inciting strife;
the same applies to the remaining cases. Here, however, [the text continues]: "What has not been seen, not heard, not sensed, not cognized..."
The meaning is that when one has previously intended, "I shall speak falsely," and at the very moment of speaking knows,
"I am speaking falsely," there is an offense called *pācittiya* for one who speaks falsely while knowing it to be so— even regarding what is seen, heard, sensed, or cognized. However,
if the person to whom one speaks does not hear it, there is no offense.
“‘Insulting speech’ (omasavāda) means one insults in ten ways: by birth, by name, by clan, by occupation, by craft, by illness, by physical mark, by defilement, by offense, and by abuse.

When this has been said, whoever reviles or disparages one who is fully ordained by these ten ways is said to “insult”; the meaning is that for him there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). [This applies] when face-to-face.
There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who speaks [in this way]; likewise for one who speaks using terms not found in the Canon, such as "thief" or "cut-purse.

There is also an offense of wrong-doing in every case for one who speaks by way of synonyms, such as "there are here certain kṣatriyas, brahmins, and caṇḍālas," and for one who speaks to a person who has not received full ordination.

To convey malicious gossip (*pesuñña*) means to report to one who is ordained, after having heard the words of another who is ordained, the disparagement of that person by birth and so forth, whether out of a desire for affection or with the intention of causing a schism. Here too,
there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) both for conveying such matters through indirect speech and for conveying them to one who is not ordained.

Regarding the term *padasodhammo*: here, "Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma of the Three Pitakas as recorded in the three councils, which was spoken by Buddhas, spoken by disciples, spoken by seers, and spoken by deities; it is endowed with meaning and endowed with the Dhamma.
[The offense applies] to one who, excluding a bhikkhu or a bhikkhunī, recites such Dhamma word-by-word, phrase-by-phrase, syllable-by-syllable, or letter-by-letter to one who is not fully ordained.
The meaning is that for one who causes [a student] to recite from one side, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). "In an enclosed place" (*sāgāre*) means:

because it is surrounded by a wall or the like to a height of at least one and a half cubits, it is entirely enclosed; and because it is covered by anything whatsoever, even a cloth canopy, it is entirely roofed.

Regarding "lodging": when one dwells together with one who is not fully ordained in such a lodging within a single precinct, from the fourth day onwards, there is a *pācittiya* offense for each instance of lying down and for each person who is not fully ordained; this is the meaning. Regarding "reviling and disparaging":
here, [it refers to] one who is fully ordained and appointed by the Saṅgha as the assigner of lodgings.
Or, desiring to act as a distributor of lodgings, a distributor of meals, a distributor of rice-gruel, a distributor of fruit, a distributor of hard food,
or a dispenser of minor items, one who— by means of a formal motion (*chanda*)—

speaks disparagingly of another fully ordained person (*upasampanna*), saying, "So-and-so assigns lodgings and designates meals," thereby censuring him and causing him to be looked down upon; whoever speaks in such a manner...
When one reveals another’s fault in the presence of a person who has received full ordination (*upasampanna*), one is censured;
it should be understood that for both such censuring and disparaging, there are two *pācittiya* offenses.
122. Regarding "in striking with the palm of the hand and causing anxiety": here, whichever monk [acts] toward a person who has received full ordination in the manner of striking...
If one raises up either the body or something connected to the body while showing [the blow], there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).

If, having missed, one gives a blow out of a desire not to strike, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); likewise, even in the case of those who are not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*), it is an offense of wrong-doing.
When being spoken to by one who is fully ordained and has been designated [for instruction], if one does so out of a desire not to train or a desire not to hear that person's words...
The meaning is that for whoever shows disrespect, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for that act of disrespect.

For one who is addressed by a person not fully ordained—whether what is said is prescribed or unprescribed—or for one who is addressed by a person fully ordained regarding what is either prescribed or unprescribed, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

For one who intentionally causes remorse in a person fully ordained by such means as saying, "I think you were ordained when you were less than twenty years old," or "I think you ate at an improper time," there is an offense of expiation. For causing remorse in a person not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Regarding the phrase "asking for permission to enter a village": here, from the time the midday meal has passed until the rising of the dawn, it is called "the improper time" (*vikāla*).
During this interval, if several [monks] enter a village for some business, they must all ask one another for permission, saying, "We ask for permission to enter the village at an improper time.
If they enter without asking permission, [they incur an offense] regarding the enclosure of that which is enclosed...

If they cross the precinct of an unenclosed [monastery], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the first step; upon lifting the second foot, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). There is no offense in cases of emergency.
Regarding "successive eating" (*paramparabhojana*): the meaning is that there is an offense of expiation for successive eating.
Here, however, having taken one of the five kinds of food—whether it be boiled rice, grain, flour-cake, meat, or...
In the manner beginning with "I invite you with fish," or by whatever synonym for an improper invitation one may be invited,
having set aside the food of whichever [person] he was first invited by, and without making a formal assignment (*vikappa*),
he partakes of any one of the five kinds of food from another and yet another family in reverse order, disregarding the original invitation.
For one who consumes [food] while another is eating, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). There is no offense in the cases of being ill, giving robes, or during the time for receiving robes;
likewise, there is no offense in all cases except for the five kinds of food.
123. Regarding "going without having put away [the bedding]," here "bedding" (seyyā) is of ten kinds: a mattress (bhisi), a felt rug (cimilika), an upper coverlet (uttarattaraṇaṃ),...
A ground-covering rug, a wooden mat, a piece of hide, a sitting mat, a bedspread, a grass mat, and a leaf mat—
whichever of these has been taken by one’s own *vassa* allotment in a communal monastery that is a secure dwelling,
whether one has spread it oneself or had it spread by one who is not fully ordained, when departing on that very day on account of travel—
One should not remove it oneself, nor cause another to remove it, so that it might not be eaten by ants and the like;
one should not leave it there, nor cause another to remove it, nor depart without having asked a suitable bhikkhu,
a sāmaṇera, or even an ārāmika, [if it is] the enclosure of an enclosed monastery, or [the area] of an unenclosed [monastery].
For one who passes beyond two throws of a clod, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

For one who departs after having spread out [a rug] in an unguarded dwelling—such as a pavilion or at the foot of a tree—there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); likewise for beds, benches, mattresses, and pillows; and even in a guarded dwelling, it is likewise an offense of wrong-doing.
Regarding the phrase "the dwellings," the connection here is with "departing without putting them away. In this context, however, the bed, the bench, the mattress...
"Kocchaka" refers to any of the four kinds of lodgings; during the eight months of the rainy season and winter,
having spread it out oneself or having had it spread by one not yet ordained,
or having left that lodging unremoved or uncaused to be removed, when one has passed beyond two *leḍḍu*-throws from that lodging.
[If she goes], it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Regarding other requisites such as brooms and the like, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

Regarding "going on a journey with a woman": here, having made an appointment with a woman by saying, "Let us go, sister," or "Let us go, lady," and having fixed a time—such as "today," "tomorrow," or "the day after tomorrow"—but without making an appointment regarding the place or the route, [she commits an offense]. Regarding the appointment for the door or the appointment for the path...

Even for one who goes from village to village after having [prepared the seat], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for each interval between villages. In a forest where there are no villages, there is an offense for every half-yojana traveled.
Regarding the phrase "for each sitting mat" (*nisīdana*): here, the meaning is "one [mat] for each woman.

124. Regarding "frightening": here, it refers to one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*) desiring to frighten another who is fully ordained by means of things such as robbers, wildernesses, or forests infested with beasts of prey.
If one describes [something] or shows a terrifying form, sound, or the like—whether that person fears it or not—for each such act, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If the person is not ordained (anupasampanna), it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
"Beating" means giving a blow. If an ordained person, being displeased with another ordained person, even with a lotus leaf...

If one gives a blow, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). If one gives a blow to one who is not fully ordained—whether a householder or a renunciant, whether a woman or a man, and even down to an animal—it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) only.
Having engaged in improper conduct, if one is being questioned in the midst of the Saṅgha regarding an offense or the matter [of the offense], and being unwilling to speak about it...
By means of other statements such as, "Who has fallen [into an offense]? What has he fallen into? In what has he fallen?", he conceals that statement;
thus he speaks otherwise. This is one who speaks otherwise (*aññavādaka*).
When someone sees a transgression in that person who speaks otherwise and says, "Friend, you have done this," he does not wish to speak and remains silent toward the Saṅgha.
"He harasses" means one who harasses the Saṅgha; the meaning is that there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for that harasser.

However, in this case, when one has been charged with being a "one who speaks otherwise" or a "harasser" by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and a second (ñattidutiyakamma), there is an offense of expiation for one who speaks further or harasses again.
It should be understood that if he has not been so charged, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

Regarding the phrase "he conceals a grave offense" (*duṭṭhullapakāsachādeti*): although it is stated here that "grave offenses are the four *pārājika*s and the thirteen *saṅghādisesa*s," nevertheless, in this context only the *saṅghādisesa*s are intended.
Therefore, [it refers to] a monk’s grave offense—such as "this man, having emitted semen, has incurred a *saṅghādisesa*"—without the formal authorization of the Saṅgha.

Having connected the offense with the basis according to the rule, excluding both monks and nuns, for anyone who reports it to one who is not fully ordained, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
For reporting a non-grave offense such as a serious transgression (*thullaccaya*), there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Even in the case of concealing a grave offense, it is intended that it is an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*). Furthermore, whichever monk [conceals] a grave offense of a monk...
If, having known an offense oneself or having heard of it from others, one sets aside the duty with the thought, "Having learned of this, they will reprove me, accuse me, and make me feel dejected;
therefore, I will not disclose it," there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Even if one discloses it after having set aside the duty, it does not protect [the person] at all.
"Hāsodaka" (laughter-water) should be understood as meaning both laughter by means of poking with a finger and laughter in water.

If one who is ordained, with the intention of causing laughter, touches the body of another who is ordained with his own body, there is an offense of *pācittiya*; what need is there to mention the case of rubbing [the body] in the armpits and so forth?
In the case of one who is not ordained, it is an act of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); likewise for touching something connected to the body of a monk.

And [it applies] to that which is connected to the body by means of what is forfeitable (nissaggiya) and to a seat. Herein, even a bhikkhunī stands in the place of one who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna).
"The nature of laughing in water" refers to such acts as diving, surfacing, and swimming with the intention of playing in water reaching above the ankles.
In this context, "laughter" is said to mean play.
“Monasteries for expulsion” means monasteries belonging to the Saṅgha that are used for ejecting [someone]. Herein, however, if one who is angry seizes an ordained person by the hand or elsewhere,
or says “Get out,” and causes him to pass through as many doors as possible with a single effort,
then— without counting the number of doors— one offense arises because the effort is singular.
It should be understood in this way. If one causes [the robe] to pass through by various means, it should be reckoned there according to the number of doors.
There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for dragging out his requisites; likewise for one who is not fully ordained, and for dragging out his requisites.
However, there is no offense in the case of those who are shameless and so forth.

"Sleeping in encroachment" means: in a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, having recognized that [someone] is "senior," "sick," or "assigned by the Saṅgha," one spreads out a bed or has it spread out within the vicinity of a bed or chair as it is being entered or exited, with the intention: "Whoever finds it cramped shall depart."
For one who sits down or lies down [in such a manner], a *pācittiya* offense is to be understood according to the count of the act. The determination of the *pācittiya* offenses is concluded.
The commentary on the exposition of the *pācittiya* rules is finished.
13. Commentary on the Exposition of the Ascetic’s Mode of Life (*samaṇakappa*).
125. *Bhūtagāma* means a "village of beings," referring to those beings that have been born and produced.

*Samārambha* means cutting, splitting, cooking, and so forth. The meaning is that regarding that destruction of the village of beings (*bhūtagāmasamārambha*), on account of such destruction, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
The connection is: "But what has been made allowable becomes allowable for the recluses. What is allowable for recluses is *samaṇakappiya*. Now, by which... [text continues]
What is allowable becomes allowable for a recluse; to demonstrate that, he said, "with the fingernail," and so forth. For it is said:
"I allow you, monks, to consume fruit by means of five allowable practices for recluses:
that which is prepared by fire, that which is prepared by a knife, that which is prepared by the fingernail, that which is seedless, and fifthly, that from which the seeds have been removed."
126. Now, in order to show that class of living beings (*bhūtagāma*), he said, "with roots," and so forth.

Therein, *sa* means "that," referring to what is called the class of living beings; it is stated that it is produced by the five kinds of seeds, beginning with root-seeds. Among these, a "root-seed" (*mūlabīja*) refers to turmeric, ginger, and the like.
A "stem-seed" (*khandhabīja*) refers to the *assattha*, the *nigrodha*, and so forth. An "apex-seed" (*aggabīja*)... [text continues]
“*Nāma*” refers to *ajjukā*, *phaṇijjaka*, and so forth. “*Phalubīja*” refers to sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, and so forth. It is said:
“‘*Bījabīja*’ means grain for the morning meal and grain for the evening meal, or whatever else there is that is produced from a seed and grows from a seed;
this is called ‘*bījabīja*’. Now, because it has been stated [in the training rule], “He abstains from the destruction of seeds and plant life,” [the following is] in accordance with the Dhamma:
In order to show the undertaking of the commencement of seeds and vegetation, he said, "In the undertaking, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," and so forth.

Therefore, after first having the release from the danger to living beings performed by saying, "Make it allowable (*kappiyaṃ karohī*)," one must again have it made allowable for the sake of releasing the seeds and vegetation.
127. "Produced seed" refers to mangoes, jackfruits, and the like. "Non-seed" refers to young mango fruits and the like; all of this—
The meaning is that even what is unallowable (*akappiya*) is permissible. "Seeds bound in a basket" refers to seeds such as those of the *kapittha* fruit. Or, "having it made outside":

it is permissible to have them made even in a bowl, provided they are connected as one unit; this is the meaning. However, once released from the basket, they must be made [into separate units] by breaking them apart. 128.
Whether in a vessel or on the ground, when the seeds are connected as one unit, if one seed is made allowable (*kappiya*), then all of them [become allowable].

The meaning is: "it has been made allowable. And just as in the case of a seed, so too should the decision be understood even when a thousand trees or a thousand sugarcanes have been cut down and joined together into a single mass. 129.

When a plantation of seeds has been deposited after being made allowable, if roots and leaves should grow again, one must make it allowable once more; this is the meaning. "Then" means when the roots and sprouts have grown.

130. "Arisen from water" means born from water. Regarding the phrase "in shrines and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes those produced in houses, gateways, walls, railings, and the like.
That which has produced two or three leaves is indeed a "community of beings" (bhūtagāma); that which has not yet produced [leaves] is included within "seed-germs" (aggabīja).
Furthermore, as long as the seed has not sent forth even a root or a leaf, it remains merely a "community of seeds" (bījagāma). And regarding the root...
The meaning is that when the leaves have fallen and new green shoots have grown, it becomes as if it were a living organism (*bhūtagāma*).
131. *Makuḷa* means unblown (unopened). An *ahichattaka* is a mushroom growing on a tree.
132. The connection is "taking [it] from a moist tree. Therein, the connection is "cutting [it] from a moist tree" or "planting [it]."
134. It is not permissible to speak by specifying [the object] in such a manner as, "Cut this tree, cut this creeper, split this bulb," and so forth.
However, it is permissible to say simply, "Cut the tree," and so forth, without saying, "This" or "That.
This concludes the determination regarding the ascetic’s mode of conduct (*samaṇakappa*).
The commentary on the description of the ascetic’s requisites is finished.
14. Commentary on the Description of the Grounds.
136. Now, [the Buddha said]: “I allow you, monks, four kinds of allowable grounds: one formally authorized (*ussāvanantika*), one like a cow-pen (*gonisādika*),” and so forth.
Having stated, “the householder’s agreement,” he spoke the words beginning with “and the proclamation of the agreement” in order to show the four types of allowable grounds (*kappiyabhūmi*).
Regarding the phrase “in which”: it refers to those allowable grounds.

Now, in order to show where an allowable shed (*kappiyakuṭi*) should be desired, he spoke the words beginning with “for the purpose of dwelling. Regarding the phrase “for the purpose of dwelling”: [text continues]

By this it is indicated that for whatever else is constructed for the purpose of residence—such as storehouses, dining halls, cetiya-houses, privies, or pavilions—there is no requirement to construct a *kappiya-kuṭi* (a formalized "proper" hut) in each of those places.

However, they say that a dining hall is indeed a lodging (*senāsana*), and therefore one must certainly construct [a *kappiya-kuṭi*] there. Regarding the phrase "in what belongs to the Sangha or to an individual": here...
The term *ekasantaka* (belonging to one) should be understood as belonging to one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*).
Now, in order to show the manner in which it should be performed, he says: "In a house," and so forth.

Therein, when a dwelling or a monastery is being built for the Saṅgha or for an individual, acting in this way—saying, "We are making a *kappiya-kuṭi* (an allowable storehouse); we are making a *kappiya-kuṭi*"—one should proceed.
If one says, "This is a *kappiyakuṭi*, this is a *kappiyakuṭi*," while placing the first brick, pillar, or other foundation, it is called "established by proclamation" (*ussāvanantikā*);
the meaning is that it is established by the utterance of such words.
Alternatively, a monastery (*ārāma*) that is mostly unenclosed, or even entirely unenclosed, is called "a place where cattle lie down" (*gonisādī*).
[This is] the connection. Herein, however, even if the dwellings are enclosed, there is no need to construct a *kappiya-kuṭi* (a "proper" hut) within an unenclosed monastery.

When those who are making the formal agreement have finished it, they should take the name of that hut—whether it be called a "monastery," a "half-gabled house," a "pavilion," a "grotto," a "grass hut," or a "canopy"—and either stand within arm's reach of it, or...
Having entered inside it, it should be authorized by means of a formal act consisting of one motion and a second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*) according to the method already described.
Regarding the statement, “by others, excluding the bhikkhu”:

the meaning is that a house given for the sake of a *kappiyakuṭi* (a storehouse for allowable goods) by other fellow practitioners of the Dhamma, or by gods and humans—being their own property—is considered and known as a “householder’s dwelling” (*gahapati*).
The intention is that, setting aside what belongs to the Saṅgha and what belongs to individual bhikkhus, the house of everyone else is considered a "householder's dwelling.
(141) "Mixed with ghee and so forth" means mixed with the five items beginning with ghee, as well as turmeric, ginger, and other lifelong medicines.
"One should avoid [food] stored overnight" refers here to the two preceding time-periods known as "for-a-lifetime" (*yāvakālika*) and "for-a-watch-of-the-night" (*yāmakālika*).

The meaning is: even if something belonging to the Saṅgha, or to a bhikkhu, or to a bhikkhunī, has been stored within one’s own *kappiyakuṭi* (permissible storehouse), it becomes "stored within" [and thus subject to the rules] if it is mixed with other items stored in an *akappiyakuṭi* (impermissible storehouse).
142. *Teheva*: by those very things—such as ghee, oil, and so forth—that were stored in an *akappiyakuṭi*. *Sāmapākataṃ*: the meaning is that it reaches the state of being "cooked by oneself."
143–4. Now, in order to show when these allowable huts (kappiyakuṭi) have lost their basis, he said, "ending with the proclamation," and so forth.
If they move the pillars or the base of the walls, it remains established wherever each one stands;
the meaning is that by this means, even when all [the components] are moved, it has not lost its basis. In the case of an enclosed [hut]:

The *goṇisādika* [offense] has its basis abandoned. The remaining [offenses] are "destructions of the covering" (*chadanavibbhama*); the intention is that they are "destructions of the covering" (*chadanavināsa*) whose basis has been abandoned.
This concludes the determination of the grounds (*bhūmivinicchaya*).
The commentary on the exposition of the grounds (*bhūminiddesa*) is finished.
15. Commentary on the Exposition of Duties Toward the Preceptor and Teacher (Upajjhācariyavattaniddesavaṇṇanā) 145.

Regarding the term "preceptor and teacher" (*upajjhācariya*): here, a teacher (*ācariya*) is fourfold—namely, the teacher of dependence (*nissayācariya*), the teacher of going-forth (*pabbajjācariya*), the teacher of full ordination (*upasampadācariya*), and the teacher of the Dhamma (*dhammācariya*).
For among these, as long as one who is a resident pupil under dependence lives in dependence upon a teacher, [he must perform the duties].

To that extent, all the duties toward the teacher must be performed. However, for those who have gone forth as students—whether they are under formal dependence (*nissaya*) or independent from the beginning—the duties must be performed starting from the dyeing of the robes and continuing until that point.

Yet, there is no offense for them in giving their alms-bowl or other items without first asking permission. Among these, both the student who has gone forth and the student who has received full ordination [belong] to the teacher.
It lasts for as long as one lives; and for a dependent resident pupil (*nissayantevāsika*) and a Dhamma pupil (*dhammantevāsika*), it lasts only as long as they reside in proximity.

"Of very amiable character and pleasant" means that he is desirous of training. When giving a tooth-stick, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, three types of tooth-sticks—large, medium, and small—should be presented. Among these, whichever...
He takes it for three days; having observed that, from the fourth day onwards, one should give him exactly the same amount with both hands.
If he takes this or that [specific portion], one should bring whatever has been obtained.
Regarding "water": having brought both cold and warm water, that which was used for three days, from the fourth day onwards—
Such [food] should be brought forward. If he uses both [hands], both kinds should be brought forward. If there is rice-gruel, the vessel should be washed and brought forward. 146.
One should observe the proper conduct regarding the bowl: having given water to one who has drunk the gruel, and having received the vessel, [one should hold it] low.
"Having washed it thoroughly and wiped it dry, it should be put away"—this is what is meant by "one should observe the proper conduct regarding the bowl.
"One should observe the proper conduct upon entering a village" applies in this same way in all instances.
"If the preceptor or the teacher wishes to enter a village, the inner robe should be given [to them], the outer robe should be received [from them], and the waistband..."
“[The bowl] must be given; having folded it, the outer robes (saṅghāṭī) must be given;
having washed it, the bowl with its water must be given”—this is called the proper conduct regarding entering a village.

“If the preceptor or the teacher desires an attendant monk, [the attendant], covering the three circles and wearing the lower robe (nivāsana) properly, having fastened the waist-band (kāyabandhana), and having folded [the robes]...”

The conduct regarding going is that which is stated in such a manner as: "Having arranged the outer robe (saṅghāṭī), having put it on, having fastened the toggle (gaṇṭhikā), having washed the bowl and taken it, one should act as the attendant monk (pacchāsamaṇa) to one’s preceptor (upajjhāya) or teacher (ācariya).
The conduct regarding returning is that which is stated in such a manner as: "Returning, one should arrive first and prepare a seat."
“Duty” (vatta) means: the duty regarding seats and so forth, as stated thus: “When the preceptor has risen, the seat should be lifted up;
the water for washing the feet, the footstool, and the foot-washing stone should be put away. The duty regarding sandals is as follows: “The sandals should be wiped;
by one wiping the sandals, they should first be wiped with a dry cloth, and afterwards with a wet one,” and so forth.

It has been stated. Regarding "the duty concerning robes" (*cīvaravatta*), it is stated as follows: "If a robe is damp, it should be dried for a short while in the heat, but the robe must not be left to dry in the heat," and so forth. 147.
Regarding "in the places for water for washing, drinking water, excrement, and urine": here, if there is no drinking water, [one should provide] drinking water...
It should be provided. If there is no water for washing, water for washing should be provided.
If the restroom is dirty, the restroom should be swept. The meaning is that the duty should be performed in this same way in the urinal as well.
By the passage beginning, "One who cleans the dwelling should first take out the bowl and robes and set them aside," and so forth...
The duty regarding the cleaning of the dwelling has been stated according to the method [in the Vinaya].

The duty regarding the re-spreading [of the bedding] is that which was stated by the passage beginning: “Having dried the floor-covering, having cleaned it, having shaken it out, and having brought it back, it should be spread again as it was originally arranged.
Now, in order to show how the dwelling must be cleaned by one who is cleaning it, he says: “One should not shake it out,” and so forth.

The meaning of this is: while cleaning the dwelling, a bhikkhu should not shake out the bedding and furniture—such as floor mats and so forth—in a place that is downwind, in a courtyard, or near the water. "Courtyard" (*paṅgaṇa*) refers to a place where many people gather.
149. Regarding bathing: "If the preceptor wishes to bathe, the bath should be prepared. If he wishes for cold [water]..."
The "duty regarding bathing" is that which is stated by the passage beginning, "When there is need, cold [water] should be prepared," and so forth.

The "duty to be performed for one who has bathed" is that which is stated by the passage beginning, "The water from the preceptor’s body should be wiped away, and his lower robe should be given," and so forth.
Regarding "the dyeing of cloth": "If the dyeing of the preceptor’s or the teacher’s robes must be done, it should be done by the student..."

It is said: "The resident pupil (antevāsika) must cook [the food]. Regarding washing: it is said, "If the robe of the preceptor (upajjhāya) or the teacher (ācariya) is to be washed, it must be washed by the co-resident (saddhivihārika) or the resident pupil, or else he must make an effort [to have it done].
Regarding sewing: "If the robe is to be made by the preceptor or the teacher, [it must be done] by the co-resident..."
It is said: "It must be done by the resident pupil. The meaning is that while dyeing, one should not depart while even a drop of cloth remains. For it is said:
"One who is dyeing a robe must dye it by turning it over thoroughly and repeatedly;
one must not depart while even a drop remains."

150. "Of a certain person" means of a teacher or preceptor who is of a different character, one who does not wish him well, or an enemy. "Without asking permission" means without having informed the teacher or preceptor. "Anything at all" means whatever it may be.

151–2. "Of him" means of that certain person. "To carry out" means to take away. "Service or assistance" means personal service, or assistance such as massaging the back, or performing service for him oneself, or having him perform service for oneself.
The meaning should be understood in this way.
153. If the teacher and preceptor have gone elsewhere, it is permissible for those who do not see them to enter the village after going to the courtyard.
They say that if one sees them while entering the village, one must certainly ask for permission. [Regarding] the preceptor...
For it is said: "One must not depart for another region without having asked permission.

One's own duties (*attano kicca*) include, even within the monastery, such tasks as boiling one's own alms-bowl, making robes, and shaving hair. Duties dependent upon the Sangha (*saṅghāyattakamma*) include probation (*parivāsa*), penance (*mānatta*), rehabilitation (*abbhāna*), censure (*tajjanīya*), demotion (*niyassa*), banishment (*pabbājanīya*), reconciliation (*paṭisāraṇīya*), and suspension (*ukkhepana*).

155. He causes them to wait for his recovery, for it is said: "If the preceptor or the teacher is ill, he should attend to him for as long as life lasts; one must wait for his recovery. Thus ends the analysis of the duties toward preceptors and teachers.
The commentary on the exposition of the duties toward preceptors and teachers is finished.
16. Commentary on the Exposition of the Place for Defecation and Urination.
156. The connection is: "one should not act according to seniority. The connection is: "it is obtained according to the sequence [of arrival].

However, the intention is this: among these three places, whichever person—whether senior or junior—arrives first, that person is entitled to perform the duties and bathe according to the order of their arrival.
157. "Having lifted up" means that one should not enter after having tossed aside the lower garment from afar. "And one should not enter hastily"—this is the connection.

Because it is stated, "One standing outside should cough," and "The privy should be entered with care and without haste," the meaning is that one should enter after coughing and without being in a hurry. "One should not enter by lifting [the garment] up..."
Because of the statement, "It should be lifted while standing on a cow-hide sandal," it is said: "One should lift [the stool] while remaining on the sandals themselves.
158. One should not do both; one should not do either. 159.
*Kūpeti* means in the feces-pit. *Kaṭṭhaṃ* means a scraping stick. One should not spit into the urinal vessel.

The meaning is as follows: "One should not scrape with something rough" means that one should not scrape with split wood, or with anything harsh, or with a knot, or with a thorn, or with a hollow, or with something putrid.
"And even what has been removed" means that one should wash away even that which is smeared with excrement, whether it was done by oneself or by another; this is the intended sense.
160. Regarding the phrase "having lifted [the garment], one does not exit":
here it is stated that "one should cover oneself while standing on the defecation sandals," and further it is stated that "one should lift [the garment] while standing on the rinsing sandals.
The meaning is that one should not rinse while making the sound "capu capū. This concludes the determination concerning the place for defecation and urination.
The commentary on the description of the place for urine and excrement is finished.
17. Commentary on the Description of Making a Request.
161. "By the elder" means by the senior of the Saṅgha.
162. Among all those assembled here and there, the one who is the most senior is the "elder" (*vuḍḍha-vuḍḍhatara*).

When that most senior person has arrived, there is no need for further formal permission (*āpucchana*). Regarding the phrase "and he expresses his appreciation at the meal hall" (*bhattagge cānumodati*), they say that it is permissible for a junior elder who has been requested by the donor to speak without having obtained permission from the [senior] elders.

163. “In a single dwelling” (*ekavihārake*) means that while staying in one room with an elder, one should not recite [the scriptures] without having asked permission; this is the meaning. “He does not give the recitation or the interrogation” (*uddesaṃ paripucchañca no dadeti*) means that he would not grant either the recitation or the interrogation.
164. “One should neither open nor bolt it”—this is the connection [of the sentence]. A “door” (*dvāra*) refers to a large gateway; in that case, there is no requirement to ask permission. 165.

“Even while walking back and forth on the walkway (*caṅkama*) with an elder, one should turn around toward where the elder is”—this is the connection. This concludes the analysis of the procedure regarding asking permission (*āpucchakaraṇavinicchaya*).
The commentary on the exposition of requesting permission is finished.
18. Commentary on the Exposition of Being Naked: 166.
Because it is stated, “One must not come naked; whoever should come so incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” it is said, “One should not travel the road naked.”
167. *Paṭicchādisūti*: "Now at that time, monks were scrupulous about performing massage both in the sauna and in the water.
'I allow you, monks, three kinds of coverings: a sauna-covering, a water-covering, and a cloth-covering'—the meaning is, regarding these three coverings thus spoken of. *Duve* means two."
The intention is that among these three types of coverings, those that cover a water-jentāghara (a bathhouse with water) are permissible for the purpose of preparation.

"Cloth-covering" means a covering made of cloth. "In all cases" means they are allowable for all tasks, such as those involving solid food, drinks, and so forth. This concludes the determination regarding nakedness.
The commentary on the explanation of nakedness is finished.
19. Commentary on the explanation of the rules regarding bathing: 168.
“In front” means in front of the elders or above them; the meaning is that one should not bathe [there].
169–171. Regarding the phrase *kuṭṭathambhataruṭṭāne*: here the meaning is that one should not rub the body against a wall, a pillar, a tree, or a wooden board.
A "gandhabbahattha" (wooden puppet hand) is made of wood or similar materials and resembles the hand of a monkey. "With a kuruvindakasūci" means with a kuruvinda needle.
[One should not rub] with a water-pot or against each other. "Monks, you must not... [The rest of the rule follows].
"Having quarreled, one should have the preparatory work (parikamma) done. Whoever should have it done, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
This was said with reference to the "quarreling preparatory work," which is why it is stated as "or mutually.
Now, in order to show what is allowable (kappiya), he says "fragments of potsherds and bricks," and so forth. The connection is that this is permissible for all.
For both the sick and the healthy, these items such as skull-shaped stones and potsherds are permitted for rubbing the body.
"Puthupāṇi" refers to hand-massage; therefore, it is permitted for everyone to perform back-massage with the hand.
What is called "akatamallaka" is that which is made by carving out a single tooth-mark. Stones and the like are [permitted] only for rubbing the feet.
Permissible. The determination of what is permissible regarding bathing.
The commentary on the exposition of what is permissible regarding bathing is finished.
20. Commentary on the Exposition of Those Not to Be Venerated.

172. Because it is stated, “One who belongs to a different community (nānāsaṃvāsaka) who is senior and speaks contrary to the Dhamma is not to be saluted,” here the term “one who belongs to a different community” refers to one who holds a different view (laddhinānāsaṃvāsaka).

Those deserving of probation (pārivāsika), those deserving of being sent back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanāraha), those deserving of penance (mānattāraha), those practicing penance (mānattacārin), and those deserving of rehabilitation (abbhānāraha) are included here as being of heavy status.
However, these individuals receive salutations and other honors from one another according to their seniority.
The intention is that one who is a *pakatatta* (one of normal status) is not to be saluted. The determination regarding those not to be saluted is concluded.
The commentary on the exposition of those not to be saluted is finished.
21. Commentary on the Exposition of Leather.
173. Now, in order to show the hides mentioned in the passage, “I allow you, monks, in all border regions, hides as coverings:
sheepskin, goatskin, and deer skin,” he said, “deer, goat, and sheep skins,” and so forth.
“To use” means that it is permissible to spread them on beds or anywhere else and lie down or sit upon them.

The meaning is as follows: the *rohitena* and the *pasada*, the *kuruṅga*, and by the word "and" (*ca*), the intention is that other wild beasts (*vāḷamiga*) such as the *migamātuka* and others are also of the same class of deer.
174. Regarding the phrase "another because it has been permitted":
"The monkey, the black lion, the *sarabha*, and the *kadalī* deer;"
"And whatever wild beasts there are, their hides are not permitted.

Here, by the mention of "wild beasts," it should be understood that all remaining animals, down to cows, buffaloes, and so forth, are included. "Thavika" (a bag) should be understood as a bag for sandals, a case for a knife, or a key-case; it does not refer to bags for bowls and the like. The determination regarding hides is concluded.
The commentary on the description of hides is finished.
22. Commentary on the Description of Sandals (Upāhananiddesavaṇṇanā) 175.
"Sandals with multiple layers" refers to those starting from four layers upwards, not those starting from one, two, or three layers. [The Buddha said:
"Monks, I allow sandals with a single layer; monks, sandals with double layers must not be worn."
Because it was said: "Sandals with triple layers must not be worn; sandals with multiple layers of straps must not be worn. Whoever should wear them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
And because it was said: "I allow you, monks, sandals that have had their straps removed;
but new sandals with multiple layers of straps must not be worn, monks. Whoever should wear them, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Therefore, [the word] "new" is used.
It has been stated. It should be understood that in all cases within the Middle Country, even a sick person does not receive a new multi-layered sandal;

they may receive only one that has been used by others and is classified as a discarded sandal. However, in the outlying regions, it should be known that even a sick person receives a new one. Thus [the Buddha said]: "I allow you, monks, in all outlying regions..."
Because it is stated without distinction as "sandals with many layers of leather" (*guṇaṅguṇūpāhana*).

"Of all" means of both the sick and the healthy. Even in the Middle Country or the Border Countries, whether in a monastery (*ārāma*) or in its vicinity (*ārāmūpacāra*), for both the sick and the healthy, [the Buddha said]: "Monks, I allow you to wear sandals within the monastery."
The meaning is that it is "allowable" because it has been so stated. "In all places" means both in the monastery and in the village. "For one who is not well" means for one who is ill.
Herein, in the Middle Country, sandals with multiple layers of leather that have already been used by the sick are permitted both in the monastery and in the village;

in the bordering regions, they are permitted even if they have not been used. Furthermore, in both the Middle Country and the bordering regions, [this applies] only for the sick, as ordained by the Blessed One.
Footwear was permitted because it was stated: "Monks, I allow one whose feet are painful, whose feet are cracked, or who has the affliction of corns on the feet, to wear footwear";
and also because it was stated: "Monks, I allow a sick monk to enter a village wearing footwear.
Furthermore, in the Middle Country, a sick person may wear new, multi-layered footwear.
If it is obtained, how is it a partial prescription (*padesapaññatti*)? In all cases, however, sandals were permitted by the Blessed One only for one who is ill;
therefore, they say that in the Middle Country, one who is ill may take new sandals with multiple linings.
176–9. "All blue" means entirely blue. This same method applies everywhere regarding white and so forth. As for "white,"...
It should be understood that this is not prohibited in either the *Pāḷi* or the *Aṭṭhakathā*, but rather it is prohibited here by way of its being contrary to the rule (*anuloma*).
"Dyed with the great dye" means having the color of the back of a centipede. "Dyed with the great-named dye" means faintly dyed. "Mañjeṭṭhika" has the color of the *kaṇavera* flower.
"Variegated" means adorned with various flowers, fruits, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "increased by blue, yellow, and so on," the word "and so on" (*ādi*) [includes other colors].
The dyer is included by way of [dyes] such as yellowish-white, red, madder, vermilion, and the dye of the Mahānāma tree.
The connection is with the hides of lions, tigers, leopards, and dholes. "Anyone" refers to both the sick and the healthy.

(180) The meaning is that one may use it after wiping the entire or a partial portion of the dye with a cloth. However, everything such as the leather straps must be discarded before use. This concludes the determination regarding sandals.
The commentary on the description of sandals is finished.
23. Commentary on the Description of Not Looking At: 181.
"A woman" refers even to a girl born on that very day. She might look at her own face in a mirror or in a bowl of water.

“For him there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)” is the connection [of the sentence]. Because it has been stated, “Monks, I allow you, on account of illness, to look at the reflection of the face in a mirror or in a bowl of water,” it is permissible to look at the reflection in a mirror and so forth, or to look at the formative factors of life (āyusaṅkhāra) in this way: “Am I decrepit, or am I not?
This is the determination regarding what is not to be looked at.
The commentary on the description of the looking-glass is finished.
24. Commentary on the Description of the Eye-Cosmetic Box (Añjanī) 182.
The meaning is that an eye-cosmetic box is suitable provided it is round or has eight or sixteen facets, is polished, and is undecorated with flowers, fruit, and so forth.
All three are permissible; the intention is that there is no discussion regarding only one or two.
"Lines" refers to circular lines. "To bind" means for the purpose of securing a lid.

183. "Form" refers to the form of a bird and so forth. If one obtains such an object made by others, it may be used after rubbing it down, cutting it, or wrapping it with thread in such a way that its original appearance is no longer recognizable.
184. *Thavikā* means an ointment box (*añjanī-thavikā*). It is connected [with the following] as "the ointment stick (*añjanī-salākā*) is also permitted.

185–6. *Aṭṭhi* (bone) refers to all bones except for human bone. Regarding horns and tusks, there is nothing that is considered *akappiya* (unallowable). "Made of fruit" refers to those made from *āmalaka* (myrobalan) paste and the like. "Made of that" (*tammaya*) means produced from exactly those materials mentioned here. This concludes the determination of the ointment box (*añjanī-vinicchaya*).
The commentary on the description of the ointment box (*añjanī-niddesa-vaṇṇanā*) is finished.
25. Commentary on the Description of Improper Beds (Akappiya-sayana-niddesa) 187–9:

Because of the statement, “A high chair has arisen; I allow you, monks, even a high chair,” [it is permitted] to have legs exceeding eight finger-breadths of the Sugata’s measure by one side, provided that side is equal to half the measurement of a bed.
Here, "stool" (āsandi) is what is intended; however, a four-legged stool is permitted even if it exceeds the prescribed measure.
"Cushion" (tūli) refers to a natural cotton mattress. A "divan" (pallaṅka) is said to be one made with imported animal skins.

Regarding that very point, they say: "Furthermore, one made displaying figures such as lions is permitted. "Blanket" (paṭika) is a white covering. "Cow-hide patterned" (gonacittaka): here, the hair must not exceed four finger-breadths.
A *kojava* is called a "woolen rug" (*gonaka*). Because it is stated in the *Cīvarakkhandhaka* that "I allow, monks, a *kojava*," a standard *kojava* made of four-finger-widths of wool is permitted.
One with jewel-patterns or decorative designs is not permitted.
A *paṭalī* is a thick, red floral coverlet. A *vikatī* is a woolen coverlet variegated with the forms of lions, tigers, and so forth.
*Uddalomī* is a rug with the nap rising on one side. *Ekantalomikā* is a rug with the nap rising on both sides.
*Kutta* is a woolen carpet suitable for sixteen dancing girls to stand upon and perform a dance.
*Koseyya* is a spread made of silk thread, sewn around the edges with gems. *Kaṭṭissa* is [a spread] sewn around the edges with gems.
A cotton or silk bedspread (*paccattharaṇa*). Silk and wool that are sewn with gems are not permitted;
those that are plain are permitted. "Elephant, horse, and chariot rugs" refers specifically to the rugs spread upon those [animals].
"Antelope-skin mats" (*ajinappaveṇī*) means mats made by sewing together antelope skins to the size of a bed; by this, the skin of the *kadalī* deer is meant.
A "pre-eminent spread" (*pavarappaccattharaṇa*) is one made by spreading out and sewing together white cloth; a "pre-eminent spread of kadali-deer skin" is one spread with that.
And when it is spread upon that, it is "spread upon a pre-eminent spread of kadali-deer skin and a layer of antelope skins.
Even beneath a white canopy, if there is an improper spread, it is not permitted; [it is only permitted] if there is a proper spread.
If it exists [as a separate item], it is permissible; however, even if there is a suitable cloth spread beneath a red canopy, it is still not permissible.
A pillow for the head or a pillow for the feet—that is, a pillow with red borders on both sides—is not permissible.
But if there is only one pillow, and it is red, lotus-colored, or patterned at both ends, provided it is of the proper size, [it is permissible].
It is permissible; however, the *mahāupadhāna* (large cushion) is prohibited.
190. Regarding the "triad beginning with the *āsandi*": *āsandi*, *tūlī*, and *pallaṅka*—this is what is called the triad. "Monks, I allow you to sit upon anything except these three:
the *āsandi*, the *pallaṅka*, and the *tūlī*; the rest may be used as household furniture. It is not, however, [permissible to lie down].
For it is said, "to lie down upon. The meaning is that it is permitted to sit on the remainder belonging to householders.

If, even on a Dhamma-seat belonging to the Saṅgha, the monastery attendants and others, without being instructed by the bhikkhus, themselves prepare and remove items such as woolen rugs (*gonaka*), this is called "removal of what was brought by householders" (*gihivikaṭanīhāra*);
it is permissible by means of this removal of what was brought by householders. [The term] *bhattagga* (refectory) is...
The place for giving is indeed within the monastery.
(191) By way of four legs and three supports on the sides, it is seven-limbed; when joined with one side, it is five-limbed.
These seven-limbed and five-limbed [beds] are referred to by the rule: "Monks, I allow even high seven-limbed [beds]."
Because it has been so stated, they are permissible even if they exceed the prescribed measurements. Therefore it is said: "with high legs.
The connection is that beds and chairs upholstered with wool are allowable only for sitting upon within the house.
192. "Cīvaracchaviyo" means the surface of any one of the six types of robes or the six types of *anuloma* robes.
The meaning is: "In all places" means on a bed, on a chair, in the dining hall, or within a house.
Furthermore, there is no fixed limit for the size of these mattresses; one should determine the size by observing what is appropriate for beds, chairs, and so forth.
193. "A cotton mattress (tūlikā) has arisen. I allow you, monks, having unraveled it, to make a bolster (bimbohana); three..."
Because it is stated, "cottons: tree-cotton, creeper-cotton, and pod-cotton," these three types of cotton are permitted for stuffing (*bimbohana*).
It should be understood that by means of these three types of cotton, the cotton of all trees, creepers, and grasses is authorized.

However, in the case of a mattress (*bhisi*), no cotton whatsoever is permitted. Regarding "the interior of the mattress" (*bhisigabbha*), this refers to the fivefold group beginning with cloth (*coḷa*) mentioned in the context of the mattress, which is used for stuffing.
The connection is with the word "allowed" (anuññātaṃ). Regarding "beasts and birds": the hair of all four-footed animals such as lions, and of all birds such as swans and peacocks, is permitted.
The connection is with the phrase "allowed for a cushion" (masūrake anuññātaṃ). 194.
Now, in order to show what is permitted and what is not permitted regarding a mattress (bhisi), he said "human hair," and so forth. Regarding "wool" (uṇṇāya): this refers to a woolen mattress.
The meaning is that human hair is not permitted. Regarding the woolen mat (*uṇṇābhisi*), with the exception of human hair, the hair of any kind of bird or quadruped is suitable;
this is the meaning. Regarding the leaf mat (*paṇṇa*): neither a leaf mat nor flowers nor pure *tamāla* leaves are permitted;
the meaning is that any other kind of leaf whatsoever is permitted. As for the *tamāla* leaf...
"It is permissible for it to be mixed with other [materials]. There is nothing that is *akappiya* (unallowable) among cotton, bark-fiber, or grass.

The statement regarding the seat was made by way of extension because, due to its commonality as a "seat," an unexamined seat is not permitted. This concludes the determination of what is unallowable regarding beds.
The commentary on the description of unallowable beds is finished.
26. Commentary on the Exposition of Sitting Together (Samānāsanikaniddesavaṇṇanā) 195.

"The interval of three years" (*tivassantara*) means within the space of three years. For it is said: "I allow you, monks, to sit together with one who is within the interval of three years. Whether he is senior or junior, one who has been ordained for two years is called "within the interval of three years.
196. "The Sage" (*muni*) refers to the Buddha, the Sage. "All indeed" includes even those who are not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*).
197. "The last [measure] is the minimum. Because it was said, "Monks, I allow that which is sufficient for three;

this much is the minimum length for a long seat," therefore, whatever is sufficient for three—whether it be portable or not portable—even on such pieces of wooden planks, it is permissible to sit. "For two" means for two people who share the same seat.
“Monks, I allow a bed for a group of two and a bench for a group of two,” because it was said thus, two who are *samānāsana* (those sharing a common seat) are permitted to sit together.

However, even if there are two, they are not permitted to sit with others who are not *samānāsana*, or with those who have not received full ordination (*anupasampanna*), and so forth. This is the determination regarding *samānāsana*.
The commentary on the exposition of those who share a seat is finished.
27. Commentary on the exposition of those who are not in communion. 198.
"One who has been suspended" means one who has been suspended for not seeing an offense, for not making amends for an offense, or for not relinquishing an evil view.

“Or one who has been suspended”—here, all three types of those suspended are included. By the term “one not fully ordained,” it should be understood that the trainee nun (*sikkhamānā*), the novice monk (*sāmaṇera*), the novice nun (*sāmaṇerī*), and those who have renounced the training are included.
One whose roots are severed is one who has committed an ultimate offense (*antimavatthu*). One of a different communion is one whose communion is different due to their views.
“One might perform an act with a fourth member standing within a different boundary; one might perform an act with a fourth member standing in the air by means of psychic power.”
Because it is stated, "it is not an act and is not to be performed," these too are called "those who do not live in communion" (*asaṃvāsika*).
However, one who performs the *uposatha* and other ceremonies together with those who have been suspended (*ukkhitaka*) incurs an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).

For one who performs them with those who are outside the boundary (*nissīmaṭṭha*), those who are insane (*vehāsaṭṭha*), or those who have renounced the training (*sikkhaṃ paccakkhāta*), the formal act (*kamma*) is invalid and there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); for the others, there is an offense of wrong-doing. This is the determination regarding those who do not live in communion.
The commentary on the description of those who are not in communion is finished.
28. Commentary on the Description of Formal Acts (Kammaniddesa) 199.
Regarding the phrase "an illegal formal act" (*adhammakamma*): if it is asked how an act becomes illegal, it has been stated by the Blessed One as follows:

“And what, bhikkhus, is an illegal procedure (*adhammakamma*)? If, bhikkhus, in a procedure that requires a motion and a second [announcement], one performs the act with only the motion and does not proclaim the formal statement (*kammavācā*), it is an illegal procedure.
If one performs the act with two motions and does not proclaim the formal statement, it is an illegal procedure.
If one performs the act with one formal statement and does not [complete it]...”

If one establishes a motion (*ñatti*) [but does not proceed with the formal act], it is an illegitimate legal procedure (*adhammakamma*). If one carries out the legal procedure with two proclamations (*kammavācā*) but does not establish a motion, it is an illegitimate legal procedure.

In this same manner, it should be understood that in the case of the remaining legal procedures as well, performing them otherwise than the prescribed method—by failing to do what has been stated—is an illegitimate legal procedure.
"By an incomplete assembly" means by an incomplete *saṅgha*. And how is it incomplete? If as many bhikkhus as are entitled to participate in the formal act have not arrived;
or if the consent of those entitled to give their consent has not been brought;
or if those present raise an objection—by any one of these factors, it is an incomplete act.
“By a unanimous assembly” means by a Saṅgha that is complete. If it is asked, “How is it complete?”: as many bhikkhus as are entitled to participate in the formal act have arrived;
the consent of those who are eligible to give their consent has been brought forth; those present do not protest; thus it is a “unanimous act.
“The fourth” refers to that which is lawful and performed by a unanimous assembly. To this extent, [it is said]: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of formal acts: those contrary to the Dhamma...”

It should be understood that these four formal acts (*kamma*) have been thus defined: a factional act, a united act contrary to the Dhamma, a factional act in accordance with the Dhamma, and a united act in accordance with the Dhamma.
200–202. [The groups] of ten, twenty, and ten-and-twenty; [the formal acts of] rehabilitation, full ordination, and the invitation (*pavāraṇā*).
The connection is: "having set aside [others], he has reached the stage for the formal act (*kamma*) in all [other] acts. The same applies to the remaining cases.
"The other" refers to both a group of twenty and a group exceeding twenty. 203.
Now, in order to show those who have reached the stage for the formal act and those who are eligible to give their consent (*chanda*), it is said: "by a group of four," and so forth. Therein—

"Those who are regular members" (*pakatattā*) means those who are not of a different communion due to having been expelled for a *pārājika* offense or due to other grounds. "Others" refers to regular member monks residing within the same boundary.

If regular member monks have entered and are staying in any village boundary, or in any of the river, ocean, or lake boundaries, they are neither eligible to participate in the formal act (*kamma*) nor entitled to give their consent (*chanda*). For it is not [the case] for them...
Either the consent (*chanda*) or the purity (*pārisuddhi*) arrives [from outside] because [the person] is standing within another boundary (*sīmā*).

"The rest also" means even in the case of formal acts (*kamma*) to be performed by a group of five or more. 204. Or, having made a group that does not constitute a formal assembly (*asaṃvāsa-gaṇa*) complete, the act performed is invalid (*kuppa*), and there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for those who perform it.
"If the Saṅgha performs a formal act against someone, and one who belongs to that [person's] faction acts as the fourth member, it is not a valid act and should not be performed."
Because it has been stated [that the assembly must consist of those worthy of the act], it is said: "or a group sufficient to complete the number for the act.

Now, in order to show the deficiency of the assembly specifically regarding acts such as *parivāsa* (probation), it is said: "or a group sufficient to complete the number for a grave matter. That too is said with reference to one who has not relinquished his duties;
however, one who has relinquished his duties is indeed a completer of the number in every case.
205. *Vāreyya* means one should object. For it has been said: "I allow you, monks, to protest when an illegal act (*adhammakamma*) is being performed.
