The meaning is: "If there is an obstacle [to the proceeding]. The meaning is that two or three [monks] should mutually manifest their view, saying: "This is an illegal act; this is not acceptable to me. If there is only one, he should say: "This is not acceptable to me."
The meaning is: "One should make a formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) in this way. Up to this point, these [monks] become free from offense and are released from obstacles;
however, because the legal act (*kamma*) is contrary to the Dhamma, it remains indeed invalid. Regarding the phrase "preventing those who exceed that," it says here:
"Monks, I allow you to protest against four or five [monks], to make one's view known to two or three, and for one person to make a formal determination: 'No...'"
Because it is said, "Does this agree with you?", the meaning is that four or five [monks] stop [the proceedings]. 206.
Now, in order to show those by whom [the action] is rejected, the words beginning with "one deserving of a formal act" (kammāraha) are spoken.

Therein, by the inclusion of "one whose mind is deranged" (khittacitta), one who is insane (ummattaka) is also included. The meaning is that for those of the aforementioned types, the rejection does not hold.
207. Now, in order to show for whom a protest is valid, it is said: "of a regular monk (pakatatta) who stands within the same boundary and is of the same communion.
The meaning of this is: a protest against such a monk is valid even when voiced by one who is immediately next to him.
"Monks, [the protest] of a regular monk who is of the same communion and stands within the same boundary..."
It is said: "Even when making a request to a monk who is sitting right next to him, an objection raised in the midst of the Saṅgha is valid.

(208) The meaning is: "If he should object in the presence [of the Saṅgha]. "In the absence" means behind their backs. The meaning is: "If he should not give either his physical cooperation or his consent, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
This concludes the determination of the legal act. The commentary on the exposition of legal acts is finished.
29. Explanation of the Description of Avoiding Wrong Livelihood (Micchājīvavivajjanāniddesavaṇṇanā) 209.
"Powders" (cuṇṇa) means such things as sirīsa-powder and so forth. "Clay" (mattikā) refers to either natural clay, five-colored clay, or pure substances such as red arsenic (kuṅkuma) and the like.
"Gathering families" (kulasaṅgaha) means the act of gathering families for the purpose of obtaining gain from those who have been gathered by these [means].

This is the meaning. Furthermore, it is not permissible to give anything belonging to the Saṅgha or to an individual to those included among these [categories] with the thought, "I shall receive something from them.
By this same principle, what is obtained [in such a manner] is not permissible even for one's five fellow practitioners of the Dhamma, and it constitutes wrong livelihood.
210–211. "Lifting up children for the sake of gain from donors" refers to the state of being a servant (*pāribhaṭaka*);
the connection is that one should not live by such servitude. The same method applies to the remaining cases as well.

"Sending errands" (*paheṇakamma*) is the act of going when dispatched to fields and so forth. "Messenger work" (*dūtakamma*) is the carrying of messages and counter-messages. "Going from house to house" refers to the movement of one who has been dispatched from one residence to another.
*Jaṅghapesaniyaṃ*: the giving and offering of bribes out of a desire for gain. *Aññena vā*: by means of other [methods], such as the science of bodily marks (*aṅgavijjā*) and so forth.
212. *Viññatti*: requesting from one who is not related. *Anesanā*: the seeking of requisites by means of the previously mentioned giving of flowers and so forth. *Kuhanādīhi*:
by means of hypocrisy (*kuhana*), flattery (*lapana*), hinting (*nemittakatā*), belittling others (*nippesikatā*), and pursuing gain with gain (*lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatā*).
The meaning is: "by these five grounds. The analysis of wrong livelihood is concluded.
The commentary on the exposition of the avoidance of wrong livelihood is finished.
30. Commentary on the Exposition of Conduct.
213. Now, in order to show the duties for newcomers and so forth, the heading-word “duties” (*vatta*) is raised.

Having reached the enclosure of an enclosed monastery, or, in the case of an unenclosed one, a place defined by two stone-throw distances, one should remove the sandals, set them down low, dust them off, take hold of the sandals with a staff, and put away the sunshade.
The meaning is that one should enter the monastery carefully and without haste, having uncovered the head and placed the robe over the shoulder.
214. Regarding "one should ask about the lodgings": the meaning is that one should ask in this way: "Which lodging has fallen to me? Is it already occupied or unoccupied? 215–6.
Wooden articles such as beds and chairs, and earthenware articles such as dye-vessels and the like. "Having asked permission" refers to [asking] the bhikkhu.
The meaning is: having addressed a novice (sāmaṇera) or a monastery attendant (ārāmika), saying, "Friend, look after this.
"Otherwise" means not doing it in this way. 217–8.
Regarding "an elder who has arrived": if, having seen him from afar, one recognizes that he is an elder, then even before he has arrived—
The meaning is that the duty of arranging the seats and so forth must be performed.
"Starting with water for the feet" means that water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot-scraper should be set out.
When asking for drinking water, if he drinks all the water brought once, he must ask again. He arranges it [saying], "This is your lodging."
The meaning is that it should be explained in this way: "He attains [it].

219–20. The alms-village should be described as being either "far from here" or "near," or it should be described as a "range" where one must go for alms early in the morning, or where one must go among one's supporters. A non-range refers to those who hold wrong views.
“Village” means a village where alms are distributed, or a village where alms are given to only one or two [monks];
that is what should be pointed out—this is the meaning. “Agreement” (katikā) refers to a place where the Saṅgha has made an agreement.
The time for entering and the time for departing should be announced in this way: “One should enter at this time; one should depart at this time. In some places...
Or there may be non-human beings or wild beasts; therefore, it must indeed be announced in this way. "While sitting" indicates merely the absence of an offense;
even having stood up, it is entirely permissible to perform all [the required duties]. The analysis of the duties is concluded.
The commentary on the description of the duties is finished.
31. Commentary on the Exposition of the Allocation (Vikappanāniddesa) 221.

"In the presence" (*sammukhā*) means: standing in the presence [of the person]. "To one who is competent" (*byattassa*) means: to one who knows the procedure for allocation (*vikappanā*) as well as the procedures for relinquishing (*paccuddharana*) and so forth.
The meaning is that an incompetent person, even if they take it thinking, "This has been given to me by him," might still depart. "Of one" (*ekassa*) means: of a single monk.

222. *Nidhetuṃ vā* means precisely for the purpose of storing away; the meaning is that it does not become an article to be forfeited (*nissaggiya*). The meaning is that it is not permitted to use, to dispose of, or to formally resolve upon (*adhiṭṭhātuṃ*) it.

224–5. *Aparā sammukhā vā* means that this is indeed a formal resolution (*vikappanā*) in the presence [of another]. These two types of resolution are called "resolutions in the presence" because, after one has resolved them oneself, they are caused to be relinquished (*paccuddharāpita*) by another.
227. *Mitta* means a firm friend. *Sandiṭṭha* means merely someone seen, not a very firm friend. "By the other... previously... [refers to]... [text fragment].
According to the method already stated, it should be said, “Three bhikkhus,” or “To the bhikkhunī Tissā.
Then, having made the assignment by saying, “I give [this] to the bhikkhu Tissa, or to the bhikkhunī Tissā,” he himself should say, “Use what belongs to the bhikkhu Tissa,
or to the bhikkhunī Tissā, or dispose of it, or do with it as you see fit.”
The reading should be understood as: “it must be relinquished.
Regarding the phrase “one should discern distance and proximity, unity and plurality”: here the meaning is, “having discerned distance, proximity, unity, and plurality.
Because it is stated, “An extra robe may be kept for a maximum of ten days,” the expression “for ten days” is used.
Because it is stated, “The time for robes is called: when the *kathina* has not been spread, the last month of the rains;
when the *kathina* has been spread, five months,” it is said, “for one month or for five. The meaning is: for one month or for five months.
“If an out-of-season robe should arise for a monk, that monk, if he so desires, may accept it.”

"Having received it, it must be made up immediately. If there is no completion, that monk may store that robe for at most one month, provided there is a hope for the completion of what is deficient. Because this was said, it is stated: "If there is hope, [the period is] one month.
"He does not incur [an offense]" means he does not generate a *nissaggiya* offense for failing to formally determine (*adhiṭṭhita*) or assign (*vikappita*) [the robe].
The meaning. The Determination of the Formal Acts of Assignment (*Vikappanāvinicchaya*).
The commentary on the exposition of the formal acts of assignment (*Vikappanāniddesavaṇṇanā*) is finished.
32. Commentary on the Exposition of the Support (*Nissayaniddesavaṇṇanā*).

230. Regarding the term "byatta" (learned): if one asks, "To what extent is one learned?"—one must, by means of the very minimum requirement for release from dependence, make both the Mātikās (matrices) thoroughly mastered and committed to memory, both in their meaning and in their phrasing.

Furthermore, on the fortnightly observance days, for the purpose of reciting the Dhamma, four recitation-sections (bhāṇavāra) from the Suttanta should be mastered for the sake of those assemblies who have gathered.
There is one method of discourse, such as the *Dhammakkhandha* spoken to Mahā Rāhula at Andhakavinda, for the purpose of general instruction;

three kinds of thanksgiving (*anumodanā*) for the purpose of expressing gratitude on occasions such as meals provided by the Saṅgha or auspicious and inauspicious events; the determination of what constitutes a formal act (*kamma*) and what does not, for the purpose of understanding the Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, and other procedures;
and [the practice] by way of concentration (*samādhi*) or insight (*vipassanā*) for the purpose of performing the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).
This single meditation subject, culminating in Arahantship, is what must be mastered. To this extent one is called "proficient" in the four directions;
otherwise, one is unproficient. 231.

Now, in order to show the manner of taking formal dependence (*nissaya*), the words beginning with "on one side" (*ekamsa*) were spoken. Here, "of the Venerable One" (*āyasmato*) means [the speech] directed toward the Venerable One (*āyasmantaṃ*).
232. Now, in order to show the methods for the cessation of dependence (*nissaya*), it is said: “When he has departed,” and so forth. [The Sutta states:
“Bhikkhus, there are these five cessations of dependence from a preceptor (*upajjhāya*). The preceptor has departed; or he has left the Order; or he has died;
or he has joined another faction; or the fifth is by formal authorization. “Bhikkhus, there are these six cessations of dependence... [and so on].

"From the teacher. This refers to both cases shown here: when the teacher has departed, or has left the order, or has died, or has gone over to another faction—wherein the fifth [condition] is simply by command—or when he has come together with the preceptor.
If the teacher and the preceptor are living even in neighboring monasteries that are not enclosed, within the distance of two throws of a clod.
The dependence (nissaya) is not suspended. Some say it is not suspended even within an enclosed area (parikkhitta), but the Teachers do not accept this.
Why? Because the suspension of the taking of dependence and the suspension [of the dependence] are delimited by the precinct boundary (upacāra-sīmā).
Furthermore, the delimitation of the precinct boundary by the range of a stone’s throw is possible only in unenclosed areas, not in enclosed ones.
Therefore, one must abide by the determination of the teachers.

Regarding the term "has departed": if the teacher crosses the boundary of the precincts (*upacārasīma*) without having taken leave of the resident pupil (*antevāsika*), the formal dependence (*nissaya*) is suspended.
If he turns back without having crossed the boundary of the precincts, it is not suspended.
The same rule applies when a pupil goes away without taking leave of his teacher.
If the teacher wishes to go somewhere and asks the pupil for permission, and the pupil accepts by saying, “Very well, very well,” then at that very moment the offense is extinguished.
The same applies when the pupil goes away after having asked the teacher’s permission. Even when both remain within the monastery, if the teacher—
If a teacher or a pupil goes beyond two *leḍḍu-pāta*s (the distance of a stone’s throw) without having first requested permission from one another, the offense is extinguished.
It is also extinguished at that very moment if the pupil has gone over to another faction, has left the Order, or has died.
"Command" (*āṇatti*) means the granting of formal dependence (*nissaya*). "Combination" (*samodhāna*) is twofold, by way of seeing and hearing.
233. Regarding the term *alajjī*:
here it refers to one who intentionally commits an offense and conceals that offense.
"He goes upon a wrong course;
such a person is called one who lacks a sense of shame.
Thus it was said. For it has been stated: "Monks, you should not live in dependence on one who lacks a sense of shame. Whoever should so live, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."
234. “I allow, monks, for a monk traveling on a journey who cannot obtain formal dependence (nissaya) to live without dependence,” because this was said, the term “for one on a journey” is used.
And the connection is: “and for one who has requested [to attend] the sick. “I allow, monks, for a monk attending the sick who cannot obtain formal dependence...”
"For it is said: 'When one is being asked, [one should give] a site without being dependent. By 'observing what is comfortable' is meant observing a comfortable dwelling.

However, this exemption is not obtained by a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer or the like, nor by an ordinary worldling who has attained firm serenity and insight. But for one whose serenity and insight are still tender...

One who has reached firmness (thāmagata) receives it. If there is no one to provide formal support (nissaya), one may stay until the full moon of Āsāḷhī by making the mental resolve: "When a suitable provider of support arrives, then I shall dwell under his support.
However, if one does not find a provider of support during the month of Āsāḷhī, one must go to a place where one exists. During the rains retreat (antovassa)...

However, it is not permissible to reside [in a monastery] without being under formal dependence (*nissaya*). The application of the rule should be made in all instances thus: "If there is no suitable donor [to provide support], one is permitted to reside.
This concludes the determination regarding dependence (*nissaya-vinicchaya*).
The commentary on the exposition of dependence (*nissaya-niddesa-vaṇṇanā*) is finished.
33. Commentary on the Description of the Waistband (Kāyabandhananiddesa) 235.
“Without a waistband” means not having fastened a waistband. From that point onward, the robe should be put on;
from that very point onward, the waistband should be fastened. “Monks, one should not enter a village without a waistband.”
"One must enter. Whoever should enter, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). For it is thus said.
"Gone while absent-minded" means that one who has gone absent-minded must fasten [the belt] at the very place where he remembers.

However, once he has remembered, it is not permitted to wander for alms until he has fastened it. If he remembers while inside the village, provided there is a waist-band, [he should fasten it] in a secluded spot.
It is said that one should fasten it after standing; if not, they say one should go out, fasten it, and then re-enter for alms.
236. Because it was stated, "Monks, I allow two kinds of waistbands:
the *paṭṭika* and the *sūkarantaka*," it is called "twofold. Therein, the *sūkarantaka* is so named because its ends are made hollow like a key-case.
“Pounded” (*koṭṭitaṃ*). “And a single cord” (*rajju ca ekaṃ*) means a cord that is a single strand. “Suitable for those two” (*tadanulomikā*) means suitable for those two [types of cloth].

237. Regarding the phrase “fish-bones, dates, smooth strips, and so forth,” the intention here is that these—namely, the fish-bones and so on—which are smooth and free from alteration, as well as the strips, are included therein.
“Four fringes are permissible” (*labbhā dasā catasso*) means by one...
The intention is that there is no conversation at all regarding two or three [fingers]; beyond that, it is not permitted.
"At the ends" means at both ends. "Double-string" means a string of double strands.
Regarding the phrase "starting from the makara-mouth," by the word "etcetera" (ādi), the head of the *deḍḍubha* (crocodile) is included. "At both ends" means at both extremities.

"Kassā" means "of which. "Ghaṭakā" means "from the border. "Lekhā" means "by the line. The meaning is that no other painting is permitted than from the border and by the line. 240. "Deḍḍubhaka" means resembling the head of a water-snake.
"Muraja" refers to [a drum] made by gathering many strings together on one side.
Having wound it with a single string, which string? The *maddavīṇā* is like a *pāmaṅga*. The *kalābu* has many coils.
However, none of these are permitted. Regarding "two middle ones among the ten fringes": only the *muraja* and the *maddavīṇā* are of medium size.
"Kappare" means they are permitted (*kappanti*).
241. "And knots" means even the knots for robes. That those made of bamboo and so forth are allowable is mentioned as a corollary. This concludes the analysis of the waistband.
The commentary on the description of the waistband is finished.
The first recitation section.
34. Explanation of the Description of Earth (Pathavīniddesavaṇṇanā) 242.
"Earth is twofold: arisen and unarisen"—this is the meaning. Now, in order to show both of these, he said:
"Pure clay dust," and so forth. Therein, "pure clay dust" refers to that which has not been burnt; "abundant clay dust" refers to a heap of clay and dust more than four months old.

And this is to be connected with the phrase "earth that has arisen. Here, however, "unburnt" means not burnt in various ways, such as by being placed on a hearth for cooking, or by being baked into vessels by a potter, and so forth. This [kind of earth] does not exist separately;
it should be understood as one among pure sand, pure clay, and the like—namely, mostly sand, mostly clay, or a heap of clay and sand that has been rained upon for more than four months.
And "and what has not been burnt" refers to all the earth that has been produced;

this is how it should be understood. 243. "The second" means the earth that has not yet been produced. "The aforementioned heap" means a heap of clay and a heap of soil; the meaning is that these are the earth that has not yet been produced for the purpose of the Cātumāsa rain-rest.
244. Now, regarding those things described as being "mostly clay," "mostly soil," and "mostly gravel":
In order to show what constitutes a "majority," he said, "two parts," and so forth. Therein, the connection is as follows:
of the three parts, that ground which has two parts of clay is "one where the majority is clay.
Even those [grounds] with half sand and so on are indeed allowable, because they do not exceed the allowable portion. "A majority of clay, a majority of sand."
For it is said [in the Vinaya]: "not half clay and half dust. "In the remaining cases as well" means even in the case of those that are mostly dust and so forth.

245. "An offense of expiation (pācittiya) for one who perceives it as grown" is the connection. "A wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who is in doubt" means for one who is uncertain. "There is no offense for one who perceives it as not grown when it is actually grown. 246.

"One [offense] by a single command" means that if he is commanded only once, even if he digs for the whole day, there is only one offense for the one who gave the command. "By speech" means by each individual utterance.

247. In this context, it is not permissible to say, "Dig for fire with nets. However, without specifying [the object], it is permissible to say, "Dig a lotus pond," "dig the earth," "dig a reservoir," "dig a pit," or "dig for tubers. 248.
Regarding the phrase "such as this," the intended meaning here is that other similar expressions of allowable terminology (*kappiyavohāra*) are also permissible.
249. The connection is with the word "to stir up" (*kopetuṃ*). It refers to mud that can be scooped out by means of jars and the like, and which is capable of being drawn out.
"251–2. *Udakasantike patite* (fallen near water) is the connection. However, that which has fallen into water is allowable (*kappiya*) at all times;
therefore, in order to show what is not allowable, it is said "*udakasantike*" (near water).
The connection is: "dust clinging to a stone, and dust fallen from a new sieve. The meaning is: "an anthill situated in the open air, and a mud wall"; likewise [the following].
The meaning is that none of these, even if they exceed four months, should be disturbed.

(253–5) The connection is: "It is not permissible to disturb the ground in order to take up pillars and so forth. (256) "By a stream" means by a stream of urine. The connection is: "I shall show the footprint.
(257) "Sprinkling" (*seka*) means pouring. The connection is: "having placed a wet hand upon the ground."
258. "When there is need" means in times of misfortune such as burns from fire on the hands and so forth. This concludes the analysis of earth (*pathavī-vinicchaya*).
The commentary on the description of earth (*pathavī-niddesa*) is finished.
35. Commentary on the Description of Requisites (*parikkhāra-niddesa*).

259–260. *Girikūṭa* refers to a makara-tooth (makaradantaka) ornament. The phrase "it is not permitted to sew or to cut" is to be applied in all cases. *Daṇḍe* means on the handle of a parasol (*chattadaṇḍe*). 261. The connection is as follows:
it is permissible to draw lines on the handle for the purpose of sewing, for weaving a lattice, or for binding [the cloth] to the handle so that the parasol remains firm.
If one obtains an unallowable parasol of the aforementioned type, [one may use] even a knob (*ghaṭaka*) or a tiger-skin image (*vāḷarūpa*).
Having cut it, it should be worn; even a seam-mark should be rubbed away, or the staff should be wrapped with thread.
262. With reference to the windward side, it is said, "or at the end. With reference to the place where two strips are joined together, it is said, "or at the edge of the strip.
With reference to sewing in the manner of a *varaka*-flower bud, it is called a "plait" (*veṇikā*); and with reference to the form of a hundred-petaled flower...
With reference to sewing, it is said, “or even a chain. The meaning is that other needlework such as that resembling a *satapadi* (centipede) is not permitted;
only ordinary needlework is allowed. The connection is that items such as *pāḷikaṇṇika* (ear-flaps) are not permitted on a robe.
263–4. The connection is that only those with four corners are permitted. *Agghika* means a *agghiya*, which is like a shrine (*cetiyasadisa*). “In this regard” [is the phrase].
Regarding "the cloth for the knotted cords": not only are square knotted cord cloths allowable, but also those with corner-threads and buttons are allowable; this is the meaning.
"Scent or oil" means either scent or oil.

265. "Stained" (*ratta*) means colored. "Or by another" means by a mallet or similar object. "Having made" means having placed. "And not with a fist-blow" means one should not strike with a fist. 266–7.

The connection is that after placing a mark on the rim of the umbrella, a mark is not permitted on the water-vessel (*dhammakaraṇa*). The connection is that a key, a spindle, a jar (*maṇika*), and a pillow (*pīḷaka*) are not permitted. In this context, "jar" (*maṇika*) refers to...
There is only one round gem. There are many pustules resembling the lines on a cowrie shell.
(268–9) Regarding “garlands and so forth on the fire-drill”: the connection is that it is not permissible for the fire-drill to be decorated with garlands and the like for the sake of beauty;

this applies everywhere in the same way. The meaning is that neither painting nor wall-work is permitted on the bowl’s rim when it is smeared with sesame husks. “Having abandoned” means having set aside.
The *sūcisaṇḍāsaka* (needle-tongs) is made of wood for the purpose of pinching a needle to hammer it; it is made so that one may strike it after having bitten it with the needle.

Because it was stated, "Monks, I allow you to carve a *makaradantaka* (crocodile-tooth pattern)," the *makaradantaka* is permitted on the bowl-rim (*pattamaṇḍala*), but no other decorative work such as wall-paintings and the like is permitted.
Therefore, it should be understood that while the *girikūṭa* (mountain-peak pattern) is allowed when placed upon the bowl-rim, it is not permitted in any other location.
272. "Senāsana" means a dwelling such as a palace and so forth. 273.
"Devoid of male and female forms" means devoid of the form of a man and the form of a woman. The analysis of the requisites is complete.
The commentary on the description of the requisites is finished.
36. Commentary on the Description of Medicines (Bhesajjaniddesa) 274–5.
The connection is: "The preparation of medicine is to be obtained from those who share the same Dhamma.

Not only is the preparation of medicine obtained through begging, requesting, or one's own means from these five types of *sahadhammikas* (fellow practitioners), but it is also [obtained] from another five.
Showing that this is possible, he said, “of parents,” and so forth. “Of parents” means of mother and father.
Those mother and father who look after and attend to [one] are called “those who provide attendance. One who lives depending solely on a bhikkhu is called “one dependent on a bhikkhu.
One who desires to go forth is called “a candidate.”
276. It is also appropriate to perform [the offering] for another ten people; to show them, he said, “The father-in-law, the mother-in-law,” and so forth.

Here, however, by taking these eight—namely, the father-in-law, the mother-in-law, the elder brother-in-law, the younger brother-in-law, the elder sister-in-law, the younger sister-in-law, the father’s sister, and the mother’s brother—and including [them] with the word “etc. (*ādi*), there are ten. Of these, however...
It should be made with one's own medicine. The phrase "and when there is no property of one's own" (*attaniye ca asati*) is an ellipsis [to be supplied].

277. Furthermore, it is said "those who corrupt the family" (*kuladūsana*) and so forth in order to show that it is permissible for these ten [types of relatives], as well as for those connected by marriage such as sons, grandsons, and so on, up to the seventh generation of the lineage, to perform [the service]. Also, any other guest...

Whether it be a thief, one defeated in battle, a lord abandoned by his kinsmen, a traveler, or one who has fallen ill, if such a person enters the monastery, medicine should be prepared for all of them without expecting anything in return. 278.
For these—namely, a mother, a father, an attendant, one dependent on a bhikkhunī, a *paṇḍupalāsa*, and a lay servant—[medicine should be provided].

The meaning is that almsfood that has been covered and not touched is "unrestricted. Furthermore, it means that there is no restriction on giving [the food] to a bandit-thief or to one who holds power.
279. "Of them" refers to householders. "Immersed in the Dispensation" means that protective charms (*paritta*) such as the *Ratana-paritta* and the *Āṭānāṭiya-paritta* should be recited.

280. “Having come, may he grant the precepts (sīla) and recite the Dhamma and the protective chants (paritta)” — this is the connection [of the sentence] as sent by someone. “It is proper to give” means it is permissible to give the precepts; the sense is that it is allowable to speak the Dhamma and the protective chants.
The Analysis of Medicines (Bhesajjavinicchaya). The Commentary on the Description of Medicines is finished. 37. Commentary on the Description of Acceptance (Uggahaniddesa).

281. "Even tenfold" means that if someone brings ten kinds of gems as shown below and says, "I give this to the Saṅgha, or to a cetiya, or for new construction work, or to another person, or to a group of Suttantika monks," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who accepts it by saying, "Very well. This is the meaning.
282–3. Among those, the meaning is “in the ten kinds of treasures. Regarding the two [kinds], namely silver and gold:

the meaning is that when one says, “I give this bullion and gold to the cetiya,” or “I give it for the construction work,” without specifying a group, a community, or an individual, [the recipient] does not refuse it.
If it is asked, “What should be done?”—to show that, it is said: “One should say,” and so forth: “These [treasures] are thus...”
The meaning is that this should be explained to the attendants (kappiyakārā). 284.
Not only gold, silver, and so forth, but other improper things such as fields and land should also not be accepted;
to demonstrate this, he said, "fields, land," and so on. "Dāsapa-su-ādikaṃ" means slaves, cattle, and so forth. For if someone...
If one says, "I have a large tank that provides me with a harvest of grain; I give it to the Saṅgha," and the Saṅgha accepts it, there is an offense both in the acceptance and in the use.
The same applies to the remaining cases. The connection is: "One should accept [the gift] by means of a permissible procedure.
When it is said, "I give a field," having refused it by saying, "It is not allowable,"...
If he says, “Enjoy these four requisites from here,” or “I give this for the purpose of enjoying the four requisites,” it may be accepted.
The same principle applies to a building site as well. If he says, “I give a pond,” one should refuse it;
however, if he says, “Enjoy the four requisites,” or “The Saṅgha will use the water and wash its utensils,” [it may be accepted].
When it is stated according to this method beginning with "I give," it should be accepted. When it is said, "I give a slave," one should refuse;
but when it is said, "I give a monastery attendant, a laborer, or a preparer of allowable things (kappiyakāraka)," it should be accepted.
When it is said, "I give cows, buffaloes, goats, sheep, and so forth," one should refuse; but when it is said, "For the purpose of consuming the five products of the cow," it should be accepted.
With reference to the taking of what has been prepared for oneself, it is said: "Having refused [the gift], one may take it. 285–6. Regarding the ninth matrix:
the work of irrigation channels, fields, and tanks; and the removal of earth from a tank that was previously taken after refusing it under the pretext of it being allowable;
and the binding of the embankment at a broken place; and the strengthening of the wall at a weak spot.
Furthermore, taking an extra portion from an old field when one’s own share has not yet been measured, or demanding a coin from a new field where the portion has not been delimited by saying,
"Give so much of the crop,"— all such things are not permitted for a bhikkhu to do. If he should do them,
the meaning is that such acts as these are unallowable for everyone.
287–9. Now, in order to show that very same improper act, the passage beginning with “without saying” is stated. Its meaning is as follows:

if, however, one does not say “plow, sow,” and so forth, but instead establishes [the boundary] by saying, “so much land is to be given, such a portion of it,” or if the plowman says, “so much crop has been grown on this portion of land; take so much,” [and one accepts it]—[this is improper].

If one measures [the field] with a staff or a rope for the purpose of determining its size, or stands upon the threshing floor to perform acts such as guarding it, that is indeed improper for him. 290.
If one should store away even what belongs to his father under the pretext of being a steward (*bhaṇḍāgārika*), the meaning is that it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
291–2. "Of his parents" means of mother and father. It refers to an allowable object such as a garment or the like. It was said: "Having stored it away, give it."

The connection [is as follows]: Because it becomes an impediment by way of the training rule concerning staying within a monastery (*ajjhārāma-sikkhāpada*) when one has gone after having laid [the items] down, therefore they may be kept;
this is the meaning. 293–4. "One's own tools such as axes, etc. is the meaning. It should be shown that this place is guarded. However, one should not say, "Place them here.
295. Here [one should consider]: "No one else enters here; perhaps it will have been taken by monks or novices."
"Transferred" (saṅkantī) means "gone. "In the object" (vatthumhi) means "in an object such as an ornament," etc. "In such [an object]" (tādise):
the connection is "when such an object as one for which there would be suspicion if it were lost has been lost.
296. Now, in order to show the places where there is no offense, he said: "Within the monastery or dwelling," and so forth. Of the monastery...
"And of the house" means [the same]. "Jewel" (*ratana*) refers to the ten kinds of jewels. "What is considered a jewel" (*ratnasammatam*) refers to items such as garments and head-wraps.

"Having taken" (*gahetvāna*) means that if there is no one to act as a steward (*kappiyakāraka*), one may take it oneself and set it aside; this is the meaning. "On the road or in the forest" (*magge raññepi*) means both on the road and in the forest.
"In such a place" (*tādise*) means in a place where there might be the apprehension that "it will be taken by monks. "Appropriate" (*patirūpam*).
Regarding "it is being made": if one sees such an article on a path or in a forest, one should step off the path and sit down;
when the owners arrive, that place should be pointed out. If one does not see the owners, one should take up the rag-robe (paṃsukūla) if it is considered a treasure.
If it is indeed a treasure, the meaning is that one should depart while remaining silent. This refers to [the rules concerning] paths and forests.

Practice. Within monasteries or dwellings, however, having seen such a thing, one should release the goods and deposit them after making a mark by means of a coin, a seal, or a scrap of cloth, according to the method of "here are so many kahāpaṇas," and so forth.
Then, when departing from there, it should be reported to suitable bhikkhus. This is the determination of what has been received.
The commentary on the exposition of the acquisitions is finished.
38. Commentary on the exposition of the corrupter of families: 297.
“He corrupts families with flowers, or fruits, or powders, or clay, or tooth-sticks...”

Because it was said, "by means of a flower, or by means of a reed, or by means of medicine, or by means of massaging the shanks," he spoke the words beginning with "flower" in order to show those eight grounds.
By this wrong practice, one corrupts and destroys the confidence of families toward other virtuous persons;
thus, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa* known as "corrupting a family. That, moreover, should be understood to apply both to what belongs to oneself and to what belongs to others.
298. Now, in order to show that in these cases one incurs not only the offense of *dukkaṭa* for defiling a family, but also offenses such as *thullaccaya*, he says "thullaccaya" and so forth.
The connection is that there is a *thullaccaya* for one who gives away heavy property belonging to the Saṅgha as if it were his own.
However, flowers and the like designated for the purpose of lodgings constitute heavy property.
The remainder of the text is: "For one who gives with a thieving mind what belongs to the Saṅgha or to another, there are offenses such as *dukkaṭa*;

the meaning is that depending on the value of that property, there are *dukkaṭa*, *thullaccaya*, or *pārājika* offenses. (299–300) "In every way" means not [by means of] appropriate terminology, inappropriate terminology, indirect speech, hints, signs, actions, and so forth.
The meaning is "it is permissible. This includes the act of making fences and so forth, as well as tending [the trees]. "For one's own use" means for the purpose of consuming the fruit.
"Planting and so forth" refers to having them planted and so on. By the word "and so forth," having them watered, having them pruned, and other such acts are included.

Having brought hoes, spades, axes, hatchets, water vessels, and so on, and placing them nearby, and by way of the sign—having taken up the hoes, spades, and so forth, as well as the flower creepers—[one may do so].

The connection is as follows: when [the site] is established, the planting and so forth are obtained through the perception that "seeing novices and others, [the people] come thinking, 'The elder wishes to have it done,' and do it," through the conventional expression of what is allowable such as "Know this tree, know this pit," and through such methods as "A wise man should have flower seedlings and the like planted; before long they will lead to benefit."
301–2. Now, in order to show the remaining two bases among the eight, it is said: "Medical practice and sending on errands have already been mentioned.
Therein, medical practice has already been explained previously; the meaning is that I shall now explain the determination regarding sending on errands and so forth.
"Father" refers to both mother and father. "The goods" refers to one who desires to go forth [into the religious life]. "The bhikkhu’s own personal attendant" means...
The meaning is that, with the exception of these, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for conveying a message regarding household tasks such as farming or trade.
The meaning is that even if one has not first received a message but later sees the person or goes to them and speaks, it is likewise an offense of wrong-doing.
However, for those who have come without having received a message, [if one asks], "Venerable sir, what is the news concerning so-and-so in that village?"...
When asked, it is proper to speak; there is no fault in answering a question that has been asked.

(303) Thus, these requisites arise through the corruption of a family. Because it is stated, "even for five," such [actions] performed even by one who is not fully ordained are likewise not permitted, as they constitute wrong livelihood.
In this regard, the case of Ātumā serves as an illustration. If one asks, "How so? [the answer follows:]
To demonstrate that, it is said: “False proclamation, material form, misrepresentation, and so forth.
In this context, “and so forth” means things similar to the conditions arising from those [factors].
304. Now, in order to show for whom it is permissible to give flowers and such, and for whom it is not permissible to give them:

He said, “Having caused to be taken away,” and so forth. The connection is that it is permitted to give [the merit] to one’s parents. It is for the sake of other relatives who have attained [the path].
“Liṅga” means the Śiva-liṅga. 305. Likewise, regarding “fruit”: even after having taken or caused to be taken the fruit, it is permitted to give it to one’s mother and father; such is the meaning.
In order to show that it is not only for parents but for others as well that [the gift] may be given, he said, “for the sick,” and so forth.
Regarding the phrase *saparasantaka* (including what belongs to others): here, “others” (*para*) is intended specifically to mean one’s own trusted kinsmen.

306. Regarding the word *bhājentā* (when they are dividing): the connection is that when fruit or flowers are being divided among the Saṅgha, they should be given by one who has been formally appointed (*sammatena*). By the other [method], it means they should be given after obtaining permission (*apaloketvā*) by one who has not been appointed.
307. “It should be given to those who have come after delimiting” means having delimited either by way of fruit or by way of tree.
“To the other” refers to the owner and so forth. “Having made an agreement” means having said, “So many fruits are obtainable from this tree.”

308. "Sesa" refers to clay, tooth-sticks, and bamboo. Regarding the phrase "the method is as previously stated," the meaning is that the legal determination (vinicchaya) should be understood according to the method explained below, starting with: "For one who gives what belongs to himself or another for the sake of maintaining family ties, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," and so forth.
As for "even a leaf," although the giving of a leaf is not mentioned in the Pāḷi, nevertheless, in the case of corrupting a family...
The meaning is "to cause to enter. The determination regarding the defiler of families is finished.
The commentary on the exposition of the defiler of families is concluded.
39. Commentary on the Exposition of the Entrance for the Rains.
309–310. Now, in order to show the entering upon the rains retreat (*vassūpagamana*), he said, “the earlier,” and so forth.

Herein, the meaning is that there are two ways of entering the rains retreat: the earlier and the later. Alternatively, the remainder of the reading is that the “entering upon the rains” consists either in the taking up of a dwelling or in a verbal declaration.
Now, with reference to what is to be said, it was stated, “of such a kind. Herein, the arising of the thought, “I will dwell for the rains here,” is [the factor].

This is the *ālaya*. However, the "taking possession of an *ālaya*" (*ālayapariggāha*) is permitted for one who wishes to enter the rains retreat (*vassa*) in a caravan, a caravan camp, or on a ship, provided he does not obtain a lodging (*senāsana*) there; this is because it is not allowed to enter the rains retreat in caravans and such places.
If, however, a lodging with closed doors is available in a caravan or similar place, one may enter there. By one who enters...
And one must say three times, "I enter the rains residence here. However, in the monastery, a verbal expression may also be made.

If there is the intention, "I will dwell for the rains here," but one does not enter the rains residence due to forgetfulness, one has not broken the rains residence and is indeed permitted to perform the *pavāraṇā* ceremony.
311. Regarding the phrase "one who does not wish to enter the residence should not cross [the boundary] on that very day":

the meaning is that for one who crosses [the boundary], it is as if the *vassūpanāyikā* (the commencement of the rains) has occurred on that very day. This connects with the phrase "should cross the residence.

As for the expression "or knowing [that the time has passed], he does not enter," the intention here is that even if one sits within the monastery, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa* for one who does not enter.
312. The connection is: "One whose rains-residence has been interrupted, or who for some obstacle has not entered the first [period], may enter the second.
"Three months" means either the first three months or the last three months.
"Monks, having entered the rains-residence, one should not set out on a journey without having dwelt for either the first or the last three months. Whoever should set out..."
"For there is an offense of wrong-doing," it is said.
313–5. "I allow you, monks, to go on account of seven kinds of business even if not requested, much less if requested:
[the business] of a monk, of a nun, of a trainee nun, of a male novice, of a female novice, of a mother, and of a father."

Because it was stated, "A seven-day postponement may be made with the thought: 'I will seek food for the sick,' or 'I will seek food for those attending the sick,' or 'I will seek medicine for the sick,' or 'I will inquire after them,' or 'I will attend to them,'" it was said:
"For the sake of mother and father... [and so on]... I will attend to them. Herein, this is the summary: "For mother and the others..."

Whether sent or unsent, one may go on a seven-day mission with the thought: "I will seek out or procure sick-rice, or rice for those attending the sick, or medicine for the sick," or thinking: "I will go to those who are sick and inquire after them," or "I will attend to them.
Now, with reference specifically to fellow practitioners of the Dhamma, it is said: "If he is dissatisfied," and so forth. "Having seen a form of a different sex..."
The meaning is that it is also permissible to go with the intention: "I have no pleasure [here]; therefore, I shall withdraw from this place, take that [offense], and go elsewhere.
The connection is: "I shall either dispel the remorse (*kukkucca*) and separate from the wrong view (*diṭṭhi*), or I shall cause others to do so.
Or, there is the formal exit (*vuṭṭhāna*) by means of probation (*parivāsa*), penance (*mānatta*), and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), if...

The meaning is that it is permissible to go with the thought: "A formal act (*kamma*) has been performed by the Saṅgha; I shall make an effort regarding the proclamation and so forth for its pacification.
"By means of a seven-day task" means by means of a business to be accomplished within seven days.

"He who is invited for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma may go thus"—this is the meaning. "Venerables" (*garū*) refers to teachers (*ācariya*) and preceptors (*upajjhāya*); it is fitting to go for one who has been sent by them on the business of washing robes—this is the meaning.
317. Regarding the phrase “not [allowing] the washing of vessels... nor seeing,” here the connection is that one does not incur an offense even in these cases.

Regarding the word “obtainable” (*labbhanti*), if one has gone not very far with the thought, “I will return this very day,” and has not yet arrived, then it is “obtainable”; this is the connection. What is meant?
For one who has gone to a neighboring monastery with the thought, “I will return this very day,” while on the way back—
It is stated that if dawn breaks, there is no interruption of the rains retreat, nor does one incur an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) due to the interruption of the night.
318. "By other relatives" means by brothers, sisters, and so forth. The connection is with the phrase "sent by one residing with a bhikkhunī. "Having pointed out" means [saying] such things as:
"May the venerable ones come; I wish to give a gift, to hear the Dhamma, and to see the bhikkhus."
When one has been sent after pointing out something specific, it is permissible to go. However, the meaning is that if it is said merely, "Let the bhikkhus come;
I desire the arrival of the bhikkhus," without having pointed anything out, one does not receive permission to go.
319. "If there is even a moment's delay" means if there is even a single moment of delay for oneself among the ten kinds of obstacles.
The meaning is this: there is no offense in breaking the rains-retreat for the sake of harmony in the Saṅgha. For this has been said:
"In this case, monks, a monk who has entered the rains-retreat sees many monks striving for a schism in the Saṅgha.
If it occurs to that monk: 'A schism in the Saṅgha is indeed declared by the Blessed One to be a grave matter. Let it not happen while I am present...'"

"If the Saṅgha is split, one may depart; there is no offense for interrupting the rains-retreat. This means that one whose rains-retreat has been interrupted in this manner does not perform the *pavāraṇā*.
320. Regarding "in the hollow of a tree": here, it is not permitted [to stay] in a mere clean hollow of a tree;
however, having constructed a small hut with a wooden floor-covering inside a large hollow and provided an entrance door, it is permissible to approach it.
It is permissible. Regarding "the branch of a tree": here too, it is not permissible [to stay] in a mere bare branch;
however, it is permissible to build a small hut by erecting a frame on a large branch and then entering it according to the method described above.
They say that a "chavakuṭi" is a stone hut; it is one where stones are piled up on three sides and covered on top with a stone.

321. Furthermore, the connection is that one who has boarded a boat or similar vessel is permitted to perform the *pavāraṇā* ceremony. This concludes the determination regarding the commencement of the rains residence (*vassūpanāyika*).
The commentary on the exposition of the commencement of the rains residence is finished.
40. Commentary on the Exposition of Non-Sharing (*avebhaṅgiya*).
322–4. Regarding "monasteries and monastery sites": here, a *ārāma* (monastery) refers to either a flower garden or a fruit orchard.
Beds, stools, cushions, pillows, and so forth constitute the furniture for reclining and sitting. The iron pots and such are made of black iron, copper, and other metals.

A *bhāṇaka* is a water vessel. These five are "not to be divided" (*avibhājīya*); the meaning is that they must not be taken after being divided; even if they have been taken, they remain the property of the Saṅgha. Here...
First, "a monastery" and "monastery site"; second, "a dwelling" and "dwelling site";
third, "a bed, a bench, a mattress, and a pillow"; fourth, "an iron pot... [and so on] ...a wooden peg"; fifth, "a creeper...
[and so on] ...wooden articles and earthenware. Thus, these are five by way of groups, but they are numerous by way of their individual forms.
And there are these verses on this:
“Two are comprised of two factors, the third is comprised of four;
The fourth has nine divisions, and the fifth has eight distinctions.”
325. "Monks, these five things are not to be disposed of; they must not be disposed of by a Saṅgha, a group, or an individual.
Even if disposed of, they remain undispensed. Whoever should dispose of them commits a thullaccaya offense.
Because this was said, it is stated that "even if distributed, they are not distributed. These five types mentioned are called "precious goods" (*garubhaṇḍa*).
And by the word "ca" (and), it is meant that they are also called "not to be given away" (*avissajjiyāni*) and "not to be divided" (*avebhaṅgiyāni*).
Now, since everything among the first three groups consists of heavy goods (*garubhaṇḍa*), those are not touched upon;
rather, because there is also some light goods (*agarubhaṇḍa*) among the latter two groups, [the author] begins to demonstrate that, even while addressing those two.
It should be understood that the phrase beginning with “even as much as a creeper the length of half an arm” was spoken in order to demonstrate the first [type of material] as having many objects.
This is its summary: even a creeper the length of half an arm, or a bamboo even eight finger-breadths long, or grass and so forth even the size of a handful;
here, by the word “and so forth” (ādi), he includes *muñja* and *pabbaja* grasses, as well as even a single leaf, or clay, whether natural or of five colors.
The phrase "or lime, kaṅgu-grain, ginger, and so forth" includes, by the word "and so forth," substances such as red arsenic, vermilion, and the like.

Whether they were given to the Saṅgha by anyone even if they are only the size of a palm fruit, or whether they grew on grass-fields belonging to the Saṅgha, or arose in a protected and guarded plot of land—such items produced there, being the property of the Saṅgha and kept secure, must not be divided; this is the meaning.
Now, in order to show those things which are to be distributed here, he says "when completed," etc.;

the intention is that it is to be distributed when the work for the Saṅgha or for a cetiya has been finished. In this context, however, whatever—such as creepers, bamboos, grass, leaves, clay, and so forth—has been given to the Saṅgha, or has grown on land belonging to the Saṅgha such as a grass-field, or is heavy property that has been guarded and protected; [all these are to be distributed].
When that [property] has been used for the business of the Saṅgha or for the business of a cetiya, it is permissible to give what remains even for the personal business of an individual;

because it is not a "heavy commodity" (*garubhaṇḍa*), it may also be distributed. Only that which is guarded and protected for the purpose of a dwelling place constitutes a heavy commodity, and nothing else.
In the island of Siṃhala, at the Tumūla-Soma monastery, even the *pākavatta* palm leaf belonging to the Saṅgha was sold.
It is made so. Why? Because there is no need for leaves there; all [buildings] such as palaces are roofed with bricks.
Thus they say that it is made so in other cases as well. 329.
Now, in order to show the items among metal vessels and the like that must be divided exclusively, he says "bowl, etc. Here...

Furthermore, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), iron pots, copper vessels, water-pots, ladles, bowls, eye-ointments, ointment-sticks, ear-cleaners, needles, tweezers, walking sticks, and so forth, are indeed included.
"In that same way" means it should be divided accordingly. "Both unfinished and finished.
"A foot-measure" (*pādagaṇhaka*) refers to the taking up of five *nāḷi*s of Magadha measure.
331–2. "Permitted to dwell" (*anuññātavāsi*) refers to that which can be carried about by being placed inside a box, as it has been stated.

"Hewn but not finished" (*tacchita-anidḍhita*) means unfinished. If it is hewn, it is indeed "heavy property" (*garubhaṇḍa*). However, ivory that is neither hewn nor finished must simply be distributed.
Unfinished items such as bed-legs and the like are heavy property. Now, in order to show earthenware (*mattikabhanda*):
He says, “in the requisites for monks,” and so forth. This refers to the requisites for monks such as alms-bowls, stands, water-pots, and the like.
“A foot-holding jar” means a jar with a handle for the feet, made of clay; it is to be distributed and shared. A conch-shell stand is likewise to be shared.
(333–4) Deer-skin and other such allowable skins are to be shared; lion-skin and other such unallowable skins are heavy goods (*garubhaṇḍa*).
However, it is permissible to use that as a ground-covering. As for the deer-skin, because it falls under the category of a spread, it is considered a valuable article (garubhaṇḍa).
Now, these five [types of skins] may not be exchanged for the sake of robes, almsfood, or medicine;
rather, having exchanged a valuable article for another valuable article, or a durable item for a durable one, they should be used.
To demonstrate this, he said, "By a heavy object," and so forth. Therein, the connection is:
"One may exchange a heavy object for a heavy object and for a stable object. And one may exchange a stable object for a stable object only, not for a heavy object;
this is the intended meaning. Among the five categories, the latter three are heavy objects, while the former two are stable objects.
It should be understood thus. And the meaning is: "Having done so, let him eat"—that is, having exchanged it, let him consume the allowable goods brought from there.
If one asks, "How is this known?"—for it is said in the Parivāra:
"The Great Seer has declared five things that are not to be relinquished and not to be shared."
“There is no offense for one who exchanges or uses [the goods];
this question has been considered by those skilled in the Dhamma.
Herein, regarding the method of exchange: heavy goods may be exchanged for heavy goods, or immovable property for immovable property, and immovable property may be exchanged for immovable property.

With this in mind, it is said: "There is no offense for one who gives away [the property]. Furthermore, to demonstrate that it is permissible to use the four requisites produced from that [gift], it is said:
"There is no offense for one who uses [them]. This is the intended meaning of this verse.
"The rest" means that the monastery and so forth are not to be divided. This is the determination regarding what is not to be shared (*avebhaṅgiya*).
The commentary on the exposition of what is not to be broken off is finished.
41. Commentary on the miscellaneous exposition. 335–336.
"In a place where the six doors are closed... falling asleep, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" means: by one who falls asleep during the day in such a place.

Regarding the connection: however, in a place enclosed by any kind of enclosure, even in an open space or at the foot of a tree, as long as one is lying down in an area suitable according to this characteristic, one must indeed bolt the door.
"When there is a wise person" means when there is anyone—whether a bhikkhu, a sāmaṇera, or even a lay follower or a monastery attendant.
The meaning is as follows: even the thought, "He will watch over it," is not permitted; thus, it is not allowed to merely ask a bhikkhunī or a woman [to do so].
"In one's own power" (*savase*) means under one's own control, that is, in a place not shared with many others.

"Without that manner" (*taṃ vinākāraṃ*) means without that aforementioned manner consisting of locking the door or making a formal resolve. This is a summary regarding the commission of an offense without conscious intent.
337. "Jewels" refers to the ten kinds of jewels, beginning with pearls. "Grains" refers to the seven kinds of grain. 338.
Regarding the phrase "with honey-cakes, oil, or water-oil": herein, if one smears the hair with honey-cakes mixed with oil, or with oil mixed with water, or with any other such preparation;
or [if one uses] any kind of paste upon objects made of ivory and the like—
The meaning is that if one performs the function of fanning with a cloth or with the hand, or if one contracts [the fingers] with the fingers, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
339. "Not one covering" means not a single covering. "They lie down together" means they should lie down. What is meant?
If they were to lie down together on a single covering, or on a single spread, or on a single bed, it is not permitted; there is an offense of wrong-doing.
This has been stated. The connection is: "One should not eat from a single vessel. 340. The connection is:

"One should not chew a tooth-stick less than four finger-breadths in length. "More than eight finger-breadths" means exceeding eight finger-breadths. "Likewise" means one should not chew it [if it is too long]. One who is ill should not eat garlic. 341.
By means of low or high birth and so forth, one should not address another as "high" or "low," such as saying, "You are a caṇḍāla," and so on.
The meaning is: if one speaks with the intent of mere sport, without the intent to revile, using either a direct method such as "There are here some Caṇḍālas,
Veṇas, or Nesādas," or by way of a designation for another, whether addressing one who is fully ordained or one who is not,
it is a *dubbhāsita* (an ill-spoken word).
342. The connection is that one should not keep the nails, hair, or the hair of the nose long. It has been said:
"Monks, I allow you to clip the nails to the size of a grain of rice," and "Monks, I allow [the hair] up to two months' growth or two finger-breadths.
Regarding the phrase "it is not permitted to polish even a single nail," it is not allowed here to make even a single nail glossy.
Thus it was said: “Monks, one should not have [the hair] removed by more than twenty [strands]. Whoever should have it done so, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Monks, I allow you to remove only the surface dirt. Therefore, it is permissible to remove only the surface dirt from the nails.
Regarding the phrase “removing hair from the private parts,” here “private parts” refers to both armpits and the urinary organ.
“It is permitted, monks, for one who is ill to have hair removed from the private parts,” so it was said. 343.
*Yathāvuḍḍhaṃ* means that which is to be received according to seniority. *Na bādheyya* means he should not refuse.
*Saṅghuddiṭṭhaṃ vā* refers to lodgings and such things given by lay followers and others after they have offered them with the words, “May the venerable ones enjoy them,” according to seniority.
“For monks, even that which has been specifically prepared for someone should not be withheld according to seniority. Whoever should withhold it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Thus it was said. The connection is: “one does not step with unwashed feet or with wet feet.

“Or a place where one whose feet are well-washed [should step]” means a place to be stepped upon by those whose feet have indeed been washed. “In the same way” means one should not step [there] wearing sandals; such is the meaning.
“For monks, one must not step onto a lodging with unwashed feet, with wet feet, or wearing sandals.
Whoever should so step, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). This has been said.

Furthermore, because it was said, “Monks, I allow you to lie down after having spread out [a mat],” one may use ground that has been plastered or a bedding-place consisting of a floor-cover belonging to the Saṅgha.
One should lie down only after having spread one’s own bed or chair with its own covering cloth.

(344) “One does not wrap oneself in the outer robe” means that one should not make a double-folded bundle (*pallatthikā*) with the robe—whether in a monastery or in an inhabited area—once it has been formally determined as one’s own.
One should not lean against a wall or similar surface that has been prepared for use. “Monks, [you should not lean] against a prepared surface... [and so forth].
"For it has been said: 'A wall must not be leaned against. Whoever should lean against one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Therefore, neither a white-plastered wall nor a wall decorated with paintings must be leaned against.

Not only the wall, but also door-frames, window-frames, pillars, and so forth that have been prepared for work must not be leaned against. Here too, the offenses are determined by the counting of hairs."

It should be understood thus: when water is available, it is not the case that one does not rinse the mouth, nor is it permissible not to rinse; the meaning is that it is not allowed not to perform purification with water.
By the word "when present" (*sante*), it is indicated that there is no offense when [water] is absent.
345. Regarding "undertaking what is unallowable": this refers to one who urges a bhikkhu, or other fellow practitioners such as a novice (*sāmaṇera*) and so forth, toward what is unallowable.
It is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). For it has been said: “Monks, one who has gone forth must not encourage another in what is unallowable.
Whoever should so encourage, there is an offense of wrong-doing. The meaning is: for the confession of a similar offense.

Here, what is intended is similarity in the *vatthu* (the objective basis), not similarity in the *āpatti* (the offense itself). “Monks, a similar offense must not be confessed. Whoever should confess [it],” [there is an offense].
And it is said: "There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," and "Monks, a similar offense must not be accepted. Whoever should accept one, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
It is not even permissible to disclose an offense that is similar in its basis; therefore it is said: "In disclosing [a similar offense], there is wrong-doing.
"Friends, I have committed such-and-such an offense; I shall [confess] it from this..."
"Having emerged [from the offense], I shall make amends"—this is what is called "disclosing another's words.
346. "Of the other," however, refers to one whose mind is impure. 347.

"A man's height" means it is permissible to climb a tree to the height of a man; for it has been said: "Monks, I allow you, when there is a purpose to be served, to climb a tree to the height of a man, and in times of distress, as much as necessary."
348. The connection is that it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who travels half a *yojana* without a water-strainer.

It has been stated: “The time of traveling on a journey is when one should eat [with the thought], ‘I shall go half a *yojana’”; therefore, it should be understood that exactly half a *yojana* is the final limit of a journey.
And regarding the training rule on traveling together with a woman, it says: “On a single road... (*ekaddhānamaggaṃ*).
Because it was stated with such specific qualification—“one should travel, even as far as between villages”—it is said:
“In a village where chickens can fly, for every interval between villages, there is an offense of *pācittiya*,” and not by way of the definition of a journey (*addhāna*).

If a journey were defined merely by the delimitation of the space between villages, then even in the training rule regarding eating in a group (*gaṇabhojana*), [the phrase] “the time of traveling on a journey” would include even the interval between villages.
If one should say, "I will go; [therefore] it may be eaten," that has not been stated. Therefore: "Monks, a journey should not be undertaken without a water-strainer.
Whoever should undertake it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If there is no water-strainer or a water-pot, even the corner of one's outer robe (saṅghāṭī) should be designated: 'Having strained with this, I will drink.'"
Even in the case of the stated location, the measurement of the journey should be understood as being by way of half a *yojana*.
However, for the residents of the Abhayagiri monastery, there is a textual passage stating that "the measurement of the journey is by way of two *gāvutas*.
"To one who asks" means to one who is requesting. "And monks, a monk traveling on a journey must not fail to give a water-strainer when it is asked for."
"For he who should not give [it], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," so it is said.
349. "Except on account of illness, regarding the remaining limbs such as the ears, nose, and so forth, it is an offense of wrong-doing"—this is the connection.
When there is an illness, it is permissible to cut off fingers and the like. However, it is absolutely not permissible to cut off the genitals or seeds. Regarding self-destruction:

And the connection is with the term *dukkaṭa*. For it has been said: “Monks, one must not cause oneself to be killed. Whoever should cause [himself] to be killed, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). 350.
“And monks, a picture intended for decoration depicting the form of a woman or the form of a man must not be caused to be made. Whoever [should do so],” [there is an offense of wrong-doing].
If one should have it done, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Because it was said, "Monks, I allow flower-work, creeper-work, shark-tooth work, and the fivefold pattern," it was stated: "One should neither make nor cause to be made paintings or cloth-paintings.
"Eating" refers to interrupted eating. "Monks, a monk who is interrupting his meal should not be dismissed. Should anyone dismiss him..."
“For this there is an offense of wrong-doing,” so it is said.
351. Regarding “vehicles”: a cart, a chariot, a wagon, a palanquin, and so forth, are permitted for one who is ill to mount;
a litter is also permitted. This applies in all such cases. “I allow, monks, a vehicle for one who is ill, drawn by men.”
For it is said: "A hand-carriage, a palanquin, or a litter. 352. *Dava* means sport. For it is said:
"Monks, no sport (*dava*) should be made concerning the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha.
Whoever should do so, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Therefore: "Is the Buddha Silakabuddha, or rather..."

It should be understood that for one who makes sport in such a manner as saying, "He has woken up," or "What is the Dhamma? Is it the Dhamma of cattle, or the Dhamma of goats? or "What is the Saṅgha? Is it the Saṅgha of goats, or the Saṅgha of deer? and so forth, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Likewise, for one who says to a novice or a fully ordained monk, "We will give you a robe," or "We will give you a bowl," and so forth—even to another person—[it is an offense].
The meaning is that for one who is immoral, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in flattery for the purpose of making himself an attendant to a gathering of his own followers.
For it is said: “Monks, another’s assembly must not be flattered. Whoever should flatter it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
(353) The connection is: “Having uncovered either the body, the thigh, or the private parts, he must not show them to the bhikkhunīs.”
The meaning is that those bhikkhunīs should not be sprinkled with mud, water, or the like. It is not only with mud, water, and so forth;
for anyone who sprinkles them with anything—even with clear water, dye, mud, or the like—it is indeed a dukkaṭa offense. 354.

Regarding the term "fool" (*bāla*): here, a "fool" is one who, having received the exhortation (*ovāda*), reports it to the reciter of the Pātimokkha on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pāṭipada*).

He does not know how to bring back [the message]. One who is "sick" is one who, having received the exhortation (*ovāda*) and gone to the Uposatha hall, is unable both to announce it and to bring back [the response].
One who is "to be sent" is one who wishes to go to the place of confession.
[The Buddha said: "Monks, the exhortation must not be neglected. Whoever should neglect it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). And: "I authorize..."
"Monks, except for one who is foolish, one who is ill, and one who is about to travel, the rest should receive the exhortation"—
and because it is said, "Monks, the exhortation must not be declined; whoever should decline it incurs an offense of wrong-doing"—
on the thirteenth or fourteenth day, the nuns should come and say, "This Uposatha is on the fourteenth."
Or, when asked, "Is it the fifteenth? or "When is the Uposatha, Venerable Sir?", he should reply, "It is the fourteenth," or "It is the fifteenth," or "Tomorrow, Sister, is the Uposatha.
On the Uposatha day, those bhikkhunīs, having arrived, should say:
"Venerable Sir, the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha pays homage at the feet of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and requests the approach for the exhortation."

"May the community of bhikkhunīs, noble sir, receive the invitation to approach for instruction"—thus should it be requested. Having accepted that speech, at the Uposatha hall, one should say to the reciter of the Pātimokkha:

"Venerable sir, the community of bhikkhunīs pays homage at the feet of the community of bhikkhus and requests the invitation to approach for instruction; may the community of bhikkhunīs, venerable sir, receive the invitation to approach for instruction."

It should be announced. The reciter of the Pātimokkha, if there is a monk designated as the instructor of the nuns, should say: "The monk named so-and-so has been appointed as the instructor of the nuns; let the community of nuns approach him. If there is no such person, he should ask:
"Which venerable one is able to instruct the nuns? and if there is someone [endowed] with the eight factors...
Once a monk has been appointed for that purpose, he should inform the one who receives the exhortation in the manner already described.
If there is no monk at all who has been appointed as an exhorter of the nuns, it should be said: "May the Saṅgha of nuns be accomplished through inspiring confidence.
Having accepted with "Very well," that monk [should go] on the first day of the fortnight to the nuns...
"It should be said: 'There is no monk appointed as an instructor of bhikkhunīs; let the community of bhikkhunīs be accomplished through inspiring confidence.
They too should accept it, saying, 'Very well, Venerable Sir. In this same manner, the distinction in speech should be understood for groups and individuals as well."

355. *Lokāyata* refers to the treatise on caviling (*vitaṇḍasattha*). Because it was stated, “Monks, one should not eat from a vessel with a handle like a ladle. Whoever should so eat, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*),” it is said that one should not eat even from a basket.
356. “One should not wear what is worn by householders” means one should not put on the lower garment of a householder. It was stated:
“Monks, one should not wear the lower garment of a householder—[namely] that which has an elephant-trunk [cut-out], a fish-scale [pattern], four corners, or a palm-leaf [fringe].”
“[It shall be] with seven folds. Whoever should wear it [otherwise], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). For thus it is said.
Dressing other than in a circular manner—all this is called “the dress of a householder. The meaning is that one should not dress in that way.
“Saṃvelliya” means: one should not wear it by tying up the hem there. “Dāya” means a forest. It is to be connected with “nālimpayeyya” (one should not smear).
357. One should not cause it to increase; one should not give it to those who are not relatives or who have not invited one; nor should one ask for it. Regarding the phrase "to another":
here, that which has been given after specifying, "May you yourselves enjoy this," is not permitted even to be given to fellow practitioners of the Dhamma.
The meaning is that one might take the best portion, or eat it for a few days, and then give it away again.

358. "Soliciting for a specific purpose" (*uddissa-yācanā*): here the meaning is soliciting protection specifically for [a person] by saying, "In our monastery, such-and-such was done by so-and-so," or "They will do this and that.
"Whether knowing or not knowing": the meaning is whether, while being solicited by us, they know those punishers [will punish them], or whether they do not know. By them...
However, when he has been punished, that punishment becomes a debt to be paid like a fine for stolen goods to those who requested it on his behalf; this is the meaning.
But as for his personally causing him to be punished by saying, "This and that was done by him;
take such and such an amount as the fine," one should know that depending on the value of that fine, there are offenses of *pārājika*, *thullaccaya*, or *dukkaṭa*; this is the meaning.

359. The connection is with the phrase "speaking for the harm of that thief. The meaning is that when kings, royal ministers, and others inflict punishment upon that thief, this [offense] constitutes an equivalent debt for the monk. 360.
Whether it be leavings, excrement, rubbish, or urine, if one should discard these outside the enclosure walls or the ramparts, it is an *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing).
By the phrase "without looking at the place of use," it is implied that one must not discard anything without first looking at it even at a time when it is not being used.

It indicates that it is permissible. The meaning is that it is not only in that specific case, but rather, for one who discards [seeds] in a green field or in a plantation of rice, coconut palms, and so forth, there is likewise an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Regarding the phrase "when it was said, 'Let us make an offering,'" the intended sense is "when it was asked."

362. The meaning is that for one going to see a royal palace, a lotus pond, a pleasure grove, a picture gallery, or a monastery built for the purpose of recreation, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) at every step.

363. One should not refuse a seat with a new one; one should not lay one’s robe out in the heat. “By a teacher,” etc.: the connection is that one who has been dismissed by a teacher or the like should ask for forgiveness.

364. "And with seven offenses": the intention is that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for reviling a bhikkhu in his absence by means of the seven offenses, or by reviling him with other [terms] such as "faithless, lacking confidence, a consumer of seeds," and so forth.
365. "A robe or alms-food given in faith" is the meaning. For it has been said: "Monks, what is given in faith must not be squandered.
Whoever should squander it, there is an offense of wrong-doing. "I allow you, monks, [to give] to one's mother and father..."
Because it was stated, "it should be given," it was said, "it may be received from one's parents.
(366) The connection is "having spent the rains elsewhere"; the meaning is "in another monastery. "Elsewhere" means from another monastery.
"Monks, one who has spent the rains elsewhere must not accept a share of the robe-cloth elsewhere. Should anyone accept it..."
“For there is an offense of wrong-doing,” it is said. “Of them” means: by the relinquishing of responsibility by those monks who were fit to divide and take that robe in that monastery;
the meaning is that it must be dealt with according to the value of the goods.
367. “With an inner and an outer garment” means *santaruttara*; the meaning is: “one should not enter a village [in such a manner]. “Monks, you should not...”
“A village should be entered with the inner and outer robes [properly arranged]. Whoever should enter otherwise, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Thus it was said. “Fit” means not being ill. “One should not enter a village wearing sandals” is the connection [of the rule]. “Monks, a yak-tail fan should not be carried.
Whoever should carry one, there is an offense of wrong-doing”; and, “Monks, I allow three kinds of fans.”
Because it is stated that [fans] may be made of bark, of *usīra* root, or of peacock feathers, it is said: "One should not carry a yak-tail fan (*cāmara*) or a mosquito fan (*makasabījani*).
However, a mosquito fan with a handle made of ivory, horn, or wood is permitted.
368. The connection is "outside the monastery grounds. "Monks, a sunshade must not be carried. Whoever should carry one, there is an offense..."

Because it has been said, "It is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," and "I allow, monks, a sunshade for one who is ill," a person who is not ill is not permitted [to use one] outside the monastery grounds;
however, the meaning is that even one who is not ill may use it for the purpose of protecting robes and so forth.
369. *Gāheyya ubhatokājaṃ*: one should not take [a sunshade] made of both types of wool. *Ekantarikakājakam*: [one made of] alternating wool. *Ekatokājañca*: and [one made of] a single type of wool.
And a shoulder-yoke. “Monks, a double-sided yoke must not be carried.
Whoever should carry one, there is an offense of wrong-doing,” and because it was said:
