“Monks, I allow a single-sided yoke, a shoulder-yoke, a waist-yoke, a head-carry, a shoulder-carry, a waist-carry, and a hanging bag.”
It should be understood that the "double-sided" (ubhatokāja) [robe] is not permitted, while the others are permitted.

370. "Without having made an occasion" means: if one should accuse another of an offense without first having made an occasion by saying, "Friend, give me an opportunity; I wish to speak to you," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for him; such is the meaning. "Likewise" means: likewise an offense of wrong-doing; such is the meaning. 371.
"By a standard finger-measure" means: not by a Sugata-finger-measure; such is the meaning.
372. If one were to undertake the ascetic practices (vata) of other sectarians, such as the vow of silence (mūgabbata), it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
this is the meaning. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the cow-vow (govata), the dog-vow (kukkuravata), and others are included.

Likewise, if one who was previously a barber should carry a barber’s kit, it is likewise an offense of wrong-doing; this is the meaning. 373. "Whatever" means any manual labor, such as the work of a barber or a tailor; this is the meaning. "In accordance with that" means...

The meaning is: "in accordance with a request for manual labor. If, when requested in this way, he gives only the basis for manual labor, it is permissible to have him perform it by having someone else give that [labor] to him; this is the meaning.

However, as for work without wages—that is, not requesting manual labor but saying, "Come, do this"—it is allowable to have him perform it even without such a request; this is the meaning. "Whatever belongs to another" refers to anything such as wood, grass, and so forth.
The intention is that it is permissible to have someone bring what belongs to another person and is unclaimed. 374.
"Of householders" means belonging to householders. "Guardians" means protectors. The meaning is that one may take as much as they give.
"According to the limit" means [the amount specified as] "every day this much sugarcane, coconut, or ripe mango."
The meaning is that when they give [something] after having determined, "You may eat," it is obtained only from among those who are giving. 375.
"One would incur [an offense] in two ways" means one would incur it by means of two. If it is asked, "By which two?", in order to show them, it is said, "By body and speech.
For it is said: "One incurs an offense in two modes: one incurs it by body, and one incurs it by speech."
One who commits an offense through body and speech commits it in six ways; to demonstrate these, he said, "due to shamelessness, ignorance, remorse, and being of a fickle nature," and so forth.
Herein, one who commits a transgression while knowing its improper nature does so out of shamelessness (*alajjitāya*).

One who commits it without knowing what is proper and what is improper does so out of ignorance (*aññāṇatāya*). One who commits it while in doubt, thinking, "Is this proper or not? [does so out of uncertainty].
Having overcome that [thought] which has arisen, one who commits a transgression falls into it because of being overcome by remorse (*kukkucca*).
One who falls into sleeping in the same bed and so forth does so through the drifting away of mindfulness; the meaning is "through the loss of mindfulness.

When eating bear meat thinking it is "pig meat," or pig meat thinking it is "bear meat," this occurs through the perception of what is unallowable as allowable, and the perception of what is allowable as unallowable.

And it should be understood that one incurs [an offense]. 376. The meaning is: by shamelessness or by ignorance, one conceals an offense through body or speech. "Either with one person" or "in one [instance]":

because of the change of gender (*liṅga*), the emergence from an offense occurs in these four ways; such is the meaning. [This refers to] the settling methods (*samatha*) such as the "covering over as with grass" (*tiṇavatthāraka*) and rehabilitation (*abbhāna*).
It should be understood that an offense is cleared within the Saṅgha by means of [formal procedures] such as relinquishment (*nissajjana*) and so forth when performed before a group.

Clearing an offense in the presence of a single individual is self-evident. Furthermore, from the statement, "Those offenses which are not common to both monks and nuns—there is no offense for those offenses," it should be known that there is a clearing of offenses upon the change of gender (*liṅgaparivattana*).
377. "In the two conditions" means in the case of robes and almsfood. And it is not only these;

even the act of making a sign (*nimittakamma*) is not permitted at all, though it was not mentioned here for the sake of the metrical convenience of the verse. In this context, "making a sign" refers to any bodily or verbal action that prompts others to give requisites.
[This applies] when someone is going along after having taken solid food (*khādanīya*).
Having seen him, his conduct should be understood through such methods as asking, "Did you receive any solid food? and so forth.
"Indirect talk" (*parikathā*) means speaking by turning the subject around in whatever way he might obtain it;
his conduct should be understood through such methods as saying, "At present, the monks are weary from alms-food," and so forth. "Hinting" (*obhāsa*) means talk connected with the requisites.

But making a formal request (*viññatti*) is clearly not permitted. Regarding the third [offense], concerning lodgings (*senāsana*): in the case of a lodging, gestures (*nimitta*), hints (*obhāsa*), and indirect talk (*parikathā*) are permissible, but only a formal request is not permitted.
In this context, "making a sign" (*nimittakamma*) refers to such things as preparing the ground for the sake of a lodging upon seeing lay followers.
A "hint" (*obhāsa*) is, for example, saying, "Lay followers, where do you live? to which they reply, "In a mansion, Venerable Sir."

The statement beginning with, "When it was said, 'Why is a dwelling for the bhikkhus not permitted? [is an example]. "Indirect talk" (parikathā) refers to the statement, "The lodgings for the bhikkhus are crowded. "In the remainder" means in the case of the requisite of medicine.
378. "Does not succeed" means it does not come to pass. "Giving after the lapse of time" means *accayadāna*. Among the five types of fellow practitioners (*sahadhammika*), by whichever...
If someone, while dying, says, "After my passing, let my requisites belong to my preceptor, or to my teacher, or to anyone else," they do not come to belong to those [individuals];
therefore it is said, "it does not take effect. And that belongs to the Saṅgha alone:
if this has been said by monks or novices, then even upon his death, they belong to the monastic Saṅgha alone.
If it was spoken by bhikkhunīs, sāmaṇerīs, or sikkhamānās, then upon their death, it belongs to the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs;
this is the meaning. As for "it is valid for householders," this means that the gift of atonement (accaya-dāna) for householders is indeed valid for all of them.
379. "In the residence" (upassaye) means in the bhikkhunī vihāra. "The inheritance" (dāyajja) means the inheritance of those requisites. "And in the rest" (sesepi) [means...]
If nuns, female trainees, or female novices pass away in a bhikkhu’s dwelling, the meaning is that the Sangha of bhikkhus alone is the heir to their requisites.
Regarding the phrase "to the former alone":
this refers to what was given with the instruction, "Having taken these requisites, give them to so-and-so," which belongs to the former [the donor].
The meaning is "it belongs. However, that which is given with the words, "I give it to so-and-so," belongs to the last [monk] alone, because it was given after having been relinquished.
Having understood this procedure, one should either take it on trust or determine it as a robe for the deceased; such is the connection.
As for the determination of a robe for the deceased: having struck the gong and announced the time, and having waited a short while, if...
If monks arrive, they should be shared with them; if they do not arrive, one should resolve: "These robes are my portion.
When resolved in this way, all of them belong to him alone, but the formal assignment (*ṭhitikā*) does not remain fixed.
If, having set aside each one, he thinks: "This first portion falls to me; this second portion [falls to me],"...
In this way he takes it up; what has been taken is well-taken, and the stability remains. Even for one who takes it after having brought it to such a state, it is indeed determined. 381.
Having placed a striker upon a metal vessel, everything is allowable; and in the case of wooden vessels, [everything is allowable] including a wooden bowl.

With the exception of sandals, a couch, and a high-backed chair, everything is permitted; with the exception of a wooden scrubber and a clay pot, everything made of clay is permitted—this is the meaning. "Monks, I allow all metal utensils except for a hammer;
I allow all wooden utensils except for a high-backed chair, a couch, a wooden bowl, and wooden sandals."
"Except for the *kataka* and the *kumbhakārikā*, all earthenware vessels," so it is said.
Here, *kataka* refers to a bowl made in the shape of a lotus calyx. A hut made entirely of clay, like that of Dhaniya, is called a *kumbhakārikā*.
This concludes the miscellaneous analysis.
The commentary on the Exposition of Miscellaneous Topics is finished.
42. Commentary on the Exposition of the Teaching: 382.
The meaning is that the relinquishing of the state of being a bhikkhu is the confession of a *pārājika* offense. For this has been said: "One who desires purity..."
“Whether one wishes to be a householder, or wishes to be a lay follower (*upāsaka*), or wishes to be a monastery attendant (*ārāmika*), or wishes to be a novice monk (*sāmaṇera*).

Therefore, for one who has committed a *pārājika* offense, purification exists only in the state of becoming a householder and so forth; for another [type of offender], there is no purification at all.

According to the method stated previously in the passage beginning, “If he conceals it, knowing that he has committed it, he should undergo the probationary period (*parivāsa*) for that duration,” etc.
With reference to this, it is said: "emergence as previously described. 383.
With reference to what is now to be stated, it is said:
"thus. 384. "I confess" means I announce. "These, I [confess]; these, indeed, I [confess]."
386. (Ka) "Except otherwise" means that which the Saṅgha grants as permission for one who is ill to be separated from his three robes.

(Kha) "Out-of-season robe" (*akālacīvara*) means: "That which arises during the eleventh month when the Kathina has not been spread, or during the seventh month when the Kathina has been spread, or even if given at the proper time, provided it is given specifically [for that purpose]—this is called an out-of-season robe.
(Ga) "Old robe" (*purāṇacīvara*) is said to be "that which has been worn once or wrapped around once. "A non-relative" (*aññātikā*) means...

(Cha) "Neither related on the mother’s side nor on the father’s side, up to the seventh generation of ancestors"—for washing a sitting mat or a rug-covering, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

(Gha) "Except in exchange": here, even a piece of myrobalan fruit is permitted. "Robe" (*cīvara*) here refers to that which is fit for formal assignment (*vikappaṇa*), starting from the smallest allowable size.
(Ṅa) "Except on an occasion": here, the meaning of "occasion" is as stated: "The monk is either one whose robe has been stolen or one whose robe has been lost."
(Ca) Because it is stated, “That monk may accept robes from him up to the limit of an inner and an outer robe,” the phrase “beyond that” (*tatuttari*) is used.
In this regard, however, it is stated: “If three have been lost, two may be accepted; if two have been lost, one may be accepted;
if one has been lost, nothing need be accepted.”
(Cha-ja) “Venerable sir, what kind of robe do you need? What kind of robe shall I have purchased for you?”—this is the meaning of “not being invited.
*Vikappeti* means to undergo a special modification or an additional arrangement.
Here, the first [term] is stated with reference to one person, while the second is stated with reference to many; this much is the distinction.

(Jha) Regarding the phrase "more than three times": here, when someone has brought some kind of unallowable thing and says, "Venerable sir, this robe-fund has been brought for the sake of the venerable one;
may the venerable one accept the robe-fund," [the monk] should say: "Friends, we do not accept robe-funds; we accept robes."
It should be said, "At the proper time, it is allowable. When this has been said, if he says, "Is there anyone who acts as a steward?
then the one seeking robes should designate anyone except for the five types of co-religionists, saying only this: "Friend, this person is a servant to the monks.
When this has been said, if the donor [places] an unallowable thing in his hand...
Having given [the money] and saying, "He will purchase this robe-cloth for the noble one and give it to him," he departs.
One should then approach him and, after urging and reminding him two or three times, say only: "Friend, I have need of a robe-cloth.
One must not say, "Give me a robe-cloth," and so forth. If, through such urging three times, one obtains that robe-cloth, [it is permissible].
This is good. If he does not obtain [an audience], he should remain silent for at most six times;
he must not sit on a seat, nor accept material gifts, nor speak the Dhamma.
When asked, "For what reason have you come?", he should say only this much: "Know it yourself, friend. If he performs acts such as sitting down, he breaks his standing.
They say that one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for breaking the rule.

However, if one does not act in this way, but instead brings it about by urging more than three times or by standing more than six times, the meaning is that it is an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*).

(Ña) What is called "spread" (*santhata*) is that which has been made by spreading [the material], not woven. Even if one makes it by mixing in even a single thread of *kosiya* silk, it is an offense involving forfeiture.
(Ṭa) "Pure black" means unmixed with anything else. It is said: "Black [wool] is of two kinds: natural black or dyed black. (Ṭha) Regarding the phrase "without taking... [up to] equal":

here the rule is that however much sheep's wool one intends to use, of that amount two portions must be taken of black wool, one portion of white, and one portion of "go-cariya" (tawny/brown). Even of a single...
(Ḍa) If there is an excess portion of black wool, it is indeed an offense involving forfeiture.
(Ḍha) Regarding "less than six years": this means within the period shorter than six years.
Furthermore, by one who has a sitting rug made, from one side of the old rug, a circle or a square—
Or, having cut it so that the portion taken up is about a span in size, one should take it and spread it out either in sections or by unraveling it.
(Ta) It is not only in the case of washing that there is an offense of expiation; it is likewise an offense of expiation in the case of dyeing as well.

Since the acceptance of silver itself has been prohibited, they perform various kinds of exchanges of gold—such as exchanging what has been acquired for what has not yet been acquired—failing to see the fault in such transactions; it is with reference to this that the term "of various kinds" is used.
(387–9) The word "then" (*atha*) is used to show what should be done after confessing the offense.
"He tells a layperson" means that if a monastery attendant (*ārāmika*) or a lay follower (*upāsaka*) comes there, he should speak to him. When addressed in this way, he [says]: "With this..."
The meaning is: "What shall I bring? [This is what he would say. "Without speaking" means without saying, "Bring this or that.

Because of the statement, "What is allowable (kappiya) must be pointed out," one should point it out by saying, "For those who have gone forth, ghee, oil, honey, or molasses are permitted"; one must certainly not say, "Bring such-and-such a thing."
"Both these two" means both the one who accepts money and the one who deals in money; this is the meaning.
"By another" means that even a portion obtained by a monastery attendant (ārāmika) is not permissible.
"Even so much as the shade of a tree produced from it is not permissible" means that even if it has been relinquished, it is still not permissible to accept.

In this context, just as cloth obtained from one who has engaged in trade with silver is not allowable, so too these three items—the blanket mixed with silk and the others—are not allowable. It is not only that specific case;
they are likewise not allowable for others as well, because it is stated: "If he obtains and uses what has been made by another, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."

391. If one does not obtain it in this way, the meaning is that the monastery attendant or others should be instructed, saying, "Discard this. If one still does not obtain it even in this way, the meaning is that an appointed monk should discard it.
392. The phrase "these" is said with reference to both accepted gold and exchanged gold.

A "second bowl" is defined as a bowl for which one has requested another new bowl while possessing a bowl with fewer than five mends; [for such an act] there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
The connection is that both this [robe] and these [other items] may be forfeited to the Saṅgha. Because it is stated, "It must be forfeited in the midst of the Saṅgha;
it must be forfeited in an assembly of bhikkhus," it is not permissible to forfeit them to a group (gaṇa) or to an individual (puggala).
However, as for the remaining three bases, such as the robe-cloth and so forth, it is said: "It must be forfeited to the Saṅgha, or to a group, or to an individual."
Because it is stated [as] "or," it is permissible to relinquish [the item] to the Saṅgha and so forth.
"Even in another language" means that for one who is unable to speak according to the Pāḷi, it is permissible to relinquish it even in any other language such as Tamil;
this is the meaning. 393. (Ka-ga) "Of various kinds" refers to robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites as support for the sick.
“Even as little as a lump of powder, a tooth-stick, or even a thread of cotton”—thus it is stated in the Pāḷi. “Cetāpito” means taken after having requested it. 394.
“Having appointed a bowl-receiver, [he should give] the last bowl to the Saṅgha”: the meaning is that he should cause him to give away whichever is the final bowl.
395. (Kha) Regarding “the rain-cloak, when worn, is to be relinquished,” the field for seeking a rain-cloak is established here.
The field is fourfold: the field for seeking, the field for making, and the field for wearing;
and the time is twofold: the time for the belly and the time for the back. How so?
During the months of the summer, the first half-month of the last month is the field for seeking; the latter half is both the field for making and the field for wearing.

It is permissible to search for [medicines], but it is not permissible to resolve [upon them]. However, the four months of the *vassika* (rains) season are the field for all four activities, including searching.
These same five months are called the "belly period" (*kucchisamaya*). The other seven months are the "back period" (*piṭṭhisamaya*);
during that time, it is not permissible to bring about the arising of mindfulness.

(Ga) "Seizes": here, having given a robe with the perception, "Whoever shall carry my bowl, robes, and so forth, will travel with me," if one later sees that person not performing his own service and seizes it back with the same perception [of ownership], he incurs this offense.
One who has given after completely relinquishing [the object] does not even have the right to take it back.
(Gha) "Having requested thread": here the meaning is that one has requested thread for the purpose of sewing robes and so forth during the robe-making season and other such times.
Otherwise, it is not even permitted to request thread [for personal use]. The meaning is: "having obtained [the cloth] from weavers [of thread] through such a request.
When the thread and the weavers are unallowable (*akappiya*), [the robe] may be only a span (*vidatthi*) in length and a cubit (*hattha*) in width.
If it is finished, there is an offense of expiation (*nissaggiya*); if it is on one side [of the robe] and not yet fit, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
(Ṅa) "Has undergone alteration" means it has undergone an excessive arrangement, such as saying, "Friend, this robe-cloth is being woven for me; make it long and wide," and so forth.
(Ca) "Urgent robe-cloth" (*accekacīvara*) refers to that which is given by those wishing to go to an army, and so forth.
(Cha) "Exceeding three nights" means more than six days. Regarding the benefits stated thus: "For you, monks, who have spread the kaṭhina, five things shall be permissible:

wandering without having been invited, wandering without having formally undertaken [the robe], eating in a group, a robe as much as one desires, and whatever robe-material arises there—that shall be for you," [this refers to] wandering without having formally undertaken [the robe] during the month of robes.

The remaining benefits are obtained by setting this aside. If it were possible to go about without having formally undertaken the robes, the monks of Pāvā would not have approached the Blessed One with their robes still wet after the rains retreat;

because that is not possible, they approached the Blessed One even during the robe-month while carrying their triple-robe set. Therefore, it should be understood as an exemption from going about without having formally undertaken the robes.
They say that only those for whom the *kathina* has been spread receive [the robe],
and not others. As for the passage written in certain manuscripts— "Venerable sir, I have committed one offense entailing confession (*pāṭidesanīya*), two, or many offenses entailing confession"—
this is according to the *Khuddasikkhā* of the inhabitants of Abhayagiri.
It seems this has been demonstrated. For therein it is said: "Venerable sir, I have fallen into several *pāṭidesanīya* offenses;
I confess them. Venerable sir, I have fallen into one *pāṭidesanīya* offense; I confess it. But for us, there is no such method of confession.
[One says: "Friend, I have committed a blameworthy thing..."
“It is an unwholesome offense entailing confession; I confess it,” so it is said. In the *Samantapāsādikā*, it is stated:
“‘It is blameworthy, friend,’ and so forth, is the demonstration of the manner in which it should be confessed. Since it is also stated in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*:

“The manner in which it should be confessed is indeed shown in the training rule by way of the method beginning with ‘It is blameworthy, friend’,” the procedure for confession follows the very method found in the text.
It should be understood as follows: If there are two [offenses], one should say, "Friends, I have committed two blameworthy, unsuitable, offenses entailing confession;

I confess them," and "Venerable sirs, see these offenses. If there are many, one should say, "Friends, I have committed many blameworthy, unsuitable, offenses entailing confession; I confess them," and "Venerable sirs, see these offenses."
And thus, the method of instruction should be understood according to what is appropriate. The remainder is of the same kind as already stated.
398. "In that which does not lead to confession" means one does not confess a *pārājika* or a *saṅghādisesa*.
"And [in] a non-offense" means one does not confess even a non-offense as being an "offense. "Even a light offense previously confessed, one does not confess again."
"Connection" means that one should not confess [an offense] in the presence of those who live in different residences or outside the common boundary (*sīmā*).

"By four or five" means that here, as in the case of the *pavāraṇā* ceremony for those of the same seniority, one should not confess together with four or five others in the presence of a single person;
rather, it is permissible for two or three to do so. If one asks, "How should it be confessed? [the answer is: in the presence of one person.
When all three have sat down together and one has said, "Venerable sir, I have committed one offense entailing confession (*pācittiya*);
I confess it in your presence," and after he has been asked three times by the other, "Friend, do you see that offense?", he replies, "Yes, venerable sir, I see it" or "Yes, friend, I see it. Then...
When it is said, "You should exercise restraint in the future," or "You should exercise restraint," one should say, "Very well, I shall exercise restraint thoroughly.
This is how it should be confessed. "By mind" means that one does not confess by means of vocal expression alone, but solely with the mind.
"Of those who have not been dealt with" refers to one who has committed the ultimate offense or one who has been suspended; for such persons, the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā [are not valid].
The meaning is that one does not confess [the offense] in the presence of someone who has been set aside. "Not various" means that one does not confess various offenses by saying they are "one.
However, one [offense] may be confessed as "many. This concludes the analysis of confession.
The commentary on the exposition of confession is finished.
43. Commentary on the Exposition of the Granting of Consent (Chandadānaniddesa) 399.
"When the Saṅgha has assembled at the place of the formal act" (*kammappatte*)—this is the connection [of the phrase].
By this, they say it is shown that the granting of consent does not take effect when the Saṅgha has not assembled. Herein, this is the investigation: in a monastery with five bhikkhus, for one...

Having brought forward the *chandapārisuddhi* (consent and purity), it is permitted in both the Canon (*pāḷi*) and the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) for the rest [of the monks] to perform the Uposatha and other rites.
Among them, there is one who gives the consent and one who receives the consent; excluding these two, the Saṅgha is not considered "assembled" here because of the existence of three separate groups.
Therefore, it is permissible to give [the consent] even when [the full assembly] has not gathered. However, by the one making the announcement, they must indeed have assembled.
It must be announced. Here too, it is said "he should take [the consent]," not "he should confess.
In that regard, the assembly of those eligible for the formal act (kamma) together with the one who conveys the consent should be understood.
Now, in order to show the procedure for giving consent, he says "one bhikkhu," and so forth.
401. (Ka) If it is asked: "Is it not sufficient merely to say 'I give my consent' (*chandam dammi*)? What is the purpose of saying 'Take it' and 'Announce it'?

It is said in reply: Because the Blessed One has stated, "Monks, I allow that when one gives purity (*pārisuddhi*) on the Uposatha day, he may also give his consent," one who is carrying out the Blessed One’s instruction says, "I give my consent."
It has been said: “Monks, if the one who carries the consent (*chandahāraka*) departs on the way after the consent has been given, the consent remains uncarried.

Because this was said, when someone gives the purification (*pārisuddhi*) so that another person carrying the consent does not depart, and instructs them by saying, “Do this and that,” it is said, “Carry my consent.
“Monks, if the one who carries the consent... [and so forth].
Because it is stated: "When consent has been given and [the messenger] has reached the Saṅgha, if he does not announce it intentionally, the consent is considered brought;
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the one who brings the consent," therefore, when one says to him, "If you do not announce it intentionally, you will incur an offense;
so please announce it," and speaks thus, saying "Announce it," this is how these words are purposeful in this context.
[The details] are to be understood.

The same applies to the giving of the *pārisuddhi* (declaration of purity). 402. "Remaining business" (*sesakamma*): if the Saṅgha performs another act, such as an act of formal authorization (*apalokanakamma*), within the boundary of the Uposatha, that [Uposatha] act is obstructed;
the meaning is that it is disrupted. 403. "Both": the meaning is both the Uposatha and the remaining business. "Not by oneself": one does not accomplish the Uposatha for oneself.
405. “Having arranged the upper robe over one shoulder and sitting in the kneeling posture,” etc.; the meaning is: having performed all the formalities of service. 406.
Having announced, “The invitation has been given by such-and-such a name.

408. Regarding the reading *paṭijāneyya nāhaṭā*: *nāhaṭā* means “not brought”; the meaning is that it has not been brought. Likewise, *heyya* means “one would perform [acts] such as leaving the order,” etc.

409. "Or one who is asleep would not inform [the Sangha]"—this is to be connected with the phrase "it is brought. "Anāpatti vā" means simply "there is no offense. This concludes the determination regarding the giving of consent (*chandadāna*).
The commentary on the exposition of the giving of consent is finished.
44. Commentary on the Exposition of the Uposatha.
411. The recitation of the Suttas is for the Saṅgha alone. "For the rest" means for two or three [monks]. 412.

Regarding "the preliminary duties (pubbakaraṇa) and the preliminary tasks (pubbakicca), having brought them to readiness": the "preliminary duty" is that which must be done first of all. That which must be done immediately thereafter is called the "preliminary task.
Herein: "The broom, the lamp, and water, together with the seat;"
“These are called the preliminary duties for the uposatha:
the giving of consent, the declaration of purity, the announcement of the season, the counting of the monks, and the exhortation.
These are called the preliminary tasks for the uposatha.”
In this way, the preliminary duties (*pubbakaraṇa*) and the preliminary tasks (*pubbakicca*) should be understood according to the method stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
“The Uposatha [is valid] as long as there are monks who have attained the status for the formal act (*kamma*),
and no common offenses (*sabhāgāpatti*) exist.”
"And there are no persons to be avoided therein;
it is called 'the proper time' (pattakalla).
By virtue of what was said, when the proper time has been ascertained, the meaning is "attained" (pajjita). "Monks, there are these five recitations of the Pātimokkha."
Having recited the Nidāna, the remainder should be announced by means of oral transmission; this is the first recitation of the Pātimokkha.
Having recited the Nidāna and having recited the four Pārājikas, the remainder should be announced by means of oral transmission; this is the second recitation of the Pātimokkha.
Having recited the Nidāna, having recited the four Pārājikas, and having recited the thirteen Saṅghādisesas, the remainder...

The rest is to be announced by means of what has been heard; this is the third recitation of the Pātimokkha. Having recited the Nidāna, having recited the four Pārājikas, having recited the thirteen Saṅghādisesas, and having recited the two Aniyatas, the remainder is to be announced by means of what has been heard;
this is the fourth recitation of the Pātimokkha. The fifth is by way of full detail. "These, monks, are the five recitations of the Pātimokkha."
Because it has been stated thus, the meaning is that this recitation of the Sutta is explained in five ways.
(413) "Without obstacles" means that the brief recitation is excluded—that is, prohibited—without the ten kinds of obstacles, such as the obstacle of a king.
"The Elder" refers specifically to the Elder of the Saṅgha. "In this" refers to the five recitations, or alternatively, to two.

The intention is that, because it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary) that "the Elder alone is the authority even in three separate locations," it is permissible to recite [the Pātimokkha] in brief even when an obstacle is present.

If one asks, "Where is this stated?"—it is in the commentary on the canonical passage which says, "It should be under the authority of whichever monk there is who is experienced and capable. Regarding the phrase "whichever monk there is who is experienced and capable":
Although the Pātimokkha has been authorized for one who is both young and competent, nevertheless, this is the intended meaning here:

if five, four, or three recitations of the Pātimokkha do not come to the senior of the Saṅgha, but two remain unbroken and well-mastered by heart, then the Pātimokkha depends entirely upon that senior. But if even this much...
The meaning stated is that he is unable to make it clear and remains dependent upon a learned bhikkhu.
This is also stated in the Pāḷi: "Those bhikkhus, monks, should straightway dispatch one bhikkhu from a neighboring residence, saying:
'Go, friend; having mastered the Pātimokkha either in brief or in detail, return.'"

414. While the Pātimokkha is being recited, or while it is being recited, if others should arrive who are equal in number or fewer, [the thought is: "It has been recited, it has been well-recited; one should sit together with them and listen to the remainder"—this is the meaning. 415.
Or, when the assembly has just finished reciting, or when the entire assembly or a portion of it has departed, if others should arrive who are equal in number or fewer—this is the connection.
"Pārisuddhim" means the Uposatha of purity. "Kareyyesan" means they should perform it.
"He should do so for them" means "in their presence. "And if many" means "and if there are many," or again, "if many have returned.
Regarding the phrase "when it is being recited, when it has just been recited, when some have left, or when all have left":
the meaning is that after performing the preliminary duties among all the aforementioned cases, one should recite the Pātimokkha once again from the beginning.
“*Itarānan*” means “of the newcomers. “*Sacetaro*” means “if it is the fourteenth day”; this is the meaning.
“*Samānetarenuvattantū*” means “let the others—whether equal in number or fewer—follow the former residents”; this is the meaning.
“*Sacēdhikā*” means “if the newcomers are more numerous, let the former residents follow them”; this is the meaning. This same method applies to the remaining cases as well: “of the newcomers...”

The meaning is that the legal decision (*vinicchaya*) should be understood according to the method beginning with: "It is the fifteenth for the residents, the fourteenth for the incoming monks," and "May the incoming monks who have arrived on the day of settlement follow the residents," and so forth.
417. "The root-stayers" refers to the residents. "Of the incoming monks who have arrived on the day of settlement. "Desiring to grant harmony" means: if they wish, let them grant it.

418. If they do not give [consent], the meaning is that the Uposatha should be performed by those who have arrived, having gone outside. The connection is: "Consent should be given through a majority, even if there is no desire [to attend].
419. Because it has been said: "Monks, the reciter of the Pātimokkha must not intentionally fail to announce [the time].
Whoever does not announce it incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," it is therefore stated: "He should announce the Sutta. [And further: "Monks, I allow the reciter of the Pātimokkha..."

Because it is stated, “How will they make an effort to cause [the sound] to be heard? There is no offense for one who makes such an effort,” it is said that “for one who intentionally causes [the sound] to be heard, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

420. “In that way” means an offense of wrong-doing. “Fit” means not being ill. “Sent” means commanded. It is said: “Monks, when commanded by the Elder, one who is not ill must sweep. Whoever does not sweep incurs an offense of wrong-doing,” and so forth. 421–3.
Now, in order to show the Uposatha of Purity, it is said, “Having swept,” and so forth. “Having raised the hands in añjali” means...

“Connection”: the meaning is that those remaining two [cases] should be stated as being thus brought forth. The meaning is that those two bhikkhus, having previously completed the undertaking by way of arranging the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) and so forth over one shoulder, should be addressed by the newcomer in this manner. 424–5.
Now, in order to show what must be done by the two, it is said: “By the elder among the two.”

426. Up to this point, having shown both the *saṅghuposatha* (the Uposatha of the Saṅgha) and the *pārisuddhiuposatha* (the Uposatha of purity), as stated in the passages: “I allow you, monks, to recite the Pātimokkha for four [monks],” and “I allow you, monks, to perform the *pārisuddhiuposatha* for three [monks],” and “I allow you, monks, to perform the *pārisuddhiuposatha* for two [monks].”

Now, in order to show the *adhiṭṭhāna-uposatha* (the observance day by formal resolution) permitted for a single bhikkhu who dwells alone, he said, beginning with “The preliminary duty” (*pubbakicca*).
Here, “preliminary duty” refers specifically to the sweeping and so forth.
427. The connection is: “If they should perform this or that Uposatha according to the Sangha-uposatha, the purity-uposatha, and the resolution-uposatha.”

428. For one who perceives a group that is actually united as being "a group," and for one who is thus doubtful, thinking, "Is this a group or is it united?", there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

However, for one who, knowing the presence of monks who have not yet arrived, performs the Uposatha with the intention of causing a schism, thinking, "Let them perish, let them be destroyed; what use have I for them?", there is a grave offense (thullaccaya).
The meaning is as follows. Both of them, perceiving it as a "complete assembly," are free from offense. 429–430.
Those called "the rest of the fellow-followers of the Dhamma" refers to the remaining four, excluding the bhikkhu. Regarding the term "one incapable":
here this refers to a paṇḍaka, one who lives in the company of a woman, one who has gone over to another sect, an animal, a matricide, or a patricide.
The murderer of an arahant, the defiler of a bhikkhunī, the schismatic of the Saṅgha, the shedder of blood [of a Buddha], and the hermaphrodite are included as being incapable [of progress].
Herein, however, it should be understood that the Nāga youths and others belong to the class of animals.
The connection is: "And the Pātimokkha is not to be recited in an assembly where these are seated."

"So be it": however, even that Saṅgha which shares the same offense should not recite [the Pātimokkha]; the meaning is that it should not be recited even by one whose consent (*chanda*) has been conveyed.

In this context, there are four kinds of "being excluded" (*pārivāsiya*): exclusion from the assembly (*parisapārivāsiya*), exclusion for the night (*rattipārivāsiya*), exclusion by means of consent (*chandapārivāsiya*), and exclusion by intention (*ajjhāsayapārivāsiya*).

In this case, however, when the bhikkhus have assembled for some business and are beset by rain clouds and the like, they rise up without having relinquished their consent, thinking, "We are without a place [to stay];
let us go elsewhere. This is called the exclusion of the assembly (*parisapārivāsiya*).
Although it is an exclusion of the assembly, because consent has not been relinquished, it is permissible to perform the formal act (*kamma*).
Furthermore, when monks have assembled at night with the thought, "We shall perform the Uposatha and other rites," and while they are listening to the Dhamma, the dawn breaks.
If they were sitting down thinking, "We shall perform it on the fourteenth day," it is permissible to perform it on the fifteenth.
However, if they were sitting down intending to perform it on the fifteenth, it is not permissible to perform the Uposatha on the first day of the fortnight (pāṭipada), which is not an Uposatha day.
However, it is permissible to perform other business of the Saṅgha. This is what is called "staying overnight [with the consent].

Again, suppose monks have assembled, thinking, "We shall perform some formal act such as rehabilitation (abbhāna)," and there a reciter of the constellations says, "Today the constellation is inauspicious. By his word, they [postpone] the *chanda*...
Having relinquished [their consent], they remain seated right there. Then another person comes and says, "What is the use of the lunar mansion? Go ahead and do it.
This constitutes both the relinquishment of consent (*chandapārivāsiya*) and the relinquishment of intention (*ajjhāsayapārivāsiya*).

It is not permissible to perform a formal act (*kamma*) while that relinquishment remains without bringing back the purity of consent (*chandapārisuddhi*) once more. It is with reference to this that it is said: "by one whose consent has been relinquished" (*chandena parivutthena*).
431. Having committed an offense and not confessed it, or having said, "Friends, I am uncertain regarding this such-and-such offense;

when I become certain, I shall make amends for that offense," yet failing to disclose one's uncertainty—or because it has been stated, "Monks, the Uposatha should not be performed on a non-Uposatha day except for the sake of the Sangha’s concord."
The meaning is that it is not permissible to perform [the Uposatha] on the following Uposatha day either. 432.

Because it was said: “Monks, on the Uposatha day one must not go from a residence where monks are present to a residence where no monks are present, or to a non-residence, except with a Saṅgha or except due to obstacles,” it is called “a residence where the Uposatha has not been performed.”
It has been said: "One should not go beyond the boundary. Regarding the phrase "one may even resolve upon the boundary":

if they perform the Uposatha within the monastery, one should not go either to the boundary or to the river for the purpose of resolving upon the Uposatha. However, if there is a certain bhikkhu present there, it is permissible to go into his presence.
It is also permissible to go from a residence where the Uposatha has been neglected; having gone in this manner...
"One may also make a formal resolution. This concludes the analysis of the Uposatha.
The commentary on the exposition of the Uposatha is finished.
45. Commentary on the Exposition of the Pavāraṇā.
433. Because it was said, “I allow you, monks, to perform the *pavāraṇā* within the Saṅgha for five [monks],” it is therefore called “the remaining *saṅghapavāraṇā*.

434. Regarding the phrase “today is the *pavāraṇā*”: here, on the fourteenth day (*cātuddasikā*), one should perform the preliminary duty by saying, “Today is the fourteenth-day *pavāraṇā*”; on the fifteenth day (*pannarasī*), one says, “Today is the fifteenth-day *pavāraṇā*. 437.

While the elders are performing the *pavāraṇā* sitting in the *ukkuṭika* posture (on their heels), the junior monk himself must likewise remain in the *ukkuṭika* posture until he has completed his own *pavāraṇā*.
The meaning is "he should sit. For it is said: "Monks, one should not sit on seats while the elders are sitting in the *ukkuṭika* posture and performing the invitation (*pavāraṇā*).
Whoever should so sit, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Monks, I allow you to sit in the *ukkuṭika* posture during that interval until the invitation is performed;
having performed the invitation, one may sit on a seat."

440–2. Having thus shown the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) consisting of three utterances, he now says “by means of giving,” etc., in order to show what is to be done regarding the invitations consisting of two utterances, one utterance, and those for those of equal seniority (*samānavassika*).
Therein, “by means of giving” (*dānena*) means either by way of giving (*dānena*).

By the term “discussion of the Dhamma” (*dhammasākacchā*), discourses on the Dhamma, the compilation of the Suttas, the determination of the Vinaya, and so forth, are included. [The phrase] “either by means of giving or by discussion of the Dhamma” [is thus explained].

The connection [of the sentence] is: "Either by means of a dispute, or because the night has been spent, or when there is no opportunity for the *tevācika* (threefold) invitation, one should invite after having established a motion (*ñatti*) in accordance with the ten kinds of obstacles.
Now, in order to show how the motion is established in accordance with the circumstances, he says: "Let the Sangha hear me," and so forth. Regarding "the motion established as it was":
In this context, if a motion that encompasses all [modes] is put forward, one should perform the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) by means of the threefold, twofold, or singlefold formula;
however, only the invitation for those of the same year (*samānavassika-pavāraṇā*) alone is not permitted.

If it is put forward with the words, "Let the Saṅgha invite by the threefold formula," then only the threefold formula is permitted, while the twofold and other formulas are not permitted. When it is said, "Let [the Saṅgha] invite by the twofold formula," then the twofold formula...
The *tevācika* (three-voiced) invitation is permissible; the *ekavācika-samānavassika* (one-voiced and same-year) is not permissible.

However, when it is said, "One should invite with one voice," all are permissible except for those of the same year (*samānavassika*). But when it is said, "Those of the same year," then everything is permissible.

And here, regarding the phrase "bring [the requisites] at the beginning," since this was stated previously in relation to the Uposatha, if [it is asked], "If there are those of the same year... [the rest follows].
In the section beginning with "they might come," the meaning is that he brings [them] forward.
443. Now, with reference to what is about to be said, it is stated: "Thus. The group of three and the group of four constitute the "three-and-four groups.
450. Because it has been stated: "Monks, one who is guilty of an offense should not perform the *pavāraṇā*. Whoever should perform it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)."
When one who has committed an offense, or one who is doubtful, or one who, while performing the *pavāraṇā*, remembers an offense, should proceed according to the method stated for the Uposatha.
From the verse beginning with "In a complete assembly, perceiving it as incomplete,
or being in doubt," until the final verse ending with "or resolve upon an obstacle, or the Saṅgha, or the boundary itself," [the procedure] is the same as for the Uposatha.
“Verses spoken” refers to those intended [here]. 451. “And when the invitation has been performed”:
the intention is that the invitation has been performed before the Saṅgha during the first invitation ceremony. Here, “one who has not spent the rains” refers to one who has entered the later period;

because it is not yet concluded, he is called “one who has not spent the rains. 452. “The four-month [period]” means the full moon of Kattika. Here, “those who have spent the rains” refers to those who have entered the later period. This concludes the determination of the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā-vinicchaya*).
The commentary on the exposition of the Pavāraṇā is finished.
46. Commentary on the Exposition of Restraint (Saṃvara-niddesa). 453.
"By way of the divisions of eye, ear, and so forth" means by way of the six faculties reckoned as the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

The meaning [of the compound] is as follows: "In the range of visible forms, sounds, and so forth" means in the six ranges comprised of visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects.
Herein, covetousness arises in one who attends to things unreasonably by grasping at the beautiful aspect—such as the distinctions of hands, feet, smiles, speech, or glances.
[It arises] through such thoughts as: "He has done me harm, he is doing me harm, he will do me harm," and so on.
By way of this method, ill will arises in one who grasps the sign of resistance and attends to it inappropriately.

However, in this context, for one who does not grasp the sign of a woman or a man, nor any other sign that serves as a basis for defilement such as the sign of beauty, but instead proceeds with regard to what is seen merely as "seen" and so forth, and cultivates appropriate attention toward the sign of foulness— [The remainder of the sentence follows: ...for such a person, [ill will does not arise].

There is the abandoning of covetousness. Or, for one who attends wisely by means of such thoughts as, “He has done me harm; what can be gained from that? or by means of the development of loving-kindness (*mettā*), there is the abandoning of ill-will (*byāpāda*).

Thus, in brief, this virtue of restraint of the sense faculties (*indriyasaṃvara-sīla*) should be understood as having the characteristic of avoiding the grasping of signs, such as the pursuit of defilements, regarding forms and so forth.
"Should restrain" means should ward off.
"Whatever streams there are in the world— mindfulness is their warding off," [said the Blessed One to Ajita].
“I declare the restraint of the taints;
by means of wisdom they are shut off.

Because this has been said, it is stated as “mindful and clearly comprehending. Herein, clear comprehension is fourfold, by way of purposefulness, suitability, the field of activity, and non-delusion. This concludes the analysis of restraint.
The commentary on the exposition of restraint (*saṃvaraniddesa*) is finished.
47. Commentary on the Exposition of Purification (*suddhiniddesa*). 455.

Because there are the divisions of teaching (*desanā*), restraint (*saṃvara*), search (*pariyeṭṭhi*), and reflection (*paccavekkhaṇa*), there are purification by teaching (*desanāsuddhi*), purification by restraint (*saṃvarasuddhi*), and purification by search (*pariyeṭṭhisuddhi*).

"Purification by review" (*paccavekkhaṇasuddhi*): such is the meaning of "fourfold purification. Now, in order to show that which is purified by those purifications, he said, "the restraint of the Pātimokkha is esteemed," and so forth. 456.

Since the restraint of the sense faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*) is purified by the restraint consisting in the mental resolve, "I shall not do it again," therefore the restraint of the sense faculties is called "purification by restraint" (*saṃvarasuddhi*); this is the connection [of the text].
457. "Having abandoned improper search" (*pahāyānesanaṃ*): the sense is that for one who produces requisites in accordance with the Dhamma, having abandoned what is not a proper search;
"requisites" (*paccaya*) is the word to be supplied. 458. "Reflecting wisely, I use the robe... [and so on] ...for the purpose of warding off the afflictions of arisen ailments...
for the sake of the highest state"—thus the meaning is the purification through the aforementioned reflection regarding all four requisites. Herein, however, it is twofold:

Reviewing occurs both at the time of acquisition and at the time of use. For at the time of acquisition, having reviewed [the robes] either by way of their elements (*dhātu*) or by way of their repulsiveness (*paṭikkūla*), the subsequent use of the robes and other items thus set aside is blameless;
so too at the time of use. This is the determination of purity.
The commentary on the exposition of purification is finished.
48. Commentary on the Exposition of Contentment 459.
“Monks, there are these four things that are both small and easy to obtain, and they are blameless. Which four?”
What four? Monks, among robes, the rag-robe is few, easy to obtain, and blameless.
Among foods, the alms-residue is few, easy to obtain, and blameless. Among lodgings, the foot of a tree is few, easy to obtain, and blameless.
Among medicines, fermented urine is few, easy to obtain, and blameless.

"Little and easy to obtain, and that too blameless. Because of this statement—"Monks, these four things are indeed little, easy to obtain, and blameless"—the phrase "with little," and so forth, was spoken.
Regarding the term "contented" (*santuṭṭho*):
here, with respect to each requisite, there is contentment according to what is obtained, according to one's strength, and according to what is appropriate.
By taking these three for each of the four requisites, there are twelve kinds of contentment. Regarding the term "one who knows the proper measure" (*mattaññū*), here there are four measures:
the measure of seeking, the measure of receiving, the measure of using, and the measure of relinquishing.
One who subsists with whatever is available is called "easy to support. This concludes the exposition on contentment.
The commentary on the description of the *santosa* (contentment) is finished.
49. Commentary on the Description of the Four Protections. 461–2.
“*Asubha*” means the meditation on the foul (*asubhabhāvanā*). The intention is that these four are called the “four protections” (*caturārakkhā*). Now...

To demonstrate these, he said, "By way of being remote, etc. Regarding the phrase "by way of being remote, etc.": here, the Blessed One is to be recollected as "Arahant" for these four reasons: because he is remote (āraka); because he has slain his enemies (arī) and the spokes (ara) [of the wheel of existence];
because he is worthy (arahati) of requisites and the like; and because there is an absence of secrecy (raha-bhāva) in his doing of evil. For this has been said: ... [text continues] ...
Thus, by these four reasons, the Blessed One is to be recollected as "Arahant. It has indeed been stated: [citation].
“Because he has driven away and slain the enemies that are the defilements,
because he has destroyed the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra, because he is worthy of receiving requisites and the like,
and because he commits no evil deeds in secret— for these reasons, he is called an Arahant.”

But the Blessed One stands at a very great distance from all defilements because the defilements, together with their latent tendencies, have been destroyed by the Path; therefore, he is called "Arahant" because of his remoteness (*ārakattā*). For it has been said:
"He is called 'remote' from that, for whom there is non-possession of it."
“And because he is without faults, the Lord is therefore considered ‘Arahant.
Furthermore, the Blessed One has destroyed all enemies that are the defilements; therefore, he is called “Arahant” because he has slain his enemies. For this has been said:
“Because all enemies, reckoned as lust and the rest,
have been slain by the Lord with the sword of wisdom, for that reason too he is considered an Arahant.
Furthermore, regarding this [wheel] which has ignorance, existence-tendency, and craving for its hub, and meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable volitional formations for its spokes...

The wheel of saṃsāra— which has aging and death as its rim, which has been pierced by the axle consisting of the origin of the taints (āsava) according to the statement "with the origin of the taints,
there is the origin of ignorance," and which has been yoked to the chariot of the three realms of existence— has proceeded from beginningless time.
At the foot of the Bodhi tree, the Blessed One established it upon the earth of the fourfold pure virtue by means of the feet of right exertion and energy.
Having taken up with the hand of faith the axe of knowledge that brings about the destruction of karma, all the spokes have been destroyed.
Therefore, he is called "Arahant" because of the destruction of the spokes (arānaṃ hatattā). For it has been said:
"Since the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra Have been destroyed by the sword of knowledge..."
“Because of this, he is called ‘Arahant’ by the Lord of the World.

Because he is the foremost among those worthy of offerings, the Blessed One is entitled to the requisites such as robes and to the highest form of worship; therefore, he is called “Arahant” because he is worthy of the requisites and so forth. For it has been said:
“The distinguished honor, together with the requisites...”
"Since this Lord of the World is worthy (araha),
and in the world those who are worthy of their purpose are called 'arahants,' therefore the Conqueror (Jina) deserves this name."

Just as some in the world who pride themselves on being wise commit evil deeds in secret out of fear of ill repute, the Blessed One never does so; therefore, he is called "Arahaṃ" because of the absence of secrecy in his doing of evil. For it has been said:
"Since for one such as he there is no such thing as secrecy regarding evil deeds, By virtue of that absence of secrecy, he is renowned as 'Arahaṃ'."
In this way, "arahant" should be developed by way of being far removed (*ārakatta*) and so forth.
Furthermore, he is the "Sammāsambuddha" because he has perfectly and individually awakened to all phenomena. "Perfectly" means by way of the proper method:

he has fully understood phenomena that are to be fully understood, fully known phenomena that are to be fully known, abandoned phenomena that are to be abandoned, and realized phenomena that are to be realized.

The meaning is: "Because the states that are to be realized have been realized, and because the states that are to be developed have been developed. "By oneself" means by one's own self. For this has been said:
"What is to be directly known has been directly known; what is to be developed has been developed;
what is to be abandoned has been abandoned by me; therefore, O Brahmins, I am a Buddha."
“When it is said, ‘Such indeed is the Blessed One: the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Well-Gone, the Knower of the Worlds,
the Unsurpassed Leader of persons to be tamed, the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One’—

this is called *anussati* (recollection) because it arises again and again as the recollection (*sati*) of the ninefold qualities of the Blessed One, or because it occurs precisely within the sphere where they are to be practiced.”

"Recollection" (*anussati*) means mindfulness (*sati*) appropriate for a clansman who has gone forth out of faith. Recollection arisen with reference to the Buddha is "recollection of the Buddha" (*buddhānussati*).
The meaning is that this mindfulness which occurs in nine ways is what is called "recollection of the Buddha.
Furthermore, the recollection of the Buddha has been explained in all its aspects by the teacher Buddhaghosa in the *Visuddhimagga*.
However, one who has need [of it] should expect it from that [source].

463–4. It should be understood that when the Elder, in demonstrating the development of loving-kindness (*mettā-bhāvanā*)—which must be cultivated morning and evening through the fourfold protection—he presented it by way of the development of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) that is universally applicable.
Otherwise, according to the statement: "Making oneself the analogy, one should neither kill nor cause to kill," [the practice would not be universal].

Having first developed it in this manner—“May I be happy, free from enmity,” and so forth—and having thus made the mind unimpeded within oneself, one should subsequently develop it toward the teacher, the preceptor, and others in due order.
However, no absorption (*appanā*) occurs with respect to oneself. The connection [to the phrase] “in the village of one’s resort” refers to those who are influential there.
“Therein” means in that village of one’s resort. Having delimited [the object] starting from the Saṅgha residing within the boundary...

"Paricchijjati" means "delimits. Thus, by cultivating loving-kindness toward the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he generates a gentle mind in those who live together with him, and consequently, there is pleasant living for him.

Through loving-kindness toward the deities dwelling within the boundary, he becomes well-protected by those deities whose minds have been softened by loving-kindness, through their righteous protection.
Through loving-kindness toward the people in the village where he seeks alms, [he is protected] by those whose mental continuums have been softened by loving-kindness.
He is well-guarded by his requisites through the protection of the righteous lords. Therein, he wanders about unassailed by those people whose minds are gladdened by loving-kindness toward him.
Through loving-kindness toward all beings, his movement is unobstructed everywhere. 465–6.
[One should contemplate] the sections beginning with hair, according to their color, shape, location, direction, and delimitation.
“Having determined” is the connection [to the following]. Here, “by way of color” means by way of the color of the hair and so forth.

“By way of shape” means by way of the shape of those very same things. “By way of location” means by way of the respective location of each part, thinking: “This component is established in this particular location.
“By way of direction” means that in this body, the direction above the navel is the upper direction, and below it is the lower direction.
Direction: therefore, the direction must be defined by determining that "this portion belongs to this particular direction.
Regarding delimitation: there are two kinds of delimitation, namely, delimitation by the similar and delimitation by the dissimilar.
Therein, delimitation by the similar should be understood as follows: "This portion is delimited below, above, and across by this [boundary]."
“Hair is not body-hair; body-hair is not hair”—thus is the delimitation of dissimilar parts by way of non-confusion.
Having thus shown the mode of defining in five ways, he now says “by way of sequence,” etc., in order to show how it should be attended to by one who is attending:
“by way of sequence” means from the time of reciting [the text].
Starting from there, one should not attend to them by skipping every other item as "hair, nails," or by reversing the order as "body hair, hair";
rather, they should be attended to in the correct sequence as "hair, body hair," and so on.
Even when attending to them in the correct sequence, one should attend to them neither too quickly nor too slowly, [directing the mind] externally...
The distraction of the mind toward diverse objects must be warded off. The reading should be taken as: “Having transcended the designation, releasing it gradually.
For when this is the case, the meaning becomes easy to understand through the sequence of meditation.

Without attending to the designation such as “head-hairs, body-hairs,” etc., the mind should be established in this way by means of the repulsive nature alone. As for the phrase “releasing it gradually”: whoever...
The meaning is: for one who gradually releases each part that does not come into the range of vision.
Now, in order to show how the contemplation of repulsiveness (paṭikkūla-manasikāra) is to be practiced, he says: "By color, location, and shape," and so forth. The connection is:
"the development [of insight] as repulsive by means of these parts, such as color, etc. Herein, first, the head-hairs (*kesā*) are [considered] even by way of color...
They are repulsive. For instance, upon seeing even a hair-like speck in their rice gruel or food, people feel disgust. They are repulsive in shape as well;
for instance, those who eat at night feel disgust when touched by the shape of a hair or by such things as a flake of cotton.
Furthermore, they are extremely repulsive in smell when devoid of oil and ointments and when thrown into a fire. Thus, they are repulsive in odor as well.

Repulsive: it is repulsive by way of its receptacle because it is produced from the discharge of pus, blood, urine, feces, bile, phlegm, and so forth, like a leaf used for soup grown in a place of filth.
It is repulsive by way of its location because it is produced upon a heap of thirty-one parts, like a fungus that has arisen on a mound of dung.
[The corpse] is bloated, livid, festering, torn apart, and gnawed.

The meaning is that "foulness" (asubha) refers to the meditation that proceeds by taking the aspect of foulness in these subjects— such as the bloated corpse (*uddhumātaka*), the mutilated and scattered corpse (*hatavikkhittaka*), the bloody corpse (*lohitaka*), the worm-infested corpse (*puḷavaka*), and the skeletal remains (*aṭṭhika*)— beginning with the bloated and so forth. Furthermore,

there is this "death by eradication" (*samucchedamaraṇa*), which for Arahants is the total cutting off of the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*) and the cessation of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*).
Momentary death, which consists of moment-by-moment dissolution, and conventional death, such as "the tree is dead" or "the metal is dead," are not what is intended here.
Here, however, "death" is intended as the cutting off of the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) belonging to a single existence.
That, too, is twofold: timely death and untimely death. Among these, timely death...
It occurs either through the exhaustion of merit, or through the exhaustion of the life-span, or through the exhaustion of both; untimely death occurs by way of obstructive or interrupting karma.
The connection is: having developed it thoroughly [with the thought], "Death will come to me," or "Life will be cut off," or "Death is death."
469–70. However, for one in whom access concentration does not arise even at this point, death should be recollected through these eight aspects:

as the presence of an executioner, as success and failure, as the drawing in [of the breath], as the body being shared by many, as the frailty of life, as signlessness, as the delimitation of the duration, and as the brevity of the moment. Now, in order to show these:

He said, “It is like waiting upon an executioner,” and so forth. The connection is as follows: death is indeed present, standing right there like an executioner who has raised his sword to cut off one’s head;
thus, this meditation is called “mindfulness of death.
This applies in every case. All health ends in illness; all youth ends in old age; all life—

Death has death as its conclusion; therefore, one should recollect death by way of seven aspects: from the perspective of success and failure, thinking, "This excellence of the body, beginning with youth, shines only so long as misfortune known as death does not occur," and so forth;
and from the perspective of bringing [all things] together, namely, from the greatness of fame, the greatness of merit, the greatness of strength, and the greatness of psychic power.
[The greatness of death is considered] from the perspective of the greatness of wisdom—from a Paccekabuddha to a Sammāsambuddha.

In that regard, [it is considered] from the perspective of the greatness of fame: "This thing called death falls even upon those of great renown and great retinues, such as Mahāsammata, Mandhātā, and others; how much more so, then, will it not fall upon me? Thus [is it considered].
“Jotika the dreadlocked ascetic, Ugga,
Meṇḍaka, and Puṇṇaka—
these and others who are in the world,”
"Renowned as possessing great merit,
they have all met with death;
what talk can there be of those like me?"
Thus, because of the greatness of their merit:
“Vāsudeva, Baladeva, Bhīmasena, and the others were great;
yet even they fell under the power of Death. What then can be said of those like me?”—so it was said.
Thus, by way of the greatness of his fortitude;
by way of the greatness of his supernormal power (iddhi), thinking, "He surpasses even those of great psychic power such as Mahāmoggallāna and others—what need to mention those like me?";
and by way of the greatness of his wisdom (paññā), thinking, "He surpasses even those of great wisdom such as Sāriputta and others—what need to mention those like me?"
Likewise, having reflected upon the greatness of the other Paccekabuddhas and Sammāsambuddhas as well, one should apply the reflection by thinking:
"Even for them death falls [upon them]; how much more so, then, will it not fall upon me? And:
"This body is shared by many; it is common to the many hundreds of internal diseases and to external things such as snakes, scorpions, and the like."
Because the body is shared with many others, and because life is weak— according to the method beginning with, "Life is dependent upon inhalation and exhalation"—
and because: "Life, disease, time,
the laying down of the body, and destiny;"
“These five [factors] in the world of the living are signless and do not move.
Thus, because there is no fixed determination of time, it is said: “Monks, he who lives long lives for a hundred years.”
Because it is stated as "or even more," the meaning is that mindfulness of death is called *maraṇassati* by way of such methods as defining the duration of the life-span.
Furthermore, mindfulness of death should be developed from the perspective of the brevity of a moment.
[As it is said: "Life and the physical form..."
“Both pleasure and pain in their entirety / Are joined within a single mind;
/ Swift indeed is that moment’s passage.”
Thus it was said. The Analysis of the Four Protections is finished.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Four Protections is completed.
50. The Commentary on the Exposition of Insight (Vipassanā).

471–2. Regarding the phrase "having discerned name-and-form": here, one who wishes to perform the discernment of name-and-form should first enter and emerge from any meditative absorption (jhāna) other than the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Then, having delimited the jhāna factors such as applied thought (vitakka), etc., and the states associated with them such as contact (phassa), etc., by way of their characteristics (lakkhaṇa), functions (rasa), manifestations (paccupaṭṭhāna), and proximate causes (padaṭṭhāna), [one should realize]: "All this..."
It should be defined as "name" in the sense of bending, because it bends toward the object.
Then, while seeking its condition, one sees that "it proceeds depending on the heart-base (hadayavatthu).

Furthermore, having seen both the primary elements that serve as the condition for the base and the derived matter (upādārūpa), one discerns: "All this is 'form' (rūpa) because of its susceptibility to being affected (ruppana) and its liability to change."
Furthermore, he defines both of these in brief as "name has the characteristic of bending, and form has the characteristic of being affected.
All this has been stated from the perspective of one whose vehicle is serenity (samatha-yānika).

However, one whose vehicle is insight (vipassanā-yānika), having delimited the primary and derived forms by way of the definition of the four elements, [sees] that "all this, because of its being affected..."
He sees it as "form. Then, for one who has thus delimited form, even the immaterial phenomena (arūpadhammā) occurring in dependence upon the eye and so forth come into range.
Thereafter, having unified all those immaterial phenomena by means of their characteristic of bending (namanalakkhaṇa), he sees them as "this is name" (nāma).
He thus defines them twofold: "This is name; this is form. Having defined them in this way,
He sees that "beyond name-and-form, there is no other being, person, individual, deva, or Brahmā.
For just as when the parts are assembled, the word "chariot" comes into being,
so too, when the aggregates exist, there is the conventional designation "being."
In the same way, when the five aggregates of clinging exist, there is merely a conventional designation such as "a being" or "a person.
In this manner, the meaning is that one discerns name-and-form by means of knowledge consisting of purification of view, which is defined as seeing name-and-form as it truly is.
Then, "and its conditions" means that one further discerns the conditions for that name-and-form. By the method already stated...
Having grasped name-and-form, while searching for its cause by asking, "What indeed is the cause of this?",
he perceives the fault in theories of no-cause and irregular causes; and like a physician who, having perceived a disease, searches for its origin and source,
he searches for its cause and condition, [finding] these four factors— ignorance, craving, clinging, and kamma— to be the cause of name-and-form.
One sees that they are called "causes" (hetu) because they are the condition for arising, and "nutriment" (āhāra) is called a "condition" (paccaya) because it is the condition for support.
Thus, regarding the material body: "For this body, the three factors beginning with ignorance are the support like a mother is to a child;
kamma is the progenitor like a father is to a son; and nutriment is the sustainer like a nurse is to a child. In this way, [one contemplates] the material body.

Having performed the discernment of conditions, he further discerns the causal condition for the mental body (nāmakāya) by way of the method beginning: "Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises," and so forth.
Discerning in this manner, he reaches the conclusion: "Past and future phenomena also proceed in exactly this same way."

Regarding him, those fivefold doubts that were stated concerning the past—namely, "Did I exist in the past? Did I not exist? What was I? How was I? Having been what, what did I become in the past?"—and likewise those concerning the future: "Shall I exist in the future?"... [text continues] ...the fivefold doubts that were stated concerning the future—namely, "Shall I exist in the future? Shall I not exist? What shall I be? How shall I be? Having been what, what shall I become in the future?"—all these are abandoned in him. Thus, with the abandoning of these six classes of views, he is said to be one who has abandoned all views. This is called the "abandoning of views. As for the "abandoning of doubt": whatever doubt there was regarding the past, whatever doubt there was regarding the future, and whatever doubt there was regarding the present—namely, "Is this the Noble Truth of suffering? Is this the origin of suffering? Is this the cessation of suffering? Is this the way leading to the cessation of suffering?"—all these are abandoned in him. Thus, with the abandoning of these four classes of doubt, he is said to be one who has abandoned all doubt. This is called the "abandoning of doubt. As for the "abandoning of underlying tendencies": whatever underlying tendency toward sensual desire there was, whatever underlying tendency toward aversion there was, whatever underlying tendency toward views there was, whatever underlying tendency toward conceit there was, whatever underlying tendency toward restlessness there was, and whatever underlying tendency toward ignorance there was—all these are abandoned in him. Thus, with the abandoning of these six underlying tendencies, he is said to be one who has abandoned all underlying tendencies. This is called the "abandoning of underlying tendencies. As for the "abandoning of fetters": whatever fetter of sensual desire there was, whatever fetter of aversion there was, whatever fetter of views there was, whatever fetter of conceit there was, whatever fetter of restlessness there was, and whatever fetter of ignorance there was—all these are abandoned in him. Thus, with the abandoning of these six fetters, he is said to be one who has abandoned all fetters. This is called the "abandoning of fetters. As for the "abandoning of bonds": whatever bond of sensual desire there was, whatever bond of aversion there was, whatever bond of views there was, whatever bond of conceit there was, whatever bond of restlessness there was, and whatever bond of ignorance there was—all these are abandoned in him. Thus, with the abandoning of these six bonds, he is said to be one who has abandoned all bonds. This is called the "abandoning of bonds. As for the "abandoning of attachments": whatever attachment to sensual desire there was, whatever attachment to aversion there was, whatever attachment to views there was, whatever attachment to conceit there was, whatever attachment to restlessness there was, and whatever attachment to ignorance there was—all these are abandoned in him. Thus, with the abandoning of these six attachments, he is said to be one who has abandoned all attachments. This is called the "abandoning of attachments. As for the "abandoning of cravings": whatever craving for sensual pleasure there was, whatever craving for existence there was, and whatever craving for non-existence there was—all these are abandoned in him. Thus, with the abandoning of these three cravings, he is said to be one who has abandoned all cravings. This is called the "abandoning of cravings. As for the "abandoning of thirsts": whatever thirst for sensual pleasure there was, whatever thirst for existence there was, and whatever thirst for non-existence there was—all these are abandoned in him. Thus, with the abandoning of these three thirsts, he is said to be one who has abandoned all thirsts. This is called the "abandoning of thirsts. As for the "abandoning of fevers": whatever fever of sensual desire there was, whatever fever of aversion there was, and whatever fever of views there was—all these are abandoned in him. Thus, with the abandoning of these three fevers, he is said to be one who has abandoned all fevers. This is called the "abandoning of fevers. As for the "abandoning of hankerings": whatever hankering after sensual pleasure there was, whatever hankering after existence there was, and whatever hankering after non-existence there was—all these are abandoned in him. Thus, with the abandoning of these three hankerings, he is said to be one who has abandoned all hankerings. This is called the "abandoning of hankerings. As for the "abandoning of clingings": whatever clinging to sensual pleasure there was, whatever clinging to views there was, whatever clinging to precepts and observances there was, and whatever clinging to a doctrine of self there was—all these are abandoned in him. Thus, with the abandoning of these four clingings, he is said to be one who has abandoned all clingings. This is called the "abandoning of clingings. As for the "abandoning of obsessions": whatever obsession by sensual desire there was, whatever obsession by aversion there was, whatever obsession by views there was, whatever obsession by conceit there was, whatever obsession by restlessness there was, and whatever obsession by ignorance there was—all these are abandoned in him. Thus, with the abandoning of these six obsessions, he is said to be one who has abandoned all obsessions. This is called the "abandoning of obsessions. As for the "abandoning of corruptions": whatever corruption of sensual desire there was, whatever corruption of aversion there was, whatever corruption of views there was, whatever corruption of conceit there was, whatever corruption of restlessness there was, and whatever corruption of ignorance there was—all these are abandoned in him.
