Thus, with the abandoning of these six corruptions, he is said to be one who has abandoned all corruptions. This is called the "abandoning of corruptions. As for the "abandoning of taints": whatever taint of sensual desire there was, whatever taint of existence there was, and whatever taint of ignorance there was—all these are abandoned in him. Thus, with the abandoning of these three taints, he is said to be one who has abandoned all taints. This is called the "abandoning of taints. As for the "abandoning of floods": whatever flood of sensual desire there was, whatever flood of existence there was, and whatever flood of ignorance there was—all these are abandoned in him. Thus, with the abandoning of these three floods, he is said to be one who has abandoned all floods. This is called the "abandoning of floods. As for the "abandoning of bonds": whatever bond of sensual desire there was, whatever bond of existence there was, and whatever bond of ignorance there was—all these are abandoned in him. Thus, with the abandoning of these three bonds, he is said to be one who has abandoned all bonds. This is called the "abandoning of bonds. As for the "abandoning of clingings": whatever clinging to sensual desire there was, whatever clinging to views there was, whatever clinging to precepts and observances there was, and whatever clinging to a doctrine of self there was—all these are abandoned in him. Thus, with the abandoning of these four clingings, he is said to be one who has abandoned all clingings. This is called the "abandoning of clingings. As for the "abandoning of uprisings": whatever arising of sensual desire there was, whatever arising of aversion there was, whatever arising of views there was, whatever arising of conceit there was, whatever arising of restlessness there was, and whatever arising of ignorance there was—all these are abandoned in him. Thus, with the abandoning of these six uprisings, he is said to be one who has abandoned all uprisings. This is called the "abandoning of uprisings. As for the "abandoning of acquisitions": whatever acquisition of sensual desire there was, whatever acquisition of views there was, whatever acquisition of precepts and observances there was, and whatever acquisition of a doctrine of self there was—all these are abandoned in him. Thus, with the abandoning of these four acquisitions, he is said to be one who has abandoned all acquisitions. This is called the "abandoning of acquisitions. As for the "abandoning of barrens": whatever barrenness of sensual desire there was, whatever barrenness of aversion there was, whatever barrenness of views there was, whatever barrenness of conceit there was, whatever barrenness of restlessness there was, and whatever barrenness of ignorance there was—all these are abandoned in him. Thus, with the abandoning of these six barrens, he is said to be one who has abandoned all barrens. This is called the "abandoning of barrens. As for the "abandoning of ties": whatever tie of sensual desire there was, whatever tie of aversion there was, whatever tie of views there was, whatever tie of conceit there was, whatever tie of restlessness there was, and whatever tie of ignorance there was—all these are abandoned in him. Thus, with the abandoning of these six ties, he is said to be one who has abandoned all ties. This is called the "abandoning of ties. As for the "abandoning of hindrances": whatever hindrance of sensual desire there was, whatever hindrance of aversion there was, whatever hindrance of sloth and torpor there was, whatever hindrance of restlessness

The fivefold [doubt] stated as: "Is it not so? What indeed? How indeed? Having been what, shall I indeed become what in the future time?"—and also that which, regarding the present time, makes one inwardly wavering: "Do I exist? Do I not exist? What am I? How am I? Is this..."
“From where has the being come, and where will he go?”—thus the sixfold doubt is stated;

all of these are abandoned. Thus, by discerning conditions and having resolved uncertainty regarding the three periods of time, the knowledge that stands firm is called “purity by overcoming doubt,” “knowledge of the stability of phenomena,” and also “right vision.”

In this context, there are three mundane full understandings (*pariññā*): full understanding as knowledge (*ñāta-pariññā*), full understanding as investigation (*tīraṇa-pariññā*), and full understanding as abandoning (*pahāna-pariññā*).

Among these, the wisdom that proceeds by way of observing the individual characteristics of various phenomena—such as "matter has the characteristic of being molested (*ruppana-lakkhaṇaṃ*), feeling has the characteristic of being felt (*vedayita-lakkhaṇā*)"—is called full understanding as knowledge.
[The wisdom that proceeds] regarding those very same phenomena by way of [seeing them as] "matter is impermanent, feeling is impermanent," and so forth...
The wisdom of insight (vipassanā-paññā) that takes the characteristics as its object after having applied the general characteristic is called "full understanding by scrutinization" (tīraṇa-pariññā).

Furthermore, the insight that takes the characteristics as its object and proceeds by way of abandoning the perception of permanence and so forth regarding those very same phenomena is called "full understanding by abandonment" (pahāna-pariññā).
In this context, from the discernment of formations up to the discernment of conditions, it is [included] within full understanding by knowledge (ñāta-pariññā).

The stage [of full understanding] begins from the contemplation of the aggregates (*kalāpasammasana*) up to the contemplation of rise and fall (*udayabbayānupassanā*); this is the stage of the full understanding of scrutinization (*tīraṇapariññā*).

From the contemplation of dissolution (*bhaṅgānupassanā*) onwards is the stage of the full understanding of abandoning (*pahānapariññā*). For from that point on, contemplating as impermanent, one abandons the perception of permanence;
contemplating as suffering, one abandons the perception of pleasure; contemplating as non-self, one abandons the perception of self.
“Becoming disenchanted with delight, becoming dispassionate toward lust, causing cessation of arising, and relinquishing grasping, one abandons.
By abandoning in this way, one exercises sovereignty over the seven contemplations that accomplish the abandoning of the perception of permanence and so forth.
Thus, because the delimitation of formations and the discernment of conditions have been accomplished within these thorough understandings (*pariññā*), [the path is established].
By this, the yogi has attained full understanding through knowledge (*ñātapariññā*).
Furthermore: "Whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle;
inferior or superior; far or near—all form, by its very nature, is non-existent."
It is impermanent; it is suffering because it is oppressed by arising and passing away;
it is non-self because it is subject to lack of mastery. Whatever feeling, whatever perception, whatever formations, whatever consciousness—whether past, future, or present;
internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; whether far or near—all that is...
“Consciousness is impermanent because, having come to be, it ceases to exist; it is suffering because it is oppressed by arising and passing away; it is non-self because it is devoid of mastery.
In such a manner, one performs the comprehension of the aggregates (*kalāpasammasana*). It is with reference to this that it was said:
“Having applied the three characteristics, he comprehends the conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra*).”
Having thus performed the comprehension of the aggregates by way of impermanence, suffering, and non-self regarding formations, he again sees only the arising and passing away of those formations.
How? By seeing the condition for the arising of the aggregate of form in the sense of "With the arising of ignorance there is the arising of form;
with the arising of craving, kamma, and nutriment there is the arising of form"—thus, in the sense of seeing the arising through conditions, of the aggregate of form.
“He sees the arising; even while seeing the characteristic of production, he sees the arising of the aggregate of form.

Thus he sees the arising of the aggregate of form in five ways. “With the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of form; with the cessation of craving, karma, and nutriment comes the cessation of form.
Thus, in the sense of seeing the cessation of conditions, he sees the passing away of the aggregate of form.
He sees [the characteristic of change]; even while seeing the characteristic of change, he sees the passing away (*vaya*) of the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*).

Thus he sees the passing away in five ways. Likewise, [he sees the arising of the aggregate of feeling]: "With the arising of ignorance comes the arising of feeling; with the arising of craving, karma, and contact comes the arising of feeling.
Even while seeing the characteristic of production, he sees the arising (*udaya*) of the aggregate of feeling.
“With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of feeling; with the cessation of craving, karma, and contact, there is the cessation of feeling.
Thus, even while seeing the characteristic of change in the aggregate of feeling, one sees the passing away of the aggregate of feeling. The same applies to the aggregates of perception and the rest.
However, this is the distinction: for the aggregate of consciousness, in place of contact, it is the arising of name-and-form, and the cessation of name-and-form.

It should be applied in this way. Thus, for each individual aggregate, by way of the arising of conditions, the characteristic of generation, the cessation of conditions, and the characteristic of change—counting ten for each through the vision of rise and fall—fifty characteristics have been stated.
By means of these, it is said: "This is the rise of form; this is the fall of form."
He applies attention in detail both by way of condition and by way of characteristic.
As he does so, his knowledge becomes clear: "Thus, indeed, these phenomena, having not been, come to be; having been, they vanish. He perceives:
"Thus, indeed, these phenomena, unarisen, arise; arisen, they cease"—ever new.
Having been sacrificed, conditioned phenomena (saṅkhārā) appear. They do not remain constant or new;

rather, like a drop of dew at sunrise, like a bubble on water, like a line drawn with a stick on water, like a mustard seed on the point of an awl, and like a flash of lightning, they endure for only a brief moment.
They are like an illusion, a mirage, a dream, a circle of fire from a whirling torch, a city of the Gandharvas, a lump of foam, a plantain trunk, and so forth.

They appear as if they were devoid of substance. To this extent, by means of this mode—namely, that "only that which is subject to fall arises, and what has arisen meets with fall"—he penetrates the fifty characteristics.

Thus he attains the first knowledge of tender insight called the contemplation of rise and fall (*udayabbayānupassanā*), the attainment of which constitutes the stage of one reckoned as a "commenced-insight practitioner" (*āraddhavipassaka*).

Then, for that clansman who has begun insight, ten imperfections of insight arise: illumination, knowledge, rapture, tranquility, pleasure, resolution, exertion, establishment, equanimity, and attachment.
Herein, "illumination" means that at the moment of insight, because of the power of knowledge, the blood becomes clear, and through that, an illumination is produced from the skin.
Seeing that, this yogi relishes that very radiance, thinking, "The path has been reached by me. "Knowledge" refers specifically to insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*);
seeing it proceeding with clarity and courage as he contemplates conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), he relishes it as "the path," just as before.
"Rapture" (*pīti*) is simply insight-rapture; for at that moment, fivefold rapture arises within him.
"Tranquility" refers to the tranquility of insight (*vipassanā-passaddhi*).
At that time, there is no distress, heaviness, rigidity, unwieldiness, sickness, or crookedness of body or mind. "Bliss" is simply the bliss of insight.
It is said that at that time, an exceedingly refined bliss arises, drenching his entire body like a soaked wick.
Adhimokkha (resolute confidence) is the faith that arises at the moment of insight (vipassanā).
At that moment, there arises a powerful faith that is an extreme clarity of both mind and mental factors. Paggaha (exertion) is the energy associated with insight.
For at that moment, there arises energy that is neither lax nor over-exerted, but well-exerted. Upaṭṭhāna (establishment)...

Mindfulness associated with insight (*vipassanā-sampayuttā sati*). For at that moment, well-established mindfulness arises. Equanimity (*upekkhā*) is twofold, by way of insight-equanimity and advertence-equanimity.

At that moment, the knowledge known as equanimity of insight—which is characterized by neutrality toward the grasping of all conditioned phenomena—arises powerfully; and there is also advertence-equanimity at the mind-door, which [directs] to each respective object.
As he adverts, the energy becomes sharp and flows. "Inclination" refers to inclination toward insight (vipassanā-nikanti).
A subtle, peaceful form of inclination arises, forming an attachment to the light and other such phenomena.

Here, the light and so forth are called "defilements" (upakkilesa) because they serve as the basis for defilement, not because they are unwholesome (akusala). Inclination, however, is both a defilement and the basis for defilement.
But when illumination and the other [signs] arise, the wise bhikkhu, without falling into distraction, defines what is the path and what is not the path, thinking:
"The phenomena such as illumination are not the path; rather, the knowledge of insight that has entered the right course and is free from defilements is the path.
His knowledge, established thus by knowing "this is the path" and "this is not the path," is [the knowledge of discrimination of the path].
This is called "purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path.

From this point onward, the insight-knowledge that has reached its culmination by means of the eightfold knowledge is known as "purification by knowledge and vision of the way" (*paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi*).

These are: the knowledge of contemplation of arising and passing away, the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution, the knowledge of appearance as terror, and the knowledge of contemplation of danger.
The knowledge of contemplation of disenchantment, the knowledge of desire for deliverance, the knowledge of contemplation of reflection,
and the knowledge of equanimity towards formations— these are called the eight knowledges. Since the mind, when overwhelmed by the secondary defilements (upakkilesas),
becomes incapable of penetrating the characteristics [of formations], one who wishes to produce these knowledges must again contemplate their arising and falling away.
For one who sees arising and passing away, the characteristic of impermanence appears as it truly is;
and because of being oppressed by arising and passing away, the characteristic of suffering appears, as one sees that "only suffering comes into being, suffering stands, and suffering passes away";

and the characteristic of non-self also appears. And herein, the impermanent is the characteristic of impermanence, the suffering is the characteristic of suffering, and the non-self is the characteristic of non-self.
This distinction should be understood. Here, "impermanent" refers to the five aggregates. Why?
Because they possess the nature of arising, passing away, and change, or because they cease to exist after having come to be. "Change" means aging;

the characteristic of impermanence consists in arising, passing away, and change, or it is a single transformation of state defined as ceasing to exist after having come to be. According to the statement, "What is impermanent, that is suffering," it is precisely those same five aggregates [that are meant].
It is suffering. Why? Because it is constantly oppressed. The mode of constant oppression is the characteristic of suffering (*dukkha-lakkhaṇa*).
From the statement, "That which is suffering is non-self," that same pentad of aggregates is non-self. Why? Because it does not admit mastery.
The mode of not admitting mastery is the characteristic of non-self (*anatta-lakkhaṇa*). These three characteristics also become the objects for one who perceives arising and passing away.
Furthermore, he contemplates even those very same material and immaterial phenomena as "impermanent," and so forth; consequently, formations enter his field of awareness very rapidly.
Then, without making either arising or stability the object, his mindfulness becomes established as he sees only their destruction, decay, and cessation.
This is called the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution (*bhaṅgānupassanā-ñāṇa*). From this point, starting from arising...
When that yogi contemplates only cessation, thinking, "Just as these formations— the five aggregates— break up, so too did formations break up in the past,
and they will break up in the future," his mindfulness becomes established. As he cultivates and develops this knowledge of contemplation of dissolution,
all formations in all states of existence, wombs, destinations, stations, and abodes of beings appear to him like a pit of glowing embers and the like.
They appear as if they were a great terror. This is called the knowledge of the appearance of fear (*bhayatupaṭṭhāna-ñāṇa*).

For one who cultivates that knowledge of the appearance of fear, all states of existence and so forth appear like glowing embers, like enemies with raised swords, providing no refuge and being fraught with danger.
This is called the knowledge of contemplation of danger (*ādīnavānupassanā-ñāṇa*). For him, thus [regarding] formations...
For one who sees the danger in existence and the dangers inherent in formations, there arises a weariness and dissatisfaction toward all formations.
This is called the knowledge of contemplation of disenchantment.

For one who is disenchanted with and weary of all formations, there arises a desire to be liberated from and a desire to escape from the entire realm of formations. This is the knowledge of the desire for liberation.
Furthermore, in order to be liberated from those formations, one applies the three characteristics to those very formations by means of the knowledge of contemplation of reflection;

this is called the knowledge of contemplation of reflection. One who thus grasps the formations after applying the three characteristics, because he has clearly seen the characteristic of non-self (*anattalakkhaṇa*) among them, [does not perceive them] as "self" or "belonging to self."
Or, not grasping [at them], having abandoned both fear and delight regarding formations (*saṅkhāra*), he becomes equanimous and neutral toward formations;
he does not grasp at them as "I" or "mine. Being equanimous and neutral toward all formations, he is indifferent toward the three realms of existence (*bhava*).
That knowledge of his is called "knowledge of equanimity toward formations. Furthermore, this [knowledge] pertains to the occurrence of all formations.
Having relinquished [the object], it becomes inclined toward Nibbāna and leaps toward Nibbāna;

yet, if it does not see Nibbāna as peace, it continues to proceed with the formations themselves as its object by way of the threefold contemplation—either as "impermanent," "suffering," or "non-self.
And while it persists in this manner, it attains the state of being an entrance to liberation by way of the three liberations: the signless, the desireless, and the void.
"Having attained, he remains. For it is said that the three contemplations are the three gateways to liberation (*vimokkhamukha*).
And herein, one who attends to [the object] as impermanent and is abundant in resolution attains the signless liberation (*animitta-vimokkha*).
One who attends to it as suffering and is abundant in tranquility attains the desireless liberation (*appaṇihita-vimokkha*). One who attends to it as non-self...
Practicing this, one who abounds in wisdom attains the liberation of emptiness (*suññatavimokkha*).
In this context, the "signless liberation" (*animittavimokkha*) refers to the Noble Path that proceeds by taking Nibbāna as its object through the aspect of signlessness.

For it is "signless" because it has arisen from the signless element (*animittadhātu*), and it is "liberation" because it is freed from the defilements (*kilesa*). By this same method, [one takes] Nibbāna through the aspect of desirelessness (*appaṇihita*).

That which proceeds by making an object its support is called "the wishless" (appaṇihita); that which proceeds by making Nibbāna its object in the aspect of emptiness (suññatā) is to be understood as "emptiness" (suññata).
For a clansman who has attained equanimity regarding formations, insight has reached its culmination.
This very [insight] is what is called "insight leading to emergence. As he cultivates and develops this knowledge of equanimity regarding formations...
A sharper equanimity towards formations arises.

Thinking, "Now the Path will arise for him," he comprehends formations as "impermanent," or as "suffering," or as "non-self" with that equanimity towards formations, and then sinks into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
Emerging from the life-continuum, [he again enters] through equanimity towards formations...
Having attended to [the object] in its aspect of impermanence and so forth by the very same method as previously described, mind-door adverting consciousness arises.
For one who continues attending to that very same thing, the first impulsion consciousness arises, which is called "preliminary work" (*parikamma*).
Immediately after that, a second impulsion consciousness arises in the same manner, which is called "access" (*upacāra*). Immediately after that as well...
In the same way, the impulsion consciousness arises, which is called "conformity" (*anuloma*). This is its specific name.
However, generally speaking, this threefold [consciousness] is called "repetition" (*āsevana*), "preliminary work" (*parikamma*), "access" (*upacāra*), and also "conformity" (*anuloma*).
This knowledge of conformity (*anuloma-ñāṇa*) is the culmination of insight (*vipassanā*) leading to emergence, which has formations as its object.
...exists. However, in the absolute sense, it is the knowledge of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhu-ñāṇa*) alone that is called the culmination of insight.

Following that, there arises the knowledge of change-of-lineage which takes cessation—Nibbāna—as its object, which transcends the lineage of worldlings (*puthujjana-gotta*), and which constitutes the first mental application directed toward the object of Nibbāna; it is irreversible. This knowledge, moreover, ...

It does not partake in either purification by knowledge and vision of the way (*paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi*) or purification by knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassana-visuddhi*); it remains merely intermediate and indeterminate.
However, because it has entered the stream of insight (*vipassanā*), it is reckoned as "insight.

However, with respect to a single article (*ekabhaṇḍa*), the application should be understood by way of taking or stealing—as previously described through methods such as forceful seizure—from a slave who has an owner, or from an animal, by means of taking or stealing.

Furthermore, for one explaining these six terms, [the following categories] are to be considered: various articles, a single article, taking with one's own hand (*sāhatthika*), prior preparation (*pubbappayoga*), theft (*theyya*), and acquisition (*āvahāra*).
By combining five groups of five, twenty-five modes of theft (*avahāra*) are to be shown, because all modes of theft are included within these six categories.
Those modes of theft are differentiated merely by the diversity of the means employed, such as forceful seizure (*abhiyoga*) and so forth;
it is on account of this that they are termed "five-fives. For when thus explained, this *pārājika* offense of taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*) is well-expounded.
It should be understood that [the name] "there is" applies here. In this context, the first two sets of five are obtained by way of the five phrases beginning with "should take up.
As for this sixth phrase, "should pass the time," it should be applied to the third and fifth sets of five by way of the relinquishment, the imagining, and the taking.

In this context, by the term *sāhatthika* (by one's own hand), taking the pentad associated with it in a figurative sense, it is called the "sāhatthika-pentad" either by the phrase "that which is *sāhatthika* and that which is the pentad," or by the elision of the middle word (*majjhepadalopa*) as "the *sāhatthika*-pentad. The same applies to the subsequent cases.

Furthermore, that [pentad] consists of: (1) by one's own hand (*sāhatthika*), (2) by command (*āṇattika*), (3) by relinquishment (*nissaggiya*), (4) accomplishing the purpose (*atthasādhaka*), and (5) laying down the burden (*dhuranikkhepa*).
In this context, *sako hattho* means "one's own hand"; that which is produced by one's own hand is *sāhatthiko*. Likewise for *āṇattiko* (that which is done by command).
Standing inside the designated area of a toll-house or a slaughterhouse and relinquishing [the goods] outside is *nissaggo*; that itself is *nissaggiyo*.

Regarding the taking of another's goods when commanded without a fixed time limit, and in the case of sandals or similar items that must necessarily be used with oil from another's oil-jar, [the amount] worth one-quarter of a *paṇa*...
It is called "accomplishing the purpose" (*atthasādhaka*) because it accomplishes the matter designated as a *pārājika* offense even before the oil-pot has been placed down.

This consists of the act of commanding and the act of depositing items such as sandals. Furthermore, the "laying down of the burden" (*dhuranikkhepa*) refers to the relinquishing of one's responsibility in cases of a formal accusation against a monastery, in regard to goods deposited for safekeeping, and in the non-return of goods lent for a limited time.

The "fivefold preliminary effort" (*pubbappayoga-pañcaka*) consists of: preliminary effort (*pubbappayoga*), simultaneous effort (*sahappayoga*), the act of arrangement (*saṃvidhāvahāra*), the making of a sign (*saṅketakamma*), and the making of a signal (*nimittakamma*).
In this context, "preliminary effort" refers to the act of commanding, because it occurs prior to the taking of the goods.

"Simultaneous effort" refers to that which occurs together with the effort of moving [the goods] from their place, digging, or crossing over. When [the thieves] have gone after having made arrangements and deliberated, even by one person [moving] the goods from their place—
When [the goods] have been moved away, the taking away of all [of them] is "taking away by arrangement" (*saṃvidhāvahāra*).

"Making a signal" (*saṅketakamma*) means making a sign for the purpose of recognition by way of delimiting a time such as the forenoon and so forth. "Making a gesture" (*nimittakamma*) means making a winking of the eyes and so forth for the purpose of producing a perception.
He said "or else," etc., in order to show the pentad of taking away by theft himself. But is it not [already] included within the six [categories]?
It was stated, “of all forms of theft. This being so, why is this pentad mentioned as if it were distinct, under the heading of an alternative view with the words “or else”?
Did we not say that they are differentiated merely by the diversity of modes such as accusation and so forth?
Because such a distinction is possible, it was stated in this way as being appropriate even from the perspective of an alternative view.
However, the separate mention of this pentad [of offenses] should be understood as being by way of conventional usage (*pasiddhi*).

By the word *kusa*, the act of stealing *kusa* grass is intended through the metaphorical application of identity (*abhedopacāra*). "Theft" (*theyya*), "force" (*bala*), "kusa," "concealment" (*channa*), and "pretext" (*parikappa*)—[the compound] *theyyā...
parikappaṃ* has a long vowel due to euphonic combination (*sandhi*). The connection is: "by means of that, the one who takes away becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense."
However, one who takes by means of concealment is, in actual fact, a taker of what is concealed;
thus, even when included within a *dvanda* compound, there is no contradiction, and this word *channa* should be understood as having an abstract (bhāva-sādhana) sense.

In that context, a thief-taker is one who takes after having committed acts such as breaking a breach (*sandhicchedana*), or having deceived by means of false weights, false measures, or counterfeit coins (*kahāpaṇa*). By force...
One who takes what belongs to another is a "stealer by force. One who takes after shifting it to *kusa* grass is a "stealer by means of *kusa*.
One who first conceals something with grass, leaves, or the like, and later steals that which was concealed, is a "stealer by concealment.
One who takes after imagining it in terms of an object such as a garment, or in terms of a location such as the entrance to a womb, is a "stealer by imagination."
In this context, however, it should be understood that there is a *pārājika* offense when one takes an object that has been designated as such, or when one exceeds the designated limit.
Now, in order to demonstrate the legal determination (*vinicchaya*) regarding this matter, the passage beginning with “by the object, time, value, and place” was stated.

Here, the meaning is that the determination in the case of taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*) must be made by means of these factors—the object, the time, the value, and the place—as well as by means of the usage.
In this regard, having investigated whether the goods taken away have an owner or not, and if they have an owner, whether that owner is attached to them or not:
if the goods were taken while the owner was still attached to them, the legal decision regarding the goods must be made after having them appraised.
If they were taken while the owner was no longer attached to them, there is no offense of defeat (*pārājika*); however, if the owners subsequently cause the goods to be brought back...
It must be given. For that same article may at one time be of great value and at another time of little value;
therefore, the legal decision must be made according to its value at the very time the article was stolen—this is called "decision by time.
The value of a new article decreases later on; therefore, [the decision] must always be made according to its original value.
The determination should not be made [based on the original value], but rather the determination should be made according to the current value.

If the goods were of low value at the place where they were stolen but of high value elsewhere, then the determination must be made according to the value at the very place where the goods were stolen;
this is "determination by locality. Furthermore, through use, the value of goods such as a cloth garment diminishes.
Therefore, having examined whether or not there has been a lapse on his part by way of that consumption, the determination should be made;
this is the determination by way of consumption.
Second.
5–7. Now, in order to show the third [offense], the passage beginning with “a human being” (*manussaviggaha*) is commenced.
Therein, “a human being” (*manussaviggaha*) refers to the body of those belonging to the human species while they are still living, starting from the stage of the embryo (*kalala*).

“Having intended and planned” (*cicca pāṇo*): together with the perception that it is a living being, having formed the murderous intention thinking “I shall kill,” and having resolved upon it. “Or deprives of life”: whichever monk...

When a drop of oil is extracted with a fine woolen cloth at the stage of the *kalala*, or by means of heating and so forth, or even beyond that by a corresponding means, if there is an assault upon the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*), it is possible to deprive both types of life because the immaterial life (*arūpa-jīvita*) exists in dependence upon it;
thus one would deprive both lives. The word "or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative. "Intention for death" (*maraṇacetanā*) refers to [the intention] regarding death.
“Whose intention” means whose intention is for death. “One who brings a weapon” (*satthahāraka*): it is called *hāraka* because it takes away life;
it is a “weapon-bringer” (*satthahāraka*) because it is both a weapon (*sattha*) and a bringer (*hāraka*). This refers to that human being. “Places near” means one should place it in close proximity.
By this, he shows the method involving stationary objects. “Should cause [him] to take up a means of death” means “a weapon or…”
Or one might cause [the person] to adopt a means for the sake of death by such methods as saying, "Eat this," or "Consume poison. By this, the application of a command (*āṇatti-payoga*) is shown.
Or one might proclaim the excellence of death through body, speech, messengers, or letters, by such methods as saying, "He who dies in this way obtains wealth," and so forth.
In both cases, the word "or" (*vā*) is used in the sense of an alternative.
It should be brought forth. The connection is that "that monk has cut [the fetters]," and it is understood as being from the Teaching (sāsana).
Now, in order to demonstrate its sixfold application (payoga), he says "applications" and so forth.

Therein, the connection is that these six applications—beginning with "manual" (sāhatthika) and ending with "consisting of supernormal knowledge" (iddhivijjāmaya)—are the six applications. However, here the word is stated as "sāhatthī" due to the elision of the letter *ka*.

Alternatively, the derivation of the word *sāhatthī* should be understood as follows: since there are multiple meanings and the possibility of various secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), this application [of the hand] is called *sāhatthī*.
Then, *sāhatthi*, *nissagga*, *āṇatti*, and *thāvara* form a *dvanda* compound. Regarding *iddhivijjāmayā*: *iddhi* and *vijjā* exist in these [applications], thus they are *iddhivijjāmayā*;
what is meant is "consisting of psychic power" (*iddhimaya*) and "consisting of knowledge" (*vijjāmaya*). These are the six applications (*payoga*).

The meaning is that they are so called. In this context, for one who kills by oneself, the physical striking with the body or with something connected to the body is "direct application" (*sāhatthika-payoga*).
For one wishing to kill someone standing at a distance, the releasing of weapons such as spears or arrows from the body and so forth is "sending forth" (*nissagga*).
For one commanding another, saying "Kill such-and-such a person," and so on, the act of commanding is "commanding" (*āṇatti*), as is the digging of a pit.
The stationary [type of killing] consists of the preparation of weapons such as swords and the like, or placing them within reach.

The magical [type] consists of employing the power born of the ripening of kamma for the purpose of killing. This power born of the ripening of kamma includes the "royal magic" (*rājiddhi*) and so forth of kings and others.
In this regard, the royal magic should be understood as the killing of the merchant Cūḷasumana by King Sīhaḷinda of Siṃhala through the striking of his fangs.
The employment consisting of supernatural power (*vijjāmaya*) is the recitation of spells such as *athabbaṇa* for that very purpose.
Having thus shown the six types of employment, the words beginning with “time” (*kāla*) are spoken in order to show the determinants of the employment of command (*āṇatti*).
In this context, those which determine the aforementioned command—delimiting it by way of convention (*saṅketa*) and non-convention (*visaṅketa*)—are the “determinants of command.”
The meaning is that these consist of four factors—time, object, weapon, and posture—and likewise six, when the specific action and location are included by way of numerical classification.
Therein, "time" refers to forenoon and so forth, as well as youth and so forth. "Object" is the being to be killed.
"Weapon" is the sword and so forth. "Posture" is the movement, such as walking, of the one to be killed. "Specific action" is the act of piercing and so forth.

"Place" refers to a village or similar location. For instance, if one is told, "Kill him in the morning," without specifying whether it is today or tomorrow, and the person kills him at some point during the morning, there is no breach of agreement (*visaṅketa*).
However, if one is told to kill him "in the morning" but he kills him at midday or another time, a breach of agreement occurs;
in that case, there is no offense for the one who gave the command. Thus, the determining factor [of the offense] depends on whether the time is specified or not.
It should be understood. By this same method, the analysis regarding the basis (*vatthu*) and so forth should also be understood.

This concludes the third [section]. 8–9. Now, in order to show the fourth, he says: "The classification according to jhāna, etc. Therein, that which does not exist within oneself, yet is attributed to oneself (*attupanāyika*), and...

The connection is as follows: having categorized the various divisions such as *jhāna*—which are based on the present existence and free from other designations—either collectively or individually, one who demonstrates them through the body or speech within the range of intimation (*viññatti*), being not conceited, is "one fallen from what is known" (*ñāte cuto*).
In this context, "not existing in oneself" means not existing in one’s own continuum precisely because it has not yet arisen; thus, it is non-existent. Herein...
*No santī* is a *tappurisa* compound in the sense of "not existing. Regarding *jhānādibheda*:

*jhāna* is the first of those things mentioned as "liberation, concentration, attainment, knowledge and vision, development of the path, realization of the fruit, the abandoning of defilements, freedom from hindrances, and delighting in an empty dwelling";
that is *jhānādi*. That itself is the *bheda*, meaning the distinction or particularity; such is the compound. It refers to that *jhānādibheda*, the superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*).

*Attupanāyikaṃ*: It is brought to oneself (*attan*) by way of announcing, "This exists in me," or it is brought to this state (*dhamma*) by way of the self being presented there, thinking, "I am manifest here"—thus it is *attupanāyika*, referring to the various types such as jhāna and so forth; that [is what is meant]. *Paccuppannabhavassitaṃ*:

"Present existence" (*paccuppannabhava*) means the personal entity (*attabhāva*) currently occurring right now; "based on that" (*tannissita*) is the compound; and that too refers specifically to the various types such as jhāna and so forth; that [is what is meant].

"Free from the designation of another" (*aññāpadesarahita*): This is a *tappurisa* compound meaning "devoid of the designation of another," such as in the manner of saying, "The monk who lived in that monastery attained the first jhāna.
Alternatively, it is a *bahubbīhi* compound meaning "that which is devoid of that [designation].
It refers specifically to the distinctions of jhāna and so forth. "Or having made them into portions" (*koṭṭhāsaṃ katvā vā*) means: "the first jhāna, the second jhāna... and so on.
Or by dividing it into sections in the manner of: "I attained the first jhāna, I attained the third jhāna," and so forth.
Or by treating each one individually in the manner of: "I attained the first jhāna, I attained the second jhāna," and so forth.
And here, the doubling [of the suffix] occurs due to the distributive sense (*vicchā*) applied to the word *eka*. In this context, however, "having made" (*katvā*)—

The desire for connection regarding a meaning—such as jhāna and so forth—that is differentiated by each individual instrument (karaṇa) and action (kiriyā), should be understood as *vicchatti* (separation).
However, in the *Ṭīkā*, it says: “Regarding the phrase ‘or part by part (*koṭṭhāsaṃ vā*)’:

here the meaning is ‘part by part’ according to such a method as ‘I am an attainer of jhāna, an attainer of liberation, an attainer of concentration, an attainer of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*)’”; and: “Or ‘one by one (*ekekaṃ vā*)’: [regarding] the first...”
It is said: "The meaning is that one speaks of each [jhāna] in such a manner as 'I am an attainer of jhāna,' 'I am an attainer of the second jhāna,' and so forth.
This should be understood as a sequence not mentioned in the Pāḷi or the Aṭṭhakathā. "By body" means by means of the body through hand gestures and so on.
Regarding the word "vācā" (speech), here the letter *ya* is indicated as elided, as in words such as "alajjitā" (shamelessness). "In the sphere of intimation" (*viññattipathe*).
"Standing in a place suitable for the perception of bodily and vocal intimation" is to be supplied [from the context]. "Expounding" means making it known:
"By this and that reason, this Dhamma exists in me. "Not over-proud" (*nādhimānika*): pride (*māna*) is the conceit consisting in the perception of having attained what has not been attained;
one who does not possess this is "not over-proud," namely, the bhikkhu. "Known" means by a wise person of human kind.
When it is understood according to the method explained under the "Renunciation of Training" (sikkhāpaccakkhāna), it is understood that one has fallen away from the Dispensation (sāsana).
However, for one who indicates [the renunciation] by means of a pretext for ignorance, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya).
And here: "An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is described as being merely preliminary to the first [offense]."
"But for the remaining three as well, a thullaccaya is declared.
This is the fourth [section].
Now, in order to illustrate the state of non-residence and incapacity for all four of these, the passage beginning with "Those who have committed a pārājika" is commenced.

The connection is as follows: these four persons who have committed a *pārājika* offense are "not in communion" (*asaṃvāsa*), just as they were previously during their time as householders and during their time before full ordination.

Because all those who possess a sense of shame dwell together in these three matters—namely, formal acts (*kamma*), recitation (*uddesa*), and training (*sikkhā*)—and not even one of them appears outside of that group, these three are called "communion" (*saṃvāsa*). Specifically, they are: being subject to the same formal acts, being subject to the same recitation, and being subject to the same training.

In this context, the fourfold formal act of the Saṅgha, beginning with the *apalokana* (announcement), is called "a single act" (*ekakamma*) because it must be performed together by the regular monks within the boundaries of the *sīmā*.
Likewise, the fivefold recitation of the *Pātimokkha* is called "a single recitation" (*ekuddesa*) because it must be recited together.
Furthermore, the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) that has been laid down must be practiced equally by all modest individuals.
“Those of equal training” means they train together. “Non-residents” (asaṃvāsā) means those with whom one does not share communal residence.

In phrases such as “incapable,” the dative case (*bhikkhubhāvāya*) is used in the sense of the infinitive; therefore, the meaning is that these four persons are incapable of becoming monks—that is, incapable of existing as monks—just as one whose head is severed is incapable of living.
11. Now, in order to show how [the offense] arises through indirect methods (*pariyāya*) and commands (*āṇatti*), he says, "And the indirect method," and so forth.
The connection is that both the indirect method and the command are found in the third category of persons (*manussaviggaha*).

In this context, the bodily and verbal application consisting of words—which makes known such things as, "He who dies in this manner will obtain wealth"—by means of the body and so forth as previously described, is the indirect method (*pariyāya*).

“By way of a method. This explains as follows: just as in the case of taking what is not given, one is exempted by a figurative explanation because it is stated there that one “might take,” it is not so here.
One is not exempted even by a figurative explanation when it says “one might praise.
In the passages beginning with “But in the second,” etc., the meaning is quite evident. We shall likewise leave the subsequent parts as they are evident.
12. Now, in order to show the constituent factors (*aṅga*) of sexual intercourse and so forth, he says "should practice" and so on.
"The mind desiring to practice": one who desires to practice sexual intercourse is "desirous of practicing" (*sevetukāmo*); the state of such a person is craving (*taṇhā*).
"The mind associated with that desire to practice" is a *tappurisa* compound. "Of sexual intercourse" (*methunadhammassa*): this belongs to the pair (*mithuna*), namely the woman and the man.

*Metu-naṃ* (sexual intercourse); that very thing is the *dhamma*, thus it is *methuna-dhamma*. Here, however, by way of figurative usage (*upacāra*), the offense of defeat (*pārājika-āpatti*) is called *methuna-dhamma*.

Alternatively, the *dhamma* born of sexual intercourse—the offense of defeat—is *methuna-dhamma*; [the phrase] "of that *methuna-dhamma*" refers to the offense of defeat consisting of *methuna-dhamma*.
"The pair of factors" (*aṅga-dvayaṃ*) means a pair of factors or causes. "The wise ones" (*budhā*) refers to those learned in the Vinaya.

13. *Manussasanti*: the peace (*santi*) of humans is human-peace (*manussasaṃ*); it is that which has its basis dependent upon them. By this, one excludes [peace] dependent upon ghosts (*peta*) or animals (*tiracchānagata*).
"Perceiving thus" (*tathāsaññī*): such a perception as that is "perception thus" (*tathāsaññā*); he who possesses that is "one perceiving thus" (*tathāsaññī*).

The meaning is: "one whose perception is dependent on another. These explanations emphasize the state (*bhāva*); or, there is an elision of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapaccaya*), as in "in the Buddha" (*buddhe*).
As in the cases of "jewel" (*ratana*) and so forth; likewise for similar instances above. "Thieving mind" (*theyyacitta*) means a mind characterized by the state of theft.
"Heaviness of the object" (*vatthuno garutā*) refers to the heaviness of the goods by virtue of their being worth more than one-quarter [of a *pāda*].

If it is less than five *māsaka*s or more than one *māsaka*, there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*). If it is exactly one *māsaka* or less than one *māsaka*, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). "Taking away" (*avahāra*) refers to the twenty-five...

Theft by means of any one of the various methods of taking what is not given—these five causes of theft are the constituent factors for the offense of a *pārājika* involving the taking of what is not given. 14.

"A living being" (*pāṇo*) means a being connected to the human species; for in common parlance, a "living being" (*pāṇo*) refers to a sentient creature (*satto*), but in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), it is called the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
"Perceiving it as a living being" (*pāṇasaññitā*) means perceiving it as a living being. "Killing" (*ghāta*) is the act of killing; that itself is...
The meaning is as follows: volition refers to the volition of killing, which occurs with the thought, "I shall kill";

and that [volition], the means (payoga) consisting of any one of the six types such as "by one's own hand" (sāhatthika) which is originated by that volition, and death by means of that means—these five aforementioned causes of killing are the constituent factors (aṅga) for the offense incurred through the destruction of living beings.
15. "Not existing within oneself" means the non-existence of superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*) within one's own continuum.
"Proclaiming evil desires" refers to the proclamation of superhuman states by one who possesses such evil desires, as described in the passage beginning, "Here, someone being immoral thinks:
'Let people know me to be virtuous,'" and so forth. "To him" means to the person to whom one makes the proclamation.
"Human birth" (*manussajātitā*) means the state (*bhāva*) of one who has the birth of humans;
and "not a designation for another" (*na aññāpadeso*) means the absence of being a designation for another, as well as the knowing at that very moment—
these five [factors] are here, in this continuity (*santāna*), for the purpose of manifesting superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussadhamma*) that do not exist in one who lacks them.
"In the *pārājika* [offenses], the factors are the cause"—this is the meaning.

(16) Having thus shown their state of non-residence (*asaṃvāsa*), incapacity (*abhabbatā*), and so forth, he now says "they are not only those four, but there are others as well," in order to present all of them together;
therein, "non-common" (*asādhāraṇā*) refers to the *pārājikas*.

"Phenomena" (dhammā) is intended here; for this reason, the masculine gender is used in this context. Therefore, the meaning should be understood here as follows: "the four phenomena of defeat (pārājika) that are not shared by nuns with monks.

However, by way of figurative extension (upacāra), those who have fallen into defeat—such as one who has gone above the knees—are included. Among them, she who is lustful toward a lustful human male [at his] collarbones...
She who consents to bodily contact above the knees and below the collarbones is one who [commits] the offense of *ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalikā*.
She who conceals a *pārājika* offense committed by another nun is a concealer of faults (*vajjappaṭicchādikā*).
She who follows along with a suspended monk (*ukkhitaka*) by way of adopting his view is one who follows a suspended monk (*ukkhitānuvattikā*). [This is said] because of the lust for bodily contact.
Taking hold of the hand of one who is lustful; taking hold of the corner of his outer robe; standing within arm’s reach of a man for the purpose of bodily contact;
conversing [with him]; going to a rendezvous; consenting to a man’s arrival; entering a concealed place;
and standing within arm’s reach while making a bodily advance—these eight bases belong to whichever woman is lustful; she is thus called "one who has the eight bases."

"Eleven who are incapable": herein, the eleven who are incapable are as follows: the paṇḍaka, the one living in communion by theft, the one who has gone over to another sect, the animal, the matricide, the patricide, the murderer of an arahant, the defiler of a bhikkhunī, the schismatic, the shedder of blood [of a Buddha], and the hermaphrodite.
Among these, "paṇḍaka" refers to those who are paṇḍakas by means of artificial means (opakkamika-napuṃsaka-paṇḍaka).
And here, both those who are permanently impotent (*paṇḍaka*) and those who are temporarily impotent (*pakkhapaṇḍaka*) are intended.

However, the going-forth and full ordination of those who are "sprinkled" (*āsitta*), "jealous" (*ussūya*), or "impotent by nature" (*paṇḍaka*) are not prohibited. As for the one who dwells in communion through theft (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*), he is threefold: by way of stealing the [monastic] sign (*liṅga*), by way of stealing the [monastic] requisites, and so forth.

Among these, one is called a "sign-thief" (*liṅgatthenaka*) because, having gone forth himself, he merely steals the outward sign. [This includes] the counting of a monk’s years of seniority, and so on.

One who deceives regarding co-residence is a "deceiver regarding co-residence" (*saṃvāsatthenaka*). The same principle applies to one who, having formally renounced the training, practices in such a manner.

One who deceives regarding both as previously stated is a "deceiver regarding both" (*ubhayatthenaka*). Aside from these three types, however—whether due to fear of kings, famine, wilderness, disease, or enemies—
"He who here assumes the outward mark for the sake of obtaining robes,
as long as he does not consent to living in communion with the pure-minded,
is not called a 'thief-living' (theyyasaṃvāsaka) at that time."
Those who have gone over to other sects (titthiyapakkantaka) and so forth should be understood according to the specific meaning of each term.
An animal (tiracchānagata), however, should be understood as everyone except those of human birth.

These eleven persons are called "defeated" (pārājika) because they are incapable of the state of a bhikkhu and are thus similar to those who have committed a pārājika offense. A nun who has left the order (vibbhantā bhikkhunī) is one who is dressed in the clothing of a householder.
And a bhikkhunī: for she, at this point, has committed a pārājika offense. And he whose back is soft:
for when he, oppressed by lack of lust, inserts his own male organ into his own anus or urinary passages, he then becomes one who has committed a pārājika offense.
17–18. One whose male organ hangs down is called "lambī. He, having inserted it as described above, is one who has committed a pārājika offense. By means of the mouth...
"Taking another's sexual organ with the mouth" refers to one who, oppressed by lust, takes the sexual organ of another—whether they be sleeping or dead—with his own mouth;
he is "one who takes another's sexual organ with the mouth.
"Sitting down right there" refers to one who, oppressed by lust, sits down right there upon another's sexual organ via the anus; he is "one who sits down right there."
These four, which are conducive to sexual intercourse, are the causes for entering the path [of defilement] even in the absence of the actual mutual union.
"The four that have come here" refers to the four offenses such as the *pārājika* involving sexual misconduct as described in this Minor Training (*khuddasikkhā*).
Thus, by way of combining and aggregating them, there are twenty-four *pārājikas*; this is the remainder [of the explanation]. Herein...
And by way of composing it in verse, it was made short and stated as “pārājikā. Here it is asked:
“The matricide and others have fallen into the third pārājika; the violator of a nun and the four beginning with the ‘soft-backed’ have fallen into the first pārājika;
so how can there be twenty-four? It is replied: For the four beginning with the matricide are here not ordained (anupasampanna).

These are what is intended. Although the four [cases] beginning with "one with a supple back" are included under the first *pārājika*, they are stated separately because, by one particular method, they do not involve the practice of sexual intercourse.
The commentary on the exposition of the *pārājikas* is finished.
2. Commentary on the Exposition of the Saṅghādisesa Rules 19.
They are called *saṅghādisesa* because they are heavy (*garuka*) due to the gravity of their formal rehabilitation (*vuṭṭhāna*). "Nine" is the numerical limit of them.
Now, why is it said "nine" when one should have said "thirteen"? This is not a fault, for [the remaining four] are to be incurred only after a long time.
Excluding the four [offenses] that are incurred only upon the third admonition, those which are to be incurred at the very moment of transgression are called "first-offense" (paṭhamāpattika).
Now, in order to demonstrate them, the passage beginning with “mocetukāmatā” is commenced.

Therein, “of semen” (sukkassa) refers to any kind of semen among the ten types—blue and so forth—due to the diversity of the bodily elements in the seat [of emission]. “With the desire to emit” (mocetukāmatā) means by way of the desire to emit.

The letter *ya* is indicated as being elided. By this statement, however, among the eleven kinds of gratification—namely, the gratification of emission, the gratification of being emitted, the gratification of having been emitted, the gratification of sexual intercourse, the gratification of touch, the gratification of scratching, the gratification of seeing, the gratification of sitting together, the gratification of speech, the gratification of worldly affection, and the gratification of forest-dwelling—it shows only one: the gratification of emission.

In this context, the gratification (*assāda*) in being released is the gratification of the pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā*); the gratification in being liberated by one's own nature is the gratification of liberation.
Thus, in all instances, the meaning should be understood through the genitive *tappurisa* compound.

By these nine terms, greed (*rāga*) is expressed under the heading of the gratification associated with them. Attachment to those dependent on the household, such as mother and so forth, is "the household" (*geha*).

“*Sitaṃ pemeti*” means attachment to the household; by this very expression, lust (*rāga*) is stated. “*Vanabhaṅgiyan*” refers to flowers and so forth sent to a woman for the purpose of establishing intimacy;
by this, lust is stated by way of its objective basis (*vatthu*). The gratification of sexual intercourse (*methunassāda*) is also to be understood through the effort of seizing a woman.
Furthermore, in all these cases, when there is volition (*cetanā*), a sign (*nimitta*), exertion (*upakkama*), and release (*mocana*), there is no absence of the agreement (*visaṅketa*).
It should be understood as follows: "By means of an effort" (*upakkamma*) refers to making an effort with the hand or other such means against the [sexual] organ.

"Except in a dream" (*aññatra supinantā*): *supinanta* means a dream itself; this is because, as in expressions such as "the act itself is the action" (*kammameva kammanto*), the word *anta* functions here to denote identity with that state.
"Releasing except in a dream" means discharging semen. Any ascetic whatsoever—meaning any monk—who, while discharging semen, commits what is called a grave offense (*garuka-āpatti*).
"He might touch" means he would incur a *saṅghādisesa* offense; this is what is meant by "he would fall into [an offense].

And here, when any one of the four methods—namely, internal form, external form, both forms, or the shaking of the hip-joint—is present, and at any time when the lustful stiffening and so forth occur, and whichever member has attained pliability, then by whatever intention such as "for the sake of health," etc., whatever object constitutes the basis for that intention—

The intention must be understood in every respect as follows: one incurs a *saṅghādisesa* offense by intentionally discharging semen through an act directed toward an object, out of a relish for the discharge.
This is the first [case].
20. *Kāyasaṃsaggarāgavatī*: bodily contact; passion for that; one who possesses that [passion] is called *vantu*; the meaning is "one endowed with passion for bodily contact.
It is connected with the phrase "the ascetic perceiving her as a woman. *Upakkamma* means having exerted oneself with the body. "Touching a human woman" is to be construed as:
even by touching her with a single hair, he incurs a grave offense (*garukaṃ phuseti*). [This refers to those who are] human beings.

“A woman” (*amatā*) refers to a human female. In this context, by the phrase “one who has lust for physical contact,” [the text] excludes affection such as that for one’s mother, as well as a woman’s intention to have attained liberation.
For one who is doubtful about whether she is a woman, or for one who perceives her as a *paṇḍaka*, a male, or an animal, there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*).
However, when there is physical contact with a woman, or when one makes use of what is connected to her body, or when one makes use of one’s own body while she is connected to his body...
There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for physical contact with a female *yakkha*, a female *petī*, or a paṇḍaka, as well as for physical contact with a male animal or a female human;

likewise for physical contact with a female *yakkha* and others, or contact with what is connected to the body (*kāyappaṭibaddha*). However, in the case of a dead woman, there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*).
Furthermore, if one who is being touched by a woman—even if he intends sexual intercourse—does not exert himself physically, there is no offense.
The second [offense].
21. "Perceiving her to be a woman" means perceiving her as a female. "Hearing" means hearing one's own words while she stands within the range of communication (*viññatti-patha*).

"And a discerning person" refers to a human female capable of distinguishing between what is grave (*duṭṭhulla*) and what is not grave. "Or the path" refers to the urinary tract (*vacca-magga*) and the anal tract (*passāva-magga*).
The connection is: "by way of either the path or sexual intercourse. Regarding "through lust for improper speech" (*duṭṭhullavācārāgena*):
it is "improper" (*duṭṭhulla*) because it is "corrupt" (*duṭṭha*) due to being associated with what is not the true Dhamma, and it is "gross" (*thūla*) because it is common to base people.

That very speech is "improper speech" (*duṭṭhullavācā*). Lust is that which is associated with gratification therein; this is the compound, and [the phrase means] "by means of that. "Having illuminated" (*obhāsitvā*)—

Having spoken words contrary to the True Dhamma by means of praising or disparaging, or by requesting sexual intercourse, and so forth; however, there is no offense if she does not hear it, provided it is communicated by a messenger or by letter.

In that regard, by means of two paths—either through praise and disparagement, or through requests for sexual intercourse and so forth—or by any one of these three abusive expressions: "You are a *sikharaṇī*," "You are a *sambhinnā*," or "You are a hermaphrodite (*ubhatobyañjanakā*")."

If one speaks in praise of [the genitals] while illuminating them, there is a *saṅghādisesa*; if one speaks in praise of the area below the collarbone and above the kneecaps (*adhakkhaka-ubbhajāṇumaṇḍala*), there is a *thullaccaya*.
The same applies when speaking in praise of the anus or the urinary passage of a female *yakkha*, a female *peta*, or a paṇḍaka, as well as in cases such as requesting sexual intercourse with them.

However, for those [beings], regarding the area below the collarbone and so forth, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense; likewise, for human women, regarding the area above the collarbone, below the kneecaps, and anything connected to the body.
The third [section]. 22. *Attakāmupaṭṭhānaṃ*: attendance out of desire is "desire-attendance" (*kāmupaṭṭhāna*), meaning attendance motivated by the desire known as sexual intercourse.
Attendance out of desire for one's own sake is "self-desire-attendance" (*attakāmupaṭṭhāna*). Alternatively, that which is desired is "desire" (*kāma*); for oneself...
"Kāma" means one who desires themselves; the meaning is that they have made a wish by way of lust for sexual intercourse. "Attakāmupaṭṭhāna" means that service which is desired by oneself.

Its "vaṇṇa" (praise) is its quality; that [he spoke]. "Vatvā" means having proclaimed—even by means of a hand gesture—that "this which is called 'service through sensual desire' is the foremost among services," thus making known to women that this is the praise for service through sensual desire.
The meaning is as follows: *vācā* [is used] by way of the elision of the letter *y* from *vācāya*. *Methunayuttena* means "by one joined with sexual intercourse";

through a shift in gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*), it refers to that speech connected with the act of sexual intercourse—such as "You ought to give me the practice of sexual intercourse"—and thus the connection is: "those who lust after sexual intercourse" (*methunarāgino*) when there is a solicitation for sexual intercourse. Sexual intercourse is the passion (*rāga*); he who possesses that is a "lustful one after sexual intercourse" (*methunarāgī*).

"Of him. "It is grave" means that it is a grave offense (*garukāpatti*); the letter *ma* is used for metrical or syntactical connection. Herein, if one perceives a paṇḍaka as a paṇḍaka, there is a serious offense (*thullaccaya*); if one perceives that same person as a woman, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
This is the fourth [section].
23. "Having received a message from a woman or a man" is the connection. Regarding "from a woman":
this refers to either a woman of twenty kinds—as described in such passages as "ten kinds of women protected by their mother, protected by their father," and so on, and "ten kinds of wives:

Or: they send a message by means of a woman, a man, or both their mothers and so forth, saying, "Come, venerable sir, speak thus to such-and-such a woman or man. This refers to a message concerning the status of husband and wife.
Having accepted it means having received it with the words "Very well," either by body or by speech. Having investigated means where—
"Having been sent," means having examined their intention oneself, or having had it examined by another.

"Returns the message" means whether a woman or a man, whether they accept with "Very well" or not, whether they are the one who sent them or the one returning the message or having it returned, and whether they are husband and wife or not—this is no cause [for an offense]. By this fulfillment of three factors...

However, some, having conjectured a variant reading of "haraṃ pacchā," construe it as "pacchā haraṃ" (take later);

now, three spans of a medium-sized man are called a *sugata-vidatthi* (the Sugata’s span);

It is a *dukkaṭa*. Now, thinking "I shall finish it with two morsels," there is a *thullaccaya* at the giving of the first morsel;

by the second giving, when the plaster has been joined together, if it is either such that its material has not been confessed (*adesitavatthukā*) or if it exceeds the proper measure, there is one *saṅghādisesa*, and two *dukkaṭas* for the presence of injury and the lack of a path around it—if both [faults] are present.
