this is the sixth [section]. 25. "Large" (*mahallaka*) means, by virtue of being requested from its owner, it is larger than a hut; having caused the site to be designated...

It is called *mahallaka* because it takes on (*lāti*) or assumes (*ādadāti*) greatness (*mahattaṃ*) due to its vastness, both by way of exceeding the proper dimensions and by way of being something that ought to be done.

When the form *mahattalaka* is established, there is the elision of the *tt* and the doubling of the *l*. "Vasana" means dwelling; thus, *vasanattha* means for the purpose of dwelling, [and it is] by means of that.
Herein, however, if the site has not been designated, there is one *saṅghādisesa*; the rest is exactly the same as in the immediately preceding case.
There is no offense for one who has various types of dwellings built here and there— such as shelters, caves, grass huts, leaf-roofed huts, or houses—
or who builds even a small hut or establishes a dwelling room for the sake of another’s residence, or constructs a meeting hall for the Uposatha and other such purposes.
This is the seventh [case].
26. "By means of a groundless [charge] on account of the final matter" is the connection. "Groundless" (*amūlaka*) means that which has no root (*mūla*);
it is called "groundless" because it lacks a root consisting of seeing, hearing, or the suspicion arising from what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
Whether he (the monk) has actually committed that offense or not is irrelevant here; in this context, that [allegation] is the decisive factor. In that regard, the monk...
Seeing a woman in such a place and suspecting her, this is suspicion based on what is seen (*diṭṭha-parisaṅkā*).

Hearing the voices of a monk and a woman in the dark or in a concealed place, and suspecting them without knowing that another person is present, this is suspicion based on what is heard (*suta-parisaṅkā*).
[The case of] ruffians with women in border monasteries, using flowers, perfumes, liquor, and so forth...

Having experienced it and seen the place where it occurred, while investigating, "By whom was this done?", he perceives that some monk there has performed an offering with perfumes and the like, or has drunk an *ariṭṭha* medicinal tonic for the sake of medicine;
having smelled its scent, he suspects, "This must be the one. This is called suspicion based on what has been released (*muta-parisaṅkā*). And by the last...
Beyond that, because it occurs at the end due to the absence of further [offenses], it is called "final" (*antima*).
Regarding the phrase "by means of a basis" (*vatthunā*): it refers to any one of the nineteen *pārājika* offenses appropriate for a monk.

Here, the particle *ca* is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), thereby excluding the *saṅghādisesa* and other [offenses]. Alternatively, the particle *ca* is used in the sense of impossibility (*aṭṭhāna*).

"Whether accusing or causing to accuse" (*codento vā codāpento vā*) should be construed [with the following]. "In order to cause to fall away" (*cāvetuṃ*) means for the purpose of causing one to fall away from the holy life (*brahmacariya*).

By this, having taken one intention—that of causing to fall away—the text rejects the remaining seven intentions, such as the intention to revile, the intention to cause to leave the community, and so forth.
"While listening" (*suṇamānaṃ*) is the object of the verbs "accusing" and so on; by this, it refers to an accusation made in the absence of the person.
He rejects it. However, for one who speaks in the absence [of the accused] by means of the seven classes of offenses (āpattikkhandha), there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

"Accusing" means either accusing oneself by way of the four types of accusation stated in brief—namely, "pointing out the basis," "pointing out the offense," "rejecting co-residence," and "rejecting proper conduct"—or causing another to accuse by any means whatsoever.
Or by exhorting him. Therefore, [this applies to] one who stands near a bhikkhu and, by way of pointing out the matter, says:

"You have engaged in sexual intercourse; you are no longer a samaṇa," and so forth; or by way of pointing out the offense, says: "You have fallen into the offense of sexual intercourse," and so forth;
or [says]: "You are no longer a samaṇa; there can be no Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, or Saṅgha-transaction with you; you are no longer a samaṇa," and so forth.

Alternatively, by way of rejecting social association—since association such as salutation and so forth has been rejected—one who, when asked "Why are you not a recluse?", indicates this matter through words such as "You are no longer a recluse," or by way of rejecting proper conduct, or even by a mere gesture of the hand, without having requested permission in this manner:
"Venerable sir, grant me leave; I wish to speak to you."
By speech, there is both a *saṅghādisesa* offense and a *dukkaṭa*; however, for one who reproves after having obtained leave [to speak], it should be regarded as a *saṅghādisesa* only.
This is the eighth [case].
27. "Of another" means of another person belonging to the *khattiya* caste or other castes. "Act" refers to the act consisting of the transgression of sexual intercourse.
"By 'ten'" means by way of indicating sexual misconduct as another form of transgression, acting as the instrument. "By 'lesas'" (stains):

since birth and so forth are called "lesas" because they stain (*lissati*) another basis beyond themselves, and because they adhere (*silissati*) to what has been briefly stated in detail through mere conventional expression, it is by means of those stains—namely, the stain of birth, the stain of name, and so on. "Another" refers to one who is transgressing.

The connection [of the text] is as follows: having seen one [person], they then accuse another monk of a final offense (*antima-vatthu*) in order to cause him to fall away from the community. How so? Someone of the Khattiya caste is seen transgressing;
then, seeing another monk who is also of the Khattiya caste and is his own enemy, he seizes upon that man’s Khattiya lineage as a pretext and says: "I have seen a Khattiya transgressing."
"You are a khattiya who has fallen into a *pārājika* offense"—thus one accuses or causes another to accuse.
In this same manner, the various types of names and so forth are to be understood. The rest of the analytical discussion is exactly as stated in the eighth [chapter].
Ninth.

28. Having thus shown in detail what was briefly indicated by the phrase "heavy and new," the following is now stated—"He conceals it, knowing he has fallen into [an offense]"—in order to show the manner of procedure to be followed when one has committed such offenses.

In this context, whatever number of days a bhikkhu conceals or hides an offense of *saṅghādisesa* that he himself has committed, knowing it as such both in terms of its legal nature (*āpatti*) and its underlying basis (*vatthu*), [that duration determines the penalty].
The meaning should be understood through the connection of the words as follows: "for that many days, his probation (parivāsa) lasts for that long.
In this context, probation is threefold: concealed probation (paṭicchanna-parivāsa), pure-end probation (suddhanta-parivāsa), and combined probation (samodhāna-parivāsa).
Even when these are shown merely by way of their headings in an extremely concise manner, there exists the possibility of entering into a detailed analysis.
We shall show merely the beginning with the word "it may be.
In that regard, what is called "probation for concealed [offenses]" (paṭicchannaparivāsa) is to be granted according to how long the offense was concealed;
therefore, having observed both the days of concealment and the offenses themselves, if it has been concealed for one day, [one says]: "Venerable sir, I [have committed] many..."

Having made him request [the formal act] according to the method set forth in the Khandhaka—beginning with, “I have committed offenses concealed for one day”—and having recited the *kammavācā* (formal proclamation) according to the very same method set forth in the Khandhaka—beginning with, “Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me:

this monk named so-and-so has committed numerous offenses concealed for one day”—the probation (*parivāsa*) should be granted. Regarding the case of having committed one offense, [one says] “numerous.”
It is said, "a number [of them]," because one is also cleared even while performing a disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*).

This same method applies even when the offenses have different bases. Now, if they have been concealed for two days and so forth—whether concealed for more than a fortnight, more than a month, or more than a year—one should state, "those concealed for two days," and so on, and mention the name of whichever individual has committed the offense.
Having grasped this, the interpretation should be made.

And at the conclusion of the formal act (kammavācā), if the residence has few monks and it is possible to dwell there without incurring a breach of the night-limit, one should undertake the duties right there, saying:
"I undertake the probation; I undertake the duties. Having undertaken the duties, one should remain right there.
After announcing to the Saṅgha, "Venerable sirs, I have committed several *saṅghādisesa* offenses concealed for one day," and so forth,
if— while announcing this again to each monk as they arrive— one shares a roof with a regular (*pakatatta*) monk even when it is covered, lives apart from him,
or fails to announce it to incoming monks and others who have entered the vicinity, then by even one of these [factors], [the offense is incurred].
One should dwell [in the probation] without interrupting the nights and without breaking the duties.

If it is not possible to complete the probation, and one wishes to live having set aside the duties, then right there—either in the midst of the Saṅgha or in the presence of a single person—one should say: "I set aside the probation; I set aside the duties."
The probation must be set aside. From the moment it is set aside, he stands in the position of a regular monk (*pakatatta*).

Then, at the time of dawn, together with one other monk, having stepped two stone-throw distances beyond the enclosure of an enclosed monastery, or beyond the place where an unenclosed one ought to be enclosed, and having descended from the main road into a concealed spot—
Having sat down and undertaken the formal observance (vatta) before dawn itself, it must be announced.

If one hears or sees those standing outside, it must be announced even after going a long distance; if one fails to announce it, there is both a breach of the night-period (ratticcheda) and an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the breach of the observance.
If they enter the boundary of the precinct (upacārasīma) while one is unaware, there is only a breach of the night-period, but no breach of the observance.
When dawn has risen, having laid aside the duties toward him, one should go to the monastery. In this manner, one must undergo the probation until the nights are completed.
This, first of all, is the concealed probation (*paṭicchanna-parivāsa*).

The end of purification (*suddhanta*) is twofold: the minor end of purification (*cūḷa-suddhanta*) and the major end of purification (*mahā-suddhanta*). Therein, that which [begins] from the time of full ordination...

Having subtracted as much time as he knows himself to have been pure, the remainder of the nights should be combined into one and the probation (*parivāsa*) to be given is called the *cūḷasuddhanta* (the minor purification).

However, for one who does not know at all, does not remember, or is uncertain regarding the limit of the nights, the *mahāsuddhanta* (the major purification) should be given. Let him know the limit of the offense.
Whether it be so or not, this is not the reason.
There are three kinds of *samodhāna-parivāsa*: *odhāna-samodhāna*, *aggha-samodhāna*, and *missaka-samodhāna*.
In that regard, one who—whether his *parivāsa* has been completed or his *mānatta* has been completed—has not relinquished his observances and commits another offense...

If, having committed [the second offense], he conceals for as many nights as he concealed the first offense— or for fewer nights— then, by means of sending him back to the beginning (mūlāya paṭikassanā),
those days already spent in probation and those days spent in the trial period (mānatta) must be subtracted and wiped away;
having then combined the subsequent offense with the limit of the days of the original offense, the probation must be granted again from the very beginning.

This is called "equalizing by value" (*agghasamodhāna*). If someone has one offense concealed for one day, another for two days, and so on up to ten days, then by equalizing them according to their value—namely, by way of the ten-day concealment of those [offenses]—the *parivāsa* that must be given for the remaining offenses, such as those concealed for one day and so forth, is called "equalizing by value. Furthermore, whoever...
The mixing together of offenses with various bases into one, so that the probation (*parivāsa*) may be granted, is called "the combination of mixed [offenses].
However, the procedure for granting it is to be understood everywhere according to the method set forth in the *Khandhaka*.
A monk who has thus completed his probation must observe the *mānatta*—the state of being honored by the monks—for six nights without interruption.
"Having done" means he should practice, perform, or accomplish it; this is what is meant.

In that regard, having had the duty performed by the Saṅgha, the Gaṇa, or an individual undertaken by that bhikkhu in the midst of the Saṅgha—having made him request [the penance] according to the method stated in the Khandhaka, beginning with "Venerable Sir, I have fallen into many offenses"—and likewise having [the Saṅgha] grant the *mānatta* penance and so forth according to the method stated right there:

It should be understood. By this [method], one who wishes to relinquish the formal practice (vatta) should relinquish it and go with four or five companions to a place of the kind described for the probationer;

there, in the same manner as before, they should proceed while avoiding the faults of wandering in a group that is deficient—namely, one short of four—as well as the faults regarding co-residence and so forth, which were mentioned below. This applies to one whose offense has not been concealed.

However, without granting the *parivāsa* (probation), the *mānatta* (penance) itself should be granted. To that monk by whom the *mānatta* has been thus practiced, performed, and brought to completion:
a group (*gaṇa*) consisting of twenty members of the Saṅgha is called a "group-of-twenty" (*vīsati-gaṇa*), with the vowel lengthened;
that Saṅgha should rehabilitate him—that is, accept him—meaning it should restore him by means of the act of rehabilitation (*abbhāna-kamma*), or rather, it should summon him back.

The meaning [is as follows]. Here too, the formal undertaking, the announcement, and the request, as well as the formal act (*kammavācā*), are to be understood according to the method explained in the *Khandhaka*.
29. Having thus shown the manner in which one should proceed regarding those [offenses], he now says "an offense," etc., in order to show the constituent factors (*aṅga*) of concealment.

In that context, "one who has not been suspended" means one who is not suspended; "one for whom there is no obstacle" means one who is unobstructed (*anantarāya*). This is by means of the suffix *-tta* used in its own sense (*sakatthe*).

Alternatively, *pahutta* is the state of being many (*pahūna*); one who possesses that by way of faith and so forth is *pahūta*. "Not thrown down," "unobstructed," and "many" form a *dvanda* compound;
the state of these qualities—being not thrown down and so forth—is "the quality of being not thrown down... [etc. ...the state of being many" (*anukkhittādi-guṇa*, *anukkhitta...pe...

pahuttatā*). "Offense" (*āpatti*) and "the state of being not thrown down... [etc. ...the state of being many" form a *dvanda*: "offense... [etc. ...the states of being many" (*āpatti...pe... pahuttatāyo*). The letter *m* arises from euphonic conjunction (*padasaṃdhi*).

"In that way" means in that manner; "perceiving as such" (*tathasaññī*) refers to perceiving [the object] as an offense and so forth among the four categories beginning with offenses, by way of brevity.
The state of being that is "perceiving as such" (*tathasaññitā*); what is meant is "the state of perceiving the aforementioned offenses and so forth.

The particle *ca* has the sense of a cumulative conjunction. "Desire" (*kāma*) is the longing or aspiration; "desiring to conceal" (*chādetukāmo*) is one who wishes to hide [the offense]. Thus, there are nine as previously stated, and then "concealing" (*chādanā*).
"And so," meaning "those ten factors. At the rising of the dawn—when the first rays of the young sun, known as dawn, have risen—it becomes concealed;
the word "offense" (*āpatti*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
Herein, this is the intended meaning: whichever monk [is concerned with] kings, thieves, fire, water, humans, non-humans, wild beasts, reptiles, threats to life, or obstacles to the holy life...
Being one who is not an obstacle due to the absence of even one of the ten [conditions], yet perceiving himself as being without an obstacle;
being capable of going to a monk and announcing [the offense], yet perceiving himself as being capable;

being one who has not been suspended because the three kinds of *ukkhepanīyakamma* (acts of suspension) have not been performed against him, yet perceiving himself as not suspended; and perceiving it to be a grave offense while desiring to conceal that very grave offense.
Having confessed it, he conceals it; thus, this offense of his becomes concealed.

However, if in this case he perceives it as not an offense, or perceives it as belonging to another class of offenses, or is in doubt, they remain unconcealed. But the one confessing should announce it in such a manner as: "Know that I have fallen into one offense," and so forth.
However, if [the offender] has committed an offense similar to the basis [of the original offense]...
As soon as she announces it, she incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense on that account.
The commentary on the exposition of the *saṅghādisesa* rules is finished.
3. Commentary on the Exposition of the *Cīvara* Rules.
30. By forming a dual compound (*dvanda*) through the neuter gender in the phrase beginning with “khomañca koseyyañca,” [the list] results in *khoma...
pe... bhaṅgāni*. Therein, *khoma* is a species of tree. Metaphorically, however, it is called *khoma* because it is woven with *khoma* [fibers] or *khoma* thread;

thus, by means of a derivative suffix (*taddhita*) or a metaphorical designation, *khoma* refers to a robe made of *khoma* cloth. The remaining [terms] are likewise [to be understood]. *Sāṇa* is that which is woven with *sāṇa* (hemp) fibers.
*Clothing* (*cīvara*): By mixing all or some of the constituent materials, such as linen thread (*khomasutta*) and so forth, one weaves it into cloth.
Some say it is made only of flax. *Blanket* (*kambala*): This refers to what is woven from the remaining types of wool, excluding human hair and animal fur.

*These*, namely the aforementioned linens and so forth, together with their corresponding secondary materials (*anuloma*), constitute the six types of allowable clothing according to their origin (*jāti*).
31. Now, with the words beginning “dukūla,” he shows their synonyms. Therein, “dukūla” refers to a robe woven from a particular kind of flax known as *dukūla*.
The particle “ca” (and) is used for conjunction; it should be drawn forward to connect with what follows.
“Paṭṭuṇṇa” means that which is produced in *paṭṭuṇṇa* [countries]. Since words denoting a place take the plural number, the analysis is made using the plural. Likewise...
*Somāra* and *cīna*: that which is produced from these is "born of *somāra* and *cīna*" (*somāracīnaja*). These three are made of thread spun by insects.
"Born of psychic power" (*iddhija*) is that which arises through the merit and psychic power of those who come as monks (*ehibhikkhu*); it is one or another of the fabrics such as *khoma*.

"Given by the gods" (*devadinna*) is a robe produced on the wish-fulfilling tree (*kapparukkha*) bestowed by the gods. This refers to each of those aforementioned materials, such as *dukūla* and so forth.
It is "conducive" (*anulomika*) with respect to hair and so forth. In this context, "conducive" (*anuloma*) means following along;

just as a hair that follows the direction of other hairs is called "conducive" because it is favorable to them, so too anything of that same kind which is favorable to anyone is, by way of common usage (*ruḷhī*), called "conducive. That very thing is "conducive," meaning it is favorable. How so?

Dukūla is the appropriate [material] for hemp; paṭṭuṇṇa and the other two are the appropriate [materials] for silk; and that produced by supernormal power or given by deities is the appropriate [material] for linen and the rest.
(32–3) Having thus shown the robes together with their appropriate materials, he now says “the triple robe,” etc., in order to show the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and so forth.
In this context, even though it is not explicitly stated, the word "and" (ca) must be supplied everywhere because it is necessarily required;

thus the connection is: "one should determine the three robes and so forth... and the itch-cloth, but one should not allocate them. Therein, the collection of the three robes is "the three robes" (*ticīvara*).

That which is both a requisite (*parikkhāra*) and a cloth (*coḷa*) is "requisite-cloth" (*parikkhāracoḷa*). That which is suitable for the rainy season is "rainy-season" (*vassikā*); that very [cloth] is...
*Saṭikā* is a rainy-season robe (*vassika-saṭikā*). That by which one wipes is a "wiping cloth" (*puñchana*); wiping for the mouth is "mouth-wiping" (*mukha-puñchana*).
That upon which they sit is a "sitting mat" (*nisīdana*); the mouth-wiping and the sitting mat together are "mouth-wiping and sitting mat" (*mukha-puñchana-nisīdana*).

It is spread out depending on the comfort of lying down and so forth, thus it is a "counter-spread" (*paccattharaṇa*), and that very thing is a "counter-spread cloth" (*paccattharaṇaka*). [It is used for] itching...

"It covers" means it is a "cover for itching. One should perform the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) by taking up the names of the nine [robes], beginning with, "I determine this outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*)," and so forth.
"One should not assign" means one should not assign it by taking up the name of each individual [robe];
rather, the intention is that one should assign it without taking up the name of each individual one, saying, "I assign this robe to you."

"Herein" means among these nine robes. "The three robes" refers to that which is determined by the name "three robes. For indeed, prior to such determination, there is no such thing as a "three robes" per se; this is because it is permitted to determine even a robe sufficient for a *saṅghāṭī* and so forth for the purpose of a rug or similar use.
"Without that," meaning without [the determination], one should not dwell for even a single day (*ekāhaṃ*)—that is, for a single day—if one has not obtained formal permission (*sammuti*).
The meaning is: "A bhikkhu should not dwell elsewhere than within the boundary of non-separation.

This indicates that if this were the case, one would have to relinquish the triple robe (*ticīvara*) and would incur an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). The connection is: "One should not dwell for four months without a sitting mat (*nisīdana*).
The compound *catumāsaṃ* is the collection of four months; that itself is "for four months" (*cātumāsaṃ*). That...
By way of absolute conjunction. 34.
Now, with the words beginning “this,” he shows the determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) mentioned as “one should determine.
The connection is: one determines the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) by saying, “I determine this outer robe. In that context, “one determines” means [the robe] is standing within arm’s reach.
One should resolve thus: "Within arm's reach" (*ahatthapāsanti*). "Arm's reach" (*hatthapāsa*) means the vicinity of the hand;
it is within two and a half cubits (*aḍḍhateyyahattha*), though some say it is within twelve cubits. "Without arm's reach" (*ahatthapāsā*) means that which has no arm's reach;
"one resolves for that" is the grammatical connection. What is meant? Having gone on that very day either into an inner chamber or onto an upper terrace—
It means that having observed the robe-cloth situated in a place suitable for returning, one should resolve upon it, saying, "I resolve upon this outer cloak (saṅghāṭi).
They say that even if it is situated at a distance from there, it may still be resolved upon.

"In the others as well" refers to the remaining robes, beginning with the upper garment (uttarāsaṅga) and ending with the skin-eruption cover (kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi). "This method" means this very same method.
Just as with the outer robe (*saṅghāṭī*), so too it is said that the method is as previously described, beginning with: “I resolve upon this upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*).

However, when resolving, one should do so either by means of the body—taking hold of it with the hand, making a bodily gesture, and applying mental attention (*ābhoga*) with the thought, “I resolve upon this outer robe”—or by means of speech, merely uttering the words.
“Requisite cloth” (*parikkhāracoḷa*) means a separate storage opening; thus, it is permissible to determine even the requisite cloth as one’s own set of three robes (*ticīvara*).

35. Now, in order to show that when one has determined [the robes] in this way, if another [robe] is obtained and one wishes to determine it, one must first relinquish the former before determining the latter, he says:
“When determining,” and so forth. In that context, “beginning with the outer robe” (*saṅghāṭippabhuti*) refers to that which has the outer robe as its beginning.
In the phrases “resolving upon this” (*etaṃ adhiṭṭhahanto*) and “he should resolve,” the word is a verb;
however, in the phrase “the previously [designated] robe” (*pubbacīvaraṃ*), it stands as a qualifying attribute. “Having relinquished” (*paccuddharitvā*) means having given away.

Having resolved upon them under the name of “requisite-cloth,” he makes the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) and so forth from the fabrics kept aside; once they are finished, dyed, and cut into patches, [he uses] this...
Having relinquished the requisite cloth, it must be determined again. Regarding "the determination of the bowl" (*pattādhiṭṭhāna*): this refers to the determination of the bowl.
The word "likewise" (*tathā*) means that just as it is with the robe, so too for the bowl, all [procedures] such as determination and so forth apply.
However, in this case, the distinction is made by saying, "this bowl," or "that bowl."
36. Now, in order to show the procedure for relinquishing (*paccuddhāra*), he says "this" (*etaṃ*) and so forth.
Therein, the word *va* in "imaṃ va" is indicated as being shortened; it should be construed after the word *iti*.
Therefore, the connection should be understood as either "I relinquish this outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*)" or "I relinquish this outer robe. *Saṃseyya* means one should say.
Thus, the meaning is that just as the *saṅghāṭi* (outer robe) is to be relinquished by name, so too are the *uttarāsaṅga* (upper robe) and the others.

*Vidū* is the agent-noun for "one who relinquishes," meaning "one who is wise. In all instances, whether [the robes] are distant or near, they should be understood according to the method already stated. 37–8.
Now, he shows the measurement and limits of the six [robes], beginning with the *saṅghāṭi*, with the words "The *saṅghāṭi*... and so forth. The last...
*Anto* means the inner end; by that, the meaning is "the western limit. *Dīghaso* means "in length.
*Muṭṭhipañcakā* is that which has five [fingers] together with a fist; however, through a change of gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*), it is called *muṭṭhipañcako*.
Here, by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), the word "fist" refers to the hand itself when it is made into a fist. The compound is "deficient compared to the robe of the Sugata. *Api* means...
In the *Vuttasamuccaya*, the meaning is that this is the supreme measure (*uttamappamāṇa*), whereas the previously mentioned is the final measure (*pacchimappamāṇa*).

The phrase "by the final limit" (*pacchimantena*) should be understood by repeating it here as well [from the rule regarding] the fist-measure and the horizontal measurement. The word "and" (*ca*) includes the following:
"it is also permissible even if it is slightly less than the supreme measure of a Sugata’s robe. In this context, for a man of medium stature—
Three spans (vidatthi) make one Sugata-span; nine spans in length by six spans in width is the measure of a Sugata’s robe.
That, however, by the carpenter’s cubit (vaḍḍhakihattha), is thirteen cubits and one span in length, and nine cubits in width.
By means of that [measure], the deficiency in both respects is to be understood.
In order to show that the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) is also made in that same way, he said: "Likewise, even for the one-shouldered [robe]. *Eka-aṃsa* means "one shoulder";

that which is to be made there is called *ekaṃsika*, by means of a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*). By the words "inner garment" (*antaravāsaka*), etc., he indicates the lower robe (*nivāsana*).
In this context, *antara* refers to the middle region; a cloth (*vāsa*) worn in the middle—that is, on the hip region—is an *antaravāsa*, and that itself is the *antaravāsaka*.
*Cāpi* is a collective term, or it is a single conjunction. *Aḍḍhateyya* means "two and a half.
Here, when two full units of a cubit (*hattha*) are combined with a third unit, the span (*vidatthi*) indicated by the word *aḍḍha* (half) serves as the instrument for effecting that third part;
thus, that very [span] is designated as the "third. Consequently, the third part consisting of half a cubit is called *aḍḍhateyya*.
Furthermore, since a measurement of two *hattha*s and three *vidatthi*s cannot be obtained by simply adding them together, it is two *hattha*s and one *vidatthi*, which is two and a half.

In this context, however, it should be understood that the *antaravāsaka* (inner robe) itself is what is meant by "two and a half" because of its association with that measurement. The term "two *hattha*s" (*dvihattha*) is a *bahubbīhi* compound meaning "one whose [measurement] is two *hattha*s.
It is stated as "two *hattha*s" because it is possible to cover the navel even with the upper robe (*pārupana*).

The word *vā* provides two alternative options (*vikappa*). "The end of the horizontal" (*tiriyassa anto*) is a genitive tappurisa compound; or, "the horizontal itself as the end" (*tiriyam eva anto*) is a kammadhāraya compound, as in the case of expressions such as "the edge of a village" (*gāmanto*).

By the phrase "of the sitting mat" (*nisīdanassā*) and so forth, he indicates the sitting mat robe (*nisīdana-cīvara*). Here, "sitting mat" (*nisīdana*) refers to [a cloth] on a level portion of ground.

A specific type of requisite made by layering sheep’s wool one upon another, sprinkling it with sour gruel and other liquids, and then splitting it in two places so that it is provided with three fringes.
"Two spans" means two *vidatthi*s. "In width" means in breadth. 40.
By the words "kaṇḍuppaṭicchādī" and so forth, he shows the itch-covering cloth (*kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi*). Therein, "itch" (*kaṇḍū*) does not [refer to] the actual meaning...
"Various" (*nānaṃ*): by this term, however, the affliction of large boils and severe skin eruptions (*piḷakā-avathulla-kacchābādha*) is included here.

It is called "a covering for itching" (*kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi*) because it covers the aforementioned boils and so forth. Alternatively, "covering" (*paṭicchāda*) means the act of concealing; a covering for the aforementioned itching is "a covering for itching" (*kaṇḍuppaṭicchāda*).
One who possesses that is "one who has a covering for itching" (*kaṇḍuppaṭicchādī*), [referring to] him. "Horizontally" (*tiriyanti*) means across (*tiriyato*).
41. By the words beginning with “*vassikā*,” he shows the *vassikasāṭika* (the rainy-season robe); that is easy to understand. 42.

Having thus shown the measure for those things that possess a measure, he says “*ettha*” and so forth in order to show the fault in exceeding the stated measure, as well as the absence of measure and the absence of counting for certain things.
Therein, “*ettha*” means among the robes that possess the stated measure. “*Taduttari*... [and so on].
Then, by means of the prefix *uttari* (meaning "beyond") following the aforementioned measure, there is a *tappurisa* compound. "For one who makes" or "for one who completes.

"An offense entailing expiation involving cutting" (*chedanapācitti*) means an expiation (*pācitti*) accompanied by cutting; what is meant is that having cut it beyond [the limit], an expiation must be confessed.
However, that which exceeds the stated measure as well as that which is deficient should both be determined as "requisite cloth" (*parikkhāracoḷa*).
That with which they wipe the face is "connected with the face"; thus, in the compound *mukhacoḷa*, there is a *dvanda*.

"Desired measure" (*ākaṅkhitappamāṇa*) is a *kammadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is desired as a measure. "Those who have this [measure] for themselves" (*ākaṅkhitappamāṇikā*) is formed by adding the suffix *-ika*.

And here, even though the number and division are not explicitly stated regarding the three robes (*ticīvara*) and so forth, starting from the beginning and excluding the bedspread (*paccattharaṇa*), the face-wiping cloth (*mukhapuñchana*), and the requisite cloth (*parikkhāracoḷa*), [the rest are counted].
Only one of each [item] is permitted. It should be understood that there may even be many face-cloths (*mukhapuñchanacoḷa*) and bedspreads (*paccattharaṇa*).

43. Regarding the "number" (*gaṇanā*): here, because there is no grammatical connection between a neuter noun and a feminine term, the word "not explained" (*na dīpitā*) must be linked by changing its gender;
the meaning is that it was not set forth in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. However, regarding these three, it is only by way of the maximum limit (*ukkaṭṭhapariccheda*)...
It has been stated that there is indeed a final measurement for the last [type of cloth] suitable for assignment (*vikappanūpaga*). Now, because not all of that has been illustrated there,
he says "likewise" (*tathā*) and so forth, showing that everything suitable for assignment— such as a *thavika* (bag), etc.—
should be determined either by calling it a single "requisite-cloth" (*parikkhāracoḷa*), or by calling them "requisite-cloths" (*parikkhāracoḷāni*) after grouping many together.

By this, he shows that what is called "requisite-cloth" (*parikkhāra-coḷa*) is a separate heading for requisites. "Thavikādi" is a compound meaning "that of which a water-strainer (*parissāvana*), etc., is the beginning.
"Vikappiya" means that which comes under the category of assignment (*vikappa*); and that he will explain further on. 44.
Now, in order to show the counterpart to the three robes, the passage beginning with "unwashed" (*ahata*) is commenced. Therein, by "unwashed" (*ahatena*)...
*Navenādhotakappam*: like new, even though washed; *ahatakappam*: like unwashed, [meaning] once-washed. *Ahatāhatakappāni*:

those that are both unwashed and like the unwashed; [this refers to] robes (*vatthāni*), of which. That which has two strands or layers is "two-stranded" (*duguṇā*). For the *Abhidhānappadīpikā* states:
"Strand (*guṇa*) [refers to] a layer and a collection. Two-stranded means double-layered. That which is fastened to the upper part of the body is the "upper shoulder-strap" (*ukkarāsaṅgo*).
"One who has a certain single panel" (*ekaccī*) means one who possesses a certain single panel (*ekapaṭṭa*); or *ekaccī* is a particle. "Likewise" (*tathā*) is used as a conjunction;
thus it is said, "and the inner robe. Or, in the sense of a comparison: just as the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) is a single panel, so too is the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*); such is the meaning.
45. “Utū” means that many seasons are included; thus, “extracted from the season” (*utuddhaṭā*) means extracted from a long period of time.

The meaning is: “of those [rags] (*tesaṃ pilotikānaṃ*). "The rest" refers to the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) and the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*). It is called *paṃsukūla* because it is loathsome (*kucchitaṃ*) like dust (*paṃsu*) and it moves about (*ulati*) or occurs there.
It is a piece of cloth situated anywhere on carriage roads, charnel grounds, heaps of refuse, and so forth. “Whichever preference” means whatever is desired.
In the case of an *abyayībhāva* compound, according to one’s preference, even a hundred cloths may be used for as long as they serve the purpose; this is the intended meaning. 46.
Now, in order to show the procedure to be followed when it is impossible to make [the robes] by cutting them from three [pieces], he says, "In the case of three," and so forth.
Therein, because two [of the three] and one are extracted from the aggregate of the three robes (*ticīvara*) by way of number and quality, [they are designated as such].

The locative case in "tīsu" is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). Since the singular number cannot be construed with a plural object, one should transpose the number to refer to the plurality designated by the two robes;
thus it should be connected as follows: "those which are sufficient, even if they are two, may be cut [into the required size]," and "that which is sufficient, even if it is one, may be cut.
"Sufficient" means they are sufficient when cut to the measurement of the final robe.

*Apīti* means "perhaps" (*sambhāvane*); the sense is: "what [offense] would there be in the three cases? *Anvādhi* refers to the guest-bowl (*āgantukapatta*). It is called *anvādhi* because it is placed after (*anu pacchā ādhīyati*);
that which is to be placed upon the robe in the manner of an outer cloak (*saṅghāṭi*) is the *anvādhi*. *Anādiṇṇaṃ* means not placed as an *anvādhi*.
*Na dhāreyya* indicates that if one were to wear it, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

47–8. Now, in order to demonstrate the characteristic of non-separation (*avippavāsa-lakkhaṇa*) for the three [robes] mentioned in the rule, “One should not dwell apart from the triple robe even for a single night,” he states the exception as it is set forth in the *Udosita-sikkhāpada* beginning with “In a village,” etc.

Therein, the connection is: “having deposited the triple robe in a village... or in a monastery. In this context, just as in expressions such as “the cloth is burnt,” the term may refer to a part [of the whole].
By way of collective designation, even one [robe] among the three is called "the triple robe" (*tricīvara*).

"Except by formal authorization of the Saṅgha" means without the authorization for separation from the robes being granted by the Saṅgha to a sick bhikkhu. "To be separated" means outside of a village that has a single access point or multiple access points;
or else, outside of dwellings and so forth, and there, outside of inner rooms or upper chambers, having gone beyond arm’s reach of the robe.

...to live separated from one's robe. In this context, the fact that villages and so forth have either a single precinct (*upacāra*) or multiple precincts should be understood by way of the enclosure and the space of the enclosure belonging to a village or the like that is owned by a single family or multiple families, as well as by way of the seven *abbhantara*s for the open spaces (*abbhokāsa*).
Therein, one internal *abbhantara* is twenty-eight cubits (*hattha*). And herein, dwellings (*nivesana*) and so forth—

It should be understood that these are situated outside the village, since the village itself has been mentioned separately. Likewise, "dwelling" refers to a residence other than a storehouse (*udositādi*).
In this context, a *udositā* is a hall for goods such as vehicles; a *pāsāda* is a long mansion; a *hammiya* is a mansion with a flat roof;
a boat, a watchtower (*aṭṭa*), a multi-storied building (*māḷa*), and a park (*ārāma*)—that is, in a boat... [and so on] ...in a park. A *aṭṭa* is [a structure used by] rival kings and others.

A *paṭissaya-viseso* is a particular type of dwelling constructed with thick walls of bricks for the purpose of warding off [enemies], consisting of four or five stories. A *māḷo* is a square palace enclosed by a single roof-peak.
An *ārāmo* is either a flower-garden or a fruit-garden. "Caravan (*sattho*), field (*khetta*), and threshing-floor (*khala*)" is a copulative compound (*dvanda*).
A "caravan" (*sattho*) refers to either a foot-caravan or a cart-caravan. A "threshing-floor" (*khala*) is said to be a place where grain is processed.

A "tree" (*dumo*) refers to the root of a tree; the area touched by its shade is included by way of its vicinity. An "open space" (*abbhokāsa*), however, is intended here specifically as a forest (*arañña*) that is not near a village.
49. Now, although the relinquishment (*paccuddhāra*) has been stated in nine items beginning with “this... [robe] cloth (*saṅghāṭī*)”, the time limit for those [items] was not mentioned;
therefore, the passage beginning with “diseases” (*rogā*) is commenced in order to demonstrate that. In this context, Devadatta is referred to by a partial name, such as *Datta*.

The *vassikasāṭikā* (rain-season robe) is called simply “robe” (*sāṭikā*) by way of conventional designation, because its meaning is understood through the context of the treatise. And the *kaṇḍuppaṭicchādikā* (itch-covering cloth) has as its limit the sickness and the rainy season.
The analysis of the compound is as follows: “sicknesses and rainy seasons” (*rogavassānā*) refers to the months of sickness and the months of the rainy season;
it is so called because they are the limits beyond which it must be relinquished.
What is meant? It is said that the *vassikasāṭikā* (rain-season robe) must be relinquished precisely on the full moon day of the month of Kattika once the months of the rains have passed.
Likewise, the *kaṇḍuppaṭicchādikā* (itch-covering cloth) must be relinquished when illnesses have subsided.

For it is stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) that "having relinquished it, it should be assigned [to another]. However, regarding this, some teachers [interpret] "having relinquished" as [relinquishing it] from its status as a *vassikasāṭikā*.

To say, "having taken it back," is not tenable. This is because the word *paccuddhāra* (renunciation) is seen only in the context of formal acts of renunciation (*paccuddhāravinayakamma*), and because of the scriptural statement:
"One may determine [the robe] for four months, and beyond that, one may assign it.
Furthermore, in the phrase "one may determine for four months," an absolute connection (*accantasamyoga*) with the determination for the duration of four months is shown; therefore—

By this, the distinction between formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and assignment (*vikappa*) is understood. For that very reason, the Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā also states: "One may determine [the robe] for four months of the rains; beyond that, one should assign it. Thus, it is said that after returning [the robe] on the full moon of Kattika, it should be assigned during the winter. Therefore, even if the rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭikā*) exceeds the [four] months of the rains, the itch-covering cloth (*kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi*)— [The text continues: ...is not subject to the same rule. It is said: “One also relinquishes the formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) by means of the subsiding of an affliction.
In the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* as well, the meaning should be understood thus: “One relinquishes the formal determination even by way of relinquishing (paccuddhāra).

For it being so, all the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā) are brought into agreement and the logical consistency (yutti) remains uncontradicted. “Thereafter” means after the relinquishing. “One should designate” refers to the itch-covering cloth (kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi).
Having relinquished it, one may assign it [to another]. Having relinquished the rain-cloak on the full moon of Kattika, one may assign it on the first day of the winter season;
the intention is that if this is not done, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). "The rest" means the remaining seven robes.
They are called "without limit" (*apariyantikā*) because they have no such temporal restriction as was stated for those [others].
50. Now, in order to show that among the four types of robes beginning with the *paccattharaṇa*, only those such as the *sadasa* are permitted and no others, he says:
“*Paccattharaṇā*,” and so forth. Therein, “*parikkhāro ca mukhapuñchanan cā*” is a *dvanda* compound. “*Parikkhāramukhapuñchanameva coḷakan*” is a *kammadhāraya* compound.
However, because the word *coḷaka* is heard at the end of the *dvanda* compound, it [is understood] from the word *parikkhāra*.

And furthermore, it should be understood as "requisites-cloth" (*parikkhāra-coḷaka*). However, setting aside the five robes because they are established under their specific names despite being included in the general designation, the remainder should be understood by the name "requisites-cloth. This group of four robes consists of:
the bedspread (*paccattharaṇa*), the cloth for wiping the face and requisites (*parikkhāra-mukhapuñchana-coḷaka*), the bedspread... [etc. ...the cloth, and the sitting mat (*nisīdana*).

The connection [of the words] is as follows: even when with a fringe (*sadasaṃ*), even when without a fringe (*adasaṃ*), and even when not of the prescribed measure (*anādiṇṇakappaṃ*), they are obtained.

*Sadasaṃ* means "together with whatever fringes (*dasā*) there may be. When that which has a fringe (*sadasakaṃ*) is obtained, that which does not have a fringe (*adasaṃ*) is also indeed obtained; thus, the meaning here is "even when with a fringe, even when without a fringe, and even when with flower-fringes" (*pupphadasaṃ*).

The particle *pi* (even/also) serves the purpose of including both what has been stated and what has not been stated. *Arattaṃ* means even when it has not been dyed with colors such as blue, yellow, and so forth.
By the word "pi" (also/even), it includes those dyed blue, yellow, and so forth, as well as those whose *kappa* (formal authorization) has not been granted.
That which has no *kappa* granted to it is "anādiṇṇakappam" (one whose authorization is not granted). By the word "pi," it also includes those whose *kappa* has been granted.
But is it not the case that, by such rules as "Monks, robes that are entirely blue should not be worn," robes that are entirely blue, entirely yellow, and entirely red [are prohibited]?
Regarding the statement that these are prohibited by way of general rule (*sāmaññena*): how is it that this fourfold set of robes, including those made of grass and so forth, is permitted;
and how is it that even what is of "unrestricted-period" (*anādiṇṇakappa*) is permitted? It is said:

in the context of the various items arising [in the Vinaya], such as "At that time, a certain monk, having put on a garment of *kusa* grass," it is stated: "Monks, a garment of *kusa* grass... [and so on]... the banner of the heretics must not be worn."

Because wearing—defined as the donning and wearing [of robes]—is prohibited by such passages as, "Whoever should wear [them], there is an offense of thullaccaya," according to the specific circumstances that have arisen;
and because it is stated right there in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "All-blue and other [robes] should be washed of their dye and dyed again before being worn;
if they cannot be washed, they should be made into bedspreads (*paccattharaṇa*), or [used for] a double-layered robe (*dupaṭṭacīvara*)."
Or they should be given in the middle; if the fringes are cut off or the fringes are too long, they should be worn after cutting the fringes.
Having obtained a tunic (*kañcuka*), it is permissible to tear it, dye it, and use it. The same rule applies to head-wraps (*veṭhana*).

Furthermore, because wearing and using [robes] are described specifically in terms of the lower garment (*nivāsana*) and the upper robe (*pārupana*), in the training rule concerning making robes discolored (*dubbaṇṇakaraṇa-sikkhāpada*), [it refers to] "that which one should wear as a lower garment or as an upper robe..."

Or, it should be understood that "that very robe" refers to the fact that only five types of allowable stains were permitted; thus, the five robes— namely, the triple robe (*ticīvara*), the itch-covering cloth (*kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi*), and the rainy-season garment (*vassikasāṭika*)—

are indeed for the purpose of protecting the body, and they must not be entirely blue or otherwise [prohibited colors], but must be dyed with allowable dyes and have their allowable marks applied, rather than being subject to strict [color] requirements.

"The other four are excluded" means that even a set of four robes (*cīvaracatukka*) that is new, along with its accessories, is permissible even if it has not been formally accepted (*anādiṇṇakappa*).
51. The construction is as follows: "The remaining five types of robes are permissible only if they have been dyed and only if they have been formally accepted.
"Dyed" means dyed with allowable dye. In order to prohibit [the use of] a sitting mat in all cases where it has not been formally accepted, according to the meaning already stated—
“It is called ‘a sitting mat that is always [used]’; for a qualification is purposeful when there is both possibility and ambiguity.

Now, in order to show what the procedure is regarding that which has not been formally resolved (*anadhiṭṭhita*) and that which has not been relinquished (*anissaṭṭha*), he said, “not resolved,” and so forth.
Therein, “not resolved” means not resolved as one of the three robes (*ticīvara*) and so on. “Not relinquished” means [not relinquished] to anyone whatsoever.

It is "not given" by virtue of the characteristic of giving. One should use it after having made a formal assignment (*vikappana*), having observed and assigned its status as single or multiple, and its state of being stored or not stored, according to the method that will be explained.
However, because this is understood through the method that will be explained, the word "having relinquished" (*paccuddharitvā*) is not stated here.
Now, regarding the term "having determined" (*vikappetvā*) which was mentioned, [the author] says "hands," etc., to explain what kind of object is determined according to the minimum measurement.
Therein, "hand-long" (*hatthadīgha*) means that whose length is a hand. "From there" (*tato*) means from that hand.
"Half-a-span-wide" (*upaḍḍhavitthāra*) means that whose width, measured in detail, is half a hand—that is, the second part known as a *vidatthi*.

53. Now, while the procedure described above applies specifically to one who possesses only the three robes (*tecīvarika*), the text says "of one with the three robes" (*ticīvarassa*) and so forth in order to show that another might practice otherwise.
In this context, "one with the three robes" (*ticīvara*) refers to one who has three robes formally determined (*adhiṭṭhita*) by name;
the meaning is "of such a person who possesses the three robes according to the Vinaya," not of one whose robes are determined merely as "requisites-cloth" (*parikkhāra-coḷa*).
However, there is no exemption stated for one who wears a robe [as part of his requisites] in the *Udosita-sikkhāpada* of the *Vinaya*. Regarding the term *parikkhāracoḷika*:
it means "one who has a *parikkhāracoḷa*," where the suffix *-ika* (in the form of *-ya*) is applied. "All" refers to the entirety of the nine kinds of robes.
"Having spoken thus" means having recognized the state of being singular or plural, and the state of being present or absent, [he says]: "This *parikkhāracoḷa*..."
Having said, "I resolve," and so forth, [the text] uses the term *adhiṭṭhāti*, meaning "he resolves.
Now, showing how the resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is lost when one uses a robe that has been resolved (*adhiṭṭhitacīvara*), it says, "By cutting off," and so forth.
In this context, "cutting off" (*accheda*), "giving away" (*vissajjana*), "taking up" (*gāha*), and "departure" (*vibbhama*) form a dvanda compound.
"Seizure" (acchedo) means taking [an item] after it has been snatched away by thieves and the like. "Relinquishment" (vissajjana) means giving to others. "Taking" (gāho) means taking with trust.
"Departure" (vibbhamo) means returning to the state of a householder without having formally renounced the training.

Even then, for him, there is a relinquishing of the robe through its lack of attachment, just as in the case of giving it to another. However, in the *Ṭīkā*, it says that one who begins with the letter *b* is indeed a monk (*bhikkhu*).
The statement that "she does not abandon her formal resolve" (adhiṭṭhāna) refers to a nun’s return to lay life after having made a conceptual distinction regarding the meaning;
that [interpretation] is not to be accepted. As for the reason here, our own teachers have stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*:
"Because it was not specifically stated regarding a nun that she would 'return to the lower state,' there is no abandonment of the formal resolve when a nun returns to lay life."
It is said: "There is nothing to be stated separately regarding her, because by her very act of leaving the order (vibbhama), she ceases to be a female ascetic.

But surely, it was stated that for a monk who has not formally renounced the training, his state of being without a dwelling place (*nirālayabhāva*)—due to his transition to the status of a householder and the consequent abandonment of his formal commitment (*adhiṭṭhāna*)—serves as the cause [for the loss of the vow].
This being so, since one who has changed gender lacks the state of being without a dwelling place, how can there be a formal commitment for him?
"Does he relinquish it? Yes, this is true. Nevertheless, there is no fault here, because the commentators who knew the Buddha’s intention stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
"However, the triple robe and the bowl that were determined for him during his state as a monk—he relinquishes that determination; they must be determined again."
The "training regarding the mark" (*liṅgasikkhā*) refers to the changing of one's gender marks or the renunciation of the training;

it is called "training regarding the mark" by means of a compound with the elision of the final member or through figurative usage. Thus, these eight [offenses] constitute the separation from the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) of any of the nine robes;
the phrase "they are the causes thereof" is to be supplied to the text. However, for the three robes, there are not only these eight.
The phrase "the cause for the loss of the resolve through being pierced" (*vinividdhachiddañca adhiṭṭhānaviyogakāraṇaṃ*) should be construed by changing the gender and number [of the terms].

In this context, "pierced" (*vinividdha*) refers to a hole made by piercing through, which, due to the absence of even a single thread within, is the size of the back of the fingernail of the little finger.
Among these, from the long edge of both the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) and the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*), [a portion] measuring one span (*vidatthi*)— [...]*

If a hole occurs within an area measuring eight finger-breadths across from the edge of the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*), or within an area measuring four finger-breadths across from the edge of the robe that is one span long, it invalidates the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
After performing needlework, it must be determined again. When performing the needlework, one should cut out and remove any weak spots.
It should be made without showing any gaps. 55.
Now, in order to show what is unallowable, the passage beginning with “grass” is stated.
Therein, “grass,” “bark,” and “wooden planks”—the robes made from these are “grass... robes. Among these, that which is made by weaving grass is a “grass robe. Likewise...
"Bark-cloth" (*vākacīra*) refers to that which is made by sewing together strips of bark; it is the garment of ascetics.

"Wood-shield cloth" (*phalakacīra*) refers to that which is made by sewing together pieces of wood shaped like shields. "Born of hair and wool" (*kesavālaja*) is a compound meaning a blanket (*kambala*) produced and woven from both hair and wool.
"Owl-wing and antelope-skin" (*ulūkapakkhājinakkhipa*) refers to the wing of an owl—that is, the bird *kosiya*—or a garment made from its wing.
The connection is as follows: for one who wears a lower garment made of antelope skin, or the hairy skin of wild antelopes complete with hooves, there is a *thullaccaya* offense.
56. Regarding "in *kadali*, *eraka*, and *akka* cloth": *kadali*, *eraka*, and *akka*—their cloths are garments;
for these, and also for rugs made of *makaci* fibers, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense. This locative case is used in the sense of a sign (*nimitta*). By the term "*kadali*-cloth" and so forth...
That which is intended here is the wearing [of such cloth]; therefore, the meaning is that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the purpose of wearing it.
This applies in all cases. The phrase beginning with “*nīlako cā*” (and blue) is a *dvanda* compound. The expression “all [types of] blue... up to black” is a *kammadhāraya* compound.

By virtue of being connected with colors such as blue, the cloth is called “blue,” and so forth. Blue is the color of the flax flower (*umāpuppha*). Mañjeṭṭha is the color of the mañjeṭṭhika flower. Yellow is the color of the kaṇikāra flower.

The red [color] has the hue of the *jayasumana* flower; the black has the hue of *addāriṭṭhaka*. Here, the word "all" (*sabba*) should be applied to each [term]. 57. Regarding "dyed with mahā... pe ... ratta":

this refers to those dyed with *mahāraṅga* and *mahānāmaraṅga*. Here too, the word "all," which is heard again, is to be understood by continuing it [to the following], such that the meaning is "all things dyed with *mahāraṅga*" and so forth. And by this, [it excludes] those that are not entirely blue and so on.
It indicates that there is no fault for one who uses cloth dyed with allowable dyes. In this context, *mahāraṅga* is the color of the back of a hundred-footed centipede.
*Mahānāmaraṅga* is a variegated color; it is the color of a withered leaf, though some also say it is the color of a lotus.
*Tirīṭaka* refers to the bark of a tree of that name. *Acchinnadīghadasaka* means "unsevered long border" because it is entirely uncut.
The compound *phalapupphadaso* is an *aññapadattha-samāsa* (possessive compound) meaning: "that which has long fringes (*dasā*) and a cloth-edge (*vatthakoṭi*) cut in the middle.
Regarding the term *phalapupphadaso*: the fringes made by weaving them together so as to resemble fruits are called "fruits" (*phala*);

those resembling flowers, such as the *ketaka* and others, are called "flowers" (*puppha*). Thus, it refers to one whose fringes are both fruits and flowers—that is, fringes resembling fruits and fringes resembling flowers.
And such is the meaning. "In wrapping" means in wrapping the head. By the word "likewise," the offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) regarding all-blue garments and so forth is extended by analogy.
"All" refers to the entirety, such as grass-cloths and the like. The connection is: "he who obtains an uncut robe.
The commentary on the description of robes is finished.
4. Explanation of the Description of Colors (Rajananiddesavaṇṇanā) 58.
"Root, trunk, bark, leaf, fruit, and flower"—this is a genitive tatpurisa compound meaning "the classification of these.

Alternatively, since the word *pabheda* (classification) functions as an accusative object, it is a karmadhāraya compound meaning "those very things are the classifications"; [the verse continues] from there: "they color... (rajanti).

“By these” refers to dyes, such as those from roots and so forth. It is said, “There are six kinds of dyes permitted by the Teacher,” because the Blessed One authorized them with the words, “I allow, monks, six dyes: root-dye,” and so on. 59.
Regarding “in the case of roots”: in the context of root-dyes, everything is permissible except for turmeric; this is the connection. The same applies everywhere.
"Mañjeṭṭhi and tuṅgahāraka" forms a dvanda compound. By means of the words *alli* and *nīli*, the leaves of those respective plant species are understood through metaphorical usage;
likewise, by the words *lodda* and *kaṇḍula*, the bark is understood, and by the words *kusumbha* and *kiṃsuka*, the flowers.
For that very reason, these [words] are neuter. *Tuṅgahāraka* is the name of a certain thorny tree.
Its dye for the trunk is the color of green palmyra. It is permissible to dye it once with the leaves of the *allī* plant when they have been used by a householder.
For dyeing with fruits, everything is permissible.
The commentary on the description of dyes is finished.
5. Commentary on the Description of the Alms Bowl (Pattaniddesavaṇṇanā) 60.

An "iron bowl" (*ayopatta*) is a bowl made from iron, that is, black metal (*kālaloha*). [The classification] is by way of the commonality of types such as "excellent" (*ukkaṭṭha*) and so forth. "By measure" means by way of its dimensions. The phrase "three bowls" is an elliptical addition to the text. 61.
Where one should say "in Magadha," the form "Magadhe" is used through a transposition of the case ending (*vacanavipallāsa*), just as in expressions such as "paccāsā satī" and so forth.
Or it is stated with the elision of the word *su*. Regarding the phrase "prepared from two *nāḷis* of rice":
here, although the word *nāḷi* refers to Magadha, it forms a compound with the word *dvaya* because it functions as a common noun (*gammakattho*); thus, "two of a *nāḷi*" is *nāḷidvayaṃ*.
In this context, a Magadhan *nāḷi* consists of twelve and a half *palas*. And here they say that twelve and a half *palas* are [the weight of] *māsas*. By means of two *nāḷis*...
"Measured rice" refers to well-husked and purified rice—unblemished, old *sāli* rice consisting of two *nāḷi* measures; "cooked by them" means prepared and boiled with that [rice].
"Boiled rice" (*odana*) means rice that has been properly prepared and drained. "Soup" (*sūpa*) is measured at one-fourth the amount of the rice;
it should be neither too thick nor too thin, easily taken up by the hand, and composed of all its necessary ingredients.

"Muggasūpaṃ" (mung bean soup). "And sauce that is suitable for it" means he takes an abundant amount of sauce—such as fish, meat, and so forth—that is suitable (*upiya*) or appropriate for that rice, sufficient even for the very last morsel;
this is the connection. 62. "Of that" refers to the aforementioned rice and so forth.
"Half-full" (*upaḍḍha*): it is called "half-full" because it possesses half a *nāḷika* measure of rice and so forth.
By the word *eva* (only), he excludes anything additional. "From that" means from the aforementioned *nāḷika*-measure of boiled rice and so forth.
The construction is: "the large-large and the small-small are not [permissible] bowls. "The small-small" refers to that which is smaller than the small.

By this further demonstration of two types of bowls, he illustrates that although there are three bowls by measure, they become nine when divided by their sub-classifications. Among these, in that [measure] where the boiled rice and so forth of two Magadhan *nāḷis* [fit],...
If everything placed on the side for enlargement remains level with the lower rim of the bowl’s mouth,
or if, when cutting it with thread or a saw, the bottom edge of the thread or the saw touches [the rim],
this is called an "excellent" (ukkaṭṭha) bowl. If it stands protruding beyond that rim, this is an "excellent-inferior" (ukkaṭṭhomaka) bowl.
This is called the "attained" (patta). If it does not reach the upper rim (*rājī*) but remains entirely within it, this is called the "exceedingly superior" (*ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭha*) bowl.

"When even a single *nāḷika* of rice and so forth, when placed inside, stands level with the lower rim according to the method already described, this is called the 'middling' (*majjhima*) bowl"—and so on, [defining] the middling-middling, middling-inferior, and middling-superior [sizes]. "In which [bowl] half a *nāḷika* of rice and so forth..."
"Even when all [the sand] is thrown in, it remains level with the lower line; this is called the 'inferior' bowl," and so forth.

By this method, the bowls that are inferior, more inferior, and most inferior should be understood in the same way as the superior ones were described above. Among these, two are not valid bowls (*apatta*);
they may be used for holding food, but they are not fit for formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) nor for assignment (*vikappana*).
63. The construction is: "One may keep a permissible (kappa) and one's own (saka) extra bowl for a maximum of ten days. In this context, *kappa* means "permissible.

*Saka* means "belonging to oneself. Because they are permissible and because they belong to oneself, it should be understood that all seven [types of bowls] are subject to the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and the assignment (*vikappa*).
Among these, an iron bowl is suitable for determination after being fired five times, while a clay bowl is suitable for determination after being fired twice.

And it should be understood that both [the bowl and the robe] are subject to formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and assignment (*vikappana*) when they are given away without leaving even a single *kākaṇika*’s worth of their original value remaining, and when they are fully recognized as having become the property of another.
Furthermore, regarding the "extra bowl" (*atirekapatta*), it is so called because it has not been formally determined or assigned;
however, the procedures for formal determination and relinquishment (*paccuddhāra*) here are exactly the same as those stated for the robe (*cīvara*).
However, the one making the assignment (vikappana) should ascertain whether the bowls are one or many, and whether they are present or absent;
having done so, he should say either "this bowl" or "these bowls," or "that bowl" or "those bowls," and then say, "I assign this to you.

The distinctions such as "in the presence of" (sammukhā) and so forth should be understood here according to the method that will be explained regarding the robe (cīvara). "At most ten days" (dasāhaparamaṃ): [the rest follows].
"Having ten days as its maximum limit" means a period for which ten days is the highest limit; this is the accusative case used in the sense of absolute connection (*accantasaṃyoga*).
"Should be kept" means it should be kept by way of use. The construction is: "When that time has elapsed, the bowl becomes subject to relinquishment.
"Elapsed" means having passed; it becomes subject to relinquishment upon the rising of the sun on the eleventh day, or [if not returned] to the Saṅgha.
The bowl must be relinquished according to the method stated in the *padabhājanīya* for either a community (*gaṇa*) or an individual (*puggala*);
the intention is that when this is done, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for him.

64. As for the phrase beginning with “by cutting,” it is self-evident because the method is the same as that stated regarding robes. However, this is the distinction: [the bowls] are designated by death.
*Uddharaṇaṃ* means *uddhaḷaṃ*, which is *paccuddhāra* (renunciation). *Maraṇañca uddhaṭañca* means death and renunciation; therefore, it is *maraṇuddhaṭā*.
"With a hole" means with a hole two finger-breadths wide below the rim of the mouth, through which broken rice grains (*kaṅgusittha*) both enter and exit.
"He abandons the determination regarding the bowl" means he abandons—that is, relinquishes—the determination concerning the bowl.
65. Now, by the words beginning with "the bowl" (*patta*), he shows that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in handling it otherwise.
Therein, the construction is: "one should not put away the bowl while it still contains water. "One should not put away" means one should not place it in a secure location;

and this should also be construed with the passage beginning, "one should not dry the bowl while it still contains water in the heat," and so forth. "One should not dry" means one should not even slightly warm it. "One should not hide" [means...]
Even if one makes it waterless, one should not burn it excessively; even if one makes it watery, one should heat it only slightly—this is the meaning of the contrast.
One does not place it on the ground; one should not place it on hard ground.
However, on such ground as has been plastered with clay where the color does not spoil, or on similar sand, having turned it upside down and then righted it again...
It is permissible to set it down. However, one must not hang it; that is, one should not suspend it from walls, pillars, or similar supports.
Having stated "or at the edge of a drip-ledge" and so forth, it should be connected thus: "it is not allowable to set the bowl down.
"At the edge of a drip-ledge" means at the edge of drip-ledges such as those on porches or eaves. But if, having been turned over, it settles back into place right there, [it is permissible].
It is permissible to place [the bowl] upon such an extensive support. "Or on the edge of the rim" means on the edge of a thin support made on the outer side.
Here, the word *vā* (or) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), and it should be applied to each item.
Furthermore, it is permissible to place it on the shoulder [of a person] by fastening it to the shoulder-blade with a shoulder-strap. Regarding the umbrella, with the equipment...
It is permissible to place [the bowl] either by tying it together with another or by making a stand for it.
It is also permissible to place a bench by tying it together with another, or to hang it from a peg. 67.
“One should not carry away used water or scraps of food with the bowl” is the connection. Regarding “used water”:
Water for rinsing the mouth; fish bones and meat bones with the flesh already stripped away, and bones with the flesh still attached;

using the bowl as a receptacle to wash one’s hands, or pouring water into the bowl to carry it out after washing, or taking hold of the clean bowl with a hand that has been used for eating (and is thus soiled).
It is not permitted. When eating fish, meat, fruits, or other such foods, if one wishes to discard any bone or core therein, one is not allowed to place it in the bowl.
Furthermore, whatever has been removed from the mouth with the intention of not eating it again is not allowed to be placed back in the bowl.
However, after biting into ginger or similar items, one is permitted to set them aside. "With bowl in hand" means...
The analysis of the compound is: "one whose bowl is in the hand" (*pattahattha*). Furthermore, the phrase "bowl-in-hand, like a door-panel" (*pattahattho, kavāṭan*) is merely an illustration.

For wherever there is a bowl on any part of the body, one is not permitted to push open a door-panel with any part of the body, nor to lift a bolt, nor to open a latch with a key. However, if the bowl is on the shoulder...
Having fastened it, one is able to open it at one’s convenience.
68. A floor-stand is that which is connected to the ground; a ring-stand made from ivory, creepers, rattan, or the like;
a wooden stand made from a single piece of wood; and a staff-stand made from many sticks—wherever [the bowl] is placed upon these...
The construction of the words is as follows: "one should place two such bowls upon that bowl which has been well-fastened so that, when turned over, it does not fall.
However, a wooden stand resembling the end of a lathe, bound with three sticks, or a stick-stand, is not a suitable place for even a single bowl; even if one were to place [the bowl] there—

Having taken it with the hand, one should sit down. Regarding "on the ground": the construction is that one should place a single bowl on the ground covered by a mat of grass or similar material, either turned upside down or turned right-side up. 69.
Now he shows the improper bowls with the words beginning "wood" (*dāru*). In this context, *sovaṇṇa* means simply gold. *Dāru*...
And silver, gold, gems (*maṇi*), beryl (*veḷuriya*), wood... [etc. ...beryls; that which is produced from these is "made of wood" ... [etc. ... "made of beryl.
However, the term "made of beryl" (*veḷuriyamayā*) was used in the long version for the sake of metrical ease in the verse composition.
One should understand similar cases in the subsequent sections as well. In this context, "gems" refers to indranīla and others. Brass, glass, tin, lead, and crystal—

“Copper and bronze” is a *dvanda* compound; [the objects] produced from these are brass (*kaṃsa*)... [and so on] ... produced from them. Therein, by the word “brass,” round iron is also included. White is tin, black is lead. 70.
“Made of human skull” means the head—the skull—of a corpse, that is, a dead person; what is produced from that is “made of human skull.”

"Ghaṭī" means a water-pot; "tumba" means a gourd; "kaṭāha" refers to their basins. Thus, they are called "born of pots and gourds" (*ghaṭitumbakaṭāhajā*). In this context, the construction is as follows:
all these bowls are stated to be unallowable (*akappiya*), and they are also stated to be grounds for an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭavatthu*).
In that regard, if among the four items such as gold and so forth, a householder prepares a curry in golden trays and the like at the meal-grounds (*bhattagga*), [and offers it].
If they offer them, it is not permissible to touch them. However, vessels such as trays made of bronze, glass, or crystal are not permitted for personal use;
they are permitted for communal use by the Saṅgha, or if they are gifts from householders.
But having obtained vessels such as jars or basins that have been fashioned, it is not permissible to keep them permanently; they may be used only temporarily.
The commentary on the description of bowls is finished.
6. Commentary on the Description of Basins (Thālaka-niddesa). 71–2.
Basins made of wood … [and so on] … or of beryl are unallowable; basins made of crystal, glass, or bronze that belong to householders or to the Saṅgha [are also unallowable].

"And they are allowable" (*kappiyā*); the connection is that those made from gourds or jars are "allowable for a limited time" (*tāvakālikā kappiyā*). They are called *kappā* because they are deemed suitable (*parikappanti*) precisely by way of being non-conflicting;
likewise, they are *kappiyā*. Those which are not *kappā* are *akappā*. These belong to the Saṅgha, thus they are "belonging to the Saṅgha" (*saṅghikā*). The word *tāva* indicates a limit.
They are "for a limited time" (*tāvakālikā*) because their duration is limited to the time of eating; the intention is that they are to be discarded after being eaten and must not be kept.
The commentary on the explanation of *thālaka* is finished.
7. Commentary on the explanation of *pavāraṇā*.
73. By whatever posture he is characterized, while eating any kind of food among the five kinds of food...

The construction of the words is as follows: "If this bhikkhu, having been invited [to eat] of the five kinds of permissible foods brought within arm's reach, should eat—while not being *atiritta* (leftover)—any *yāvakālika* (food for the day) by means of a posture other than the one from which he was invited, there is an offense of *pācittiya* for him.
However, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa* in the act of accepting it for the purpose of eating. In that context, *iriyā* refers to physical activity.
The "path" (*patha*) is the means for proceeding, namely the postures (*iriyāpatha*): standing, walking, sitting, and lying down.

One who "invites" (*pavāreti*) [food] and then "refuses" (*paṭikkhipati*) is called "one who has been invited" (*pavārito*). Alternatively, the invitation itself—the act of refusing—is "the invitation" (*pavārita*); one who possesses that is "one who has been invited. The meaning is: one who has performed the invitation and performed the refusal.
Alternatively, one is "invited" (*pavārito*) by the server, meaning one is offered [food] and then refused [if one does not wish to take more]. "Not leftover" (*anatirittaka*)...

That which has been made permissible by means of the seven modes of formal disciplinary acts (vinayakamma), such as the declaration of "enough, this is all" when rising from one's seat after having performed the invitation (pavāraṇā);
that which is brought forth with the thought, "I will eat it today or whenever I wish";
and the leavings of one who is ill—these are called "leftover" (atiritta) or "extra" (adhika). Other than these is what is "not leftover" (anatirittaka) or "not extra" (anadhika).

The meaning is as follows: it causes a wholesome mind to fall away, thus it is *pācitti*; therefore, when the letter *t* in the word *itthi* becomes *c*, and there is doubling [of the consonant], it is *pācitti*.

For one who accepts food for the purpose of nourishment that is to be taken within a watch (*yāmakālika*), within seven days (*sattāhakālika*), or for life-long use (*yāvajīvika*), there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
for every swallow, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
74. Now, in order to show that the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) by which one is invited is indeed called an invitation only when it is endowed with five factors, he said "eating" (*āsana*), and so forth.
Therein, "eating" (*āsana*) is the act of eating for one who is eating. By this, he shows that food which has been partially consumed.
"And the food itself" means that it is indeed food sufficient for an invitation. "Bringing" (*abhihāro*) refers to [the gift] by the body of the donor.
The bringing [of the invitation] is by means of physical delivery, not by word alone. "In the vicinity" refers to the vicinity measured at two and a half cubits.
In this regard, if the monk is sitting, it is from the rear edge of his seat;
if he is standing, from the edge of his heels; if he is lying down, from the far edge of the side on which he lies.
Starting from the donor— whether standing, sitting, or lying down—
one should understand the "three-and-a-half-cubit range" as being delimited by the near side of whichever limb is closest, excluding the outstretched hand.
"Rejection by body or speech" means [rejection] of that food brought forward either by a bodily gesture such as moving a finger, or by saying "Enough," and so forth.

Or the refusal by means of a verbal modification. Thus, the connection is: "the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) is a fivefold invitation (*pañcaaṅga-pakāravāraṇā*)," meaning it possesses five factors (*pañca-aṅgāni*). That which has five factors is "fivefold" (*pañcaaṅgā*). 75.
