Now, having shown the five kinds of food beginning with rice among these, and in order to show them again by way of analysis:
The passage beginning with “rice” (*odana*) is commenced. Therein, “*sālī*” refers to the entire genus of *sāli* rice, including red *sāli* and so forth.
“*Vīhī*” refers to the entire genus of grain named *vīhi*. “*Kaṅgū*” refers to the entire genus of *kaṅgu*, distinguished as white, red, and black.
“*Kudrūsa*” is black *kodrava*. “*Varaka*” is white-colored *kodrava*. As for barley (*yava*) and wheat (*godhuma*), there is no further subdivision. Thus, of those mentioned above...
The connection is: "boiled rice and boiled rice gruel made from the seven kinds of grains that grow in accordance [with the season]. Regarding "boiled rice gruel" (*bhojjayāgu*):
it is that which leaves a residue in the place where food is taken at the time of eating, whether one is eating hot or cold;

that is boiled rice gruel. By the word *ca* ("and"), the connection is "and boiled rice" (*odano ca*); the meaning is "that which is called boiled rice. However, if water, sour gruel, milk, and so forth are [added] to the meal...
If they pour it out and give it saying, “Take the gruel,” even though it is thin, it generates an invitation (*pavāraṇa*).
But if they put it into water or other liquids, cook it, and then give it, it is included within the category of gruel.
Furthermore, if even a tiny piece of fish or meat, or a strand of sinew, as small as a mustard seed, has been placed into the thin gruel, it generates an invitation.
76. The construction is as follows: *sāmākāditiṇaṃ* (the grass beginning with *sāmāka*) is included within *kudrūsaka*; *varakacoraka* is included within *varaka*;
and *nīvāra* is included within *sāli*. Regarding *sāmākāditiṇaṃ*: it is a compound meaning "that very grass which has *sāmāka* as its first [member]," i.e., "grass-corn."
77. *Bhaṭṭhadhaññamayo*: this means made from seven kinds of grain that have been parched until they are hard and then ground;

even the mere flour or the husks are called "sattu" (grain meal). However, they do not allow [the consumption of] either the meal or the husks of rice grains that have been roasted evenly or dried in the sun. That which has its origin or production (*sambhava*) in barley (*yava*) is [called *yavasa*].
That which originates from grain is *kummāsa*; this is what is called *kummāsa*. However, that made from mung beans and the like does not produce satisfaction (*pavāraṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "and it is allowable" (*kappiyo ca*): the construction is that even meat which is indeed allowable is referred to by the word "meat. The particle *ca* is used for emphasis. But that which is unallowable must certainly be rejected.
Even if rejected, it does not satisfy. That which has its origin in water is called "fish. Now, regarding these two [cases]: if...
If, while drinking rice gruel, even a single grain of rice or a single piece of fish or meat has been eaten and remains either in the hand or in the bowl,
and he then refuses further food, he has invited [the host to stop].
Even if two have been eaten and not even a mustard-seed’s worth remains in the mouth, if he still refuses further food, he has not invited [the host to stop].
78. Now, keeping in mind the objection, “In what manner eating, and having said what, does one ‘invite’ (pavāreti) while prohibiting what has been brought forward?

he says, beginning with “Eating,” etc. Therein, a bhikkhu who is eating any kind of food among the five types of edible foods—whether it be allowable (kappa) or unallowable (akappa)—[is speaking] by that name, namely, by the name of those foods which generate the invitation.

Or, having spoken generally with the word "this," one should invite [the guest] while repeatedly refusing that which has been brought and placed within arm's reach—namely, the permissible and allowable food mentioned above;

such is the connection between the words. This is the intended meaning here: by whomsoever [the food is brought], even if it includes unallowable meat, or is obtained through corrupting families, medical practice, or claiming superhuman qualities, or acquired through money and so forth...
If food that has been prepared— which may be either unallowable or otherwise allowable—
is swallowed even in the amount of a single grain of rice, and while there is still food remaining in the bowl, mouth, or hands, he, being still intent on it,
invites another person standing within arm’s reach by name or by a designation sufficient for an invitation, such as "Take some rice," and so forth; [he commits an offense].

"‘This’ means that one rejects or refuses—either by body or by speech—a meal that has been brought specifically for oneself, which possesses the aforementioned characteristics and is exclusively or partially permissible; this applies whether it is mixed or unmixed.
However, it is permissible to say: ‘Sprinkle! Sprinkle! Grind! Grind! Fill it up!’"
79–80. Now, in order to show those things that do not generate the invitation (*pavāraṇā*), he says “fried grains,” and so forth.
Therein, the connection is: “fried grains... fruits, etc., do not generate the invitation. “Fried grains” (*lāja*) refers to fried grains made from rice and other such crops.

“Flour and cooked rice made from them” (*taṃsattubhattāni*) means both the flour and the cooked rice made from those fried grains. “Milk product” (*gorasa*) means the milk and so forth that is the product of cows. “Plain snack food” (*suddhakhajjaka*)—

“Pure dry food” (*suddhakhajjaka*) refers to that which is not mixed with fish or meat. As for “sesame balls” (*sattuguḷa*), these are made by kneading sesame seeds and, while still uncooked, they are offered under the designation of “sesame cakes” (*sattumodaka*).
“Rice grains” (*taṇḍula*) refers to the grains of *sāli* rice and so forth when roasted to an even degree;
or it may refer simply to roasted grains. “Roasted flour” (*bhaṭṭhapiṭṭha*) is any pure flour that has been roasted. “Puffed grains” (*puthuka*)...
The *puthuka* (unhusked grain) of rice and so forth. For the term *puthuka* is understood both separately and collectively according to the logic of the textual tradition (*tanti-āgama-yutti*).
Therefore, it is connected as "the meal consisting of the remaining items mentioned, such as *puthuka*, bamboo [grain], and so on. By "bamboo" (*veḷu*), their grains are meant. The compound is:
"those for which *puthuka* and bamboo are the firsts. Furthermore, the word "and" (*ca*) should be applied here in every instance.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), bulbs, roots, and fruits are also included. Regarding the phrase "of those remaining from what has been mentioned": it refers to those remaining after the seven kinds of grain already stated.

"Savoury gruel" (*rasayāgu*) is gruel mixed with savours such as cooked meat and so forth; the savour itself is of the same nature. "Plain gruel" (*suddhayāgu*) is pure gruel unmixed with meat and the like.
Regarding "fruits, etc.," by the word "etc.," bulbs and so forth are also included. Furthermore (*api ca*):
The particle, or a combination of particles, is used in the sense of conjunction; it should be applied to each [term] individually.

81. Now, since an offense of expiation (pācittiya) is stated for that which is left over and not made *atiritta* (rendered permissible by the formal act) through the seven modes of disciplinary action (*vinayakamma*), whereas there is no such offense when it is made *atiritta*, therefore, one who makes something *atiritta* should do so in this manner.

He spoke the words beginning with “by one who has finished his meal” (*pavāritena*) in order to show this. Therein, the connection is as follows: having risen after finishing his meal, one must not make [food] leftover;
and one must not make food leftover without having eaten. "Food" (*bhojana*) here refers to food sufficient for a formal invitation (*pavāraṇa*).

"Without having eaten" (*abhuttena*) means by one who has not consumed even a single grain of rice. Regarding the phrase "whatever was previously made by whom," the word *eva* (indeed/only) is used here.
It is indicated with a long vowel, and it is connected with the word *taṃ* brought forward from the previous context; therefore, the meaning should be understood by construing it thus:
"That very monk by whom that very food was previously made *atiritta* (leftover) must not make that same thing *atiritta* again.
Therefore, when one who has had it made permissible (*kappiya*) is eating, if they pour other food over it, he—
One may not do it again; for while that food is being prepared, it is considered as having been prepared together with the first portion already made.
However, it is permissible to have it prepared by him or by someone else at another time.
82. The words beginning with “kappiyaṃ” (suitable) are the objects of the verb “karonto” (making). [It must be] suitable, taken, and announced.
The construction is as follows: "Let him speak thus: 'This is sufficient for all,' while making both what is within hand's reach and what is of the proper time into leftover food.

In this context, whatever fruit or root-crops and so forth have been made allowable by the five monastic rules (samaṇakappa), and whatever allowable meat or allowable food there is—this is called "allowable" (kappiya). It has been taken by the bhikkhu.

"Accepted. "Uttered" means that when a monk who has come to have [the food] made allowable (kappiya) has lifted it up even slightly or moved it aside, that must be done by the one making it leftover (atiritta), saying, "Enough of all this.
"Within arm's reach" means that it has come within arm's reach of the one who has come to have it made allowable. "Making it leftover" means [making it] endowed with these four modes.

A monk who has perfected the sevenfold manner of performing formal acts of the Vinaya (*vinayakamma*) is one who, when making food leftover, either rises from his seat after having invited others to stop eating (*pavāretvā*), or—even without having invited them—has finished eating in every respect.
"Let him speak thus: 'Enough, all is sufficient,'" means: let him speak, "Enough, all is sufficient.
Thus, while accomplishing this sevenfold manner of performing formal acts of the Vinaya, he makes a vocal utterance.
The meaning is: having done so, one might say this even once. 83.
However, when making something allowable (*kappiya*), it must not be placed in the hand of one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*). Therefore he said: "One should not... [etc. ...in the hand.
One who is other than the fully ordained is "not fully ordained"; that which has gone into his hand is "gone into the hand of one not fully ordained" (*anupasampannahatthaga*).
"Even having sent [the food]," means: if there is no other competent monk (*bhikkhu*) there, then even after having sent it to where such a one exists.

"One who has not made it *atiritta* (leftover)"—this should be connected as follows: everyone other than the one who made it *atiritta*, whether they have already finished eating (*pavārita*) or have not yet finished eating, is permitted to eat it.
However, one who has finished eating must eat it after having cleansed both the mouth and the hands.
The commentary on the exposition of the *pavāraṇā* is finished.
8. Commentary on the Exposition of the Timely (*kālika*): 84.
"Timely" means that these possess a time characterized by occurrence at midday, during the last watch of the night, for seven days, or for as long as life lasts.
"Kālika" refers to all things comprised within the categories of what is to be chewed, eaten, licked, and drunk.

These, however, are four in number according to their numerical limit. One might ask: "Do these receive the designation 'kālika' by their very nature even when not formally accepted, or is it otherwise?

To this he says: "Accepted. Only when they have been accepted do they receive the designation of "kālika," such as "yāvakālika" (to be used until the end of the day) and so forth; it is not otherwise.
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). He now demonstrates it by means of the passage beginning with "that which is for the time being" (*yāvakālika*).

In this context, because it must be consumed from sunrise until the time of midday has passed, it is "for the time being" (*yāvakālika*)—meaning that its duration is the period up to midday—referring to such substances as flour-based foods (*piṭṭhakhādanīya*).
From the moment midday has passed, it is no longer possible to consume it; thus, [the term is used] for the purpose of knowing the limit of the permitted time.
Either it should be combined with the time-staff, or the meal-duty should be performed at another time.
Because it may be consumed until the watch that is reckoned as the last watch of the night, it has "watch-time" (*yāmaka*) as its time; thus it is *yāmakālika*.
Because it may be stored for seven days after being received, it has "seven-day-time" (*sattāhaka*) as its time; thus it is *sattāhakālika*. With the exception of water, all the remainder—
Because it is to be used when there is a need after having been accepted and kept for as long as life lasts,
it is called *yāvajīvika* (lifelong) because that which has the limit of "as long as life" (*yāvajīva*) belongs to it.
But surely, since— as elsewhere— there is no mention of time here in the term "*yāvajīvika*," how can it be said that "there are four types of [medicines] according to time"?

Is it appropriate [to say this]? It is appropriate; because for the followers of the Sugata there is no time existing apart from the aggregates, and since the life-faculty (jīvitindriya)—which is designated as "life" (jīva)—is included within the aggregates, that too is simply time.

But is it not the case that those things indicated by the phrase "as long as time lasts" (*yāvakālika*) and so forth are called "time-bound" (*kālika*), and thus one should have said "kālikāni"? This is not to be understood in that way.
The terms beginning with "kālika" are stated in connection with the substance (*vatthu*), whereas "kālikā" is stated in connection with the word *attha* by way of a different grammatical gender;
thus, there is no contradiction. 85.

Now, among those [categories], he shows what is "for as long as life lasts" (*yāvakālika*) by means of the passage beginning with "flour" (*piṭṭha*). Therein, "flour," "root," and "fruit" [are examples].
There are flour-based foods, root-based foods, and fruit-based foods. Among these, the flour of the seven grains, the grain-like vegetables,
and the flours of the breadfruit (*panasa*), jackfruit (*labuja*), mango (*ambāṭaka*), and the washed *tāla* palm, etc.—
according to the natural dietary habits of people in various regions— fulfills the function of food and sustenance for human beings.
“Flour” (*piṭṭha*) refers to flour for solid food (*piṭṭhakhādanīya*). There is no end to the enumeration when counting those such as “unwashed palm-flour,” “flour of milk-creeper,” and so forth;
however, their defining characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) is simply their capacity to fulfill the function of solid food or soft food.
Even if one were to speak at great length, one must remain within this very definition, and thus we do not elaborate further. This applies in all cases.

Roots such as *tambaka* and *taṇḍuleyya* are edible roots (*mūlakhādanīya*). Fruits such as the jackfruit (*panasa*), breadfruit (*labuja*), and coconut (*nāḷikera*) are edible fruits (*phalakhādanīya*).
Edible food made from the primary grains (*pubbaṇṇa*) and secondary grains (*aparaṇṇa*), such as *sakkhali* and sweetmeats (*modaka*), is also edible food (*khādanīya*).

Cow’s milk refers to the products of cows known as milk, curd, and buttermilk (*gorasa*). Grain-food refers to the food consisting of rice, barley, millet, and so forth, specifically that which is designated as boiled rice (*odana*), roasted grain flour (*sattu*), and gruel (*kummāsa*).
In the *Ṭīkā*, however, it is stated: "The seven grains together with their by-products and the five kinds of food";
this is not correct, because there is no purpose for mentioning the grains separately, and even if there were a purpose, they could have been included simply by mentioning the fruits themselves.

"Consisting of gruel, soup, and so forth" (*yāgusūpappabhūtaya*) means those for whom gruel and soup are the beginning; the connection is that these are "things to be taken at the proper time" (*yāvakālika*).

And here, by the word "and so forth" (*pabhuti*), there is included food other than grain-based meals—namely, fish and meat—as well as bulbous roots, fruits, and edible roots such as lotus stalks, which are distinct from flour, roots, and fruits.

He includes them. Among these, the bulbous roots such as the *bhiśa* (water-lily) and so forth, and the round tubers such as the *utpala* (blue lotus) stalk and so forth, constitute the edible tubers (*kanda-khādanīya*).
The roots of the *paduma* (lotus) and so forth, as well as similar ones like the roots of the *eraka* grass and so forth, constitute the edible rhizomes (*muḷāla-khādanīya*).

The tops of the *tāla* palm and other trees, known as *kaḷīra*, constitute the edible tops (*matthaka-khādanīya*). The trunks of sugarcane and so forth, and the stalks of blue lotuses and so forth, constitute the edible stems (*khandha-khādanīya*).
The leaf-soft-food consists of the leaves of the *tambaka*, *taṇḍuleyya*, and so forth; the bark-soft-food consists of the single flavor of sugarcane bark;
the flower-soft-food consists of the flowers of the *tambaka*, *siggū*, and so forth; the bone-soft-food consists of the seeds of the *labuja* and the seeds of the *panasa*, and so forth.
(86) By the words beginning with "honey" (*madhu*), he shows what is permissible for a watch of the night (*yāmakālika*). Honey, grapes, lotus-root, *coca*, and *moca*—

“*Amba* and *jambu*” form a *dvanda* compound. The word *muddikā* is used in the feminine when referring to the fruit; the remaining [words for fruits] are in the neuter. The word “*jambu*” is a neuter term denoting the fruit.
That which is produced from it—such as honey-drinks and so forth—is called *madhu*...
pe ... *jambuja*. The construction is: “*phārusañca pānakaṃ*” (and the drink made from *phārusa*). Therein, the drink called *madhuja* is the natural juice of *muddikā* fruits mixed with water.
"Having made it, having prepared the drink. This refers to a drink prepared by oneself before the meal; it is permissible whether it contains meat or is meatless.

However, if one receives a drink prepared by those who are not fully ordained (anupasampanna) and accepts it before the meal, it is permissible whether it contains meat or is meatless; but after the meal, only that which is meatless is permissible.
This same principle applies to all drinks. A "drink made from grapes" means [a drink] of grapes...
This refers to what has been crushed in water and drunk. In the same way, the remaining drinks should be understood according to their respective natures:
*sālūka* is the root-stock of the red lotus (*rattuppalādi*) and other such plants; *coca* is the seeded plantain fruit; *moca* is the seedless [plantain].
These eight drinks are permissible whether they are cold or ripened by the sun, but those ripened by fire are not permissible. Therefore he said: "not heated by fire."
As for the remaining minor fruit drinks—such as those made from vetta, tintiṇika, mātuluṅga, kapittha, karamanda, and so forth—they fall under the same category as the eight [types of] drinks.
Therefore, he said: “Grains together with their derivatives, excluding the juice produced from fruits.

Furthermore, regarding one [type of drink] and those to be mentioned later, such as “flower juice” and so forth, it is said: “Whether it be boiled by the sun after being crushed while cold, it is to be consumed within a watch of the night (yāmakālika).”

The connection should be understood as follows: the nine great fruits—namely, the palm, coconut, plantain, breadfruit, bottle-gourd, pumpkin, squash, pigeon pea, and elephant foot yam—and all other non-grains follow the seven grains; thus, they are "with their followers" (*sānuloma*).
The taste of these grains and their followers is "for the time being" (*yāvakālika*). The term "grains with their followers" refers to the fruits.
They are understood. In the *Phalasuttaya*, although it should have been stated as “born from the remaining fruits,” it was not mentioned because it is already implied.

“Except for the *madhuka* flower” means setting aside the *madhuka* flower. “The juice born of ripe *ḍāka* vegetables” means the juice produced from ripe *ḍāka* vegetables that are fit for immediate consumption (*yāvakālika*).
“Cold water” is *sītoda*; “ground in cold water like [in] the milk-ocean” is a *tappurisa* compound. The word “Ādicca” refers to sunlight.
The compound *vattati upacārato* means "that in which cooking occurs by way of proximity" (*ādicce pāko yassa*). 89.

He shows what is permissible for seven days (*sattāhakālika*) with the words beginning "ghee" (*sappī*). Therein, "permissible for seven days" refers to ghee and the other items mentioned above as being permissible for seven days.
Now he analyzes ghee and the others with the words beginning "ghee. Therein, those [products] of cows and buffaloes...
The meat of animals that are permitted is allowable; regarding them, [the text] states the definition of ghee with the words "ghee, ghee by name," and so forth.

Since it will be explained later that even for ghee made from the meat of unallowable animals, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) if seven days have passed when an allowable substance is available, the phrase "the meat of which is not prohibited" is stated here specifically to show the object subject to relinquishment (*nissaggiya-vatthu*). For, among milk and the other [liquids],...
For them, there is nothing called "unallowable" (akappiya). Because fresh butter is similar to ghee, its specific characteristics have not been stated separately.
When they place a lump of ghee on top and serve cool rice porridge, that portion which is unmixed with the porridge is "seven-day permissible" (sattāhakālika);
however, when it is mixed, it must be cooked in the sun and strained, and likewise after adding milk.
Regarding "cooked oil" (*pakkatelam*): among those, "fresh butter" (*navanītam*) is that which has been recently extracted; "clarified butter" (*sappi*) is that made from it. 90.
"Sesame, fat, castor seeds, madhuka, and mustard"—this is a *dvanda* compound. Its external meaning is "that which originates from these," which is the sense of "oil" (*telam*).
"Small" refers to small honey-bees and bees; "small bee" (*khuddabhamaram*) is the small bee and the bee together.
The singular neuter form is used because it refers to a small creature (*khuddajantu*). "Honey-makers" (*madhukariyo*) means those who make honey;
they are bees, thus "honey-making bees" (*madhukarimakkhikā*). This is a *kammadhāraya* compound meaning "the small bee itself is the honey-making bee.
The meaning is that the honey made by them is called "honey" (*madhu*). In the commentary (*ṭīkā*), however, the word *madhukarī* is treated separately [as follows]: "In the stalks..."
It is said: "The *madhukara* is the bee known as the honey-bee.

Whether it be a honeycomb or honey-dregs, if they are smeared with honey, they belong to the same category as honey. However, the honey resembling resin from *tumbalaka* trees and *cīrika* trees is permissible for life (*yāvajīvika*).
"Rasādi" means that which has juice (*rasa*) as its first [ingredient]. By the word "ādi," molasses (*phāṇita*) and so forth are included.
That is a preparation of sugarcane. "Cooked" means either cooked without a base (solid substance), or it means molasses; such is the meaning.
However, molasses made from madhuka flowers with cold water falls under the same category as molasses. Mango-molasses and the like are "to be used only during the day.
These aforementioned items, such as ghee and so forth, may be used even with solid food before the meal, but from after the meal onwards—
However, those [medicines] received after the meal must be stored for seven days and then consumed without being treated as a non-meat (nirāmisaparibhoga) food.

Now, having shown the distinction regarding what is permitted specifically by way of what has been cooked, he says "savatthu" and so forth in order to show [the distinction] regarding ghee and the other [medicines].
Therein, "before the meal" means either by oneself (*sāmaṃ*), that is, by one's own self; by the word "or" (*vā*), it is implied that it may also be [received] from others.
"Non-human" means devoid of human fat. "Fat" refers to the fat of non-permissible animals such as bears and the like, and the fat of permissible animals such as pigs and the like.
"Cooked with its own base" means it is cooked having been made into a base; this is the intended meaning here: if, however, one has received the fat before midday and then cooked it...
Oil that has been strained may be used for seven days, provided it is used without meat.
Furthermore, if it was prepared by others and accepted before midday, it is permissible even with meat before midday; from after midday onwards, however, it must be used only without meat.
Otherwise, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Moreover, here, by the metaphorical application of the cause to the effect, "fat" refers specifically to oil.
It has been stated [that fat is] "only for the duration of a day" (*yāvakālika*).

However, in the *Ṭīkā*, after stating, "There is no place where fat is mentioned as being for seven days," it says, "That must be examined," thereby expressing doubt regarding whether fat is indeed for seven days.
What is there to be examined here? By the one who authorized medicine...
The Blessed One stated that only ghee and the other medicines are to be used for a period of seven days, saying:

"Whatever medicinal requisites are to be consumed by sick bhikkhus—namely, ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses—having accepted them, they may be used after being stored for a maximum of seven days.
This is also stated in the *Bhesajjakkhandhaka*.
“I allow you, monks, having accepted those five medicines, to consume them both at the proper time and at the improper time.
Having thus spoken of those very five as “medicines,” he specifically permitted oil, saying:
“I allow you, monks, the medicinal fats—namely, bear fat, fish fat, porpoise fat, pig fat, and donkey fat—if received at the proper time, [to be used] at the proper time.”
It is said: "When it has been processed at the proper time and mixed, it may be used for the consumption of oil.

And in the commentary on the Medicinal Substances Training Rule (*Bhesajja-sikkhāpada-aṭṭhakathā*), after showing the regulations for fat-oil (*vasātela*) with the words, "any kind of fat except that which is under human control," the commentator (*aṭṭhakathācariya*) states:
"It is certainly not permitted to cook the substance for other things that are to be consumed only during the day (*yāvakālika*)."

The meaning explained here is that, having set aside the case of those things that are *yāvakālika* (to be used during the day), it is not permissible to cook the substance of other *yāvakālika* substances;
thus, by this [rule], it is understood that "only those which are *yāvakālika*" are meant. What is the subtle principle here?
[It is this: from among other fats and oils, regarding those specific *yāvakālika* substances—such as ghee (*sappi*) and so forth—which are *yāvakālika*.
The connection is that one does not cook milk and so forth—which are reckoned as "temporary" (*yāvakālika*)—as the base substance (*vatthu*). This is the intended meaning here:

just as it is permissible to cook at the proper time after having received [milk] during the proper time for the purpose of seven-day consumption, it is not so with milk and the like which serve as the base substance for ghee (*sappi*) and other medicines; for that [base substance], even at the proper time, [is not permissible] for the purpose of seven-day consumption.

It is not allowable. For if those [foods] were made by oneself after receiving them, they are not allowable from after midday onwards because they have been received with a physical basis (*savatthuka-paṭiggahita*);

they are not allowable as "with meat" (*sāmisa*) because they have been prepared by oneself; and they are not allowable even before midday because they have been excluded from the category of "timely foods" (*yāvakālika-vatthu*).
However, if they were made by others, even if they contain meat, they are allowable before midday.

They are permissible because they have been prepared by oneself. However, regarding mustard seeds, madhuka, castor, and bones—which are kept for life—one may accept them for the purpose of making oil;
the oil made on that very day is "seven-day" (sattāhakālika). Oil made on the second day is permissible for six days.
Likewise, up to oil made on the seventh day, it is permissible on that very day. If the dawn has risen, it becomes an offense of forfeiture (nissaggiya) on the eighth day.
On that day, it is as if one has consumed something not fit for consumption; it is equivalent to having taken up anything whatsoever.
For mustard seeds and the like received for the purpose of oil, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) after seven days have passed.

Ghee or butter that has been produced may be accepted either at the proper time or at the improper time, and it is permissible to cook it. However, even on that very day, before the meal, it is considered "with meat" (*sāmisa*).

It is not permitted; because of the risk of association, even food that is for a limited time (*yāvakālika*) might become food prepared by oneself (*sāmaṃpakka*). However, if it is non-material (*nirāmisa*), it is permitted even for seven days. 92.
Now, with the words beginning "turmeric" (*haliddi*), he shows what is for life-long use (*yāvajīvika*).

Although there might be confusion regarding the synonymous terms being stated therein—such as "turmeric is called *nisā*" and so forth—we shall not cause excessive confusion by means of those specific terms; therefore:
These [terms] are to be understood from the instructional commentary (*upadesa*) itself. In this context, the word "haliddi" (turmeric) is stated with the addition of a nasal vowel (*bindu*).
However, by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), the roots and other parts are expressed by the words "turmeric" and so forth.

Some of these, such as turmeric, are exclusively feminine in gender. Regarding the phrase "mūlaphale vacattañca…pe… bhaddamuttañca ativisāti," the word division is: *mūla-phale*, *vacattañ-ca*, …pe…, *bhaddamuttañ-ca*, *ativisa-iti*. By the term "five roots" (*pañcamūla*), both the minor five roots (*cūḷapañcamūla*) and the major five roots (*mahāpañcamūla*) are intended.
[These terms] have been taken up. By the word "etc. (ādi), there is an inclusion of such terms as *jaraṭṭha* in the root of the *vajakaḷi* tree, and so forth.
93–5. Regarding the statement that they call it *goṭṭhaphala*, they mean the *madanaphala*. That which contains three fruits is *tiphalā*. By the word "etc.
in *eraṇḍakādīnaṃ*, there is the inclusion of the *jāti* tree and others. [The phrase] *sulasādīnaṃ paṇṇaṃ* means the leaves of the *sulasā* and other plants.

The connection [is as follows]. By the word "etc. (ādi), there is the inclusion of Aśoka and others. "Vegetables for curry" (sūpeyyapaṇṇa) refers to leaves suitable for curries, such as *tambaka* and *taṇḍuleyya*.

"Except for sugarcane juice" (*ucchuniyyāsaṃ ṭhapetvā*) means all juice; and "except for the sap of sugarcane and its bark" (*sarasaṃ ucchujaṃ tacañca ṭhapetvā*) means all bark—this is the connection.
In that context, everything including the juice of *hiṅgu*, *kaṇikāra*, and so forth, is called "all juice" (*sabba-niyyāsa*). "Sapless sugarcane bark, etc. (*nirasa-ucchutacādi*)...
All skin is so called. Salt refers to that from the ocean and so forth. Iron refers to iron, copper, bronze, and so forth.
Stone refers to black stone and so forth. 96. "Plain boiled rice" means not smeared with honey; however, that which is smeared with honey is permitted for seven days.
"Whatever has been well-roasted" means whatever has been roasted properly, rather than poorly roasted. "The various kinds beginning with vikaṭa," etc.
The external meaning is: "that whose variety has as its beginning what is called foul excrement, clay, urine, and dung";

that [is the referent]. The connection is with the phrase "whatever it may be. Here, moreover, by the word "etcetera" (ādi), in the case of bulbous edibles, there are such things as milk-yams and *kākolā*;
in the case of root edibles, such things as turmeric and ginger roots; and in the case of head edibles, such things as turmeric, ginger, and lotus rhizomes.
It should be understood that among the "solid foods" (*khādanīya*), items such as lotus stalks and stems are included; among the "flower foods," items such as *campaka* flowers are included;

among the "seed foods" (*aṭṭhikhādanīya*), items such as the seeds of *madhuka*, castor-oil plant, and mustard are included; and among the "flour foods" (*piṭṭhakhādanīya*), items such as uncleaned palm flour are included. 97.

Now, because it is impossible to describe them all individually, both those mentioned and those not mentioned are stated together in order to demonstrate everything that lasts for life (*yāvajīvika*).
Summarizing these points and establishing the characteristic therein, he says, "The root," and so forth.

In this context, where "essence" (*sāra*) should have been said, he says "essence" (*sāraṃ*) by means of a change of gender; for the *Nighaṇḍu* states: "Essence (*sāra*) [is used] in the sense of strength and firmness.
"Nutritional purpose" (*āhāraṭṭhaṃ*): the meaning or function produced by nutriment is the "nutritional purpose"; that itself is the "nutritional purpose," which is to say, the function of nutriment.

98. Now, with the words beginning “all,” he shows the distinction between what is allowable and what is unallowable among the four [kinds of medicines]. Therein, “all” refers to those that are *kālika* (timely);
their enjoyment is the experience—this is the compound. “At the proper time” means at the forenoon. “Of all” means for one who is ill and for one who is not ill.

“When there is a requisite” means that among the three [types of *kālika*], the *yāmakālika* (afternoon) is permitted when there is a cause such as thirst, and the *sattāhakālika* (seven-day) and *yāvajīvika* (lifetime) are likewise permitted when there is a cause.

The meaning is: "when there is a reason of illness. *Vikāla* means "past the proper time"; in that regard, if one consumes *yāmakālika* (medicines for a watch of the night) for the purpose of food at an improper time, it is an offense.
Furthermore, regarding *sattāhakālika* (seven-day medicines) and *yāvajīvika* (lifetime medicines), even the mere act of receiving them for that purpose constitutes a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing). 99.

*Ubho* (both) refers to *yāvakālika* (medicines for as long as it lasts) and *yāmakālika*. Therein, if *yāvakālika* has passed its own proper time, it is [treated] by the rule on eating at an improper time.
It incurs a *pācittiya* offense; [food] that was kept overnight becomes "past the watch" (*yāmātikkanta*) by virtue of the training rule on storage (*sannidhi-sikkhāpada*).

The connection is that both of these produce both "kept overnight" (*antovuttha*) and "storage" (*sannidhi*). The expression "kept overnight and storage" (*antovutthaṃ sannidhiṃ*) is a designation where the abstract state is emphasized;
the meaning is "the state of being kept overnight and the state of being stored."

100. *Atināmitā* means "having passed. *Pācittiya* means that there is both a forfeiture offense (*nissaggiyapācittiya*) and an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for exceeding seven days according to the training rule on medicines;

this is the meaning. If what belongs to two people has been accepted by one and not yet divided, there is no offense for either of them upon the passing of the seven days, yet it is not permitted to consume it. *Pāḷināruḷhe* means "not having ascended into the Canon" (*pāḷiyaṃ anāruḷhe*).
The connection is: "seven days are spent on ghee and so forth. "Ghee" (sappi) refers to the ghee of humans and others.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), their fresh butter (navanīta), coconut oil and other oils, and honey-phlegm (phāṇita) made with cold water are included. 101.

"Obtained from what has been relinquished" (nissaṭṭhaladdha): it is both that which has been relinquished (nissaṭṭha) by means of a formal act of discipline (vinayakamma) and that which has been obtained (laddha).
"Again, in that same way" means obtained from one who has relinquished it. "Having taken that" is the remainder [of the sentence].

The procedure for relinquishing, however, should be understood according to the method that will be explained later. The phrase "a limb," etc., is merely illustrative; by this, robes such as the saffron-colored cloth that have been smeared with [impurities] are indeed not to be used.
However, physical use by another person is permitted. Regarding the phrase "for a novice for seven days while he is assigning it," here [it says] in the *Ṭīkā*:

The text in the section on offenses states: “If, having recited ‘I assign this ghee to you’ and so forth, taking the names of various individuals and demonstrating the purpose by way of assigning it both in their presence and in their absence, one perceives it as assigned when it has not been assigned, it is a *nissaggiya pācittiya* offense.
[It continues: “If one assigns it to one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*), it becomes his own property.”

Having stated the fault that "one does not relinquish even the acceptance," the absence of ownership in one's own possession regarding the assignment (*vikappana*) to one who is not fully ordained, as well as the relinquishment of acceptance, are stated as the purpose.
Regarding this, we say: in the section on offenses (*āpattivāra*), there is no such canonical text as "if not assigned" (*avikappite*); rather, it says:

"If [a robe] has not been determined (*anadhiṭṭhite*) and one perceives it as determined, it is an offense of expiation with forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*); if it has not been given away (*avissajjite*) and one perceives it as given away..."

Because it has been handed down in the Pāḷi by way of such passages as “it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession” (nissaggiya-pācittiya), the text in the section on non-offenses (anāpatti-vāra) likewise follows that very sequence, appearing as “he resolves it,” “he gives it away,” and so forth.
If this were the case, there ought to be a commentary (aṭṭhakathā) since it would constitute a point requiring explanation;
yet no such commentary is found here. Furthermore, how [could there be an offense] in the act of assigning [an item] to one who is not fully ordained?
One relinquishes formal acceptance because it is not included within the six causes for relinquishing acceptance, such as the renunciation of the training;
therefore, this [relinquishment] is not the meaning here.

We state the meaning here as follows: in the phrase "of one who makes a transfer" (*vikappentassa*), "transfer" (*vikappana*) means "arranging" (*saṃvidahana*), as in the expressions "mental intention" (*cittasaṅkappo*) and so forth.
However, there is merely a difference in the prefixes used in both cases;

therefore, the meaning is that there is no offense for a novice who, within seven days, makes an assignment or an arrangement, generating a perception of relinquishment, a volition of relinquishment, and an intention of relinquishment toward anyone [to whom he gives].
And this has been stated based on the opinion of the Elder Mahāsumma. For it is said:
In explaining the intention behind such Pāli expressions as “with that mind,” etc., [the commentator] says: “Why was this said?
It is for the purpose of showing that there is no offense for one who gives [the food] within the seven days and subsequently receives and consumes it.
However, the Venerable Mahāpaduma Thera said: “This was said for the purpose of showing that there is no offense in consuming [it] after the seven days have elapsed. This [latter view] alone...

Among these, the former interpretation is more excellent. The connection is as follows: for one who has resolved upon ointments and so forth for seven days, there is no offense even if he gives them to another.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it includes anointing ointments and the like. This is the intended meaning here:

there is no offense for one who has resolved upon ghee and so forth, anointing ointments and the like, honey, ointments for wounds, molasses, or house-smoke. "To another" means to one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*).
Or [the offense] of one who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna). 102.
The connection is that "yāvakālika" and so forth, being associated with oneself, cause the state of intimacy (*sabbhāva*) to be grasped.
"State of intimacy" (*sabbhāva*): *sa* means "one's own" (*attano*), and *bhāva* is "state"; thus *sabbhāva*. "Therefore" (*tasmā*): because it is thus, therefore. "Thus declared" (*evamudīritaṃ*).
Thus it is stated: "For one who makes a formal assignment (vikappa), within seven days," and so forth. This is the intended meaning here:

because things that are mixed with oneself—such as those to be used for a limited time (yāvakālika) and others—cause one's own status [to be attributed to them], therefore, when they exceed the seven-day limit, those things to be used for seven days (sattāhakālika) that produce an offense of expiation (pācittiya) cause an offense of expiation even when mixed with oneself; thus, in the case of non-assignment and so forth.
The three statements beginning with “of one who makes a formal assignment” (*vikappentassa*) are stated to illustrate the offense of *pācittiya* from the perspective of its exclusion (*byatirekato*).

However, it is stated in the *Ṭīkā*: “It was said ‘thus’ (*evaṃ*) with reference to what will be explained hereafter. How can that be appropriate, given that what is about to be explained cannot logically be described as having been uttered in the past?
Alternatively, [the reading] might be “thus uttered” (*evam udīritaṃ*), both in the canonical text (*pāḷi*) and in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
The meaning is: "it is said thus. The word *eva* is used for emphasis.

103–5. Now, in order to demonstrate by way of its specific form the apprehension of the existence of things associated with oneself, such as those that are *yāvakālika* (to be consumed until the same day), he says "before," and so forth.
Therein, *sattāhaṃ* means that which has seven days; it is *sattāhakālika* (seven-day time-limited).
The word "and" (ca) is used in the sense of a non-appropriate occasion; it should be construed as "for seven days and for life.

"Mixed with other *kālaka* [foods]" means mixed with the remaining *kālaka* foods received on that very day—namely, those designated as *yāvakālika* (to be consumed during the day) and *yāmaka* (to be consumed within a watch of the night).

"Pācittiya" refers to the offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) according to the training rule concerning stored food (*sannidhi*). "Received on that very day" means received before the meal on that same day.
"Tadaheva" means on that very same day, specifically before the meal. "The rest" refers to the seven-day medicines and the life-long medicines.

"Thus" is connected to the understanding that one should consume [the seven-day medicine] only during the watch of the night. "The other" refers to the life-long medicine, which is distinct from the seven-day medicine.
The commentary on the exposition of the timed medicines is concluded.
9. Explanation of the Description of Receiving (Paṭiggāhaniddesavaṇṇanā) 106.
“Desires to give” means one who wishes to give (*dātukāmo*). His “offering” (*abhihāro*) refers to the act of bringing forward even slightly by inclining the body and so forth;

thus it is a *tappurisa* compound. The “hand’s reach” (*hatthapāso*) is the range of the hand. However, by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhī*), a distance of two and a half cubits is called the “hand’s reach. And that...
If the monk is sitting, starting from the back edge of the seat; if he is standing, starting from the heels;

if he is lying down, starting from the far side of whichever side he is lying on—excluding the hand that has been extended—if it is the donor who is sitting or standing, then [the limit is] by the near side of whichever limb is closest.
It is to be understood by way of delimitation. "Able to bear tossing" means capable and fit for being tossed by a man of medium strength.
Its neuter gender is relative to the word *vatthu* (the object). "Giving in three ways" refers to the giver giving by means of three modes:
namely, by way of the body, what is connected to the body, and what is to be relinquished (*nissaggiya*). Therein, by any part of the body, even down to...

Even when giving with a toe, it is called "given by means of the body. When giving with anything connected to the body, such as a spoon or the like, it is [given] by means of what is attached to the body.

However, having released [the object] from the body or from what is attached to the body, and then handing it over to one standing within arm's reach by means of the body or by means of what is attached to the body, it is called "given" through the act of relinquishment (*nissaggiya-payoga*). "Grasping in two ways" means:
The grasping of whatever is being given by anyone, in two ways—by means of the body and by means of what is attached to the body.
Thus, the application is that "acceptance has five factors. "Five factors" (*pañcaṅga*) is a *bahubbīhi* compound meaning "that which has five factors. 107.
Now, in order to show the acceptance and the mounting [of the seat] even for something that cannot withstand being carried and for anything else attached to the body:
He spoke the passage beginning with “asaṃhāriye. Therein, “asaṃhāriye” means on things such as wooden planks or stones that are impossible to carry away.
“Tatthajātā” refers to things such as the leaves of the *kiṃsuka* or *padumini* that grow upon those very trees;
the connection is with the delicate leaves of the *ciñcā* and so forth, for they are unable to support [the weight]. However, it is permissible on their branches. By the word “ādi,”...
The word “aṅga” and so forth includes [the other factors]. The particle *vā* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).

“In a burden that is unbearable” means in a burden that cannot be borne or sustained even by a man of medium strength. The phrase “acceptance of all” is connected with the words “does not succeed. 108.
Now, he shows the relinquishing of acceptance with the words beginning “the training,” and so forth. Therein, “by means of the training, death, and the signs”:
[The loss of the status of a monk occurs] by renouncing the training, by death, and by the transformation of gender.

Regarding "through the departure of one who is indifferent": one who has no longing (*apekkhā*) is "indifferent" (*anapekkha*); that itself is the "departure" (*visagga*), and it is from that. Regarding "through seizure": through being seized after being robbed by thieves and others.
Regarding "through giving to one not fully ordained": through giving [the robe] to one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*). The word "and" (*ca*) is to be supplied in every instance.
“Gāho” means receiving. “Upasammati” means it is relinquished.
Now, in order to show the fault in using what has not been received, he says “appaṭiggahitaṃ,” and so forth.
Therein, “sabbam” means the entirety included within the four time-periods. Now, [he explains] that which may be used without having been received.

He said "pure," etc., in order to show this. Therein, the connection is as follows: pure water that is not too thick, and likewise tooth-wood (*dantakaṭṭha*) that is unbroken, and feces (*gūthaka*), and salt (*loṇa*), and dung (*karīsa*)—these are allowable.
Therein, "pure" means completely clean due to being unmixed with dust, pollen, or other substances. "Not too thick" refers to that which [is found] in a ploughed place... [text continues].
It does not stick to the mouth or the hand, like thick water. "Uninterrupted" means it has not gone away after being severed from the body.
"Teeth, eyes, and ear" refers to the teeth, eyes, and ear; because these are parts of the body, the term *dantakkhikaṇṇa* is a *tappurisa* compound meaning "excrement of those [parts].
"Salt" is that which arises from the body. "Siṅghāṇī" means nasal mucus. That which is severed [from the body] must not be accepted.
111. Now, with the words beginning “excrement,” he shows the time of Kālodāyin. “At such a time” (tathāvidhe) means at a time such as that of being bitten by a snake and so forth.
It is a *bahubbīhi* compound meaning: “one for whom such a kind of time exists. “He would resort to” (seveyya) means he would practice resorting to it;

what is meant is that he would consume it. Regarding the phrase “when there is no one to make it allowable” (*asante kappakāre*), here even one who is difficult to speak to or incapable is considered a maker of what is allowable (*kappiyakāraka*).
It should be understood that it remains for exactly the duration of the time [of the meal].

However, because it is seen to be the right time, if there is no ash, it is permissible to cut fresh wood from a tree and use it; if there is no clay, it is also permissible to dig into the ground and take clay.
112. Regarding "badly performed" (*durupaciṇṇa*): what has been poorly performed or touched upon is "badly performed. If a monk [takes] what has not been formally offered...

If one moves a vessel containing food from its place and touches it, touches the lid, discards refuse or the like that is on top of it, or shakes it by grasping a branch or creeper growing thereon, this is called "bad conduct" (*durūpaciṇṇa*).
The connection is that for this, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). However, [if one does so] to lean against a fruit tree or to [remove] a thorn there—
Or it is permissible to tie [it up]. It is permissible to bring wild mango fruits and the like that have fallen in the forest, thinking, "I will give them to the novice," and then give them.

Regarding the phrase "covered with dust" (*rajo-kiṇṇe*): it means covered with dust; for one who accepts anything in such a bowl or similar vessel, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*vinaya-dukkata*).
If dust falls into the bowl while one is walking for alms, having accepted it...
Alms should be accepted. Even when told, "Having received it, give it [to me]," they may pour it out;
one should accept it by leading it to the person who is to receive it without letting it leave the hand.
If a strong wind blows dust from here and there so that it is impossible to accept alms, one should form the intention with a pure mind: "I will give this to one who is not fully ordained."
It is permissible to take [the food] after having [received it]. However, once it has been given by him or accepted through trust, it is permissible to consume it.
The word *atha* indicates the commencement of what is about to be said. Regarding the term *uggahappaṭiggaho*: that which is taken up (*uggahita*) is called *uggaho*;

it is the taking up. Its acceptance is *paṭiggaho*. [The phrase refers to] "in that [acceptance]. The intended meaning is: for one who knows the state of not having formally accepted it, it is the taking [of it] by oneself after having personally picked it up.
However, it is permissible to take oil and such items for the sake of one’s parents without receiving them as a gift, or to take branches and such for the sake of shade;
likewise, it is permissible to receive and consume things out of a desire to eat later.

When sugarcane and the like have been split, no impurity is perceived; nor is there any fault in the sitting mats, small stools, mortars, or pestles used by those grinding or pounding root medicines and the like.
They spoil; when there is fine meat stuck between the teeth, its flavor is no longer perceived—it is not an offense.
"Dwelling inside" means dwelling within the interior of the roof of an unallowable hut. "Cooked by oneself" means cooked by oneself anywhere whatsoever.
Even if one heats an axe or similar tool and puts it into buttermilk or other liquids, one is still not released from the offense of cooking for oneself.
Furthermore, with the exception of what has already been cooked, it is not permitted for a bhikkhu to cook any kind of foodstuff whatsoever.
Even if they add things such as *sulasī* leaves or ginger to hot gruel, it is not permitted to stir them.
Having received rice that is still unhusked, it is not permitted to cover it [with water]. "Inside a non-permissible hut" means inside a hut that is not allowable.
"In cooked. The connection is "in all cases, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
The commentary on the description of receiving [food] is finished.
10. Commentary on the Description of Improper Meat.

113–4. The meaning should be understood by connecting it as follows: "among those meats, namely the meat of humans, elephants, and horses... [and so on] ... and of snakes, as well as meat specifically prepared for someone, and meat that has not been inspected.
In this context, *taracchā* are a specific kind of bear that moves with its head and neck held high. By the term "of snakes" (*uragassa*), all species of long-bodied creatures are included.
"Included. "Meat prepared specifically for a monk" (*uddissakatamaṃsaṃ*) means meat prepared having designated a particular monk; that is *uddissakataṃ*, and it is also *maṃsaṃ*.
Here, by the mention of "meat," the inclusion of fish should also be understood, either by way of illustration (*upalakkhaṇavasena*) or by the word "and" (*ca*).
Among the five types of fellow practitioners of the Dhamma, anything prepared specifically for them is not allowable for any of them; that too—
It is permissible [to accept meat] that is pure in three respects by virtue of not having been seen, heard, or suspected.

"Unexamined" means not investigated; the meaning is "without asking. For one who is fearful of an offense, even when observing the appearance [of meat], it should be accepted and consumed only after asking.
The construction is: "In the case of the flesh of humans, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya). This is because there is a grave transgression (*thūlo accayo*) therein.
In the case of a corpse and a double corpse, there is a *thullaccaya* offense. Apart from the *pārājika* and *saṅghādisesa* offenses, there is no fault (*vajja*) greater than this.
"In the remaining" means in the eleven remaining cases.
115. Now, in order to show that even the bones and so forth of humans and others are unallowable, he says "even bone," etc. The word "even" (*pi*)...

The term "blood" (*lohita*) and so forth should also be understood as recurring [in the following list]. Among the ten items, such as human [flesh], [the first] belongs to humans and the rest. However, among the fats (*vasā*), only one—the human fat—is not permitted.
Regarding milk and the other liquids, there is nothing called "unallowable" (*akappiya*). The construction is:

"only that which is specifically intended (*uddissakata*) is 'with consciousness' (*sacittaka*). It is called "with consciousness" because it occurs together with the consciousness that knows the state of being specifically intended. It does not occur with the consciousness that fails to recognize the transgression regarding the object (*vatthu*).

For herein, the state of being "with consciousness" refers only to the offense and not to the meat; nevertheless, it should be understood that the offense itself is expressed by way of the term "meat.
The commentary on the description of unallowable meat is finished.
11. Commentary on the Exposition of the Nissaggiya Offenses 116–117.
“One should exchange non-monetary goods for money, and money for other [goods]” is the connection [of the text].

In this context, “with money” means by means of an article subject to forfeiture (nissaggiya-vatthu) designated as money. “Non-monetary” refers to an article subject to an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa-vatthu) designated as non-monetary.
And "an allowable object" (kappiyavatthu). "By the other" means by that which is not money (arūpiya). "Forfeiture" (nissaggi): forfeiture (nissagga) is the act of relinquishing;
this is the name for the formal monastic procedure (vinayakamma) to be performed prior [to the confession]. That which has forfeiture as its characteristic is "forfeiting" (nissaggi);

what is it? An offense of expiation (pācittiya). However, regarding the initial taking of money, there is a forfeiting offense of expiation according to the training rule on accepting money (rūpiyappaṭiggahaṇasikkhāpada).
Now, in order to show silver and so forth, the passage beginning with “here” (*idha*) is commenced.

Therein, the connection is as follows: “a *kahāpaṇa*, a *sajjhu*, a *siṅgī*, or a *māsaka*—this is what is meant here by ‘silver’ (*rūpiya*). Among these, a *kahāpaṇa* is made of gold or made of silver;
it may also be the ordinary *kahāpaṇa* currently in circulation. *Sajjhu* means silver. *Siṅgī* is a variety of gold; nevertheless, in this context, gold is intended in its general sense.
"Vohārūpagamāsakaṃ" means that which approaches (upagacchati) trade (vohāra), namely buying and selling; thus it is "vohārūpaga," and that together with the *māsaka* coin.
Furthermore, that [coin] is said to be made of metal, wood, and so forth, whether its form has been fashioned (*samuṭṭhāpita-rūpa*) or not yet fashioned (*asamuṭṭhāpita-rūpa*).

In this context, "rūpiya" refers to what is called "rūpiya" in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*). Cloth, pearls, and so forth are allowable, while the objects of an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa-vatthu*) are otherwise.
The construction is "the other. Therein, the compound is "that of which cloth, pearls, and so forth are the beginning" (*vatthañ-ca muttañ-ca ādi yassa*).

The word "beginning" (*ādi*) should be applied to each [term], as in "cloth, etc., pearls, etc. Therein, by the first word "beginning," any allowable object such as cotton, thread, silver, and so forth is meant;
by the second, gems, conch shells, stones, coral, rubies, and cat's-eye gems.
The seven types of grain, female and male slaves, fields, lands, flower gardens, fruit gardens, and so forth—this includes the category of *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).

The meaning is that other non-material items (*arūpiya*), such as cloth and other allowable goods (*kappiyavatthu*), as well as pearls and other items that constitute *dukkaṭa*, are included under the term "the other.
118. Having thus far demonstrated the exchange of money, he now speaks in order to demonstrate the buying and selling of allowable goods (*kappiyabhaṇḍa*).

“*Imaṃ*,” and so forth. Therein, the construction is as follows: when one has entered into buying or selling, it is an offense of relinquishment (*nissaggiya*) if [one says], “Having taken this, give that; do this; bring that,” or “Having eaten this, give that; do this; bring that,” or “I give this, you give that;
do this; bring that. In this context, *imaṃ* refers to rice and so forth. *Bhutvā* refers to cooked rice and so forth.
"Having eaten. "Give this" means: give this cloth or other article. "Make this" means:
make this dyeing, boiling, and so forth. "Bring this" means: bring this dye-wood and so forth. "I give this" means: I give this cloth or other article to you.
"Has finished" means: it has been completed. Therefore, when one is exchanging allowable goods with those who are not relatives, [one should say]: "This..."

Three offenses are stated: for one who says, "Give [it]," there is an act of intimation (*viññatti*); for one who says, "Take this," there is the misappropriation of what was given in faith (*saddhādeyyavinipātana*);

and for one who says, "Give this by means of that," there is buying and selling (*kayavikkaya*). However, with regard to one's mother and father, one may exchange goods with them provided one avoids even the mere semblance of buying and selling.
For this buying and selling is forbidden except among the five types of persons who share the same Dhamma (*pañcasahadhammika*).

It is not permissible for householders or those who have gone forth [to dedicate gains]. However, if one has new buildings constructed, one should confess an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) according to the measure of the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
119–120. Now, in order to show the classification of offenses by way of dedication, the passage beginning with “for oneself” is commenced. Herein, this is the summarized meaning:
if one should dedicate to oneself a gain intended for the Saṅgha, it is an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*). [If one dedicates] from elsewhere to an individual...
If one should divert it [to oneself], it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). If one should divert it to another *saṅgha* or to another *cetiya*, it is an offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*).

The construction is as follows: if one should divert that gain—which belongs to another individual or to another *cetiya*—either to oneself, to the *saṅgha*, to another individual, or to another *cetiya*, it is an offense of wrongdoing.
In this context, "that" (*taṃ*) refers to [the gain] by way of body or speech.
Or it has been made low-lying. "Gain" means robes and so forth that ought to be obtained. "From one to another" means from one person to another person, or to a shrine (*cetiya*);

however, in the case of a shrine, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). "Of another" refers to anyone other than the shrine, down to even a dog. "Or from one [to another]" means to a shrine and so forth.
As for the phrase "of the Saṅgha," this term "should not divert" applies to both cases by way of the maxim of the crow’s eyeball (*kākakkhigoḷaka-nyāya*).
The connection is that if one does not give back [an item] while perceiving it as one's own, it is a *dukkaṭa*. "In another way" means by another manner;
it is stated that if one does not give it back while perceiving it as stolen, [the offense is different].
"The other" means that, depending on the object, there are other offenses—*pārājika*, *thullaccaya*, or *dukkaṭa*. This is the meaning.
The commentary on the exposition of the *nissaggiya* rules is finished.
12. Commentary on the exposition of the *pācittiya* rules.
121. Regarding the phrase "in falsehood... in taking," the locative case is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*). This is connected with the words "a *pācittiya* offense is stated."
The connection [is as follows]. Thus it is in all cases. "In lying" (*musāvāde*) is a *tappurisa* compound with the indeclinable (*nipāta*).
The meaning is: for one who knew previously and also knows at the moment of speaking, it is the cause for uttering a falsehood.

Furthermore, "speaking" here refers to the act of making what is unreal appear as real, or making what is real appear as unreal, through the application of communication by means of body or speech. These are the failures of conduct regarding the *pārājika* and *saṅghādisesa* offenses.
For one who accuses [another] on groundless charges, there are, respectively, offenses of *saṅghādisesa*, *pācittiya*, and *dukkaṭa*.

There is no offense for one who speaks impulsively without having reflected, or for one who says something else thinking, "I will say something else," provided that the person to whom he speaks does not hear him.
It is called *omasa* because by means of it one reviles (*omasati*), as if piercing the ears with what is unpleasant; and this is both that reviling and speech (*vāda*).

In that [context], however, the vowel is long due to the requirements of metrical composition; this applies everywhere in such cases. Regarding the ten bases—namely, birth, name, clan, age, occupation, craft, illness, gender, defilement, and offenses—the meaning of "abusive speech" is:

with the desire to revile a bhikkhu, whether by body or by speech, using either true or false statements under no other pretext than these ten bases, such as saying, "You are a khattiya," or "You are a caṇḍāla. "There are some here... [and so forth].

Whether by using indirect designations such as "Caṇḍāla" and so forth, or by words outside the canonical texts (pāḷimutta) such as "You are a thief," "You are a pervert," or "You are a matricide," it is a *dukkaṭa* offense for one who reviles a bhikkhu or,
in any manner whatsoever, a person not fully ordained (anupasampanna) in their absence. However, if one speaks out of mere frivolity, it is a *dubbhāsita* in all cases.
Regarding "carrying off slander" (*pesuññaharaṇa*): *pesuñña* is the state of being a slanderer (*pisuṇa*).

It refers to the carrying off of that slander by a monk who, having heard the words of another monk—either because he himself desires to be liked or with the intention of causing a rift among others by reviling them on account of their birth and so forth—conveys that slander to someone else.

If it is conveyed to one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*), it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). "Word by word" (*padaso*) means according to each individual word; this is used in the sense of distributive repetition (*vicchā*).
Thus, the meaning is "part by part. The term *padasodhamma* is a third-case tappurisa compound consisting of *pada* (word) and *saha dhammena* (together with the Dhamma).

This refers to the recitation of the aforementioned Dhamma together with those who are not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*), categorized part by part according to divisions such as single syllables and so forth. This Dhamma includes both that which is contained in the Three Councils—the Tipiṭaka Dhamma—and that which is not so contained, such as the *Rājovāda* and other discourses. Thus, *padasodhamme* means the recitation of the Dhamma as described, along with those who are not fully ordained, division by division, starting from single syllables.
The meaning is as follows: For the phrase "reciting word-for-word" (*padasodhamma*) is expressed by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).

When one recites or studies together with one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*), or when receiving instruction from them, or when reciting or rehearsing a text that is for the most part well-mastered together with them—if a mistake occurs in such instances, [the rule states]: "In this way..."
There is no offense even if one speaks while another person is speaking at the same time.
Even if it is entirely covered by means of anything such as cloth and so forth, a dwelling that does not touch the roof, even if it is one and a half cubits high,
is intended here as a "house" (agāra) if it is completely enclosed, or if it is mostly covered and mostly enclosed.

In this context, with the exception of a monk, even a lower animal—even one as low as a female born on that very day—is called "one with a house" (*sāgāra*) by way of metaphorical usage. One who is "with a house" is a *sāgāra*, namely a monk.
Furthermore, the state of being "with a house" (*sāgārabhāva*) consists in sharing a bed with one who is not fully ordained and with a woman, even if only by way of metaphorical proximity.

The name should be taken [of the person]. "Ujjhāpanaka" (reviling) refers to that speech by which those who desire fame, being fully ordained monks, cause others to revile, despise, look down upon with contempt, or consider someone as inferior—this being authorized by the Sangha and consisting of various roles such as the assigner of lodgings.
"Khīyana" (denigration) is that by which they cause [the person] to be disparaged everywhere, proclaiming his ill-repute.
122. *Tala* refers to the palm of the hand as intended here. By taking that [term], however, the body itself is the *tala*.
*Satti* means a spear, a specific type of weapon attached to the body; but because it is used as a characteristic term (*upalakkhaṇa*), everything attached to the body is also a *satti*.
Thus, *tala* and *satti* together form *talasatti*. In this context, however, the brandishing of the *talasatti* by a monk out of anger is what is meant by *talasatti*. If...
However, if one strikes [someone] by mistake, it is a *dukkaṭa* because it was given without the intention to strike; if it was given with the intention to strike, it is a *pācittiya*.
If [the person struck] is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*), it is a *dukkaṭa*. There is no offense for one whose intention is to release [the blow].
Disrespect consists in showing disrespect toward one who speaks according to what has been prescribed, whether it be the one who is fully ordained or the teaching being spoken by him.

For one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*) being spoken to by one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*), or for one being spoken to by another—whether that other person is authorized or unauthorized—if there is disrespect, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Causing a monk to feel remorse by saying things such as, “I think you are less than a year in seniority,” is an offense of wrong-doing for the one who is not fully ordained.

Regarding “entering a village without having asked permission”: by the natural phrasing [of the rule], this refers to the vicinity of sight within the inner boundary (*upacāra-sīmā*) where it is appropriate to ask permission.

Upon seeing a bhikkhu, if one enters a village at an improper time without having asked for permission—thinking, "I shall ask for permission regarding entering the village at an improper time"—there is an offense for entering the village at an improper time without asking.
However, the word *dīgho* (long) is used here due to euphonic combination (*sandhi*). There is no offense in cases of emergencies (*āpadāsu*).
Regarding "successive eating" (*paramparabhojana*): "another and another" is *paramparā*; the letter *m* is due to euphonic combination (*sandhi*), therefore it is *paramparā*.
This is a statement regarding the ablative case (apādāna) denoting the source of arising; the meaning is "eating after having received [food] one after another.

This is the intended sense here: for one who has been invited by receiving names for five kinds of food, from whichever food he was first invited, he may, in reverse order from that food, say, "I give my portion of almsfood to you," or "I assign it to you."
Or, having received various kinds of food, such as the five types of cooked food, either in the presence of others or out of their sight, or without making a specific designation, one eats them.
There is no offense at the time of giving medicine for the sick or when robes are being made. 123. The connection is:
"going without putting away the bedding or the lodgings. The word *vā* (or) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). In that context:
“Among the ten kinds of bedding mentioned— namely, a mattress, a pillow, an upper coverlet, a floor-covering, a wooden board, a piece of hide, a sitting mat,
a rug, a grass mat, and a leaf mat— one should take even one of these from among one’s own annual requisites and,
having spread it out or having had it spread out in a communal dwelling that is well-sheltered and secure, leave it exactly as it was placed.”

It is not eaten by ants and the like; likewise, when one has gone beyond the enclosure of a monastery that was fenced in—having been left unremoved by way of being set down—or the precincts of one that was unfenced;

and likewise, when bedding and seats consisting of beds, stools, mats, and cushions have been spread out or caused to be spread out in the open air during the rainy season and have not been removed by one who is not fully ordained.
The meaning is: "having gone beyond the distance of a clod-throw by a man of medium strength.
However, in any case other than that which has been described, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Regarding a woman traveling on a journey: having made an appointment with one another, saying, "Let us go, sister; let us go, noble lady,"...
The meaning is: even without making a time-agreement (such as "today or tomorrow"), if one makes an agreement regarding the door or the path and travels a long-distance road together with a woman.
"Sitting alone with one" means "one by one"; the meaning is "her sitting" together with one [man]. "With one" refers to one [man] together with one [woman].

There is no such thing as sitting alone with one person; therefore, the intended meaning is that when there is sitting together with one person, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for the monk who is sitting. Alternatively, the reading is "ekāyeka-nisīdane" (sitting one with one).

124. In the case of causing fear to one who is fully ordained by means of presenting forms and so forth, or by telling terrifying stories, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who is not fully ordained.

In the case of striking, for one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*), even giving a blow with a lotus leaf constitutes an offense. For one who is not fully ordained, even toward an animal, it is an act of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). There is no offense for one whose intention is to release [the person being struck].

When one is being interrogated by a master of the Discipline (*vinayadhara*) in the midst of the Sangha, "speaking otherwise" (*aññavāda*) is answering one thing when questioned about another, or evading the question with something else.
Likewise, when being questioned in that same manner, remaining silent out of a desire not to speak is "harassment" (*vihesana*).

Harassment (*vihesā*). When a formal act consisting of a motion and a second (*ñattidutiyakamma*) has been performed against one who speaks otherwise or who harasses—namely, an act for speaking otherwise or for harassing—if he subsequently speaks otherwise or harasses, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). However, if the formal act has not been performed, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Having seen some transgression and being told, "Friend, you have done such-and-such," if he remains silent because he does not wish to speak about it, [he should inform] the Saṅgha...

"He harasses," thus he is a harasser (*vihesaka*). One who, having practiced improper conduct, when being questioned in the midst of the Saṅgha regarding an offense or its basis, does not wish to speak of it and conceals that matter with other words—saying things such as "Who has committed [an offense]?
or "In what has one committed?"—this person is called one who speaks otherwise (*aññavādaka*).
“Gross offense” (duṭṭhulla) refers to offenses involving defeat (pārājika) or formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa); here, however, it refers specifically to a saṅghādisesa.
“Manifest and concealed” (pakāsachāda) means the manifest and the concealed; thus, “the manifest and concealed [nature] of a gross offense” is a tatpurusa compound.

For a monk who repeatedly commits offenses, whether or not he has established a limit on the number of offenses or a limit on the number of families for the sake of future restraint, he should seek permission three times.

It should be done. Setting aside the formal authorization of the Saṅgha (bhikkhusammuti), when one reveals or reports a grave offense (duṭṭhulla) by connecting the basis with the offense—such as saying of one who is not fully ordained, "This person, having emitted semen, has committed a saṅghādisesa"—and when one conceals that very same grave offense after having learned of it by any means whatsoever;
and when one reports or conceals a non-grave offense (aduṭṭhulla).

Furthermore, for one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*), there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) even for the other [type of] indecent speech under the fifth training rule mentioned previously.

Regarding the term *hāsodake*: here, the analysis of the words should be understood as *hāse udake* (in laughter, in water). It refers to touching the armpits or other parts of the body with any part of one's own body while intending to laugh.
For touching with the purpose of laughter is itself "laughter. In the case of one who is not fully ordained, it is an offense of wrong-doing.
"In water" means: in water reaching above the ankles; for one who intends to laugh, it is by way of playing while emerging and submerging.

For "laughter" is what is meant here by "play. For one who plays with a boat, or strikes the water with his hands or with sticks and such, or even plays at tossing things like bowls or sour gruel into the water, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). There is no offense for one who does not intend to laugh.
"Expelling from the monastery" means the act of ejecting a bhikkhu or causing him to be ejected from a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha.
In this regard, there is one offense for a single instance of action; however, if there are multiple instances of action, there are as many offenses as there are doors [through which he is ejected].

In the case of ejecting an individual (not a bhikkhu), ejecting his requisites, or ejecting a non-ordained person or his requisites, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). This does not apply to those who are conducting themselves properly.
There is no offense in ejecting one's own resident pupils (antevāsika) or co-residents (saddhivihārika), or in ejecting someone who has placed his trust in oneself from a monastery;
however, there is no offense in ejecting a quarrelsome person from the entire monastic compound (saṅghārāma).
Regarding "lying down intruding upon another": having recognized that [the other] is "senior," "sick," or "authorized by the Saṅgha," [one may lie down] on beds or chairs...
When that bhikkhu enters or exits, if one sits or lies down on a bed in a communal vihāra by encroaching upon his vicinity and intruding into it—
with the intention, "Whoever finds it cramped will depart"— there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the case of a private [dwelling].
And here, having pointed out "an offense of expiation" (*pācittiya*), some well-known instances have been shown.
However, those not explicitly mentioned, being of the same nature, should be understood as included by this very general term. How so?

In the case of giving with one's own hand any kind of material gift to any member of other sects, such as the naked ascetics (*acelaka*) and others; and [the giving] of what are reckoned as ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, molasses, fish, meat, milk, and curd—
In eating exquisite foods having requested them for one's own sake; in entering and taking a seat in families suitable for men and women who are overwhelmed by lust;

and in going before a meal or after a meal without having asked a present monk, when one has been invited with any of the five kinds of cooked food and that food has either been eaten or not yet eaten.
Or, having been invited to a particular family, excepting the occasion of giving robes for the sick, upon entering another family;
