or, excepting a single day, upon eating alms-food at a lodging on another day while not being ill;
or, having set a limit of nights or a limit of medicines, beyond that which was invited to, except for a further invitation—other than these cases.
In requesting a constant invitation; in going to see an army that has marched out from a village, except on such a specific occasion;

in staying with an army for more than two nights even when one has gone there for a specific purpose; in going for the sake of seeing the place of battle, the location of the troops, the military camp, or the divisions of the army while staying there;
[and] in regard to *surā*, which is liquor made from flour and so forth, and *meraya*, which is intoxicant made from flowers and so forth.
Furthermore, for one who is not ill, the lighting or causing to be lit of a fire out of a desire to warm oneself—without the purpose of drinking, lighting a lamp, boiling water, or cooking;
the use of a new robe without taking the *kappa-bindu* mark; the use of a robe after having personally designated it as such without subsequently relinquishing that designation;
and the hiding of a bowl or other items belonging to a monk, even if only with the intention of joking.

in causing [another] to take up [a wrong view]; in intentionally depriving a being of the animal realm of life; in intentionally reopening for a second trial a legal issue that has been settled according to the Dhamma;
in intentionally traveling along the same road in company with a band of thieves;
and in saying, when being addressed by monks regarding the training rules, "I will not train in that," without considering the other matter.
In the disparaging of the training rules; in eavesdropping at a place where those who have fallen into dispute are speaking without the intention, "Having heard it, we shall desist";
in falling into the state of criticizing after having given one's consent for legal acts that are in accordance with the Dhamma;

in departing from the Saṅgha without giving one's consent while a formal decision is being carried out by the Saṅgha; and in falling into the state of criticizing after a robe has been given by a unanimous Saṅgha.
"Except within a monastery or a dwelling, taking or causing another to take a jewel or what is considered a jewel is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The commentary on the exposition of the offenses of expiation is finished.
13. Commentary on the Exposition of the Ascetic’s Mode of Dress.

125. *Samaṇakappā* means the designations for ascetics (*samaṇa-vohārā*). *Bhūtā* means they have come into being (*bhavanti*), or they have been (*ahesuṃ*); it is a suffix applied to either the present or the past.

It is a "village of beings" (*bhūtagāma*) because it is a collection (*gāma*) or a multitude (*samūha*) of beings—namely trees, creepers, and so forth—which are designated as such when they have attained the state of having developed roots and so on and are growing, or when they have grown and reached a state of greatness.
Alternatively, the beings themselves are the village; thus it is a "village of beings."

His undertaking consists of cutting, splitting, and so forth; this refers to that [action]. This locative case is used in the sense of "on account of" (nimitta), meaning that on account of that, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

The connection is with the phrase: "it becomes what is permissible for a recluse" (*katakappiyaṃ samaṇakappiyaṃ bhavati*). In that regard, it is a *bahubbīhi* compound meaning "that for which what is permissible has been made.
To the question "by what?", he says: "by the fingernail," and so forth.

126. Now, in order to analyze and demonstrate that category of living beings (*bhūtagāma*) which is the object of undertaking (*samārambha*), the passage beginning with "with its roots" (*sa mūlā*) is commenced.

"It" (*so*) refers to the category of living beings. It is called *pabhāvita* because it is applied (*payojeti*) toward becoming or arising; the suffix *-tappaccaya* is used in the sense of an agent (*kāritanta*). Thus, the meaning is "that which has been brought forth" (*pabhāvita*) or "produced.
Alternatively, "origin" (*pabhava*) means the act of originating (*pabhavana*), that is, arising; it is "that which makes an origin" (*pabhāvaṃ karoti*), derived from a verbal root (*nāmadhātu*).
The suffix *tappaccaya* is used here; the meaning is "produced from" or "arisen from. Root, trunk, seed, tip, and fruit—[these are] roots...
[up to] fruits. "Fruit" (*phalu*) means a joint (*pabba*). These very things are the seeds; it is produced or brought forth by them.
Alternatively, it is produced or arisen from them as limits or as causes. Thus, there are two alternative interpretations in sequence.
Two types of seeds should be understood. Among them, "root-seed" refers to turmeric, ginger, and so forth.
"Stem-seed" refers to the *assattha* (pipal) tree, the *nigrodha* (banyan) tree, and so forth. "Seed-seed" refers to paddy, barley, and so forth. "Tip-seed" refers to *hirivera* grass and so forth.
"Joint-seed" refers to sugarcane, reeds, and so forth. Among these, the five beginning with root-seeds constitute the category of seeds.
That which has arisen from it is the community of beings consisting of trees, creepers, and so forth.

Now, by means of the word *aparaddha*, he shows that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in the undertaking of the commencement of a plantation of seeds among those [beings]. The connection is: "There is an offense of wrong-doing in the undertaking of seed separated from the community of beings.
"Separated from the community of beings" (*bhūtagāmaviyojita*) is a *tappurisa* compound. "Seed" (*bīja*) refers to that which is in the earth.

Planted and unplanted seeds include those from which a leaf-sheath (pattavaṭṭi) measuring at least one span has emerged; these are root-seeds (*mūlabīja*). Regarding the word "undertaking" (*ārambhe*):

when used in connection with the suffix *-ita*, since no specific case is stated for the object (*kamma*), the sixth case arises optionally, and thus the second case may be used in both instances. "Undertaking" means "commencement.
Therefore, by means of a formal declaration of suitability (*kappiyavacana*) such as, "Know this to be a flower or fruit; make this permissible," [the monk may accept it].
The collection of seeds, having been separated from the mass of living beings, may be consumed after being made permissible once again for the sake of liberating them from the mass of seeds.
Regarding the five ways of making fruit permissible for consumption that were stated as: "I allow you, monks, to consume fruit by means of these five monastic methods:

that which is overcome by fire, that which is overcome by a knife, that which is overcome by the nail, that which is seedless, and fifthly, that which has produced its seed," three of these—beginning with that overcome by the nail—are here shown.
127. Now, in order to show the remaining two, he spoke the first half-verse beginning with “the seed for production.
Therein, “the seed for production” (*nibbattabīja*) means that which is produced (*nibbatta*)—from the root *vat* preceded by the prefix *ni*, with the suffix *-ta*.
That whose seed is produced is “the seed for production”; it is that which, having had its seed produced, should be enjoyed separately [after the seed has been extracted].

“Mangoes, breadfruit, and so forth. “Non-seed” (*nabīja*) refers to young mango fruits and the like. Now, in order to show the specific methods for making seeds and forest-grown plants permissible (*kappiya*), he says “in a vessel,” and so forth.
Therein, the external meaning is: those whose seeds are bound within a vessel. (128) The construction is:

when the seeds are joined together in a single unit, whether in a container or on the ground, and one [of them] has been made permissible. “In seeds” means among seeds and forest-grown plants; for here, even what is “forest-grown” (*bhūtagāma*) is called “seed” by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhī*).

129. *Nikkhitte* means "placed. *Kappiyaṃ puna kareyyā* means: because it has become a living plant (*bhūtagāma*) due to its state of having roots and leaves, one should again make it allowable (*kappiya*) for the purpose of releasing it from the category of seeds (*bījagāma*).
Therefore he said: "For that is then a living plant (*bhūtagāma*). The word *hi* indicates a reason. *Tadā* means at the time when the roots and leaves have grown. If...
If only the root has arisen, and a sprout arises in the upper part, it is permissible to cut it off at the lower part. Alternatively,
once only the roots or only the leaves have emerged, even if branches as large as a jewel emerge,
they are included within the category of "seed-forest" (bījagāma).

130. "Water-born" refers to *sevāla* (moss) and such; the connection is that moss on *cetiyas* and the like constitutes a "community of beings" (*bhūtagāma*). By the word "and the like" (*ādi*), walls and so forth are included.
If two or three leaves have not yet grown, it is classified under "seed-heads" (*aggabīja*).
However, if it is dry, it may be swept away. When roots and leaves have emerged, even the seed is a "community of beings"—this is the connection. By the word "leaves" (*paṇṇa*)...
He rejects even a mere sprout. 131.
The connection is that moss on the surface of a jar or similar vessel, and the unopened bud of the *ahichattaka* mushroom, are indeed grounds for a *dukkaṭa* offense.

By the word "surface" (*piṭṭha*), he shows that what is inside is not subject to this designation. "Blooming" (*phulla*) refers to a fully opened *ahichattaka*. "Not fit for consumption" (*abyavahārika*)— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the portion available.]
The meaning is that it is not suitable for use as a conventional designation for an offense.
132. The connection is that there is an *pācittiya* offense for one who, having destroyed the lac, resin, or parasols on fresh trees, takes them, or even cuts letters therein.
"Therein" means on the fresh trees. The reading "vikopaya" (having destroyed) is seen in the manuscripts.
That reading is incorrect because there is no reason for it to end in the nominative case. Instead, the reading “vikopiyā” should be accepted.
By the word “vikopiyā,” it is indicated that there is no offense if one takes [the object] without having disturbed it.
133. Regarding “wooden monkeys and the like”: having carved a peg and fashioned a wooden frame, they hang a thorn upon it.
This is called the "wooden monkey" (dārumakkaṭaka). By the word "etc. (ādi), the binding with thorns and so forth are included. The construction is:
"It is not allowable to cut grass, etc., nor to make a knot. "To cut" (chindituṃ) means the act of cutting. 134.
"Or a grove of living beings" (bhūtagāmaṃ vā) means "or a grove of living beings. "Or seed" (bījaṃ vā) means "or a grove of seeds. In all instances, [the phrase] "cut, or... and so forth applies.

The particle *vā* should be connected [to the preceding]. "Or cook" (*paca vā*) means "or perform the act of cooking. Alternatively, there is the reading "cloth" (*paṭa*), the meaning of which is "produce it.
However, rather than saying "cut this tree," etc., it is permissible to speak without specifying, as in "cut the tree," and so forth.
135. "This" (*imaṃ*) refers to that tree or other object. Regarding "clean this" (*imaṃ sodhehi*), the meaning should be stated by adding the particle *iti*.
The commentary on the description of the ascetic’s requisites is finished.
14. Commentary on the Description of Grounds (Bhūminiddesa) 136.

Those grounds upon which what has been stored or cooked is allowable are the permissible grounds (*kappiya-bhūmi*): namely, a formal authorization (*sammuti*) and an authorized hut (*sammuti-kuṭī*). … [as above] …
The meaning should be understood by connecting the phrase: "the householder and the householder’s hut—these four [are the types].

In this context, it is called *sammuti* (formal authorization) because, by means of a second proclamation (*dutiyakammavācā*) as stated in the *Bhesajjakkhandhaka*, or by means of a motion (*apalokanakamma*), one causes it to be properly authorized after having announced it.
The term *uggamana* refers to the rising up of the pillars or the foundations of the walls.
“Ussāvanantā”: that which has its conclusion (*anta*) consisting of the laying out (*ṭhapana*) and the formal proclamation (*sāvana*) by speech, saying, “We shall build a *kappiyakuṭi*.
And thus it is said: “The fixing of the pillars and the completion of the speech must occur simultaneously.
“Gonisādi”: *nisāda* means entering or settling; that which has a *nisāda* like that of cattle is a *gonisādi*. [A] bhikkhu...
Excluding those, all remaining fellow-practitioners (sahadhammika) and all gods and humans are intended here by the general term "householder" (gahapati).
In this context, however, a hut associated with a householder is called "long" (dīgha) because of the commentarial statement:
"That which was stayed in a house capable of accommodating one's own bed on an improper site."
Whatever the Saṅgha desires—whether a *vihāra*, a *aḍḍhayoga*, a *pāsāda*, a *hammiya*, a *guha*, or a *leṇa* and so forth—the term "monastery" (*sāmañña*) is understood to apply to them as well.

Therefore, it should be understood that *leṇas* and the like, which possess their respective characteristics and are sufficient for a single person to sleep in, are included within the four types of huts (*kuṭīs*).
Among these four types of places sufficient for a single person to sleep in, whatever...

Whether belonging to the Saṅgha or to an individual, anything belonging to a bhikkhu that has been stored for even a single night by one who is not fully ordained—whether it be cooked food, *yāvakālika* (food to be consumed during the day), or *yāmakālika* (food to be consumed during the watch of the night)—does not incur the designation of "stored overnight" (*antovuttha*) or "cooked inside" (*antopakka*). This is even more so for the other two types of food.
However, even if it has been stored on an improper ground (*akappiyabhūmi*), cooked food is permitted. Therefore it is said: "In those [grounds], what is stored and cooked is allowable."

137. The connection is as follows: "In a house built for the purpose of lodging, belonging either to the Saṅgha or to a single individual, and sufficient for one to lie down in, a *kappiya-kuṭi* (a lawful storehouse) may be obtained.
In this context, the phrase "for the purpose of lodging" excludes that which was built for any purpose other than lodging.

"Belonging to a single individual" means belonging to one monk. "A *kappiya-kuṭi*" is a designation where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is emphasized; for it is not the case that a house [is itself] a house.
"It is appropriate to obtain" means a "proper hut" (*kappiyakuṭi*). However, the long vowel [in *kuṭī*] is due to the requirements of the verse;

alternatively, it should be understood as a descriptive compound meaning "a hut that is proper. Regarding the phrase "sufficient for sleeping together," here "sleeping together" refers to a lodging (*senāsana*) possessing the characteristics described in the definition of a dwelling place (*vāsāgāra*).

138. Now, having shown those huts in sequence, [the author] spoke the verse beginning with “In the house” (*gehe*) in order to show the method for practicing therein and the complete abandonment of them.
Therein, the connection is as follows: they set about [building], saying, “We shall make a *kappiya-kuṭi* (a lawful hut), we shall make a *kappiya-kuṭi*.
Regarding the term *iṭṭhakā-thambhā*: when it should have been said “bricks and pillars” (*iṭṭhakā ca thambhā ca*), the vowel is shortened; thus it is *iṭṭhakathambhā*.
“Of which the palace is the beginning” (*ādi yassa bhittipāsādassa*) is a *bahubbīhi* compound. Subsequently, it forms a *kammadhāraya* with the word *paṭhama*.
The meaning should be understood by connecting the words *ce*, *sā*, and *ussāvanantikā* as follows:

“If she were to set it aside, that [act] would be subject to the formal proclamation. 139. The connection is: “Even an entire, unfenced monastery (*ārāma*). Whether the dwelling (*senāsana*) is fenced or unfenced, that is not the determining factor.
140. The construction is: "given by others for the purpose of a *kappiyakuṭi* (a storehouse for allowable goods)," or "belonging to them.
141. Because of their state of being non-opposing, they are *kappā* (allowable); from the word *kappa*, with the feminine suffix *āp* due to its capacity (*sāmatthiya*), the form is *kappā*.
That which is not *kappā* is *akappā*; and that which is *akappā* and a *kuṭi* (hut) is an *akappakuṭi*, [by] that. By the phrase "ghee, etc.,"...
The seven-day [medicinal] substances and those for life-long use have been taken up.

142. "With those very same" means that because they are mixed with the seven-day substances—such as ghee and so forth—which were stored in an improper storehouse, it is stated that "they are allowable for seven days. "Together with material things" means together with the first two categories known as material things. "Raw meat" (sāmapākata) [is explained as follows].
That which is cooked by oneself is *sāmapāka*; that which is cooked together with what is permissible for seven days (*sattāhakālika*) is *sāmisa* (mixed with food).

The state of being such is *sāmapākatā*. The intention is that because it is cooked by oneself, through its association with that [other food], it makes even that other food fall under the category of *sāmapāka*, and thus it possesses the quality of *sāmapākatā*.
143. *Adhiṭṭhitā* means established. The word *eva* should be understood as following the word *tiṭṭhati*.

144. *Sabbesu* means in all [of them], such as the pillars and so forth. *Jahitavatthukā* refers to that whose ground-material (*vatthu*) has been abandoned; it is a hut-ground (*kuṭibhūmi*) from which the material has been discarded.
The connection is: "enclosed and having its ground-material abandoned. *Sesā* refers to the other two types of huts. *Chadanavibbhama* means the removal of the roof-covering.
“Through the destruction of the covering. Here too, the phrase “having abandoned the basis” (*jahitavatthukā*) should be supplied.
The commentary on the description of the planes (*bhūminiddesa*) is finished.
15. Commentary on the Description of the Conduct Toward Preceptors and Teachers (*upajjhācariyavattaniddesa*).
145. One is called an *upajjhā* because one reproves by saying things such as, "This was badly done by you;
it was ill-spoken," and because one causes mindfulness to arise in one who has forgotten their own fault, or because one causes them to proceed in right practice by reminding them or urging them on.

One is called an *upajjhā* because one closely contemplates—that is, thinks deeply about—what is faulty and what is not. An *upajjhā* is precisely an *upajjhāya*. "In this way, the word of the Buddha by you..."

"One should recite [the scriptures], one should step forward in this manner, and one should step back in this manner"—because he practices and acts in such a way as to instruct in conduct (*ācāra*), he is called an *ācariya*.
And he is fourfold, by way of the *nissaya-ācariya*, the *pabbajjā-ācariya*, the *upasampadā-ācariya*, and the *dhamma-ācariya*.

Both the preceptor (*upajjhā*) and the teacher (*ācariya*) are "preceptor-teachers" (*upajjhācariyā*). By the phrase "dwelling in dependence," [the text refers] to those who are *nissaya-students*, *pabbajjā-students*, *upasampadā-students*, and *dhamma-students*.

This shows who it is that must live in dependence. For among those four types of residents, only the resident dependent on formal support (*nissaya*) must perform all the duties toward the teacher (*ācariya-vatta*) for as long as he lives in dependence upon him;
not the others. As for the others—even those who are independent of formal support—they must perform duties such as dispelling boredom and so forth, up until the time of dyeing the robes.
However, regarding the giving of the bowl and robes and other such matters, they need not do so without having first asked permission.

However, there is no offense for these [other cases]. But for a preceptor who does not attend to his resident pupil—from the dyeing of the robe until the removal of boredom and so forth—there is indeed an offense, whether he has been released from formal dependence (*nissaya*) or not.
For certain individuals, there is an offense starting from the giving of the bowl and so forth, even while still under formal dependence. Among those, two are for the teacher.
They are a burden for as long as one lives. The others, however, are a burden only as long as they dwell nearby;

therefore, even the teacher must behave properly toward them, whereas there is no need for the preceptor to speak to his resident pupils. *Supesalo*: one who possesses a pleasing character (*sīla*) is "pleasant" (*pesalo*);
by the elision of the suffix *-ya-* and the substitution of the vowel *ī* with *a*, [the form] is derived. One who is very pleasant is "supesalo."
The meaning is "one who desires to train. Regarding the phrase "tooth-stick," etc., "should give" is its verb.
"Should give" means one should give properly, with care, and according to the intended purpose. "At the proper time" means at a time suitable for that.
146. The connection is: "One should perform the duty regarding the bowl... and the robe. "Should perform" means one should do it. In that regard, "lowly... [the text continues].

The proper conduct regarding the bowl is as follows: having washed it thoroughly without rubbing it, warming it for a short while over heat, and having inspected the place where it will be set down, one should place it away from anything such as leather that might cover it.
The proper conduct upon entering a village is to provide the lower robe, the waistband, and the outer cloak to those entering, and to give back the bowl after it has been washed and rinsed clean.
If they so desire, the proper conduct for going is to put on the lower robe and the upper robe evenly, walking neither too far nor too near, and taking up the bowl and its contents.

As for returning, the proper conduct is to arrive first, prepare a seat, set out water for washing the feet and other necessities, and receive the bowl and robes as they approach. While they are speaking...
The duty in all cases is to interrupt the conversation. The duties regarding the seat are: laying out the seats;
when they have risen, removing the seats; placing footstools and foot-scrubbers nearby; and putting them away from the seats, the footstools, and the foot-scrubbers.
A footstool is for placing washed feet upon it. A "scrubber" (kathala) is something else. "Sandals and robe" is a copulative compound (dvanda).

In that regard: wiping with dry, clean cloths is the duty concerning sandals. Briefly drying a damp robe and folding it after pulling back a four-finger-width border is the duty concerning robes. 147. The duty concerning the washing bowl...
[and so on] ...and regarding the cleansing of the urinal and excrement disposal areas, as well as their re-arrangement, is the duty.

The connection is "likewise" (*tathā*). "Excrement and urine" (*vaccapassāvā*) is a copulative compound (*dvanda*) of excrement (*vacca*) and urine (*passāva*). "A place for them" (*ṭhānī*) means a hut (*kuṭi*), as it is that wherein one stands (*tiṭṭhati*).

"A place for excrement and urine" (*vaccapassāvānaṃ ṭhānī*) is a dependent determinative compound (*tappurisa*). Alternatively, "a place" (*ṭhānaṃ*) is that wherein one stands; this is the same compound, meaning the place where excrement and urine fall.
That which possesses such a place is a latrine, a house, and so forth. And "requisites for use" (*paribhojanīyaṃ*).

The duties concerning the water for drinking and the places for excrement and urine are as follows: providing warm, cold, and bathing water for washing the feet is the duty regarding the water for use (*paribhojanīya*).

Inquiring about and providing the water for drinking is the duty regarding the drinking water (*pānīya*). Sweeping and providing water for the places for excrement and urine is the duty regarding those places.
First, having the bowl, robes, and so forth brought out, they are to be placed aside, and so on.
Beginning from the time of looking up, the duty (*vatta*) consists of sweeping and cleaning the monastery after setting aside the monkey’s lineage [of mischief].

Having dried it, cleaned it, beaten it out, and brought it back, the duty is the spreading of the floor-coverings and so forth in their proper places, as well as replacing them when they have been moved.
By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), this refers back to the instruction "one should practice."

148. The connection is as follows: while cleaning the monastery, a bhikkhu should not shake his bedding or seating near the drinking water, whether in a place with a counter-wind (*paṭivāta*), in a crowded place (*saṅgaṇa*), or near the drinking water.
By the word "drinking water" (*pānīya*), the water for washing (*paribhojanīya*) is also included.

"In a place with a counter-wind" means in an upper wind. "In a crowded place" means in an open area where many people have gathered. "Bedding and seating" (*sayanāsana*) refers to floor coverings, couches, and so forth.

149. Regarding the phrase "One should observe the proper conduct for bathing" (*nhāne vattaṃ care*), the connection should be understood as dependent on the person, in the sense that "one should observe what is to be done after having bathed.
"Proper conduct for bathing" (*nhāne vattaṃ*) refers to the receiving of robes, the cleansing of the body, and so forth.

"One should observe what is to be done" (*kātabbe care*) means one should engage in the duties such as wiping the body with water and providing a lower garment. In the phrases beginning with "in the forest thickets" (*vanappagumbe*), etc., [the same principle applies].

The form [of *kātabba*] is like the substitution of the vowel *e* for the suffix *-ya*. Therefore, it should be understood by connecting it as: "one should perform the duty that ought to be done" (*kātabbaṃ vattaṃ careyya*).
However, the Buddhas explain the meaning by connecting it as: "one should perform the duty toward one who has bathed when bathing is to be performed" (*nhāne nhātassa kātabbe vattaṃ care*).

This being so, because the word *kātabba* functions as the object (*kamma-sādhana*), the duty itself is what is called "that which ought to be done"; thus, [the phrase] reads: "one should perform the duty regarding the duty" (*vatte vattaṃ care*).

It contradicts [the reading] "it is as if it were said. Alternatively, the reading is "by one who has bathed, by one who has bathed," meaning that after first bathing the Elder by means of washing his limbs in water, he himself also bathed. There is also the text: "having first emerged from the water by one who has bathed.
Then, the connection is: "he should perform the duty regarding dyeing, washing, and sewing"; [this refers to] the dyeing process.
The meaning is: "in washing robes" and "in sewing robes. The connection is: "when dyeing, he does not stop while the drops remain on the robe.
"Dyeing" means dyeing the robe. "While the drops remain" means while the drops of dye remain. 150.
"Of a certain person" refers to the bowl or robes belonging to a person who is an enemy of the teacher or preceptor. Anything whatsoever—
The connection is: "one should neither give nor take requisites.
In this context, "should neither give nor take" means that one should not give even for the purpose of receiving back, nor should one take it back.

The word *kiñcana* should be understood as in the expression "ākiñcana" (nothingness), where its meaning is "anything whatsoever. Alternatively, the reading may be *kiñcinaṃ*, which is to be construed as "any requisite whatsoever."
The use of the word *ta* (him) here is made by way of establishing the sense of the word *naṃ* (him). 151–2.
“To act as an attendant behind” means to act as a *pacchāsamaṇa* (attendant walking behind). “Of him” means of a certain person. “Behind” means having become an attendant behind.
“To lead out” means to escort a certain person. In all cases, it should be understood that it is not permissible [to do these things] without having asked for permission.
“Or some duty”: any kind of duty such as service and so forth. *Kiccayaṃ* is simply *kicca*; it is a possessive form, as in the case of words like *seniyo*.
“Or some preliminary service”: such services as massaging the back and so forth. “To have performed by someone else”:
to have it performed by another person on one's own behalf. “Or to do it oneself”: to perform it for him by oneself.

153. "Outside the boundary" means that which has gone out from the boundary and is beyond it. Even if the teacher (ācariya) and preceptor (upajjhāya) have gone far away on alms-round without saying anything, one may enter the village without seeing them.
However, from the point where they were last seen, it is proper to inform them.
"Or for one's own business" means that even within one's own boundary, [one may go] for one's own sake, such as boiling rice-porridge, dyeing robes, and so forth.
Or even to perform what ought to be done.
154. *Aratiṃ*: lack of delight in the Teaching. *In matters dependent on the Saṅgha*:

in those formal acts (*kamma*) connected with the Saṅgha, such as probation (*parivāsa*), censure (*tajjanīya*), and so forth. *Or even to exert oneself*: when teachers or preceptors have committed a grave offense (*garudhamma*).
And among those worthy of work, there is also the exertion [of thought], such as: "How indeed might the Saṅgha grant him probation?
etc. 155. Regarding the sick, "one should attend to them" means: "Monks, one who possesses five qualities is fit to attend to the sick;
he is capable of providing medicine, he knows what is suitable and what is unsuitable..."
He sets aside what is unsuitable and offers what is suitable; he attends to the sick with a mind of loving-kindness, not for the sake of material gain;
he is not disgusted by removing excrement, urine, spittle, or vomit;
and he is capable of instructing, urging, inspiring, and gladdening the sick from time to time with a discourse on the Dhamma.”
The meaning is: "Having become endowed with these five factors as thus described, one should attend to those who are ill.
By this, he indicates the conduct toward the sick that must be practiced by everyone. "Recovery" means having emerged from illness.
"Should wait upon" means one should wait upon or look after them. And if among the co-residents or pupils of the preceptors and teachers, they should be ill—
From the very beginning, one must perform all the duties, from the dyeing of the robes at their conclusion down to the dispelling of discontent;
furthermore, for those who are not ill, one should provide assistance through recitation, interrogation, exhortation, instruction, and the giving of bowls, robes, and other requisites.
For this very reason, it was stated above: "Therefore, the teacher must also conduct himself properly toward them, and the preceptor toward his co-residents."
"There is simply nothing that needs to be said.
The commentary on the exposition of the duties toward preceptors and teachers is finished.
16. Commentary on the exposition of the places for defecation and urination.
156. *Vaccapassāvaṭṭhānikaṃ*: that which exists in a place for excrement and urine is "belonging to a place for excrement and urine.

The connection is: "one should not void excrement according to seniority" (*yathāvuḍḍhaṃ*). "According to seniority" means whichever individuals are senior; the sense is that one should not abandon the order of arrival and instead follow the order of seniority.
"Excrement" (*vacca*) is merely an illustration; the intention is that one should not void urine or bathe [in that manner] either. That very same...
It establishes [the meaning] by means of the passage beginning with “yātānupubbiyā. “Yātānupubbiyā” means: the sequence or succession (*anupubbī*) of those who have gone or departed (*yātānaṃ*);
that is *yātānupubbi*, and [the phrase means] “by means of that. The sense is that this triad—“vacca... pe ... titthañca”—is applicable; it is understood to refer to a “bhikkhunī. The connection is:

“having lifted up and having entered hastily, one should not [enter]. “Ubbhajitvā” means having tossed the robe from afar. “Sahasā” means quickly. The construction is: “having coughed, one should enter.”
158. “Outside the receptacles for feces and urine” is the connection [of the phrase]. “Both” means both feces and urine.
159. “In a well” means in a cesspool. “A stick” means a scraping stick. “With a rough one” means with a harsh scraping stick.
“And even that which has been struck” means even that which has been struck by oneself or by another, and is smeared with feces; such is the meaning. “Wash it.”
If there is water, [one should rinse]; if there is no water, one should clean it even with wood. 160.

"Does not cause to come out" means he should not cause it to come out. *Capu capūti* is an onomatopoeic imitation; when doubled in the sense of scattering, *capu capu katvā* is an adverbial modifier of the action.
"He should not sip" means he should not wash his mouth. However, if there is water, he should sip.
If there is none, one should wipe [the hands] with anything available and then depart. Furthermore, in a place used by everyone, one must not leave any water remaining in the rinsing-pitcher.

"Uklāpa" means refuse. "Visodhaye" (one should clear) means that, just as in the cleaning of the monastery, one should sweep the latrines and urinals, as well as the surrounding courtyards and gate-houses.
In all these cases, however, a *dukkaṭa* offense is incurred for any breach of the proper conduct (*vatta*).
The commentary on the description of the place for urine and excrement is finished.
17. Commentary on the Description of Making an Announcement (Āpucchakaraṇaniddesa) 161.

"Making an announcement" (āpucchakaraṇaṃ) means the act of making an announcement (āpucchāya karaṇaṃ). "Without having been requested" (anajjhiṭṭho vā) means without being commanded, that is, without even being asked.

Or: "And he does not answer" means that he should not fail to answer a question asked; the intention is that having requested permission or being asked, he is permitted to do what has been stated. 162.
"Of one who speaks after having requested permission" means of one who speaks on the Dhamma or other matters after having requested permission from those senior to himself.

"Again, when another elder arrives" means when another elder comes again. "There is no need for a further request" means that apart from what has already been spoken, there is no further requirement to ask for permission.
This same rule applies even if the Sangha-thera is absent, provided one does not interrupt what has already begun.
And for one who offers the blessing of thanksgiving (*anumodanā*) in the dining hall (*bhattagga*), there is likewise no need for a request.

The connection is with the word "there is not. "Rejoicing" refers both to one who, being requested by donors, delivers a Dhamma talk by way of rejoicing in their respective merits, and to the act of rejoicing itself.
For it is said: "I allow, monks, that the senior monk should give the blessing of rejoicing in the meal hall.
Furthermore, if people have a certain person perform the rejoicing according to their own preference— [End of provided text]
"In the *Aṭṭhakathā* it is said: 'There is no offense for the one who expresses approval, nor does it become a burden for the Mahāthera.
For the Mahāthera should be asked for permission only when people are engaged in conversation while sitting together.
(163) "Living in a single dwelling with one who is senior" is the connection [of the phrase]. "With one who is senior" means together with one who is senior. "In a single dwelling" means...
In a small dwelling (*khuddakavihāra*) near the place of the three daily recitations (*savana*), not in a large monastery (*mahāvihāra*). For the suffix *-ka* has the sense of contempt here.
"He should not recite" means he should not perform the recitation (*sajjhāyana*).
Regarding the phrases "he should not proclaim the Dhamma," etc., it should be connected with the word "without having asked permission. He does not inform [others] either.
And it should be extinguished. One should not open nor bolt the window-lattice, the door-panel, or the window-shutter—the word "not" (*na*) is to be construed with every instance. 165.
While walking on the same walking-path as an elder, one should turn in the direction where the elder is; this is the construction. Where...

"Tenā" (by that) is an instrumental expression used in the sense of a locative; the meaning is "where the elder is, there [he must stay]. The intention is that one should not go elsewhere, leaving the elder behind.
"So" refers to the junior monk. "Enaṃ" refers to the elder. In all such cases, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). For this is the rule of the Khandhaka:
wherever there is a prohibition by means of the negative particle *na*, there it is an offense of wrong-doing.
The commentary on the exposition of "requesting permission" is finished.
18. Commentary on the Exposition of "Nakedness" (Nagga-niddesa) 166.

In the phrases beginning with “*vaje*,” the word *na* (“not”) should be connected. Therein, however, having supplied the appropriate verbal expressions such as “eating” and so forth, the meaning should be understood as “he does not eat food,” and so on.
167. "He does not perform services such as hand-massaging" means that he himself should also not perform them.
"In the cases of the bathhouse, water, and robes" uses the locative case in a selective sense; the meaning is "among the bathhouse, water, and robes.

This is to be connected with "two [types of] services are allowable. Regarding "services": this refers to the sphere of services to be performed for one's preceptor and others, whether in the bathhouse or with water.
Not in the case of salutations and so forth. *Duve* refers to the sauna and the water-covering. It is called *chādi* because they cover (*chādenti*);
the covering for a cloth is *vatthacchādi*. *Sabbattha* means in all formal acts.
The commentary on the exposition of nakedness is finished.
19. Explanation of the Description of Bathing (Nhānakappaniddesavaṇṇanā) 168.

*Kappa* means suitability or what is allowable (*kappiyatā*). *Nhānakappa* is the allowance regarding bathing. "A new bhikkhu should not bathe in front of or above the elders"—this is the connection. *Na ca* means "indeed not. *Purato* means "in front of" or facing. *Upari* means "above," as in being upstream of a river. 169–171.
"He should not rub his body against a wall, a pillar, or the base of a tree"—this is the connection. In this context, a *kuṭṭa* (wall) is defined as follows: [text continues]
"Brick, wood, stone, or wall. A "pillar" (*thambha*) is that which is set up after being buried at a bathing place. "Tree" (*taru*) means a tree.
An "altar" (*aṭṭhāna*) is a wooden board buried at a bathing place, having been cut and marked with lines in the shape of a checkerboard.
"One should not rub body against body"—that is, one should not rub the body with the hand of a *gandhabba* (a musician), or... [as before] ...or with a water-jar, or with the body itself.
Connection. "With a wooden hand" means with a hand made of wood.
"With a string of kuruvinda beads" means with a string threaded through a series of beads made by binding kuruvinda stone powder with lac.
"With a water-pot" means with a water-pot shaped like a lotus calyx, made after carving it from a *makara* tooth. "With his own body" means with his own person. Of one another...
The doubling [of the word] occurs in the sense of reciprocal action or mutual performance.
The connection is as follows: "the bowl... pe ... and the broad hand are suitable for all. "Bowl and brick" refers to their fragments.

"Broad hand" (*puthupāṇi*) means various or manifold hands (*puthu nānā pāṇi*); it is a conventional term (*ruḷhīvasena*) for manual labor. "For all" means for both the sick and the healthy. For the sick person...
The connection is with the phrase "it is allowable as an unmade bowl. An "unmade bowl" (akatamallaka) means the opposite of a made bowl (katamallaka).
"Foam" (pheṇa) means sea-foam.
The commentary on the description of the permissible for bathing is finished.
20. Explanation of the Non-Veneration (Avandiyaniddesa) 172.

"One who is suspended" (*ukkhitto*) refers to three types of those who have been suspended: one suspended for not seeing an offense, one for not making amends for an offense, and one suspended for not relinquishing an evil view.
One who belongs to a different community (*nānāsaṃvāsako*) is either one who differs in tenet (*laddhi*) or one who differs in formal act (*kamma*).

"And one who is subject to a heavy penalty" (*garukaṭṭha*) refers here to one who is on probation (*pārivāsika*), one deserving to be sent back to the beginning (*mūlāyapaṭikassanāraha*), one deserving the trial period (*mānattāraha*), one undergoing the trial period (*mānattacārī*), and one deserving rehabilitation (*abbhānāraha*).
However, it is permissible for these individuals to pay homage to one another.
The commentary on the description of those not to be paid homage to is finished.
21. Commentary on the Description of Skins (Cammaniddesavaṇṇanā) 173.
"The skins of deer, goats, and rams"—this is a compound. An *aja* is a goat; an *eḷaka* is a ram.
He indicates the types of deer with the words "the *rohitā*," and so forth. The mention of the *rohitā* and others is merely illustrative; it includes the *vātamiga*, *migamātuka*, and so on as well.
These are included right here. 174.

"Because it is permitted" means because it is permitted as one of the three types of hides mentioned above. The connection is: "All non-human hide is allowable for bags and sandals. "Bags" refers to cases for knives and so forth.
The commentary on the description of hides is finished.
22. Commentary on the Description of Sandals (Upāhana-niddesa-vaṇṇanā) 175.
"New sandals with multiple layers of leather are not permitted in the central regions"—this is the connection [of the rule]. "New" means those that have not been worn even once.
In this context, "sandals with multiple layers of leather" refers to those starting from four layers. A qualification is used when there is the possibility of ambiguity.

Regarding the phrase "it is purposeful": since the qualification "in the Middle Country" deviates from cases outside the Middle Country, it should be understood that sandals with double layers of leather (*guṇaṅguṇūpāhanā*) are permitted even outside the Middle Country.
Likewise, by the word "new," they are not permitted even in the Middle Country if they are not new.
However, by this statement, it is established that even a single pair of sandals with double layers of leather, if once bound on in the Middle Country, is permitted elsewhere.
It is permissible for these, but not for the rest; thus it is understood that what has been transgressed [is forbidden].

Nevertheless, because it was stated, "Monks, I allow sandals with a single sole," it should be understood that even those with a single layer of leather are permitted. "Of all" means for everyone—whether sick or healthy—in both the Middle Country and the border regions.
For it has been generally authorized by the rule: "Monks, I allow one to wear sandals within the monastery precincts."
"In all places" means whether in a village or in the forest, or elsewhere than in a monastery.
"And for one who is not well" means for one who is indeed ill. 176–9. If anyone should wear sandals that are entirely covered with snakes, or entirely covered with scorpions and lizards...
or sandals fashioned from the skins of leopards, or from the skins of cats... or sandals and shoes that are variegated, [it is a rule of training].

The construction is: "it is an offense of wrong-doing" (*dukkaṭa*). Although there is no white [cloth] mentioned in the Canon (*pāḷi*) or the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), it appears here as if stated by way of analogy.
The compound "blue and white," etc., is a *dvanda*. The compound "all those which are blue... pe ... black" is a collective compound (*samāsa*).
In such cases as "great dyers" (*mahāraṅga*), the meaning should be understood by applying the word "all" (*sabba*) according to the context, even though it is not explicitly used.
“It is by means of purpose, context, gender, propriety, and time and place that word-meanings are analyzed, not words alone. Thus it has been said. *Citrā* means variegated (*vicitrā*).
The compound is formed as “those which have blue, yellow, and so forth as their increase” (*nīlapītādī vaddhā yāsanti*). By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*), white and other colors are included.
"Grasping" (*gahaṇaṃ*): A variegated color resembling a partridge feather is grasped by the term "partridge-feather" (*tittirapatta*).
Those who possess this are called *tittirapattikā*. Regarding the phrase "having protrusions like the horns of a ram and a goat," this refers to the external object (*bāhirattha*).

However, those [protrusions] are made by attaching growths shaped like the horns of rams and goats to the position of the *kaṇṇika* (the central knob). This same method applies to the *vicchikāḷika* and others.

The analysis of the compound is: "that which has a leather strap (*khalla*) bound to its sole for the purpose of covering the heel. It is a *bahubbīhi* compound meaning "that which has a covering (*puṭa*) bound from the shank down to conceal the entire foot.
It is an *aññapadattha* (possessive) compound meaning "that which is filled with cotton (*tūla*) or lint (*picu*).

It "covers over" (*paliguṇṭheti*), thus it is a "covering" (*paliguṇṭha*); this refers to a binding that covers only the upper surface of the sole. Having joined [the foot] with that, it is made into a "pāliguṇṭhimā" (a covered shoe).
The formation of secondary derivatives (taddhita-vutti) is indeed diverse. "Vicchikālikā" refers to those [beds] that have tails like scorpions or tails like spiders.
Regarding the phrase "and with the skins of lions, tigers, leopards, and dīpīs," by way of context, "ajina" refers to deer.
"Ulūka" refers to owls and flying cats. They are called "saṅkamanīyā" because one moves or walks upon them; furthermore, these are portable items made from palm leaves and the like.

180. The construction is: “having wiped either the whole or a part. By the word “etcetera” (*ādi*) in the phrase “shoes, etc.,” everything including sandals with ram-horns, leather straps, and so forth is included.
The commentary on the description of shoes (*upāhana-niddesa-vaṇṇanā*) is finished.
23. Commentary on the Description of Not Looking At (*anālokiya-niddesa-vaṇṇanā*).
181. *Sāratto* means impassioned; the meaning is that one whose mind has given rise to lust. Regarding "a woman":

even if she is one born on that very day, or one dressed in a hundred pieces of cloth, if one gazes at her while standing outside [the house], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) even for animals. "The giver of alms" is merely an illustration;
whether it be a woman or a man, at the time of giving alms, one must not look at their face, even if one is not impassioned. *Ujjhānaṃ*.

“Deliberately thinking of it as inferior” means having the perception of anger toward that; thus, one has the perception of reproach (*ujjhānasaññī*). Here, however, even the sick person is not exempt.
By the words “in a mirror or a bowl of water,” the reflection of the face is perceived in the remaining items such as bronze bowls and in substances like sour gruel;
these are included. Furthermore, [one might wonder]: “Is my complexion still fresh, or not? Am I old, or not?”
It is proper to look [at it]. "Assa" means of the bhikkhu.
The commentary on the description of "not looking" is finished.
24. Commentary on the Description of the Eye-Salve Box (añjanī).
182. The construction is: "A round or eight- or sixteen-sided polished eye-salve container (añjanī) is suitable.

The analysis (*viggaha*) is: that which has eight and sixteen sides, that is, corners (*koṇa*). It should be understood that when there is an eight-sided [container] divided into sixteen sections, by implication (*sāmatthiya*), a four-sided one divided into eight sections is also included;
for it says in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*): "Or else, it may be straight and four-sided."
It has been stated. "Añjanī" means an ointment tube. The construction is: "three lines are also suitable at the base. "At the base" means at the bottom; that is what is meant by "below.
"Lines" refers to circular lines. The connection is: "only one line is suitable on the neck for tying.
"For tying" means for the purpose of securing the lid.

183. “Whatever form” means any form whatsoever, such as the form of a woman, and so forth. “Flower-work” means work involving garlands or creepers. “Half-moons, etc.”: here, by the word “etc.,” items such as the *agghiya* (sacrificial altar) and others are included.

“Therein” refers to the ointment-box (*añjaniya*). 184. “Bag” means an ointment bag. “Case” means a razor-case. “A stick, even if without a design, may be obtained”: this is the connection. “Stick” means an ointment-stick.
“Without a design” (*acittaka*) means that which has no painting (*citta*) upon it. Having obtained such [an item], however—
It should be used after discarding it like a pair of sandals.
185. By the word "bone," any bone whatsoever is included, with the exception of human bone.
186. "Smoke-tubes" (dhūmanettā) refers to smoking pipes; it is stated thus by means of the substitution of the vowel *ā* for *i*. "Sword-handles" (satthakadaṇḍāni) refers to sword-hilts.

They give a nose-ornament (*natthu*) to her; thus, they are "nose-ornament givers" (*natthudānā*). For [the suffix] *ī* is applied without restriction after words such as *nada*. Made of those—meaning produced from conch shells, navel-shells, and so forth.
The commentary on the description of eye-collyrium boxes (*añjanī*) is finished.
25. Commentary on the Description of Improper Beds (*akappiya-sayana*)
187–9. "Unsuitable beds" refers to high beds and large beds. However, they are called "beds" (*sayana*) by way of their function as places for reclining;
chairs and other such items are also included here, just as the remaining items are included under the term "ointment box.
The connection is that these—namely, the *āsandi*... [and so on] ...up to the "pillow on both sides"—are unsuitable. In this context, the *āsandi* is measured by the Sugata-finger.
Couches and stools with legs exceeding eight finger-breadths in length. In this context, a "stool" (*pīṭha*) is said to be not too long, similar to a couch (*mañca*).
A "cushion" (*tūlī*) is so called because it possesses three kinds of stuffing; it refers to a natural-stuffing cushion.

Regarding the term "divan" (*pallaṅka*), since the *Aṭṭhakathā* states that it is "made by placing animal figures on the legs," the placing may be done in any manner whatsoever, and the logic [of its construction] is as follows.

Regarding the statement in the *Ṭīkā*, “It is said that it is permissible if one displays a lion-form or the like right there,” this must be rejected by asking, “Why do they say such a thing? For it is stated even in the *Sārasamāsa*:
“A couch made from an improper material is called a *pallaṅka*; the *āsandi* and *pallaṅka* are high beds, while the rest are large beds.”
*Paṭikā* is a white woolen spread made of sheep’s wool. *Goṇa* is a large woolen rug (*mahākojava*) with hair more than four finger-breadths long.
*Cittaka* is a woolen spread variegated by weaving. *Uṇṇā* refers to sheep’s wool. *Paṭalikā* is a thick, tufted rug. *Vikatī* means variegated with figures such as lions, tigers, and so forth.
*Uddalomī* is one where the hair stands up on one side. *Ekantalomikā* is one where the hair stands up on both sides.
A *kutta* is a place suitable for dancing where sixteen female dancers stand.
A *koseyya* is a silk bedspread made of silk thread, embroidered with jewels. A *kaṭṭissa* is a silk rug made of silk, embroidered with jewels.
"Elephants, horses, and chariots" is a collective compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) used to denote the plurality of the components of an army; thus, [the term refers to] elephants, horses, and chariots.
*Tappurisa* (a tatpuruṣa compound) refers to "spreading upon their backs. *Ajinappaveṇī*:

having made double or triple layers of antelope skins—that is, the hides of the *ajina* deer—equal in size to a bed, they are sewn together to form a *paveṇī*. *Kadalimiga*: this belongs to the *kadalimiga*;
what is it? It is the hide. *Pavarapaccatthara*: that which is both excellent (*pavara*) and a spread (*paccatthara*), and it is spread over the white cloth.
“Kadalimigañca taṃ pavarapaccattharañca” is a compound; the meaning is: “the excellent deer-skin rug spread over white cloth,” which is what is designated as the “excellent deer-skin rug.
It is said that they prepare it in this manner.

However, in the *Ṭīkā*, something else entirely has been stated regarding what was spread by the two aforementioned [materials]; that is not correct, for [it says]: “an antelope-skin rug... [and so forth].

Because it is stated separately in the passage beginning with "should be kept" (*dhāretabbā*) that these refer specifically to the spreadings (*attharaṇa*). For when those [other items] are mentioned, it would already be implied that they serve as spreadings;
thus it was said above: "separately, such as the rug (*paṭika*) and so forth.
"A canopy with red borders" (*salohitavitāna*) is an epithet for the last [item], "having two red pillows on both sides" (*ubhatorattūpadhānaka*), meaning together with a red canopy.
"Vattamānaṃ" (the existing) is a compound. Even a white canopy is not permitted if there is an improper covering beneath it.

"Ratta-upadhānaṃ" refers to a red pillow, including a head-pillow and a foot-pillow; "rattūpadhānakaṃ" is a compound formed by eliding the middle term (*alopa-samāsa*), meaning a red pillow placed at both ends of the bed, at the positions for the head and the feet.
However, that which is a single pillow on both sides, colored red and so forth—
It must be variegated and its dimensions must be appropriate. Herein, these are the dimensions:

in width, the distance between two of the three corners is four fingerbreadths (vidatthi), while in the middle it is one fist-span (muṭṭhi-ratana); in length, however, it is one and a half spans or two spans.
By the word "using," [it is implied] for one who makes it or causes it to be made, in some cases...
"It is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) involving cutting off," thus it is explained.

190. Regarding the phrase "on a formal seat, in the dining hall, and also in a house, on the remaining three types of seats belonging to a layperson, or when they are provided by a layperson, it is permitted to sit"—this should be understood as a syntactical connection (*ajjhāhāra*) that links the words. By the term "belonging to a layperson" (*gihisantake*), [it is indicated that...]

One may also mark it as belonging to the Saṅgha. It was stated in general terms: “I allow you, monks, [the use of furniture], except for the three: the high chair (āsandi), the divan (pallaṅka), and the stuffed mattress (tūlikā), as well as what is manufactured by householders.
However, because a general statement can apply to specific instances, the meaning here—regarding the "three beginning with the high chair"—should be understood by connecting it as follows:
among the three beginning with the high chair, [only] those other than the Dhamma-seat (dhammāsana) are permitted. For in the Commentary it says: “The high chair... [and so forth].
In the sequence of the Pāḷi beginning with “pallaṅko gonako,” after omitting the first two items such as the *āsandī*, it is stated:
“The *gonaka* and the others are not permitted to be used by spreading them over beds or chairs, whether in a communal monastery (*saṅghika-vihāra*) or a private dwelling (*puggalika-vihāra*).

However, they may be used on a Dhamma-seat (*dhammāsana*) under the condition that it is regarded as a household item; even there, it is not permitted to lie down. Regarding the dining hall (*bhattagga*):
The place for giving is in a monastery (*vihāra*). However, the Dharma-seat (*dhammāsana*) may be anywhere. "In a house" means inside a house.
By the phrase "it is permitted to sit," it is indicated that lying down is not allowed. "Folding" (*saṅkhepa*) means inclusion;
"the bed has its folding upon the floor-covering" is the compound (*samāsa*). From that floor-covering which constitutes the inclusion—namely, the floor-covering—...
It should be understood as "only a ground-covering. "And to lie down" means that one may lie down or sit down after having spread out one's own allowable ground-covering.

For it is said in the Commentary: "One must lie down only after having spread out with one's own ground-covering either the floor that has been swept, or a lodging-place consisting of a ground-covering, or a bed or chair belonging to the Saṅgha."
This has been stated. Furthermore, this is a statement of the defining characteristic regarding the use of items such as high seats (*āsandi*) when they have undergone a change of state.
For it was said by the Blessed One: “I allow you, monks, to cut off the legs of a high seat and use it; to break off the tassels of a couch (*pallaṅka*) and use it;
to pull apart the stuffing of a cushion and make it into a bolster; and to use the remainder as a floor-covering.”

191. Regarding the phrase "four-armed seats... and five-limbed [seats] with high legs are allowable": the connection should be made by transposing the words according to their meaning, or it should be understood as being connected with the word "allowable" (*kappiyā*). In this context, the compound is to be analyzed as:
those which have four arms (i.e., corners) and are also seats. This refers to [seats] by way of three backrests and four legs.
The compound consists of seven factors. There are five factors by way of the single shelter (*ekāpassaya*).
However, because it is stated that four-legged stools have a separate status as allowable (*kappiya*), it is understood that "seven factors" and so forth refer to long [forms].

Since the *bhattagga* (hall for meals) is taught in a single grammatical connection (*ekayoga*) in the Canon, for those things taught in a single connection, there is either simultaneous occurrence or simultaneous cessation; thus, [the term] "in the house" (*ghare*) [is used].
By this, the dining hall (*bhattagga*) is also included. The word *eva* is used in the sense of "only" (*aṭṭhānappayutta*).
Therefore, the connection is: "Cotton-filled beds and chairs are permitted only for sitting, whether in a house or in the dining hall. In this regard, the canonical text (*pāḷi*) says:
"Now at that time, people were arranging cotton-filled beds and chairs in the dining hall within the village."

The bhikkhus, being apprehensive, did not sit down. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. "I allow you, bhikkhus, to sit down on what has been prepared by a householder, but you must not lie down upon it.
However, for one who does so, or causes it to be done, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) involving tearing [the robe].

192. The analysis of the compound is: "one of these six types of robes that are suitable [is] the skin. "Five kinds of cotton" refers to the fivefold enumeration based on the counting of cotton from *coḷa* (hemp) and so forth. "In all places" means everywhere, including the monastery, beds, chairs, and so on. 193.
"The three kinds of down" refers to the three kinds of down from trees such as the *simbali*, from milky creepers and the like, and from grasses such as *eraka*.
"The inner lining of the cotton" refers to the fivefold inner lining made of *coḷa* and so forth. "The hair of beasts and birds"—this includes everything.

The rest is as follows. By the word "deer" (*miga*), all four-footed animals such as lions and so forth are included; by the word "birds" (*pakkhi*), all [birds] such as swans and peacocks are included.

Now, one might object: "Since wool is already contained within the term 'lotus-stalk core' (*bhisigabbha*), and since the hair of deer and birds is also thereby included, does not the fault of tautology (*punaruttidoso*) arise when they are mentioned separately?
This fault does not arise, because there is a specific purpose in distinguishing them by excluding human hair.

But is it not the case that even here there is the same fault? For since [the text] says, “with human hair and wool,” and so forth, it is understood from the fact that they are being led over the interior of the *bhisī* (cushion covers) that this very same *bhisī*-interior is also present in the bolster (*bibbohana*). True;

nevertheless, there is no fault, for there is freedom of usage regarding the employment of a word whose meaning is already understood. One should connect [the passage] by modifying it as follows: “In the *masūraka* (pillow), cotton is permitted.”
They say that what is called *masūraka* is a stuffed cushion made of leather or skin.
194. Regarding wool and human hair: if leaves, pure *tamālaka*, or flowers have not been inspected, they do not qualify as a seat;
this is the connection [of the rule]. By the term "human hair," it is indicated that here "wool" does not refer exclusively to sheep's wool.
Now, he shows that even the feathers of birds and the hair of four-footed animals may be either allowable or unallowable meat.
"Flowers" refers to flowers such as the *piyaṅgu* and *bakula*. By the word "tamālaka" itself, the leaf is taken metaphorically, and thus it is called "tamālaka.
"Unexamined" means not investigated. But what kind is to be examined, and what kind is not to be examined?
That which is understood through formal adjudication need not be examined; the other [type] must be examined by one feeling it with the hand.
The commentary on the description of improper furniture is finished.
26. Commentary on the Description of Sharing a Seat.
195. The connection is: "A single seat for monks is permitted within three years' interval.
In this context, "a single seat" (*ekāsana*) refers to two persons sitting together on one seat, such as a bed or similar furniture; the letter *m* is a euphonic conjunction (*sandhi*).

To the question "Of what kind?", he says: "within three years' interval" (*tivassantara*). That which has an interval of three years is "three-year-intervalled"; that is, [the senior monk] is more than two years older, or [the junior monk] is younger.
Or, "a bhikkhu who has three years' difference" means one who possesses a three-year interval; that is, one who has a gap of three years [between ordination and age].
However, for one who is older by one year, younger by one year, or exactly one year [older], there is no need to speak of such a state of possessing an interval.
Alternatively, "tivassantaraṃ" is in the accusative case used in the sense of the instrumental; the meaning is "together with a three-year interval."
He establishes that very point with the words “seven years,” and so forth.
196. The connection is: “the Sage permitted. “All indeed” means together with all, both those who share a seat and those who do not.
197. He shows what a long seat is with the words “the edge,” and so forth. That which is sufficient for three people to sit upon is the edge; that is a long seat.
The connection [is as follows]: "End" means the last. However, showing that those who share the same seat may sit on a long seat, he said, "On a couch," and so forth.
In all cases, because it is not done according to the rule, it is an *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing).
The commentary on the description of those who share the same seat is finished.
27. Commentary on the Description of Non-Communion (Asaṃvāsa-niddesa) 198.

"One who has been suspended" (ukkhitto) refers to one who has been suspended for not acknowledging an offense, for not making amends for it, or for not relinquishing an evil view—being thus designated as one who is in a state of non-communion due to a formal act (kamma).

"One who is not fully ordained" (anupasampanno) refers to those designated as female trainees (sikkhamānā), male novices (sāmaṇera), female novices (sāmaṇerī), and those who have renounced the training (sikkhā-paccakkhāta).
“Not fully ordained”: one who has cut off the root, meaning one who has committed an extreme offense (antimavatthu). Regarding those who have been suspended (*ukkhitto*):

one whose communion is different because he holds the view that has arisen, “These are speakers of Dhamma,” is called “one of different communion” (*nānāsaṃvāso*), specifically referring to one who follows the views of those who have been suspended.

“Outside the boundary” (*nissīmā*) means having departed from the boundary; it refers to the intermediate zone between boundaries (*sīmantarikā*) and the area outside the boundary (*bahisīmā*). Within that [area], within arm’s reach (*hatthapāse*)...

Even if one is standing within [the boundary], if one does not share communion with those within the boundary, one is "standing outside the boundary" (*nissīmaṭṭhita*). Standing in the air, in the sky, is "standing in the air" (*vehāyasaṇṭhita*), according to the method of *bindu*-addition.
In this regard, even in a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) such as "nānāsaṃvāso ca," the neuter gender sometimes deviates;
thus, there is an absence of the neuter gender, as in the case of "maggāmaggo. "A single legal act" (*ekakamma*), "a single recitation" (*ekuddesa*), and "identical training" (*samasikkhatā*).

This is what is called the threefold "communion" (saṃvāsa). Those who do not possess this are "those outside of communion" (asaṃvāsā); they are to be excluded by being kept beyond the reach of one's hand.

For when these three types of those suspended (ukkhitaka) exist, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for one performing a formal act such as the Uposatha, while for others there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
The commentary on the description of "those outside of communion" is finished.
28. Commentary on the Exposition of Kamma (Kammaniddesavaṇṇanā) 199.

“There are four kinds of kamma: a factional illegal kamma, a unanimous illegal kamma, a factional legal kamma, and a unanimous legal kamma”—this is the remainder [of the text]. Therein, “a factional illegal kamma” means [a kamma] performed by a faction.
An illegal act (adhammakamma) is that which is to be performed by the Saṅgha. This same principle applies in all cases. Furthermore, "faction" (vagga) refers to a group;

and in the context of formal acts (kamma) requiring a quorum of four or more, it is intended here when there is the absence of as many members as are entitled to participate in the act, or when those entitled to give their consent have not brought their consent, or when those present raise an objection—even if only one among them does so.
Regarding the term *adhammakamma* (an illegal act): here, "dhamma" refers to that which has been handed down as follows:

"If, monks, in a formal act (*kamma*) requiring a motion and a second [announcement], one performs the act with only a single motion and does not proclaim the formal statement (*kammavācā*), it is an illegal act";

likewise, [it applies] to those cases handed down as being performed with only a single motion, or similarly with two motions and only a single formal statement, or similarly with two formal statements.
Likewise, by way of the nature of omitting or altering [the formal act], setting aside a *ñatti*-kamma, and performing seven kinds of formal acts—
namely, the *tajjanīya*, *pabbājanīya*, *paṭisāraṇīya*, *niyassa*, *tassapāpiyyasika*, and *ukkhepanīya*—
which are introduced in the text both for one who is not entitled to such acts and for one who is entitled to them but performs them in violation; and by way of the text as it has come down.

There is the inverted text, the text arrived at by way of formal acts such as full ordination (*upasampadā*), and the text arrived at by performing the seven types of formal acts as they occur—namely, those designated as *sammukhāvinaya*, *sativinaya*, *amūḷhavinaya*, *paṭiññākaraṇa*, *yebhuyyasika*, *tassapāpiyasika*, and *tiṇavatthāraka*.
By means of that, there are four kinds [of formal acts]: those designated as *apalokana*, *ñatti*, *ñattidutiya*, and *ñatticatuttha*.
Kamma is *dhamma*-kamma; its opposite is *adhamma*-kamma. By way of contrast, that which is performed by a unanimous assembly (*samagga*) should be understood as *dhamma*-kamma.
It is *dhammika* because it possesses the *dhamma*, meaning the aforementioned *pāḷi* (scripture), or because it is performed according to the *dhamma*.
Its opposite is *adhammika*. "The fourth alone" refers to the completion of the four types of kamma among those four; it is the one performed by a unanimous assembly and is *dhammika*.

"By the state of the remaining actions, the state of being an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) is characterized for the monk"; thus, in the phrase "in the remaining actions," the locative case is used in the sense of a characteristic of a state (*bhāvalakkhaṇe*).
"Offense of wrong-doing" means that it is a *dukkaṭa* because of having performed illegal formal acts (*adhammakamma*) and factional formal acts (*vaggakamma*) which are subject to subversion.
200. Now, as for this so-called "legal act performed by a unanimous assembly," the classification of those assemblies by whom it should be performed is as follows:
In order to show this, he said, “a group of four,” and so forth. Because the words *cattāro* (four) and the others function as numerals (*saṅkhyeyya*), the analysis is:

“a group of four” (*catunnaṃ vaggo*), and so on. “One who belongs to a group of ten or twenty” (*dasavīsativaggiko*): the analysis is “a group of ten and twenty” (*dasavīsatīnaṃ vaggo*) by way of the division into groups of ten and twenty;
the suffix *-ika* is used in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*). “A group of twenty” (*vīsatiyā vaggo*): the analysis is “a group accompanied by more than [twenty]” (*atirekena sahito vīsativaggo*).

201–2. He determines [the number] for five types of formal acts (*kamma*) by means of the words “four,” and so forth. It should be understood that, having applied the phrase “a group of four” and so on—excluding the acts of rehabilitation (*abbhāna*), full ordination (*upasampadā*), and the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*)—it is shown that one is eligible for all formal acts.
In those various instances, the word “and” (*ca*) includes the groups of four and so forth in the performance of the act. However, here the word “all” (*sabba*)...

Because certain [procedures] such as rehabilitation (*abbhāna*) have been set aside, the term "all" (*sabbe*) is understood here as "partial all" (*padesasabba*). "Qualified for the act" (*kammappatta*) means one who has reached, is fit for, or is suitable for the formal act (*kamma*).

"The other" refers to a group of twenty or more than twenty. Regarding the phrase "in all acts," the word "all" (*sabba*) here signifies "absolute all" (*sabbasabba*). But is it not the case that while a group of twenty is qualified for the act, a group of more than twenty is not?
It is understood that [the number] must be complete. If that is so, why was it stated [in the rule]? True;

nevertheless, it was stated for the purpose of making it known that the formal act (kamma) which is to be performed by a Saṅgha consisting of four groups or more cannot be validly carried out by one with fewer members, whereas it is valid when there are more.

203. Now, he shows by means of the words beginning with “four” that the requirement must be fulfilled by the bringing of consent from a group of four or more. Because they have not fallen into the state of being pārājika or other such offenses...

Those whose self (attā) remains in its natural state (pakatiyā), by its very essence (sabhāvena), or those whose self is not departed from that [state] regarding their actions, are "those of natural status" (pakatattakā);

they are others than those who have committed a *pārājika*, those who have been suspended (*ukkhitaka*), those who have received [a penalty], and those who belong to a different community (*nānāsaṃvāsaka*). "Others" (*pare*) refers to those of the same kind who are within the same boundary (*ekasīmaṭṭhā*).
"In the rest as well" (*sesepi*) means even in the remaining matters to be performed by a quorum of five or more.

204. Now, in order to show the validity or invalidity of a formal act (*kamma*) based on defects in the site, the motion, the proclamation, the boundary, and so forth—and therein to demonstrate the nature of the offense and other factors regarding the assembly and opposition to the act—the author says "fourfold," etc.

A formal act to be performed by a quorum of four or more may be fulfilled either by a group of those who are not in communion (*asaṃvāsa*), or by a group sufficient for one eligible for the act (*kammāraha*), or by a group sufficient for one subject to a heavy penalty, such as the formal act of probation (*parivāsa*).

The construction [of the sentence]. And here, one who is worthy of the formal act (*kamma*) is distinct from one who is "heavy" (*garukaṭṭha*); however, one who has laid down the training (*nikkhittavatta*), though heavy, certainly serves to complete the quorum.
"Done" means performed by a quorum of four or more. "In the absence of an obstacle" (*vāreyya*):
even if there is not even a single obstacle, it is called "in the absence of an obstacle"; the meaning is that when obstacles are being created by wicked persons.
When there is an obstacle to the holy life (*brahmacariya*). If they do not prevent it despite it being an obstacle, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
"Having seen" means that each reveals their own view and conviction to one another, saying, "This is an illegitimate legal act (*adhammakamma*);
this is not acceptable to me. "A single resolve" means a single monk's resolution, thinking, "This is not acceptable to me."
"Should do" is the remainder [of the phrase]. "More than that" means more than three. However, those [three] are capable, when acting as a Saṅgha, of bringing their own legal procedure to completion.
206. "One with a distracted mind" means one who is insane. "Afflicted by pain" means one overcome by painful sensation. "Does not take root" means that it does not take hold once grasped.
207. The connection is: "even if he reports it to someone immediately following him... ... "the monk. Within a single boundary...

"Stays" means residing within the same boundary (*ekasīmaṭṭha*). "Of equal communion" (*samasaṃvāsa*) means one whose communion is equal. He is both one who stays within the same boundary and one of equal communion;
he is both a regular member (*pakatatta*) and one who stays within the same boundary and is of equal communion; and he is also this monk—thus, in all cases, it is a *kammadhāraya* compound. Of him.
Here, however, "regular member" (*pakatatta*) is intended to mean one whose virtue (*sīla*) is unimpaired. "Of one who announces" means [one who announces] his own view.
"Of one who reveals. "It takes root" means that the objection takes root. 208.
"A legal act" (*dhammikakamma*) refers to an act such as a formal motion (*apalokanakamma*) that ought to be performed according to the Dhamma.

"One should object" (*paṭikkoseyya*) means one should prevent it. The meaning should be understood by connecting the word "or" (*vā*) with the phrase "either bodily unity or consent" (*tirokkhā kāyasāmaggiṃ vā chandaṃ vā*). "Tirokkhā" means in the absence of [the person].
Thus, *sammukhā* is a particle, like the word *sammukhā*; or else, its meaning is "beyond," that is, outside from the range of the sense faculties (*indriyavisaya*).
The commentary on the description of action (*kamma-niddesa*) is finished.
29. Commentary on the description of the avoidance of wrong livelihood (*micchājīva-vivajjanā-niddesa*).

209. That by which one lives having come to it is "livelihood" (*ājīva*). What is that? It is the effort in seeking the requisites. Wrong livelihood is *micchājīva*; the avoidance of that is the avoidance of wrong livelihood.
As for this [avoidance], in terms of its meaning, it is shown as the practice consisting in the perfection of restraint according to the Pātimokkha, as in the passage:

"Here, a bhikkhu dwells restrained with the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort. Thus, it is by way of demonstrating the practice through the attainment of restraint according to the Pātimokkha.
The conduct has been set forth in due order as the cause for the offenses of *pārājika*, *saṅghādisesa*, *thullaccaya*, *pācittiya*, *pāṭidesanīya*, *dubbhāsita*, and *dukkaṭa*;
it consists of the transgression of those training rules proclaimed for the sake of livelihood— namely, making false claims, acting as a go-between, making claims under another pretext,
requesting exquisite food, requesting food from a nun, and requesting rice-gruel and boiled rice— as well as hypocrisy, flattery, and hinting.

And there is the virtue of purification of livelihood, which consists in the avoidance of wrong livelihood, occurring through such evil qualities as extortion (*nippesikatā*)— the seeking of gain by means of gain— and so forth. Now, as for its manifestation here in some cases,
it is shown according to the training in higher virtue (*adhisīlasikkhā*), known as restraint by the Pātimokkha, and by way of the fourfold protection and insight (*vipassanā*).
It should be understood that this is for the purpose of illustrating the factors conducive to the two trainings known as higher mind (*adhicitta*) and higher wisdom (*adhipaññā*).

Such things are to be understood in this way; he shows this by means of the passage beginning with "wood" (*dāru*). In that context, "wood" and so forth are the appropriate actions (*pattikamma*) for the word "I give" (*dade*).
"Powder" (*cuṇṇa*) refers to bathing powders such as *sirīsa* powder and the like. "Bathing water and mouth-water" (*nhānamukhodaka*)—

"Bath and face": this is a compound meaning "water for that [purpose]. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), one includes leaves and so forth. "By means of gathering families" (*kulasaṅgahā*) means by performing the act of gathering families. 210.
One who carries about (*paribhaṭati*) other people's children—that is, looks after them—is a *paribhaṭa*; the work of a *paribhaṭa* is *pāribhaṭaka*.
In its literal sense, it means "mere buffoonery. This is a name for the way a man of good family is attended to through decoration and the like.

Just as when bean soup is being cooked, only some beans might not be cooked while the rest are cooked, so too, in the case of a person whose speech contains only a small portion of truth while the remainder is false, that is called "bean-soup" (muggasūpa). It is simply "bean-soup" (muggasūpo).
