Just as when bean soup is being cooked, some beans indeed do not cook while the others do, so it is with the person whose words contain only a certain amount of truth and the rest is untruthful.
This person is called "bean-soup" (*muggasuppa*) by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) because of his resemblance to bean soup; the state of being such is *muggasuppatā*.
This is a designation for making a livelihood through truth and falsehood. *Vatthuvijjā* is the science related to house sites and so forth.
By the compound *pāribhaṭakatā cādi*, there is a dual compound; due to the absence of the neuter gender, [the form is] *pāri... vijjā*; by that. But the short vowel—
By way of composition in verses, it is likewise long. *Paheṇa* is the dispatching or assigning of various persons to various tasks.
Any task that must be performed by a messenger with care is *dūtakamma*. *Pesana* means sending; sending by means of the leg or foot is *jaṅghapesana*;
because one possesses that, it is called *jaṅghapesaniya*. Of those various...
This is a designation for the carrying of messages or counter-messages between householders in different villages, regions, and so forth.

211. Giving a bribe out of a desire for gain is "anuppadāna" (bestowing). By means of something else that is censured by the Fully Enlightened One, condemned by the Buddha—such as the science of limbs (*aṅgavijjā*), the science of constellations (*nakkhattavijjā*), the science of dreams (*supinavijjā*), the science of spirits (*bhūtavijjā*), or the like.
212. "Viññatti" (solicitation) is the making known of things to those who are not related and have not invited one; it is an application of body and speech proceeding by way of requesting.
Seeking requisites through a wrong livelihood that is censured by the Buddhas is *anesanā* (improper search).

*Abhūtullapanā* (boasting of what is unreal) is the speaking or declaring of superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*) that are non-existent and not found within oneself. "By means of scheming and so forth" refers to scheming, boasting, and the rest.
Therein, for one who is dependent on gain, honor, and fame, it consists of the seeking of requisites, whispering to neighbors, and the assuming of postures.

Deceit (*kuhana*) is the act of causing wonder among people. *Lapanā* (flattery) is the act of addressing people who have come to the monastery with such phrases as, "For what purpose have you gentlemen come? Are you inviting the monks?
or "The king has confidence in me, and so-and-so and so-and-so, the king’s high ministers, also have confidence in me," and so forth.
It is also [the act of asking] when seeing people leaving after taking solid food, "Did you receive any solid food? and so on.

Giving hints and so forth by means of indirect methods is *nemittikatā* (hinting). Reprimands such as "one who lacks faith, one who lacks confidence," and so forth, as well as verbal disparagement and the like by means of such methods as "you should speak thus on this matter," constitute *nippesikatā* (belittling).
Desiring to take much by deceiving with little gain is *lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatā* (seeking gain through gain). [The term] *kuladūsaka*, etc., refers to those who corrupt families and so forth.
Here, by the word "etcetera," the acceptance of money and trading in money are included.
The commentary on the exposition of the avoidance of wrong livelihood is finished.
30. Commentary on the Exposition of the Course of Conduct.
213. "One who wears sandals... [etc. ...or one who enters the monastery with his robe placed on his head"—this is the connection.
"With an umbrella" means having an umbrella placed on the head. "Veiled" means having covered oneself including the head.
"The vicinity of the boundary of the precincts" refers to the enclosure of a walled monastery, or for an unwalled one, the area suitable for an enclosure; this is what is stated.

Having reached [the monastery], having performed all such acts as removing one's sandals, and so forth, one should enter the ārāma; this is the meaning obtained here through the method of exclusion (*vyatireka*).

214. "One should not wash one's feet with drinking water" is the connection. Having reached the place for returning, having set aside one's bowl and robes in a secluded spot, and having sat down in a suitable place, one should ask for and drink drinking water; [one should also use] the water for washing, as previously described.

The intention is that the feet should be washed. By the phrase "one should also pay homage to those residing there who are senior," it is indicated that after inquiring about the rains-residence (*vassa*), the junior resident monk should cause [the senior] to be paid homage. Regarding "he should inquire about the lodging":
he should inquire about the lodging, asking, "Which lodging has been reached—is it one already occupied or not yet occupied? And this is for the purpose of inquiry.
This is the statement of the characteristics. Therefore, one should inquire about whether the bed has been slept upon and so forth, as prescribed in the duties for resident monks (*āvāsika-vatta*).

If they say, "It has not been slept upon," one should knock on the door, wait a moment, open the latch, push the door open, look inside while standing outside, enter, and perform all the duties regarding the lodgings (*senāsana-vatta*). This is the duty for visiting monks (*āgantuka-vatta*).
"215–6. ‘One who is about to depart should set out’ is the connection. ‘Having put away,’ etc., are the preliminary actions for this.
‘Wooden and earthenware goods’: here, wooden goods refer to items such as beds and chairs; earthenware goods refer to items such as dye-vessels and the like. ‘Having put away’ means:
if there is [such property], having arranged it in a place sheltered from rain. ‘Having shut’ means: having closed the doors and windows."
"Having carefully protected it" means: having prepared a bed on four stones, and having carefully protected it by stacking the lodgings one upon another—placing bed upon bed and stool upon stool.
"Not" (*na ca*) means "neither. (The duties of one departing on a journey. 217–8. "A resident" (*āvāsiko*):
this is the subject for the verbs "should prepare" (*paññapeyya*) and so forth. Because of the completion of tasks such as the performance of new construction work (*navakamma*).
One who has a dwelling (*āvāsa*) as his residence is called an *āvāsika*. However, one for whom there is merely the act of residing in a monastery (*vihāra*) is a *nevāsika* (resident).

Both of these are included here under the term *āvāsika*. Regarding the phrase "starting with the washing of the feet" (*pādodappabhuti*), the word "starting with" (*pabhuti*) includes the footstool and the foot-washing stand.
The construction is: "having gone out to meet him, he should take [his] bowl and robe."
"Arranges a bed and seat" means he should arrange or designate a bed and seat, saying, "This resting place belongs to you.
(219) "Inhabited" means previously occupied by monks. He tells [the donor] whether it is within range for alms-gathering or not, saying, "This is a village for walking for alms..."
The meaning is that he might speak of the alms-resort (*gocara*) as being "far" or "near," or "one should wander for alms early in the morning, or during the day";
or he might speak of what is not a proper resort (*agocara*), such as "a village of those with wrong view" or "a village where alms are restricted," and so forth.

The phrases beginning with "places for defecation and urination" are also the objects of the verb "he should speak. "The authorization for trainees" (*sekhasammuti*) refers to a family to which the Saṅgha grants the authorization for trainees, and that family itself.
220. Regarding the time for entering and departing: this refers to the time for entering and departing, thinking, "In certain places there may be wild beasts or non-human beings;

at this time one should enter and depart. Furthermore, all these duties, beginning with the preparation of seats, must be performed except when an elder has arrived, or when setting aside work on robes, or medicine for one who is not excessively ill.
[The usual duties] must be performed. However, for one who is seriously ill, only medicine should be provided.
Even one performing the duties at the shrine courtyard (cetiyaṅgaṇa) should begin to perform his [the sick person's] duties as well. For a wise visitor would say, "First prepare medicine;
sweep the shrine courtyard. Furthermore, he should be fanned with a fan, his feet should be washed, and [he should be anointed] with oil.
[The seat] should be smeared [with oil]. If the back aches, it should be massaged. However, for a new arrival, one should point out [the seat], saying, "This is the seat;
sit here," and so forth; showing this, he said, "Even while sitting," and so on. By the phrase "even while sitting," he indicates [the other postures] such as "even while standing" and so forth.
"Should designate" means one should speak with care. This is the duty of a resident monk (*āvāsika-vatta*).
However, because it is indicated by the general term "conduct" (*vatta*), one should not sit too close to the elder monks;
rather, having left space for one or two seats from the seat where the Great Elder is sitting, one should sit when told, "Sit down.
One should not block junior monks from their seats, nor should one sit covering oneself with the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*). [One should maintain] silence...
The water-rite (udakakicca) must be performed; one should take a portion of rice sufficient to leave room for the soup.
The senior monk (thera) should say: "Set aside a small amount of rice and so forth, and distribute everything equally to all.
The senior monk must not eat yet; once he has finished eating, he must not receive water [for washing] until everyone else has finished.
When returning from the meal hall, one should exit in a manner appropriate to the occasion and proceed along a sparse path;
furthermore, one should fulfill the training rules (sekhiyavatta) corresponding to that situation. This is the duty regarding the meal hall.
One should enter the village with great care and without haste, thinking as one enters a dwelling: "By this way I shall enter; by this way I shall exit."
One should observe [the situation]; one should not enter too hastily, nor should one leave too hastily; one should stand neither too far away nor too close;
one should not stand for too long; one should turn back without being too light; one should stand after having perceived the sign of a desire to give;
whoever returns first from the village must perform all the duties, such as preparing the seat and so forth.

He who comes later must perform all such duties as the clearing away of the seats; furthermore, he should fulfill the training rules (*sekhiya-vatta*) appropriate to that situation, and this practice of the alms-round (*piṇḍacārika-vatta*) must also be carried out.
Having fulfilled all the duties in the place of residence, he should then depart from there, properly dressing himself and putting on his robes.
One must perform the entire code of conduct for alms-gathering, beginning with the instruction that one should enter a village without hurrying.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the following duties for forest-dwellers have already been prescribed: drinking water, water for washing, fire, a tinder-box, and a walking stick must be kept ready;
the constellations and lunar mansions, either in their entirety or in part, must be mastered; and one must become skilled in the directions.
The commentary on the exposition of the cycle (*vattaniddesa*) is finished.
31. Commentary on the Exposition of Alternatives (*vikappanāniddesa*) 221.

Regarding the terms *sammukhā* (in the presence) and *parammukhā* (in the absence): the analysis (*viggaha*) is "one's own face" (*sassa mukhaṃ*) and "another's face" (*parassa mukhaṃ*). [They are used] by way of being in the presence (*sammukhena*) and by way of being in the absence (*parammukhena*).

The meaning is as follows: the construction is that two types of *vikappanā* (formal assignment) have been stated, namely the distinction between *sammukhā-vikappanā* (assignment in the presence of the person) and *parammukhā-vikappanā* (assignment in the absence of the person).
"Distinction" (*bheda*) means specifically. Alternatively, it is a compound: *sassa mukhaṃ* (the face of him), and *mukha-sambandhi-vacanaṃ* (a word related to the face) belongs to this *vikappanā*;

thus [it is] *sammukhā*. Likewise for *parammukhā*. *Sammukhā* and *parammukhā*—their distinction (*tassā bheda*), from that [distinction]. [The locative case form: *sammukhāya*, [meaning] by way of *sammukhā-vikappanā* (assignment in the presence).
"By one who knows" means by one who understands the procedure for assigning (*vikappana*) and the procedure for relinquishing (*paccuddhāra*).

222. "By him" means by that monk in whose presence one assigns it. "Use, etc. refers to use (*paribhoga*), giving away (*vissajjana*), and formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*). 224–5. Regarding the phrase "another [assigns] in the presence":
here the word *vā* has the sense of an alternative; the meaning is "or else" (*atha vā*), serving the function of the particle *api*.
Or the word *vā*—it should be understood as following the word *aparā*. The meaning is: "There is also another kind of face-to-face assignment.

To explain how this is so, he says: "Of a bhikkhu," and so forth. Because it was stated, "of five who share the same Dhamma," [the rule applies] in cases such as "of the bhikkhu Tissa," and likewise for a bhikkhunī Tissa, a female trainee (sikkhamānā) Tissa, a novice nun (sāmaṇerī) Tissa, or a male novice (sāmaṇera) Tissa.
It should also be understood that this applies to a novice (sāmaṇera). 226.

*Parammukhāvikappanā* means by means of an assignment made in the absence [of the recipient]; or it should be taken as *parammukhāvikappanā*, the meaning of which is "how is the assignment made in the absence?
227. A *mitta* is a firm friend. A *sanditṭha* is a friend merely seen. Herein, however, regarding the two types of assignment...
What is the distinction? First, regarding *sammukhāvikappanā* (assignment in the presence): having made the assignment oneself, one has another perform the relinquishment (*paccuddhāra*);
it is for this reason that it is called *sammukhāvikappanā*. Regarding *parammukhāvikappanā* (assignment in the absence):
having had another make the assignment, one has another perform the relinquishment; it is for this reason that it is called *parammukhāvikappanā*. This is the distinction here.
228. Regarding "nearness and distance, unity": here, the state of being near or far is to be understood in the same manner as explained in the section on formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*).

229. "Ten days... [etc. ...when there is expectation, one does not incur an offense of forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) for a *māsaka* coin that has neither been formally determined nor assigned to another" is the syntactical connection.
"Ten days" (*dasāhaṃ*) refers to ten days taken together. In all these instances, the accusative case is used to express continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*). Therein:

The dawn of the day on which the robe was obtained is dependent upon that day of its acquisition; therefore, when the dawn rises on the eleventh day from the day the robe was acquired, it becomes subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*). Thus he said, "within ten days. Regarding the phrase "or one month":
because it is stated that "when the *kathina* has not been spread, [the period is] the last month of Kattika," it follows that when the *kathina* has been spread, the period is five months.
*Kathinaṃ atthataṃ yasmiṃ vihāre* is a compound meaning "the monastery in which the kaṭhina has been spread.
*Pāripūratthaṃ* is analyzed as "that whose purpose is fulfillment" (*pāripūri attho yassa*). It is an adverbial modifier; the sense is "having made fulfillment the objective.

*Ūnassa* refers to that which is deficient by whatever amount is required for the robe to suffice for the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*), namely, by the deficiency of either eleven months or seven months.

Regarding the root robe that has arisen during the period following the robe season: "If there is expectation" means if there is an expectation based on the thought, "I shall receive it from somewhere, such as from the Saṅgha.
Both [terms] are indicated here with the elision of the letter *ya*. Alternatively, *sati* is a particle, or it is stated with a change of gender.
In this context, however, by way of contrast, there is an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) in cases such as exceeding the ten-day limit.
"It should be understood as an offense entailing expiation (*pācittiya*).
The commentary on the exposition of formal assignment (*vikappanā*) is concluded.
32. Commentary on the exposition of dependence (*nissaya*).
230. *Byattassa*: In the phrase “*kāriyan*,” the sixth case (*chaṭṭhī*) is used for the agent (*kattari*) in connection with the word *kitaka*.
One who is called “learned” (*byatta*) is one endowed with five factors, monks:
he knows what is an offense, he knows what is not an offense, he knows a light offense, he knows a heavy offense, and furthermore, both of these...
“The Pātimokkhas are welcomed in detail, well analyzed, well expounded, and well determined, both in terms of the rules and their specific phrasing.
It is with these five factors, monks, that a monk endowed with them may live independently.
Thus should one understand what is meant by being “experienced” and “learned and experienced.”
In this context, "well-analyzed" (*suvibhattāni*) means thoroughly analyzed, being free from the faults of confusion regarding words and their sequence.

"Well-proclaimed" (*suppavattīni*) means they have become familiar and have been mastered through recitation. "Well-determined by the Suttas" (*suvinicchitāni suttaso*) means they have been well-determined according to the suttas to be drawn from the Khandhaka and Parivāra.
"Well-determined by the phrasing" (*anubyañjanaso*) means they are well-determined through the completeness of syllables and words, and are thus unbroken.
The syllables are not inverted. By this, the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary) is indicated; for this determination arises from the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

Furthermore, one who is learned and proficient—at the very least, having mastered two *mātikās* by heart, and having mastered four recitation-sections (*bhāṇavāra*) from the Suttanta for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma on the fortnightly days for the assembled assemblies—[is qualified].
There is one method of discourse, such as the *Andhakavinda*, *Mahā-Rāhulovāda*, and *Aṅguttara* (Ambaṭṭha) suttas, for the purpose of giving expositions;

three types of thanksgiving (*anumodanā*) for the purpose of expressing gratitude on occasions such as meals provided by the Saṅgha or auspicious ceremonies; the determination of what constitutes a formal act (*kamma*) and what does not, for the purpose of understanding the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā rituals;
and one practice for the purpose of performing the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*), consisting of either concentration (*samādhi*) or insight (*vipassanā*) culminating in the path to Arahatship.
This much of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) has been mastered; this is what is being said. Regarding the phrase "there is no duty to be performed in dependence" (natthi nissāya kāriyaṃ):
there is nothing to be done by living in dependence upon a teacher or others. Alternatively, the reading is "nissayakāriyaṃ," which is a compound meaning "duties to be performed through dependence.
As for "the limit of life" (jīvassa yattako paricchedo): it means "for as long as one lives" (yāvajīvaṃ).
231. To show that one who lives in dependence must receive dependence in this manner, it is said:

“Ekaṃsaṃ,” etc. The analysis of the compound *ekaṃsaṃ* is: “that robe which has one shoulder [bared]. It is either an adverbial modifier for the action or an accusative used in the sense of the locative;
the meaning is “on one shoulder. *Añjali* is the hollowed palms joined together. One should speak up to the third time regarding full ordination (*upasampadā*) by one with sixty years of seniority.
Or, one who has been ordained for seventy years should make the request up to three times in the presence of one who is capable, even if he is newly ordained.

The phrase *yāvatatiyo vāro* is a descriptive compound (*kriyāviśeṣaṇasamāsa*) meaning "the third time [of the request] having been reached. *Āyasmato* means "to the Venerable One. *Vacchāmi* means "I shall dwell.

When receiving the status of a preceptor (*upajjhāya*), one should also say, "Venerable sir, please be my preceptor. That [request], however, is [made] in the context of the term "teacher" (*ācariya*).
Regarding the word "preceptor" (*upajjhāya*), it is a specific term; here, it is not mentioned separately because it is already included within the category of verbal distinctions.

Not only in this case when taking formal dependence (*nissaya*), but also in matters such as entering a village and so forth, one should proceed in exactly the same way, saying "I, friend" or "Venerable sir," and then stating, "I ask for permission to enter the village," and so on.
232. He shows the cessation of dependence (*nissayapaṭippassaddhi*) with the words "when [the preceptor] has departed," and so forth.

"When he has departed" means when the preceptor (*upajjhāya*), teacher (*ācariya*), co-resident pupil (*saddhivihārika*), or resident pupil (*antevāsika*) has gone to some place such as a village, either having asked for permission or not having asked for permission.
When any one of them says, "I am going to such-and-such a village," then by any one of those very persons—

Even if [the student] has consented by saying “Very well,” if he departs having transgressed one or another of those observances, the formal support (*nissaya*) is suspended; furthermore, it is suspended if he departs without asking permission and crosses the boundary of the monastery precinct (*upacāra-sīmā*). Regarding "one who has gone over to another faction":

whether he has gone over to the faction of the heretics (*titthiya*), or has renounced the order (*vibbhanta*), or dies, it is suspended at that very moment. "Command" (*āṇatti*) means: "I am sending you away."

The phrase "that" refers to the formal dismissal of support (*nissaya-ppaṇāmanā*), such as saying, "Do not enter here," and so forth. One who has been dismissed by that [act] must ask forgiveness from his preceptor (*upajjhāya*) and teacher (*ācariya*).

If they do not forgive him, he should perform a disciplinary act (*daṇḍakamma*) and then ask for their forgiveness by taking the senior monks (*mahāthera*) of that monastery, or even by taking monks from neighboring monasteries.
If they still do not forgive him, [he must ask for forgiveness] in the presence of those who are like-minded with the preceptor and teacher.

One should dwell [there]. If, for any reason whatsoever, it is not possible to dwell there in the presence of one's teachers—the preceptor (upajjhāya) and the teacher (ācariya)—who are of like status, one should return to that very same monastery, take formal dependence (nissaya) under another, and dwell there.
Regarding this, it is said: "Monks, when a preceptor does not admit a student (saddhivihārika) who is endowed with five qualities..."
He incurs an offense, while the one who dismisses him incurs no offense. He does not have excessive affection for his preceptor;
he does not have excessive confidence in him; he does not have excessive moral shame toward him; he does not have excessive reverence for him; he does not have excessive devotion toward him.
It is by these five factors, monks... [as before] ...it is so. Endowed with five factors, monks, [one...]
However, because it is stated, “When not assigning a resident pupil...

[the teacher] becomes [at fault],” it should be understood that teachers and preceptors incur an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) when they do not assign a resident pupil or co-resident student who is conducting himself improperly. "Cultivation" refers to the cultivation of loving-kindness (mettā).
Furthermore, the meeting with the preceptor should be understood by way of seeing and hearing him.
233. "Shameless" means:
one intentionally commits an offense;
one conceals an offense.
“He goes on a wrong course;
such a person is called one who lacks shame.

Regarding the one lacking shame (*alajjī*) defined by these characteristics thus spoken, even when granting formal dependence (*nissaya*), it should be granted only to those who possess shame (*lajjī*). “Monks, [it should not be granted to one who lacks shame].”
“Support should be given to those who are shameless. Whoever should give it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). For this is what was said.
To one who has not been seen before, support should be given after observing his conduct for a few days. Regarding the word “apubba”:
here, because it is a relative term, the word *pubba* refers to a former residence; “apubba” means that which has no prior [residence], i.e., it is new. Four or five...

The analysis (*viggaha*) is: "these have a measure (*parimāṇa*). Here, however, by the proximity of the word *parimāṇa*, even those [words] expressing the things to be numbered (*saṅkhyeyya*) come to express mere number (*saṅkhyāmatta*);

thus, it refers to the very number four or five as the thing to be numbered. Therefore, since a distinct external referent (*aññapadattha*) different from the referents of the words in the analysis is possible, there is a compound (*samāsa*).
Regarding the alternative sense (*vikappattha*) of the word *vā*, this [compound] applies therein as well.
*Samāso*: four or five; *catupañca-ahāni* means the collection (*samāhāro*) of those days is *catupañcāhaṃ*.

*Bhikkhusabhāgataṃ*: those who have a common (*samāno*) portion (*bhāgo*), that is, a part consisting of a sense of shame (*lajjitāsaṅkhāto koṭṭhāso*), are "those who share the same [qualities] as monks" (*bhikkhūhi sabhāgā*);
the state of being such is *bhikkhusabhāgatā*, which means "the state of being well-behaved" (*pesalabhāvaṃ*). By one who knows, "The elder is conscientious" (*thero lajjī*).
However, one who has gone to a place where support is normally provided must receive it on that very day; there is no allowance for even a single day’s delay.

If one lies down thinking, "I will receive it at dawn since I cannot find an opportunity," and does not realize that the sun has already risen, there is no offense. It is also permissible to stay with the benefit already obtained.
234. Regarding the word “labbhati” (is obtained): because it is formed as a passive verb (*kammani*), the agent is not explicitly stated;

thus, in phrases such as “addhikassa,” the genitive case is used for the agent, meaning “by a traveler,” and so forth. However, in the phrase “sallakkhentena,” the agent is indicated by its own form [the instrumental]. “Vasituṃ” (to dwell) refers to the action already mentioned;
for here the suffix *-tuṃ* denotes the abstract state (*bhāve*), meaning “dwelling. “Yācitassa” (of one who has been asked) refers to “the attendant of the sick person.”
And here, "and" (*ca*) is a qualifying particle. However, if even when being told, "Please ask me," a sick person does not ask because of pride, one should go.

Or, for one who is forest-dwelling (*āraññaka*), while observing whether it is "conducive to comfort" (*phāsuka*)—meaning that for one dwelling there, there is a state of comfort by way of participating in the specific excellence of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) already attained—one should observe such a comfortable dwelling in the forest. [Regarding] the donors...
*Asanta* is the word-division (*padacchedo*). *Tāva* indicates a limit; it means "as long as" the provider of dependence (*nissayadāyaka*) is available from those such as travelers (*addhika*), etc.

However, for a forest-dweller (*āraññaka*), having formed the intention, "If there is a suitable provider of dependence, I shall dwell under dependence," the meaning is "as long as [the time until] the full moon of Āsāḷha.
But if the teacher (*ācariya*) does not arrive in the month of Āsāḷha, where [should] the dependence [be sought]?
"It is possible; one should go there. However, during the rains retreat, one must dwell in a fixed residence and receive formal dependence (*nissaya*)," so it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
But some of our resident pupils (*antevāsika*) say: "Monks, the rains retreat must not be bypassed. Whoever does not enter it..."
"there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," and "Monks, on the day of the commencement of the rains, one who does not wish to enter the rains residence must not intentionally bypass his dwelling.

Whoever should bypass it, there is an offense of wrong-doing"—because of these words of the Canon (Pāḷi), even if one is unable to obtain formal dependence (nissaya) for some reason, it is not permissible to fail to enter the rains residence during the rains season. "During the rains..."
Regarding the phrase "panā" and so forth, they said: "But in these cases, the word *ca* has the sense of an addition (*anvācaya*), therefore by that [word] one must indeed enter for the rains.
However, we have spoken here as follows: "The Blessed One stated that an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) occurs only for one who does not enter [for the rains] when there is no obstacle;
for that very reason, it is said in the Commentary: 'If one has not entered for the earlier period due to some obstacle, one should enter for the later period.'"
It has been said: "Obstacle" (*antarāya*) means that which comes in between, in the middle; thus it is an obstacle.
Whatever is intended as a hindering condition is called an "obstacle," as in such passages as, "They do not obtain a suitable attendant;

this very thing is an obstacle, therefore one should depart. Therefore, being a hindering condition is what is intended. Furthermore, the non-attainment of dependence (*nissaya*) is also understood to be an obstacle.
For it can indeed be said: "The entering of the rains-retreat is an obstacle, as it provides a basis for those who have attained the nascent stages of serenity and insight, much like a granted leave.
For even in the case of those who have attained the nascent stages of serenity and insight, when leave has been granted, the Commentary states emphatically:
"But if the teacher does not arrive by the month of Āsāḷhi, one must go to wherever support is obtainable."

It has been stated. Furthermore, our teachers, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, have stated that even on the day of the entry into the rains residence (*vassūpanāyikadivasa*), one should indeed go for the sake of receiving formal dependence (*nissaya*), saying:
"If the day of entering the rains residence falls while one is still waiting for a teacher, let it be so;
one must go there wherever one can obtain a giver of dependence. Moreover, the Blessed One, though possessed of great compassion, said: "I allow..."
"Monks, for a monk who is attending to the sick, if he is unable to obtain formal dependence (*nissaya*) and is being requested [to stay], he may live without dependence (*anissita*).
Thus, even in the case of the sick, he established formal dependence as a weighty matter.
However, that which is without dependence is like entering the rains residence (*vassūpagamana*) for one who is free from dependence and free from obstacles. Furthermore, for one traveling by boat...
However, it is stated that there is no offense for one who goes by boat even when the rains retreat has arrived, provided they do not obtain formal dependence (*nissaya*);

thus, the exemption from offense is mentioned specifically for those traveling by boat. Therefore, the failure to obtain formal dependence is an obstructive condition for entering the rains retreat, whereas entering the rains retreat is not an obstructive condition for obtaining formal dependence;

hence, the failure to obtain formal dependence is indeed an obstacle [to the rains retreat]. For this very reason, the *Ṭīkā* states: "But during the rains retreat, by one who is without formal dependence..."

It is said: "The dwelling place is not permissible. For that very reason, in passages such as "But during the rains," since there is a provider of formal dependence (nissaya), one must both dwell in a fixed residence and receive formal dependence;
thus, the word "and" (ca) should be understood as a conjunction in the sense of the act of going being exhausted [by these requirements].
The commentary on the exposition of dependence is finished.
33. Commentary on the Exposition of the Girdle (Kāyabandhana): 235.
It is called a "girdle" (bandhana) because one is bound by it; a girdle for the body is a "body-girdle" (kāyabandhana); he who has no body-girdle is [described as such].
"Without the waistband. Regarding "an offense of wrong-doing" (*dukkaṭa*): if one should enter [the village] either intentionally or unintentionally, it is an offense of wrong-doing.
The connection is that if one has gone out of mindfulness, one should fasten [the belt] at the very place where one remembers. "Gone" means having gone into the interior of the village.
Having remembered, as long as one does not fasten it, one must not go on almsround.
236. By the words “paṭṭikā,” etc., he defines the waistband (*kāyabandhana*) as that which encompasses all types.
“Paṭṭikā” refers to either ordinary woven cloth or cloth woven from fish-bone or date-palm fibers. “Sūkaranta” means the intestine of a pig; here, however, it refers to something resembling it.
Including even a cord-like waistband that has been prepared without being made square, it is called “a single cord.”
This has been stated. Furthermore, when tying that rope, it is permissible to tie it as a single strand; it is not permissible to split it in the middle and tie it as a double strand.
However, without making it a double strand, it is permissible to tie it even a hundred times by repeatedly twisting it together;
yet, even a single [strand] in the shape of a *pāmaṅga* (a braided ornament) is not permissible. [This applies to] many ropes.
If one makes [the strips] into one and wraps them continuously with a single [piece], it should not be called "many-corded" (*bahurajjuka*); that is permissible. Regarding "conforming to those":
these two [types of strips] are respectively conforming to those two, namely, the *paṭṭikā* and the *sūkaranta*. 237–8.
As to what kind of *paṭṭikā* is permissible, he says "fish," etc. The *paṭṭikā* [should be like] a fish’s fin, a thorn, or a date-palm leaf.
The connection is: "or it is obtained as smooth (*maṭṭhā*). By the words *kaṇṭaka* (thorn) and *patta* (leaf), their respective shapes are expressed;
for, by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), this [plant] has the shape of a fish's thorn and the shape of a date-palm leaf—thus is the compound formed.

"Smooth" means naturally polished. In the commentary (*ṭīkā*), however, it says: "These fish-thorns and so forth are smooth, meaning they are free from deformity, and the strips (*paṭṭikā*) are included therein."
This is what is meant by "the intended meaning. How are they included therein? Because those very things are called "strips" (*paṭṭikā*).
And so it is said in the Commentary: "A plain strip or one woven with fish-bone [patterns] is suitable.
Here, however, the date-palm leaf is included within the very category of "fish-bone" patterns. The connection is that all four types of fringes (*dasā*) may be obtained.
“Forty” is stated as the maximum limit; therefore, even fewer than that are permissible.

Regarding the phrase “at both ends,” the connection is that a double-stranded cord is obtained at both ends of the waist-band (*kāyabandhana*). A *guṇa-suttaka* is a cord serving as a fastening. For the *Abhidhānappadīpikā* states:
“*Guṇa* [is used] in the sense of a membrane, a heap, a benefit, and a fastening. [This refers to] two such fastening cords.
A "samāhāra" (compound) is a double-stranded cord. It is appropriate to twist that for the sake of making the fringe-strips firm, not for the sake of beauty.
Therefore he said, "garlands, etc.
Having shown garlands, crab-patterns, and elephant-patterns, [he indicates that] a strip twisted from a double-stranded cord is not permitted.
Regarding the connection: in the phrase "mālādi" (garland, etc.), the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes any such form of modification.
The compound means "that which has eyes like those of crabs, and so forth. Similarly, there is "kuñjaracchādi" (elephant-protector). 239.
"Ghaṭaka" refers to a circular line in the shape of a small jar. Regarding "makaramukhādi," here "makaramukha" (crocodile-mouth) is—
The shape is that of a crocodile’s mouth (*makaramukha*). As for the dot (*bindu*), it is mentioned on the basis of traditional authority (*āgama*). By the word “etc.

(*ādi*), any other form resulting from modification, such as the head of a water-snake (*deḍḍubha*), is included. Regarding the phrase “at the ends of the fringe” (*dasāmukhe*): the connection is that these [ornaments] are not permitted at the ends, which constitute the faces of the fringe.
Regarding the phrase “on both ends of the border”: the connection is that neither pots, nor lines, nor any other embroidery is permitted. “Pots” (*ghaṭakā*) means from the pot-shaped [ornament].

*Lekhā* means *lekhāya*. There is an elision [of the case ending] due to the fifth case (*pañcamī*). *Vidha* refers to a device made of ivory, horn, or other materials, which is to be placed at the end of the waist-band near the fringe of the cloth for the purpose of providing stability.
(240) *Deḍḍubhaka* means resembling the head of a water-snake. *Muraja* means having the shape of a drum-body (*murajavaṭṭi*) made with threads of various colors.

It was made by wrapping [the strings] around. However, in the *Ṭīkā* it is stated: "A *muraja* is a lute made by gathering many strings together on one side, wrapping them with a single string, and then making the strings.
This contradicts the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) cited below, which says: "[It is made] by putting many strings together on one side," and so forth.
A *maddavīṇā* is shaped like a *pāmaṅga*. A *kalābu* has many strings. For these, [it is said]: "It is not allowable."
This is the connection. "Two middle ones" means two that are in the middle, namely those known as the *muraja* and the *madda-vīṇā*.
"And also the knots" means also the knots of the robe. "Made of that" means produced from those [materials] such as bamboo and so forth. This, however, was stated by way of digression.
The commentary on the description of the waistband is finished.
The commentary on the first recitation section of the sub-commentary titled *Sumaṅgalappasādani* is completed. 34.
Commentary on the Description of Earth (*Pathavīniddesa*).
242. "Of two kinds: born and unborn"—the meaning is that earth is twofold, namely "born earth" and "unborn earth. By this, he shows both born earth and unborn earth.
He shows their distinction with the words beginning "pure," and so on.
Pure clay and dust, as well as that which is not burnt and contains much clay and dust, and a heap of clay and dust that has been rained upon for more than four months—this is "born earth."

The connection [is as follows]: "clay and dust" (*mattikā ca paṃsu ca*) is a *dvanda* compound. Its external meaning is: that of which the clay and dust are pure, due to the absence of gravel and other such impurities.
"Unburnt" (*adaḍḍhā*) means not burnt in various ways by means of a hearth, cooking, and so forth.

However, that [unburnt state] does not exist separately; it should be understood as being one or another among the pure clay and so forth. "Four months"—together with those, it is "exceeding" (*atireka*).
The compound is *kālo tasmiṃ ovaṭṭho* (“black, moistened by that”). As for “moistened” (*ovaṭṭho*), it means moistened by any kind of water.
However, the Buddhas say: “Only by water fallen from the sky, not by drops falling after being struck elsewhere.
And because it is stated generally as “moistened,” thin mud standing in a lotus pond is permissible, but thick mud is not.

Furthermore, because it has been stated, "When a matter requiring a formal decision on discipline (vinaya-vinicchaya) arises, one must stand firm," and because it contradicts the definition of the Vinaya, this [position] is not acceptable to us.

A "heap of dust and clay" (paṃsu-mattika-rāsi) is a collection of dust and clay. The compound *catu-pe-vaṭṭho paṃsu-mattika-rāsi* is either an *aññapadattha* (possessive compound) meaning "one who has a heap of dust and clay that is fourfold, etc.," or a *kammadhāraya* (descriptive compound).

243. "Sand and burnt earth, mostly gravel and so forth, and the earth for the four-month rain-retreat, and the second ground which has been piled up"—this is the connection. "Gravel, stones, sand, potsherds, and sand" is a *dvanda* compound.
The analysis (*viggaha*) is: "that of which the pure gravel... pe... sand [is the constituent]. It is of a measure that can be grasped by the closed fist.
Gravel, stones larger than that, potsherds, sand, and fragments of skull-bone are to be understood as "stones.
"The second" refers to those not yet formed. "The aforementioned mass" refers to the previously mentioned layer of clay and dust.

244. To the question of what kind of soil consists mostly of clay and so forth, he says: "two parts," etc. "Of whatever ground" means of whichever ground. "In the remaining cases as well" refers to those cases where the soil consists mostly of dust, mostly gravel, mostly stone, and so on.

245. By the words “*pācitti*,” etc., he shows the analysis (*vinicchaya*) therein. The connection is: “If [the tree] has grown and one perceives it as having grown, there is an offense of expiation (*pācitti*) for cutting it.
“Grown” (*jāte*) means on a plot of ground where growth has occurred; or it is a change of gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*), meaning “to that which has grown” (*jātāya*). The connection is:

“If it has grown and one is in doubt or uncertain, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). If it has grown and one perceives it as not having grown, there is no offense. The same applies to commanding another to do so.

The construction is: "there is no offense" (*anāpatti*). "One who has the perception that it is not yet dug" (*ajātasaññissa*): the perception that it is not yet dug is "perception of the undug" (*ajātasaññā*);

one who possesses this is "one with the perception of the undug" (*ajātasaññī*), [meaning] for such a person. 246. "By a single command, 'once'": if one who has been commanded once digs even for an entire day, the meaning is that there is only a single offense for the one who gave the command. This is to be connected with the phrase "an offense by word" (*vācaso āpatti*). "By word" (*vācaso*) is used in the sense of distribution; the meaning is "by each individual word.
247. It should be construed as: "Dig this spot," and so forth. The construction is: "Or light a fire here."

"‘Vattuṃ’ (to speak)" means that this is a verbal expression for the agent of the phrase "it is not allowable. Alternatively, the meaning is that it is not allowable to speak in such a manner as "Dig up this spot," and so forth.
By the word "niyametvā" (having specified), he indicates that it is allowable to speak without specifying, such as by saying, "Dig a pit," or "Dig a bulbous root," and so on.

248. The connection is as follows: such words as "Know the pit for this pillar, or make it allowable," and "Know the clay, or bring the clay, or make the clay allowable" are permissible. It is called "such" (*edisaṃ*) because it appears like that; what is it?
The thing to be compared (*upameyya*), namely, "Give me clay," and so forth. "Clay..."

The phrase beginning with "one knows" (*jānāti*) is the simile (*upamāna*). The commonality of properties (*samānadhammatā*), designated as *kappiya*, between those similes and the objects of comparison (*upameyya*), is the "simile" (*upamā*).
Thus it has been stated by us in the *Subodhālaṅkāra*: "The state of having common properties between the simile and the object of comparison may constitute a simile.
Otherwise, the very sequence of syllables that serves as the simile would be identical to the sequence of syllables that is the object of comparison.
It should be understood that in this sentence, the word *viya* alone indicates the simile. 249.
It is possible to stir up dry mud and the like, or thin mud that is to be scooped up, even if they are not connected to the earth;
here, by the word "ādi" (etc. in the phrase "mud and the like," the scum of water in places where water has flowed is included.
It is so called because it includes whatever is moved by the force of the wind. "Mud fit for bailing out" means mud that can be removed by means of jars.
This should be connected with the passage beginning, "The *gaṇḍuppāda* [mud] that has been standing for more than four months," and so forth. *Gaṇḍa* refers to the surface of the earth.
They are called *gaṇḍuppādā* because they produce a heap of clay resembling a tumor (*gaṇḍa*).
Here, however, the excrement produced by them is designated as "tumor-produced" (*gaṇḍuppāda*). In manuscripts, however, the reading *gaṇḍuppādo* is found;
that [reading] is not tenable here, as it would have to be [interpreted] as an object in the phrase "one should not disturb it" (*na kopaye*). *Mūsikukkiraṃ* means the scattering of mice.
"A heap of dust made outside after digging" refers to a mouse's burrow. Regarding "clods and so forth": here, "clod" (*leḍḍu*) means a lump of clay cut by a plough in a tilled field.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), mud cut by the hooves of cows is included.
When [these] fall near water, or when stones cling to the banks of tanks and the like, or when dust falls into fresh dung—[in these cases, it is not an offense].
The connection is: "and likewise in the case of a royal road, an open space, an anthill, and a mud wall.
By the word "likewise" (tathā), this extends the rule to everything else, such as riverbanks and so forth, which do not become disturbed even after four months or more;
thus he says "mostly" (yebhuyyena) and so on. "Mostly consisting of gravel" (yebhuyyakathalā) refers to ground where there is mostly gravel.
“*Ṭhānaṃ*” means that which stands (*tiṭṭhati*) here; it refers to a place where there is mostly stone.

The intention is that a brick wall is like a place consisting mostly of stone. The intention is that there is no offense for one who destroys such a wall. “A wall made of bricks” is a compound (*samāsa*). 253–5. The connection is:
“having moved [it], while disturbing the ground, in order to take hold of a pillar or the like. In that context, they disturb [the ground].
The nominative case is used in the sense of the instrumental; the meaning is "one who violates. Otherwise, how could there be the possibility of the first case here?
For the first case might occur when the word "bhava" (be) is stated, but in cases such as "gaṇhitum" (to take), there is nothing stated by means of the infinitive suffix (*tuṃ*-paccaya).
When the infinitive suffix denotes the abstract state (*bhāva*), then nothing [of the agent] is stated; thus, even in the case of the primary action expressed by "it is not allowable" (*na kappati*).
In all instances, it should be understood according to the method explained below: that the agent is indeed another.

However, when the sense of the third case (instrumental) is present, it is highly appropriate [to interpret] that for one who moves here and there and disturbs the ground, it is not permissible to take hold of a pillar or similar object.
"Dhārāya" means by a stream of urine. The construction is: "to make the uneven even, or to scrub with brooms. "Visamaṃ" means an uneven place.
The connection is: "He broke the ground in order to walk, thinking, 'I shall show the footprint. "Bhindanto" means by one who is breaking. The construction is:
"Or, being afflicted with the disease of itch (kaṇḍu), he might rub his limbs against the bank and so forth. "Kaṇḍurogī" means by one suffering from the disease of itch.
The word "ca" is used in the sense of restriction (avadhāraṇe).
256–7. *Suddhacittassa* means of one whose mind is completely pure, being devoid of the intention to split the earth. 258. The connection is as follows:

when there is no fuel (*anupādāne*), it is possible either to let the fire fall upon a potsherd or a brick that lacks fuel, or, if it must be contained, to let it fall upon the ground. *Upādāna* is fuel; that which is not fuel is *anupādāna*.
In that [place]. *Vaso* means "enjoyed. For the *Nighaṇḍu* states: "When *vaso* is enjoyed, it is dependent (*āyatta*).
That which is not *vaso* is *avasō*; the meaning is: in that which is not enjoyed. It is permissible to make a fire by placing fuel only in the place where it has fallen.
However, it is not permissible to set fire to dry stumps, dry trees, and so forth. But if one thinks, "I will go after extinguishing it before it even reaches the ground," [it is permissible].
If he gives it and it is permissible [to throw it], but he is unable to extinguish it afterwards because it is beyond his capacity, there is no offense.
It is also not permissible to say, "Throw it on the ground.
The commentary on the description of earth is finished.
35. Commentary on the Description of Requisites (Parikkhāraniddesa) 259–60.

The connection is as follows: it is not permitted to sew a sunshade (*chatta*)—that is, a sunshade made of palm leaves—with threads of five colors both inside and out, nor is it permitted to cut patterns such as mountain peaks (*girikūṭa*) or half-moons upon the leaves.
"Mountain peak" (*girikūṭa*) refers to the "tooth" design of a sea monster (*makaradantaka*).
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), other such types of modified forms (*vikārarūpa*) are included. "A pillar" (*ghaṭaka*) refers to a pillar being constructed like those found in the supports of a house.
"A staff" (*daṇḍa*) refers to a parasol-staff. "Lines" (*lekha*) refers to the lines drawn here and there. "Similar" (*sādisa*) is specified by the long vowel [in *sādisī*].
"In the bundle" (*bundamhi*) means at the base.
261. The connection is as follows: "It is permissible to sew [the umbrella] with a single color for the sake of stability, or to bind the frame.
"To sew" means to sew both inside and out. "With a single color" means with one color such as blue and so forth. "The frame" refers to the frame of the umbrella-staff holders and the ribs.
By the phrase "for the sake of stability," he shows that it is not for the sake of a glossy finish. It is permissible to draw lines on the staff for the purpose of binding.
"Connection" (*sambandho*): This refers to the act of binding by means of ropes to hold a circular umbrella (*chattamaṇḍalika*) steady against the force of the wind.
"Lines" (*lekhāvā*): These are lines drawn as if engraved in the form of a ring. "It is permissible" (*vaṭṭati*):
Even if it does not actually bind [the umbrella], it is permissible because it is a suitable place for binding with ropes.

262. "Whether at the edge of the robe, or at the tip of a patch, or on a seam, or on a ring, or on any other needle-work such as a border-ear (*pāḷikaṇṇika*) or even a permissible dot (*kappabindu*), it is not allowable"—this is the connection [of the sentence]. "At the edge" (*ante*) means at the limit of the robe;
"along the fold" (*anuvāte*) is what is meant. "At the tip of a patch" (*paṭṭamukhe*) means at the end of a patch, or the place where two patches are joined together.
This was said with this intention: "Veṇī" refers to sewing in the shape of a braid of hair; "saṅkhalikā" refers to sewing in the shape of a chain-link bond;
"or any other needle-work" refers to any other kind of needlework being done for the purpose of decorating a robe.
However, in the *Ṭīkā*, it is stated: "Any other needlework such as the 'hundred-petalled' [flower] pattern is not allowable."
This was stated as a general rule. However, because it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:

“When they sew [robes] with various threads into a hundred-fold pattern for the purpose of decorating the robe, or when they place an *āgantuka-paṭṭa* (an incoming patch), or perform any other kind of needlework transformation—all this is not permitted,” therefore, whether it be of various colors or of a single color, for those who sew together for the purpose of decorating the robe—
It is said with reference to alterations made by needlework; therefore, it is our view that it is permissible to sew even a hundred-fold patch onto robes for the purpose of strengthening a torn area.
By the words *pāḷi* and *kaṇṇikā*, either through the elision of the word *kappa* or by figurative usage, only the *pāḷikappa* and so forth are intended.
*Pāḷi* and *kaṇṇikā* together form *pāḷikaṇṇikāyo*; these are the "beginnings" (*ādi*).

The analysis of the compound is: "of another such as that. Therein, a *pāḷikappa* (textual arrangement) is made in such a way that it shines with a row of dots having the shape of a blue garland (*nīlāvaḷi*) and so forth.
Likewise, a *kaṇṇikakappa* (central arrangement) is made by showing [the pattern] in some part of a collection of dots.
263. *Gaṇṭhipāsakapaṭṭā* refers to the strips that should be placed at the locations where the knots and the loops are fixed.

Regarding the word *vaṭṭati* (is permissible): here, having formed the compound *gaṇṭhipāsakā* (knots and loops), one should connect it by transposing the phrasing according to the sense as “only those with four corners are permissible.
*Agghiya* refers to sewing in the shape of a *cetiya*. Sewing in the shape of a mallet, making the base and the tip identical, is called a *muggara*.
*Vikāraṃ*: this is *vikāra*; it is stated with a transposition of gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*). *Ettha* (here).
Regarding the knots, loops, and bands: 264.
"Corner-threads" (*koṇasutta*) is a neuter designation; it refers to the ends of threads drawn out from the corners of the knots, loops, and bands.
"Bulbs" (*pīḷaka*) refers to those very same [threads], which, having been turned back, are fashioned in the shape of bulbs. "Difficult to discern" (*duviññeyyāva*) means that at their ends, once—
Alternatively, by making a knot or by sewing it back again, it is indeed difficult to discern. "Fragrant oil" means either fragrance or oil;
vinegar, flour-paste, and so forth are also permitted. 265.
"With a gem" means with a stone such as *masāragalla* (emerald) and the like. "And he should not rub it" means he must not rub it at all. "Or with something else..."
"With a club, a mace, and so forth. However, it is permissible to do so with shoulder-straps or waist-bands.

"Having placed it in a tub, one should not scrub it" means that having placed it in a tub used for washing raw-dyed cloth, one should not scrub it by kneeling on the ground and rubbing it back and forth.
266–7. *Kaṇṇakoṇakasuttāni*: These are threads fastened by making loops in the four corners when hanging [the robe] in the wind at the time of dyeing the robes.

They were thus authorized by the statement: "I allow you, monks, ear-threads (*kaṇṇasuttaka*). The corners, being called "ears" (*kaṇṇa*), are the *kaṇṇakoṇakā*; the threads are those [attached] to them. [This refers to] the knotted loops and the strips.
However, since the permissibility of the ear-flaps and corner-threads—which are indeed difficult to discern—was stated previously, there is no need to cut them once the robe has been dyed;

yet, because it was stated that the ear-flaps and corner-threads must be cut, it should be understood that even threads drawn out along the grain (anuvāta) must be cut. [Regarding] the mark on the handle of the water-strainer...
The construction is: "Except for the lines, it is not permitted. "On the rim of the umbrella" means on the mouth-rim of the umbrella.
"Lines" refers to any other lines, whether above, below, or on the interior. The connection is: "A key, a spindle, a jewel, and a pill are not permitted.
"Jewel" refers to a single round gem. "Pill" refers to a substance the size of a mustard seed, resembling a urinary stone.
“Many circular lines. Regarding “on the handle”: on the handle of the *pipphala* (grinding stone). 268–9.
It should be understood that it is not appropriate to have garlands and the like on the fire-drill (*araṇi*), nor wall-painting on the leaf-patterned surface.
By “fire-drill” (*araṇi*) is meant the upper fire-drill, the lower fire-drill, and the fire-drill bow, taken collectively. By “leaf-patterned surface” (*pattamaṇḍala*) is meant...
On a leaf-dish made of tin, lead, and so forth; however, a crocodile-patterned handle is appropriate here. "Below" means below the walking staff (kattarayaṭṭhi);
"above" means above that very same staff.
Regarding "in a broom," there is a change of gender from *sammuñjanī*. "Not forbidden" refers to the female form, which is indeed forbidden.
"Even one made of gold" means even one consisting of gold. A "horn-tube" (*visāṇanāḷi*) is a tube made of horn.

Furthermore, it should be understood that whatever other items are not explicitly mentioned here—such as those made of *āraka* wood, ivory, tooth-sticks, water-jars, water-basins, bowls, powder-cases, and so forth—are to be regarded as permissible in accordance with those already mentioned.
Moreover, if one who knows the Vinaya should see such an article [made of bone] and cut it [into a permissible material], [it is allowed].
"Or if he should have it cut, he is to be understood as being without offense.
The commentary on the description of requisites is finished.
36. Commentary on the Description of Medicines.
274–5. It should be connected as follows: "It is not permitted to make, to give, or to speak medicine for people.
Regarding the word "it is permitted" (*labbhati*), "by a bhikkhu" is the agent (*kattā*) and "medicine" (*bhesajja*) is the expressed object (*vuttakamma*).

Now, since "to make" (*kātuṃ*) is a verbal noun derived from the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva-sādhana*), it must necessarily have an unstated object (*avuttakamma*), because the suffixes *-ta* and *-ka* prescribed in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*) are employed even when there is an active case-role (*kammakāraka*).

Is it not to be desired? True; nevertheless, when the power of the object (*kamma-satti*)—which constitutes the primary factor—is expressed, the power of the object, though subordinate due to its connection with the action of making (*kiriyā*), is understood as if it were itself expressed. Thus it was said by us in the *Yogavinicchaya*:
"Because it follows the primary factor, in the expression of the primary truth according to common usage, the subordinate power appears as if it were itself expressed."

"Of the people" (*janassa*) means of the people who have arrived one after another. The connection is that [the following] may be obtained for fellow practitioners of the Dhamma, for parents, for the nuns who attend to them, for the owners of the requisites, and for the attendant:
the preparation of medicine by means of what is obtained through begging and requests.

Therein, "fellow practitioners of the Dhamma" (*sahadhamminam*): the Dhamma to be practiced together is the "Dhamma," consisting of virtue, faith, and wisdom; those who possess this are "fellow practitioners of the Dhamma."

"Those who possess this [dharma]" (*sahadhammī*) means those who share the same dharma; there are five: the bhikkhu, the bhikkhunī, the *sikkhamānā*, the *sāmaṇera*, and the *sāmaṇerī*. "Of them" refers to these five.
"Father and mother" (*pitaro*) is formed by the rule of single remainder (*ekasesa-naya*), or it is a collective designation for both; "of them" refers to these two.

One "dependent on a bhikkhunī" is a bhikkhu who lives in dependence upon a bhikkhunī while performing all the duties in the monastery. One "desirous of going forth" (*bhaṇḍu*) is one who is seeking ordination.
As long as he has not yet prepared his bowl and robes, he may stay in the monastery; such a person is like a withered leaf.

Regarding "to one who performs services": this refers to one's own attendant. However, among these [dependents], if one's mother and father expect [service] even while established in royalty, it is not permissible not to do it.
One who does not touch his mother must perform all the preliminary service; but as for the father, [he should serve] with his own hands.
One should attend to [the parents] by performing such services as bathing and massaging.
276. "Father, mother, brother, and sister" is a *dvanda* compound: father...pe... sisters. "The great and the small" refers to the great and the small;
"those who are the father...pe... and the sisters" is a *kammadhāraya* compound. "Those who have these as their beginning" is a possessive (*aññapadattha*) compound.
The terms *mahācūḷa* should each be joined with the words *pitā* (father) and so forth, as in the expression “of the great father, of the minor father,” and so on.
By the word *ādi* (and so forth), one includes here the paternal aunt (*pitucchā*) and the maternal uncle (*mātula*), as well as the lineage of sons up to the seventh generation for all ten of them.
The construction is that they receive the preparation of medicine from their own [relatives]. Of these...
The meaning is that if [medicines] belonging to a great uncle or others are available, it is permissible to prepare medicine with them. "If not" means if they do not exist.
"In one's own possession" means if they belong to the bhikkhu himself. "It should be given on loan" means it should be given after making it a temporary loan.
If they return them, they may be accepted; if they do not give them back, they should not be pressed for them.
*Tāvakālikaṃ* means "temporary," in the sense that as long as there is giving for him, so long is it [the time].

The suffix *-ika* occurs at the end of a compound. 277. Regarding the phrase "preparation of medicine, etc.," the word "etc. includes the giving of uninvited alms-food (*anāmaṭṭha-piṇḍa*) and so forth. The word *hi* is used in the sense of a cause;
because corruption of families and the like do not take root in these [cases], therefore the preparation of medicine is permissible for them, as they are one's own.
And when [the medicine] exists, it should be given; this is how the meaning should be understood here.
"It does not grow" means it does not take root, it does not proceed, it does not come into being; the intention is that it does not produce an offense.

For their sake, medicine should be caused to be brought by relatives or novices, or having caused it to be brought for one's own sake, it should be given. By them also, thinking, "We shall bring it for the preceptors and others," [it should be done].
It should be brought under the heading of one’s duties (*vatta*). If others who are ill also enter the monastery, you should prepare medicine for all of them without expecting anything in return.

If there is a faithful family that stands in the place of mother and father to the Saṅgha of monks, and if someone there becomes ill, for their sake [one should ask]: "Venerable sir, what is the medicine for such-and-such a disease?"
When they ask, "Are you making [it]? after having made it allowable (*kappiya*), saying, "It is permissible;
take this and that and make it," then the monks may converse with one another.

278. It is not forbidden to give almsfood (*piṇḍapāta*) that has not been specifically designated for the six classes of people, beginning with mothers, nor for a murderous robber, as long as it is given under their authority.
It should be joined [to the following]. "In the midst of the six" means in the midst of the six beginning with the mother.
"Of the mother and so forth" refers to the remaining five beginning with the mother, excluding those dependent on the bhikkhunī.

However, this application of the term "in the midst of the six" contradicts the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), for there it mentions only seven beings, omitting those dependent on the bhikkhunī, by stating "of the mother and father," and so on. And the Elder Ācariya Buddhadatta has stated exactly the same thing.
“Alms should be given by one who understands,
even if not requested, to both parents, to their attendant,
to a master, and to a jailer of thieves.”
“[It is] for Bhaṇḍuka himself and also for his attendant. (Vinaya II 493–495).
“A robber-thief” means a notorious thief who aspires to kingship.
“Unclaimed” means that which has been obtained from the hand of one who has not gone forth, and which has not been taken up by oneself or by another who has gone forth; this is “unclaimed alms-food.”
“Hospitality means: seeing a visitor who has arrived at the monastery, whether he be poor or otherwise, one should give him water to drink;
oil for rubbing the feet should be given; to one who arrives at the proper time, rice-gruel and food; to one who arrives at the improper time, if there is rice, rice should be given;
a place to sleep should be provided; and even property belonging to the Saṅgha should be given to those who are robbers.”

...has been said. However, the remaining forms of hospitality should be performed by one who does not expect anything in return. Likewise, the hospitality of the Dhamma should be given to anyone at all.
279. "Of them" refers to householders who are strangers and so forth. "One should do" means that when told, "Please speak," one should do so; [but] "we will not do it" means...
If, when it has been spoken, they should feel remorse, [the rite] should be performed. "Not by oneself" (na-attanā) is to be construed as "not to be done by one's own water and thread.
Having thus shown the method of practice for the *paritta* in general, he now says "it should be recited," etc., in order to show the method of practice for the Āṭānāṭiya *paritta*.
"Causing to recite" (*bhaṇāpento*) means preceded by the request, "Recite! (*bhaṇatha*).
The construction is as follows: having first recited the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta— which is a protective charm (paritta) included within the Teaching—
and then having recited for seven days these suttas included within the Teaching, namely the Metta Sutta, the Dhajagga Sutta, and the Ratana Sutta,
one should then recite the Āṭānāṭiya Paritta as the preliminary rite (parikamma).

280. “Having come, let him give the precepts and recite the protective Dhamma (paritta). This is the connection: it is permissible for someone sent by another to go and either give the precepts or recite the protective Dhamma.
The commentary on the description of medicines is finished.
37. Commentary on the Description of Acceptance (uggaha).
281. Since it is possible for the word *puggala* (person) alone, when used in conjunction, to include even the self (*attan*), the word *añña* (other) is employed to exclude that possibility.
When there is a possibility of deviation, a qualification serves a purpose. Thus, the "jewel" (*ratana*) is of ten kinds, namely:
pearl (*muttā*), gem (*maṇi*), beryl (*veḷuriya*), conch shell (*saṅkha*), crystal (*sila*), coral (*pavāḷa*), silver (*rajata*), gold (*jātarūpa*), ruby (*lohitaṅka*), and cat’s-eye (*masāragalla*).
The tenfold jewel has been described. "Of one who learns" means of one who takes up or accepts. 282–3.
Among those, the connection is with "two [offenses] involving relinquishment for one learning for one's own sake. "Among those" means among those ten.
"Two" refers to the two objects involving relinquishment consisting of silver and gold. By the word "for one's own sake,"...
It indicates that for the sake of the five [purposes] beginning with new construction (*navakamma*), there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

Regarding the phrase "in the remaining cases there is an offense of wrong-doing," the meaning is that for all the remaining eight [purposes], there is an offense of wrong-doing for one who accepts [the gift]. This should be connected as follows:

even when it is said, "I give this for the new construction of the shrine (*cetiyassa navakamma*"), without specifying a group, a Saṅgha, or an individual, one does not refuse it. "Does not refuse" means...
This explains the rejection [of the gift] when it has been stated that the *saṅghāḍi* has been touched.
Once it has been rejected, if he says, "It will be in the hands of those who prepare what is allowable (*kappiyakāraka*), or in the hands of my own men, or in my own hands;
you may simply enjoy the requisites," it is permissible. And whatever has been given for the sake of the four requisites, for whichever one there is need—
If there is need for robes, it should be applied toward that purpose. What has been given for the sake of their robes should be applied toward robes themselves.

If there is no such need for robes, and the Saṅgha is suffering due to alms-food and other requisites, one may apply it for those purposes as well after seeking permission for the welfare of the Saṅgha.
This same method applies to what is given for the sake of alms-food or medicinal requisites for the sick. Regarding what is given for the sake of lodgings:
However, because it is a heavy object (*garubhaṇḍa*), once given, it must be returned to that very place.
If lodgings (*senāsana*) are being lost, one should consume only what is necessary for maintenance, without cutting off the root or giving it away, for the sake of looking after them.
(284) To show the means of accepting certain grounds for wrongdoing, such as fields and so forth, [the text] says "field," etc.
It has been stated. Therein, "field" (*khetta*) refers to a place for growing paddy and other grains. "Ground" (*vatthu*) refers to a place for growing vegetables, sugarcane, fruits, and so forth.
"Slaves, cattle, and so on" refers to slaves, cattle, flower gardens, fruit gardens, and the like. The connection [of the sentence] is:

"having rejected [these], one should accept [them] by means of what is allowable (*kappiya*) and through the proper procedure (*kamma*). Regarding the phrase "by means of what is allowable and through the proper procedure," here the word *kamma* [refers to...]
It is a term that follows conventional usage; therefore, the meaning is that it must be done for others and for oneself strictly according to the sequence of allowable (kappiya) conventions.

Regarding fields and lands, for instance, one may say to others: "Please enjoy these four requisites," or "They shall be in the hands of the kappiya-kārakas," or "Let the Saṅgha enjoy the allowable goods," or "We give the boundary. Thus [it is said].
Having said, "Excellent, lay follower! The birds and wild animals will live here in safety and comfort," he himself [thinks] of the pond as previously described:
"They will use the water, they will wash their belongings, and the birds and wild animals will drink";
or others [say], "Excellent, lay follower! The Saṅgha will drink the drinking water," and so forth, while he himself [thinks]...

Or, regarding slaves, it should be understood as when one says, "I give [this person] as a monastery attendant (ārāmika)," or "I give [him] as a servant (veyyāvaccakara)," or "I give [him] as a preparer of allowable things (kappiyakāraka)";
or regarding livestock, "I give [these] for the purpose of consuming the five products of the cow"; or regarding a monastery, "I give a grove," and so forth.
However, if someone who is incompetent accepts a field or the like, or causes it to be built, by means of an improper expression (akappiya-vohāra), then that—
It must not be used by the bhikkhus; even a permissible article obtained in dependence upon it is indeed impermissible.

However, although the formal acceptance (*paṭiggahaṇa*) is permissible when a construction is commissioned by a conscientious bhikkhu who is incompetent [in the Vinaya], it is nevertheless impermissible because it is mixed with what arose through the bhikkhu’s own initiative, like food containing poison or like the eating of forbidden meat.
And it is difficult to dispose of; all such things are indeed unallowable.

285–6. Nine [types of grain]...pe... the act of plowing, the removal of clay, the binding, the making firm of the embankment, the taking of an extra share in an unplowed field, and the demanding of a coin for the crop when it is not yet harvested and the portion has not been demarcated, saying, "Give this much."
The connection is that all these are "unallowable" (*akappiya*). *Mātikā*, *kedāra*, and *taḷāka* form a *dvanda* compound: *mātikā... taḷākā*.
The compound is [formed by] their action (*tesaṃ kiriyā*). "In an old one" (*anave*) refers to an old pond accepted as one of the four requisites.

However, if it is accepted on account of its water, it is permissible for those with pure minds. "Binding" (*bandha*) means a binding according to the Canon (*pāḷiyā*). In an ancient field (*porāṇakedāre*).

Because the portion of the field has been fixed, he says, “in a field. Regarding “in an undetermined portion”: this refers to a case where the portion is not delimited by saying, “on such-and-such an area of land, such-and-such a portion must be given.
[Sutta 287–9: Without stating, “Plow and sow,” etc., but rather saying, “on such-and-such land, such-and-such a portion must be given,” [he designates] the land.
The connection is: "for him who establishes [the field], this is indeed what is not allowable. The word *ca* (and) is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇe*).
"Establishes" means: whichever monk establishes it. "For him alone" means: for that very monk who is the establisher.

"This" refers to the grain obtained from the land that was established, when someone says, "A crop has been grown on such-and-such an area of land; take this much," in order to take a measured portion.

Whether measuring with poles or ropes, or standing in a threshing floor to guard it, or having it removed, or putting it back into a storehouse and so forth—this should be connected as being "unallowable for him alone.
"And he establishes it" means that the monk establishes it.
"Made" means made by us. "While the farmers are speaking" means while the cultivators are speaking thus. "Measure" means the measure of the ground.
"Causing to be removed" means causing it to be removed from the threshing floor to the house. "This" refers to what has been obtained from a friend, protected [by another], and so forth.

"Of that very person" means of the one who possesses the honorarium, the protector, and so on. Because it has not been produced as something previously unknown, it is allowable for others; thus he said, "this is unallowable for that very person. 290.
In connection with the topic of returning [the robe], he said, "one should return it," and so forth. "Whatever belongs to a householder" includes even that which belongs to one's father.
Regarding the connection: "Belonging to the parents" means the parents are both the father and the mother; it is their property.
By the phrase "belonging to the household," it is indicated that it is permissible to store away any kind of requisite belonging to the five who share the same Dhamma.
"Any kind whatsoever" includes what is allowable (*kappiya*) or unallowable (*akappiya*), even down to a mother’s ear-ornament or a palm leaf.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the treasurer’s head": here, by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), anything that is primary is called "head," just as the head is the foremost part of the body. Likewise, the word *bhaṇḍāgārika* (treasurer) also emphasizes the state (*bhāva*). Thus, in the compound *bhaṇḍāgārikasīsa*, it is a *kammadhāraya* where the subsequent term is a qualifier:
"the treasurer-ness is the head, the primary thing. Therefore, the meaning is: "by means of making the state of being a treasurer the primary factor."
291–2. "Must be put away" means it must necessarily be stored away. "Even when told" means even when told by one's mother or father. 293–4. The construction is:

if carpenters and the like, or royal favorites, should say, "Give [this] back after you have put away your own tools or bed-furniture," one should not do so either out of desire or out of fear. "Tools" (*parikkhāra*) refers to implements such as axes, hatchets, and so forth.
"Out of desire or even out of fear" means: out of desire in the case of carpenters and the like, and out of fear in the case of those favored by the king.
(295–6) "It is allowable to take it back" is how the construction should be joined. "Suspicion" (*saṅkā*) means:
in whatever place they give rise to the suspicion that "it will have been taken by monks or novices," in such a place, within the monastery or dwelling, is how the construction should be joined.

“Of a monastery and a dwelling” means of both a monastery (*vihāra*) and a dwelling (*āvasatha*). “A treasure” refers to the ten kinds of gems. “An object considered a treasure” refers to items such as cloth and the like.

“He should deposit” means that when the owner is seen, he should deposit it after making a restriction, or having made a sign or mark—such as a clay seal or the like—corresponding to the amount, saying, “There are so many kahāpaṇas,” and so forth. “Having taken” [means] in the absence of such [an owner].
"Having taken it oneself": when there is such a thing as a jewel or something regarded as a jewel. "Knowing that the owners have not arrived":
if they suspect [the theft] regarding themselves, they step off the path, sit down, and subsequently realize that the owners have not come.
"Appropriate": taking refuse rags when there is something regarded as a jewel, or departing without concern for a jewel—such things are suitable for monks.
The commentary on the exposition of acquisition is finished.
38. Commentary on the exposition of defilement (dūsana): 297.

"Giving" means giving both what belongs to oneself and what belongs to another. "An offense of wrong-doing for defiling a family" (*kuladūsanadukkaṭa*): defiling families through one's own misconduct—that is, destroying their faith—is "defiling a family" (*kuladūsana*); the wrong-doing arising from that is "an offense of wrong-doing for defiling a family."
298. Here, the connection is that for one who gives heavy property belonging to the Saṅgha with a sense of ownership (*issara*), there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*).

"Here" means among these things such as flowers and so forth. "With a sense of ownership" is stated with the elision of a *taddhita* suffix; the meaning is "by means of mastery" or "by way of lordship.
"Giving" refers to giving with a sense of lordship for the purpose of winning over families. "Grave offense" [refers to] for the purpose of winning over families.

Regarding the giving [of requisites], there is the *dukkaṭa* offense for defiling a family (*kuladūsanadukkaṭa*), together with the general *dukkaṭa* prescribed [by the rule]; furthermore, there is the *thullaccaya* mentioned thus:
"Monks, these five things are not to be distributed; they must not be distributed by a Saṅgha, a group, or an individual.
Even if distributed, they remain undistributed. Whoever should distribute them, there is an offense of *thullaccaya*."
