[The offense is] *dukkaṭa*. In other cases, it is merely a *thullaccaya*. The same principle applies even when [the property] has been designated for the purpose of providing lodgings.
Regarding "one who gives what belongs to the Saṅgha through theft," the connection to the *dukkaṭa* and other offenses should be understood. "Of one who gives" refers to the method already stated.

As for "the *dukkaṭa* and others," this includes the *dukkaṭa* for corrupting a family incurred by one giving [gifts] for the sake of winning over a family, along with [the offense regarding] a *māsaka* or less than a *māsaka*.

The meaning is that there is a *dukkaṭa* for [a value] less than one *māsaka*, a *thullaccaya* for more than one *māsaka* up to less than five *māsakas*, and a *pārājika* for five *māsakas* or more than five *māsakas*;
thus, the offenses such as *dukkaṭa* occur accordingly. In other cases, there are only *dukkaṭas* and so forth.
299–300. For the sake of supporting a family, one may in every way plant or cause to be planted a tree bearing fruit or flowers.

"And it is not permissible to prepare" is how the connection should be made. The word "and" (ca) includes those things not explicitly mentioned: picking [flowers] oneself or having them picked, and weaving [garlands] oneself or having them woven.

It is called "approaching for fruits and flowers" (phalapupphūpaga) because it approaches [the tree] for the purpose of procuring fruits and flowers. "In every way" means by every possible manner, namely:
through the use of allowable terminology (*kappiya-vohāra*), unallowable terminology (*akappiya-vohāra*), indirect speech (*pariyāya-obhāsa*), signs (*nimitta*), and formal acts (*kamma*).

In this context, "allowable speech" (*kappiyavohāra*) refers to such statements as: "Know this tree," "Know this pit," "Know this flower seedling," or "Know that there is water here," as well as the straightening of a dried-up irrigation channel.
By way of its opposite, "unallowable speech" (*akappiyavohāra*) is defined. "Indirect method" (*pariyāya*) means: "A wise person should have flower seedlings and the like planted; before long..."

The statement beginning with “they conduce to assistance” and so forth [is made]. What is called “illumination” (obhāsa) is standing while holding a hoe, a spade, and so forth, as well as garlands and cuttings.
What is called “making signs” (nimittakamma) is bringing a hoe, a water-vessel, and so forth, and placing them nearby.
They say that “tending” (jaggituṃ) means having performed tasks such as sprinkling water and so forth. However, regarding the tying and untying of knots, all six varieties of flowers [are used].
It should be understood that [these flowers] are knotted, tied with a loop, pierced, wrapped, filled, or woven.

Their specific distinctions, however, should be understood by their names alone. Furthermore, apart from gathering them from a family [of donors], it is not permitted for a bhikkhu to make them himself or to have them made by means of an improper request, saying:
"Know this; when made thus, it will look beautiful, so that these flowers do not scatter."

However, it is permissible to have [the work] done by means of allowable speech (*kappiya-vacana*), such as "Please do so," without [explicitly] engaging in the act of gathering a family (*kulasaṅgaha*).
Regarding "planting and so forth": this refers to having [seeds] planted or watered in unsuitable soil, or planting and so forth elsewhere.

301–2. Now, in order to show the remaining two among the eight bases for gathering families (*kulasaṅgaha-vatthu*) beginning with the offering of flowers, he said, "It has already been stated," and so forth.

The avoidance of wrong livelihood has already been stated; it is precisely as stated there. "The explanation regarding the sending of messengers on foot shall now be told"—this is the remainder of the text.

The connection is as follows: having appointed one's own attendant (*veyyāvaccakara*) to serve one's father, if one carries a message or dispatch for household affairs by means of a messenger, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Since there is nothing at all that ought to be said concerning fellow practitioners of the Dhamma, only fathers and the like are mentioned. Regarding "in household affairs":
This is a locative of object (*visaya-sattamī*). "By way of words" (*padavārena*) means by way of sequence; the intention is "word by word. It should be connected thus:
even for one who speaks again without having first received the message, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). "Again" (*puna*) means afterwards.
There is an offense of wrong-doing for one who descends from the road thinking, "Now this is that village; come, let me announce the message," and for one who speaks at every step.
This is the intention. However, it is permissible for one who, having rejected that [monastic] instruction,
has himself remained in a state of compassion and gone there to announce a message appropriate to his own status— such as "Worship the feet of the Blessed One in my name"—
to carry such a layperson’s allowable (kappiya) message.

303. *Abhūtārocanarūpiyasaṃvohāruggahādisā*: those which indicate, state, or explain the false proclamation (*abhūtārocanā*), the trading in money (*rūpiyasaṃvohāra*), and the acquisition (*uggaha*)—that is, the conditions that have arisen—are called *abhūtā...hādisā*; what is meant is "those similar to them. 304.

Having caused [the flowers] to be brought and having brought them oneself, one may give the flowers for the purpose of worshipping the site (*vatthupūjā*); it should be construed thus: "to give for the purpose of worshipping the site for the remaining relatives who have arrived.
When it is said, "having caused to be brought and having brought," it means "having summoned and having caused to be summoned."

The phrase “or” (*vā*) was not stated because it would have been redundant; it is already implied by what has been said. “Of those who have arrived” (*pattānaṃ*) includes those who have arrived by being summoned.

“For the purpose of worshipping the physical relic” (*vatthupūjatthaṃ*) means for the purpose of worshipping the Triple Gem. However, it is indeed permissible to give [the gift] for the purpose of worshipping the physical relic even to lay followers (*upāsaka*) who have arrived.
“For the purpose of worshipping symbols and so forth” (*liṅgādipūjatthaṃ*) means for the purpose of worshipping the Śiva-linga, the Giṇḍu image, and so on.
305. By the phrase "likewise they bear fruit," he refers back to everything stated regarding the flower.

"Those who are destitute of provisions" (*paribbayavihīnānaṃ*) is a compound meaning those guests whose provisions (*paribbaya*), that is, their travel rations (*pātheyya*), have been lost or exhausted. "Together with their own" (*saparaṃ*) means those who are one's own trusted friends.
In the Commentary, however, the statement "only what belongs to oneself" was spoken in order to exempt [the donor] from the classification of grave offenses (*thullaccaya*) and so forth.

306. "By one who is authorized" (*sammatena*) means it should be given; "should be given" (*deyyaṃ*) means a fourth part should be given. However, by the other [method], it should be connected as "having asked for permission, it should be given. But by the other, namely by one who is not authorized (*asammatena*). 307.

"Having delimited" (*paricchijja*) means having delimited either by way of a fruit-delimitation, such as "this many fruits should be given," or by way of a tree-delimitation, such as "these trees should be given. "From that" (*tato*) means from the fruits thus delimited.
"Or from a tree. This should be connected with "to one who asks, whether sick or otherwise.

Regarding "or the tree should be shown": without saying, "The fruits here are beautiful; take them from here," one should simply point out the tree, saying, "It is permitted to take [fruits] from here.
308. Now, having shown the determination of the four items beginning with flowers among the eight, [he shows] the determination of fruits and flowers as previously stated.
Referring to the remaining four [substances], he says "sirīsā" and so forth.

Regarding "sirīsacuṇṇakasāvacuṇṇe": *kasāva* is that which has "anything" as its beginning; that itself is the powder (*cuṇṇa*). Thus, it is a compound meaning "the sirīsa powder and the powder of astringent substances (*kasāva*) and so forth.
For it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā: "The sirīsa powder or another astringent substance. Although one should have said "kasāvādi," it is stated with a short vowel (*rassa*).
“Sesesu” means among the three [substances], such as bamboo and so forth. Although it was not mentioned in the Pāḷi, because it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā, he said:
“One may insert even a leaf here. “Here” refers to among the flowers and so forth.
The commentary on the section concerning defilement (dūsana) is concluded.
39. Commentary on the Exposition of the Entrance into the Rains Retreat (Vassūpanāyika-niddesa) 309–310.
The connection is: "There are two entrances into the rains retreat, namely the earlier and the later.

That which is to be entered upon the first day of the fortnight immediately following the full moon of Āsāḷha is "prior" because it occurs before the later one; that very [period] is the "earlier" (purimikā).
After that, the *pacchimikā* (the later rains-residence) is to be entered on the first day (*pāṭipadadivasa*) immediately following the next full moon.
"Upanayana" means reaching or approaching; it is the act of entering. "Vassa" means rain;
however, here the rainy season is taken metaphorically as "vassa," and dwelling there is likewise called "vassa" by way of metaphor. Of the rains—
The "approaching for the rains residence" (*vassūpanāyikā*) is the act of approaching, either by means of verbal expression or by means of making a formal commitment (*ālaya*).
In this context, there are two ways of approaching for the earlier rains residence (*purimikā vassūpanāyikā*): the undertaking of the commitment and the verbal expression;

and there are two ways of approaching for the later rains residence (*pacchimikā vassūpanāyikā*): the undertaking of the commitment and the verbal expression—thus it should be connected with these two. "In this context" (*tattha*) refers to among those [two types].
Regarding these two: in order to show both of them, the passage beginning with “such as this” was stated.

That grasping of a dwelling place and the verbal expression—namely, “I enter the rains residence for this three-month period in this monastery; I enter the rains residence here”—is of such a kind; the meaning is “of this sort.
And here, the verbal expression is mentioned first, disregarding the order of their arising. This is because one may enter the rains residence in either of the two ways.
It is permissible. For this very reason, it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:

"Even if there is an attachment [thinking], 'I shall spend the rains retreat here,' yet the rains retreat is not entered due to a lack of mindfulness, the lodging already taken is well-taken, one does not become one whose rains retreat is broken, and one is indeed permitted to perform the *pavāraṇā*.
For even without a verbal declaration, by the mere act of forming an attachment, the rains retreat is indeed entered."

Thus it was said. However, for one who has searched for a dwelling place among those excluding ships and caravans and still does not find one, he may enter merely by making a mental reservation (*ālayakaraṇa*).

And when entering, he should enter after having looked after the monastery, provided drinking water and water for washing, and completed all the formal acts of respect such as the worship of the cetiya.
Regarding the taking possession of the dwelling (*ālayapariggahe*), the reservation—
To show this, he said: "In this context, the arising of consciousness is the *ālaya*.
"In this" refers to the two [cases]. 311. "On that day" means on the day of entering the rains retreat (*vassūpanāyikā*). "Knowing" means knowing, "Today is the day of entering the rains retreat";

"not having entered" is an epithet for him. 312. "The second" refers to the later period (*pacchimika*). "Not having entered" means not having entered the earlier period (*purimika*) due to some obstacle. "Three months" means...
[This applies] during either the first three months or the last three months [of the rains].

However, having entered the rains residence, if one departs on the very same day for a seven-day business—even if one does not wait until dawn—and returns within those seven days, there is no offense. 313–5.
For the sake of one's mother and father, or for five fellow practitioners of the Dhamma, [one may accept] food for the sick and for those attending the sick.
"Whether sent or not sent with the purpose of a seven-day task— thinking, 'I will go and seek medicine for him, or ask for it, or attend to him;
I will cause one who is dissatisfied to depart, or dispel his anxiety, or separate him from wrong views,
or perform or cause to be performed the formal act of reconciliation (vuṭṭhāna) for a heavy offense, or exert myself or cause such exertion to be made'— " [in such cases, there is no offense].
Or they may go for a distance of a league (*yojana*).
Here, however, the meaning should be understood by applying the method that will be explained according to what is possible.

By the mention of "mother" and so forth, those very persons are included by the term "the sick" (*gilāna*); their attendants are "those who attend to them" (*tad-upaṭṭhāka*); thus, there are both the sick and those who attend to them.
And "their meal" (*tesaṃ bhattaṃ*) is a compound. "Medicine" (*osadhaṃ*) means the remedy for those very same sick people. "I shall seek" (*esissāmi*) means I shall search for it.

"I shall ask" (*pucchissāmi*) means I shall ask those very seven persons who are sick. "I shall attend" (*upaṭṭhissāmi*) means I shall nurse those very same sick people. "He delights" (*abhiratīti*) means he is delighted;
not delighted in the Teaching because of seeing forms and so forth that are discordant with it, [he is] not delighted. Delight (*abhiramaṇaṃ*).

"Or one who is not delighted": he who has no delight is "not-delighted"; such a person. One who is not delighted among those who share the same Dhamma—him I shall set apart, meaning I will lead him elsewhere for the purpose of removing his distraction.
"Remorse" (*kukkucca*) refers specifically to remorse regarding the Vinaya that has arisen in these very five.
The accusative case is used here due to its connection with *kitaka* (a small amount) and by way of option. "View" (*diṭṭhi*) refers to the wrong view of those very same individuals.

*Garukamādikam*: the analysis is "that which has a grave offense as its beginning. By the word "beginning" (*ādi*), the inquiry regarding the seniority of novices, the desire to undertake the training rules, and the performance of formal acts such as *tajjanīya-kamma* are included.

*Vuṭṭhāna*: the restoration of a monk from a grave offense through the granting of probation (*parivāsa*), penance (*mānatta*), and so forth. *Ussukka*: the zeal for such matters as the inquiry regarding seniority.
By the phrase "and so forth" (*evam-ādinā*), the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes such things as engaging in discourses on the Dhamma regarding views (*diṭṭhigata*) and the like.
Regarding the permission to go: one who goes must do so while remaining within the precinct boundary (*upacāra-sīmā*), having made the mental resolve (*ābhoga*), "I will return within seven days.
If one crosses the precinct boundary without making this resolve, the rains-residence is broken (*chinnavassa*).

They say it "occurs. Regarding "by means of a seven-day function" (*sattāhakiccena*): a function obtainable within seven days—whether already mentioned or yet to be mentioned—such as a formal act of the Saṅgha (*saṅghakamma*) and so forth, is called a "seven-day function.
Because [the robe] must be brought out from the monastery at the very moment of the seventh dawn, the entire duration of the seven days is taken into account.
316. "In a formal act of the Saṅgha" (*saṅghakamme vajeti*): in a function of the Saṅgha, such as in the Uposatha hall, in dwellings, or in relation to the parasols and railings of a *cetiya*.
The meaning is that one should avoid even the slightest signs of private dwellings. One may go if invited for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma;
one may go if sent by one's teachers; or one may go to see one's teachers—thus it should be construed. Regarding the word "invited":
if an agreement has already been made beforehand, such as, "We must assemble on such-and-such a day," [then one may go].
"Invited" means he has been invited. "By elders" means by preceptors (upajjhāya) and teachers (ācariya). "Sent" means dispatched for the purpose of washing clothes and so forth.
"To see" applies even when one is not ill. 317. "Washing clothes... pe ...
seeing" should be construed as "he does not incur an offense. Here too, the locative case is used in the sense of a sign (*nimitta*). "Clothes" [etc.]... [as above].

"By name" refers to the robe. "Relatives" means other than mother and father. "Attendants" refers to lay followers (*upāsakas*). "If he does not arrive today"—meaning one who has not gone far—should not reach [the destination];
this is the connection for obtaining [the robe]. "Obtaining" refers to the formal act (*kamma*) stated regarding his failure to arrive. Regarding "if he will arrive today":
if dawn breaks while he is on the road after having gone to a neighboring monastery and returning again, there is even a breaking of the rains retreat (*vassaccheda*).
They say that [the robe] does not exist, and thus there is no offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for interrupting the night.

318. "By other relatives" means by relatives other than one's mother and father. "Having pointed out" refers to acts such as giving gifts or listening to the Dharma. And here, regarding the phrase "when sent or dispatched," it should be understood as "it is permissible. 319.

"When there is an obstacle for oneself" refers to obstacles to life or to the holy life (*brahmacariya*) caused by thieves, reptiles, or coral; it includes even the non-availability of medicine or a suitable attendant.
“Even the interruption of the rains-residence (*vassa*) may constitute a ‘seven-day business’ (*sattāhakaraṇīya*),” some ancient teachers say; this appears reasonable.

For in every respect, how could there not be a reason for interrupting the rains-residence by spending even seven days outside the monastery—since staying outside is permitted for such reasons—and then resuming residence within the monastery?
The grammatical connection is: “one whose rains-residence has been interrupted should not perform the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*).”

320. Although the meaning is already understood by the phrase "one who has no bed or seat" (*asenāsanika*), the expression "and in the open air" (*ajjhokāse*) was stated for the purpose of turning away from dwelling [in a shelter], thinking:
"I am one who dwells in the open; what need have I for a bed or seat? "In the hollow of a tree" means in a clean hollow of a tree.
However, inside a large hollow, having constructed a small hut with a thatched roof and an entrance door—
It is permissible to approach after having joined [the parts]. The phrase "having tied a platform even to a branch," etc., follows the same method already stated.
Likewise, it should be understood accordingly for umbrella-stands as well. A "hovel" (*chavakuṭi*) refers to a hut consisting of various types such as a bedstead with spikes, and so forth.
Among these, a "bedstead with spikes" (*ṭaṅkitamañca*) is one made by boring holes in the middle of long bed-legs and inserting cross-pieces (*aṭaniyo*).
A bedstead made by placing a stone on top of four stones is also [included]. 321.

"By one who has no lodging" means: by one for whom there is no lodging provided with any one of the five types of roofing—namely, grass, leaves, bricks, stone, or plaster—and which is equipped with a fitted door and fastenings. This, however, refers to a verbal expression.
They say that this was said with reference to having made a formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*), but that is incorrect;

for if that were the case, there ought to be a separate rule [for it], just as there is for boats and so forth. By the phrase "one who has entered upon [the rains] in a boat, etc.," it is indicated that it is permissible for one who does not possess a dwelling (*asenāsanika*) to enter upon the rains in boats and such. And in that regard, if one seeks out a hut and obtains one, there—
Having entered [a village], because there is no monastery (*vihāra*) present, one should not say "in a monastery," but rather say three times, "I enter the rains residence here.

If none is available, one should establish a dwelling place (*ālaya*). By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and to perform the *pavāraṇā*," it is included that there is no offense for breaking the rains residence due to a cause for interruption.
"In the army, in a caravan, and on a boat—in these three places, there is no offense for breaking the rains residence."
And it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā: "One may perform the Pavāraṇā.

Regarding the interruption of the rains residence (*vassaccheda*), since it was said, "Monks, I allow you to go wherever there is a caravan," and because this refers to the very nature of traveling by land or by boat, it should be understood as being spoken with reference merely to going elsewhere without remaining in the place where one entered the rains residence.
The commentary on the explanation of the commencement of the rains residence (*vassūpanāyika*) is finished.
40. Commentary on the explanation of the non-divisible (*avebhaṅgiya*):
322–5. "The monasteries... up to... clay vessels"—these five should be connected as "are not to be divided. "Five" means: [the five items listed].
By way of grouping them together as "gardens and garden sites" and so forth, there are five;
however, by their individual forms, these become twenty-five when the five types of grass are added. Thus it is said:
"Two are comprised of two [categories] each, while the third is comprised of four."
The fourth consists of nine sections, and the fifth is divided into eight parts.
Thus, with five groups, the Protector, whose eyes are the fivefold stainless vision, has explained the twenty-five kinds of heavy goods.
In this context, a "monastery" (*ārāma*) refers to either a flower garden or a fruit garden.

A "monastery site" (*ārāmavatthu*) is the location where those very gardens were established, or, when they have perished, the original plot of ground. A "dwelling" (*vihāra*) refers to any kind of lodging, such as a palace and so forth.
An "iron cauldron" (*lohakumbhī*) is a cauldron made of either black iron or copper; the same principle applies to basins and similar vessels.
"Here, 'the reciter' refers to the forest-dweller (*arañjaro*). 'The turn' refers to the water-pot (*ghaṭo*). The masculine designation 'these' is used in reference to the heap.
'Indivisible' means not to be shared by way of cutting off the root. However, there is no offense for one who uses or gives away [the goods] by way of exchange.
By the word 'and' in the phrase 'and not to be given away,' it includes what was not explicitly stated, namely, 'not to be shared.'"

326–8. Having set aside the first three heaps because they consist exclusively of heavy articles, the section beginning with “a creeper” (*vallī*) is commenced in order to distinguish between heavy and light articles starting from the fourth heap.

Even a creeper the size of half an arm, a bamboo eight finger-breadths long, even a single blade of grass or the like the size of a fist, or even a leaf—whether naturally colored or of five colors—even if it is the size of a palm fruit.

The construction is as follows: even clay the size of a palm fruit, or lime the size of a palm fruit, or *kaṅgu* grain, husks, and so forth—whether given there or grown on-site—if they belong to the Saṅgha and are protected, they are not to be divided; likewise, ropes, cords, and so forth, if belonging to the Saṅgha, are not to be divided.
A bamboo may be taken [for use] if it is as thin as a leaf-needle or a reed-stalk. Grass, *muñja*, *pabbaja*, and so forth are included by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*).
"Except for the rest, whatever grass there may be. A leaf measuring eight finger-breadths [is permitted]; an empty book is indeed a heavy article. "Ordinary" means naturally occurring.
"Five colors" refers to the five colors beginning with red and white. "Lime, kaṅguṭṭha, and so forth" includes these under the category of clay.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in "kaṅguṭṭha and so forth," substances such as *sajjurasa* and *hiṅgulaka* are included. "Given" means...

It has been given to the Saṅgha. "Grown there" means grown on land belonging to the Saṅgha. "Ropes, cords, and so forth" refers to ropes and cords made of thread, hemp, flax, coconut fiber, or leather.
By the word "and so forth," single-stranded ropes made by twisting hemp, flax, and the like are included.

However, by way of contrast, it should be understood that in this context, the others [the remaining items] are to be distributed among the fourth group in the case of work for the Saṅgha or for a Cetiya.
"When the work is finished, it should be distributed"—this is how it should be construed.
Regarding metal vessels: "metal vessels suitable for a monk," such as a bowl (*patta*) and so forth; likewise, metal vessels that are unfinished or unmade;
or a water-pot (*vāraka*) with a foot-base—these are what are to be distributed. "And so forth" (*ādi*) refers to an iron bowl, an iron ladle, a copper vessel, and a bronze dish.
An eye-salve stick, an ear-wick for removing earwax, a needle, a leaf-needle, a small pair of forceps, a small awl, a key, a gong-stick, and so forth.
"Unfinished" means not yet completed. "Not made at all" means entirely unmade.
"A foot-measure" refers to that which measures a foot in the island of Sri Lanka. A "foot" is a fourth part; it is equal to five Magadha *nāḷis*. A Magadha *nāḷi*...
And this should be understood as being less than five *satas*. Likewise for a water-jar and an oil-container.
A *vāsī* (adze) by which one cannot perform any major work other than cutting tooth-sticks or trimming sugarcane is a *bhājiyā* (small adze).
However, a handle for a broom that is merely a piece of wood without a shaft, which can be placed inside a small box—this is simply a fruit [of a tree].
This is what may be kept. Among the tools for working with tin: the small knife for cutting tin; among the tools of the goldsmith:
the small knife for cutting gold; among the tools of the leather-worker: the small knife for cutting leather;
and among the tools of the barber and tailor: setting aside the large scissors, the large tweezers, and the large pair of nippers.
All items that are to be shared out (*bhājanīya-bhaṇḍa*). Likewise with keys. However, by reversing what was stated [previously], it should be understood that metal utensils are not to be shared out.

330. By the phrase “In bamboo,” etc., wooden utensils are shown. But by including them under the category of “wooden utensils,” all manufactured articles made of wood, bamboo, leather, sandals, and so forth, should be understood.
“The umbrella handle and the tally-stick” is a *dvanda* compound. Regarding the sandal...
A staff is a walking-staff. 331.
"The staff for one permitted to stay" means the staff for one who has been granted permission to remain.
"Collyrium-box, horn, etc."—by the word "etc.," the collyrium-rod, umbrella, folded leaf, sandals, water-strainer, foot-wiper, and a non-residual vessel for *āmalaka* fruit are included.
This includes such things as a jar made of *āmalaka* fruit, a gourd-vessel, a jar made of gourd, and a horn-vessel.
(332) Among wooden articles, anything other than those already mentioned is a "heavy article. The construction is:
"a clay foot-jar" means a bowl (*bhājī*). "Foot-jar" (*pādaghaṭaka*) refers to a jar sufficient for one person's share. By this term, he characterizes it as a clay vessel.
Therefore, the bowl, the platter, and the water-pot—these are items to be distributed;

the remainder mentioned are not to be distributed. 333–4. One should construe it thus: "One may exchange heavy property for heavy [property], and one may exchange immovable [property] for immovable [property].
By "heavy" is meant a bed, chair, and so forth. By "immovable" is meant the monastery and so forth—the first two groups of requisites. Having done so...
"And he may consume" (*bhuñjituṃ*): the meaning is that having thus exchanged [the goods], he may consume the allowable articles (*kappiyabhaṇḍa*) brought from there;
here the suffix *-tuṃ* is used in the sense of a procedure (*vidhi*). "He takes rice and so forth by way of interest" (*phātikammena*)—this is how it should be connected.
"Interest" (*phātikamma*) means an increase in value, whether equal to, exceeding, or equivalent to the original price. "The rest" refers to the first heap.
The commentary on the explanation of the "Non-Dispersal" (Avebhaṅgiya) is concluded.
41. Commentary on the Miscellaneous Explanation (Pakiṇṇaka-niddesa): 335.
For one who sleeps during the day in a place where the six doors are secured and there are stakes and loops, the door must be turned [to face inward].

"Should fasten" (*bandheyya*) refers to the connection. "The door and the door-fastening" (*dvārañca dvārabandhanañca*) becomes *dvārabandhanāni* by elision of the middle term (*majjhepadalopa*), or else the word "fastening" (*bandhana*) itself denotes the door-posts;
thus, "together with the door-fastenings" (*sadvārabandhanaṃ*) refers to the place.
"Below, the mortar and above, the peg" (*heṭṭhā udukkhalakañca upari pāsako ca*) forms a compound meaning "together with the mortar and peg" (*saudukkhalapāsakehi*). In such [a manner]...
The phrase "enclosed" (parikkhitta) is understood to mean that the site must be surrounded by a boundary such as a wall.

And they say that this [boundary] is of the same measure as that prescribed for sleeping with another; that is, sufficient in height to allow for lying down together. "Lying down" (sayanta) means reclining after having released one's feet from the ground.
"Reversible" (parivattaka) means suitable for being turned here and there by way of opening and closing. "Door" (dvāra) includes even a door made of cloth or a curtain.
"Should fasten" means that by the minimum method, one should fasten it even to the extent that it does not enter the head; "should restrain" is what is meant.
336. "And also attention": "attention" in the sense of "he will watch over this.
By the word *ca* ("and"), the expression "watch over the door" is also included. "In its own power" (*savase*) means in a place dependent upon one's own control, where—
However, because many people frequent it, even though the gate is closed, it does not remain secure in its place;
lacking a gate, they even climb over the wall and wander about. In such a pariveṇa, there is no need for guarding.
Alternatively, the crop is dependent on him (the farmer), not on the *yakkhas* and so forth, since it was seized by them and made to lie down after being bound.

And by the phrase "and by non-existence," it means in every way. When that exists, the meaning is the mode (ākāra) designated as the restraint, the application of effort, and the verbal expression, which were previously mentioned as the doors.

337. "Jewels" refers to the ten kinds beginning with pearls. Among those, however, all gems—whether crystal, beryl, ruby, or cat's-eye—are untouchable, whether they are polished or unpolished and pierced; and so too are glass-gems and water-shells.
Raw grain, even if washed, is untouchable; stone, even if polished and pierced, is untouchable; and gold, even if melted together with it and turned the color of mung beans, is untouchable.
For the keepers of a shrine-house, it is permissible to remove only refuse from a golden shrine. Base metal (ārakūṭa) is also of the same category as gold.
"Female forms" includes even female figures made of dough. "Grain" includes even that which grows there [in the field].
Even seven kinds of grain spread out on a path are untouchable. Even other foods such as palm fruits and so forth, when [the owner] is playing, are untouchable;
one must not pass by them even if they are spread out without crushing them. If there is no path, one should go after resolving upon a path.
"Women's ornaments" includes even a palm-leaf skirt or a ring placed merely for the purpose of wearing it.
338. “With wax, oil, and lac” means with any kind of resin mixed with oil—such as honey, wax, or nutmeg—or with oil mixed with water.
“With hand-fans” means like a fan, it is a fan; because the hand performs the function of a fan by means of the fingers, the hand itself is the fan, thus a hand-fan.
It refers to any kind of fan made of ivory or other materials that is both a fan and a hand-fan.
*Duvaṇḍo*. "Osaṇṭheyyā" means having rubbed [the body] with [unguents], one should cause them to sit down together. 339.
"They did not lie down with a single upper garment or a single bedspread"—this is to be construed as "they did not lie down on the same couch.
The analysis of the compound is: those for whom there is one upper garment (*pāvuraṇa*) and one bedspread (*attharaṇa*). "Na tuvaṭṭayuṃ" means they should not lie down.
One should connect [the phrase] as "nor should one eat from a single vessel. 340.
*Aṭṭhaṅgula* is a compound meaning "that which has eight finger-breadths according to the human standard-finger (*manussānaṃ pamāṇaṅgulena*), together with what is in excess of that.
The connection is: "one should not eat garlic born in Magadha, nor garlic in the form of an emblic myrobalan (*āmalaka*) cluster."
"Not unwell" means not being ill. 341.

Regarding "whether superior or inferior": whether one speaks of someone as superior or inferior on account of birth and so forth—whether straightforwardly, under another pretext, or jokingly—the connection is that this constitutes "wrong speech.
"On account of birth and so forth" refers to insults concerning birth, name, clan, occupation, craft, illness, gender, defilements, or offenses.
"Superior" (ukkaṭṭhaṃ) means one who is superior by birth and so forth, whether ordained or unordained. "In jest" (davaṃ) means with the intention of joking.
"Directly" (ujuṃ va) means by way of saying, "You are a caṇḍāla," and so forth. "By means of another pretext" (aññāpadesena vā) means by way of saying, "There are some caṇḍālas here," and so forth.

342. "Long nails" refers to their length in terms of the measure of flesh. "Long hair" refers to [a length] of two finger-breadths; even if they are not that long, [it applies] from the point where it exceeds a month's growth.
One is not permitted to let even a single day pass [without attending to these]. "The long nose-hair" means that which has protruded from outside the nostrils.
"Polished twenty" refers to the polish of the twenty nails. Regarding "the private parts": it should be connected as follows—shaving the hair in both armpits and the urinary organ is not permitted.
"Is not permitted" means that these things, such as polishing and so forth, are not allowed; this is the sense of the particle *na labbhati*.
Or it may be obtained. However, for the sake of illness, it is permissible to gather hair in a cramped space.
343. The construction is: "One should not cause obstruction according to seniority regarding bedding and seating designated for the Saṅgha or belonging to the Saṅgha.
"Designated for the Saṅgha" (*saṅghuddiṭṭha*) means assigned to the Saṅgha; the intention is that it was made for the sake of the Saṅgha. Whosoever is the elder...
"According to seniority" means in the order of seniority. "One should not obstruct" means one should not prevent [others from entering].
"Wet-footed" refers to those by whom water is seen in the place they have stepped upon. "Lodgings" refers to beds, chairs, and so forth;
by this, it is also implied that the ground has been swept and cleaned. The connection is: "or likewise with well-washed feet and wearing sandals. "Well-washed feet" means...
It is the place that must be stepped upon with feet already washed. "One whose feet have been washed for the act of stepping" is a descriptive compound (*kriyāviśeṣaṇasamāsa*).
However, if the resident monks (*nevāsika*) make use of it even with unwashed feet, it is permissible to use it in that same way.
"In that same way" means one should not step on ground or a dwelling that has been plastered or smoothed.
344. *Saṅghāṭiyā* means with a saṅghāṭi that has been formally determined (*adhiṭṭhita*). Having wrapped the feet and crossed the legs, one forms a sitting posture;
the form *pallattheti* comes from the verbal root *pallatthati*, meaning "he crosses. The intended meaning is: "One should not sit in a cross-legged posture either in a monastery or within a village.
The phrase "prepared by work" (*parikammakataṃ*) refers to a wall or similar surface; this is how it should be construed. "Prepared by work" means [prepared] with white pigment.
Or it is that which has been prepared by means of mental action (*cittakamma*). The word "etc. (*ādi*) includes doors, windows, and so forth.

"Not leaning against" means one should not lean against it without having covered it with a robe or similar garment. "No na ācameti" means "not not rinsing"; the sense is that one should indeed rinse.
Regarding the two negations, they convey the original affirmative meaning. By the word "being present" (*sante*), he indicates that there is no offense when water is not present.
345. *Akappiyasamādāne*: in the undertaking of what is unallowable for monks and novices.
*Dava* is a particle; the meaning is "with the intention of sport. *Silāpavijjhane*: even including the throwing of pebbles or anything as small as a hand-fist.
It should be construed that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) both in the teaching of something similar and in making it known. *Sabhāgāya*: by way of the subject matter.
The analysis of the compound is: "her share is equal to that of this offense. The word *ca* (and) includes the mere acceptance of such [an agreement].
346. "Agreement" (*paṭissava*) means the promise: "We both shall dwell here for the rains retreat; let us recite [the Pātimokkha] together," and so forth.
"Breach of agreement" (*paṭissavavisaṃvāda*) is the failure to act upon it later; in that [breach], the locative case is used in the sense of the instrumental (i.e., by reason of).
“Of one with a pure mind” means: at the time of speaking, one whose mind is directed toward the thought, “I shall do it. “The other” means another person with an impure mind. 347.
“In the case of a need” refers to when there is a need to take dry wood and so forth; the connection is that one may then mount a vehicle of human size (*porisa*).
“In times of distress” means in situations such as seeing wild beasts. 348. The connection is: “without a water-strainer. “On a journey” means, at minimum, a distance reckoned as half a *yojana*.
On a journey. If there is no water-strainer (*parissāvana*) or a water-pot (*dhammakaraṇa*), even a corner of one’s outer robe (*saṅghāṭikaṇṇa*) may be designated [as a strainer].
"To one who asks" means to one who asks for a water-strainer. 349. The construction is:

"Except on account of illness, in the case of the remaining limbs and in the case of self-destruction, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). "The remaining limbs" refers to the cutting off of parts other than the genitals, such as the ears, nose, and so forth. "Self-destruction" refers to killing oneself by means of withholding food and the like.
350. "Paintings" refers to figures such as women and men being made on canvas or cloth, and "scrolls" refers to paintings made on wood and other materials;
these are the terms used in this compound. However, one may have the *Jātaka* stories and so forth made by others.
One may also perform floral arrangements and the like oneself. One should not cause someone who is eating in a monastery, a forest hermitage, or a house to rise.

It should be joined [as follows]. The compound is a *dvanda* consisting of the monastery (*ārāma*)—meaning the monastery complex—and the forest (*arañña*), as well as the house (*geha*)—meaning the interior dwelling.
Although one should say "in monasteries... and in houses," it is stated thus by means of the *gāthā* meter through the substitution of the vowel *e* with the vowel *a*.
Once the space has been made, when it is said, "Enter," one should both enter and sit down nearby.
351. The connection is that it is permissible for one who is ill to mount vehicles drawn by males, as well as palanquins (*sivikā*) and hand-carts (*hatthavaṭṭaka*).
"Drawn by males" means drawn by horses, oxen, or men; they must not be drawn by cows.
As for the charioteer, it is permissible whether he be a woman or a man. The same rule applies to hand-carts. "Vehicles" refers to chariots, carts, and so forth.
*Śivikā* means a chair-litter; the meaning is a wheeled carriage. *Pāṭaṅkī* means a swing-cot.

Regarding the term "for one who is ill": here, one should not understand "ill" merely by a slight affliction such as a headache; rather, it should be understood as one who is unable to go without a vehicle.
For it was in the Kosala country that the Blessed One, while permitting the use of vehicles, [made this distinction].
While the Blessed One was traveling to Sāvatthī to see him, [the Buddha] saw a certain sick monk sitting at the foot of a tree because he was unable to go;
when people learned of this situation and said, "Come, venerable sir, let us go," he replied, "Friends, I will not go, I am sick. It was in reference to this account that [the rule] was authorized.

And it is understood that when that bhikkhu speaks thus, he refers specifically to an illness that necessitates the cessation of travel, because [the journey] has been interrupted for the sake of accomplishing the intended purpose;
moreover, by the commentator who establishes the limit for sandals as being the same as the limit for a vehicle, [it is stated]:
"In the phrase 'a sick bhikkhu with sandals,' here 'sick' means..."

"He who is unable to enter a village without sandals"—this is what is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. Therefore, it should be concluded that only one who is ill in the manner previously described is considered "ill" in this context. 352.

"In making sport" means in engaging in play. "To another" means even to one who is immoral (*dussīla*). "In coaxing" means by saying things such as, "I will give you a bowl," "I will give you a robe," and so forth.
353. It should be connected as: "Having opened [the door], she does not show [them] inside. Those nuns. 354.

Regarding "exhortation" (*ovāda*): when the nuns have arrived on the thirteenth or fourteenth day, asked about the Uposatha, and the monk has announced it by saying "It is the fourteenth," and so forth, they must again assemble on that Uposatha day and make a formal request for the approach to the exhortation (*ovādūpasaṅkamanayācana*).
Having informed the one who recites the Pātimokkha and having received his formal authorization, it must be brought back on the first day of the fortnight (pāṭipada).
However, this does not apply to one who is ignorant and foolish, nor to one who is ill and unable to do so, nor to a traveler who wishes to depart on the first day of the fortnight;
excluding these cases, it is not permissible for another person not to take up the authorization and bring it back. Therefore, it is said: "Not [for] one who takes it," and so forth.
355. *Lokāyata* refers to the teaching of the non-Buddhist sects (tīrthika) associated with useless causes. By this very term, *tiracchānavijjā* (animal-like sciences) is also characterized.
"One should not recite" means one should not teach it to others. By this, even one's own mastery of these subjects is prohibited.
Both *lokāyata* and *tiracchānavijjā* increase lust, hatred, and delusion; they are censured by the Buddhas and others, and are obstacles to heaven and liberation.

All branches of knowledge—whether they be those that are bent, extended, or turned across, such as the dramatic arts and so forth—are included under the category of "conformable" (anuloma) or, having reached the method of the Vinaya, must be maintained with gravity;
thus they should be understood as being comprised within the logic of the Vinaya. And this is the instruction of our teachers.
Regarding the phrase "even in a box": it refers to a place where people eat happily after setting down their bowls, made of copper or iron.
Having placed it in a box made of silver, which is called an "overflowing foot-rest" (āsittakūpadhāna).

356. Regarding "the upper garment and the lower garment": this is a descriptive compound (*kammadhāraya*) qualifying the action, meaning "the upper garment and the lower garment of householders, [worn] in the manner of an elephant's trunk and so forth.
One should neither put on nor wear the upper or lower garments of householders.
Connection: "One should not wear it wrapped around" means one should not wear it by tucking in the hem, as do laborers such as Mallas.
It is not permitted to wear it in this manner even for one who is ill or traveling on a journey.
Furthermore, when traveling on a road, if one lifts up one or two corners and lets them hang over the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*), that is not permitted. Thus, without having put it on [properly]...
Without wearing [the inner robe], one should put on the outer robe evenly all around; and while concealing the three circles, one should wear the inner robe evenly all around.

Likewise, having neither put on nor worn [the robes] properly, for one who acts with negligence—whether in a monastery or within a village—committing any such improper act, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). "Dāya" means a forest. "One should not smear" refers to "all ointments."
Or one should not paint [the wall] with the intention of play, thinking, "Let it perish. 357. The construction is:

"One should not seek an increase" and "one should not request from one who is forbidden by strangers. "Of another" means even of one who is a fellow-practitioner (*sahadhammika*). It should be construed as "having eaten for a few days. *Puna* is a particle. 358.
Whether knowing or not knowing that they are staff-bearers (*daṇḍin*), if one requests protection specifically for them, there is an offense; the penalty shall be his responsibility.
The construction is as follows: "He takes up a staff" means that for one who possesses a staff due to a condition, there is the "taking up of a staff.
"With reference to" means with reference to the past or the future, such as: "This was done by so-and-so and so-and-so in our monastery," or "It will be done.
"When there is a request" means when there is a request from the administrators. "Punished" means when they have taken up the staff against them.
That punishment shall be the neck of the begging bhikkhu; the meaning is that it becomes his debt.
But when the judges ask, "By whom?", he should say: "It is not permissible for us to say 'by such-and-such'; you yourselves must know this.
We merely request protection, so grant us that, and have the goods that were carried off brought back to me. Thus...
Pointing out [the offense] without specifying [a person] is permissible. "Pārājika and so forth" refers to the offenses of pārājika, thullaccaya, and dukkaṭa.
"When the requisites are being carried away, and one says, 'A thief! A thief!'"
"Taking it for their own harm"—this must be the reading.
For only thus does it accord with the plural form "in those who carry off.
When they say "Thief! Thief! regarding those who carry off requisites, and [the authorities] take punishment upon themselves for the sake of their harm, that much shall be his debt.
It should be applied [as follows]. "While they are carrying it away" means while the thieves are taking it and going. "They search for" means they search for the thieves.

"While they are seizing" means while the judicial officials are seizing [the goods]. Whatever has been seized, that much is the debt (*gīvā*) of that bhikkhu; the meaning is that it becomes "property to be restored" (*bhaṇḍadeyya*). 360.

Outside the walls and enclosures, whether in a courtyard, or in a green plot planted with rice and so forth or coconut trees and so forth, or in a place where there is refuse, excrement, sweepings, or urine—
The connection is that it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) if one discards [food] without looking.

By the phrase "without looking at what is fit for use," it is indicated that there is no offense for one who discards food scraps and the like after having looked, or for one who discards them where they are not fit for use. "Vīhādayo" refers to rice and other grains;
"nāḷikerādayo" refers to coconuts and other fruits such as mangoes and jackfruit; thus, "vīhādayo ca nāḷikerādayo" means rice and the like, as well as coconuts and the like.
The compound *cāti* is a *dvanda*; their planting (*ropa*) is that by which rice and so forth are produced... [etc] ...it is what is planted (*ropima*).
"In green" means in a green place. "Vighāsa" refers to leftover water, dregs, and so forth. 361.
Even with regard to things connected with the Dhamma, one may cause dancing, singing, and instrumental music to be performed, or cause them to be employed when they have been performed.
And there is no connection [to the prohibition] regarding looking at it or accepting it when it is said, "We shall make an offering.
"Even that which is connected with the Dhamma" means even that which is associated with the Dhamma or merit, by virtue of being endowed with the qualities of the Triple Gem.
"Dancing" includes even the dancing of peacocks, monkeys, and so forth. "Singing" includes even "tooth-singing," which is performed prior to a formal song.
“Musical instruments” includes even musical instruments such as water-drums (*udakabheri*). “To cause to be played” means to have others perform them. “To employ” means to perform them oneself.
It is not permitted to speak even the Dhamma with a drawn-out, melodic voice.
“Employed” means performed by anyone else whatsoever. By the word “to see,” even glancing without full observation is included; thus, it also has the meaning of “to hear.”
It is understood. There is no offense for one who sees while standing within a monastery. Even if one stands on the road and turns the neck to look, it is still an offense.
If one sees or hears [the sound] at a place where one has gone for some business, there is no offense.
"To accept" means to accept by saying "Very well. To say, "It is good to perform an offering," [is also included].
It is permissible. The word *vā* (or) is used in the sense of conjunction. 362.
It should be connected with the passage beginning, "A royal palace built for the purpose of sport," and so forth. A house variegated by design is a *cittāgāraka* (painted house).
363. The construction is: "One should not exclude [another] from a new seat. Regarding "by means of a seat": this means from the seat. "Should not exclude" means not...
He should cause [the robe] to be lifted up. "He should not lay the robe out in the heat" is how it should be construed. "He should not lay it out" means he should not leave it there in excess.
"By the heavy ones" means by the teacher (ācariya) or preceptor (upajjhāya). "Dismissed" means expelled with such words as "Do not enter here," and so forth. 364.
In the case of reviling a monk or even a lay follower (upāsaka) in their absence, whether for seven offenses or for something else...

It should be construed as "an offense of wrong-doing" (*dukkaṭa*). In the phrase "and from offenses," the word *ca* (and) is used for emphasis. In the expression "and by another indeed," the combination of particles *eva ca* is a fixed formula;
or, *eva* alone is used for emphasis, meaning "by another indeed" than what was previously stated, such as "one who lacks faith," and so forth.
*Parammukhā* is a particle; its meaning is "in the absence of [the person]. For one speaking in their presence, it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). This is by way of censuring evil.

But there is no offense for one who speaks thus. 365. Regarding "what is given in faith" (*saddhādeyya*): it refers to a robe that ought to be given out of faith; by the word *ca* ("and"), it is understood that one may not misappropriate or destroy the remainder either. It is connected [to the phrase] "it is permitted for one's parents. Regarding "for kinsmen as well" (*ñātīnam pi*): the particle *pi* is used in the sense of inclusion (*sambhāvane*). 366.
"If one who has spent the rains retreat elsewhere should take a share from another, it is an offense of wrong-doing" (*dukkaṭa*)—this is the connection. "Elsewhere" (*aññatra*) means...
"In another monastery" means from another monastery. "Should restore" means he should give it back to the place from which it was taken.
The connection is: "If that object has been taken, or lost, or worn out, he is liable for its value.

"If, when exhorted, he does not restore it, by relinquishing his responsibility, he becomes liable for the value of the goods"—this is the construction. "Exhorted" means urged by the owners of the object with the words, "Give it back."
"Of them" means: of those monks who receive gains in that monastery. 367. One should construe it thus:
"One should not enter a village wearing only an inner robe and an upper robe, nor with sandals on; one should not carry a yak-tail fan or a mosquito whisk.
*Antara* and *uttara* together with *antara-uttara*; "wearing [only] antara and uttara" is *santaruttaro*. [This refers to] protection by the bolt.

It is permissible to go after having deposited one’s outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) in the monastery. However, one who dwells in the forest (*āraññaka*) should place it in a basket for goods and set it down in concealed places such as hollows in rocks or trees before departing.

This same method applies to the depositing of the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*) and the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*). "Healthy" (*kalla*) means not being ill. A "mosquito-fan" (*makasabījanī*) is a fan made from the hair of yaks (*camari*).
"Makasabījanī" is a compound. 368.

"Outside of the monastery" (ārāmato bahi) is to be connected [to the preceding]. "From the monastery" (ārāmato) means from the vicinity of the monastery. "He should not wear it" (na dhāreyya) means that one who is not ill should not wear it.
However, for one who has a burning sensation in the body, or an aggravation of bile, or whose eyesight is weak, or who has another [such condition]...
If some ailment arises that cannot be managed without an umbrella, then an umbrella is permitted for him whether in the village or in the forest.

"It is allowed for protection" means it is allowed during the rainy season for the purpose of protecting one's robes; the meaning is that it is also allowed for the purpose of protecting oneself from the fear of wild beasts and thieves. However, an umbrella made of a single leaf is permitted in all circumstances.
369. “One should not enter a double-rope carrying-net” is the connection [of the sentence]. A *ubhatokāja* is a carrying-net (*bhārabandhakāja*) with a rope at both ends of a double-staff;
this is an *alopa-tappurisa* compound. An *ekantarikakāja* is as follows: *antara* itself is *antarika*; “one and an *antarika*” is a *dvanda* compound;
“a carrying-net for one *antarika*” is an *ekantarike bhārabandhakāja*, which is a *tappurisa* compound, thus it is called an *ekantarikakāja*. It is stated as *antarikakāja*.
“*Olamba*” means that which hangs from the hand; thus it is a compound (*samāsa*). 370. *Anokāsakataṃ*:
when the accuser has requested leave by saying, “Venerable sir, please grant me leave, for I wish to speak to you,” there is no leave granted by this one who is being accused;
thus it is a possessive compound (*bahubbīhi*). *Codeyya*: with the intention of causing removal, reviling, performing a formal act (*kamma*), or causing [the person] to stand forth.

One should state it. There is no need for a formal request (*okāsakamma*) in the cases of the *uposatha*, the *pavāraṇā*, the suspension of the observance, the investigation, or the intention to give a Dhamma talk. "Of one who is pure" means of one who is pure by virtue of being free from an offense.

"In what is not a ground" means without cause. "Likewise" refers by extension to the *dukkaṭa* offense. Even when performing [the act], one should do so after investigating in this way: "Does he speak of an actual offense, or an unreal one?"
“For I have said, monks: ‘I allow you to grant permission after having weighed the individual.
(371) The construction is: one should not use a bed-leg that exceeds eight finger-breadths by the standard finger-breadth of beings, or a bed with high legs.
A “standard finger-breadth” (*pakata-aṅgula*) is a finger-breadth by nature; and that should be understood as the carpenter’s finger-breadth.
“Eight and those fingers”: this is a compound meaning “that which is exceeded by those [eight fingers]. “The foot-rest for beds”: that upon which the bed-legs are placed.
“That whose feet are eight fingers high”: this is a *bahubbīhi* (relative) compound. 372. “Mute-vow and so forth”:
this refers to the vow characterized by silence, like that of the mute, which is the first among the heretical vows such as the cow-vow and others.

Compound: *khura* itself as the object is *khurabhaṇḍa*. One who was previously bathed is *nhāpitapubbaka*; this is an instance of the inversion of the qualifier (*visesana*) to the end of the compound.
373. *Hatthakamma* is work to be done with the hand, such as the work of carpenters and the like.
*Anussaraṇa* is the following of the movement of thought, thinking: "By whom was it requested that it be made allowable for me? By us this must be given to him. This refers to that request.

"Following" means "in accordance with that"; the construction is: "to take whatever is obtained from that. "Free from action" (*nikkamma*) means that which has emerged from action, such as those who subsist on leftovers (*vighāsāda*).
The connection is: "to cause it to be done even without being asked. "To have brought" means to bring it from the forest.
"Not belonging to another" refers to wood, grass, straw, and so forth, which are not claimed by anyone else.
374. The construction is as follows: whatever a householder gives, it is permissible for cowherds to take when they are giving;
and regarding what belongs to the Saṅgha or the Cetiya, it is permissible to take according to the established limit. "Gives" means the cowherd gives to the monks. "To take" means to take that much.
"Belonging to the Saṅgha and the Cetiya" refers to what is being given by cowherds who are receiving wages. "According to the established limit" means...
Whatever has been authorized by the Saṅgha for them, saying, "Eat this much every day," one must not exceed that limit.
For there is no limit to giving when one takes [food] by means of a fee from what belongs to the Saṅgha or to a shrine (cetiyasantaka) and guards it. 375.
"One may incur an offense through both body and speech" is stated by way of the majority; however, regarding the act of sexual intercourse...

Because, when there is an action by another, it is possible for one who consents to it to have an offense originating from non-action (*akiriyasamuṭṭhāna*). Or, "by six" means that one may incur an offense through the six origins (*samuṭṭhāna*), which are the causes for the arising of offenses; this is the connection. For all offenses, there are six origins: body, speech, body and speech, body and mind, speech and mind, and body, speech, and mind.
Among these, the first three are without mental intention (*acittaka*).
The latter [offenses] are those involving consciousness.
Threefold are those originating from one source; fivefold are those arising from two sources;
twofold are those based on three or four factors; and singlefold are those arising from six sources.
In that regard, by way of origination, those consisting of the fourth, fifth, and sixth are of one kind, being of a single origination.
By way of origination, those consisting of the first and fourth; the second and fifth; the third and sixth; the fourth and sixth;
and the fifth and sixth are of five kinds, being of a dual origination. And by way of origination, those consisting of the first three and the last three [are of another kind].

There are two types of offenses arising from three origins (*tisamuṭṭhāna*): those arising from the first, third, fourth, and sixth [origins], and those arising from the second, third, fifth, and sixth [origins].
There are two types of offenses arising from four origins (*catusamuṭṭhāna*): [those arising from the first, second, fourth, and sixth; and those arising from the second, fourth, fifth, and sixth].

There is one type of offense arising from all six origins (*chasamuṭṭhāna*). The connection is as follows: "One might incur an offense through these six [factors]: lack of shame (*alajjī*)... [and so on]... and by means of perception (*saññitāya*). One who intentionally incurs an offense... [the rest of the sentence follows].
He incurs an offense, he conceals the offense, and he goes upon a wrong path; such a person is called one who is shameless (*alajjī*).
"Shameless," "ignorant," "one who is troubled by remorse," and "overcome by remorse" form a *dvanda* compound. The suffix *-tta* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).
Among these, one who knowingly disregards what is improper and commits a transgression does so out of a lack of shame.
One who is dull-witted and deluded, not knowing what should and should not be done, does what should not be done and fails in what should be done;

this one incurs [an offense] through ignorance. When remorse has arisen concerning what is allowable and what is unallowable, one who transgresses by crushing [the matter] without having consulted a master of the Vinaya incurs [an offense] through being overcome by remorse.
*Satiplava* means a raft of mindfulness; *sammoha* is a raft of delusion.

One incurs offenses through such things as sleeping together, being separated from the three robes, and so forth, by means of a lapse of mindfulness. Regarding what is allowable (*kappiya*) and what is unallowable (*akappiya*), there is the perception (*saññā*) of what is allowable and unallowable;

one who possesses that [perception] is "possessing-perception" (*saññī*). The suffix *-tā* is used to express the state of that [person]. However, by the elision of *ya*, it is stated as "state of possessing-perception" (*saññitā*);
or else, the nominative case is used in the sense of the instrumental. And those [terms] are [the objects] of "unallowable," etc.

They correspond according to their respective order. In this regard, one who eats the flesh of a bear thinking it is "pig's meat," and eats at an improper time while perceiving it as the proper time, incurs an offense through the perception of what is unallowable as allowable.

However, one who eats pig's meat thinking it is "bear's meat," and eats at the proper time while perceiving it as the improper time, incurs an offense through the perception of what is allowable as unallowable.

376. The construction is: "By way of shamelessness and ignorance, one conceals an offense through body and speech. Regarding "liṅga": this refers to the cause of the transformation of gender. The remainder of the sentence is: "In respect of gender (liṅga), the Saṅgha, the group (gaṇa), and the individual—one," thus the emergence from an offense is fourfold.
377. "In the two requisites" means in regard to robes and almsfood. "Indirect talk, hinting, and requesting"—this is merely a synonym.
However, it should be understood that the indicative act (nimittakamma) which accompanies these is also included right here. In that context, by way of sequence...
*Parikathā* (indirect talk) is speaking in a roundabout way. *Obhāsa* (hinting) is making an indirect suggestion so that one’s intention becomes clear without stating it directly.
*Viññatti* (requesting) is making one’s intention known by means of a sign so that it is understood. *Nimittakamma* (making a sign) is the act of giving a signal.
"In the third" refers to the lodging. "The rest" refers to the requisite of medicine for the sick.
378. The connection is that a gift does not take effect upon the passing away of five who share in the same Dhamma.
"A gift upon one's passing away" refers to a gift made regarding one's own departure, such as: "Upon my passing away, let what belongs to me become the property of my preceptor," and so forth.
"That" means that the robe and other items given upon one's passing belong to the Saṅgha alone, and not to an individual monk; this is the intended meaning.
"But for householders" means: as for the gift given on behalf of householders. This is the defining characteristic of giving here:
it must be something actually given, whether face-to-face by saying, "I give this to you," and so forth, or behind one's back by saying, "I give it to such-and-such a person.
When told, "Take it for yourself," if one says, "I am taking it for myself," it is well-given and well-received.
When it is said, “Make it yours; let it be yours; have it made yours,” he replies, “I am making it mine; let it be mine; I shall have it made mine. This is both badly given and wrongly grasped.
However, if, when told, “Make it yours,” he says, “Very well, venerable sir, I shall take it for myself,” [it is properly received].
"He takes it; it is well taken. 379.

If a bhikkhu or a sāmaṇera should die in the dwelling of the bhikkhunīs within the monastery precincts, if he should pass away there, then—in that case—the Saṅgha of bhikkhus alone is the heir and the owner of what belongs to both [orders]. This is the remainder. "In the remainder as well" means...
The same principle applies to the remainder belonging to bhikkhunīs, sāmaṇerīs, and sāmaṇeras. This is the method:
if they should die in a monastery belonging to the bhikkhus, the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs alone is the heir to their property; this is the meaning of "this is the method. 380.
Regarding what is given with the instruction, "Having taken this, give it to so-and-so," it belongs to the previous owner until it reaches the hand of another.
The meaning is: "It belongs to him who sends it. As for "I give," when one has given saying, "I give to such-and-such a person," it belongs only to the latter;
the meaning is that it is the property of the one to whom it was sent.

Having understood this method—that by the manner described these [robes] become the property of the owners—one should either take them on trust or determine them as the robe of the deceased; such is the construction. "Taking on trust" means...
While the owners are still living, one may take possession [of the robe] out of trust.
If those [owners] have died and no other monks are present, one may determine the deceased’s robe as one's own, thinking, "That belongs to me.
However, the belongings of a deceased person placed far away, having not been given to others, belong to the Saṅgha in each respective case. When a monk has passed away...
"The Saṅgha is the owner of the bowl and robes; moreover, those who attend to the sick are of great benefit.

Therefore, the Saṅgha should give the three robes and the bowl to the attendants of the sick. Whatever light goods or light requisites there are among them, those should be distributed by the Saṅgha present.
Whatever heavy goods or heavy requisites there are among them, those [belong] to the Saṅgha of both those present and those yet to come."
It is not to be given away and not to be divided among the Saṅgha of the four quarters. One who attends to the sick may be either a layperson or one who has gone forth—even if it be a woman;
all of them receive a share. If many attend together in harmony, an equal share must be given to all.
However, for whoever attends with particular distinction, a special allotment should be made for that person.
381. It should be applied [to the rule] beginning with: “Having placed a striking-rod upon a metal vessel, everything is allowable.
*Paharaṇi* means a weapon. *Pādukā ca saṅkamanīyo pallaṅko ca* is a dvanda compound. One should apply the interpretation:
“Having set aside a strainer and a potter’s [wheel] made of clay, everything is allowable”; for Dhaniya alone, however, every hut made of clay is considered a potter’s [work].
The commentary on the Exposition of Miscellaneous Items is concluded.
42. Commentary on the Exposition of the Teaching:
Now, by way of illustrating the teaching, certain training rules not mentioned above will be pointed out.
He said, beginning with “renunciation” (*cāga*). The connection is: that which is the renunciation of the state of being a monk (*bhikkhubhāva*) is the confession of a *pārājika* offense.

That by which something comes into being is a "state" (*bhāva*); it is the cause for the occurrence of a word. The state of a monk—the function of a monk which is the cause for the occurrence of the word "monk"—is "the state of being a monk" (*bhikkhubhāva*);
[it refers] to that. The root *dis* means "to utter"; utterance is manifestation, which is confession (*desanā*). "A rainstorm overflows a covered house... [etc. (Dhp 154).

For it is said: "The rain does not fall upon what has turned away. Here, however, the very renunciation of the state of a bhikkhu is called the "manifestation of a pārājika," which is the teaching on a pārājika.

Although it would be appropriate to say "he" (*so*) because "who" (*yo*) was stated, nevertheless, either the gender of what has already been stated by means of words such as "all" (*sabba*) is adopted, or [the gender] of what is about to be stated is adopted;
thus, with reference to the teaching that is about to be explained, it is stated as "he" (*so*).
"In whatever way" means by the manner stated in such passages as "one who conceals [an offense] while knowing it has been committed," etc.; that is, by the aforementioned method.
Alternatively, the meaning should be understood through the analysis of an indeclinable compound (*abyayībhāva*) as "without overstepping what was stated.
Here too, since the disclosure—that is, the confession—must occur precisely without overstepping the emergence from a grave offense, it is called "the confession of a grave offense as its emergence."
383. The word "thus" (*evaṃ*) is stated with reference to what is now to be said. "Of one" (*ekassa*) means of a single bhikkhu. 384.

"In your presence" (*tumhamūle*) means in your vicinity. "I confess" (*paṭidesemi*) means I make it known. "You should restrain yourself" (*saṃvareyyāsi*) means you should exercise self-restraint; the meaning is that you should establish yourself in restraint. 385.
"Having relinquished" (*nissajjitvāna*) means having ascertained whether [the object] is one or many, and whether it is present or absent, [saying]: "Venerable sir, this is mine..."
"Having relinquished [the robe] by means of the words beginning with 'cīvaraṃ'... "By him" means by the person to whom the robe was relinquished. "This... I give" should be connected as:
"The relinquished robe is to be given. It should be applied in this way: "This robe has exceeded ten days," and so forth. 386.

(Ka) "Robe" (*cīvara*) refers to any robe among the *saṅghāṭi* and others that have been determined (*adhiṭṭhita*) according to the method of determining the three robes. "Dwelt apart from" (*vippavuttha*) means dwelt while separated [from it].

(Kha) "Out-of-season robe-cloth" (*akālacīvara*) means: when the *kathina* has not been spread, it is that which arises during the remaining eleven months, excluding the last month of the rainy season;
when the *kathina* has been spread, it is that which arises during the remaining seven months, excluding that month and the four winter months.
Even if it is in season, if it is designated for the Saṅgha as "this is out-of-season robe-cloth," or given to a single individual [with the words] "I give this to you."
It was given after having been designated. The other, however, is "out-of-season robe-cloth.

"Exceeding one month" means that when out-of-season robe-cloth has arisen, if there is an expectation of receiving more to complete a deficiency from the Saṅgha, a group, or others, a period of one month is permitted; exceeding that month is what is meant.

(Ga) "Old robe-cloth" refers to any [robe] down to that which one has used as a pillow while lying down. "Robe-cloth" (*cīvara*) means any one of the six types that is fit for assignment (*vikappanūpaga*). This same method applies to all the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) concerning robe-cloth that will be explained hereafter.
(Gha) “Except by exchange” means except by exchange even for as little as a piece of *harītakī* fruit.
(Ṅa) “A householder” refers to one who has not gone forth among the monks. “Except on an occasion” means except on the occasion when robes have been stolen or lost;
however, for those whose robes have been stolen, it is permitted to wear [robes] even after they have themselves broken off branches and foliage or gathered materials such as *vāka* grass.
It is permissible, let alone [the case of] a formal request (*viññatti*). The connection is: "a robe has been requested.
To the question "What?", he says: "an unrelated person," and so forth. (Ca) "Beyond that" means exceeding the aforementioned measurement.
For a monk whose robe has been lost, having approached with either body or speech, two [robes] may be accepted from among three offered robes; when two have been lost...
One [robe] is to be accepted. For one who normally goes about wearing only the inner and outer robes, if two are lost, exactly two are to be accepted;
if one is lost, only one is to be accepted. For one who has only one robe, if that is lost, two are to be accepted.

(Six) "Without being invited" means by a householder or a housewife. "Improper modification" (*vikappa*) refers to an excessive alteration—a superior modification—such as saying "it is long," etc., out of a desire for beauty while increasing the value beyond what was originally intended.
(Ja) "To an unrelated householder" is stated merely by way of many [cases]; this is the distinction from what precedes it.
(Jha) "By means of a request" means by the request: "Friend, I have need of a robe. "By means of a standing" refers to a bodily request;
for when robe-funds have been placed in the hand of a messenger by a king or others, three [offenses] arise.
Exhortation is permitted; there are two positions for each exhortation. Therefore, if one only exhorts and does not take a position, six exhortations are obtained.
If one only takes a position and does not exhort, twelve positions are obtained.
If one does both, two positions must be deducted from a single exhortation.
(Ṭa) "And they are pure" means they are black by nature or by dye.
(Ṭha) "They weigh them with four measures" is said with reference to one who wishes to have it made;
however, in terms of the actual substance, as many sheep’s wool as he intends to use, two portions of those must be black, one portion white, and one portion of the color of a cow.
It should be understood as follows: "Tula" means one hundred *palas*. "Gocariya" refers to those of Kapila color. The construction is: "This rug was made for me.

Regarding the phrase "not exceeding three *yojanas*," the meaning should be understood through the neuter form of the abstract noun (*bhāvanapuṃsaka*): "the maximum distance of his crossing from the place where it was taken up is three *yojanas*.
"They have been crossed over" means, at the very least, the carrying away of goods even by means of a mere thread, without the goods being placed upon the back [of the animal].
Even those inserted into the ear canal for the purpose of treating a wind-affliction, if they exceed [the permitted size], are [offenses].
387–9. "Having relinquished" means having relinquished the articles in the manner already described. "Then" (atha) means immediately after the offense has been confessed.
The construction is: he tells the householder, "Know this. "He" refers to the householder, such as a monastery attendant. "What shall I bring with this?"—thus he might speak.

The connection [is as follows]: "If he should speak" means if he speaks. "Without saying 'this'" means without saying "bring this," but rather speaking of what is allowable for the monks, such as oil and so forth;
this is the connection. The word "ādi" (etcetera) contains a *niggahīta* due to euphonic combination (*sandhi*).

Having exchanged it with that, the construction is: "that which he brings, being allowable. "By that" means by the object subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya-vatthu*). "Setting aside these two" refers to these...
The connection is that, with the exception of the two—the receiver of money and the trader in money—one may consume [the goods] with the remaining [monks].
"To consume" means to eat that. "From that" means from the permissible [goods] that have been exchanged. "By another" means by anyone at all, even by a monastery attendant (*ārāmika*).
"Of them" refers to the two mentioned.
390. "At the very least, even the shade of a tree produced by that [land]"—this is the connection. Regarding "produced by that":
in a monastery acquired after purchasing it with the object relinquished, the shade of a tree is "produced by that"; thus, the compound means "produced from that.
"From the beginning, the three kinds of spreadings" refers to the three kinds of spreadings at the outset: those made of pure black silk and those made of two parts black [wool] and one part white.

391. "If we should not obtain one in this way": having thus turned [the matter over], if a kappiyakāraka (one who makes things allowable) should not be obtained, that householder should be addressed as follows:
"Discard this. Thus, if a householder who discards money should not be obtained, the connection is that an appointed monk should discard it.
"Appointed" means one endowed with the five factors described by the words, "He who would not fall into favoritism," and so forth.
A monk authorized by the formal act of appointment for the disposal of silver.

392. "These" refers to the silver that has been accepted. Regarding the second bowl: when there is a bowl with fewer than five mends, it may be stated before the Saṅgha that another bowl has been requested;
this is the connection of the words. It should be stated thus: "Venerable sirs, I have accepted silver," and so forth.
The construction is as follows: the remaining articles of forfeiture (nissaggiya-vatthu) may be spoken before either the Saṅgha or a group (gaṇa).
They may be spoken even in another language; the meaning is that they may be forfeited not only in the Pāli language, but also in Sinhalese and other tongues.

393. (Ka) *Nānappakāraṃ* means manifold, by way of allowable articles such as robes and so forth. *Kaya* is buying; *vikkaya* is giving. *Kayavikkayaṃ* is both buying and selling. (Ga) *Ūnapañcabandhanena*:
