that which has fewer than five repairs (*bandhana*) is [described] thus; this is a term used in the sense of a characteristic of state (*itthambhūtalakkhaṇe*).
However, a bowl that has five repairs in any way whatsoever, or one that has space for a fifth repair, is not a [valid] bowl (*apatta*).
It is permissible to ask for something else.

394. Regarding the phrase "having appointed": according to the word-commentary (*padabhājanīya*), this means having appointed by a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*). As for the expression "the bowl of the Saṅgha":
by the word *anta*, that which exists at the end of the bowls—that is, a worn-out bowl—is what is intended; it does not refer to a bowl that has been relinquished (*nissaṭṭha*).
Having spoken of the qualities that exist [in the bowl], he should have the Elder’s bowl taken by the second Elder;
by this same method, having had it taken down as far as the most junior member of the Saṅgha, the bowl which is the last among the bowls of the Saṅgha assembled there is "that bowl.
"Of him" means of the monk who has performed the relinquishment. "Should cause to be given" means he should cause it to be given by the appointed bowl-distributor.
395. (Ka) "Medicine" refers to ghee and so forth, which receives that designation whether it performs the function of medicine or not; it is to be kept for seven days.
(Kha) During the last month of summer, the first half-month is the period for seeking and preparing [the medicine]; the second half-month is the period for both seeking, preparing, and storing it;
and during the four months of the rains, all four [periods] apply, including the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
The field [of application] is as follows: these five months are the period of the womb, while the other seven months are the period of the back.

For one who seeks [the robe-cloth] during the period of the back, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya). And for one who wears it after having kept it for more than a fortnight during the period of the womb, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
Therefore it is said: "when more than a month remains."

(Ga) "Having given it oneself" means having given it personally while expecting services and the like in return. "Taken away" means having taken it away with the perception that it was one's own, upon seeing someone not performing [the expected service].

For taking away anything other than a robe—whether it be another requisite belonging to a bhikkhunī or any kind of requisite belonging to one who is not fully ordained—there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
This applies even when something has been given after being relinquished, provided it is done without the perception that it is one's own.
(Ṅa) One who seizes [the robe] must be made to pay the value of the goods.
(Ca) "Adapting" means making further adjustments such as saying, "Make it longer and wider," and so forth.

"A robe for one in haste" refers to [the robe] of those who are traveling, those who are ill, those who are pregnant, or those whose faith has newly arisen during any of the three months of the invitation period (*pavāraṇā*).
An urgent robe-offering is that which is given with the intention, "I shall give a rainy-season robe," starting from the fifth day of the bright fortnight.
The period for robe-material consists of one month plus eleven days when the Kathina has not been spread, and five months plus eleven days when the Kathina has been spread.
For one who exceeds this, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*). Therefore it is said: "the period for robe-material..."
"Exceeded. That is the time and that is the occasion; it is the "time and occasion for robes.

(Sixth: When a bhikkhu, having entered the rains residence in a forest dwelling that is dangerous, dwells there, he has entered the first [rains] period with one of the three robes and has been invited at the Great Invitation, and it is the month of Kattika.

If one has a dwelling that possesses the four factors described as being "not less than five *dhanus* in width and length" and "having some risk or danger," one may, having deposited the robe within an inhabited area, live apart from it for at most six nights when there is a valid reason.
If one should live apart from it longer than that, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*). Therefore, it is said: "more than six nights," and so forth.
(Ja) They know, being knowers.
396. *Ādimhi viya* means as in the first *nissaggiya*. 397.
(Kha) And in the case of receiving fresh food (*khādanīya*) and so forth from the hand of a nun who has entered among the houses.
When monks are eating at families, for a nun who makes a request in such a manner as saying, “Give me some cake here, give me some soup,” and so forth;
for one who does not show respect toward families designated as "in training"; for one who accepts fresh food and other items when not previously invited;
and for one who, while dwelling in a forest lodging that is dangerous, accepts fresh food and other items without having been informed in advance.
And the category of offenses called *pāṭidesanīya* has been mentioned. Therefore it was said: “blameworthy,” and so forth. 398.

Regarding the phrase “not leading to confession,” etc., this is the action (*kamma*) in the context of “one should not confess. The *pārājika* and *saṅghādisesa* offenses are called “not leading to confession.

“Non-offense” means that which is not an offense; that [is what is meant]. “Confessed” means one for whom confession has been performed. This applies to those who reside outside the boundary (*nissīma*) and live apart from the community (*nānāsaṃvāsa*).
The connection is with the word "does not confess. Thus, one should not confess by means of four or five [factors]: one should not confess mentally;

one should not confess for those who have not been made to acknowledge their offense (*apakatattānaṃ*); and one should not confess multiple offenses as "one. "Mentally" means solely by means of the mind.
"Multiple" refers to saying "one" when there are many offenses. However, it is permissible to confess a single offense as "multiple."
The commentary on the exposition of the *desanā* is finished.
43. Commentary on the Exposition of the Granting of Consent (*chandadāna*) 399.

"In one who has reached the business" means in one who is fit, suitable, and appropriate for the business such as the Uposatha. "When the Saṅgha has assembled" means when the Saṅgha consisting of at least a quorum of four has gathered together in one place. And here, it should be understood that even including the one who conveys the consent, there must be at least a quorum of four.

400. In order to show the procedure for giving consent (*chanda*) and so forth, he said, beginning with "one. "Having approached" means having confessed one's offense and subsequently approached [the assembly].
Regarding "he gives consent": among the three types of persons to be mentioned below, even if only one has come after performing the *uposatha* outside [the boundary], he may give his consent;
or, having gone to the place of assembly for some business, he may give it while not providing physical unity (*kāyasāmaggi*).
However, when granting purification (*pārisuddhi*), one should give consent (*chanda*).
Regarding the purpose for giving both, he says: "Purification," and so forth.
The connection is that by the granting of purification, one fulfills the Uposatha for both the Saṅgha and oneself. Purification itself is *pārisuddhi*; the giving of that is *pārisuddhipadāna*.
By that [act]. Now, one might object: "Since the Uposatha ceremony consists merely of the act of offering purity, how can the offering of purity accomplish the Uposatha for the Saṅgha as well?
It is said in reply: By accomplishing the formal legal act (*dhammakamma*) through the giving of purity, one accomplishes the Uposatha for the Saṅgha too.
In this case, if four [monks] perform the *pārisuddhi-uposatha* by bringing the consent (*chanda*) and purity (*pārisuddhi*) of one,
or if three bring the consent and purity of one and two recite the *Pātimokkha*, it is an unlawful, incomplete Uposatha act. Or,
if four perform the *pārisuddhi-uposatha*, or if three or two recite the *Pātimokkha*, [it is likewise].

An assembly that is complete but acts contrary to the Dhamma: if four monks assemble and three recite the Pātimokkha after one has brought his own portion, or if three monks assemble and two perform the Uposatha of purity after one has brought his own portion, this is an assembly that is contrary to the Dhamma but incomplete.

However, if four monks assemble and recite the Pātimokkha, or if three perform the Uposatha of purity, or if two perform the Uposatha of mutual purity for one another, [this is an assembly that is according to the Dhamma].

They perform it lawfully and with a complete assembly. Regarding the five types of *pavāraṇā* (invitation) formal acts as well: in one case, they bring the invitation of one person and establish a motion (*ñatti*) for the four-membered group, and then perform the *pavāraṇā*;
in four or three cases, they bring the invitation of one person and establish a motion for the three- or two-membered group, and then perform the *pavāraṇā*.
"An unlawful and incomplete *pavāraṇā* formal act" and so forth are to be understood according to the method already stated. The remaining formal acts [are treated] in the same way.
"It obstructs" means it obstructs the remaining business of the Saṅgha; the intention is that its purpose has not been attained. 403.
"The two" refers both to the performance of the Uposatha and the remaining business. It should be connected with the phrase "does not accomplish for oneself. 404.
"He should convey" means he should convey either the pure *chanda* mentioned previously or this present *chandapārisuddhi*.
“Let not the succession be lost” means that the succession should not be interrupted. Why? He says: “brought down the succession,” and so forth.
“By him” refers to the one who first received the *chandapārisuddhi* (the formal declaration of purity). “Brought down the succession” means:
just as in a chain of rings, the first ring reaches the second but does not reach the third, so too it comes to the second but not to the third.
It does not come. Alternatively, there is the reading: “The purity of intention (chanda-pārisuddhi) brought by succession does not go. 405.
*Sabbūpacāraṃ* means all the formal procedures (*upacāra*), such as “having arranged the robe over one shoulder,” and so forth.

406. The construction is: “He, having arrived, having announced [his arrival], should invite the Saṅgha. *Atha* is used in the sense of immediate sequence. *Āgato* refers to the monk who has arrived after taking the invitation. *Ārocetvā* means having announced it to the community of monks (*bhikkhusaṅgha*). *Evaṃ* means according to the sequence that will be explained.

407–8. The connection is: “having taken it, [he is] a carrier. “Not brought” means that it has not even been brought; this is the sense. The construction is: “the carrier, having reached the Saṅgha, should act in such a way, and [then] it becomes ‘brought. “Should act in such a way” means he might become one who has left the order (a renegade) and so forth. 409. The connection is:

“if he, having reached the Saṅgha, being careless or asleep, does not announce it, there is no offense. The word *ca* (and) includes the carrying of the consent (*chanda*) and the purification (*pārisuddhi*).
The commentary on the description of the giving of consent is finished.
44. Commentary on the Exposition of the Uposatha 410.
“Two kinds of Uposatha”: this is stated by way of their common occurrence. However, there are three Uposathas by way of the days themselves:
that of the fourteenth, that of the fifteenth, and the Uposatha for concord (*sāmaggika*). Among these, during the three seasons of winter, summer, and the rains—
By grouping two each in the third and seventh fortnights, there are six Uposathas on the fourteenth day; the remainder are on the fifteenth. Thus, there are twenty-four Uposathas in one year.

This, first of all, is the natural course of the world. However, according to such statements as “incoming monks must conform to the resident monks,” it is permissible to perform the Uposatha on another fourteenth day when such circumstances arise.
411. The construction is: "The recitation of the Sutta belongs to the Saṅgha alone. "That which is both a formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and an Uposatha" is a *kammadhāraya* compound.

"Of the others" refers to two or three [monks]. By the phrase beginning with "two," etc., it is shown that: (1) by way of the day, there are the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the communal (*sāmaggī*) Uposatha;

(2) by way of the mode of performance, there are the recitation of the Sutta, the formal determination, and the purity (*pārisuddhi*) Uposatha; and (3) by way of the assembly, there are the Uposatha of the Saṅgha, the Uposatha of a group (*gaṇa*), and the Uposatha of an individual (*puggala*).
And by way of individuals, nine types of Uposatha are thus illustrated.
412. Regarding the preliminary duties:
"The giving of consent, the declaration of purity, the announcement of the season, the counting of the monks, and the exhortation;"
“These are called the preliminary duties of the uposatha”—
thus it was said by the masters of the Aṭṭhakathā regarding the preliminary duties to be performed immediately after the preliminary preparations (*pubbakaraṇa*).
Regarding the term *pubbakaraṇa*:
“The broom, the lamp, water, and the seat—these are called the preliminary duties (*pubbakaraṇa*) for the Uposatha.
Thus, regarding the preliminary duties that must be performed first of all, as stated by the masters of the Aṭṭhakathā: “At the proper time (*pattakāle*).”

The "proper time" (*pattakāla*) is that time which has arrived through the presence of the four factors beginning with the observance day (*uposatha*); "proper time" itself is "proper occasion" (*pattakalla*). What is that?
It is the ritual act (*kamma*) such as the observance day. That, moreover, is comprised of four factors. As the teachers of the Commentary have said:
"The observance day, and as many bhikkhus as are entitled to participate in the ritual..."
“Shared offenses do not exist,
nor are there persons who must be avoided therein;
it is called ‘the right time.’”

"Collected" (*samānītā*) means properly brought together or set in motion; "it" (*so*) refers to the recitation of the Sutta. "In five ways" (*pañcadhā*) means: the introduction (*nidāna*), the section on offenses involving defeat (*pārājika*), the section on formal meetings of the Saṅgha (*saṅghādisesa*), the section on undetermined offenses (*aniyata*), and the detailed exposition (*vitthāra*); thus it is fivefold. 413.

"Without obstacles" (*vinā antarāyaṃ*) refers to the obstacles mentioned as follows: the obstacle of kings, the obstacle of thieves, the obstacle of fire, the obstacle of water, the obstacle of humans, the obstacle of non-humans, the obstacle of wild beasts, the obstacle of reptiles, the obstacle to life, and the obstacle to the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
"In the ten [recitations], whatever obstacle there may be, without it. "In brief" means without elaboration. The construction is:
because it is stated that "in this case, regarding two or three recitations (*uddesa*), the Elder alone is the master," it is appropriate even when he does not proceed.
"In this case" refers to the five recitations. "When he does not proceed" means when the Elder does not proceed with the elaboration due to being unskilled. "It is appropriate" means...
It is also permissible to recite in brief. By this very point, it is understood that it is permissible even when no one at all is acting as the reciter.
The phrase "when three" is stated for the purpose of showing that when two are present, there is nothing further to be said regarding seniority.
By the words "the Elder alone is the authority," etc., this is illustrated: [the first two] are unbroken, perfectly clear, and have reached the tongue.
The Pātimokkha is to be entrusted to the elders; however, if one is unable to make even this much clear, it falls under the responsibility of a competent bhikkhu.
Therefore, one should either recite it oneself or request another to do so.

Regarding the phrase "if they should arrive while [the recitation] is being performed—whether equally or in small numbers"—this is how it should be connected. While [the recitation] is being performed...
While the *pātimokkha* is being recited by the resident monks: "Equal or few" means that the visiting monks are either equal in number to or fewer than the resident monks.
"The remainder should be heard" indicates that even at this point, the *uposatha* ceremony is indeed considered completed.
415. "Merely recited": "merely recited" (*uddiṭṭhamatta*) means it has simply been recited. The word *matta* is used for emphasis. Throughout the entire...
The construction is: "If [the others] should come, whether they have risen from their seats, or are equal [in number], or even a few.

"Entirely" means the whole assembly. "They should perform the *pārisuddhi* in their presence" means that those visiting monks should perform the *pārisuddhi-uposatha* in the vicinity of those resident monks.
Now, if there are many, in all the aforementioned alternatives, the preliminary duty (*pubbakicca*)—
"Having made" (*katvā*) is how it should be construed. They are "alternatives" (*vikappa*) because they are conceptualized and imagined;

all those remaining procedures for the purity of the assembly and the Uposatha, together with those alternatives, are "all the alternatives. Among them. "One should recite again" means one should recite the Pātimokkha once more.

416. "The others" refers to the newly arrived monks. "The other" refers to the fourteenth-day [Uposatha]. However, in this case, for those for whom it is the fifteenth day, that [previous Uposatha] has passed.
It should be understood that they performed the Uposatha on the fourteenth day. This is the intended meaning here:

when such conditions existed, because they had already performed the [Uposatha] on the fourteenth, when the fourteenth—consisting of the third and seventh fortnights as previously described—arrived, it was not to be performed again as an *anuposatha* (a non-Uposatha); however, since the Uposatha had not been performed there [on the previous occasion], it was indeed the fourteenth.
"Has become the fifteenth. The word-division is *samā ūnā itare*. "The others" (*itare*) refers to the incoming monks (*āgantuka*).

"Let them follow the former" means that while the preliminary duties are being performed by the resident monks (*āvāsika*), such as "Today is the Uposatha of the fifteenth," let the others follow those former residents.
"If they are more numerous" means if the incoming monks are many. "The former" refers to the residents.

"Resident monks. "Let them follow them" means that when the preliminary duties are being performed by those resident monks, thinking, "Today is the Uposatha of the fourteenth," let the visiting monks follow along.

"In the rest as well" means even on the fifteenth day for the visiting monks. "This method" refers to this very same method beginning with, "For the visitors it is the fifteenth, for the others it is otherwise," and so forth.
However, in this case, for those for whom it is the fifteenth...
Or it should be understood that they have come from another kingdom or have observed the past Uposatha on the fourteenth day.

(417) Because the past Uposatha was performed on the fourteenth day, the Uposatha for the fifteenth day was effectively performed on the fourteenth; thus, for the residents, the first day of the month (*pāṭipada*) has become the fifteenth day.
Therefore he said, "for the residents, the first day. "For the others" refers to the newcomers. "Uposatha" [is the term used].
The fifteenth Uposatha. "Of those who are few" means of either those who are equal to oneself or of those incoming monks who are few.
"Those established at the root" refers to the resident monks. "Let them give according to their wish" means let them give according to their own desire. 418.
"If they do not give" means if the resident monks do not grant the formal assembly (kāyasāmaggi); however, regarding those resident monks, yesterday...

"Because the Uposatha has already been performed, there is no performing of the Uposatha today. The construction is: "One should give formal unity (*kāyasāmaggi*) even when many [monks] are unwilling.

"When many" means when there are many among those who have arrived as guests. "Or one should avoid going outside" means that the assembly of resident monks should avoid going beyond the boundary (*nissīma*).
419. "He should recite the *sutta*" means that he should, with effort, recite the *sutta* known as the Pātimokkha.
420. “To sweep... [etc. ...and to prepare a seat for water”—the connection is that one sent by the Mahāthera should not do what is improper (*akalla*).
*Akalla* means one who is not ill. *Tathā* refers by extension to the offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
In the absence of seats, even a broken-off branch should be made allowable (*kappiya*) and prepared. In the absence of oil, a fire should be lit in a skull-bowl.
421–3. "Having prepared the water and seat" means having set out both the water for drinking and use, as well as a seat.
"The motion of the group" refers to the formal motion (*ñatti*) that is to be established by the group, which will now be explained. "Those two" refers to the other two monks.
"With the commencement previously completed" means that the commencement regarding the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*), the wearing of one shoulder, and so forth, has been finished and concluded.

"Of whom" (*yassa*) is a three-word *bahubbīhi* compound. The connection is: "the newcomer (*navo*) should conduct himself (*īriya*) in this way toward them (*te*). "Them" (*te*) refers to the other two. 424. The construction is:
"having done what is to be done, having performed the preliminary duties and so forth, the newcomer (*navo*) should conduct himself (*īriya*) in this way.
427. "Wherein" (*yattha*) is connected with: "having brought the individual purity (*pārisuddhi*) of each one (*ekkekassa*) into that monastery (*vihāre*). "Of each one" (*ekkekassa*)...

In this context, *vicchā* (distribution) means a desire to pervade. *Vicchā* is the desire to pervade—that is, to connect—meanings that are differentiated by an action (*kiriyā*), a quality (*guṇa*), or a substance (*dabba*).

Here, however, *vicchā* is the desire to pervade and connect each individual [meaning] as it is divided into four, three, and two, by means of the action known as the bringing about of intention and purity.
In the phrase "one with the other" (*itarītara*), it should also be understood by way of the instrument and the action.
"Three, two, or one"—this refers to that particular *saṅghuposatha*, *gaṇuposatha*, or *puggaluposatha*. This is the intended meaning here:
having brought one from among four, three perform the *pārisuddhi-uposatha*;
or having brought one from among three, two perform the *saṅghuposatha*. This is an unlawful and incomplete formal act of Uposatha. Then...

However, if they bring [the requisites] for one person and perform the *saṅgha-uposatha* for three, or if they bring [the requisites] for one person and perform the *pārisuddhi-uposatha* for two, it is called an "illegal and incomplete" (*adhamma-vagga*) procedure.

But if all four assemble and perform the *pārisuddhi-uposatha*, or if three or two perform the *saṅgha-uposatha*, it is called an "illegal but complete" (*adhamma-samagga*) procedure. By way of the opposite of that—
It should be understood that [the act] is performed legitimately by a united assembly.
428. The connection is as follows: for one who acts while perceiving a divided assembly as "divided," or while being in doubt, it is an *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing).
"Divided" means in a divided Saṅgha. "While being in doubt" means for one who is uncertain, thinking, "Is this a divided assembly, or is it united? By this very [rule],...
One who has been made to feel remorse is also characterized [as an offender]. "He makes" refers to one performing the Uposatha; the construction is "he makes with the intention of causing a schism.
Here, however, a grave offense (thullaccaya) is stated due to the strength of the evil intent. "One who perceives" (saññī) refers to the mind by way of its function of perception;
the meaning is "one possessing a mind."
429–30. By the words “of one who has been suspended,” etc., he shows the persons to be avoided. “Of one who has been suspended” (*ukkhitassa*) is a genitive case used in the sense of the agent.
Since the word “seated” (*nisinna*) is formed with an accusative derivation, it must be that those who have been suspended, etc., are the agents.

The purpose of the qualifier “of the others” (*sesānaṃ*) is to specify the monks, as there might otherwise be ambiguity. “Of the incapable” (*abhabbassa*) refers to the eleven kinds of incapable persons, beginning with the *paṇḍaka* (eunuch).
The connection is: "One should not recite the Pātimokkha before an assembly that is seated. It should be construed thus: "One should not recite it before one who has committed a similar offense.

*Sabhāgā* means "having a similar portion" (*bhāga*), that is, a common part (*koṭṭhāsa*), because its basis—such as the matter of eating at an improper time—is the same; thus, it is a *bahubbīhi* compound meaning "one whose offense is such [a similar one].

Regarding the phrase "surrounded by consent," there are four kinds of being surrounded: being surrounded by the assembly (*parisā-parivāsiya*), being surrounded for the night (*ratti-parivāsiya*), and so forth.
"Sending away by means of a formal motion" (*chandapārivāsiya*) and "sending away by means of one's own intention" (*ajjhāsayapārivāsiya*).

In this regard, when the monks have assembled for some business, and then, due to some circumstance such as the rising of clouds (rain), there is no opportunity [to continue], they rise up and depart elsewhere without having sent away their consent (*chanda*);
this is called "sending away by means of the assembly" (*parisapārivāsiya*). Although it is indeed "sending away by means of the assembly,"...
However, because their resolve (*chanda*) has not been relinquished, it is permissible for them to perform the formal act (*kamma*).
If they request someone else, saying, "Until all have assembled, we shall listen to the Dhamma," and while that person is delivering the Dhamma talk, dawn breaks;
if they were sitting to perform the fourteenth-day ceremony, it is considered the fifteenth day.

It is permissible to perform [the Uposatha]. If they have sat down to perform the Uposatha on the fifteenth day, it is not permissible to perform the Uposatha on the first day of the lunar fortnight (pāṭipada), which is the following Uposatha day;
however, it is permissible to perform other business of the Saṅgha. This is called "postponement for the night" (rattipārivāsiya).
But while they are sitting thus, if some monk who recites the constellations says, "Today the constellation is fierce; this ritual..."
"Do not do it," he says; they, having relinquished their consent at his word, remain sitting right there.
Then another comes and says, "The time for the festival has passed by the fool who was waiting for the auspicious star. When he asks, "What is the use of the star? Do it!
this is both the relinquishing of consent (*chandapārivāsiya*) and the relinquishing of intention (*ajjhāsayapārivāsiya*). In one case of relinquishing...
Furthermore, it is proper to perform the formal act (*kamma*) after having brought about purity through desire (*chandapārisuddhi*).

431. The connection is that it is not permissible to perform the Uposatha without having confessed or revealed what has been committed as an offense or what is subject to doubt (*vematika*). "Without having revealed" means without having disclosed a grave offense (*garukāpatti*). "Not" means indeed not. 432.
"Uposatha not established" (*aṭṭhitoposatha*) is a *bahubbīhi* compound meaning that in which the Uposatha is not established or not released. "On that day" (*tadahū*) means on that [day].
On the Uposatha day, one should resolve [upon the observance] without an obstacle or the Saṅgha, or else one does not cross the boundary (*sīmā*).
By the word "resolve" (*adhiṭṭhātuṃ*), the Uposatha of a group (*gaṇa*) is also implied; by the word "boundary" (*sīmā*), even a river is included.
The commentary on the description of the Uposatha is finished.
45. Commentary on the Exposition of the Pavāraṇā 433.

Regarding the phrase "mutual invitation" (*aññamaññappavāraṇā*) and so forth: an invitation that is to be performed mutually. Among these, for a group of three or four, the mutual invitation is carried out by setting aside the formal motion (*ñatti*);
however, for two [monks], it is done without setting anything aside at all. This is called "formal determination" (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
Regarding *adhiṭṭhānappavāraṇā*: because words ending in the suffix *-yu* are invariably neuter in the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*), it is called "adhiṭṭhāna.
The remaining five, which are to be performed by groups of five or more, namely the rest of the *saṅghappavāraṇā*, must be performed by establishing a motion (*ñatti*) on behalf of the Saṅgha.
By this, the three types beginning with *saṅghappavāraṇā* among the nine have been shown. For there are nine Pavāraṇās: those on the fourteenth day and those on the fifteenth day.

"Harmony" (*sāmaggī*) is [distinguished] by way of the day—as "three-day," "two-day," or "one-day"—by way of the manner in which it should be performed—as "invitation in the Saṅgha," "invitation in a group," or "invitation to an individual"—and by way of the agent. In that regard, for those who have spent the preceding rains-retreat, the full moon of the month of Kattika is the [proper time];
however, if they are harassed by those who cause strife and postpone their invitation, then [the time is] the month of Kattika...
The fourteenth day of the dark fortnight or the full moon of the latter Kattika are the days for the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) for those who have completed the final rains retreat;
indeed, for those who have completed the final rains retreat, only the full moon of the latter Kattika is the day for the invitation ceremony. This, however, is the normal practice.

When such circumstances arise, it is permissible to perform the invitation ceremony on either of the two preceding fourteenth days of the two Kattika full moons. But for one who has [not] completed [the retreat],...
Regarding "in the harmony of the Saṅgha," any day whatsoever is a Pavāraṇā day. These are the three Pavāraṇās by way of the days.
However, they should be understood by way of the manner in which they are to be performed according to the method that will be explained below.
Regarding the phrase "In the preliminary duties" and so forth:
“The broom, the lamp, water, and the seat—
these are called the preliminary duties for the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*).
The proclamation of consent, the announcement of the season, the counting of the monks, and the exhortation.”
These are called the preliminary duties for the Pavāraṇā ceremony:
"The Pavāraṇā [should be performed] when as many bhikkhus as are entitled to participate have assembled,
and no common offenses exist."
"And there are no persons to be avoided in that [assembly];
it is therefore called 'the proper time'.
Thus should the preliminary duties and so forth be understood as stated in the Commentary. "The motion" (*ñatti*) refers to the general form which will now be explained.

The motion for the Saṅgha. However, when the motion has been thus established, if there is a reason, it is permissible to perform the Pavāraṇā by means of three utterances, two utterances, one utterance, or by way of those of equal seniority (*samānavassika*).
This very motion—wherein it says, "May the Saṅgha perform the Pavāraṇā"—is as follows: "May the Saṅgha perform the Pavāraṇā with three utterances;
may the Saṅgha perform the Pavāraṇā with two utterances; may the Saṅgha perform the Pavāraṇā with one utterance; may the Saṅgha [perform the Pavāraṇā] by way of those of equal seniority."
It is also permissible to set aside [the invitation] with the thought, "I shall invite. On the fourteenth day, however, when there is concord, it should be said: "The fourteenth-day concord. 437.
Regarding the elders who are inviting while squatting on their heels, the construction is: "Let the junior monk remain squatting on his heels until he himself has invited.

"Let him remain" means let him sit. 440–2. "Discussion of the Dhamma and quarrel" is a *dvanda* compound. Because of the state of having passed the night, [it occurs] during the occasion of the threefold recitation (*tevācikā*).
When the ten kinds of obstacles are absent, one should understand the connection as follows: having made a motion appropriate to the situation—“May it be heard by me... [etc.

...let us invite together those of the same year”—one should perform the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) in accordance with that motion as it was established. Regarding "appropriately": "May it be heard by me... [etc.
...the night has been spent by those giving gifts; if... [etc. ...the night will dawn, if for the Saṅgha..."

The meaning is: by means of [the formula] beginning with "It is appropriate," which corresponds to the night already spent; or by means of [the formula] corresponding to the obstacles such as those caused by a king, beginning with "Let the Sangha hear me, venerable sirs: this is the obstacle of a king; if the Sangha [grants] the threefold proclamation... [and so on]... there will be the Sangha, then there will be this obstacle of a king, if it is appropriate for the Sangha. Then this...

The phrase "there will be an obstacle to the holy life" (*brahmacariyantarāyo bhavissati*) is stated at the end by way of an elliptical formula (*peyyālavasena*), having taken up the obstacle to the holy life.

Furthermore, although [the formulas] beginning with "with two words" (*dvevācikaṃ*) should be recited individually, they have been stated here combined according to the order of skipping [the intermediate steps].
At the time of the actual recitation, however, one should say: "One should invite with two words," and so forth. They might come.

If those beginning with "If they should come together" and the verses spoken on the Uposatha day beginning with "If they should come together," etc., were also [to be recited], then "here" refers to this Pavāraṇā ceremony.
And this is the sequence for the citation:
"If they should come together, let those who are few indeed perform the Pavāraṇā."
If you have invited [the Sangha], it is well-invited; and others may also invite.
Whether all or some have been invited, or if they have stood up [to leave], if there are many others present, they too should invite them in their presence.
"Having performed all preliminary duties, one should point it out again.
The verses beginning with "The fifteenth day for the residents," however, are the same here as well. 443.
"Having stated the motion" means having stated the motion concerning the assembly that is about to be described.
444. *Samudīrayati*: two or three others [of the same type] should be stated according to the sequence to be explained.

446–8. *Kattabbaṃ katvā* (having done what was to be done): this should be construed [with the preceding]. "What is to be done" refers to the preliminary duties and so forth. Even with a junior [monk], one should construe it thus: "The Elder, venerable sir... [etc.]... will make amends. *Evaṃ* (thus) refers to what is about to be said. 449.
The passage beginning with *yasmiṃ* is self-evident because it follows the method already stated.
450. Regarding the "verses": these refer either to the verses stated previously, beginning with, "Perceiving [the Saṅgha] as being in harmony when it is actually divided," and so forth.
However, there is this distinction here: in the phrase "he performs," the meaning should be understood as "he performs the invitation" (*pavāraṇā*).
In the third verse, the phrase "he should not recite the Pātimokkha" should be removed and the phrase "he should not perform the invitation" should be inserted.
In the fourth verse, one should remove the metrical composition beginning with “anuposathe” and insert:
“It is not to be done at the invitation ceremony; that invitation ceremony is permissible. In the fifth verse, one should remove “aṭṭhitoposathāvāsā” and insert “pavāraṇāṭhitāvāsā. 451.
“Only when the Saṅgha has invited” means only when the Saṅgha has already invited during the preceding rains-retreat. [This refers to] the *pārisuddhi-uposatha*.
"Should perform" means that two *ñatti*s (formal motions) should not be established at a single *uposatha* boundary; this is the intended meaning.

"Having entered the later [rains] and not having completed the rains" means he has not yet entered the rains. "Not having entered" means he has not entered the rains. This is the intended meaning here:
those who have entered the earlier rains—five or more—or those who have entered the later rains, equal in number to them...
If those who have entered during the later invitation period are fewer than those who entered during the earlier period,

and they complete the quorum for a formal act of the Saṅgha (saṅghappavāraṇā) by proposing a motion (ñatti) according to that Saṅgha procedure, yet both groups together do not constitute a Saṅgha but do constitute a group (gaṇa),
then they should perform the invitation by proposing a motion of a group (gaṇañatti). Afterwards, [the invitation] should be performed in their presence.

The Uposatha of purity should be performed. However, if there is one [monk] during the earlier period and one during the later period, one should invite the other in his presence, and the other should perform the Uposatha of purity.
If those who entered the rains residence later are even by one more than those who entered it earlier, and they complete the quorum for the Saṅgha, then after first reciting the Pātimokkha...
"Later, they should perform the *pavāraṇā* ceremony in their presence. This same method applies to a group as well. In the subsequent cases as well, it should be considered accordingly.
452. "On the fourth month" means on the full moon of the later *Kattika*. "By the Saṅgha" means by the Saṅgha that has first entered the rains residence.
"Those who have completed the rains" (*vutthavassa*) refers to those who have entered the later rains residence. By the phrase "if there should be fewer," [it is indicated that...]
If they are either more numerous or equal in number, it indicates that after setting aside the formal motion for the invitation (*pavāraṇāñatti*),
the others should perform the Uposatha of purity (*pārisuddhi-uposatha*) only after those who have entered the rains-retreat first perform their invitation.
The commentary on the exposition of the Invitation (*Pavāraṇā-niddesa-vaṇṇanā*) is finished.
46. Commentary on the Exposition of Restraint (Saṃvaraniddesa) 453.
Restraint (*saṃvara*) is the closing of the doors of the eye and the other sense faculties with the bolt of mindfulness.

In this regard, although there is no restraint in the eye-faculty itself—for mindfulness does not arise depending upon the sensitive matter of the eye, nor indeed at the time of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), nor during the moments of adverting and so forth—[restraint is nevertheless established].
At another time, however, it arises at the moment of impulsion; thus, restraint exists then.

When it exists in this way, it is called "restraint of the eye-door," and so forth. The compound *cakkhusotādibhedehi* means "by the distinctions of the eye, ear, and so on"—that is, the eye and the ear, which are the first (*ādi*) among those [senses], and these very things are the distinctions (*bhedā*);
[it refers] by means of those doors. This is because [restraint] is extremely helpful in preventing the occurrence of covetousness and other such unwholesome states.
And here, the instrumental case is used in the sense of instrument (*karaṇatthe*). By this, the doors consisting of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are stated.

"In the range of visible forms, sounds, and so forth" means in the objects (*visaye*) designated as visible form, sound, odor, flavor, tangible object, and mental phenomena. "The occurrence of covetousness, dejection, and so forth":

herein, covetousness (*abhijjhā*) is that which meditates (*jhāyati*) directly upon the prosperity of others; it is intense craving. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), wrong view and other such states are included.
Many unwholesome states are comprised [therein].
454. The connection is: "One should restrain one's own mind as one would [restrain] a crop of *kiṭṭha* and so forth that is difficult to suppress.

*Kiṭṭha* refers to the grain produced in a *kiṭṭha* field. That which gives *kiṭṭha* is *kiṭṭhādi*; that [is what is meant]. "Possessing clear comprehension" (*sampajāno*) means by way of non-delusion regarding what is purposeful and suitable as a resort (*gocara*).
"Fully understanding through the four kinds of clear comprehension. By this, the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties (*indriyasaṃvara-sīla*) is explained.
The commentary on the exposition of restraint is finished.
47. Commentary on the Exposition of Purification (*suddhi-niddesa*).
455. The connection is that purity is fourfold by way of the divisions: teaching, restraint, seeking, and reflection.
Although it should have been stated as "reflection by way of division," the elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra) should be understood;
thus it is said to be fourfold: purity of teaching, purity of restraint, purity of seeking, and purity of reflection. In this context, it is called "purity" because one is purified (*sujjhati*).
Purification through confession according to the Dhamma is "purification by confession" (*desanāsuddhi*).

Here, the emergence from the offense should also be understood as being included within that very confession. As for the root offenses, it was stated above that the confession consists simply in acknowledging one's lack of restraint;
this constitutes the purification for one who has fallen into a *pārājika* offense. For since he has committed a *pārājika*, [he must undergo this process].
Remaining in the state of a bhikkhu, one is incapable of attaining jhāna and the other stages.
For the state of a bhikkhu becomes both an obstacle to heaven and an obstacle to the Path. Indeed, it has been said:
“The ascetic life, when wrongly grasped, drags one down to hell.”
Furthermore, it is said:
“For a lax wandering life only scatters more dust.
Thus, his state as a bhikkhu is not called purity. However, because [one]—having been a householder or otherwise—[practices] through giving, taking refuge, the restraint of virtue, and so forth...
One becomes capable of attaining either the path to heaven or the path of meditative absorption and liberation;
therefore, his state as a householder and so forth is called "purity. Purity through restraint distinguished by its foundation is "purity of restraint" (*saṃvaravisuddhi*).

Purity through seeking the requisites in accordance with the Dhamma and with justice is "purity of seeking" (*eṭṭhisuddhi*). Purity through reflection upon the four requisites is [purity of reflection].

Purity through review (*paccavekkhaṇasuddhi*). Regarding the passage beginning with “The bowl is fourfold,” the phrase “agreed upon as the restraint of the Pātimokkha” refers to the virtue (*sīla*) that is recognized as “the restraint of the Pātimokkha.

456. The construction is: “The restraint based on the mind is purified” means that the restraint of the sense faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*) is stated to be “purity of restraint. 457. The connection is:

for one who has abandoned wrong livelihood and acquires requisites in accordance with the Dhamma, because of the purity of their seeking (*eṭṭhi*), it is stated that “dependence on livelihood is purity of seeking. “Of one who acquires” means of one who acquires the requisites.
458. Regarding "purity through reflection" (*paccavekkhaṇasujjhanā*): the fifth case ending is used in the sense of cause (*hetumhi*).
The commentary on the exposition of purity is finished.
48. Commentary on the Exposition of Contentment (*santosaniddesa*).

459. These four requisites—the rag-robe, the alms-food lump, the root of a tree, and fermented urine as medicine—are called "few" because they are of little value, and "blameless" because they lack any basis for attachment.

They are called "easy to obtain" because they are available wherever one goes. Therefore, he said, "With few things," and so forth. One who knows the proper measure (*mattaññū*) is one who knows moderation in seeking, receiving, using, and relinquishing.
He is one who knows the measure by way of moderation in the four [requisites].

(460) How is he "content"? He says, "In the past," and so forth. "Maintaining himself with the present" means maintaining himself with the present fourfold requisites as described, according to what is obtained, according to his strength, and according to what is appropriate.
The commentary on the description of contentment is finished.
49. Explanation of the Exposition of the Four Protections (Caturārakkhaniddesa) 461–2.
“Buddhānussati … pe … maraṇassatī” — these are what is meant by the phrase “the four protections,” which is the remainder [of the sentence].

Regarding the expression “ārakattādinā”: the state of being distant is *ārakatta*; that which begins with “because of the slaying of enemies” (*arīnaṃ hatattā*) and so forth is *ārakattādi*. By means of that...
Because the spokes (ara) together with their latent tendencies (savāsanā) have been destroyed by that path, he stands far away (āraka), at a very great distance from all defilements (kilesa).
Thus, the shortening of the vowel *ā* and the changing of the consonant *ka* to the nasalized *ha* should be understood as the derivation of the word "Arahant.
Furthermore, when "āraka" is stated, because it establishes a specific meaning within a general indication, and because one who possesses that specific quality [seeks it], [the term is applied].
Because no distinction [of agent] can be applied, the term "by defilements" (kilesehi) is obtained.
"Sammā" means without error. "Sāmaṃ" means by himself; the sense is that he is not led by another.
For here, in the word "Sambuddho," the prefix *sam-* should be understood as signifying the meaning of "himself" (*sayam*). The suffix *-tā* in *Buddhatā* emphasizes the abstract state (bhāva).

The meaning is "the exposition" or "Buddhahood. Alternatively, the construction is as follows: the repeated recollection of the ninefold qualities of the Blessed One—whether as "Arahant" or as "Sammāsambuddho"—is "Buddhānussati" (Recollection of the Buddha). In the phrase "Sammāsambuddho iti," the vowel *a* has been introduced by way of euphonic conjunction (*sandhi*).
Here, the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning" (*ādi*), meaning "such as these and so forth. [This refers to] the ninefold [qualities].
“Anuttaro purisadammasārathī” (the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed) is taken as one [formula]. Here, however, only access concentration (*upacāra*) arises, not absorption (*appanā*);
the same applies to mindfulness of death (*maraṇassati*). But it should be understood that both arise in the remaining [recollections]. This concludes the Recollection of the Buddha. 463–4.

By the words “Those standing within the boundary,” etc., he shows the development of loving-kindness (*mettābhāvanā*). In the phrase “the Saṅgha standing within the boundary,” one stands within the boundary (*sīmāyaṃ tiṭṭhati*).
The Saṅgha is that which resides within the boundary. The connection is with those who hold sway in the village where one goes for alms.
Therein, it should be construed as "among all beings, starting from human beings. "Therein" means in that village. The word division is: "May they be happy and free from enmity.
By "and so forth," [it refers to] "may they be free from affliction, may they be free from distress, may they maintain themselves in happiness. Having delimited [the scope].
One delimits [the object] by saying, "All the bhikkhus in this monastery," and so forth; thus one delimits it again and again. This is the development of loving-kindness (*mettābhāvanā*).

Now, in explaining foulness (*asubha*), [the author] first shows the sevenfold skill in apprehension (*uggahakosalla*) that must be accomplished, by means of the passage beginning with "In color" (*vaṇṇe*), and so on.
For that [skill] is sevenfold, having come down through the method [of tradition], by means of vocal recitation (*vācāsajjhāya*) and mental recitation (*manasāsajjhāya*).
Together with [the following]. Therein, first, by one reciting with the voice, the four sets of five [factors] beginning with the skin should be delimited and performed in direct and reverse order.
Just as it is done with the voice, so too should the recitation be performed with the mind.
For recitation with the voice is a condition for recitation with the mind, and that, in turn, is a condition for the penetration of the characteristics.
In this context, "color" refers to the color of the head-hairs and so forth. "Shape" refers to the shape of those very things.
"Location" refers to the place where they are established. "Direction" means the upper direction above the navel and the lower direction below it.
"Delimitation" refers to the delimitation by way of similar parts, such as: "this component is delimited from below, above, and across by this [specific boundary]."
And likewise, by way of their non-confusion—such as "hair is not body-hair, body-hair is not hair"—there is the delimitation of dissimilar types.
The connection is with the phrase "having defined the sections beginning with hair. "Having defined" means having defined in the manner already stated.
By defining in this way, one accomplishes the sevenfold skill in learning as described, and the eighteenfold...
In order to show that skill in attention (*manasikārakosalla*) must be accomplished, he said, "By way of sequence" (*anupubbato*), and so forth.

Therein, these four—concentration (*appanā*) and the three discourses (*suttanta*)—should be understood as being tenfold when included within the [categories of] "not too fast," etc., which are arrived at by way of method (*naya*).
"By way of sequence" means in successive order, starting from the time of recitation (*sajjhāyakaraṇa*). "Not too fast, not too slow."

"Having done" (*katvā*) is an adverbial modifier of the action. "Warding off distraction" means warding off the mind's distraction toward external, diverse objects by relinquishing the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

"Having surmounted the description" (*paṇṇattiṃ samatikkamma*) means having transcended that description, namely, "head-hairs, body-hairs," and having established the mind on the thought "repulsive"—this is the intended meaning. "Successively" (*anupubbato*)...
“Releasing each part” means that whichever part does not appear clearly, one releases it in successive order;
this should be understood as being connected with the term “development.
Having thus accomplished both kinds of skill and having defined all the parts by way of color and so forth, [one should contemplate them] precisely by way of color and so forth.
In order to show that the fivefold repulsiveness must be defined, he said, "By color," and so forth.

The construction is: "The meditation on the parts [of the body] as repulsive by way of color... and location is the foul (asubha). Therein, first, the head-hairs are black by natural color, the color of green *ariṭṭhaka* fruit;
by shape, they are long and round, shaped like a measuring rod; by direction, they are born in the upper direction.
By way of location, the space of the head hairs is that moist skin enveloping the skull, demarcated on both sides by the ear-lobes, in front by the edge of the forehead,

and behind by the nape of the neck. By way of delimitation, the head hairs are bounded below by their own root-bases as they rest after penetrating about the thickness of a grain of rice into the skin enveloping the head,
above by space, and all around by one another.
“Delineated. There is no single hair existing as two; this is delineation by way of similarity (*sabhāga-pariccheda*).

That hairs are not body-hairs, and body-hairs are not hairs—thus, hairs are a single, distinct category unmixed with the remaining twenty-nine parts; this is delineation by way of dissimilarity (*visabhāga-paricceda*).
This is the determination of hairs by way of color and so forth. Furthermore, this is [the determination] of them by way of their color and other qualities...
The determination [of the body] as repulsive in five ways: "These hairs are repulsive by way of color, by way of location, by way of shape, by way of smell, and by way of place.
In this manner, it should be understood accordingly for the remaining parts as well.

"In the instances of the bloated and so forth" refers to the bloated (*uddhumātaka*), the livid (*vinīlaka*), the festering (*vipubbaka*), the fissured (*vicchiddaka*), the gnawed (*vikkhāyitaka*), the scattered (*vikkhittaka*), and the hacked and mangled (*hatavikkhittaka*).

The connection is as follows: meditation that proceeds by taking the aspect of foulness (*asubha*) in the ten objects of foulness—consisting of the bloated, the livid, the festering, the worm-infested, and the skeleton—which are devoid of consciousness, is called "foulness" (*asubha*). This is the meditation on foulness. 468.
Or [the thought]: "Death will happen to me," or "My life is being cut off," or "Death, death."

The construction is: “having developed it thoroughly” (yoniso bhāvayitvā). “Life” (jīvita) refers to both the material life-faculty (rūpa-jīvitindriya) and the immaterial life-faculty (arūpa-jīvitindriya).

“Thoroughly” (yoniso) means by way of the proper method (upāya). For it is precisely by practicing in this way that, for some, the hindrances are suppressed, mindfulness with death as its object becomes established, and the meditation subject reaches at least the stage of access concentration (upacāra).

469–470. However, for one who does not [attain concentration] by this much, it is shown that death should be recollected in eight ways, beginning with the appearance of an executioner, by saying "Like an executioner," and so forth.
"The appearance like an executioner" means like an executioner who, having taken up a sword with the thought, "I shall cut off his head," is moving it toward the neck.
Because death stands near; because of the ruin of prosperities, that is, the ruin and death consisting in the loss of prosperity in wealth and prosperity in life;

because of bringing together, that is, by way of these seven modes: greatness of fame, greatness of merit, greatness of strength, greatness of psychic power, greatness of wisdom, the state of a Paccekabuddha, and the state of a Sammasambuddha.

Because it is drawn toward oneself. "Common to many bodies" means because it is common to the eighty families of worms, to the hundreds of diseases, and to external causes of death such as snakes, scorpions, and so forth. "Because life is weak" means because life is dependent on inhalation and exhalation, dependent on the postures, and so on.
"Because there is no fixed determination of time" means [the thought]: "One must die at this very time, and not at another."
Thus, because there is an absence of a fixed determination of time. Regarding "the delimitation of duration":
it means that the delimitation of human life is now limited; as for the duration of one who lives long, he lives for a hundred years—thus, from the delimitation of the duration of time.

Now, we shall briefly set forth from the beginning, by way of a clansman who is a beginner, what must be done by a son of the Buddha who, having developed the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), desires to attain Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) through insight (vipassanā).
First, the fourfold virtue (sīla) must be purified. In that regard, there are three ways of purification.
Non-transgression, emerging from what has been transgressed, and not being oppressed by defilements—in this way, cultivation succeeds for one whose virtue is purified.

Furthermore, that which is called "virtue of good conduct" (*ābhisamācārika-sīla*), consisting of duties such as those performed in the temple courtyard (*cetiyāṅgaṇa*), must also be thoroughly fulfilled. Then—
“Residence, family, gain, the group, and action as the fifth;
travel, relatives, illness, study, and psychic power—these are the ten.
Regarding these ten impediments thus mentioned, whichever impediment is to be severed—by one who has thus severed the impediments—
“One who is dear, venerable, and inspiring; one who speaks and is patient with what is said;

one who delivers profound discourse and does not urge one toward what is inappropriate”—having approached a teacher possessing these stated characteristics, the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) should be learned. That is twofold.
There are two types of meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna): the universal meditation subject and the specific meditation subject.

Therein, the "universal meditation subject" refers to loving-kindness (mettā) toward the Saṅgha of monks and others, mindfulness of death (maraṇassati), and some also say "perception of foulness" (asubhasaññā).
This triad is so called because it must be cultivated and desired everywhere, and because it serves as the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for the practice of yoga intended here.
It is called the “all-purpose meditation subject. Among the thirty-eight objects, however, whichever one is suitable to a particular temperament should be constantly maintained by that person;
therefore, it is called the “meditation subject for maintenance” according to the method already stated. From that [it follows]:
“The great abode, the new abode, the old abode, and the roadside;”
A trunk, a leaf, a flower, and even a fruit that has been sought after—
A city made of wood, a field, a port with dissimilar inhabitants,
and a remote border region where no friend is to be found.
“A wise person, having understood these eighteen points, should avoid them from afar, just as one would a dangerous path.
Thus, a dwelling free from the eighteen faults of lodgings—such as that which has been described—is as follows: “Here, monks, a lodging is neither too far nor too near...”
It is well-suited for coming and going; it is not crowded by day, and at night it is quiet, with little noise, and free from the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and creeping reptiles.
Furthermore, while dwelling in that lodging, the requisites of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal supplies for the sick arise without difficulty.
Moreover, in that lodging dwell elder monks who are learned, who have mastered the traditions, and who are bearers of the Dhamma and Vinaya.
They are masters of the *mātikā*. From time to time, he approaches them, questions them, and inquires: “Venerable sirs, how is this?

What is the meaning of this? Those venerable ones reveal to him what has not been revealed, clarify what has not been made clear, and dispel his doubt regarding various points that give rise to uncertainty.

“Monks, it is in this way that a lodging is endowed with five factors. Having approached a lodging endowed with these five factors as described, one dwelling there should either have their long hair, body hair, and nails trimmed;
or perform repairs on worn robes by strengthening them through patching, darning, and so forth; or carry out needlework such as mending where threads have been broken.
"Stained garments must be dyed; if there is dirt on the bowl, the bowl must be cleaned; beds, chairs, and so forth must be swept.

Having thus dispelled the drowsiness following the meal by means of the minor impediments that have been severed as described, and having gladdened the mind by recollecting the virtues of the Triple Gem, one should attend to the mind without becoming confused over even a single word of the teacher’s instruction.
The commentary on the exposition of the four protections is finished.
50. Commentary on the Exposition of Insight (Vipassanā). 471–2.
"Name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) refers to name—consisting of consciousness and mental factors—and twenty-eight kinds of form. [Form] has the characteristic of bending (*namana*).
“Name has the characteristic of cognizing; form has the characteristic of being affected; apart from name-and-form, there is no such thing as a self or anything else.

Thus, if one is an attainer of jhāna, having emerged from jhāna; or if one is a practitioner of insight, having discerned the miscellaneous name-and-form that constitutes the object of jhāna—then there is the purification of virtue consisting of restraint by the Pātimokkha and so forth, which is described by way of the four protections and is termed “concentration with its access.”
By the phrase "and purification of mind has already been stated," purification of view (*diṭṭhivisuddhi*) is mentioned. This is connected with the following:

"Then, having discerned its conditions. "Its conditions" refers to its cause, namely: "At the moment of rebirth-linking, the dyad of name-and-form arises solely from ignorance, craving, clinging, and kamma, and not from causes such as a Supreme Lord (Īśvara)," and so forth;
by this, purification by overcoming doubt (*kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi*) is shown.
"Impermanent because of passing away after having arisen": all formations of name-and-form are impermanent because, having arisen, they reach non-existence.

"Suffering because of oppression by rise and fall": they are suffering because of being oppressed by way of arising and ceasing. "Non-self because of lack of mastery": they are non-self because they do not come under one's own control.
Having thus applied the three characteristics to the formations, [one contemplates] again and again...
"Comprehending" means a practitioner of yoga who, by the method already described, is either one whose vehicle is serenity (*samatha-yānika*) or one whose vehicle is insight (*vipassanā-yānika*).

By this, the purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path (*maggāmagga-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi*), as well as the purification by knowledge and vision of the way (*paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi*), are shown.

For, because of the contemplation of formations themselves through their arising and passing away and so forth, there arise [the purifications of] the contemplation of arising and passing away, the contemplation of dissolution, the contemplation of fear, the contemplation of disadvantage, the contemplation of dispassion, the desire for deliverance, and the contemplation of reflection.

Insight-knowledge that has reached its culmination by means of the eightfold knowledge known as equanimity about formations is called purification by knowledge and vision of the way (*paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi*).

By the phrase "may he gradually reach the destruction of all fetters," purification by knowledge and vision is shown. "The destruction of all fetters" refers to the five lower fetters (*orambhāgiya-saṃyojana*).
Because the three lower paths have already exhausted [the fetters] and because the other higher fetters (*uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) have been exhausted,
the path of Arahatship arises at the end of the destruction of all fetters.
Commentary on the Concluding Statement.
473. Because the training (*sikkhanā*) is the duty of a monk (*bhikkhu-kicca*), therefore—that is, for that reason—is the meaning.

474. "One who wanders constantly through the world" (*niccaso lokavicārino*) means one who wanders constantly in the world. The construction is: "Fatigue does not arise even for Mālu, as it does for the wind. *Mālutasseva* means "just like the wind" (*vātassa iva*). *Na sambhoti* means "does not occur" (*na hoti*).
475–6. *Tambapaṇṇi* itself is *tambapaṇṇiyo*. Like a banner (*ketu*), it is a banner; thus, *tambapaṇṇiye ketū* is a *tappurisa* compound.

The connection is as follows: this *Khuddasikkhā*, composed by him and praised by those who know the Dhamma and Vinaya, has reached its conclusion at this point, consisting of approximately five hundred verses.
The commentary on the concluding remarks is finished.
The Concluding Statement:
In this beautiful and excellent monastery,
which was caused to be built by the venerable and virtuous Purina, the chief official (mānādhikārin).
Having lived out the rains retreat, I, Vidhava, a Damila,
performed the rites for the flourishing of the Victor’s dispensation as desired.
By that merit born from the composition of this treatise—
Because of my commitment to causing the excellent arising of the Perfect Buddha’s dispensation,
I have no attachment to worldly pleasures;
I shall practice for the sake of the excellent arising of the Perfect Buddha’s dispensation.
Regarding these matters, words, and explanations,
whatever errors may exist in what has been written concerning what precedes and what follows—
let the noble ones set those aside, forgive them, and speak.
Or rather, what is the use of coaxing one who has committed an offense?
It was by the churning of the ocean of the inner jewels that the supreme wisdom,
shining forth from the Mount Mandara of the churning-stick, was obtained.
Sārāmātā, being exceedingly happy, brings happiness to others;
they surpass even my own venerable teachers in their virtues.
Through the merit I have attained by accomplishing the welfare of others, I [rejoice].
"May I, in birth after birth, be one who accomplishes the welfare of others.
The pupil said:
"To those who possess supreme fewness of wishes, manifold contentment, and tranquility..."
To those whose livelihood was pure and austere, who always dwelt in the forest,
who illuminated the Dispensation, and who had attained the status of preceptors—
the eminent ascetics known as the Udumbaragiri monks, the bull among practitioners.
Having approached his own disciple and friend,
the Elder named Medhaṅkara— a treasury of steadfast compassion and wisdom,
rich in asceticism, renowned by that name, and honored by the virtuous.
He who strove to purify the Teacher’s dispensation composed the *Subodhālaṅkāra*,
praised by the virtuous, as well as the *Vuttodaya*,
which is free from confusion and provides a certain determination of grammatical yoga for the correct formation of words.
By the wise Great Elder named Saṅgharakkhita,
who was the abode of manifold virtues such as fewness of desires and so forth,
and who acted for the upliftment of the Dispensation, this was well composed.
The commentary on the *Khuddasikkhā*,
titled *Sumaṅgalappasādanī*, is finished.
Thus ends the *Sumaṅgalappasādanī*.
The New Commentary on the Khuddasikkhā is completed.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Mūlasikkhā.
Introduction to the Text:
Having paid homage to the Protector, I shall briefly explain the Fundamental Training,
so that a newly ordained bhikkhu may train in the original language.
1. The Exposition of the Defeats (Pārājika):
A monk who emits semen while inserting [the organ] into the three paths [of a woman], or if he consents to it during the stages of insertion, maintenance, withdrawal, or once it has already entered.
If one takes human property that has not been given, by means of theft,
and if it is a grave offense among the twenty-five types of acquisitions, one would fall [to hell] upon death—
whether while taking it, while carrying it away, or even while walking about with it.
One who disturbs [the goods] from their place, even if only moving them slightly,
is defeated (parājika). In this regard, a wise person should understand that there are ten types of theft involving multiple articles, namely those consisting of five units each.
The act with one's own hand, the command, the relinquishment that accomplishes the purpose,
and the laying down of the burden— this is the pentad of "with one's own hand. Furthermore,
prior preparation and the bringing [of the object] after consultation.
The act of signaling, the sign, the fivefold preliminary effort,
theft, misappropriation, scheming, concealment, and [the taking of] grass and so forth—
these five forms of taking what is not given should be understood by the discerning one.
Knowing it to be a human being, one who with a murderous intent deprives it of life from its existence is defeated by the Teaching.
[One who claims] meditative absorptions and other such qualities that do not exist in the heart—
And if a monk should speak of another person as being of human birth without exaggeration,
he becomes defeated (parājika) at the moment he is recognized [as having lied].
2. The Exposition of the Heavy Offenses:
If, with a mind desiring to release [a woman], one makes an effort to liberate her, then, except in the case of a dream, a monk who is white (pure) shall incur a heavy offense.
If a monk, perceiving her as a woman, with lust for physical contact, makes an effort and touches a human woman, he incurs a grave offense (saṅghādisesa).
If, out of delight in indecent speech, he propositions a woman regarding the path for sexual intercourse, [he incurs a grave offense].
Shining upon a human woman while listening, one incurs a grave offense.
Having spoken praise of sexual service for one's own pleasure, one incurs a grave offense.
Soliciting a woman with lustful intent for sexual intercourse, one incurs a grave offense.
Having accepted a message from either a man or a woman,
if a monk takes it back after having investigated it, he incurs a grave offense (garuka). If,
desiring to cause [the nun] to fall away, he accuses her with a groundless matter, [he incurs a *saṅghādisesa*].
"Or, by instigating [a formal act], the ascetic incurs a heavy offense if he hears [the charge].
Taking even a mere hint as a basis,
desiring to cause [the monk] to fall away from his status through a groundless matter, he incurs a heavy offense if he hears [the charge] while instigating."
3. Explanation of the Forfeiture Rules:
If one lets a timely robe exceed ten days without having made a formal assignment or dedication, there shall be a forfeiture for that person.

Except by the consent of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, if one causes a robe that has been formally designated as one of the three robes to exceed [its size] by even one day, it is an offense of forfeiture (nissaggiya) in the absence of a formal agreement.
Furthermore, [if one accepts] an old robe from an unrelated bhikkhunī...
If she has it washed, dyed, or beaten— that may be so. If,
from the hand of an unrelated nun, one takes any root-cloth without having given anything in exchange for the robe-material,
it is declared to be an offense involving forfeiture.
For one who solicits a robe from someone who has not invited him,
except on an appropriate occasion, it is declared that he incurs an offense of expiation (nissaggiya).
[Likewise for] silver, gold, a māsaka coin, or a kahāpaṇa coin.
One who takes it, causes it to be taken, or consents to its being taken incurs an offense of forfeiture (*nissaggiya*).
One who exchanges it incurs an offense of forfeiture. Silver and so forth are of four kinds;
[the exchange] may be with a permissible thing (*kappiya*) or even with another permissible thing, provided that those who follow the same Dhamma are excluded.
If one exceeds the ten-day limit for an alms-bowl without having made a formal determination or a mental resolve regarding its size,
that bowl becomes subject to forfeiture.
Furthermore, when there is a bowl with fewer than five repairs, [one may keep it] beyond that limit.
If one requests a new bowl, there shall be an offense of expiation (nissaggiya) for him.
Furthermore, having accepted ghee, oil, and so forth, if he keeps them beyond seven days,
there shall be an offense of expiation for him.
Having given a robe to a bhikkhu, if one takes it back again— whether by one’s own initiative or by causing another to take it—
it is an offense of expiation (nissaggiya) if done with the perception that it is one’s own. Likewise,
if one asks for thread from someone who has not invited one and makes a robe oneself, it is an offense of expiation.
For one who causes [it] to be solicited, it is an offense of expiation (nissaggiya),
except when invited by relatives. But if a bhikkhu, knowing that a gain has been dedicated to the Saṅgha,
dedicates it to himself, for him there shall be an offense of expiation.
4. Exposition of the Pācittiya Offenses:
A pācittiya is declared for intentional lying;
likewise for insulting a bhikkhu, and for carrying tales that cause division.
Except for a nun or a monk, for one who recites the *Padasodhamma* from the Three Piṭakas with anyone else, a *pācittiya* is declared.
Having lain down together with one not yet fully ordained for three nights;
An offense of expiation (pācittiya) occurs for sharing a bed with another, or again, after the fourth watch of the night has passed;
for spending even a single night in bed with a woman;
or for teaching the Dhamma to more than six verses to one who is not a wise person.
If a monk speaks of a grave offense (*duṭṭhulla-vajja*) to one who is not a monk,
without the consent of the Saṅgha, it is declared a *pācittiya*.
Or if he should dig, or cause to be dug, the earth in an improper manner;
If one should disturb a grove of living plants, there would be an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for him.
But having made a bed or the like in the open air,
if one departs from what belongs to the Sangha without first performing the formal request and so forth, it is an offense of expiation.
Having prepared a bed in a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha by spreading out mats and so forth,
if one departs without performing the required inquiries and formalities, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for him as well.
If one knowingly uses water containing living beings, it is an offense of expiation for consuming it.
If a nun gives a robe to a woman who is not a relative—except in exchange for another robe—it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya); so too is sewing a robe [for her].
And if one eats food that has been formally offered after it was not made "leftover" (atiritta).
If one, seeking to provoke a monk, invites him and he accepts the invitation,
then having eaten what is not left over, an offense of expiation (pācittiya) is declared. If one eats stored food,
or eats what is suitable for the proper time at an improper time, [an offense of expiation is declared].
Or if one eats fine food while not ill, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one should eat after having requested [food], even such things as ghee and rice;
or if one should eat what has not been formally accepted, except for tooth-sticks and water.
One may give something to a member of another sect and eat it with one’s own hand;
one may sit down together with a woman, provided it is appropriate.
Regarding the drinking of fermented and distilled liquors, a *pācittiya* offense is proclaimed.
In poking with a finger, or in making one laugh, or in reproving;
in showing disrespect, or in frightening a bhikkhu; by telling a terrifying story, or by displaying something terrifying—it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
Except for a requisite, one who is not ill should not kindle a fire himself, nor should he cause it to be kindled;
for him there would be an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
This applies even when using a new robe without taking a "whitening mark" (*kappa-bindu*).
For a monk who, out of desire for amusement,
removes a robe or other such item belonging to another and hides it away, or causes it to be hidden;
or who, knowing it to be so, kills a living being— even one belonging to the animal realm— it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who wishes to conceal it conceals it, as does one who conceals a grave offense even from a nun;
likewise for one who has gone between villages, or one who has made an appointment with a woman.
Also for one who strikes a bhikkhu, or who brandishes a hand, a clod, or a fist.
Whether one reproaches or causes another to be reproached,
even on account of a grave offense; or in causing remorse, or for the sake of quarreling,
eavesdropping upon those engaged in a dispute to hear what they say— there may be an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one diverts to another person a gift that was intended for the Sangha,
even without having questioned the peaceful bhikkhu [regarding its destination], [that act constitutes an offense].
[The offense is] a pācittiya for entering a village at an improper time. 5.
Miscellaneous Explanation:
He who, being the owner, gives heavy property belonging to the Saṅgha to another;
A *thullaccaya* offense according to the specific case, such as a *pārājika* for theft,
applies to one who wears robes made of grass and so forth, woolen blankets, hair from a horse's tail,
bark cloth, rags, or antelope skins, except at the appropriate time.
In the case of surgical operations or vaginal treatments, for one who cuts the *saṃnimitta*,
there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) regarding human beings, as is also the case in consuming meat and so forth.
[Likewise for wearing] garments of bark, hemp, or linen, or cloth made of *potthaka* grass, or anything entirely blue.
There is also an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who wears any kind of yellow dye or similar colors.
Likewise, there is an offense for meat and so forth from elephants, horses, donkeys, lions, tigers,
leopards, hyenas, and even that which has been prepared specifically for oneself.
If one eats meat without having asked for it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
one should avoid meat from animals killed in sequence, as well as water from bathing places and the like.
Having forcibly caused [an animal] to be slaughtered, one should not enter or depart [the dwelling].
One should not defecate or urinate in a shed that lacks a window for ventilation.
One may defecate while sneezing, or while chewing a tooth-stick, provided it is outside the receptacles used for feces and urine.
One should likewise discharge feces and the like outside of such vessels.
One might scrape with a fingernail, drop a stick into a well,
fail to wash away what has been removed, or fail to clean away filth.
And while performing the work of water— having made a "capucapu" sound—
Even without being requested by the Elder, one may recite the Pātimokkha.
There is no offense in answering questions or explaining them without prior permission,
nor in the practice of recitation, or in lighting and extinguishing a lamp.
One may open or close the windows and shutters;
perform acts such as prostration while naked; go out, eat, and so forth;
perform or cause services to be performed; and [act] except for that which is covered by the three robes.
