Having bathed his body, he may rub it against a wall, a pillar, or a tree.
With a cord of kuruvindaka beads, he may rub one person’s body against another’s.
One who is not ill may walk about outside the monastery wearing sandals.
He who wears sandals, or even those that are entirely blue and so forth;
one who is lustful for the sign of a woman, or for the face of the giver of alms;
one who, perceiving blame, [uses] another's bowl or his own face [for such purposes].
One might see [these offenses] regarding mirrors and the like, or sitting on high seats and great thrones.
There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who performs acts such as sitting down,
and also for paying homage to those who have been suspended, those not fully ordained, those of a different communion, and so forth.
One may sit on a long seat together with learned women or with one who possesses both sexual organs, but not on a short seat. Or,
one who does not share a common seat may lie down upon a bed or a bench.
One who is unskilled might consume, or live under the dependence of,
even fruits, flowers, and so forth, given for the purpose of supporting one's family;
or he might have knots and such made, using requisites forbidden by the Conqueror.
If one speaks of medicine or medical treatment for another when it has not been authorized,
that bhikkhu incurs an offense regarding the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā.
In places such as doorways and the like, there should be a revolving door-panel.
One may lie down during the day either without exertion or with a fixed posture.
One may touch grain, women, precious gems, weapons, ornaments for men,
musical instruments, fruits on trees, and raw rice and other such crops.
With rice, water, and oil; or with hoods, hands, and hoods;
in the arranging of hair, in a vessel, and also in food;
they may lie on a single bedspread or cloak, two together on one couch.
One should chew a tooth-stick that is not exceeding the proper measure.
For one who arranges, or causes to be arranged, dancing, singing, or instrumental music,
or for one who watches or listens to them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Also in planting trees such as rice, outside the walls or enclosures,
in the disposal of excrement and so forth, in wearing long hair and the like,
in grooming the nails and so forth, and in the removal of hair from the private parts.
To step upon ground that has been prepared while wearing sandals;
to sit on a bed or chair belonging to the Saṅgha with unwashed and dusty feet;
or to touch a wall that has been prepared—there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who does these things.
Even when folded with the outer robe, a robe is difficult to use;
one should enter a village without fastening the waistband, having made a space for excrement.
One should not bathe when water is available, nor should one accept what is improper.
In the case of announcing one's confession and so forth, and also regarding a similar offense;
one should not spend the rains residence if there is a deception, but if the mind is pure, one may give a promise.
Having spent the rains residence, one may depart from the duty that was not authorized.
One should not mount a pure tree devoid of branches upon a person;
one should avoid a vessel that lacks a strainer or a lid when asked for it, nor should one give it.
Or, for the sake of one's own destruction, one might have the form of a woman or similar things fashioned.
Having set aside one's own mind for garlands and such, one should personally prepare the Jātaka and other stories.

One commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) by making someone else recite while one enjoys it oneself, or by sitting in the Sāla-hall and other such places without giving way to those who are senior, or by failing to give them space.
One should mount the foremost vehicle, taking refuge in the Triple Gem;
one should speak with diligence, avoiding the flattery of an assembly of outsiders.
Having uncovered one’s body and so forth, one should not display it before the bhikkhunīs.
One may recite Lokāyata philosophy oneself, or cause it to be recited.
Whether eating from a bowl or with one's hands in any kind of casket,
or opening a window-lattice, even if it is full of water.
One should set it aside when hot, or remove the water when it is too hot;
one should place the bowl on the ground, or in one's lap, or on a bed or a stool;
or one may place it on a mat, on the edge of a platform, on the foot of a bed, or under a parasol.
If one places a bowl on the ground, or washes hands over a bowl,
or carries away even used water with a bowl,
or uses a bowl that is unfit [for food], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
When one says "Live on! and, being disrespectful, does not train [in the rules], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) regarding the "parimaṇḍala" and other training rules (sekhiya).
He who, while engaged in the storehouse, [takes] goods...
It would be a *pācittiya* offense for one to disparage mothers;
furthermore, if one should speak ill of another on account of inferiority in birth and so forth— even if it be the highest [truth]— it would be a *dubbhāsita*.
6. The Exposition of Duties Concerning the Latrine, etc.

The duties toward preceptors and teachers, as well as those for those departing and those arriving, and the duties regarding lodgings and so forth—these should be performed by one who is affectionate and virtuous.
Standing within arm’s reach, one may give three kinds of things that are to be taken;
one who wishes to take may take two kinds—this is formal acceptance (sampaṭiggaha). [The three are:
the outer robe (saṅghāṭi), the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga), and likewise the inner robe (antaravāsaka).
“I resolve upon this,” and likewise, “I relinquish.
Or: “This, these, those, and even this robe,” or “These are requisites-cloths,” and likewise, “I relinquish.”
“I resolve upon this; I relinquish the bowl. In this way one should relinquish what has been resolved upon—the robe and so forth—according to the rule.
With the exception of matchmaking, the remaining [offenses] are heavy when committed intentionally.
Having abandoned what is uncut and transformed, the forfeiture without intent;
two on the recitation of the Dhamma, two on beds, teaching the Dhamma to a woman;
two on lodgings, and also the sewing of a robe.
Inviting [others to drink], drinking fermented liquor, the five kinds of stored food and so forth,
lighting a fire, and the Kappa-bond and Anādika; these, ending with entering a village,
are the offenses of expiation (pācittiya) committed unintentionally.
Among the miscellaneous rules: meat specially prepared [for oneself], excluding other kinds of meat;
sharing a single blanket or cloak; lying down on the same bed;
eating together; and the seven [offenses] such as dancing, singing, and so forth.
The waist-band, the bowl-rest, and the door-bolt—all these are without consciousness;
everything else here possesses consciousness.
Through a mind that transgresses [the precepts], there is both that which possesses consciousness and that which does not.
The teachers who speak likewise [say] that by means of knowing the formal designation as well,
having performed the preliminary rites and so forth, all of the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies,
illuminated in nine ways, should be performed by one of loving virtue.
The broom, the lamp, water, and the seat—
these are called the preliminary duties for the Uposatha. The announcement of consent,
the declaration of purity, the proclamation of the season, the counting of the monks, and the exhortation;
These are called the preliminary duties for the Uposatha.
[The Uposatha is valid] when as many monks as are entitled to participate have assembled,
and no common offenses exist.
And since there are no persons to be excluded from that assembly,
it is said to be "fitting.

Having completed the preliminary acts and preliminary duties, we perform the act of propitiation to recite the Pātimokkha with the consent of the harmonious Saṅgha of monks who have confessed their offenses.
By virtue of the recitation of the Sutta on the Resolution of Complete Purification (Pārisuddhi-adhiṭṭhāna-sutta), there are three ways:
by group, by individual, and by the Saṅgha; they should perform it according to the sequence.
On the fourteenth or the fifteenth day, it is threefold according to the giving of the invitation (dinata) for the sake of harmony.
Because they are not prompted by the things to be done by the day or the person,
and because they are divided into three groups of three according to the distinctions of the day and the person,
these nine invitations (pavāraṇā) are stated as having three, two, and one word respectively.
From the last fortnight of Kattika comes the winter ending on the full moon of Phagguna;
from its last fortnight comes the summer ending on the full moon of Āsāḷha;
the remainder is the rainy season, consisting of twenty-four Uposatha days.
Among these, the fourteenth, the third, and the seventh of the fortnight are to be known as the fifteenth;
the remaining [days] are the eighteen Uposatha days.
(117) “One gives consent, one carries my consent, one announces my consent”—in this way, consent should be given.
118. “I give my purity; take my purity; announce my purity”—thus should the purity be given.
119. “I give my invitation; take my invitation; announce my invitation; invite on my behalf”—thus should the invitation be given.
120. By the one confessing an offense: “Venerable sir, I have committed several offenses of various categories; [I confess them] in your presence.”
Having said, "I confess," the one receiving the confession should ask, "Friend, do you see those offenses? To which he should reply, "Yes, venerable sir, I see them.
Then the one receiving the confession should say, "Friend, you should restrain yourself in the future.
Having said this three times, the other should reply, "Very well, very well, venerable sir, I shall restrain myself," and then the confession should be made.

121. One who is expressing doubt should announce it by saying three times: "Venerable sir, I am in doubt regarding many offenses of various bases; when I become free from doubt, I shall then make amends for those offenses.
122. Having said three times, "I resolve that today is my Uposatha—whether it be the fifteenth or the fourteenth," the individual should perform the Uposatha by resolution.

123. However, in the case of two [monks], the elder must state three times: "Friends, I am pure; 'I am pure,' let you remember me. The junior monk must likewise state it in the same way. The only difference is the phrase: "Venerable sir, may you remember me. 124.
In the case of three [monks], however, having established the motion (ñatti) thus: "Let the venerable ones hear me: today is the Uposatha of the fifteenth day.
If it seems appropriate to the venerable ones, let us perform the Uposatha of mutual purity," they should proceed in order according to the method already described.
The Uposatha of complete purity should be performed.
125. Having recited three times, "Today is my invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*)," whether it be on the fourteenth or the fifteenth day, one should perform the invitation ceremony with one person. 126.
But when there are two, the elder should say: "Friend, I invite the Venerable One regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected."
Or, having said three times, "Let the Venerable One speak to me out of compassion; seeing [my fault], I will make amends," one should perform the *pavāraṇā*.
The newly ordained monk should also speak in the same manner; the only difference is the address "Venerable Sir" (*bhante*).
Or, when there are three or four [monks], they should say: "May the Venerable Ones listen to me: today is the *pavāraṇā* on the fifteenth day; as for the Venerable Ones..."
Having established the motion: "It is appropriate that we invite one another," the Elder should say three times:
"Friends, I invite you regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected; let the venerable ones speak to me out of compassion;
if I see [an offense], I will make amends. The novices should do likewise.
The invitation (*pavāraṇā*) should be performed in successive order. The address “Venerable Sir” (*bhante*) is the distinction. 128.
However, when there are more than four [monks], one should propose a motion (*ñatti*) as follows: “Let the Sangha hear me, friends; today is the fifteenth day of the invitation.
If it is timely for the Sangha, let the Sangha invite. Then, by the senior [monk], [the words] “The Sangha... [should be spoken].
Having said three times, "Friends, I invite you with regard to what has been seen, heard, or suspected; may the venerable ones speak to me out of compassion;
seeing it, I shall make amends," one should perform the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*). Even novices should likewise proceed in order, saying:
"Venerable sirs, I invite the Saṅgha with regard to what has been seen, heard, or suspected; may [the venerable ones] speak..."
"Venerable sirs, out of compassion for me, please wait; I shall make amends while seeing my fault. Having said this three times, he should perform the *pavāraṇā*.
The *Mūlasikkhā* is finished.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Introduction to the Commentary on the Mūlasikkhā:
To the Triple Gem, which bestows all desires and is the most precious of all jewels.
Having paid homage to the most excellent and the most excellent among those worthy of homage—
the feet of my teachers who lead the holy life—
I shall set aside my head at their feet and compose this commentary on the meaning of the Root Training Rules.
Commentary on the Introduction to the Work:
First of all, showing his homage to the Teacher—who is honored by all and supreme among all beings—the author says, "Having bowed to the Protector," and so forth.
Having bowed to—that is, having paid homage to—the Blessed One, who is the Protector endowed with the four qualities of a protector, at the beginning...

The summary meaning (*piṇḍattha*) is as follows: "From the time of his initial full ordination (*upasampadā*), I shall briefly and concisely explain the fundamental training (*mūlasikkhā*) for a newly ordained monk who has recently gone forth, so that he may train in the root language, the Māgadhī tongue.
As for the analysis of the parts (*avayavattha*): *natvā* means having become inclined toward, leaning toward, and bent toward that [training] through the doors of body, speech, and mind.

The meaning is "having paid homage. He is called a *nātha* because he protects; the meaning is that he aspires for and wishes for the welfare and happiness of those to be trained (*veneyya*) by way of loving-kindness (*mettā*).
Alternatively, the meaning is that he torments the defilements residing in those to be trained. Or again, the meaning is that he entreats or requests.
For the Blessed One [said]: "Bhikkhus, it is good for a bhikkhu from time to time to reflect upon his own excellence..."
By saying, "He should reflect," and so forth, even after requesting beings to practice various forms of benefit, he encourages them therein out of compassion.
Alternatively, because he possesses supreme mastery of mind and thus rules over and surpasses all beings, the Blessed One is called the "Lord" (*nātha*).
And this entire meaning should be understood according to the science of grammar (*saddasattha*).

"I shall explain" means I shall speak clearly. "Root training" (*mūlasikkhā*) refers to all three trainings—namely, the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom—in the sense that they are the root for establishing one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*), and because they must be trained in, they are called "training.
Since this is stated here by way of summarizing the texts, the book that elucidates it is called the "Root Training."
In this context, what is virtue (sīla), what is higher virtue (adhīsīla), what is mind (citta), what is higher mind (adhicitta), what is wisdom (paññā), and what is higher wisdom (adhipaññā)?
It is said: First, the virtue consisting of five factors, eight factors, and ten factors is simply virtue (sīla).
However, the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha is called "higher virtue" (adhīsīla). For that [Pātimokkha restraint] is like the sun among lights.
Like Sineru among mountains, it is both superior and supreme among all mundane virtues (*sīla*).
Furthermore, while virtue associated with the path and fruit is indeed "higher virtue" (*adhisīla*) even compared to the restraint of the *Pātimokkha*, that is not what is intended here.
For one training in that [restraint] does not engage in sexual intercourse. Rather, it refers to the eight wholesome sense-sphere consciousnesses and the eight mundane attainment-consciousnesses.

And having brought them together, it is simply the mind. However, the mind of the eight attainments that serves as the basis for insight (vipassanā) is called "higher mind" (*adhicitta*). For that is both superior and supreme among all mundane minds.
Even more so than that, the path and fruition minds are indeed "higher mind," but those are not intended here. For one training in those does not engage in sexual intercourse.
The knowledge of the ownership of action (*kammassakatāñāṇa*), which proceeds in the manner beginning with “there is what is given, there is what is sacrificed,” is *paññā*.
However, the insight-knowledge (*vipassanāñāṇa*) that delimits the aspects of the three characteristics is called “higher wisdom” (*adhipaññā*).

For that is both superior and supreme among all mundane forms of wisdom. Even more than that, the wisdom of the paths and fruits is indeed higher wisdom; however, that is not intended here. For it is not...
Training in that, he engages in sexual intercourse.

Among those three trainings, the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) must be practiced by one who undertakes both types of virtue—the virtue of conduct and the virtue of restraint—exactly as instructed, and abandoned by means of abandoning the defilements opposed to it through their specific antidotes (tadaṅga-pahāna). The training in higher consciousness (adhicitta-sikkhā)...

One should train by means of application toward the aforementioned objects, effecting the suppression-abandonment (*vikkhambhana-pahāna*) of the groups of hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) which are the opposites of jhāna.

Furthermore, the training in higher wisdom (*adhipaññā-sikkhā*) should be practiced by one who cuts off the defilements along with their underlying tendencies (*sānusaya*) through the abandonment consisting in specific counteraction (*tadaṅga-pahāna*) and eradication (*samuccheda*), as appropriate. Therefore, in the sense of establishing a firm foundation...
It is the "root-training" (*mūla-sikkhā*) because it is both the root and that which is to be trained in; thus, in the *Kammavācā*, it is called "root-training.

It is a "compound" (*samāsa*) because it is joined together or abbreviated; therefore, it is "from the compound. One who has received full ordination (*upasampanna*) by means of a complete Saṅgha through a formal act (*kamma*) consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha*), which is irreversible and fit for the occasion, is a "bhikkhu. In this regard, by the very last method...
In a formal act (*kamma*) that must be performed by a quorum of five, when as many bhikkhus as are entitled to participate have arrived,

when the consent (*chanda*) of those who are eligible to give consent has been brought forward, and when there is no objection from those present— by the Saṅgha having thus attained unanimity in a single formal act,
through the procedure known as "fourth with a motion" (*ñatticatuttha*), consisting of three proclamations (*anussāvana*) and one motion (*ñatti*).

Because it is a legal act of discipline (*vinayakamma*) that possesses the perfection of the subject matter, the motion, the proclamation, the boundary, and the assembly, it has reached a state that is not to be disturbed and not to be reviled;

thus, one who is "ordained" (*upasampanna*) is one who is fit for the occasion, fit for the reason, and fit for the Teacher’s instruction—the meaning is that he has attained a superior state and has reached [it].
For the state of being a monk (*bhikkhubhāva*) is indeed the superior state. And this [state] is [attained] by the aforementioned...
Because he has attained full ordination through the formal act (*kamma*), he is called "one who is ordained" (*upasampanno*); by that monk.

Because he is less than five years [in seniority], he is "newly ordained" (*navako*); by that newly ordained one, meaning one who has recently gone forth, one who has not long since gone forth—this is what is meant.

"From the beginning" (*ādo*) means "right at the start," or "beginning from the very outset. Furthermore, by the word "beginning" (*ādo*), the Elder [Thera] refers to those sons of good family who have gone forth out of faith.
It generates a sense of spiritual urgency in those who do not practice due to the fault of laziness, and in those who practice wrongly due to the fault of ignorance. How so?
Having obtained this extremely rare moment and this convergence of conditions, one should not waste that moment through indolence or by being intent on useless talk.
What should be done? From the very beginning, one must proceed without interruption.
"One should generate reverence for the three trainings.
"The Māgadhī is the root language, by which men were speakers from the beginning;
even the Brahmās spoke it when they had heard it, and the Fully Awakened Ones also spoke it."

"By way of speech" means by way of the root language; that is to say, by way of the Māgadhī root language, or by way of the language of natural terminology (*sabhāvanirutti*). "To train" means to learn. 1.
Commentary on the Exposition of the *Pārājika* Rules:
Now, because it is the foundation of all training, the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) is stated first. Within that [section], too—
Showing that the *pārājika* offense must be understood first of all because it is extremely blameworthy and because it proceeds by way of severing the very root [of the monastic life], he says:
"Introducing the sign... and so forth. Therein, the meaning is: a monk who introduces his own sexual organ (*saṃ nimittaṃ*) into the three paths is "one who has fallen" (*cuta*).
"The sign" (*saṃ nimittaṃ*) refers to one's own generative organ (*aṅgajāta*), even if it is as small as a single sesame seed at its minimum extent.
"His own organ" is what is meant. "A bhikkhu" refers to one who has not laid aside the training.
Regarding "the three paths": here, by way of humans, non-humans, and animals, there are three types of females, three hermaphrodites, three eunuchs, and three males;

these are the twelve beings who serve as the bases for the signs that constitute the grounds for a *pārājika* offense. For these, there are three paths by way of the anus, the urinary tract, and the mouth.
In that regard, there are three for a human female, three for a non-human female, and three for an animal female, making nine;

likewise for hermaphrodites (ubhatobyañjanaka) and others among humans. For human paṇḍakas and others, however, there are two each according to the anus and the urinary tract, making six; likewise for human males and others. Thus, by way of all these, there are thirty paths. All of them—
Having taken this up, it is stated here as “in the three paths”;
the meaning is: in those three paths, in whichever path among the three paths for the twelve types of beings.
“Fallen” (cuta) means he has fallen from the teaching—just like a being fallen from the state of Sakka or Brahmā—and thus he is one who has committed a pārājika offense.
Now, what is called "entry" occurs not only through one's own effort but also through the effort of another;
and even in that case, if there is a mind of indulgence, one becomes guilty of a *pārājika* offense. To demonstrate this, the words beginning with "entry" were spoken. Their meaning is as follows:
if a bhikkhu consents to any one of the moments—namely, the moment of entry, the moment of remaining [inside], or the moment of extraction—he [becomes guilty].
If one consents—even if at that very moment a mind of sexual intercourse arises—one has fallen and is defeated (*pārājika*).
However, he who does not consent at all, regarding it as if entering the mouth of a venomous snake or a pit of glowing coals, is without offense.
In this context, "situated" means having reached the point of emission of semen. This is the first *pārājika*.
2–7. Now, in order to show the second [offense], he says: “Human property that has not been given,” and so forth. Therein, the connection is as follows:
whichever monk, taking human property that has not been given and is of heavy value, by means of any one of the twenty-five modes of taking, becomes one who has fallen [from his status].
“Not given” refers to any kind of property belonging to another, which is owned and possessed by a master.
That which has not been given by those owners, either by body or by speech, is "not given" (*adinnam*).
It is unrelented, unrelinquished, guarded, protected, cherished as "mine," and possessed by another. "Of a human being" (*mānusam*) means belonging to a human;
it is a coordinate compound with the word "goods" (*bhaṇḍam*). "By one [person] through theft" (*theyyāyakena*) means by one person through theft, that is, by a single act of taking away.

This is the meaning. It is stated by changing the gender. Alternatively, the reading is "theyyā kenacī" (by theft by anyone). Therein, *theno* means a thief; *theyyā* is the state of being a thief (*thenassa bhāvo*). This is the nominative case used in the sense of the instrumental;

therefore, the meaning is "by some theft, that is, by some taking away. *Ādiyanti* means taking up, seizing, or grasping. Regarding "among the twenty-five modes of taking": having combined five sets of five.
There are twenty-five modes of taking what is not given (*avahāra*). Among these, the "five fives" are as follows:
the fivefold set of various articles, the fivefold set of single articles, the fivefold set of taking by one's own hand, the fivefold set of prior preparation, and the fivefold set of theft.
Therein, the fivefold set of various articles is categorized according to animate, inanimate, and mixed articles; the [first] fivefold set is according to animate articles.

The group of five on single articles. Therein, first, it should be understood according to various types of articles as follows: one who seizes a monastery incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
One who causes doubt to arise in the owner incurs an offense of serious transgression (*thullaccaya*).
When the owner relinquishes his responsibility, thinking, "It shall not be mine," there is an offense of defeat (*pārājika*). This applies when one is carrying off another's property.
If one with a thieving mind touches a burden on the head, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). If he makes it move, there is an offense of serious transgression (*thullaccaya*).

If he lowers it onto his shoulder, there is an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*). If, when addressed with the words "Give me the goods" regarding goods deposited [there], he says "I will not take them," there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If he causes doubt to arise in the owner's mind, there is an offense...
Regarding a grave offense (*thullaccaya*): if the owner gives up the effort, thinking, "He will not give it to me," there is an offense of defeat (*pārājika*).
If, thinking, "I will take him along with the goods," he moves the first foot [into the boundary], there is an offense of grave misconduct (*thullaccaya*).
If he moves the second foot, there is an offense of defeat. If, with a mind of theft, he touches goods situated on dry land, there is an offense...

[If he] touches it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). If he makes it quiver, there is an offense of serious transgression (*thullaccaya*). If he moves it from its place, there is an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*).

This is the application here by way of various articles. However, by way of a single article, if one takes, carries off, or steals a slave with an owner or an animal, by means of the aforementioned method of assault and so forth, or [if one] [alters] their posture...
"Or he provokes [the owner], or he causes him to move from his place. This is the application here by way of a single article.
There are five modes of taking away: by one's own hand, by command, by relinquishment, by accomplishing a purpose, and by laying down the burden.
Among these, "by one's own hand" means that one takes away another's article with one's own hand. "By command" means [saying] "Take the article of so-and-so..."

If he commands another, saying, "Steal it," it is called *nissaggiya*: if one standing inside a customs barrier causes [the goods] to fall outside the customs barrier, there is an offense of *pārājika*.
One who accomplishes the purpose is one who commands, "When you are able, then steal such-and-such an article.
In that case, if the other person steals it without obstruction, at the very moment of the command, the commander [is guilty].
One becomes *pārājika* at the time of the theft; this is the "accomplisher of the purpose.
However, the "laying down of the burden" is to be understood by way of the goods that have been laid down. This is the pentad of "by one's own hand.
Furthermore, there are five other modes of theft: preliminary effort, simultaneous effort, theft by appointment, making a sign, and making a gesture.
In this context, the preliminary effort (*pubbappayoga*) is to be understood by way of giving orders, while the simultaneous effort (*sahappayoga*) is by way of causing displacement from its place.

"Concerted theft" (*saṃvidhāvahāra*) means that several monks, having made an agreement, saying, "Let us go to such-and-such a house and, having broken the roof or cut through the wall, let us steal the goods," they go there; among them, one person steals the goods.

In the event of its recovery, there is a *pārājika* offense for all. "Making an appointment" (*saṅketakamma*) means making an agreement; it is the act of establishing a sign by way of delimiting time.
And here, when it is said, "Steal before the meal," whether he steals today before the meal, or tomorrow, or in a future year, there is no breach of the appointment;
[the offense occurs] at the moment the maker of the appointment gives the command, and for the other [party, it occurs] at the moment of the recovery.
If he causes [the object] to fall from its place, there is an offense of *pārājika* for both.
"Making a sign" (*nimittakamma*) means making some kind of signal for the purpose of producing recognition;

it is of many kinds, such as winking the eyes, raising the hand, striking with the palm, snapping the fingers, stretching the neck, or rising from one's seat. The thief, thinking "this is it," [recognizes] that which was spoken by the instigator after he had made a sign.

If he steals that very same thing, there is an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*) for both. Regarding what was stated as "steal this," if, thinking "this is it," he steals another object placed in that very same spot, there is no offense for the one who was the original instigator.
These are the five preliminary applications. There are furthermore five other modes of stealing: stealing by theft, stealing by force, stealing by artifice, and stealing by concealment.
"Taking by means of theft" (*avahāra*). In this context, for one who takes after deceiving others with false measures, counterfeit coins, and so forth, such taking is "taking by theft.

For one who takes what belongs to others after intimidating them or showing himself off, or who takes by force more than his own share—such as kings, royal ministers, and the like—such [taking] is likewise [taking by theft].
The taking of what is not given consists of taking by force and taking after having made a mental reservation. Taking after having made a mental reservation is "taking by reservation.

This is of two kinds, according to the reservation regarding the object or the reservation regarding the space. In that regard, if one makes a reservation, thinking, "If it is a cloth, I will take it;
if it is thread, I will not," and then takes a bag in the dark, if it is a cloth, there is indeed theft.
If it is a formal rule (*sutta*) concerning a *pārājika* offense, he is protected. This is called "conceiving of the object.
When one who has conceived of a location takes an object, for him there is a *pārājika* offense the very moment that object exceeds the boundary he has conceived.
This is called "conceiving of the space. Thus, by way of these two types of conception, for one who takes [the object] after having conceived [its limits]:

Taking away (*avahāra*) is of two kinds: taking away by means of a pretext (*parikappa-avahāra*). When one takes another’s property after concealing it, that is called "taking away by concealment" (*paṭicchanna-avahāra*).
Taking away by shifting the boundary markers is "taking away by means of a *kusa*-grass line" (*kusāvahāra*).

This refers to when, while the robes are being distributed, someone shifts the *kusa*-grass line and, while the portion for himself is being divided, [takes] from another’s portion—whether it be of lesser value, greater value, or equal value—[standing near his own share].
Having seen the portion, if he first pulls up a blade of grass from another’s portion,
he guards it against pulling while desiring to drop it into his own portion, and he guards it even at the moment of dropping;
but if he pulls up a blade of grass from his own portion, he guards it while pulling, and as soon as it has slipped from his hand while he is dropping it into another’s portion—
"Pārājika. "This is called 'stealing' (avahāra)": the meaning is that one who takes by means of any one of these twenty-five modes of stealing becomes guilty of a pārājika offense.
"Heavy" refers to five māsakas; for a kahāpaṇa consists of twenty māsakas, and a fourth part of a kahāpaṇa is a pāda.
Therefore, it should be understood that five *māsakas* or one *pāda* constitutes a heavy [fine]. In this regard, based on the statement, "Four *vīhis* are a *guñjā*;
two *guñjās* make a *māsaka*," it should be understood that by way of *vīhis*, forty *vīhis* and ten *guñjās* constitute five *māsakas*.
As for what is stated in the *Sāmaṇera-sikkhāpada* as "twenty *vīhis*," that is not...
This is found in the *pāḷi*, not in the *aṭṭhakathā*; this should be investigated. The Second Pārājika. 8.
Now, in order to show the third, it is said: "A human being, [perceiving him as] a living being," and so forth.
Therein, whichever bhikkhu, knowing "this is a human being," deprives a human being of life with the intent to kill—that bhikkhu is defeated (*pārājika*) from the Teaching.
"Occurs" is the collective meaning [of the term].
"Human life" refers to the extremely subtle *kalala*-matter that arises together with the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*) in the mother's womb;
beginning from that point, it extends gradually until the time of death for a being whose natural lifespan is one hundred years. Within this interval...
The personal existence that has reached growth—this is what is called "human life"; the meaning is "such a human life.
"Knowing it as 'life'" means knowing "this is life," and knowing "I shall deprive it of life. "With a murderous mind" means with a murderous intention;
this is an instrumental expression used for a state of being (*itthambhūte karaṇavacana*). What is meant is: having become one whose mind is murderous, having formed the intent for death.
"Life" means from the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). "He" is an indefinite pronoun. "That one" should be understood as the definite pronoun by which [the subject] is specified.

"Deprives of life" means that he deprives the human body—described in the manner already stated—of life, even at the stage of the embryo (*kalala*), by means of heating or crushing, or by the administration of medicine, or by any appropriate means thereafter; such is the meaning. "In the teaching" refers to the application of the verbal root *parā-pub-baj* (to deprive of life).
The word *nissakkavacanaṃ* means "from that," namely, from the Teacher’s instruction; this is the meaning. *Parājito* means one who has incurred defeat.
*Hoti* is a remainder of the text. This is the third *pārājika*.
Now, in order to show the fourth, it is said: "The classification beginning with jhāna," and so forth. In that regard, whichever bhikkhu [commits] a pretext...

Having abandoned conceit, if one were to speak of a state such as jhāna—which does not exist in the heart—to a being of human birth, at the very moment it is known [by that person], he becomes defeated (pārājika) from the teaching; this is the meaning.
"A state such as jhāna" refers to: jhāna, liberation, concentration, attainment, knowledge and vision, development of the path, and realization of the fruit.

"The abandoning of defilements, freedom from the hindrances, and delight in empty huts"—this refers to the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) classified as jhānas and so forth, as thus described.
"In the heart" means in the mind. "Non-existent" means not being found. "Avoiding the designation of another" means avoiding the indirect way of speaking, such as:
"The monk who lived in your monastery was an attainer of the first jhāna," and so on.
The meaning is as follows. *Vinā* is a particle used in the sense of exclusion; its meaning is "having excluded.

*Adhimānaṃ* means "conceit arisen in the form of 'I have attained,'" such is the meaning. The analysis (*viggaha*) is "conceit that has been attained" (*adhigato māno*); the meaning is "having excluded that conceit.
*Manussajātissa* means "of one born as a human," not of anyone else among the gods, Brahmas, and so forth; such is the meaning. *Vadeyya* means...

He should inform [them]. "At the known moment" (*ñātakkhaṇe*) means "at the known time" (*ñāte khaṇe*), which is a compound; the meaning is that at that very moment when it has been informed by one of human birth.
"From that" (*tena*) is an instrumental case used in the sense of the ablative; the meaning is that from that instruction [he becomes] one who has committed a *pārājika* offense.
The fourth *pārājika*. The commentary on the exposition of the *pārājikas* is finished.
2. Commentary on the Exposition of the Grave Offenses (Garukāpatti). 10.
Now, in order to explain the Saṅghādisesa offenses, the passage beginning with “with a mind desiring to release” is commenced.

Therein, “one who desires to release” means one who has the desire to release; that which is both the desire to release and the mind is “the mind desiring to release,” by means of which—that is, by a mind finding gratification in releasing.
The meaning is as follows: it is stated that an offense occurs through the gratification of release (*mocanassāda*) among the eleven types of gratification.

In this regard, these are the eleven gratifications: the gratification of release, the gratification of being released, the gratification of having been released, the gratification of sexual intercourse, the gratification of touch, the gratification of scratching, the gratification of seeing, the gratification of sitting together, the gratification of speech, worldly affection, and the pleasure of forest-dwelling.
In this regard, if one makes an effort while intending and relishing with the intention to experience the pleasure of emission, and emission occurs, it is a *saṅghādisesa*;

if no emission occurs, it is a *thullaccaya*. However, if at the time of sleeping, being overwhelmed by lust, one presses the genitals firmly with the thigh or the fist and sleeps with the resolve for emission, then while he is sleeping—

Impure matter is emitted; this is a *saṅghādisesa* offense. If one relishes the emission while it is being emitted by its own natural process, and does not make an effort [to cause it], and it is emitted, there is no offense.

If one relishes what has already been emitted, when the impurity has already fallen from its place by its own natural process, for one who subsequently relishes it without making an effort, and it was emitted [previously], there is no offense. If one relishes sexual intercourse through lust for sexual intercourse...
If he takes hold of a woman and semen is emitted because of that, there is no offense, but he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
There are two kinds of relish for touch: internal and external.

In this regard, if one causes one's own organ to move—either thinking, "I shall know whether it is stiff or soft," or out of a fickle disposition—and semen is emitted, there is no offense. However, regarding the relish for external touch, through lust for bodily contact...
If one touches or embraces a woman and semen is emitted, there is no offense; however, one incurs a *saṅghādisesa* offense for bodily contact.

If, while scratching with the desire for pleasure, semen is emitted from a part of the body being scratched due to itching caused by a rash, scab, boil, eruption, insect bite, or similar affliction, there is no offense.
If, while gazing at a woman with the desire for visual pleasure, semen is emitted... [the text continues].

If there is release, there is no offense; however, it is an act of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). In the case of sitting together in private with a woman, even if there is release for one who sits in secret, there is no offense regarding the release, but there is an offense of sitting in private.

In the case of speaking together, for one who addresses a woman with words connected to sexual intercourse, even if there is release, there is no offense regarding the release, but one incurs a formal meeting offense (*saṅghādisesa*) for indecent speech. Regarding affection based on the household...
For one who embraces his mother or others out of affection for them as mother and so forth, there is no offense even if emission occurs. Regarding the "breaking of the forest":

if one touches with pleasure a gift—such as flowers sent by a woman for the purpose of establishing intimacy—which is designated as the "breaking of the forest," thinking, "This was sent by such-and-such a woman," there is no offense even if emission occurs. Thus, it is shown that among these cases, an offense arises through the pleasure of emission.
It is said: “...may he release... [etc. ...no. Alternatively, *mocetukāmacitto* means one whose mind desires to release;
this is an instrumental construction used in the sense of a state (*itthambhūte karaṇavacana*), meaning “having become one whose mind desires to release.
*Upakkamma* means having made an effort by means of any instrument, such as the hands and so forth. *Vimocayanti* refers to whatever—even down to the smallest—[is released].
The meaning is: even if a single small fly were to drink [the semen], it is released to that extent.

"Semen" (*sukka*) refers to any kind of semen among the ten types reckoned as blue, yellow, red, white, the color of oil, honey, milk, curd, ghee, or fat. "Except in a dream" means excluding any emission of semen that occurs during sleep.
"A recluse" (*samaṇa*) refers to anyone who has received full ordination. "Heavy" (*garuka*) refers to an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*).
"To touch" means "one would commit [an offense]. Intention, effort, and emission—these are the three factors here. This is the training rule on seminal emission (Sukkavissaṭṭhi-sikkhāpada).
11. Now, in order to show bodily contact, the passage beginning with "with lust for bodily contact" is commenced.
If a bhikkhu, perceiving a human woman as a human woman, makes an effort out of lust for bodily contact and touches that human woman, it is a *saṅghādisesa*.
"Should commit" is the construction. Therein, "with lust for bodily contact" means with lust for the physical touch of grasping the hand and so forth;
that is, with lust for the mixing of bodies. "A human woman" refers to a human female who is living, even if born on that very same day.

"Touching" means while touching. "Perception of a woman" (*itthisaññā*) is the perception that she is a woman; one who possesses that is "one having the perception of a woman. "Having become one having the perception of a woman" means...

The meaning [is as follows]: a human woman, the perception of her as a woman, lust for bodily contact, the exertion arising from that lust, and the actual undertaking of grasping the hand and so forth—these are the five factors here. This is the training rule on bodily contact. 12.
Now, in order to demonstrate what constitutes "vulgar speech," the passage beginning with "by delighting in vulgar speech" is commenced. Therein, "by delighting in vulgar speech" means...
[It is] through lust for the sound of speech connected with sexual intercourse via the urinary passage or the anal passage.

Or, "with reference to a path" means with reference to either the urinary passage or the anal passage, or with reference to sexual intercourse; this is the meaning. "Shining forth" means illuminating.
"A human woman" means one who is discerning, capable [of understanding], and able to distinguish between well-spoken and ill-spoken words, and between what is indecent and what is not.
"A woman capable of discernment" means a human female. "Hearing" means she is listening.

By this, it is indicated that even for a capable woman who is situated beyond the range of vocal intimation (*aviññatti*), there is no offense of indecent speech (*duṭṭhullavācā*) for one who makes a report by means of a messenger or a letter.
[The factors are: a human female; the perception of her as a female; lust for indecent speech; and making a disclosure through that lust.
"Understanding at that moment"—these are the five factors here. This is the training rule concerning indecent speech. 13.
Now, in order to show "service according to one's own desire," the passage beginning with "praise" (*vaṇṇa*) is stated.

In this regard, if a bhikkhu, having spoken in praise of service according to his own desire, should request sexual intercourse from a woman out of lust for sexual union, he incurs a grave offense (*garuka*).*
The connection [is as follows]. "Having spoken of the praise" means having proclaimed the quality and the benefit. "Personal sexual service" (*attanokāmapāricariyā*):

sexual service through desire, which is termed the act of copulation, is *kāmapāricariyā*; sexual service for one's own sake is *attanokāmapāricariyā*. This is a compound formed by non-elision (*aluttasamāsa*).
Alternatively, *attano* is used in the genitive case to express the sense of the dative; thus, it means "desired" or "wished for" by oneself.
“Desiring oneself” means longing for oneself by way of lust for sexual intercourse; “service desiring oneself” (*attanokāmapāricariyā*) is that service which desires oneself.
Regarding that service desiring oneself, [the Blessed One said]: “Sister, this is the foremost of services:
that one should serve with this Dhamma one such as me—virtuous, of beautiful character, and living the holy life. Thus...
The meaning is "having spoken in praise. Because the root *yācati* (to ask) takes two objects, it is said: "asking for sexual intercourse with a woman.

Therein, "a woman" refers to a woman of the type described in the context of the offense of *duṭṭhulla-āpatti* (grave offense). She is a human female, she is perceived as a female, there is lust for her personal service;
the speaking in praise [of her] by means of that lust, and the communication of that at that very moment—these are what is meant here.
There are five factors. The training rule concerning the performance of one’s own desires [is the fourteenth].
Now, in order to demonstrate the act of matchmaking (*sañcaritta*), the passage beginning with “a message” (*sandesa*) is commenced.
In this regard, a monk who, having received a message from a man or a message from a woman, investigates it and then returns a reply, incurs a grave offense (*garuka*).
Connection: In this context, "sending a message" refers to a man's instruction being spoken thus: "Go, venerable sir, tell such-and-such a woman protected by her mother:
'Become, it is said, the wife of such-and-such a man, purchased for a price,'" or a woman's instruction being spoken thus: "Go, venerable sir, tell such-and-such a man: 'I shall become his wife.'"

The message. "Having accepted" means having accepted or received it by making some verbal utterance—such as saying "Very well, lay follower," or "So be it," or "I shall inform them"—or by shaking one's head, and so forth;
this is the meaning. "Having investigated" means having taken the message in the manner described, [and then considering] whether it concerns a man or a woman, or those...
The meaning is: "having informed those who must be informed, such as one's mother, father, brother, sister, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase *haraṃ paccā*, it should be understood that although one ought to say *paccāhara*, the word *hara* has been placed first out of fear of violating the meter (*chandahāni*).
Having gone to the place where the messenger was sent, let that woman accept with "Very well" or reject what has been announced by him.

Or, out of shame, he may remain silent; yet, if he returns and conveys it to that man, then by this fulfillment of three factors—consisting of the acceptance, the announcement, and the return—he, the bhikkhu, incurs a *saṅghādisesa* offense. This is the meaning.

Herein, the five factors are: their being human beings, their being capable of being spoken to, the acceptance, the inquiry, and the return. This is the training rule on matchmaking (*sañcaritta-sikkhāpada*).
15. Now, in order to explain the groundless [accusation], the passage beginning with “desiring to cause to fall away” is commenced.

The connection is as follows: a monk desiring to cause [another] to fall away, by accusing or causing another monk who hears him to be accused on account of a groundless matter, incurs a heavy offense.

In that context, “desiring to cause to fall away” means desiring to cause [him] to fall away from the holy life (*brahmacariya*). “Accusing” means: “You have fallen into an offense involving defeat (*pārājika-dhamma*).”
The meaning is that he reproaches [the other] himself with such words as, "You are not a samaṇa; you are not a son of the Sakyans.
For one who reproaches in this manner, there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense for every single word. Regarding the phrase "without basis" (*amūlaka*):

that which has not been seen, heard, or suspected by the accuser concerning the person being accused—this refers to the absence of those "bases" (*mūla*) consisting of seeing, hearing, and suspecting.
Because it has no basis, it is "rootless" (*amūla*); that *pārājika* offense for which there is a final matter is the "final matter" (*antimavatthu*);
and since it is both rootless and a final matter, it is "the rootless final matter" (*amūlantimavatthu*).
By means of that rootless final matter, the meaning is: by any one of the nineteen *pārājikas* appropriate to a monk. They cause him to be accused; he causes [him] to be accused. Of him...
The meaning is that by standing nearby and instructing another monk to charge him, one incurs a grave offense for every word spoken by that instructed person.
By the word "listening" (*suṇamāna*), it is indicated that [the offense] does not apply to one who charges someone in their absence by means of a messenger or a letter.
However, there is an *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) for one who speaks of the seven classes of offenses in the absence [of the accused]. That which he charges...

The five factors here are: (1) his being reckoned as one who has received full ordination; (2) the perception that he is pure regarding that [offense]; (3) the groundlessness of the charge of a *pārājika* offense by way of what was seen and so forth;
(4) the formal accusation in his presence with the intention of causing him to fall away;
and (5) his understanding of it at that very moment. This is the training rule on groundless charges.
16. Now, in order to show what pertains to another case (*aññabhāgiya*), he said, "merely by a slight resemblance" (*lesamattam*), and so forth. Therein, "merely by a slight resemblance" means:

having taken as a basis, having relied upon, whichever among the ten kinds of resemblances—namely, those consisting of birth, name, clan, gender, offense, bowl, robe, meditation, teacher, or lodging—is seen in that person; [and] desiring to cause the monk to fall away from the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
The meaning is that one who accuses a monk while he is listening to the recitation of the *Amūla* (Groundless) section incurs a grave offense (*garuka-āpatti*).
How so? Suppose another person of kṣatriya birth is seen by this accuser committing an offense involving defeat (*pārājika-dhamma*).
That [accuser], seeing another monk of kṣatriya birth who is his own enemy, seizes upon the mere appearance of being a kṣatriya and says: "A kṣatriya was [seen] by me..."
If one accuses another, saying, "I have seen you committing an offense entailing defeat; you, a khattiya, have fallen into an offense entailing defeat," or "You are that very khattiya, no other;
you have fallen into an offense entailing defeat"—in this way, the cases involving specific characteristics (*nāma-lesa*) and so forth are to be understood.
However, the constituent factors (*aṅga*) here are the same as those in the preceding [rules]. This is the training rule on "belonging to another case" (*aññabhāgiya-sikkhāpada*).
The commentary on the explanation of the heavy offenses (*garukāpatti*) is finished.
3. Commentary on the explanation of the offenses involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*). 17.
Now, in order to show the procedure regarding robes, the section beginning with "assignment" (*vikappana*) is introduced. [It concerns] whichever monk [takes] an out-of-season robe (*akālacīvara*)...

The summary meaning is: if a monk lets ten days pass without having performed either the formal assignment (*vikappana*) or the determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*), it becomes an offense requiring relinquishment (*nissaggiya*) for that monk.
In this context, "out-of-season robe" (*akālacīvara*) refers to a robe received at an improper time;
there are six types of robes by way of material: linen, cotton, silk, wool, hemp, and jute. Furthermore, there are [other materials]: *dukūla*, *paṭṭuṇṇa*, *somārapaṭṭa*, and *cīnapaṭṭa*.
These six types of robes—namely, those produced by supernormal power (*iddhija*) and those given by deities (*devadatta*)—are "robes in conformity" (*anulomacīvara*).

Among them, *dukūla* is in conformity with *sāṇa* because it is made of flax. The three beginning with *paṭṭuṇṇa* are in conformity with silk (*koseyya*) because they are made from threads spun by insects.

The two beginning with those produced by supernormal power are in conformity with linen (*khoma*) and the others, because they possess the nature of one or another of those materials. Any one of these six types of robes is an "out-of-season robe" (*akālacīvara*).

Regarding the phrase "assignment is determination," it should be understood here as both that which pertains to assignment (*vikappanūpaga*) and that which pertains to determination (*adhiṭṭhānūpaga*).
Herein, this is the canonical text: "I allow you, monks, to assign the lower robe (*pacchimacīvara*), eight finger-breadths in length by the Sugata’s finger-breadth and four finger-breadths in width.
For a man of medium height, [this would be] two spans in length and... in width.
A *vidatthi* (a span). There are two kinds of designations (*vikappanā*): designation in the presence (*sammukhā-vikappanā*) and designation in the absence (*parammukhā-vikappanā*).
How so? One should say, "I designate this robe to you"—this is designation in the presence.
[One says], "Use what belongs to me, or dispose of it, or do with it as you see fit," in the presence of one person: "I designate this robe to Tissa..."
The other monk should say, "I assign this to the monk [Name]," and this is another form of face-to-face assignment (*sammukhāvikappanā*).

That first monk should say, "Enjoy the property of the monk Tissa, or dispose of it, or do with it as you see fit," and [the second monk] should say, "I give this robe for the purpose of assigning it to you. He should then be asked, "Who is your friend?"

Or if [the donor] says, "I give this to the monk Tissa," then the other should say, "Three monks. Then the former should say, "I give it to the monk Tissa. This is the assignment in the absence of the recipient (*parammukhā-vikappanā*).
When it is said, "Enjoy what belongs to the monk Tissa, or dispose of it, or do with it as you see fit," that is relinquishment (*paccuddhāra*).

It is called "name. [The phrase] "bahuke" means "these," while "imāni" refers to those not within hand's reach; or "etaṃ, etāni" likewise. The meaning is: "without making such a conceptual distinction.
Regarding the measure of the three robes, it is permissible for them to be less than the Sugata’s robe according to the maximum limit;
according to the minimum limit, for the *saṅghāṭī* and the *uttarāsaṅga*, the length is five fist-breadths and the width is two fist-breadths; as for the *antaravāsaka*—
In length, five fist-breadths; in width, two cubits or two and a half cubits is permitted.
What is more or less than the stated measurement should be resolved upon as "an accessory cloth" (*parikkhāra-coḷa*). There are two ways of resolving upon a robe:

one resolves it by means of the body, or one resolves it by means of speech. When resolving upon the triple robe (*ticīvara*), having dyed it, one should apply the *kappa-bindu* (the mark of validity).

Having given away his old outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) with the words, "I relinquish this outer robe," and having taken hold of the new outer robe with his hand, he should resolve it mentally with the thought, "I determine this outer robe," and then determine it by means of the body through a physical gesture;
this is determination by the body. This [determination] may be performed by any part of the body.
It is not permissible for one who does not touch it. However, the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) by speech must be performed by making a vocal utterance;

if it is within arm’s reach, one should say, "I determine this outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*)," and if it is placed beyond arm’s reach, one should make the vocal utterance after observing the location where it is kept, saying, "I determine this outer robe.
This same method applies to the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) and the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*).
Furthermore, it is permissible to take all [robes] beginning with the three robes together and resolve upon them by saying, "I resolve that these robes are requisites-cloths.
Thus, the meaning is: "without having made such a resolution.
"Ten days" means ten days. "Exceeds" means passes beyond. "Of him" refers to that bhikkhu. "Nissaggiya" (relinquishment) [is the offense].

*Nissajjana* means "to relinquish"; this is the name for the disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*) that must be performed in its preliminary stage. It is called *nissaggiya* because it involves relinquishing;
what is that? It is the *pācittiya*. For one who lets [the period] pass beyond that, there may be a *pācittiya* offense together with the disciplinary act of relinquishment;
this is the meaning here. Furthermore, as for that robe-cloth, on the day it arose—its...
That which is dawn is dependent upon the day that has arisen; therefore, when dawn breaks on the eleventh day together with the day the robe was produced, there is an exceeding of the ten-day limit.

In this context, there are five factors: the robe being one's own property, its being of a suitable birth and measure, the state of having severed the impediments, it being an extra robe, and the exceeding of the ten days. This is the first Kathina training rule.
18. Now, in order to show the second [offense], the passage beginning with “by the consent of the bhikkhus” is commenced. The connection is as follows:

for one who, setting aside the consent of the bhikkhus and without [the permission of] time, causes the three robes (ticīvara) that have been determined to pass beyond one day, there shall be an offense entailing relinquishment (nissaggiya).
In that context, “except by the consent of the bhikkhus” means that which the Saṅgha [grants] to a sick bhikkhu regarding his three robes...
It grants permission for absence; setting that aside. “The three robes have been determined” is the accusative case used in the sense of the instrumental;
thus, by means of whichever robe among the outer cloak (*saṅghāṭi*) and the others that has been determined according to the method of determining the three robes.
“For one night” means for a single night. “He exceeds [the limit]” means he dwells apart; the meaning is that he dwells separated [from his robes]. For one who has not obtained such permission...

The meaning is that for a bhikkhu to be separated from his robe even for a single night, it constitutes an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*). "Except on an occasion" means excluding the time for making robes.

The four factors here are: having a robe formally determined (*adhiṭṭhita-cīvaratā*), not having the frame for the robe-cloth spread (*anatthata-kathinatā*), not having received formal permission (*aladdha-sammutitā*), and being separated during the night (*ratti-vippavāsa*). This is the second rule concerning the frame for the robe-cloth (*kathina*).
19. Now, in order to show what constitutes an old robe (*purāṇacīvara*), the passage beginning with “an unrelated woman” (*aññātikā*) is commenced.
Therein, “an unrelated woman” (*aññātikā*) means one who is not related by either maternal or paternal ties—just as in such passages as “having reflected thoroughly” (*paṭisaṅkhā yoniso*).
“A nun” (*bhikkhunī*) refers to one who has received full ordination (*upasampadā*) through a formal act consisting of eight proclamations (*aṭṭhavācika-kamma*). “Has [her] beaten” (*ākoṭāpeti*)...
"He causes to be washed. This means that it would constitute an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
The three factors here are: the garment being an old robe, giving the order to an unrelated nun while standing within the vicinity, and her performing the washing and so forth.
This is the training rule concerning old robes.
20. “Something brought as a gift” means something brought for alms. “In the taking of a robe” means in the receiving of a robe.

The three factors here are: that it is a robe suitable for assignment, the absence of an exchange, and the taking from the hand of one who is not a relative. This is the training rule on the receiving of robes.

21. "Not having been invited" (*appavārita*) means that one has not been invited by being prompted with the words, "Venerable sir, please say what you need," whereby a desire or preference has been aroused;

thus it is "not having been invited. "To one who requests" (*viññāpentassa*) means to one who asks. "Except at the proper time" (*aññatra samayā*) means setting aside the time when robes have been lost.

[The factors for an offense are: the robe being of a type suitable for assignment, the absence of the proper time, requesting from one who is unrelated, and the acquisition [of the robe] through that request.
Herein, there are these four factors: the training rule concerning requesting from one who is unrelated;
"silver" means bullion; "gold" means gold; "māsaka" refers to three types of māsakas: the copper māsaka, the wooden māsaka, and the lac māsaka.
Among these, the "copper māsaka" is a coin made of copper, bronze, or similar metals. The "wooden māsaka" is [made] of heartwood.
"Or having cut out an image with a bamboo scraper or even with a palm leaf, one makes a counterfeit coin (*māsaka*).
A 'gum coin' (*jatumāsaka*) is a counterfeit coin made by forming an image with lac or resin. A 'kahāpaṇa' is one made of gold, silver, or ordinary [copper].
"Should take" means: whether it is being given for one's own sake, or is situated somewhere [and one takes it].
Or, having seen something without an owner, one might take it oneself. "Causes to be taken" means one causes that very thing to be taken by another.
"Forfeiture" (nissaggi) means that for anyone who performs any of the acts such as taking, there is forfeiture according to the number of items, provided they are not fixed in value.
"Should consent" means one should acquiesce with the mind without rejecting it through body or speech. [This refers to] the nature of gold and silver.

The three factors here are: being for one's own sake, and being one of the [four] states such as taking up [the object]. This is the training rule on receiving money (rūpiyappaṭiggahaṇasikkhāpada). 23. The connection is:
"Except for fellow practitioners of the Dhamma, one may exchange the four kinds of unallowable things, such as silver, for allowable things;
it would be an offense of relinquishment (nissaggiya). In that context, "unallowable" means an unallowable thing. "For allowable" means by means of an allowable thing.
"Those who share the same Dhamma" (sahadhammika) refers to the five types of fellow practitioners:

bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, sāmaṇeras, sāmaṇerīs, and sikkhamānās. In this context, there are two factors: the state of being money (rūpiya-bhāva) and the exchange (parivattana). This is the training rule concerning the exchange of money (rūpiya-parivattana-sikkhāpada).
[24] "I assign this bowl to you," and so forth, constitutes the act of assignment (vikappana); "I resolve upon this bowl," and so forth, constitutes...
The meaning is: "and without making a formal resolution. Regarding the term *pamāṇika* (measured), this is the detailed explanation:

having taken two Magadhan nāḷis of old, undamaged rice grains that have been well-husked and purified, one cooks a meal of boiled rice with those grains—free from broken grains, not soggy, not clumped together, very clear, resembling a heap of jasmine buds, and drained of its water—and then places it entirely into the bowl.
Into that rice, one should add a portion of bean soup equal to one-fourth the amount of rice—neither too thick nor too thin—which is taken by the hand and composed of all its constituent ingredients.
Then, one should add condiments such as fish or meat in an amount corresponding to the size of a mouthful, sufficient for the final mouthful.
However, ghee, oil, buttermilk, sour gruel, and so forth, are not counted; for they belong to the same category as the rice.
They are unable either to diminish or to increase it.

Thus, all of this [measure] being set aside, if it remains level with the lower rim of the bowl's mouth, or if, when cutting with a string or an awl, the string or the awl touches its lower end—this is called the "excellent" (ukkaṭṭha) bowl. If it exceeds that rim...
It stands like a heap; this is called the "superior" (ukkaṭṭha) bowl. If it does not reach that line, it remains entirely within;
this is called the "superior-superior" (ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭha) bowl. That which is half the measure of the superior is the "middling" (majjhima).
That which is half the measure of the middling is the "inferior" (omaka). The classification of these should also be understood according to the method already stated. Thus, among these—
The two types—the extremely large and the extremely small—are not bowls; the remaining seven are called "measured" (*pamāṇayutta*).
Thus, that which is endowed with measure is "measured" (*pamāṇika*); this refers to the "bowl. Among the seven types of bowls, it is any one of them. [The factors involved are:
the bowl being one's own property, its being of the proper measure, its having been formally resolved upon (*adhiṭṭhāna*), its being an extra bowl, and the passing of ten days.
These are the five factors here: the first training rule concerning the bowl. 25.
"Whatever monk, when he has a bowl with less than five mends, should request another new bowl—there is a forfeiture for that monk as well"—this is the connection.
In this context, "another" (*para*) means a different one, [specified] by the phrase "a new bowl."
It has a common locus (*tulyādhikaraṇa*). For one who has accepted [the medicine], there are four factors here:

it being less than five days old, its being for one's own use, a formal request having been made, and the acquisition through that [request]. This is the training rule concerning what is less than five days old.
26. Whoever, having received medicinal requisites such as ghee or oil, keeps them in store for up to seven days...
The meaning is: "If one consumes [these] and exceeds seven days, there is an offense of expiation (*nissaggiya*) for him.

In that context, regarding the phrase "ghee, oil, and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes fresh butter (*navanīta*), honey, and molasses. Therein, "ghee" (*sappi*) refers to the ghee of cows and other animals whose meat is permitted;
the same applies to fresh butter. "Oil" (*tela*) refers to oils derived from sesame, mustard, *madhuka*, castor, *vasa*, and so on.

It has arisen. "Honey" refers specifically to honey from bees. However, every preparation of sugarcane—from raw juice through that which is uncooked or partially cooked—should be understood as "molasses. This concludes the training rule on the administration of medicine. 27.
Having given a robe to a bhikkhu, if one then takes back that robe, either by one's own perception [that it belongs to oneself] or by causing another to take it back...
The construction is: "or it may be an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*). In that context, "having given" means having given while expecting services and so forth in return.
"Of one who seizes" means of one who, seeing that [the other] is not performing services and so forth, takes [the robe] by force; likewise for one who causes another to seize it.

[The factors constituting the offense are: the robe being suitable for assignment (*vikappanūpaga*), having been given by oneself (*sāmaṃdinna*), the perception that it is one's own (*sakasaññitā*), the state of being fully ordained (*upasampannatā*), and the seizing out of anger (*kodhavasena*).
"Or causing it to be cut off"—these are the five factors here. This is the training rule on cutting off (Acchindana-sikkhāpada).

28. The summary meaning is as follows: for one who, having requested thread from an unrelated householder who has not invited him, causes weavers to weave a robe while excluding those who have been invited by relatives, there is an offense entailing relinquishment (nissaggiya). In this context, "thread" refers to six kinds, beginning with linen thread.
Or it may be in accordance with their [wishes]. "Having requested" means having requested for the sake of robe-cloth.

The three factors here are: that the thread was requested for the sake of robe-cloth; that it was intended for one's own use; and that it was caused to be woven by an improper weaver through an improper request.
This is the training rule regarding the request for thread.
29. The meaning is: if a monk, knowing that a gain has been assigned to the Saṅgha, diverts it to himself, for him there shall be an offense entailing relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).
In this context, "knowing" means being aware. "Gain" refers to the requisite items such as robes and so forth that are to be obtained.
"Assigned" means that it stands as something directed toward the Saṅgha, inclined toward the Saṅgha, and leaning toward the Saṅgha. "Diverts to himself" means...

By saying things such as, “Give it to me,” one makes oneself the recipient. In this context, there are three factors: the fact that the gift was dedicated to the Sangha, the knowledge of that, and the act of redirecting it to oneself. This concludes the training rule on redirection.
The commentary on the exposition of the offenses involving forfeiture is finished.
4. Commentary on the Exposition of the Pācittiya Rules 30.
Now, in order to demonstrate the *pācittiya* offenses, the passage beginning with “in intentional lying” (*sampajānamusāvāde*) is commenced.

Therein, the locative case in “in intentional lying” (*sampajānamusāvāde*) is used in the sense of a cause; therefore, for that monk who speaks a lie while being fully aware, [the offense arises] on account of that.
The meaning is that, on account of that cause and by reason of that condition, an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) is proclaimed.

"And for one who reviles a bhikkhu": the meaning is that for a bhikkhu who stabs a bhikkhu with any weapon of the mouth—whether true or false—by means of [accusations regarding] birth, name, clan, deeds, craft, age, illness, gender, defilements, or offenses, an offense of expiation is proclaimed. "And also in the case of carrying tales" means in the case of carrying tales against a bhikkhu, [regarding] birth and so forth.

The meaning is this: having heard a monk reviling another monk on grounds for abuse, if one—whether out of a desire for favor toward that monk or with the intention of causing a schism—conveys malicious gossip to that monk who is not angry, by means of body or speech, an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) is proclaimed.
31. [This applies] to anyone other than a monk or a nun who has mastered the Dhamma of the Three Baskets (*piṭaka*) as recorded in the Three Councils (*saṅgīti*).
The collective meaning is that for a monk who recites word by word together with another person, an offense of expiation (pācittiya) is declared according to the number of words.
"With one who is not fully ordained" means,
excluding a monk, even down to a common animal that serves as the basis for an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
The connection is as follows: having slept together for three nights, on the fourth day, when the sun has set, there may be an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) due to sleeping together again.

In this context, "sleeping together" refers to sitting together in one place within a dwelling that is entirely covered and enclosed, or mostly covered and enclosed, either sequentially or simultaneously. Therein, "not touching the roof-covering" [is the condition].
Even that which is delimited by a wall or the like measuring one and a half cubits in height should be understood as "completely delimited. 33.
The meaning is: for a monk who spends even a single night lying down with a woman, there would be an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
In this context, "with a woman" refers to any human female, even one born on that very day. When teaching [the Dhamma] without a person of understanding present...

The meaning is: "And a Dhamma consisting of more than six lines" refers to a Pācittiya offense for a monk who teaches a Dhamma consisting of more than six lines to a wise man in the absence of a woman.
In this context, regarding the phrase "more than six lines," one verse-quarter (gāthāpāda) is considered one line;
thus, the measure of a "line" (pada) should be understood in all such cases. Six lines constitute "six lines" (chappada); [the phrase means] "from six lines..."

"Furthermore, beyond the six [cases], it is declared that there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for one who, having set aside the authorization of the monks (bhikkhusammuti), speaks of a grave offense (duṭṭhulla-vajja) to one who is not a monk.
In this context, 'grave' refers here to an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa). 'Having set aside the authorization of the monks' means..."

Except for that which the Saṅgha, for the sake of future restraint, makes a formal agreement (katika) three times—either having set a limit on offenses and families or not having set such a limit—for a monk who repeatedly commits offenses, after having obtained his consent;
"to one who is not a bhikkhunī" means to one who is not fully ordained; "speaking" means announcing.
35. Whoever should dig, or cause to be dug, unconsecrated earth, for him there shall be an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
In this context, "unconsecrated" refers to earth that has not been burnt in such a manner as for cooking on a hearth, or earth that has already been formed [by natural processes].
That is threefold, by way of being pure, mixed, or a heap. Therein, "pure earth" means soil that is naturally pure.
Or pure clay. "Mixed earth" means that where one-third part consists of either soil, clay, stone, gravel, potsherds, pebbles, or sand.
"Heaped earth" means a heap of soil or a heap of clay that has been piled up for more than four months.
Furthermore, by the definition already stated, this includes mixed heaps as well as fine dust resting on a flat rock.
And when it rains upon the deity, if [the water] remains for even a moment, after the lapse of four months, that which has remained becomes merely a mass of earth.
"For whichever bhikkhu should damage a living organism, for him there shall be an offense of expiation (pācittiya)"—this is the connection.
In this context, "living organism" (*bhūtagāma*) means those things that "are" (*bhavanti*) and "have been" (*abhavuṃ*); the meaning is that they are born and grow, or have been born and grown.
"Village" (*gāma*) means a collection; a "village of beings" (*bhūtagāma*) is either a collection of beings or the beings themselves.
This is a designation for established green grass, trees, and so forth. To "disturb" that village of beings means to perform acts such as cutting or breaking. 36.
Whatever monk, having spread out a bed or other furniture belonging to the Saṅgha in the open air, [fails to] seek permission and so forth...
The meaning is: "If one departs without having done so, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). In this context, "belonging to the Saṅgha" means that which is the property of the Saṅgha.
Regarding "beds, etc.," the word "etc. includes chairs, stools, mats, and so forth. "Having spread them out, etc.
means either having spread them out oneself or having had them spread out. "Requesting permission, etc. means either requesting permission, removing [the items], or having them removed.
The meaning is "he goes. "He goes" means he departs.

37. The meaning is that for whichever bhikkhu, having spread out a bed or performed other such acts in a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, departs without having requested permission or performed other such formalities, there would be an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for that bhikkhu.
In this context, "in a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha" refers to that which is the property of the Saṅgha.
In a dwelling, a monastery, a room, or any other well-defined, secure lodging. "Bedding" refers to such things as a mattress,
a cotton pad, a woolen coverlet, an upper sheet, a floor-covering, a wooden plank, a piece of hide, a sitting mat,
a rug, a grass mat, or a leaf mat— whatever is used for spreading out and so forth among these.
By someone having made or caused to be made a covering cloth or the like.
38–9. However, whichever monk should knowingly consume water containing living beings, for that monk there shall be an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*);
