such is the construction [of the rule]. In this context, "knowingly [it] contains living beings" means: having seen or heard that "this contains living beings," by whom...
Knowing in some way. "Toyam" means water. "Paribhuñjaye" means he should use.
If a monk gives a robe to an unrelated nun, setting aside the exchange [of robes], it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for that monk.
In the training rule concerning the acceptance of robes, the monk was the recipient; here, it is the nun—this is the distinction.

The meaning is that even for a monk who sews a robe for an unrelated nun, it would be a *pācittiya* offense for him. "Robe" (*cīvara*) refers to what is suitable as an undergarment or an upper garment.
"Sewing" (*sibbati*): for one sewing himself, there is a *pācittiya* for each instance of inserting and withdrawing the needle, according to the count of the effort.
However, for one having it sewn by another, if he says, "Sew it," even if the entire needle-work is completed, [the offense is incurred].
It is one *pācittiya* offense; there is a *pācittiya* for each instance of the act following the command.

The meaning is that it becomes a *pācittiya* for one who eats food after having invited others to partake (*pavāretvā*) without first designating it as leftover (*atiritta*). Herein, this is the analysis:
having made a refusal of food, if one swallows even as much as a mustard seed of any one of the five kinds of staple foods—boiled rice, flour, boiled millet, fish, or meat—it is an offense.
There is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for one who, by means of another posture, consumes food without having had it declared as leftover (atiritta), thinking, "This is enough for all.

40. For whichever monk, desiring to cause [another] to offend, invites a monk who has finished eating and refused further food, saying, "Come, monk, eat or consume," with food that is not leftover—when that food has been eaten, an offense of expiation is proclaimed for him.
The meaning [of the rule]. In this context, "expecting reproach" means looking toward being reproached, being censured, or being made to feel shame.
41–2. The meaning is: for whichever bhikkhu should eat food that has been stored, there shall be an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for that bhikkhu.
In this context, "stored food" refers to food that has been received and kept overnight. "At the wrong time" refers to [food] that is to be consumed during the proper time.
The construction is: "or for one who eats, there shall be an offense of expiation" (*pācittiya*). In this context, "at the wrong time" (*vikāla*) means when the [proper] time has passed;

the meaning is from the moment the midday meal is over until the rising of the dawn. "Suitable for the duration of the day" (*yāvakālika*) refers to edible food such as forest roots, fruits, and so forth.
If a monk who is not ill should request and eat something choice, such as a meal with ghee and the like, for that monk—
The construction is: "there may be an offense of expiation" (*pācitti siyā*). In that context, "one who is not ill" (*agilāno*) means one who is healthy.
"Delicate food" (*paṇītakaṃ*) refers to refined food produced from the seven types of grain, mixed with ghee, oil, honey, molasses, fish, meat, milk, and curd.

The meaning is: if a monk, setting aside tooth-sticks and water, should eat what has not been formally received (*appaṭiggahitakaṃ*), there may be an offense of expiation. In that context, "not received" (*appaṭiggahitaṃ*) [means] by way of the body...

Or, for one who takes [an object] with something connected to their own body, standing within arm’s reach, it is called "not given" and "not accepted" if it is not handed over by means of any of the items belonging to the body or connected to the body that are subject to relinquishment. 43.
Whatever monk should give anything edible with his own hand to a member of another sect, for him there shall be an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

The connection [is as follows]: "Therein, 'of a member of another sect' means of one belonging to another religious order. 'Something to be eaten' means any kind of food. 'With his own hand' means by his own hand.
'If a bhikkhu should sit down alone with a woman in a secluded place, for him there would be an offense of expiation (pācittiya)'—this is the connection.
Therein, 'secluded' means in a hidden place. 'He sits' means he might sit. 'Alone' means together with."
44. Regarding the phrase "even in the drinking of fermented liquor and spirits" (*surāmerayapāne pi*): here, *surā* refers to intoxicants made from flour and such;

*meraya* refers to spirits distilled from flowers and such. The meaning is that for whichever monk drinks either of these two, even as much as a blade of *kusa* grass starting from the seed, an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) is declared on account of that drinking.
And regarding "also in the poking with a finger": this refers to the cause of touching the armpits and so forth with the fingers.

The meaning is: "there may be an offense of expiation" (*pācitti*). Regarding "even when the one who reproves is in a state of merriment": the meaning is that when the water reaches above the ankles and he is in a state of merriment, there may be an offense of expiation for the purpose of playing. 45.
Regarding "there is also an offense of expiation for disrespect": even when showing disrespect toward a person or toward the Dhamma, there may be an offense of expiation.

The meaning is this: when a monk, being addressed by one who is fully ordained and authorized, shows disrespect because he does not wish to act upon those words or because he does not wish to train in that Dhamma, for that disrespect there may be an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
This also applies to one who terrifies a monk by making a frightening speech or by showing a frightening form.
The meaning is "it may be an offense of expiation" (*pācittiya*). 46.
The connection is: for whichever monk, not being ill, should kindle a fire or cause one to be kindled, setting aside some [allowable] necessity, for him there may be an offense of expiation.
In that context, "some necessity" refers to the lighting of a lamp, or [the lighting of a fire] for cooking a bowl, and so forth.
"Or making it luminous" means having established such a requisite as that. "Luminous" (*joti*) means fire. 47–8. The meaning is:
for one who uses a new robe without taking a *kappa*-mark, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for one who is wearing a new robe.
A "*kappa*-mark" (*kappabindu*) is a *kappa*-mark of the size of either a peacock's eye, a round seal, or the back of a finger.

"Without taking" means not having taken. The meaning is: for a monk who, with a view toward laughter, removes a requisite such as a robe belonging to another monk and hides it, or causes it to be hidden, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
"Such as a robe" includes—by the word "such as"—the alms bowl, sitting mat, needle case, waistband, and so forth. "Hiding" means concealing.
"With a view toward laughter" means with the intention of causing laughter. [Regarding the phrase] "knowing it to be a living being":

"Should a monk kill even an animal": the meaning is that if a monk, knowing it is a living being, should kill an animal—even one belonging to the animal realm—whether small or large, for him there would be an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). 49.
"Desiring to conceal, he conceals; even from a nun regarding a grave matter": if a monk [conceals] what is reckoned as a grave matter (*duṭṭhulla*) of a monk...
The meaning is: if one, desiring to conceal a *saṅghādisesa* offense, conceals it, there is a *pācittiya* for him.
The construction is: "For a bhikkhu who has traveled from one village to another in agreement with a woman, there is a *pācittiya*.
50. "Or you should strike a bhikkhu": if a bhikkhu should strike a bhikkhu, there is a *pācittiya* for him.

The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: "He raises his hand" means that if a bhikkhu, displaying the manner of striking, should raise either his body or anything connected to his body, for him there would be a *pācittiya* offense;

such is the meaning. "Or he should accuse, or cause to accuse, a bhikkhu with groundless [charges]" means that if a bhikkhu should accuse or cause another bhikkhu to be accused of a *saṅghādisesa* offense without basis, for him...
The meaning is that it would be an offense entailing expiation (*pācittiya*). In this context, "groundless" means being devoid of a basis such as having actually seen [the offense].

51. Regarding "and also in causing remorse": if one were to cause remorse by saying things such as, "I think you are less than twenty years of age," then there is an offense entailing expiation on account of causing that remorse. This applies to whichever monk speaks for the sake of a quarrel.
The connection is as follows: if one goes to eavesdrop in order to hear the words of those engaged in a quarrel, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for him.

In this context, "for the sake of a quarrel" means for the purpose of a dispute. "Of those engaged in a quarrel" means of those who have started a dispute. "Eavesdropping" means the vicinity of hearing. 52.
Whatever monk diverts to another individual a gain that has been assigned to the Saṅgha, for him [there is an offense].
“May there be an offense of expiation (pācittiya)” is the connection [of the sentence]. Therein, “directs” means “transforms.

“Without having asked permission” means without asking permission by saying, “I ask for permission to enter the village at an improper time,” or “I will enter the village. “A present bhikkhunī” means:
having seen a bhikkhu within the vicinity of the boundary (upacārasīmā) and within the range of sight, one who is able to ask permission with ordinary speech—
"Such a bhikkhu being present": "of the village" (*gāmassa*) means "to the village"; this is the genitive case used in the sense of the accusative.

"Gone" (*gate*) is the locative case used in the sense of the dative; the meaning is "having gone. The meaning is that for a bhikkhu who has gone to the village at an improper time without having asked permission from a bhikkhu who is present, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). The rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the exposition of the *Pācittiya* rules is finished.
5. Commentary on the Exposition of Miscellaneous Matters:
Now, in order to demonstrate miscellaneous matters, the passage beginning with “belonging to the Saṅgha” (*saṅghika*) is commenced. In that context, whichever monk is the master...
If, having offered it, one gives a heavy article belonging to the Saṅgha to another, there may be a thullaccaya for that person.

If one gives it to another with intent to steal, then according to the nature of the object, there may be a pārājika offense or the like: where the matter is a dukkaṭa, there is a dukkaṭa; where the matter is a thullaccaya, there is a thullaccaya;
and where the matter is a pārājika, there is a pārājika—this is what is meant.
54. Regarding the phrase "garments made of *kuśa* grass, etc.": here, the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes bark-fiber and wooden planks;

thus, there are garments made of *kuśa* grass, garments made of bark-fiber, and garments made of wooden planks. Among these, a garment made by weaving *kuśa* grass together is a "garment made of *kuśa* grass.
A "garment made of bark-fiber" refers to the bark-clothing of ascetics. A "garment made of wooden planks" refers to [garments] made by sewing together pieces of wood shaped like planks.
*Katacīraṃ*: a woolen blanket (*kambala*). *Kesavālajaṃ* means a woolen blanket made of hair (*kesaja*) or a woolen blanket made of tail-hair (*vālaja*);
the meaning is "hair-blanket" (*kesakambala*) or "tail-hair-blanket" (*vālakambala*). A woolen blanket woven from hair is a *kesakambala*.
A woolen blanket woven from the tails of yaks (*camari*) is a *vālakambala*. "At the proper time" (*samayaṃ*) means excluding the time when one's robes have been lost. For one who wears [them]...
"Of one who wears": "owl-winged and antelope-skin" means an owl-winged antelope-skin garment.
In this context, "owl-winged" refers to a lower garment made from the wings of the owl-bird. "Antelope-skin" refers to the hide of an antelope, complete with its fur and hooves.
The meaning is that, setting aside the time when one's robes have been lost, for one who wears any of these seven types of clothing, there would be a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).
55. *Satthakamma* is the action to be performed with a knife; in that *satthakamma*. *Vatthikamma* is the action to be performed on the vagina;
in that *vatthikamma*. *Saṃnimitta* means one’s own *aṅgajāta* (genital organ). The connection is:
"For one who cuts it, there may be a *thullaccaya* (grave offense). In the phrase *maṃsādibhojane*, the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes bone, blood, skin, and hair.
He favors [them]. Therefore, the meaning is that on account of eating the flesh, bones, blood, skin, and hair of human beings, there may be a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).
56. Regarding "cloths made of *kadali*, *eraka*, and *akkavāka*": for one who wears garments made from *kadali*, *eraka*, and *akkavāka* fibers, there is a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing).

"Potthaka" refers to a cloth made of *makaci* fibers. Regarding "all-yellow and so forth," here the word "and so forth" (*ādi*)— [...]* *Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a Vinaya commentary (likely the Samantapāsādikā or a similar sub-commentary) discussing specific types of forbidden clothing and the gravity of offenses associated with their use.*
It includes all-blue, all-black, and all-madder-red. In this context, "all-blue" means entirely blue;
the same applies to the remaining colors. Blue is the color of the *ummāra* flower; yellow is the color of the *kaṇikāra* flower; red is the color of the *jayasumana* flower;
black is the color of the *addāriṭṭhaka* fruit; and madder-red is the color of lac juice. Regarding these eight types of cloth:
The meaning is: for one who keeps anything [of these], there would be an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
57–8. Regarding "elephants, horses, cattle, and deer": this refers to the meat, bones, blood, hides, and hair of elephants, horses, cattle, and deer. Regarding "lions, tigers, leopards, and dholes":
this refers to the meat and so forth of lions, tigers, leopards, and dholes. And regarding the meat and so forth of the hyena (*taraccha*).
There would be an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who eats meat that has been specifically prepared for them or meat for which permission was not requested.
Regarding the phrase "the bathing place at the ford, etc.," here the word "etc. includes the privy and the urinal.
Therefore, having abandoned—that is, having avoided—the sequence of arrival, one should avoid and not go to the bathing ford, the privy, or the urinal.
The meaning is that for him there would be an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
59. *Sahasā* means impulsively, with haste. *Vubbhajitvāna* means having lifted up the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*) from afar;
the syllable *-va-* has entered [the compound] by way of euphonic combination (*sandhi*). *Pavise* means he should enter. *Vaccapassāvakuṭikaṃ* means a privy for excrement and a privy for urination.

"Viseti" means "should enter. The construction is as follows: if a bhikkhu should enter or exit the restroom (vaccapassāvakuṭikā) abruptly, or should enter or exit by lifting the lid, or should enter it while clearing his throat, he would incur a *dukkaṭa* offense.

60. "If one should defecate while making a smacking sound, or while chewing a tooth-stick, there would be an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); this is the meaning. If one should defecate or urinate outside of the receptacles for feces and urine, there would be an offense of wrong-doing.
61. "And one should not scrape with a rough [stick]" means: one should not scrape with a split stick, or a coarse one, or a knotted one, or a rotten stick, or a hollow one;
this is the meaning. "Stick" refers to a scraping stick. "In the pit" refers to the cesspool.
"Carried off" means covered with excrement. "He should not wash it" means he should not wash it himself, nor should he have it washed by another.
"And filth" means rubbish. "He should not clean it" means he should not sweep it. 62.
The meaning is that for one who makes a "capu-capu" sound while performing water-related duties or rinsing the mouth, there would be an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
"Without being requested" means not having been commanded at all. "By the elder" means by the senior of the Saṅgha. "The Pātimokkha" refers to the recitation of the Pātimokkha.
To recite it, or to cause it to be recited, [without permission], there would be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
63. In the case of speaking questions without asking permission, answering questions without asking permission, or performing recitation without asking permission, [there is an offense].
In these four instances—lighting a lamp without asking permission or extinguishing a lamp without asking permission—he commits a *dukkaṭa* offense. 64.
"If he should open or close the window shutters without asking permission, he commits a *dukkaṭa* offense"—this is the connection [of the rule].
Regarding the phrase "vandanādi" (veneration, etc.), here the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes causing one to venerate. If a monk who is naked should perform veneration, [he commits an offense].

The connection is that for one who performs a salutation, goes [on a journey], eats, drinks, chews, takes hold of something, or gives a gift, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in every such case. 65.
Regarding the three coverings: "Monks, I allow three kinds of coverings: a covering for the sauna..."
The three coverings mentioned as "the water-covering and the cloth-covering" are combined and thus called "the triple covering.

The meaning is that, setting aside the triple covering, if one performs the preparatory work oneself or causes another to do it, there would be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). When a monk, while bathing, [stands] against a wall or a pillar...
Or if he should rub his body against a tree, there would be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for him.

66. The connection is as follows: whichever monk, while bathing, should rub his body with a kuruvindaka thread, or should rub one body against another body, there would be an offense of wrong-doing for him;
[likewise] whichever one who is not ill, wearing sandals, [stands] outside the monastery or beyond the monastery precincts.
"He should conduct himself [properly]; for him there would be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)"—this is the connection.

Regarding the phrase "even all-blue and so forth," here the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes sandals that are entirely red, yellow, black, madder-brown, mahāraṅga-colored, mahānāma-colored, or dyed with lac, etc.
For whichever bhikkhu wears sandals that are entirely blue, entirely red, and so forth, for him...

The connection is: "it would be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). If a bhikkhu, being lustful and with a lustful mind, should look at the sign of even a woman born on that very day, for him there would be an offense of wrong-doing.
If a bhikkhu should look at the face of a woman who gives alms, for him there would be an offense of wrong-doing.
68–9. If a bhikkhu, being conscious of censure, should look at another bhikkhu’s bowl, it would be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for him.
If he should look at his own face in a water-bowl such as a mirror, it would be an offense of wrong-doing for him.

For a bhikkhu who sits on a high seat or a large seat, or who performs acts such as sitting or lying down [inappropriately], it would be an offense of wrong-doing. [This applies to] those who have been suspended, those who are not fully ordained, those of a different communion, and so forth.
The connection is: "there may also be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) even in the act of paying homage. In this context, "one who has been suspended" (ukkhitto) refers to all three types:
one suspended for not seeing an offense, one suspended for not making amends for an offense, and one suspended for not relinquishing an evil view.
By the term "one who is not fully ordained" (anupasampanno), the bhikkhunīs, sāmaṇeras, sāmaṇerīs, sikkhamānās, paṇḍakas, itthi-sikkhā-paccakkhātakas, and so forth are included.

"Those who belong to a different communion" (nānāsaṃvāsaka) refers to those who hold different views regarding their communion. By the word "etc. (ādi), those whose roots of virtue are severed (chinnamūlaka) are included. 70–71.
If one should sit together with a woman on a long seat—whether with a pandaka, a woman, or a hermaphrodite—one would incur an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
"On a non-long seat" means on a short seat. If a bhikkhu [sits] on a short seat...
The meaning is: if one should lie down on the same bed or seat with someone who does not share the same seat, there would be an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for him.
Regarding the phrase "fruit, flowers, etc.," the word "etc. includes bamboo shavings, tooth-sticks, clay, and so forth. The connection is:
for one giving fruit, flowers, and so forth for the sake of winning over a family, there would be an offense of wrong-doing.
72–3. Whatever monk should himself make a knotted garment or the like, or should cause another to make it, for him there would be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Whatever monk should consume requisites prohibited by the Conqueror, for him there would be an offense of wrong-doing.
Whatever unskilled, foolish monk should dwell without relying upon a teacher or preceptor, not having taken formal dependence, for him there would be an offense of wrong-doing.

If a bhikkhu should prepare medicine for another person or speak [on its behalf] for a person other than those such as his mother or father who have been authorized, there would be an *dukkaṭa* offense for him.
The connection is that if a bhikkhu should perform the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā ceremony while being guilty of an offense, there would be an *dukkaṭa* offense for him.
In that context, "prohibited by the Conqueror" (*jinavāritā*) means prohibited by the Blessed One, the Conqueror. *Jinavāritā*.

And those conditions are "conditions prohibited by the Victor" (*jinavārita-paccayā*); these are "conditions prohibited by the Victor. One who is incompetent due to a lack of proficiency in the two matrices (*mātikā*) is [unqualified].

74. The connection is as follows: for whichever monk, having avoided intention (*ābhoga*) or application (*niyoga*), should lie down during the day after closing the door-panels and so forth in a place such as a doorway, there would be an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). "In a place such as a doorway" means by whatever [means].
In an enclosed area, even in the open air, or at the foot of a tree—even in a space that possesses this characteristic of being an open clearing.
"Having closed" means having shut it. "Without setting up a watch" means having set aside the intention, "He will guard the door.
"Niyoga" means a place where one has no choice; having set aside a place that is not under one's own control but is shared by many. "Together with the door" (savasā).
Or the reading is *savaso hutvā*, meaning "having become one's own.
*Divā* means during the daytime. 75. *Dhaññaṃ* refers to the seven kinds of grain: rice, paddy, barley, wheat, millet, beans, and kudrūsaka.
*Itthirūpaṃ* refers to images of women made of wood, metal, and so forth. *Ratanaṃ* refers to the ten kinds of gems, such as pearls and the rest. *Āvudhaṃ* refers to weapons.
All weaponry and implements such as spears and javelins; "women’s ornaments" refers to the head-ornaments and so forth of a woman;
"musical instruments" refers to all musical instruments such as flutes and conchs; "fruit trees" refers to trees that bear fruit;
"grain and so forth" refers to mung beans, black gram, and the like—the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes nets, traps, and so on. If one should touch any of these, for him...
The meaning is that it would be an *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing).
76. "With food, water, or oil" means: with honey, flour, or oil; or with water mixed with oil;
or with any kind of mud; or with hand-fans made of ivory and so forth, or with fans that perform the function of a fan.

The meaning is that there would be an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for arranging the hair with the fingers of the hand or with a brush. The meaning is that there would be an offense of wrong-doing for eating from a single vessel.
77. Two monks might lie on one bed-cover; two monks might lie under one blanket. Two monks...
The connection is: "If they should lie on the same couch, there are offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for them.
The construction is: "If one should chew a tooth-stick that is either longer or shorter than the proper measure, there would be an offense of wrong-doing for him.
In this context, "excessive" means longer than eight finger-breadths; "insufficient" means shorter than four finger-breadths.
78. If a bhikkhu arranges for, or causes to be arranged, dancing, singing, or instrumental music, he commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
The meaning is that an offense of wrong-doing occurs for one who watches those dances, listens to those songs, or listens to that instrumental music.
79. "In a place for growing rice and so forth" means in a location where rice and other crops are cultivated. "Outside the walls and enclosures" means outside the ramparts and fences.
"On account of discarding feces and so forth" means that there may be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) due to the act of throwing away or discharging excrement, urine, refuse, ashes, and the like;
this is the meaning. "Wearing long hair and so forth" means that there may be an offense of wrong-doing for wearing long hair or wearing long nails; this is the meaning.
80. Regarding the phrase "in the case of making the nails smooth, etc.," the word "etc. includes the act of dyeing.
"In the case of removing hair from the private parts" refers to the plucking out of hair in the private areas, namely the armpits and the region of the genitals. The syntactical connection is:
"A monk wearing sandals should step upon ground that has been prepared."

81. "With unwashed or wet feet": the meaning is that if a bhikkhu should step upon a bed or a bench belonging to the Saṅgha with unwashed or wet feet, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who touches with the body a wall that has been prepared [for painting].

82–3. "Even with his outer robe folded over [the shoulder]": if he should fold his robe over [his shoulder] while wearing an assigned robe (adhiṭṭhitacīvara) either in a monastery or within a village, there is an offense of wrong-doing for him. "A robe difficult to use" refers to any one of the three robes.
One might use [food] in an improper manner. "Without a waist-band" means that a monk, being devoid of a waist-band, should avoid or enter a village.

The meaning is: if a monk, having defecated, does not plunge into water when water is available—that is, does not perform purification with water—there would be an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for him. "He should accept what is unallowable" refers to a monk or a novice (*sāmaṇera*), etc.
The meaning is that if one should direct fellow practitioners toward what is improper, there would be an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

The meaning is that there would be an offense of wrong-doing due to the confession and disclosure of a similar offense. Regarding the term "similar" (*sabhāga*), here it is intended in the sense of similarity of the *vatthu* (the objective basis), not in the sense of similarity of the offense itself. 84.
*Na vase vassaṃ*: if a monk should not dwell during the rains—that is, should not enter the rains residence—for him there is an offense of wrong-doing.
"Siya" (it may be). Regarding "visaṃvāde suddhacitte," this is a locative case used in the sense of the dative;

the meaning is that for one who deceives a promise while possessing a pure mind, there may be a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). The construction is: "For a bhikkhu who, having spent the rains retreat, goes away despite not being permitted to do so because of a duty not yet authorized, there may be a *dukkaṭa*."
85. The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "If one climbs higher than a man’s height on a tree, having avoided an emergency (āpadā), there may be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
"Emergency" means an obstacle. "Of a tree" means of a wooden tree.
"A man’s height" means five cubits, which is the measure of a medium-sized person for one man’s height. As for the non-strainer: if a monk should travel on a journey, and if a monk...

The construction is: "If one does not give that water-strainer when asked for it, there would be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). "On a journey" means a journey of exactly one-and-a-half yojanas at most. 86.

"There would be an offense of wrong-doing in killing oneself"—this is the connection. If a bhikkhu should make or cause to be made an image such as the form of a woman, there would be an offense of wrong-doing for him.
[This applies] except for placing variegated items such as garlands upon a subject matter such as a Jātaka story.
The connection is: "if one should do it oneself, there would be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

87. Regarding "he makes one who is eating rise": if a monk should make someone who is eating rise, for him there would be an offense of wrong-doing. The construction is: "for one sitting [in a place] without giving space to the elders in the dining hall and so forth, there would be an offense of wrong-doing.
88. "Vehicles" refers to carts, chariots, wagons, carriages, and so on. "One who is not ill" means one who is not sick. As for "one who is not ill": [text continues].
The meaning is that if a bhikkhu should mount vehicles, there would be an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for him. "Should speak in jest" means he should speak in jest;
he should speak in jest concerning the Triple Gem—the meaning is that there would be an offense of wrong-doing for him. There is an offense of wrong-doing in coaxing another assembly.
89. Regarding "the body, etc.": here the word "etc. includes the thigh and the sexual organ. [He should not touch] the body, or the thigh, or the organ.
"Having opened [it], one should not show it to the bhikkhunīs; 'should not show' is the meaning.

One should not recite the *Lokāyata*—the knowledge of animal cries and so forth—neither oneself nor cause another to recite it. Whether one should take up a bet or cause another to take one up, there would be an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
such is the construction."
90–92. The connection is that for one who eats food having placed it in a box anywhere whatsoever, there would be an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Regarding the "bowl-in-hand" [offense]: whichever monk should open or cause to be opened a window or a door;

or should warm a bowl containing water in the heat, or dry it in the heat, or put it away; or should overheat a bowl without water, or leave it standing too long in the heat—for him [there is an offense].

The meaning is: "it would be an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). The connection is: for whichever monk should place his bowl on the ground, or in his lap, or on a couch, or on a stool, or on a bed-cover, or on a floor-covering, or on his foot, or under a sunshade—for him it would be an offense of wrong-doing.
"On the ground" means on anything that is not protected [from dust] and is mixed with soil and gravel. "In the lap" means between the two thighs.
"At the edge of the *miḍḍha*" means at the limit of the *miḍḍha*. "At the edge of the *paribhaṇḍa*" means at the end of the thin plastering made on the outer side.

The connection is as follows: if a monk should place rice-scum (*calaka*) or the like in his bowl, or if he should wash his hand in the bowl, there would be an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) on account of that washing of the hand.
93. It may be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for a bhikkhu who carries away even the water used for rinsing the mouth from the bowl after it has been used as leftovers.
The meaning is that it would be an offense of wrong-doing for whichever bhikkhu should use an improper bowl.
In this context, "improper bowl" refers to one made of wood and so forth.
94. The meaning is that if a bhikkhu, when something is thrown, should say, "Live! (*jīva*), he would incur an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

The connection is that if a bhikkhu, being disrespectful toward the seventy-five rules of training beginning with the *parimaṇḍala* (the rule on the robe), does not train in them, he would incur an offense of wrong-doing.
95. If a bhikkhu, while engaged in the storehouse, should guard the belongings of his mother or father, for that bhikkhu... [the sentence continues].
The connection is: "it may be an offense of expiation (pācittiya). In that context, *payutta* means engaged in activity within the storehouse.

*Gopaye* means he should guard. The connection is: "if a monk, out of sport, should speak of even a superior [person] as inferior by way of birth and so forth, it would be an offense of wrong speech (dubbhāsita).
In that context, whether by means of low or high birth and so forth, thus [speaking of] the superior as low or...
Or, if one should speak— either directly in the manner of "You are a caṇḍāla," and so forth; or by way of a pretext in the manner of "There are here some caṇḍālas,
venas, neṣādas," and so forth— whether the person addressed is ordained or unordained, with the intention of mere sport and without the intent to abuse,
it would be a *dubbhāsita* (wrong speech).
The commentary on the *Pakiṇṇakaniddesa* is finished.
6. Commentary on the section on duties (*vatta*) and so forth.
96. Now, in order to show the duties, it is said: "The duty toward the preceptor and teacher. Therein, the duty toward the preceptor (*upajjhāya*) and...

The connection is that the duties toward the teacher, the duties of one departing, the duties of a guest, and the duties regarding lodgings and so forth must be performed by a bhikkhu who is dear in virtue (*piyasīla*).
Regarding the term *gamikāgantuka*: it is a compound split as *gamikaṃ* and *āgantukaṃ*; the meaning is "the duties of one departing and the duties of a guest.
(97) One who wishes to give, standing within arm's reach, [should give] whatever is to be taken up by a person, provided it can be lifted.
The object (vatthu) may be given in one of three ways among the three modes; a monk desiring to receive it may take it in one of two ways among the two.
This is the meaning of "acceptance with five factors" (pañcaṅga-paṭiggaha). 98–100.
Having observed the robe placed in its designated spot while standing at a distance, one should say, "This. [If it is] within hand's reach...
Having touched it with the hand while it is standing [before him], he should say, "This.
He should determine the three robes (*ticīvara*) by joining these two phrases—"I determine this" and "I determine that"—to each one individually among the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) and the others.
How so? He should determine them thus: "I determine this outer robe; I determine that outer robe. The same applies to the remaining robes.
And regarding robes: the meaning is that one should determine or relinquish the bowl in the same manner as the determination and relinquishment of robes and so forth. 101.
The connection is that, with the exception of matchmaking (*sañcaritta*), the remaining grave offenses (*garuka*) and defeats (*pārājika*) are committed with a conscious mind (*sacittaka*).
"The last ones" refers to the defeats. With the exception of these two—the rule on [robes] being cut off and the rule on [robes] being finished—the remainder...
"Without intention" (*acittaka*) means that it is an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*).

102–3. Regarding "at the point of entering a village": these [offenses] ending with "entering a village" are the seventeen training rules (*sikkhāpada*) among the *pācittiya* offenses, beginning with "receiving food by appointment" (*padasodhamma*), which are without intention.

104–5. Among the miscellaneous rules (*pakiṇṇaka*), excluding that which is "prepared specifically for oneself," the rest—namely, "flesh of another" and "other flesh"—are without intention; this is the meaning.

Regarding the miscellaneous rules here: among these thirteen training rules, those concerning meat from another animal and so forth—where one has a bowl in hand and reaches as far as the door-panel—are without intentional thought (*acittaka*);
the meaning is that all the rest involve intentional thought (*sacittaka*).

The teachers state that, by virtue of knowing the formal rule (*paññatti*), there is intentional thought even when one acts with a mind of transgression (*vītikkamana-citta*). They call it "with intentional thought" and "without intentional thought. 106. By knowing the formal rule...
The meaning is that the teachers say, "In the same way, it is 'with mind' or 'without mind. By the word *tathā* (in the same way), the pair "with mind" and "without mind" is included.
Regarding the phrase "the preliminary duties, etc.," here the word *ādi* (etc. includes the prior tasks (*pubbakicca*). In that regard:
“The broom, the lamp, water, and the seat—
these are called the preliminary duties for the Uposatha. The declaration of consent,
the confession of purity, the announcement of the season, the counting of the monks, and the exhortation.”
“These are called the preliminary duties of the Uposatha.

Thus, the meaning is that all the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies, illuminated in nine ways beginning with the preliminary preparation (*pubbakaraṇa*), should be performed by one who is fond of virtuous conduct. 112. Regarding the phrase “in due order,” this is the intended meaning:

the group (*gaṇa*) should perform the Uposatha of purity (*pārisuddhi-uposatha*); an individual (*puggala*) should perform the Uposatha of determination (*adhiṭṭhāna-uposatha*); and the Saṅgha should perform the Uposatha of the recitation of the Suttas (*suttuddesa-uposatha*).

113. "The fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the *sāmaggī* [uposatha]—thus, from the perspective of the day, they are threefold: the fourteenth-day *uposatha*, the fifteenth-day *uposatha*, and the *sāmaggī-uposatha*.

From the perspective of the day, from the perspective of the individuals, and from the perspective of the manner in which it is to be performed, those *uposathas* are said to be nine. This is the meaning.

114. "Threefold-utterance" (*tevācikā*), "twofold-utterance" (*dvevācikā*), and "single-utterance" (*ekavācikā*): thus nine *pavāraṇā*s (invitations for criticism) have been stated. 115. "Of that" means of the month of Phagguṇa.
"The remainder from that" means from the last fortnight of Āsāḷha up to the full moon of Kattika; this is the meaning of the "rainy season. For in one year, there are twenty-four *uposatha* days.

116. "Among these" means among these three [groups]; in each of the four seasons, the third and seventh fortnights [are excluded]. "Fourteen" means six [fortnights] on the fourteenth day. The rest are of obvious meaning.
The commentary on the section concerning the training rules, beginning with the *vatta*, is finished.
This concludes the explanation of the meaning of the fundamental training rules (*mūlasikkhā*) that was undertaken up to this point.
This has been completed in brief after the passing of half a month.
Whatever merit I have acquired by explaining this matter in summary for the benefit of those newly ordained, [may it be for their welfare].
By this merit, may this world, through practice for the sake of happiness that is utterly pure,
attain Nibbāna, the ageless state.
May those who desire various wholesome deeds [dwell] amidst the multitude of diverse trees.

This commentary on the meaning of the Root Training Rules was composed by the wise Siddhi, who has attained success within the Dispensation while dwelling in monasteries, victorious in battles and mindful.
The Commentary on the Mūlasikkhā is completed.
